The USDA entry is 'Shoulder petite tender', a specific small muscle cut from the shoulder area, sold and cooked differently from a shoulder roast. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F says a different cut of meat is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because a cook would not use the petite tender in place of a shoulder roast without changing the preparation (it is small, tender, and cooks quickly, unlike a large braising or roasting cut). Condition 2 also fails because a diner would likely notice the difference in texture and appearance. The 100g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is self-rising flour, a wheat flour with added leavening (baking powder) and salt. The USDA entry is self-rising cornmeal, which is made from corn, not wheat. Condition 1 fails: a cook could not swap cornmeal for wheat-based self-rising flour without changing the batter's structure, since wheat flour forms gluten and cornmeal does not, so the dish's preparation and rise would change. Condition 2 also fails: cornmeal gives a grainy texture and a distinct corn flavour and yellow colour, which a diner would notice. Under guideline F, a different flour is not substitutable. Sifting is handling and does not change the match, and the weight is ignored.

The ingredient is 200g okra, raw. The USDA match is Okra, raw. Guideline A says to ignore the quantity, so the 200g is irrelevant. Condition 1: okra raw can directly replace okra raw in any recipe with no change in preparation, since the same food in the same raw state is used. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is literally the same food in the same state. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is plain raw ground turkey, the standard default product. The USDA match is 'Turkey, ground, fat free, pan-broiled crumbles', which is a cooked product (pan-broiled crumbles), and it is also a modified fat-free version. Condition 1 fails: using pan-broiled crumbles in place of raw ground turkey would change how the dish is prepared, because the meat would arrive pre-cooked and would not brown or cook through in the recipe the way raw meat does. Condition 2 also fails: the fat-free, pan-broiled crumbles differ in texture, moisture, fat content and appearance from raw ground turkey, and a diner could notice the difference. Under the guidelines, raw vs cooked is a different state, and plain vs fat-free is a modification, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is roasted hazelnut oil, a processed oil pressed from roasted hazelnuts with a distinct toasted, nutty flavour. The USDA match is raw hazelnuts (whole tree nuts, uncooked). Condition 1: raw whole nuts cannot be used in place of an oil; the cooking method would change entirely, since a recipe calling for oil would not work with whole nuts as a fat source. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in texture (liquid oil versus solid nut pieces) and flavour (no roasted notes, no oil richness). Guideline F explicitly excludes the raw source versus the processed ingredient, and plain versus roasted states. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is fresh casaba melon, a specific melon variety eaten raw. The USDA entry is 'Melon, frozen', a frozen product. Condition 1: Freezing changes the melon's cell structure, so thawed frozen melon is softer and releases more liquid than fresh. It cannot replace fresh casaba without changing preparation, for example in a fruit salad or as a garnish. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference in texture, juiciness and appearance, since melon is usually served fresh. The frozen entry also does not specify casaba or any named variety. Per guideline E, a frozen entry does not match when the thawed food would visibly differ where it is served fresh. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is Pacific herring, a specific fish species. The USDA entry 'Fish, herring, Pacific, raw' is the same species in the same raw state. The quantity (245g) is irrelevant per guideline A. No cooking method is implied by the ingredient, so the raw USDA entry does not alter preparation; the diner would not perceive any difference in taste, texture, or appearance because it is literally the same food in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sweet potato leaves, a fresh leafy vegetable. The USDA entry 'Sweet potato leaves, raw' is literally the same food in its uncooked state. The leading '300g' is only the quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the leaves are used the same way (typically cooked or stir-fried, which the recipe handles). Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the food is identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is heavy whipping cream, and the USDA entry 'Cream, fluid, heavy whipping' is the same product under its standard name. Condition 1: it can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since the quantity is ignored and the product is the same. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is soy creamer, a formulated product. Soy creamers are typically made with added vegetable oil, emulsifiers and stabilizers, and are often sweetened or flavoured to give a richer, thicker, sweeter mouthfeel. The USDA match is plain unsweetened soy milk, a thinner beverage with no added fat or stabilisers. Condition 2 fails: in coffee, tea or a sauce, a diner would likely notice the thinner body and lack of richness and sweetness. Condition 1 is also doubtful, since creamer's fat and emulsifiers affect how it behaves when heated or combined with acidic or hot liquids, so swapping in plain soy milk could change the preparation outcome. Because the match is a different product (unsweetened milk rather than a creamer), it is not a same-food-by-another-name case, so guideline B does not apply. The result is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried lima beans, which are the mature seeds of the lima bean plant, bought dry and typically soaked and cooked before eating. The USDA match is 'Green beans, raw', which refers to the immature pods of a snap or string bean. These are different foods, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: substituting fresh green beans would change the preparation, since dried beans need long soaking and simmering while green beans need only brief cooking. Condition 2 also fails: the dish would taste, texture and look different, with a starchy, creamy bean in place of a crisp green pod. The quantity and the 'raw' label do not change this.

The ingredient is young brick cheese, a semi-soft American cheese with a moist, open texture and a mild, slightly tangy, buttery flavour. The USDA match is Cheese, colby. Colby is a distinct variety made by a washed-curd process, so it is a sibling cheese, not the same food under another name. Its flavour is milder and sweeter, and its texture is softer and more uniformly open. Condition 1 holds, since it could be swapped in without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 is not clearly met: a diner could plausibly notice the difference in flavour and texture between brick and colby. Under guideline F, a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable. The 45g quantity is ignored.

The ingredient is green seedless grapes, a common fresh table grape. The USDA entry is 'Grapes, red or green (European type, such as Thompson seedless), raw'. Thompson seedless is the classic green seedless grape, so the USDA entry names the same food. The quantity (300g) is ignored per guideline A. The 'raw' descriptor means uncooked, which matches fresh grapes served as bought. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the entry covers the same green seedless European-type grape. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is queso chihuahua, a Mexican melting cheese, sold shredded. The USDA entry 'Cheese, mexican, queso chihuahua' names the same cheese. Shredding is knife or handling work and does not change the match (guideline C). The leading '75g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Nothing indicates a modified, flavoured, frozen, or dried version. It would be used the same way in the dish, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dry espresso grounds, an unbrewed, solid coffee product measured by weight. The USDA entry is brewed espresso, a liquid beverage prepared by restaurant brewing. Condition 1 fails: brewed espresso cannot replace dry grounds without changing the preparation. Dry grounds would have to be steeped or extracted, and the liquid would add water and change the recipe's structure. Condition 2 also fails: the dish would taste different and have different texture and appearance, since the diner would be eating a dissolved, liquid coffee rather than the dry-ground ingredient. Guideline F covers this as a different state (dry/ground vs brewed), and the match is not the same food under another name. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'bacon fat, cooked', meaning rendered fat drippings from bacon. The USDA entry 'Pork bacon, smoked or cured, cooked' describes the cooked bacon meat itself, with lean and fat tissue intact, not the separated rendered fat. Using the meat in place of the fat would change the dish: it is a solid, meaty, crisp ingredient rather than a liquid or semi-solid cooking fat, so it would alter how the dish is prepared (fat coats and fries; meat must be chopped or rendered). Diners would also notice texture and flavour differences, such as chewy bacon pieces versus a smooth fat. This is the raw/whole source versus the processed ingredient pattern, not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails, and so does condition 2.

The ingredient is fresh hearts of palm, which is raw and uncooked. The USDA match is 'Palm hearts, cooked', which is a different state. Guideline F says raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Using pre-cooked palm hearts would change the preparation, since the recipe would skip any cooking step the raw version needs, and the texture and flavour of the finished dish could differ. The food is the same plant part, but the cooked state is the deciding factor under the rules, so condition 1 fails. Condition 2 also cannot be assumed to hold, because a diner could notice a difference in texture and firmness. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is beef kidney (an organ meat from cattle), sliced. The USDA match 'Kidney beans, NFS' is a legume (Phaseolus vulgaris), a completely different food. Condition 1 fails: beef kidney cannot be substituted by kidney beans without changing the dish entirely (it would be a different protein/organ meat cooked as meat, versus a bean). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance between offal and beans. The shared word 'kidney' is coincidental; these are not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and they are not a cut or variety of the same food (guideline F).

1. The ingredient is fresh raw Asian pear, sliced. The match is canned pear in syrup. Asian pears are a distinct pear type (crisp, juicy, apple-like texture), not just another name for the same food, so guideline B does not apply. 2. Condition 1: Using canned pear would change preparation. Fresh sliced fruit would become syrup-packed canned fruit, which the cook would need to drain, and the syrup adds sweetness. 3. Condition 2: A diner would likely notice. Canned pear is soft, mushy, and sweeter, with a syrup flavour, while sliced Asian pear is firm and crisp. Guideline F rules out a different packing medium and a raw-versus-processed state. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is imitation crab, a surimi product made from processed white fish paste (usually pollock) with starch, egg white, flavourings, and colouring. The USDA match is 'Crab, canned', which is real crab meat. These are different foods, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Imitation crab is a processed product with a different composition, so guideline F's rule against substituting a processed product for its raw source applies. Condition 2 also fails: its firm, springy, fibrous texture, uniform appearance, and sweet, mild flavour differ from canned crab's flaky texture and distinct taste, and a diner would likely notice. Condition 1 is at least partly met, since the crab could be shredded and used in the same dish, but condition 2 is not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'graham cracker' and the USDA entry is 'Graham crackers'. These are the same food under the same name, with the plural being the only difference. The leading '360g' is a quantity and is ignored. No cooking method is altered, since the crackers are used as bought, and the taste, texture and appearance of the dish would be unchanged. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is berbere, a complex Ethiopian spice blend of chili peppers, paprika, garlic, ginger, fenugreek, allspice, and other spices, used for savory dishes. The USDA match is 'Sugar substitute and sugar blend,' which is a sweetener product, not a spice blend. Condition 1 fails: it cannot be used in place of berbere without changing how the dish is prepared, since it contains no chili or spices and would not provide the savory seasoning. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, as the dish would become sweet rather than spiced and its flavour, colour and appearance would change. This is a different food entirely, not a same-food alternate name, so guideline B does not apply. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is Smart Balance light buttery spread, and the USDA entry is Margarine-like spread, SMART BALANCE Light Buttery Spread. It is the same branded product, and the 'light' descriptor appears in both, so it is not an added modification. Condition 1: the spread can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation, since both are a spread used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the identical product. The quantity (30g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 60g fresh mustard greens, chopped. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Mustard greens, raw', which is the same food, uncooked, with the chopping being knife work that does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the greens can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since fresh raw mustard greens are the same product. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the match is the same food in the same raw state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain 'bamboo shoots' with no preparation state given, so the standard default is the fresh/raw shoot. The USDA match is specifically 'cooked, boiled, drained, with salt'. Under guideline F, raw vs cooked is a different state, so it is not interchangeable without changing how the dish is prepared. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a version with added salt (an added solution or additive) is a modified version, which is not a match. Salting also changes the flavour, and a diner could taste the added salt and the cooked texture. The quantity (10g) and the optional label do not affect this. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is plain "duck" with no cut, state, or modifier specified; the 290g weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is "Duck, domesticated, meat and skin, raw," which is the same food in its uncooked state. Per guideline D, a plain ingredient matches the standard default version, and whole domesticated duck is normally sold with its skin, so the skin is not an unusual modification. Condition 1: the entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is raw meat and skin as the recipe would expect. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the default duck purchased under the plain name already includes skin. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is butternut squash, a specific winter squash variety. The USDA entry is Squash, winter, hubbard, raw, a different winter squash variety. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F treats a sibling variety with a different taste as not substitutable. Hubbard differs from butternut in flesh density, moisture, sweetness and often colour, and its rough, bumpy grey-green rind looks different. Condition 2 (a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance) is therefore not reliably met. Condition 1 is plausible for cooking method, but both conditions must hold. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is turkey bockwurst, a poultry sausage. The USDA entry is bockwurst made from pork and veal. Ignoring the quantity, the core question is whether this is the same food under another name. It is not: the protein source differs (turkey versus pork and veal). Substituting pork-veal bockwurst would change the flavour, fat content, and texture, since turkey sausage is leaner and tastes noticeably different. A diner would likely notice the difference in taste and mouthfeel. Condition 2 therefore fails, and the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is canned crab, which is real crab meat from the crab itself. The USDA match is imitation crab meat, which is surimi: a processed fish paste (usually pollock) that is formed, flavoured and coloured to resemble crab. Under guideline F, the raw/natural source differs from the processed ingredient, and imitation products are not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 is arguably met, since both can be used in cold salads or sushi-style dishes without changing the preparation. Condition 2 fails: the taste (sweeter, milder, no true crab flavour), texture (uniform, springy and fibrous rather than flaky), and appearance (orange-red surface, uniform shreds) differ, and a diner would likely notice. Because condition 2 is not met, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is pickled Atlantic herring, and the USDA entry is 'Fish, herring, Atlantic, pickled', which is the same food under the same preparation. The leading '100g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Pickling is the state of the ingredient itself, not a modification, so the entry matches the plain pickled product. Substituting it would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance because it is the same product.

The ingredient is green leaf lettuce, a raw leafy green. The USDA entry is red leaf lettuce, raw, which is a sibling variety. Condition 1: the dish could be prepared the same way with either leaf, since both are eaten raw and handled identically, so the preparation does not change. Condition 2: red leaf lettuce has visibly red or purple-tinged leaf edges, so a diner would likely notice a difference in appearance. Its flavour is also slightly different from green leaf. Guideline F states that a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable, and the visible colour difference reinforces this. Condition 2 is not met.

The ingredient is plain almond yogurt, a cultured, thick, tangy product. The USDA match is sweetened almond milk, a thin, sweetened, unfermented beverage. Condition 1: almond milk cannot replace yogurt without changing the dish's preparation. Yogurt contributes body, moisture and structure, and it is often stirred, folded or dolloped, so a thin liquid would alter how the dish is made. Condition 2: the diner would notice the difference. The thin liquid lacks the thick texture and tang of yogurt, and the sweetening adds a flavour that plain yogurt does not have. The match is a different food (a milk beverage rather than a yogurt) and a modified version (sweetened). Both conditions fail.

Step 1: Identify the food. 'Poultry neck pieces' is generic. The default poultry neck is chicken neck, and the USDA entry is chicken broiler/fryer neck, so the species matches under guideline D. Step 2: Check the cut. Both are neck. The USDA entry is 'meat only', which describes the edible portion of the same cut, not a different cut like brisket versus chuck. Step 3: Check preparation. Both are simmered, so the cooking method is unchanged. Step 4: Check the diner's experience. Taste and texture should be essentially the same. The one possible difference is that 'pieces' may imply bone-in pieces, while 'meat only' is deboned. That could show in appearance, but the ingredient does not specify bone-in, so it is not enough to reject under the default-version rule. Both conditions are plausibly met, though this is the least certain part of the judgement.

The ingredient is pure sucralose, a single high-intensity sweetener. The USDA match is a baking sweetener blend that contains sugar plus sucralose. Guideline F rejects a single ingredient matched to a blend containing it. Substituting the blend would also change the dish: it adds sugar's bulk, browning, moisture and sweetness per gram, so the quantity and the final texture and appearance would differ. A diner could notice the difference, so condition 1 and condition 2 both fail.

The ingredient is sweetened shredded coconut. The USDA entry is dried (desiccated), sweetened, flaked coconut meat, packaged. Both are sweetened, dried coconut sold in packaged form. The ingredient asks for the sweetened version, so the sweetened USDA entry matches (guideline D). Desiccated is the standard dried form of this product. 'Flaked' versus 'shredded' is a cut descriptor for the same dried coconut product, and guideline B/C treats cut and trade names of the same food as matches. The weight (140g) is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient in the same recipe steps, since it is used the same way (sprinkled, mixed, or baked in) with no change in method. Condition 2: sweetness, dryness, and appearance are essentially the same, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain yogurt with no fat specification. The USDA match, 'Yogurt, nonfat milk, plain', is a fat-free version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a fat-free or reduced-fat version is a modification and does not count as the standard default. The exception for descriptors that describe how a product is normally sold does not clearly apply, because plain yogurt is sold in whole, low-fat and nonfat forms, and the plain name does not point to nonfat. Nonfat yogurt is also thinner and tangier than whole-milk yogurt, so a diner could plausibly notice the difference in texture and flavour, particularly in sauces, dressings and baked goods. Condition 1 may be met for simple substitution, but condition 2 is not reliably met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is whipped butter, which is butter with air incorporated, giving it a lighter, fluffier, less dense texture than standard butter. The USDA match 'Butter, salted' is regular stick-style butter. Under the guidelines, whipped butter is a modified form of butter, not the plain default. Condition 1: the substitution changes preparation, because whipped butter is aerated and has a different volume and density, so creaming, spreading, or melting behaves differently, and recipes that rely on its airiness would not work the same. Condition 2: a diner could notice a difference in texture and appearance, especially where the butter is served or its aeration affects the crumb or mouthfeel. Rule E on frozen/thawed does not rescue the match, since the thawed product still has whipped texture that differs from the USDA entry. Because the match fails both conditions, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a chocolate hazelnut spread, and the USDA entry is literally 'Chocolate hazelnut spread', the same food under the same name. The leading '45g' is only a quantity and is ignored per guideline A. Nothing in the recipe would change preparation, since a spread is used as-is and the USDA entry describes the same product. Taste, texture and appearance match because it is the same product type, with no modification, cooking state or added flavour that a diner would detect. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cooked black beans plus brown rice, with the leading 220g ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry names the same two components, black beans and brown rice, with no added flavour, sauce, or modification. Under guideline C, an entry that names the same dish with the same components is a match even when USDA adds a standard descriptor. The ingredient's 'cooked' state matches the usual state of a prepared bean-and-rice entry. Condition 1: the entry could replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are ready-to-use cooked components. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, as the same beans and rice are present. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is sliced sourdough bread, and the quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Bread, french or vienna (includes sourdough)' explicitly names sourdough as one of the breads it covers, so under guideline B and the spirit of guideline C it names the same food. Slicing is handling and does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: sourdough can replace the bread without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is still a sliced loaf used the same way. Condition 2: the entry is written to include sourdough, so the USDA values are intended to represent it, and a diner would not be served a different kind of bread. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dry, uncooked tapioca pearls, a starch that must be cooked (boiled or simmered) before eating. The USDA entry is ready-to-eat tapioca pudding, a finished dessert made with milk, sugar, and often eggs and vanilla. Using it in place of the pearls would not work in recipes that cook or boil the pearls, such as bubble tea or pearl drinks, and it would change the dish's texture, flavour, and appearance. A diner would notice a creamy, sweet pudding instead of chewy translucent pearls. The guidelines reject a processed or prepared product that differs in state and composition from the raw ingredient (guideline F). The quantity (300g) is ignored as instructed.

The ingredient is fresh goat milk, 100g; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Goat milk' is the same food under its plain name, with no added flavour, fat modification, or processing descriptor. Per guideline D, a plain ingredient mapping to the standard default version is a match. Goat milk is not a different cut, oil, or variety, and 'fresh' describes the normal state of milk as bought, which does not alter the match (guideline C on handling/state descriptors). Substituting it would not change cooking method, flavour, texture, or appearance in a way a diner would notice, since it is the identical product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is store-bought hollandaise sauce: an egg-yolk and butter emulsion flavoured with lemon juice, with a tangy, rich taste and a yellow, creamy, pourable texture. The USDA match is Alfredo sauce: a dairy sauce made from butter, cream, and Parmesan cheese, with a mild, cheesy flavour and a whitish appearance. These are different sauces with different components (no egg yolk or lemon in Alfredo, and Parmesan rather than a lemon-butter base), so they are not the same food under another name. Replacing hollandaise with Alfredo would change the flavour from tangy-buttery to cheesy, and the colour from yellow to white. Condition 1 can be argued as possible in a loose sense, but condition 2 clearly fails because a diner would notice the taste difference (no lemon tang, cheese flavour present). Therefore the match is not substitutable.

Hominy is whole corn kernels that have been treated with alkali (nixtamalized), sold canned or dried as whole kernels. The USDA entry is hominy grits: the dried kernels ground into a fine or coarse meal, specifically a quick-cooking, branded cereal product. Condition 1 fails: whole hominy needs long simmering or soaking, while quick grits cook in minutes as a porridge-like mush, so the cooking method changes. Condition 2 also fails: whole kernels give a chewy, distinct-kernel texture and appearance, while grits give a smooth or granular porridge that a diner would notice. The entry is a processed, ground form of the same grain, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. The quantity and the cereal brand do not change this.

The ingredient is dried rosemary, and the USDA entry is 'Spices, rosemary, dried', which is the same food in the same state (dried). The leading '15g' is quantity and is ignored. Guideline F rejects fresh vs dried herbs, but both sides here are dried, so that rule does not apply. The USDA entry names no modification such as ground, toasted or smoked, so it is the standard default version of the plain ingredient. Using it in place of the ingredient would not change preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance.

1. The ingredient is 'light tartar sauce'. The '250g' is only a quantity and is ignored. 2. 'Light' denotes a reduced-fat or lite version, which guideline D classes as a modification. 3. The USDA entry 'Sauce, tartar, ready-to-serve' is the standard, regular-fat tartar sauce, not a reduced-fat version. 4. Substituting regular tartar sauce for light changes fat content, and therefore mouthfeel and flavour, and a diner could notice the difference. 5. Condition 1 (preparation is unchanged) is met, but condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste or texture) is not reliably met. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is Canadian bacon, prepared by crisping. The USDA entry is the same food, Canadian bacon, cooked by pan-frying. Crisping Canadian bacon is typically done by pan-frying, so the USDA entry describes essentially the same end state. Condition 1: the match can stand in for the ingredient, since the cook's crisping step produces the same result as the USDA pan-fried entry, and the dish's preparation is not altered in a way that matters. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance between Canadian bacon crisped in a pan and Canadian bacon listed as pan-fried. The weight is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain dill pickles, which are normally sold as regular-sodium brined pickles. The USDA match is 'Pickles, cucumber, sour, low sodium', a reduced-sodium modified version. Per guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a low-sodium version is not the standard default, so it fails the same-food test. The sodium reduction also changes taste: brine salt contributes much of a pickle's sharp, savoury flavour, so a diner could notice the difference. The ingredient does not ask for low sodium, so the modified entry does not qualify. Condition 1 (same preparation) may hold, but condition 2 (no noticeable taste difference) does not.

The ingredient is generic protein powder, a dry protein supplement that is used as an ingredient in shakes, baking, or similar preparations. The USDA entry, 'Nutritional powder mix, protein, NFS', is the generic (not further specified) protein powder category, so it names the same kind of product without adding a flavour, sweetener, or other modification. Condition 1: it is a dry protein powder that can be measured and mixed in the same way, so the preparation does not change. Condition 2: the entry carries no specific flavour, colour, or added ingredient, so it corresponds to the plain default product; a diner would not be able to tell it apart from the protein powder in the recipe. Both conditions are met, with some uncertainty because the actual protein source and flavour of the ingredient are unspecified.

The ingredient is plain 'wheat germ' with no preparation stated. The USDA entry is 'Cereals ready-to-eat, wheat germ, toasted, plain', which specifies a toasted state. Guideline F says plain vs toasted is a different state and not substitutable. Toasting gives wheat germ a noticeably nuttier, roasted flavour and a crisper, drier texture, so a diner could taste the difference, and the USDA entry is also classed as a ready-to-eat cereal rather than a raw ingredient. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh red grapes, and the USDA entry is raw European-type grapes, red or green, explicitly including red table grapes such as Thompson seedless. The weight prefix is decoration (guideline A). Both are the same fresh, raw food with no cooking, modification, or processing, so the preparation does not change (condition 1). A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the entry covers red grapes directly (condition 2). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a plain maize (corn) tortilla, which by default is the ready-to-eat soft tortilla used warm or as a wrap. The USDA entry is specifically 'Tortillas, ready-to-bake or -fry, corn', a separate product meant to be baked or fried before eating. Condition 1 fails: substituting it would require a different preparation step (baking or frying) that the recipe does not call for, and the product is not used in place of a ready-to-eat tortilla without changing the cooking method. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (a ready-to-bake or fry tortilla is typically stiffer and less pliable, and it cooks to a different crispness) and possibly in appearance. Guideline F (a different state) and the general rule that a changed cooking method makes a match non-substitutable both apply. The quantity (115g) is ignored.

The ingredient is cream of tartar, a leavening acid (potassium bitartrate), a fine white powder used in small amounts to stabilize egg whites, prevent sugar crystallization, and act as an acid in baking. The USDA match is 'Cream, whipped', which is a dairy product: an aerated fat emulsion of milk fat and cream. These are not the same food under another name; one is a dry chemical acid and the other is a dairy topping. Substituting whipped cream would introduce large amounts of fat, water and air, changing the chemistry and texture of any dish (e.g., meringue would fail to stabilize, and the dish would gain dairy flavour and moisture). Both conditions fail: the preparation would change and a diner would notice a difference in taste, texture and appearance. The quantity (95g) is ignored per the guidelines.

The ingredient is stevia powder, a high-intensity sweetener derived from the stevia plant, used in very small amounts (quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA match is Honey, which is a different food: a viscous, natural sugar-containing product made by bees. Condition 1 fails: honey is a liquid or semi-solid, adds bulk and moisture, and would change the preparation of most recipes that call for a powdered sweetener; it cannot be used as a direct drop-in for a dry powder. Condition 2 fails: honey contributes its own floral flavour, adds substantial sugar and calories, and alters texture and browning, so a diner would notice the difference. Stevia and honey are not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and they differ in state and composition (guideline F). Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a buttery spread, a fat-based spread such as margarine or butter blend used on bread or in cooking. The USDA match is a chocolate hazelnut spread, a sweet confection-style product made mainly from sugar, palm oil, cocoa and hazelnuts. Condition 1 fails: it would not be used in the same way, since a chocolate spread is sweet and is not a fat used for cooking or baking in place of butter or margarine, so the preparation changes. Condition 2 fails: a diner would clearly taste chocolate and hazelnut and would notice the difference in flavour, sweetness and appearance. The two products are not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and they differ in flavour (guideline F). The quantity is irrelevant (guideline A). Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is chicken leg quarters, meaning the whole leg with thigh and drumstick, normally sold bone-in with skin. The USDA entry is broiler or fryer leg, meat and skin, raw, which is the same cut of the same bird in standard USDA terms. The leading weight (200g) is ignored. Condition 1: the entry can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is raw, skin-on leg with the same components, and the skin and bone-in form are standard for leg quarters. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cut with the same skin and meat. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain lime-flavoured yogurt with no fat level or style specified. Flavoured yogurts are normally low fat, so the 2% fat level is acceptable under guideline D. The lime flavour also matches the key lime blend. The problem is the Greek style. Greek yogurt is strained, so it is noticeably thicker, denser and tangier, with a different mouthfeel than standard set or stirred lime yogurt. Because the ingredient does not ask for Greek yogurt, the match is a modified version of the plain product, and a diner could notice the difference in texture. Condition 2 therefore fails, and the match is not substitutable.

Simple syrup (1:1) is a sugar-and-water solution, so its sweetness and body come from sugar. The USDA entry 'Syrups, sugar free' is a modified product, made with sugar substitutes or sugar alcohols rather than sugar. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient mapped to a sugar-free or otherwise modified version as a non-match, and guideline F treats a different sugar as a non-match. Condition 1: a sugar-free syrup could be poured or mixed in the same way, but the sweetener changes. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference in sweetness profile, mouthfeel, and possibly an aftertaste, and in cocktails or desserts the result would differ. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'light chocolate syrup', so the request itself asks for the reduced-calorie 'lite' version. The USDA entry is HERSHEY'S Genuine Chocolate Flavored Lite Syrup, a branded lite chocolate syrup. Guideline D says a plain ingredient matched to a modified version is a no, but when the ingredient itself asks for that version, the matching modified entry is a yes. Guideline G allows a branded entry of the same product type. The leading '300g' is ignored (A). Condition 1: the syrup is used the same way (drizzled, stirred, or blended) with no change in cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since both are chocolate syrups in the lite style and the 'chocolate flavored' wording describes how this product is normally sold. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is beef tenderloin steak, which is the same cut as the USDA entry 'Beef, tenderloin steak, raw'. The weight is decoration (guideline A). 'Trimmed of visible fat' is preparation handling that does not change the match (guideline C), and the entry is raw, which is the default state for a steak bought for cooking. Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since the same cut is cooked the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because trimming visible fat is done before cooking and the cut is identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'chicken patties', a formed, processed meat product, typically ground or minced chicken shaped into patties and often seasoned, bound, or breaded. The USDA entry is 'Chicken, stewing, meat only, raw', which is whole meat from an older stewing hen, a different cut and product form. Condition 1 fails: the patties would need to be formed and shaped, and stewing chicken meat is not a ground or formed product, so the preparation would change. Condition 2 also fails: the texture (tough, fibrous stewing meat versus a tender, uniform patty) and the flavour and appearance (no seasoning, binder, or shape) would be noticeable. Quantity is ignored, and the mismatch is in product type, not amount. This is not the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 10g of black garbanzo beans, dried. Black garbanzo beans (kala chana, also called Bengal gram) are a variety of chickpea, and 'garbanzo beans' is simply the regional name for chickpeas, so this is the same food under another name (guideline B). The USDA entry 'Chickpeas (garbanzo beans, bengal gram), mature seeds, raw' describes the dried legume as bought (guideline C). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient in the same preparation, since dried legumes are soaked and cooked the same way. Condition 2: the difference between black and the USDA entry's variety is a seed-coat colour difference, which USDA does not separate. The USDA entry is the generic chickpea, and the black variety is a sibling cultivar of the same food, so the diner would notice a difference in appearance (dark seed coat, which can bleed colour and make the dish look darker) and possibly a slightly earthier flavour. Under the strict reading of condition 2 and guideline F's point on sibling varieties with different taste, the appearance difference is noticeable, so this is not substitutable. However, guideline B treats regional names as the same food, and the black garbanzo is by name a garbanzo bean. Weighing these, the entry is a generic chickpea, the ingredient names a specific colour variety that visibly differs in appearance when cooked, so the match is not acceptable.

The ingredient is plain American cheese slices, the standard full-fat product. The USDA entry is specifically the nonfat or fat-free version. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient turned into a reduced or fat-free version as a modification, so this is not the default match. Condition 1: the fat-free cheese would generally melt, brown and bind differently in cooking, so the preparation can change. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference in taste, mouthfeel and meltability, since fat carries much of American cheese's flavour and texture. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is a mixture of two different sauces: plum sauce and barbecue sauce. The USDA match, 'Sauce, barbecue', covers only one of the two components. Condition 1: Substituting plain barbecue sauce for the mixture would not change how the dish is prepared, since both are sauces added in the same way. Condition 2: A diner would likely notice the difference. Plum sauce adds a sweet, fruity, tangy note and a different consistency and colour that plain barbecue sauce lacks, so the flavour of the dish would change. Guideline F rejects a single ingredient standing in for a blend that contains it, and the flavour change means the match fails. Both conditions are not met.

Ingredient: azuki beans, boiled and unsalted. USDA match: Beans, adzuki, mature seeds, cooked, boiled, without salt. Condition 1: The ingredient is the same food (adzuki = azuki, a regional/trade name variant per guideline B), already boiled and unsalted, matching the USDA's cooked, boiled, without salt state. Under guideline C, 'mature seeds' denotes the dried legume, and the cooked state matches the ingredient's state, so no cooking method change is needed. The 15g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2: The diner would taste and see the same boiled, unsalted adzuki beans; no flavour, texture, or appearance difference is implied. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'roasted edamame', a dry-roasted snack-style product with a crunchy texture and toasted, nutty flavour. The USDA match, 'Edamame, frozen, prepared', is boiled or steamed edamame that has been frozen and is soft and moist. Guideline F lists 'plain vs toasted/roasted' as a difference in state that makes items non-substitutable. Using boiled edamame in place of roasted would change the dish's texture and flavour, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 (no change to preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste or texture) both fail. The 35g quantity is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is turkey broth, a poultry-based stock. The USDA match is fish broth, which is made from fish and has a distinctly different flavour profile. Substituting it would change the taste of any dish that relies on the broth, and a diner would likely notice the fishy character. Condition 1 (no change to preparation) might hold since both are liquids used the same way, but condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste) fails. The quantity is irrelevant. Not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is 250g blueberries, a plain fresh fruit; the quantity is irrelevant per guideline A. The USDA match is 'Blueberries, raw', which is literally the same food in its uncooked, default form. Blueberries are normally eaten or used fresh, so 'raw' simply describes the standard state and does not represent a modified or processed version. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same fruit in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is spiced rum, which is rum with added spices and usually other flavourings such as vanilla or caramel. The USDA entry 'Rum' is the plain, unflavoured spirit. Guideline D treats a flavoured version of a plain product as a modification, so it is not the standard default. Condition 1 is arguably met, since rum can be poured and used in the same way. Condition 2 fails: spiced rum adds clear spice notes that a diner would taste, so the flavour of the dish changes. The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Because the flavour difference is noticeable, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is apple cider vinegar, an apple-derived vinegar with a fruity, mellow flavour. The USDA match is distilled vinegar, which is made from a grain-based alcohol and has a sharper, neutral taste. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), so the question is whether it is a different product with a different flavour. It is. Condition 1 can be met in a loose sense, since both are acidic liquids used in similar amounts. Condition 2 fails because a diner would likely notice the difference in flavour, for example in a vinaigrette, pickle brine, or dressing. The word 'raw' in the ingredient name does not change this, since it does not describe a cooking state. Under guideline F, a different product with a different taste is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw napa cabbage, a vegetable (Brassica rapa, Chinese cabbage). The USDA match, 'Cabbage salad, NFS', is a prepared dish, typically shredded cabbage combined with dressing and often other ingredients. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: using a dressed salad would change the preparation, since napa cabbage is used as a raw or cooked vegetable and not as a pre-dressed salad. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the dressing and other components and would notice a different dish with different flavour and texture. The weight is ignored per guideline A. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is a mixture of two different foods: dried goji berries and pumpkin seeds. The USDA match 'Berries, NFS' is a generic berry entry that covers neither component. It does not account for pumpkin seeds at all, so it cannot replace the ingredient without changing the dish. Even for the goji berry part, 'Berries, NFS' is an unspecified berry, not a dried goji berry (a distinct fruit, dried, with its own flavour and texture). A diner would notice the absence of the seeds and the different fruit. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance) both fail. The quantity is ignored per guideline A.

Florence fennel (finocchio) is the bulb of Foeniculum vulgare var. azoricum, the same vegetable sold in most markets as fennel bulb. The USDA entry 'Fennel, bulb, raw' is the uncooked bulb with no added modification. The leading '5g' quantity is ignored. Under the guidelines, a regional or culinary name for the same food counts as a match. Substituting it would not change preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

Renkon is the Japanese name for lotus root, the same food as the USDA entry "Lotus root, raw". Under guideline B, regional or culinary names for the same food count as a match. The quantity (30g) is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). The USDA entry is raw, and the ingredient is plain fresh renkon, so no state change is involved. Slicing or other knife work done in the recipe does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the raw lotus root can replace renkon without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same vegetable.

The ingredient is plain Swiss cheese, the standard full-fat version. The USDA match is 'Cheese, Swiss, reduced fat', a modified version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced/low-fat version is not a match, because the descriptor is a modification and not how Swiss cheese is normally sold. Condition 1 is arguably met, since it could be grated, melted or sliced the same way. Condition 2 is not met: reduced-fat Swiss is drier and firmer, melts differently, and has a flatter, less rich flavour, so a diner could notice the difference. The quantity (45g) is ignored.

The ingredient is cooked quinoa, quantity ignored (guideline A). The USDA entry is 'Quinoa, cooked', which is the same food in the same state (cooked, plain, no added components). Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the recipe would simply use cooked quinoa either way. Condition 2: a diner would not perceive any difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions hold, so the match is substitutable. The word 'optional' describes whether the ingredient is included, not the food itself, and does not affect the match.

The ingredient is fresh, uncooked Pacific cod fillets, which is raw fish. The USDA entry, 'Fish, cod, Pacific, cooked', describes the same species but in a cooked state. Guideline F explicitly lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Using cooked cod in place of raw would change how the dish is prepared, since it would already be cooked before the recipe's cooking method is applied. It would also change texture and appearance, because cooked flaked fish differs visibly and in texture from raw fillets. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 likely fails too. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is a dehydrated tomato sauce powder, a dry product. The USDA entry is a wet, canned tomato sauce, specifically labelled 'for use with vegetables', which suggests a seasoned or prepared product. Condition 1 fails: 150g of a liquid sauce carries far more water and changes the dish's liquid balance and cooking method, so it cannot replace a dry powder without altering preparation. Condition 2 also fails: the consistency, concentration of tomato solids, and flavour would differ, and a diner could notice. Under the guidelines, a different state (dried vs. wet) and a seasoned product are not substitutable. The quantity is ignored, as instructed.

The ingredient is dry textured vegetable protein, the dehydrated soy-based product sold under that name. The USDA entry 'Textured vegetable protein, dry' names the same product with the same state (dry, uncooked as bought). Under guideline B, the same food under the same name is a match. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are rehydrated or cooked the same way. Condition 2: once cooked into a dish, a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. The quantity (250g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chorizo, a seasoned pork sausage whose defining character comes from smoked or sweet paprika, garlic and often vinegar, with a red colour and a firm, cured or semi-cured texture (dry-cured Spanish chorizo) or a crumbly, spiced texture (fresh Mexican chorizo). The USDA entry is 'Sausage, Italian, pork, mild, raw', which is fresh pork sausage seasoned mainly with fennel and mild herbs, with no paprika or smoke and a pale, unseasoned colour. Condition 1: substituting it would change the preparation. Chorizo is usually cooked or eaten cured, and the raw Italian sausage would need to be cooked through, which alters the dish. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. The flavour shifts from smoky, paprika-led and spicy to fennel-led and mild, and the red colour from paprika would be missing. Chorizo is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. The match fails both conditions, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain corned beef, chopped (the chopping is knife work and does not change the match). The USDA entry 'Corned beef hash' is a prepared product that contains corned beef blended with potatoes and onions, and is usually seasoned and sometimes canned or pre-cooked. Guideline F rejects a single ingredient matched to a blend or product containing it. Condition 1 fails: substituting hash would change the dish's composition, since the potato and onion would be added, and the recipe would be built around a different base. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice potato pieces and a different texture and flavour. The entry is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply.

1. The ingredient is plain Greek yogurt with no fat level specified. The USDA match is 'Yogurt, Greek, plain, lowfat', which names a specific reduced-fat version. 2. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient mapped to a low-fat/reduced-fat version as a modification, so it fails the same-standard-default test. The exception for products normally sold low fat applies to flavoured yogurts, frozen yogurt, parfaits and buttermilk, not plain Greek yogurt, which is sold in full-fat and low-fat forms. 3. Condition 2: lowfat Greek yogurt is visibly looser, slightly tangier and less rich than whole-milk Greek yogurt, so a diner could plausibly notice the difference in texture and mouthfeel. 4. Condition 1 can hold for cooking method, but the modified fat level fails the plain-to-default rule and risks a noticeable change in texture and taste. Not substitutable.

Whortleberry is a regional name for wild Vaccinium berries. In North American usage it is commonly applied to huckleberries (Vaccinium), and the British name refers to bilberry, which is in the same genus. Under guideline B, regional names for the same food count, so this is the same food under another name. The entry is raw, the ingredient is fresh, and no processing or cooking is implied, so the preparation is unchanged. Wild Vaccinium berries of this type have similar flavour, texture and appearance, and a diner would not reasonably notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a nectarine, and the USDA entry is 'Nectarine, raw', which is the same fruit in its uncooked, fresh state. The quantity (250g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the nectarine can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation; any handling such as pitting, slicing or chopping does not alter the match (guideline C). Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is literally the same food in the same raw form. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Spam, a canned luncheon meat, and the USDA entry is named Spam, the same branded product. Guideline G says a branded entry of the same plain product type matches, and the entry has no added flavour or modification (such as lite or a flavoured variant) that would change the product. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: Spam can be used directly in place of Spam with the same preparation (slicing, frying, dicing). Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions hold.

Quahogs are the regional name for hard-shell clams (Mercenaria mercenaria), the same food as littleneck and cherrystone clams, which guideline B maps to 'Mollusks, clam, raw'. 'Shucked' is knife or handling work and does not change the match (guideline C). The USDA entry 'Mollusks, clam, mixed species, raw' is a generic raw clam entry. Quantity is ignored (guideline A). Cooking method is unchanged, since the raw clam meat is used the same way. Flavour and texture are close enough that a diner would not reasonably notice a different clam species in a dish, so both conditions hold.

The ingredient is granola made with oats, wheat and honey. The USDA entry is a branded granola with the same components: oats, wheat and honey. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. The '100% Natural' wording describes how this granola is normally sold and does not add a flavour or modification that a shopper would not expect. Granola is a ready-to-eat product, so there is no cooking method to change. Condition 1 is met because it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 is met because the components match, so a diner would not reasonably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance beyond normal brand variation.

The ingredient is a Fuji apple, and the USDA entry is 'Apples, fuji, with skin, raw', the same variety in its default fresh state. The 'Japanese' qualifier is a regional name for the same Fuji cultivar, which guideline B says counts as the same food. The weight (365g) is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). 'With skin' is the normal way apples are sold and eaten whole, and 'raw' means uncooked, which matches a fresh apple used in a recipe. Using the USDA entry would not change preparation, and a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference, since it is the same variety with the same skin. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is coconut cream, a plain pantry product made from coconut and used as an ingredient in cooking. The USDA entry 'Pie, coconut cream' is a finished baked dessert: a pie with a crust, a set custard-style filling, and typically a meringue or whipped topping. It is not the same food under another name. Using it in place of coconut cream would change the dish entirely, since the pie is a complete baked product rather than an ingredient that can be mixed in. Condition 1 fails because preparation would change, and condition 2 fails because a diner would clearly notice a different food with a crust and set texture. The 200g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Per guideline F, a different state or product form is not substitutable.

1. Identity: A pork shoulder roast is typically cut from the pork shoulder, and in USDA terms the Boston butt is the standard pork shoulder roast. The USDA entry is for that same primal cut, so it is the same food under the standard name, not a different cut (Guideline B, F).
2. Default version: The plain ingredient is the whole raw roast as normally sold, which includes its fat. 'Separable lean and fat' describes that default form, not a modified or reduced-fat version (Guideline D). 'Blade (steaks)' is USDA's sub-cut naming for the same shoulder region and does not change the product.
3. Preparation: The entry is raw, and the recipe's roasting is the cooking method applied to the raw cut. The match does not alter how the dish is prepared (Guideline C).
4. Sensory check: Since the entry is the same raw cut with the same fat distribution, a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance.
Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is hoisin sauce, a standard commercial condiment. The USDA entry 'Sauce, hoisin, ready-to-serve' names the same product. The 'ready-to-serve' descriptor only states that it is sold ready to eat, which is how hoisin is normally bought, so it is not a modification. The quantity (250g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: it can be used directly in place of hoisin sauce with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since it is the same food under the same name. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pickled beets, puréed: beets preserved in a vinegar brine, usually with sugar and spices, then blended. The USDA match is commercial baby food, strained beets, which is plain cooked beets puréed with no pickling. Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste the sharp vinegar tang and added sweetness and spice that pickled beets carry, and the colour and texture may also differ. Condition 1 also fails: the pickling is a preparation step that the plain cooked entry does not share, so the match changes the dish's flavour and preparation. Under guideline F, a different state or processing (pickled vs plain cooked) is not a substitute. Not substitutable.

Ingredient is teriyaki sauce (a soy-based sweet glaze containing soy sauce, mirin or sugar, sake, and often ginger/garlic), used for glazing. USDA match is oyster sauce, which is a thick, savoury sauce made from oyster extracts, sugar, salt, and starch, with a distinctly briny, umami flavour and a different colour and viscosity profile. Condition 1: Oyster sauce could be brushed on as a glaze, so the cooking method could nominally stay the same. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference in taste, since teriyaki's sweet-soy flavour is replaced by oyster's seafood-umami flavour, and the appearance and glaze texture also differ. These are different products, not the same food under another name, and guideline F (different ingredient/flavour) applies. Therefore the substitution fails condition 2.

The ingredient is 'frozen fish tofu', a fish-paste product (surimi-style) sold frozen and thawed for cooking. The USDA entry is 'Tofu, dried-frozen (koyadofu)', a soybean curd that has been freeze-dried. These are different foods: one is made from fish and the other from soy. Koyadofu is also a dried, sponge-like product that must be rehydrated, while thawed fish tofu is a moist, springy paste. The match fails condition 1, since using koyadofu would change how the dish is prepared (rehydration, different handling). It also fails condition 2, since a diner would taste soy and notice the lack of fish and the different texture. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F rules out the raw source versus processed product and different-state cases. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain coconut oil, presumably the common refined or virgin edible oil used in cooking and baking. The USDA match is 'Oil, industrial, coconut (hydrogenated), used for whipped toppings and coffee whiteners.' This is a hydrogenated industrial/food-service specialty fat designed for whipped toppings and creamers, not the home cooking oil. Guideline F explicitly says industrial and food-service specialty fats are not substitutable for the home ingredient, and it is also a hydrogenated fat rather than the plain oil. Condition 1 fails: using it in place of coconut oil would alter how the dish is prepared, since hydrogenated fat has different melting and whipping behaviour and is typically solid at room temperature, changing how it is measured and incorporated. Condition 2 also fails: the hydrogenated product would change the texture and mouthfeel of the dish and could be noticed by a diner. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is '100g mutton, lean', a plain raw meat ingredient that will be cooked as part of the recipe. The match is 'Mutton, cooked, roasted (Navajo)', which is already cooked and roasted. Guideline F says raw vs cooked is a different state and not substitutable. Using pre-roasted meat would change the cooking method, since the dish would not be cooked from raw. It would also change texture and appearance, and a diner could notice the difference. The quantity is ignored, and the Navajo label does not alter the verdict. Condition 1 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a whole grain baguette, which is a French-style bread made with whole grain flour. The USDA entry 'Bread, french or vienna, whole wheat' is the same product type (French bread) in its whole-wheat form. Per guideline D, the ingredient asks for the whole grain version, so the matching whole wheat entry is the correct version rather than a modified one. Condition 1: the bread can be used directly in place of the baguette with no change to preparation (no cooking-method change, same serving form). Condition 2: both are crusty, lean, yeast-leavened whole-wheat French loaves with similar crumb and crust, so a diner would not reasonably notice a difference attributable to the database match. The quantity (50g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain mozzarella cheese, which corresponds to the standard default USDA mozzarella entry. The match is 'Cheese, Mozzarella, reduced sodium', a modified version. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient mapping to a reduced/low sodium version as a modification, so it is not an acceptable match. The quantity (50g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2 also fails in practice: reduced-sodium cheese has less salt, so a diner could notice a difference in taste. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the cheese could be used in the same way, but the taste change means both conditions are not satisfied.

The ingredient is dried persimmon slices, a dehydrated product with chewy texture, concentrated sweetness, and a darker, wrinkled appearance. The USDA match is 'Persimmon, raw', which is fresh, uncooked fruit with a soft, juicy texture and a different moisture and sugar concentration. Slicing does not account for the difference, since the drying itself changes the food. Under guideline F, a different state (raw vs dried) is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using fresh persimmon would change how the dish is prepared, because dried slices are typically used as a chewy, ready-to-eat ingredient, and fresh fruit would need different handling and would not give the same result. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance between chewy dried slices and soft fresh fruit. No USDA entry for dried persimmon was offered, and the 'raw' entry is not an acceptable stand-in.

The ingredient is instant oats (oat groats that have been pre-cooked, steamed, and rolled thin for quick preparation). The USDA match is 'Oil, oat', which is an oil extracted from oats, a different product entirely. Condition 1 fails: oil cannot replace instant oats without changing how the dish is prepared, since instant oats are a solid grain product that would be cooked, soaked, or mixed in, while oil is a liquid fat. Condition 2 fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in texture, appearance, and taste. This is the raw/processed source confusion pattern (the oat grain product versus an oil derived from it), and it is not the same food under another name. Quantity is ignored per the guidelines.

The ingredient is a plain tomato and vegetable juice blend, normally sold in its regular (standard-sodium) form. The USDA match is the same product type but specifically the low-sodium version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version (reduced/low sodium) is not a match, because the ingredient does not ask for low sodium. The low-sodium version also changes the taste: it is noticeably less salty, so a diner could notice. Condition 1 might be met, since the juice could be swapped in without changing preparation, but condition 2 fails because the flavour would differ.

The ingredient is 305g of pheasant meat; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Pheasant, raw, meat only' is the same food in the same state: raw pheasant meat with no skin or bone components named, matching the plain ingredient. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since no cooking method or handling difference is implied. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, as the match is the same uncooked meat. Both conditions hold, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is canned white tuna packed in oil and drained. The USDA entry is 'Fish, tuna, white, canned in oil, drained solids', which is the same food with the same packing medium (oil) and the same drained state. The 18g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the drained solids can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the tuna is already drained and only the drained fish is used. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the product is the same canned white tuna in oil. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is tallow (rendered beef fat), used for frying. The USDA entry is 'Shortening frying (heavy duty), beef tallow and cottonseed', which is a blend of beef tallow and cottonseed-based shortening. Condition 1: Swapping in the blend would not change the frying method, since both are solid fats used for deep or shallow frying. Condition 2: The blend contains cottonseed oil/shortening, so it is not pure tallow. Guideline F says a single ingredient versus a blend containing it is not substitutable, and that different fats are not interchangeable. The heavy-duty, food-service framing of the entry also points to an industrial specialty fat rather than the home ingredient. A diner could plausibly notice a difference in flavour (tallow's beefy character versus neutral shortening) and in the crispness or mouthfeel of fried food. Condition 2 is therefore not met.

The ingredient is tomatillos that have been roasted, while the USDA match is tomatillos raw. Both are the same food, so the naming check passes. However, guideline F lists plain vs roasted as a different state that is not substitutable. Roasting softens the flesh, concentrates and sweetens the flavour, and produces charred, darker skin and a different appearance. Condition 1 fails because the dish's preparation would not match a raw tomatillo, since the roasting step would be skipped. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would notice the difference in flavour, texture and appearance. The quantity (50g) is irrelevant.

The ingredient is a ham steak, a cured and usually smoked or brine-treated pork cut that is typically sold ready to eat or quick-cooked. The USDA match is 'Pork, roast', which is fresh, uncured pork from a roast cut. Ham is a processed product, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails because ham steak is normally pan-fried or grilled as a steak, while a pork roast is prepared by roasting, so the cooking method would change. Condition 2 also fails: cured ham has a distinctly salty, smoky flavour and a firmer, pinker appearance that diners would notice compared with unseasoned fresh roast pork. Guideline F rejects a different processing state of the same meat, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is prickly pear (the fruit of Opuntia cacti), sold fresh as a whole fruit. The USDA entry 'Prickly pears, raw' is literally the same fruit in its uncooked state, with no added processing, flavouring, or packing medium. Quantity (400g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the fruit could be used in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation, since the recipe handling (peeling, slicing, etc.) does not alter the match. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the match is the same raw fruit. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smooth sunflower seed butter (made from sunflower seeds). The USDA match is peanut butter, which is made from peanuts, a legume. These are different foods with different flavours: sunflower seed butter has a distinct earthy, nutty taste and different texture and colour (greenish-grey tint in some cases), and it is not the same product under another name. Guideline F rules out switching between sources that look similar but taste different. Although both are smooth nut/seed spreads that could physically be used in a recipe, a diner would notice a difference in flavour, and the substitution would change the dish's taste and possibly appearance. Quantity (75g) is ignored. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is salad cream, a shelf-stable, emulsified, sweet-tangy dressing (egg-based or egg-free, typically mayonnaise-like with vinegar, sugar, mustard and spices). The USDA match 'Beef salad' is a prepared dish of cooked beef pieces mixed with other ingredients, not a condiment or dressing. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a component of the same product. Condition 1 fails: using beef salad in place of salad cream would change the dish entirely, since it is a solid meat preparation rather than a creamy dressing that can be spooned or mixed in. Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. The quantity of 300g is irrelevant. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is Virginia peanuts that are roasted and unsalted. The USDA entry is Virginia peanuts that are oil-roasted and salted. The food itself is the same (Virginia peanuts), so the base identity matches. However, the entry differs in two ways. First, it is 'with salt', while the ingredient is explicitly unsalted. Guideline D treats adding salt as a modification that changes flavour, and a diner would taste the salt. Second, 'oil-roasted' is a different roasting method from the plain 'roasted' in the ingredient. Oil roasting adds fat and changes the flavour and mouthfeel, which fails condition 1 (the preparation changes) and condition 2 (taste and texture differ). The 10g quantity is irrelevant under guideline A. Because the match introduces salt and an oil-roasting process the ingredient does not specify, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is sweet potato bread that has been toasted. The USDA entry is 'Bread, sweet potato, toasted', which names the same product in the same state. Guideline F rejects plain versus toasted only when the ingredient is plain and the USDA entry is toasted, or the reverse. Here both are toasted, so the toasting does not create a mismatch. The '30g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Substituting this entry does not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same bread in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw chicken feet (poultry). The USDA match is pork feet (pork, variety meats), cooked and simmered. These are different animal species, so this is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Guideline F rejects different cuts and different states, and this match is also cooked while the ingredient is raw, so the cooking method would not match. Chicken feet and pork trotters differ in size, bone structure, skin-to-bone ratio, gelatin content and appearance, so a diner would notice a difference in taste, texture and appearance. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is lamb sweetbreads (the thymus or pancreas glands of lamb, an offal meat). The USDA match is 'Spinach, creamed', a creamed vegetable side dish made from spinach in a cream sauce. These are entirely different foods: one is an animal organ meat, the other a plant product with a dairy sauce. Condition 1 fails because sweetbreads would be prepared by soaking, blanching, and pan-frying or braising, which cannot be replaced by a creamed spinach product without changing the dish. Condition 2 fails because a diner would immediately notice a difference in taste, texture, and appearance. The quantity (300g) is irrelevant. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain 'sorghum flour' with no modifier (the 170g is decoration). The USDA entry 'Sorghum flour, refined, unenriched' is the same food, the standard refined sorghum flour. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to the standard default version as a match. 'Unenriched' is a nutrient-fortification detail that does not change how the flour is handled and would not change taste, texture, or appearance for the diner. The entry is not a sibling variety, a different flour type, or a different state. Both conditions are met.

Blood sausage (black pudding, morcilla) is made mainly from pig's blood, combined with fat and/or grain and spices, and is usually sold cooked or cured. The USDA entry 'Pork sausage' refers to ground pork sausage, typically made from muscle meat, and is normally sold raw. This is not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails: using pork sausage would change the preparation, since blood sausage is usually sliced and fried or grilled as a ready product, while raw pork sausage must be fully cooked and would not behave the same way. Condition 2 also fails: the dark, crumbly, rich blood-based interior and distinctive flavour of blood sausage would be noticeable, and the appearance would differ. Under the guidelines, a different product with different components and flavour is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a mixture of two foods: ruby red grapefruit and avocado, both diced. The USDA match covers only grapefruit (Grapefruit, raw, pink and red). Ruby red grapefruit is a pink/red grapefruit, so the grapefruit half is a reasonable match under guideline B. However, the avocado component has no counterpart in the match. Using only the grapefruit entry would omit one of the two ingredients. That changes the dish's flavour, texture and appearance, and a diner would notice the missing avocado. The match therefore fails condition 1 (it cannot replace the ingredient as specified) and condition 2 (taste, texture and appearance would differ). The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is 'peanut sauce' and the USDA match is 'Peanut sauce'. They name the same food with no added modifier, preparation state, or processing difference. Guideline A says to ignore the 200g quantity. Guideline B treats the same food under the same name as a match. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to the standard default version as acceptable.
