Substituting the USDA entry would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the food is the same. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 25g of halved raw cashew nuts. The USDA entry 'Nuts, cashew nuts, raw' is the same food (raw cashews) with no added flavour, salt, or roasting. Per guideline A the weight is ignored. Per guideline C, 'halved' is knife work the recipe performs and does not change the match. Condition 1: raw cashews can be used in place of halved raw cashews without changing preparation, since the halving is a handling step the cook would do. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the food is the same nut, just cut. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'light brie cheese', meaning a reduced-fat brie. The leading weight (155g) is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Cheese, brie' is the standard full-fat default. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version is not acceptable, and the ingredient itself asks for the modified (light/reduced-fat) version. The USDA entry does not name a reduced-fat product, so it does not match the requested version. Reduced-fat brie also differs from full-fat brie in texture, melt, mouthfeel and flavour, so a diner could plausibly notice the difference. Condition 2 is not reliably met, and the match fails.

The ingredient is smoked turkey neck, and the USDA entry is raw turkey neck, meat only. Condition 1 fails: the entry is raw, while the recipe calls for a smoked product. Guideline F lists 'plain vs toasted/smoked/roasted' as a different state that is not substitutable, and smoking changes the cooking method (the smoke flavour is already built in, so the dish would not be prepared the same way). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the difference between smoked and raw turkey, and the smoked surface and colour would differ in appearance. The entry is also 'meat only', whereas a turkey neck is normally cooked with its bone and skin. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh cactus fruit, which is the fruit of the prickly pear cactus (Opuntia). The USDA entry 'Prickly pears, raw' is literally the same food under a different name (guideline B). The parenthetical '(Northern Plains Indians)' is a source or cultural attribution in the USDA name and does not change the food itself. 'Fresh' matches 'raw', and 'peeled' is knife/handling work that does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the raw fruit can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not perceive any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same raw fruit. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is frozen peas and carrots, used as a vegetable side or in cooked dishes. The USDA entry 'Peas and carrots, frozen, unprepared' is the same product in the same state (frozen, not cooked or seasoned). Per guideline E, frozen vegetables that are normally cooked or mixed match the frozen USDA entry, since freezing does not visibly change how they are served. The weight (400g) is ignored per guideline A. Using this match would not change the cooking method, flavour, texture or appearance, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is adzuki beans, which are normally bought dried. The USDA entry 'Beans, adzuki, mature seeds, raw' is the dried legume as sold, per guideline C (mature seeds, raw = dried legume as bought, as with dried chickpeas). It is the same food with the same state and no modification. Condition 1: the beans can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are soaked and cooked the same way. Condition 2: a diner would see and taste the same beans. The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is ground chia seeds (75g, weight ignored). The USDA match is whole dried chia seeds. It is the same food, so the question is whether grinding changes preparation, taste, texture or appearance. Guideline C allows home knife work or ground-at-home for meat or fish, but this does not extend to seeds. Ground chia is a powder, while whole chia seeds stay intact and visible, and they gel differently when hydrated. Using whole seeds where ground is called for would change the texture and appearance of the dish, and a diner would notice seeds where a powder was expected. Under the 'whole vs ground' state difference in guideline F, this is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain 'almond milk' with no stated sweetness or processing. The USDA entry is specifically 'unsweetened, plain, shelf stable'. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a sweetened or unsweetened version is a modification, so it is not the default match. Sweetness is a taste difference a diner could notice, especially in sweet dishes, so condition 2 is not reliably met. The 'shelf stable' descriptor is a packaging state that is unlikely to change the dish, but the unsweetened descriptor is enough to fail the match. A generic almond milk entry would be the appropriate USDA match instead.

The ingredient is plain fried tofu cubes, a single food that is fried, with no added vegetables or sauce. The USDA entry is a mixed dish: tofu combined with vegetables (excluding carrots, broccoli and dark-green leafy vegetables, and no potatoes) and served with soy-based sauce. Condition 1 fails because substituting it would change the preparation: the frying is absent and vegetables and sauce are added. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in appearance, texture and flavour, since the sauce and vegetables are visible and the fried exterior is absent. The entry is a different food, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is cranberry sauce, a cooked, sweetened, processed product, usually a jellied or whole-berry preparation made with sugar. The USDA match is 'Cranberries, raw', which is the uncooked, unsweetened fruit. Condition 1 fails: raw cranberries cannot replace the sauce without changing the preparation, since the sugar and cooking step would have to be added. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the intense tartness and notice the difference in texture (firm, whole berries versus a soft, sweetened, set sauce). This is a raw source versus a processed ingredient, and a raw versus cooked state, both of which guideline F excludes. Not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply.

The ingredient is yellow squash, which is the common name for yellow summer squash. The USDA entry 'Squash, summer, yellow, includes skin, raw' is literally the same food, a raw yellow summer squash with skin. Quantity (500g) is ignored. The entry is raw, which matches a plain fresh ingredient; the recipe's own handling (slicing, dicing, cooking) does not change the match. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same vegetable in the same form. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food with the skin included as normally eaten. Both conditions are met.

Lamb liver and beef liver are the same organ from different animal species. The USDA entry is 'Liver, beef', so the species differs. Condition 1 (same preparation) is likely met, since both are cooked the same way. Condition 2 is not met: lamb liver is generally smaller, more tender and milder in flavour, while beef liver is coarser and has a stronger, more mineral taste. A diner who knows the dish would notice the difference. Guideline F treats different cuts of meat as non-substitutable, and a different animal source is a comparable difference in the same food category. Guideline B (same food under another name) does not apply, because these are different foods, not regional names for one food.

Russian dressing is a mayonnaise-based condiment with ketchup or chili sauce, paprika, and often pickle or horseradish, giving it an orange-pink colour and a tangy, savoury-sweet flavour. Coleslaw dressing is a different product: a mayonnaise- or oil-based dressing, typically sweetened with sugar and vinegar and flavoured with celery seed, and usually pale and creamy. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B), so the first check is whether it could replace the ingredient without changing the dish. It could be spooned in, but the flavour would differ, since Russian dressing has a distinct tomato/chili tang and Coleslaw dressing lacks it. The colour would also differ, so a diner would likely notice a pink-orange dressing becoming white or pale. Both conditions fail, and the guidelines treat distinct flavoured products as non-matches (D, F). The 13g quantity is ignored (A).

The ingredient is toasted masa harina, a dry corn flour that has been toasted. The USDA entry is 'Masa harina, cooked', which describes a cooked product, not the dry flour. Guideline F says raw vs cooked and plain vs toasted are different states and are not substitutable. Toasting changes the flavour (nutty, roasted notes) and the colour of the flour, and cooking changes its texture and moisture. Adding it to a dish would alter the taste and possibly the appearance, and a diner could notice. Condition 1 is not met, because the cooked product cannot simply replace the toasted dry flour without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 is also not met, because the flavour and appearance differ. Quantity is ignored per guideline A.

1. Identity: The ingredient is chicken thighs, which are dark meat. The USDA entry is broiler or fryer dark meat, meat only, raw. Thigh meat falls within that dark-meat category, so the food is the same.
2. 'Skinless' is handling, not a different product. The entry specifies 'meat only', so the skin-free state matches, and removing skin is covered by guideline C.
3. Raw state: the entry is raw, matching the uncooked ingredient, and the recipe's cooking method applies equally to either.
4. Cut concern: guideline F rejects different cuts such as thigh versus breast. Here the USDA entry is the broader dark-meat category rather than a breast or other distinct cut, so it does not conflict with F. A diner would not reliably detect a difference between thigh meat and the dark-meat category in the same dish.
5. Both conditions hold: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, and taste, texture and appearance are not meaningfully altered.

The ingredient is dry cream of rice cereal, a finely milled rice porridge product. The USDA entry 'Cereals, CREAM OF RICE, dry' names the same product in the same dry state, so it is the same food under the same name (guideline B). The quantity prefix '260g' is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are dry cereal cooked in liquid in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same plain, unflavoured product. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a mixed dish of cooked kidney beans and white rice, and the USDA entry names the same dish with the same two components. The leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry does not state a preparation or packing state, so it is the generic food, which matches the cooked version (guideline E). Condition 1: the match could replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same components in the same form.

The ingredient is a blend of shea butter/oil and babassu oil, so it is a mixture of two different fats. The USDA entry is a single ingredient, babassu oil only. Guideline F says a single ingredient is not substitutable for a blend containing it, and a different oil or fat is not substitutable either. Using pure babassu oil would change the fat profile, and so the flavour, texture and melting behaviour of the dish. Condition 2 is therefore not met, and condition 1 is doubtful for the same reason. The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is butterhead lettuce, a soft, loose-leafed variety with tender, buttery-textured leaves. The USDA match is iceberg lettuce, raw, a crisp, dense-headed variety with a milder, watery crunch. They are different lettuce varieties, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F treats sibling varieties with different taste as not substitutable. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (soft versus crisp) and in appearance (loose, rounded leaves versus compact, pale leaves). Condition 1 is not the deciding factor, since both could be used raw in a salad, but the taste, texture and appearance differences mean the substitution is not acceptable.

Guideline B treats prawns and shrimp as the same food, so the species matches. The problem is the preparation state. The ingredient is plain cooked prawns, typically boiled or steamed. The USDA entry specifically describes shrimp that has been baked or broiled. Guideline F says a plain item is not substitutable for a roasted or toasted version, and baked or broiled is the same kind of difference. Condition 2 also fails: baked or broiled shrimp is usually firmer and drier, and may show browning or char, so a diner could notice a change in texture and appearance. Because the entry describes a different cooked state, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is low-sodium baking powder, and the USDA entry is 'Leavening agents, baking powder, low-sodium', which is the same product. Condition 1: the low-sodium entry can replace the ingredient directly, with the same mixing and baking method. Condition 2: the leavening action and sodium content are the same as the ingredient the recipe asks for, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Per guideline D, when the ingredient itself asks for a modified version (low-sodium), the matching modified entry counts. The quantity prefix is ignored (guideline A).

The ingredient is plain cooked cream of wheat. The USDA entry is Cream of Wheat, the same cereal, prepared with water, so the food is the same product in the same cooked state. Preparing it with water matches the usual way it is cooked. The 'instant' label describes a product form of the same cereal and gives a slightly finer, smoother texture, which is hard for a diner to notice in a dish. 'Without salt' is a seasoning difference that is minor and unlikely to be noticed. Condition 1 (same preparation) is met. Condition 2 (no noticeable taste, texture or appearance difference) is met, with only small variation from the instant form and salt. The quantity is ignored per the guidelines.

The ingredient is lamb shoulder, cubed, and the USDA entry is lamb shoulder (arm, separable lean and fat) raw, so it is the same cut and not a different one. Guideline C says trimming and cubing are handling steps that do not change the match, and the 300g quantity is ignored under guideline A. The USDA fat specification (trimmed to 1/4 inch) describes a normal retail trim, not a modified or processed product. Condition 1 holds: the cubed lamb can be used in place of the ingredient with the same preparation, such as braising or stewing. Condition 2 holds: after cooking, a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance from a shoulder trimmed to a standard fat level.

The ingredient is canned navel orange segments, drained. The match is raw navel oranges, so the food is the same variety, but the ingredient has been processed: the segments are heat-treated and packed in syrup or juice. Draining removes the liquid but not the processing. Canned segments are noticeably softer and more uniformly sweet than fresh raw orange, and their texture differs visibly. Guideline F lists raw vs processed/cooked states as not substitutable, and the ingredient's 'canned' state is not a knife-work or handling change that the guidelines allow. A diner would likely notice the softer texture and different taste. Condition 1 (cooking method/preparation) may be met, but condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance) is not.

The ingredient is red leaf lettuce, a specific colour variety of leaf lettuce. The USDA entry is green leaf lettuce, a sibling variety. The weight is ignored per guideline A. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B), since the two are distinct varieties. Condition 2 fails: red leaf lettuce has visibly red or bronze-tinged leaves, so a diner would notice a difference in appearance, and the flavour and texture also differ slightly. Guideline F excludes sibling varieties with a different taste. Condition 1 is met, since the same washing and tearing would apply, but condition 2 is not, so the match is not substitutable.

Step 1: Identify the food. Yardlong beans (asparagus beans) are the same vegetable as the USDA entry 'Yardlong bean, raw'. The quantity (30g) is ignored per guideline A.

Step 2: Frozen and thawed. Guideline E says frozen matches the fresh/raw entry when the food is normally cooked and freezing does not show. Yardlong beans are normally stir-fried or cooked, and the frozen-then-thawed state does not change how they are prepared or served in typical use. 'Thawed' is handling only (guideline C).

Step 3: Condition 1 (same preparation). Replacing fresh raw yardlong beans with thawed frozen ones does not change the cooking method. The dish is prepared the same way.

Step 4: Condition 2 (no noticeable difference). The diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance in a cooked dish. Freezing may soften the beans slightly, but guideline E treats this as not showing for normally cooked foods.

Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain white rice flour, weighing 100g; the weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Flour, rice, white, unenriched' is the same food, white rice flour, with the standard descriptor 'unenriched' (guidelines B and D). Enrichment is not a flavour, texture or appearance change in a way a diner would notice, and the plain product is the default version. Flour is used the same way, so the preparation does not change. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh grapes, weight is decoration. The USDA entry 'Grapes, raw' is the same food in its uncooked, fresh state. Condition 1: it can be used directly in place of fresh grapes with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since fresh grapes are raw grapes. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is turkey skin, a plain food with no modification, preparation, or processing stated. The USDA entry is 'Turkey, whole, skin (light and dark), raw', which is the same food (turkey skin) in its raw state, with the standard descriptor that it comes from both light and dark meat. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing the preparation, since it is raw skin used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The only difference is that the USDA entry combines light and dark meat skin, which is how turkey skin is normally sold and cannot be distinguished once cooked. The 320g quantity is ignored per the guidelines.

The ingredient is brewed tea, which is normally black tea, and the USDA entry 'Tea, hot, leaf, black' is hot brewed black tea made from leaves, so it is the same food. 'Strong' describes brewing strength (more leaf or longer steeping), not a different product, and the USDA entry names no strength, so it is the default brew. Brewing strength is a preparation parameter the cook controls, so the match does not change the cooking method. A cook could brew the USDA-style tea to the required strength, and the dish would be the same. The entry is not a modified or flavoured variant and not a different state (it is brewed, not dried leaf or powder). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain salami, the standard default cured sausage. The USDA match is 'Salami, made from any type of meat, reduced fat', a modified version with reduced fat. Guideline D lists reduced/low fat as a modification, and reduced-fat salami is not what a shopper would normally buy under the plain name 'salami'. Condition 2 also fails: a diner could notice the difference in fat content, which affects mouthfeel, juiciness and flavour of the slices. The cooking method is not the issue; the product differs in a way that changes taste and texture. Because the match is a modified product rather than the default version, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a chocolate-flavoured corn cereal. The USDA entry, Malt-O-Meal Coco-Roos, is a branded chocolate-flavoured corn cereal, which is the same product type. Guideline G treats a branded entry of the same plain product type as a match, and the chocolate flavour is the defining trait of the ingredient, not an added modification. Quantity (140g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the cereal can be used as-is in the same dish with no change to preparation, since it is an eat-ready cereal. Condition 2: the brand's recipe may differ slightly in sweetness or crispness from another chocolate corn cereal, but this is the same category of product, and the annotation guidelines treat a branded same-type entry as equivalent. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is green enchilada sauce, and the USDA entry 'Enchilada sauce, green' names the same product with no added modification or alternate state. The leading '10g' is quantity and is ignored. 'Warmed' is handling that the recipe does itself, so it does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the sauce can be used directly in place of the ingredient with the same preparation, since warming is a step the recipe already specifies. Condition 2: a diner would taste and see the same sauce, with no difference in flavour, texture, or appearance. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is sweetened dried beechnuts. The USDA entry, Nuts, beechnuts, dried, is the plain dried nut with no sweetening. Under guideline D, sweetened versus unsweetened is a modification, and a plain entry is not a match for an ingredient that specifies the modified version. Condition 1 is met in terms of preparation, since both are dried nuts used the same way. Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste the added sugar, which changes the flavour and possibly the texture and surface appearance of the nuts. The weight prefix is ignored. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is blood sausage, and the USDA entry is 'Blood sausage', which is the same food under the same name. The quantity (300g) is ignored per the guidelines. Preparation would not change, since the match is the same product sold in the same form, so the first condition holds. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, so the second condition holds. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'breaded turkey breast cutlets', a raw or uncooked breaded product that the recipe will cook itself. The USDA entry describes a product that has already been baked or fried, so it is a cooked state. Substituting it would skip or change the cooking step, failing condition 1. The entry also specifies 'skin eaten', while breaded turkey breast cutlets are normally sold skinless, which is a further difference in product. Light meat turkey breast does match the cut, but the cooked state and the skin descriptor mean the dish's preparation and appearance would differ, so condition 2 also fails.

The ingredient is fully cooked kielbasa, sliced. The USDA entry is 'Kielbasa, fully cooked, unheated', which is the same food with the same state (fully cooked). Slicing is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). 'Unheated' describes the product as normally sold and eaten straight from the package, so it does not indicate a different product. Condition 1: the sliced fully cooked kielbasa can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh peas and carrots, which by default means raw, uncooked produce. The USDA entry is specifically 'cooked, no added fat'. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because using pre-cooked vegetables changes the preparation: the cook step is skipped or altered, and the dish would need different handling. Condition 2 also fails because cooked peas and carrots differ from raw in texture (softer, less crisp), colour (carrots and peas dull and brighten differently), and flavour (sweeter, less grassy). A diner could notice the difference. The 50g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Because the states differ, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a plain frozen tomato sauce, thawed. The USDA entry is canned tomato sauce with salt added. Guideline E asks for the frozen USDA entry of the same product when a frozen product is thawed, and no frozen entry is offered here, so the comparison falls to the canned entry. Guideline D says a plain ingredient matched to a modified version is not a match, and 'with salt added' is an added-additive modification. The salt would change the flavour of the dish, so condition 2 fails: a diner could taste the difference. Condition 1 is not clearly met either, since seasoning changes how the sauce must be handled in the recipe. The quantity is irrelevant. Because the match alters flavour through added salt, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain oat flour. The USDA match is 'Oat flour, partially debranned', a specific product with bran partially removed. Condition 1: the match is a different flour, and guideline F says a different flour is not substitutable. It is also a modified version of a plain ingredient (guideline D), and a shopper buying 'oat flour' would not normally pick up a partially debranned product, so it does not fall under the 'normally sold that way' exception. Substituting it would change the bran content, colour, and likely the texture and flavour of baked goods, so the preparation could be affected. Condition 2: a diner could plausibly notice a difference in texture, colour, and nuttiness and fibre character, since bran contributes to these. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is 200g duck egg, a raw whole duck egg. The USDA match 'Egg roll, with shrimp' is a fried or fried-style wrapped dish containing shrimp, vegetables and a wheat-flour wrapper, not an egg. Condition 1 fails: a duck egg cannot be substituted by an egg roll without changing the preparation, since the egg roll is a finished, pre-cooked product rather than an egg used as a recipe ingredient. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance between an egg and a shrimp egg roll. Per guideline F, a ready-made composite product is not a match for a single raw ingredient, and it is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Ignoring the 200g quantity (guideline A) does not change this.

The ingredient is plain tortilla chips, which are normally fried. The USDA entry is a modified version: 'low fat, baked without fat'. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a low-fat or otherwise modified version is not a match. Condition 1 fails because the match is a different product with a different preparation, baked rather than fried, so it changes how the chips are made. Condition 2 also fails: baked, fat-free chips have a different texture (drier, less crisp-fried and less rich), a different flavour from the oil, and a different appearance, so a diner would likely notice. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is navy beans, rinsed. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Rinsing is handling that does not change the match (guideline C). The USDA entry 'Beans, navy, mature seeds, raw' is the dried legume as bought, which is the same food under the standard descriptor (guideline C, dried beans). Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation; it is the same dried navy bean that would be soaked and cooked. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the identical food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a Denver steak, which is the trade name for the beef chuck under blade center steak (Denver Cut), so the USDA entry is the same cut under its standard name. The ingredient is frozen and thawed; per guideline E, frozen meat matches the fresh/raw entry because freezing does not show once the meat is cooked. The 'trimmed to 0" fat' wording describes handling (trimming), which guideline C says does not change the match. 'Choice' is a grade descriptor; the ingredient names no grade, so the standard default applies. Cooking method is unchanged: the steak would be prepared the same way and would look and taste the same to a diner. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pecorino romano, a protected sheep's-milk hard grating cheese (PDO) that is saltier, sharper and more tangy than cow's-milk romano. The USDA entry 'Cheese, romano' is the broader romano category, which is typically cow's milk. This is a sibling product with a different taste rather than the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F treats sibling varieties with different taste as not substitutable. Condition 1 (preparation) would hold, since both are grated over dishes. Condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice the sharper, saltier, sheep's-milk flavour of pecorino romano replaced by a milder cow's-milk romano. Quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is pickled beet cubes: beets that have been cooked/cut and preserved in a vinegar brine, served as a solid vegetable with a distinct sweet-sour flavour and firm texture. The USDA match 'Beet juice' is a liquid expressed from beets, not the beet vegetable itself. It is a different food product (the processed liquid rather than the vegetable), so it cannot be used in place of the cubes without changing the dish's texture and appearance (no solid pieces, no visible cubes). Also, the pickling brine (vinegar, sugar, spices) is absent from plain beet juice, changing flavour. Condition 1 fails because a solid cubed ingredient cannot be replaced by a liquid without altering preparation. Condition 2 fails because a diner would clearly notice the difference in texture and appearance. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is goose egg yolk, an egg component from a goose. The USDA match is Goose, liver, raw, which is an organ meat from the goose's liver. These are different foods: egg yolk is an egg product, while liver is a meat organ with a distinctly different taste, texture, fat and protein composition, and appearance. It would not be used in place of egg yolk without changing how the dish is prepared (liver would not emulsify, bind, or enrich as yolk does), and a diner would clearly notice a difference in flavour and texture. Guideline B does not apply since this is not the same food under another name, and guideline F's principle that different foods are not interchangeable applies. Quantity is ignored. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is beef shin, a leg/shank cut that is usually sold bone-in, with connective tissue and collagen, and is typically braised or stewed for a long time. The USDA match is boneless beef chuck roast, which comes from the shoulder, a different anatomical cut with different fat marbling, connective tissue, and muscle structure. Guideline F states that a different cut of meat is not substitutable (e.g., beef brisket vs beef chuck). Condition 1 is not met because the swap changes the appearance and the bone/connective-tissue profile the recipe relies on, and condition 2 is not met because a diner could notice differences in texture and mouthfeel, especially in braises where shin's gelatinous texture is distinctive. Neither condition holds.

The ingredient is turkey bone, which is skeletal tissue and not edible meat. The USDA entry is smoked, cooked turkey meat with skin, with the bone removed, so it is a different food rather than a name variant of the same thing. It also differs in state (cooked versus presumably raw bone) and processing (smoked, which the guidelines explicitly say is not interchangeable with plain). Substituting it would change the dish's flavour from the smoke and the meat-for-bone swap would change how the dish is prepared (for example, a stock or broth made from bones would not be made from smoked meat). A diner would notice the difference in flavour and texture. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient 'litchi' is an alternative spelling of 'lychee', the same fruit under a regional name (guideline B). The USDA entry 'Lychee' is the generic food with no processing state, so it matches fresh or plain lychee. Lychee can replace litchi with no change to preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is '100g dried fish', meaning dried fish as a food product (the quantity is ignored per guideline A). The USDA match is 'Liver cheese, pork', which is a processed pork liver spreadable/sliced meat product. Condition 1: Liver cheese cannot replace dried fish without changing the dish's preparation; dried fish typically requires soaking, rehydrating, or grinding/flaking, and is a different food category entirely (fish versus pork offal product). Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (fishy, salty, dried-fish umami versus liver-pork flavour), texture (dry, flaky, chewy fish versus a smooth, cured pork liver emulsion), and appearance. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and it is a different source animal and a processed product (guideline F). Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is raw serrano peppers, and the USDA entry is 'Peppers, serrano, raw', which is the same food with the same state (uncooked). The leading '3g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. No cooking method is implied or altered, and the match is the same food rather than a sibling variety or processed form. Taste, texture and appearance are the same for a diner, so both conditions hold.

The ingredient is frozen guava juice, thawed, which is a plain guava juice product. The USDA match is canned guava nectar with added ascorbic acid. Guava nectar is a different product from guava juice: nectars are typically diluted, sweetened purées with pulp, while juice is a plain juice. Guideline D says a plain ingredient mapped to a version 'with added solution/additives' is a modification, so the added ascorbic acid counts against the match. Guideline E also requires the frozen entry when the source is frozen, and the match is canned, not frozen. Condition 1 (same preparation) could plausibly be met, since both are used as liquids in drinks or recipes. Condition 2 is not met: a diner could notice the thicker, sweeter, pulpier texture and different flavour of nectar compared with juice. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is cooked spiny lobster meat, and the USDA entry is cooked spiny lobster meat (mixed species) prepared by moist heat. Both are the same food in the same state (cooked meat), so the food identity matches. The weight is ignored per guideline A. The ingredient does not specify a cooking method, so the USDA entry's 'moist heat' descriptor is the standard way lobster is cooked (boiled or steamed) and describes how the product is normally prepared, not a modification. Condition 1: the cooked meat could replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since no further cooking is implied. Condition 2: a diner would not detect a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cooked spiny lobster meat. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is drumstick leaves (Moringa oleifera leaves), a green leafy vegetable used in cooking, typically as a cooked vegetable or in curries. The USDA match is grape leaves stuffed with rice, a prepared dish (dolma-style) consisting of grape leaves wrapped around a rice filling. Condition 1: Drumstick leaves cannot replace stuffed grape leaves without changing preparation; the match is a composite prepared dish containing rice and possibly meat or seasonings, not a plain leafy green. Using it would require the cook to stuff, wrap, or otherwise change the dish entirely. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance, since the match contains rice filling and a grape leaf flavour profile, whereas drumstick leaves are a distinct moringa green. Neither condition is met, and this is not the same food under another name (it is a different plant and a prepared, stuffed product).

The ingredient is pike, a fish. The USDA entry is 'Fish, pike', which names only the food with no preparation state, so it is the generic food and matches fresh pike. Condition 1: pike can replace pike with no change to the cooking method. Condition 2: the diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same fish. The leading weight (280g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is potato starch, a refined starch extracted from potatoes, used as a thickener, binder, or flour substitute in cooking and baking. The USDA match is Potato chips, NFS, a fried or baked snack food made from sliced potatoes with fat, salt, and seasonings. Condition 1 fails: potato chips cannot replace potato starch in a recipe. Potato chips are a whole, processed snack food, not a refined starch; using them would change the dish's preparation (they would not dissolve, thicken, or bind the way starch does, and would add fat, salt, and flavour). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice differences in taste, texture, and appearance. This is the 'raw source vs processed ingredient' and 'different state' pattern in guideline F, and it is not the same food under another name.

The ingredient is soursop (Annona muricata). The USDA entry is sugar-apple (sweetsop, Annona squamosa). These are different species in the same genus, not regional or trade names for the same fruit. Guideline B does not apply because they are not the same food under another name. Soursop is larger, has a fibrous, creamy pulp with a tart, acidic, citrus-and-pineapple flavour, and a softer, more stringy texture. Sugar-apple is sweeter, with a custard-like pulp, a different taste, and a segmented, bumpy appearance. Guideline F also rules out a sibling variety with a different taste. A diner would notice the difference in flavour and texture, so condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is plain "almond milk" with no sweetness specified. The USDA match is "Almond milk, sweetened", which adds a sweetener. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a sweetened or unsweetened modified version is not a match. Sweetened almond milk is not the default way the plain name is understood, so the match fails the taste condition: a diner could notice added sugar, and cooking or flavour could change. The quantity (75g) is irrelevant under guideline A. Condition 2 is not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain ground turkey, the default retail product, which is typically sold with some fat (e.g. 85/15 or 93/7). The USDA entry is 'Turkey, ground, fat free, raw', a modified version with the fat removed. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a reduced/fat-free version is not a match, and fat-free entries are not what a shopper normally buys under the plain name. Condition 1: the swap does not change the cooking method, so it passes. Condition 2: fat-free turkey is noticeably leaner, so it cooks drier and firmer, and it browns and tastes differently. A diner would likely notice the difference in texture and juiciness. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is caesar dressing, a plain, standard product. The USDA entry is 'Salad dressing, caesar dressing, regular', which names the same product with no added flavour or modification. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient in the same way, with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since it is the same dressing type at the default (regular, not reduced-fat) version. The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is whole mustard seeds. The USDA match is 'Spices, mustard seed, ground', which is a processed, ground form of the spice. Guideline F explicitly states that whole vs ground spice is a different state and is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using ground seed instead of whole changes how the dish is prepared, since whole seeds are typically toasted, bloomed in oil, or popped in a tempering step, and ground seed behaves differently in those methods. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (whole seeds pop and give a crunch, ground gives a powdery, pungent dispersion) and in appearance (visible whole seeds versus powder). The quantity prefix (4g) is ignored per guideline A and does not affect the result.

The ingredient is canned crab, meaning crab meat (a seafood product) packed in a can, used as a plain ingredient. The USDA match is 'Crab salad', which is a prepared dish made of crab meat combined with mayonnaise or dressing and other components such as celery, onion, and seasonings. Condition 1: Crab salad cannot replace canned crab in a recipe without changing preparation, because the dressing and added vegetables are already mixed in and would alter the dish's flavour and the way the crab is handled. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference in taste and texture because the crab salad carries mayonnaise-based dressing and other ingredients, whereas canned crab is plain crab meat. Guideline F (a single ingredient versus a product containing it) and the rule that a diner would notice a different food both apply. The match is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not rescue it. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh pork leg, which is the same food as the USDA entry 'Pork, fresh, leg (ham), whole, separable lean and fat, raw'. The USDA entry names the same cut (leg), is fresh, and is raw, which matches the ingredient as bought. 'Separable lean and fat' is the standard way whole pork leg is sold, so it is the default version, not a modified one. The leading '100g' is quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same raw cut and any trimming or cooking is done by the recipe. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cut of pork. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is rice noodles, cooked (quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry is 'Rice noodles, cooked', which is the same food with the same state (cooked) and the same name. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient with no change in preparation, since both are already cooked and need only to be used in the dish. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is literally the same product in the same state. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is plain tilapia with no preparation, state, or modifier specified (the 150g is ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry 'Fish, tilapia, NFS' is the generic tilapia entry, with no added state, flavour, or processing. It is the same food under the same name, so it matches the plain default version (guidelines B and D). Cooking method is unchanged because the recipe does not specify one beyond the fish itself, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance between the generic tilapia and the ingredient as described. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a bosc pear, a fresh fruit. The USDA match is cornmeal, degermed, enriched, yellow, a dried, milled cereal product made from corn kernels with the germ removed. These are entirely different foods: one is a fresh fruit, the other a processed grain product. Cornmeal cannot replace a pear without changing the dish's preparation (a pear is eaten or cooked as fruit, cornmeal is a dry powder requiring liquid and heat to become a food), and a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails. This is not a same-food naming variant, and the quantity is irrelevant.

The ingredient is plain Swiss cheese, the standard default product. The USDA entry is 'Cheese, swiss, low fat', a modified version. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to a low-fat version as not substitutable, because the descriptor changes the product from what a shopper would normally buy under the plain name. Low-fat Swiss is also not the normal form of the product; it is a reduced-fat variant. Its texture and melt behaviour differ from full-fat Swiss, so a diner could notice the difference. Condition 2 is not met, and the match fails.

Ingredient is 175g leek, a plain fresh vegetable. USDA entry 'Leeks, (bulb and lower leaf-portion), raw' is the same food (leek) in its standard raw form; the descriptor only specifies which part of the plant is included, which is how leeks are normally sold and eaten. The quantity (175g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: a raw leek can replace a raw leek without changing preparation; any trimming or chopping is handled by the recipe and does not change the match (C). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since this is the same vegetable in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is specifically fried chicken gizzards and livers, about 255 g, with the weight ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Chicken, broilers or fryers, giblets, cooked, fried'. Giblets is a mixed category that normally includes hearts and necks as well as gizzards and livers, so the entry describes a blend rather than the same two components. Guideline F says a blend or product containing the ingredient is not the same as the single ingredient. The cooking state matches (fried, cooked), but the diner could notice neck or heart pieces, which differ in texture and appearance from gizzards and livers. Because the components do not match, condition 2 is not met and the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'vegan mayonnaise', a generic egg-free mayonnaise-style condiment. The USDA entry 'Mayonnaise, made with tofu' is an egg-free mayonnaise, so it falls within the same product category and is not a different food under another name. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient at 50g in the same way, spread or mixed in the same manner, with no change to preparation. Condition 2: both are emulsified, creamy, pale, egg-free spreads. A tofu base gives a slightly different flavour and texture from some commercial vegan mayonnaises that use pea or soy protein, but the ingredient does not specify a base, so a diner would not reliably notice a difference relative to what a vegan mayonnaise is. The leading weight is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw savoy cabbage, quartered, a single vegetable. The USDA match, 'Cabbage with ham hocks', is a cooked prepared dish that combines cabbage with pork ham hocks. Condition 1 fails: using it in place of raw cabbage would change the dish, because the cabbage would be pre-cooked and combined with pork rather than used as a plain vegetable component. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the smoky, pork-derived flavour and see a different, stewed texture and appearance. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and it is a raw-versus-cooked, single-ingredient-versus-dish mismatch (guideline F). The quartering is handling only and does not affect the match.

The ingredient is whole egg (quantity ignored). The USDA entry 'Egg, whole, raw' is literally the same food in its uncooked state, which is the default form of a plain whole egg ingredient. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation, since the recipe itself determines how the egg is cooked. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, because the raw whole egg is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain yogurt with no flavour, fat level, or other modifier stated. The quantity (500g) is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Yogurt, NFS' is the generic, unspecified yogurt entry, which is the same food as the ingredient under the standard default. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since yogurt is used the same way regardless of the specific type. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the generic entry describes the same product without added flavour or modification. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain canned adzuki beans, drained. The USDA match is the same bean (adzuki, mature seeds, canned), so the food identity matches. However, the USDA entry is specifically 'sweetened', which is a modified version under guideline D (plain ingredient to sweetened version = no). Plain canned adzuki beans are normally sold unsweetened and used in savory dishes or as a neutral bean. Using sweetened beans would change the flavour of the dish, and a diner would notice the sugar. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is barley meal, which is ground barley grain. The USDA entry 'Flour, barley' is also ground barley, so it is the same food under a near-synonymous name. Both are plain, unmodified, uncooked barley products with no added ingredients, so there is no change in flavour or composition. Barley meal can be a coarser grind than flour, which could in principle affect texture in some baked goods. The guidelines treat grinding as handling that does not change the match, though, and the difference is a matter of particle size rather than a different food. Both conditions are plausibly met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is smoked turkey thigh, skinless. The USDA match is turkey thigh meat only, roasted. The cut and the skinless, meat-only form are the same, so the question is the cooking state. Guideline F says plain versus smoked or roasted is a different state, and that a different state is not substitutable. Smoked and roasted turkey differ in flavour (smoke compounds versus roast flavour), and a diner would likely notice the smoky taste and possibly the colour and texture. Condition 2 fails, and the dish's flavour would change, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is parsnip, a root vegetable (Pastinaca sativa). The USDA match is Couscous, dry, which is a granular wheat semolina product. These are not the same food under another name, and they are not sibling varieties or cuts of the same product. Condition 1 fails: couscous cannot be used in place of parsnip without changing preparation, since parsnip is cooked as a vegetable (roasted, mashed, boiled) while dry couscous must be hydrated or steamed and is a grain. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste (sweet, earthy vegetable versus neutral wheat grain), texture (firm, fibrous root versus soft grain) and appearance. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

Star anise pods come from Illicium verum, a different plant from anise seed, which comes from Pimpinella anisum. They are not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Both share anethole and a liquorice-like flavour, but star anise is more intense and woody, with a different aroma profile. A diner would notice the difference in flavour. The pods are also visibly star-shaped, while anise seeds are small and oval, so appearance would differ too. Substituting one for the other would change the dish's flavour and appearance, so neither condition is met.

The ingredient is plain bacon, which a shopper would normally buy as standard cured bacon with regular sodium content. The USDA match is 'Bacon, pre-sliced, reduced/low sodium, unprepared'. Pre-sliced and unprepared describe the same raw product and do not change the match. The reduced/low sodium descriptor is a modification of the plain product, and guideline D says a plain ingredient matched to a reduced/low sodium version is not a match. It is not the normal default sold under the plain name, so it is not an exception. Condition 2 also fails in practice: reduced-sodium bacon has less salt, so a diner could notice a difference in flavour. Because the match fails on the modification rule and the taste difference, it is not substitutable.

Keen-wah is a regional spelling of quinoa, so this is the same food under another name (guideline B). The ingredient is listed only as a weighed 'grain', with no cooking state given, so it is read as the plain grain as bought. The USDA entry 'Quinoa, NS as to fat' names only the food, with no raw or cooked state, and so it matches the generic food (guideline E). Condition 1: quinoa can replace quinoa without changing the preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, because it is the same grain. Both conditions hold. The main uncertainty is whether the USDA entry reflects a cooked product, which would be a raw-vs-cooked mismatch under guideline F, but the entry as written does not state a cooked state.

The ingredient is muscadine grapes, a fresh whole fruit (a sibling of the grape genus with a distinctive musky flavour). The USDA match is 'Beverages, carbonated, grape soda', a sweetened carbonated drink. Condition 1: a fresh fruit cannot be substituted by a carbonated beverage without changing how the dish is prepared; the beverage is liquid, carbonated, and processed, not a raw whole fruit, so the preparation would change. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in texture (effervescence, liquid vs solid), taste (artificial grape-soda flavouring and sweetness vs. muscadine fruit flavour), and appearance. This is not the same food under another name, and it is a processed beverage rather than the raw plant source. Both conditions fail.

Spanish peanuts are a variety of raw or roasted peanut, sold as crunchy, dry-roasted or raw nuts. The quantity prefix is ignored. The USDA entry 'Peanuts, boiled' is a different state: the nut has been simmered in water, so it is soft, moist and bland, with a completely different texture and flavour. Condition 1 fails because the dish would need a different preparation, since boiled peanuts cannot replace crunchy nuts used as a topping, garnish or ingredient without changing how the dish is made. Condition 2 fails because a diner would clearly notice the soft, waterlogged texture and the missing roasted flavour. The rule that raw versus cooked is a different state applies here.

Ingredient is pecan halves, a plain nut ingredient used as an add-in, likely raw or as-bought. The USDA entry 'Nuts, pecans, halves, raw' is literally the same food: pecans in halved form, uncooked. Per guideline A the 20g quantity is ignored. Per guideline C, 'halved' is handling that does not change the match. Condition 1: the pecan halves can be used in place of the USDA food without altering preparation, since no cooking method is implied by the ingredient and the USDA entry is the raw form. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, as it is the same nut in the same halved form. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is lamb leg, trimmed of excess fat, with no specific sub-cut named. The USDA entry is specifically the shank half of the leg (separable lean and fat, trimmed to 1/8" fat, raw). The trimming level is broadly comparable, and both are raw lamb, so the preparation method and fat trimming are not the main issue. However, the shank half is a distinct sub-cut with different muscle structure, more connective tissue, and a bone-in shank end, compared with the leg as a whole. Under the guidelines, a different cut of meat is not substitutable. A cook would likely notice differences in texture and cooking behaviour, such as toughness and how the meat cooks through. Condition 1 (used in place without changing preparation) and condition 2 (diner would not notice) are therefore not reliably met.

Ingredient: lotus root, cooked, used as an optional garnish; quantity is ignored. USDA match: Lotus root, cooked. This is literally the same food in the same state (cooked), with no added descriptor or modification. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the ingredient is already cooked and the match is cooked. Condition 2: a diner would not perceive any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food in the same cooked state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a meal replacement shake given by weight (500g), which implies a powder that is mixed with a liquid before use. The USDA match is a ready-to-drink liquid nutritional drink, a specific branded product (Boost) with its own flavour profile. Condition 1 fails: substituting a ready-to-drink liquid for a powder changes preparation, since the powder would normally be measured dry and mixed, and the liquid's weight and liquid content would not be comparable. Condition 2 is also doubtful: the ready-to-drink product has a fixed sweetness, flavour and mouthfeel that differ from a generic powdered shake, and a diner could notice the difference. Under guideline F, a different state (powder vs ready-to-drink liquid) and a branded product with its own flavour are not interchangeable. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is 'butter croissants', meaning croissants made with butter. The USDA entry 'Croissants, butter' describes the same product: a croissant made with butter. The leading '10g' is quantity and is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same baked product and needs no different cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food under the same name. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain cottage cheese, which the guidelines treat as the standard default product (the USDA equivalent being 'Cheese, cottage, creamed'). The match, 'Cheese, cottage, lowfat, 1% milkfat', is a reduced-fat version. Guideline D says a plain ingredient mapped to a low-fat or reduced version is a modification and not substitutable, and the 'low fat' descriptor here is not how cottage cheese is normally sold under the plain name. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the product could be used in the same way. Condition 2 fails: lower milkfat gives a drier, leaner, less creamy texture and a milder flavour that a diner could notice. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is pineapple-flavoured Greek yogurt, and the USDA entry is Yogurt, Greek, 2% fat, pineapple, which names the same product: Greek yogurt with pineapple flavouring. Guideline A says to ignore the 500g quantity. Guideline B says a same-food match counts, and this is the same food. Guideline D says flavoured yogurts are typically low fat, so the 2% fat level is how this product is normally sold and is not a modification. The CHOBANI brand is acceptable under Guideline G because it is the same product type with the same flavour. Used in place of the ingredient, the match would not change the preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is frozen chicken nuggets, a ready-made frozen product. The USDA entry 'Chicken nuggets, from frozen' names the same product in its frozen state. Under guideline E, a frozen product matches the USDA frozen entry of the same product. The weight (195g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match is the same food, so it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since it is the same nugget product prepared the same way. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is canned sprouted wheat, drained. Canned wheat is a pre-cooked, preserved product that is ready to eat and has a soft, cooked texture. The USDA entry 'Wheat, sprouted' is the sprouted grain in its basic, uncooked form. Using it would change preparation: it would need cooking to soften, whereas the canned product goes straight into the dish. The texture and eating quality would also differ, since a diner would notice firm, raw-style grains versus soft canned ones. The canned state is a processing difference, not just handling like draining, so the two conditions are not both met.

The ingredient is milkfish that has been baked. The USDA entry is milkfish, cooked, by dry heat. Baking is a dry-heat cooking method, so the match describes the same food in the same cooked state. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since the cooking method already matches. Condition 2: the same cooked fish, with no added flavour, sauce, or processing, should not show any difference in taste, texture, or appearance to a diner. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is roasted pork tenderloin. The USDA entry is pork loin tenderloin, cooked, roasted, so the cut and the cooking state both match. The ingredient is already roasted, so the 'cooked, roasted' state matches rather than conflicting with it. The USDA entry specifies 'separable lean and fat', but the ingredient does not ask for lean-only meat, so this is the standard default form of the cut, not a modification. The leading weight (115g) is ignored. Using this entry would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since tenderloin carries very little separable fat. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is bone-in chicken leg quarters with skin on: the drumstick and thigh together, with the meat, bone and skin. The USDA entry, 'Chicken, skin (drumsticks and thighs), raw', describes the skin from drumsticks and thighs as a standalone food, not the whole leg quarter. Substituting it would remove the meat and bone, so the dish would be prepared differently (a different yield, texture and appearance) and a diner would notice they were eating something different. The cut components overlap, but the entry is a different food, so condition 1 and condition 2 both fail.

The ingredient is queso chihuahua, a Mexican melting cheese, specified as low-fat. The USDA entry is Cheese, mexican, queso asadero. Queso asadero and queso chihuahua are closely related melting cheeses, and the names overlap in common usage, so the base food is arguably the same or very close. However, the ingredient explicitly asks for a low-fat version. Per guideline D, a plain product matched to a modified version is not substitutable, and when the ingredient asks for a modified version the match must also be modified. The USDA entry names no low-fat or reduced-fat descriptor, so it is the standard full-fat default. Substituting full-fat cheese for low-fat changes the fat content, which affects melting, texture (greasiness, stringiness), and how the cheese appears in the finished dish. A diner could plausibly notice the difference, so condition 2 fails.

Poha is flattened (beaten) rice, a processed rice product that is typically soaked or dry-roasted before cooking. Bulgur, dry is parboiled, dried and cracked wheat, a different grain from a different plant. The two differ in species, appearance (flat flakes versus cracked kernels), cooking method (soaking or light cooking versus boiling or simmering to absorb water), and taste and texture. A diner would notice the difference. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a cut, variety or form of the same product. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would change, and condition 2 fails because taste, texture and appearance would differ.

The ingredient is chicken rib, a bone-in cut of chicken ribs with meat attached. The USDA entry is chicken heart, an organ meat with a different texture, flavour and appearance. Condition 1 fails: the cooking method is not guaranteed to be unchanged, and a heart is not a rib cut. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (dense, muscular organ meat versus meat around bone), taste (organ flavour), and appearance (small whole hearts versus rib pieces). The quantity is ignored per the guidelines. This is a different food, not the same food under another name.

The ingredient is dried orange slices, a dehydrated product with a chewy texture, concentrated flavour, and different appearance. The USDA match is 'Oranges, raw, navels', a fresh, uncooked, juicy fruit. Guideline F lists a different state (raw vs dried) as not substitutable. Using fresh navel orange would change the texture (juicy rather than chewy), concentrate the flavour (dried slices are sweeter and more intense), and alter the appearance (translucent and shriveled rather than fresh). Cutting or slicing does not account for this difference, and the quantity is irrelevant. Condition 1 fails because fresh orange cannot stand in for dried orange without changing the preparation, and condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in texture and flavour.

The ingredient is fresh or dried chestnuts (170g, quantity ignored). The USDA match is 'Flour, chestnut', which is a processed, milled product made from dried chestnuts. Condition 1: chestnut flour cannot replace whole chestnuts without changing preparation. Whole chestnuts are roasted, boiled, puréed, or chopped, while flour is a dry powder used in batters and doughs, so the cooking method and dish structure would change. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice a difference in texture (chunks or pieces versus fine powder) and appearance. This is the raw source versus a processed ingredient, which guideline F explicitly marks as not substitutable.

Tomato concentrate is a thickened, concentrated tomato product, the same food as tomato paste under another name, so the identity matches. The USDA entry is canned tomato paste with no added salt. The 'without salt added' descriptor does not make it a modified version, because plain canned tomato paste is commonly sold unsalted, so it describes the normal product rather than a reduced or altered one. Using it in place of tomato concentrate does not change the cooking method. The quantity (8g) is ignored. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is purple corn meal. The USDA entry is whole-grain blue corn flour, labelled in Spanish as harina de maiz morado. Purple corn (maiz morado) and blue corn are close relatives and similar in colour and flavour, so the variety difference is minor. The deciding issue is the grind. Cornmeal is coarser than corn flour, and the two are not interchangeable in cooking. Using a finer flour in place of a meal changes the texture of dishes such as tortillas, arepas, cornbread or polenta-style preparations, and a diner could notice the difference in mouthfeel. Because the entry is a flour and the ingredient is a meal, the match fails condition 2 and is not a same-food-under-another-name case. This is a borderline call, but the guidelines treat distinct milling grades as non-substitutable.

The ingredient is cider vinegar, a single plain vinegar used as a splash for flavour. The USDA match is Italian dressing made with vinegar and oil, a prepared blend that contains vinegar along with oil, herbs, spices and typically other seasonings. Condition 1: substituting a splash of cider vinegar with Italian dressing would change the preparation, since it adds oil, herbs and other components rather than just acidity. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in flavour, because Italian dressing carries herb and oil notes absent from plain cider vinegar, and the dish's taste profile would change. Guideline F rejects a single ingredient versus a blend containing it. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is dried eel, a fish product (eel, typically smoked or dried as a preserved fish). The USDA match is Currants, zante, dried, which is a dried fruit (small seedless raisin-like grape). These are entirely different foods: one is an animal protein, the other a fruit. Condition 1 fails because currants cannot replace eel without changing the dish's preparation entirely. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would immediately notice fish versus fruit in taste, texture, and appearance. The quantity (20g) is irrelevant. There is no naming or regional equivalence between the two foods.

The ingredient is quick oats, a plain dry cereal product. The USDA entry is 'Cereals, QUAKER, Quick Oats, Dry', which is the same product under a brand name (guideline G: a branded entry of the same plain product type matches). The weight '135g' is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: quick oats can be used in place of Quaker Quick Oats with no change to preparation, since both are used dry or cooked the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dark soy sauce, reduced to a paste. Dark soy sauce is a distinct product from standard soy sauce: it is aged longer, has added molasses or caramel, and is thicker, sweeter, and much darker. Reducing it to a paste concentrates these qualities further. The USDA match is 'Soy sauce, reduced sodium', which is a modified version of regular (light) soy sauce with sodium reduced. It is not dark soy sauce. Condition 1 fails: using it would not produce the same paste, since it is a thin, salty, light sauce that would need reducing and would lack the molasses-like sweetness and colour. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the flatter, saltier flavour and the lighter colour and texture of the dish. The match is not a naming variant of the same food; it is a different product type with a modification, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is '200g egg whites' with no stated preparation, so it is the plain, raw ingredient as bought. The USDA match is 'Egg, white, cooked, no added fat', which is a different state. Guideline F explicitly lists raw vs cooked as not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using cooked whites where raw whites are called for would change how the dish is prepared (e.g., they could not be whipped into a meringue, folded into batter, or used to bind and emulsify in the same way). Condition 2 also fails: cooked egg white has a firmer, rubbery texture and different appearance compared with raw whites, which a diner could notice. Because the cooking state differs, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is beef bouillon powder, a seasoned, salted, savory stock product whose flavour is primarily beef, salt, MSG/yeast extract and spices. The USDA match is tomato powder, dehydrated tomato, which has a sweet-acidic tomato flavour, no beef or savory meat character, and a different colour and texture profile. Condition 1: substituting tomato powder would change the dish's flavour base; the cooking method could technically stay the same, but the ingredient's function (adding beef savoury flavour and salt) is not preserved. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice a tomato taste instead of beef broth flavour, and the colour would also differ. Tomato powder is not the same food as beef bouillon under any regional or trade name, so guideline B does not apply. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is cottonseed oil for cooking, a plain oil. The USDA entry 'Oil, cottonseed, salad or cooking' is the same food under its standard name, with no added flavour, modification, or different state. Using it changes neither the preparation method nor the taste, texture, or appearance of the dish. The 80g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

Condition 1 (interchangeability): The ingredient is a honey oat cereal with strawberries, used at 30g. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is Honey Bunches of Oats with real strawberries, a ready-to-eat cereal with the same components (honey, oat, strawberry). Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type is a match, and the 'with strawberries' descriptor matches the ingredient's own description, so it is used the same way with no change in preparation. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference): The product type, flavour profile (honey and strawberry oat cereal) and form (ready-to-eat cereal) are the same, so a diner would not expect a different taste, texture or appearance. The only possible difference is brand-specific formulation, which the guidelines treat as acceptable for a branded match of the same product type. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is unsweetened soy milk, and the USDA entry is 'Soy milk, unsweetened', which is the same product. The leading '250g' is only quantity and is ignored. 'Cold' describes storage or serving temperature, which is handling and does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the soy milk can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not detect a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same unsweetened product. Both conditions hold.

Chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) is the same fish that the US trade and USDA name 'Pacific mackerel'. The entry 'Fish, mackerel, Pacific and jack, mixed species, raw' covers that species. Its 'mixed species' label also admits jack mackerel, which is a different genus with a somewhat leaner, milder flesh. However, both are small oily mackerel-type fish with similar appearance and texture, and the raw entry needs no change to cooking method. Under guideline B (regional/trade names count) and the spirit of the 'same food' rule, the match is acceptable. The quantity (135g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is 250g of crushed Spanish peanuts (raw or roasted whole peanuts, crushed; the weight is ignored per guideline A). The USDA match is 'Peanut sauce', which is a prepared condiment/sauce, typically a blend of peanuts with other ingredients such as oil, sugar, soy sauce, spices, and coconut milk. Condition 1: it cannot replace crushed peanuts without changing the preparation; the dish would receive a liquid, seasoned sauce rather than solid crushed nuts, and the sauce would have to be added in a different way or amount. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference in texture (smooth/liquid versus crunchy particles) and in flavour (added seasonings and sweeteners). Per guideline F, a single ingredient versus a product containing it is not substitutable. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is a generic light milk-based protein powder. The USDA entry is 'Protein supplement, milk based, Muscle Milk Light, powder', which is a branded, light, milk-based protein powder in powder form. The 'light' descriptor is requested by the ingredient itself, so the matching modified version applies (guideline D). Guideline G treats a branded entry of the same plain product type as a match. The quantity (100g) is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the powder can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since both are dry powders of the same type. Condition 2: the ingredient names no particular flavour or brand, so a diner would not reasonably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance from using this product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 390g of shucked oysters, which is a raw seafood ingredient, as shucked oysters are normally sold raw for use in a recipe. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Oysters, baked or broiled' is a cooked product. Per guideline F, raw versus cooked is a different state, so the match changes the food's preparation and texture, and a diner would notice the difference (firm, cooked texture versus soft, raw texture and briny flavour). Condition 1 fails because the dish would need to be cooked to use the match, and condition 2 fails because the taste and texture differ.

The ingredient is turkey salami, a ready-to-eat sliced deli meat. The USDA entry 'Salami, cooked, turkey' names the same product with the same components. Turkey salami is normally sold as a fully cooked, ready-to-eat product, so the 'cooked' descriptor reflects how it is normally sold rather than a modification or a different state (guideline D). Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since neither version requires cooking before serving. Condition 2: it is the same food, so a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh jujubes. The USDA entry 'Jujube, raw' is the same fruit in its uncooked, fresh state, so it is the same food under the same name (guideline B). The quantity (150g) and the '(optional)' label are decoration and do not affect the match (guideline A). Nothing in the ingredient implies cooking, drying, or processing, so the preparation method is unchanged. A diner would not notice a difference between fresh jujubes and 'Jujube, raw' in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh ugli fruit (a single citrus, a tangelo hybrid) cut into segments. The USDA match is 'Fruit mixture, frozen', a blend of several fruits in frozen form. Condition 1: it is a multi-fruit blend rather than ugli fruit, so it would change the dish's composition and flavour profile, and freezing and thawing would alter how the fruit is prepared and served. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice a different fruit mix, and fresh citrus segments would look and feel different from thawed frozen fruit pieces. Guideline F rejects a single ingredient versus a blend containing it, and E says frozen does not match where the food is served fresh. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is plain vegetable shortening, a common household baking fat. The USDA entry 'Shortening, vegetable, household, composite' is the same product under USDA naming: 'household' indicates the home-use version, not an industrial or food-service fat, and 'composite' is a standard USDA descriptor for a blended vegetable fat. Condition 1: the shortening can be used directly in place of the ingredient, with the same creaming, rubbing-in, or melting method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same type of fat. It is not a different oil, a blend containing other fats, or a modified version. Both conditions are met.
