Both are uncooked, so the cooking method is unchanged. The USDA wording 'separable lean only, trimmed to 0" fat' describes trimming. Guideline C treats trimming as handling the recipe does, not a change in the food, so it does not alter the match. Grade and cut are the same, and the entry is not a different cut, a processed product or a cooked state. A diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance once the roast is cooked, since the only variable is the degree of external fat trim. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sesame paste (tahini), a ground sesame seed paste that retains the solids of the seed, giving it a thick, creamy texture and a nutty, earthy flavour. The USDA match is 'Oil, sesame, salad or cooking', which is the pressed liquid fat extracted from sesame seeds with no solids. Condition 1 fails: the oil cannot stand in for a paste without changing the preparation (a paste contributes body, emulsifying and bulk, which oil does not). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (smooth and thick versus liquid) and in flavour and mouthfeel. Guideline F applies, since this is a different state and product (processed seed paste versus extracted oil). The quantity (50g) is ignored.

The ingredient is plain ground chicken, which is raw, uncooked ground meat. The USDA entry is raw ground chicken but explicitly 'with additives', meaning it has added solution or additives such as broth, salt, or phosphates. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to a version 'with added solution/additives' as a modified version, which is not substitutable. Condition 1: the match could be used in the same cooking method, since both are raw ground meat, but the added solution changes how the meat behaves. Condition 2: the added water and salt-based solution would typically make the cooked meat juicier and firmer or spongier, and it can change seasoning and texture compared with plain ground chicken. A diner could plausibly notice the difference in texture and taste. Because the descriptor changes the product from what a shopper would normally buy under the plain name, the match fails.

The ingredient is ravioli with no sauce, and the USDA entry is ravioli, not specified as to filling, with no sauce. Both describe the same dish with the same components. The ingredient does not name a filling, so the 'not specified as to filling' entry is the generic default version (guideline D) and does not add a modification. The 220g weight is decoration (guideline A). Preparation would be unchanged, and a diner would notice no difference beyond what the unspecified filling already allows. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain 'chicken skin' with no cut specified. The USDA entry is raw chicken skin from drumsticks and thighs, which is the standard, most commonly sold and used chicken skin, so it is the default version of the plain ingredient. Both entries are raw, so there is no change in cooking state. The leading '265g' is quantity and is ignored. Skin from these cuts has essentially the same taste, texture and appearance as other chicken skin in a dish, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is hard cider, an alcoholic, fermented apple beverage. The USDA match, Apple cider, is the unfermented, non-alcoholic apple juice product. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B), so the question is whether it can replace the ingredient. Condition 1: the preparation could be followed as written, since both are liquids that can be added in the same step. Condition 2: the flavour would change. Hard cider is drier and tangier, with alcohol and fermentation character, while apple cider is sweeter and more juice-like. Simmering may reduce the alcohol, but the flavour difference would remain, and a diner could notice it. Guideline F also rejects a different state of the same source (fermented vs unfermented). Because condition 2 fails, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is tub margarine, and the USDA entry 'Margarine, tub' is the same product under the same name. The leading '5g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Using the USDA entry changes no cooking method, since margarine is used the same way. A diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain sunflower seed kernels, ground, with no mention of toasting. The USDA entry is 'Seeds, sunflower seed kernels, toasted, without salt'. Condition 1: toasting is a prior cooking step, so using toasted kernels in place of plain ones changes the preparation the recipe assumes. Condition 2: toasted kernels have a noticeably different nutty, roasted flavour and a darker golden-brown colour, so a diner would likely notice a difference in taste and appearance. Grinding is handling that does not affect the match, but the toasted state does. Guideline F classes plain vs toasted as not substitutable. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is Tabasco pepper sauce, a specific branded product. The USDA entry 'Sauce, ready-to-serve, pepper, TABASCO' is the same product, named by the same brand and type. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is a ready-to-serve sauce used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not taste or see a difference, because it is the same product. The leading '13g' is quantity and is ignored. Guideline G covers branded entries of the same plain product type. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 500g rhubarb, a plain fresh vegetable stalk with no specified preparation. The USDA entry is 'Rhubarb, raw', which is the same food in its uncooked state. Per guideline A, the quantity is ignored. Per guideline C, 'raw' means uncooked, and any handling such as chopping or trimming does not change the match. Condition 1: the raw rhubarb can replace the ingredient without altering preparation, since the recipe's own handling applies equally. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pork rinds, which are fried or puffed pork skin, a crispy, airy snack-style product. The USDA match is 'Pork, fresh, backfat, raw', which is raw pork back fat (adipose tissue), not pork skin. Under guideline F, the raw source is not the same as the processed ingredient: pork skin is a different tissue from backfat, and the rinds have been cooked and puffed. The match fails condition 1, since using raw backfat would change the preparation (it would need rendering or frying rather than being used as a crisp rind) and condition 2, since diners would clearly notice a greasy, raw, dense fat instead of a crisp, light texture. Quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is a navel orange, a commercial orange variety. The USDA entry 'Oranges, raw, all commercial varieties' is the generic raw orange and explicitly includes navel oranges. Unlike the guideline F example of navel vs blood orange, where two specific sibling varieties taste different, this entry is the general food rather than a different variety. Condition 1: the orange is used raw in the same way, and peeling, segmenting or juicing does not change the match. Condition 2: a diner would not reliably notice a difference, since the entry describes the same fruit type sold under its general name. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient 'Japanese horseradish paste' is a regional/culinary name for the paste made from wasabi (Wasabia japonica), the same product USDA lists as 'Wasabi paste'. Under guideline B, regional or trade names for the same food count as matches. Both are a plain, ready-to-use condiment paste with the same preparation: it is spread or mixed in, not cooked, so the cooking method is unchanged. The match is a plain paste, not a modified version (no added flavour, reduced-sodium, or other alteration is indicated). Any taste difference between commercial 'horseradish' wasabi-style pastes and USDA wasabi paste is within the normal range of the same product sold under these names, so condition 2 is also met. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is quick-cooking farina, a plain cooked-wheat cereal sold dry. The USDA entry is farina, enriched, in the quick (1-3 minute) form, dry, and names CREAM OF WHEAT, which is the standard quick-cooking farina product. Enrichment is the normal default for farina sold in the US, so it is not a modification. The quantity prefix is ignored. Used in place of the ingredient, the dish would be prepared the same way, with the same cooking time and the same resulting taste, texture and appearance. Both conditions are met.

Indian mustard (Brassica juncea) is the same species commonly sold as mustard greens. The ingredient is the fresh leaves, and the USDA entry 'Mustard greens, raw' is the uncooked leaf. Under guideline B, regional or culinary names for the same food count as the same food, so 'Indian mustard leaves' maps to 'Mustard greens, raw'. The 10g weight is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions hold: the leaves can be used in the same preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance because it is the same plant type. Only minor cultivar differences could exist, which guideline B does not treat as a different food.

The ingredient is fresh elderberries. The USDA entry, 'Elderberries, raw', is the same food in its uncooked state. 'Stemmed' is knife or handling work that does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since no cooking method or handling step differs. Condition 2: the food is the same, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain grits, the standard dried corn product. The USDA entry 'Grits, with cheese, fat added' is a prepared, flavoured version that contains added cheese and added fat. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient turned into a modified or flavoured version as not substitutable. Guideline F also rejects a different state or product containing added components. Using cheese-and-fat grits would change the dish's flavour, and a diner would notice the cheese and extra fat in taste and texture. Both conditions fail, so this is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'maize relish'. 'Maize' is the British/Australian name for corn, so this is corn relish, the same food under a regional name (guideline B). The 12g quantity is ignored (guideline A). The USDA entry 'Relish, corn' is the same pickled condiment with no modifying state or flavour that would differ from a shopper's expectation (guideline D). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is used as a ready-made condiment. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product under another name. Both conditions are met.

1) Same food: the ingredient is canned tart (sour) red cherries, and the USDA entry is canned sour red cherries, so the food identity matches. 2) Draining: 'drained' is handling the recipe does itself, and guideline C says such handling does not change the match. The 'solids and liquids' wording describes the full can contents, and the recipe discards the liquid, leaving the same drained fruit. 3) Packing medium: the ingredient does not name a packing medium, so the plain default canned sour cherry (water pack) is the reasonable match. The water-pack entry is the standard plain product, not a sweetened or flavoured modification. 4) Preparation and appearance: the drained fruit would be used the same way, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is black tea, which is dry tea leaves bought to brew or infuse. The USDA entry is a ready-to-drink beverage: iced tea, bottled, black, with diet (artificially sweetened) added. These are not the same food under different names. The match is a processed liquid beverage, not the dry leaf. Using it in place of 500g of dry leaves would change how the dish is prepared, since there is no leaf to steep, and it would add water, sweetener and processing. The added 'diet' sweetener is a modification, which guideline D says to reject. Condition 1 fails, and diners would taste the sweetener and the iced-tea character. Condition 2 also fails. The entry is not substitutable.

The ingredient is canned figs and the USDA entry is 'Fig, canned', which is the same food in the same processed state. Canned fruit is normally packed in syrup or juice, so the USDA entry does not describe a modified version. The quantity (45g) is ignored. Used in place of the ingredient, the figs would not change the preparation, and a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is tinned (canned) sweetened milk, which in common usage means sweetened condensed milk. The USDA entry 'Milk, canned, condensed, sweetened' is the same product: canned, condensed, and sweetened. Guideline D says that when the ingredient itself asks for a modified version (here, sweetened), the matching modified entry counts as a match. Condition 1: the entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are used the same way in recipes. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. The quantity prefix is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is teriyaki sauce, and the ingredient itself asks for the low-sodium version. The USDA entry is 'Teriyaki sauce, reduced sodium', which is the same product in the same reduced-sodium form. Guideline D says that when the ingredient asks for a modified version, the matching modified entry counts as a match. The weight prefix (35g) is ignored per guideline A. Using the reduced-sodium sauce in place of the low-sodium one requires no change to cooking method. Its flavour is the same teriyaki profile, and the sodium difference is the one the recipe asked for, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance beyond what the recipe intends. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is adobo sauce, a seasoned chili-based sauce (typically dried chiles, vinegar, garlic, oregano, spices) used as a condiment or marinade. The USDA entry 'Adobo, with rice' is a prepared dish of rice seasoned with adobo seasoning, a Puerto Rican/Latin dry seasoning blend, or a mixed rice dish. It is not the same food: it is a cooked rice product, not a liquid sauce. Condition 1 fails: using cooked rice in place of a sauce would change how the dish is prepared, since the sauce is an added liquid or paste, not a grain dish. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice rice in place of a sauce, with different texture, appearance and flavour. Per guideline F, a different state and a different product type are not substitutable.

The ingredient 'karela' is the Hindi/South Asian name for bitter gourd, which is the same vegetable as balsam-pear (bitter gourd). The USDA entry is 'Balsam-pear (bitter gourd), pods, raw', which names the same food in its raw form. Per guideline B, regional or culinary names for the same food count as a match. The leading '215g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). The 'raw' descriptor matches fresh karela used as a vegetable. Condition 1: it can replace karela without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same vegetable. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is mature winged bean seeds, the dried legume as bought. The USDA entry 'Winged beans, mature seeds, raw' is the same food. Per guideline C, 'mature seeds, raw' for beans is the dried legume as bought, so it matches. The 75g quantity is ignored (guideline A). The match is the same food under the same state, so it could be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is frozen apple juice concentrate, thawed, which is a concentrated, syrupy liquid. The USDA entry is apple juice reconstituted from concentrate: diluted to drinking strength, with added vitamin C, and shelf stable. Condition 1: Substituting the reconstituted juice for the concentrate would change the preparation. Because it is far more dilute, 250g of it would deliver much less apple flavour and sugar, so the recipe would need different quantities or reduction to compensate. Condition 2: A diner would likely notice a weaker, thinner apple flavour and possibly a looser texture. The entry also adds 'with added vitamin C', which guideline D treats as a modification of a plain ingredient, and the concentrate itself is not described that way. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain cream cheese, softened. Softening is handling (room-temperature preparation) and does not change the product, per guideline C. The USDA entry 'Cream cheese, regular, plain' is the standard default version of the same product, per guideline D. The quantity (300g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since softened cream cheese is used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh loquats, sliced. The USDA match is 'Apple, baked', which is a cooked apple product. Condition 1: loquats are a different fruit from apples (Eriobotrya japonica vs Malus), so they are not the same food under another name, and substituting baked apple would change the dish's preparation, since the loquat is used fresh and sliced rather than baked. Condition 2: loquats have a distinct tangy-sweet, apricot-like flavour and a juicier, softer texture with a different appearance; a diner would notice baked apple instead of fresh loquat. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is toasted Italian bread, a crusty Italian loaf. The USDA entry is Grecian/Armenian bread, which is a flatbread in the pita or lavash family, not the same product under another name. Guideline B does not apply because these are different breads, not regional names for one food. Condition 1: swapping in a flatbread changes the bread's structure and how it would be cut, toasted and used, so the preparation changes. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in texture (soft, thin, pocketed flatbread versus a crusty loaf with an open crumb) and in appearance. The word 'toasted' matches, but that is not enough to make the bread types equivalent. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is puff pastry dough, meaning unbaked dough that will be cooked in the recipe. The USDA entry 'Puff pastry, frozen, ready-to-bake, baked' describes the baked product. Guideline C matches unbaked ready-made products to the ready-to-bake USDA entry, but the 'baked' descriptor means the food is already cooked. Condition 1 fails: using baked pastry in place of raw dough would change the preparation, since the dough would no longer rise and bake in the dish. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, rise, flakiness and appearance. Guideline F treats a different state (raw vs cooked) as not substitutable. Therefore the match is not acceptable.

The ingredient is canned sorghum, which is pre-cooked and packed in liquid, then drained. The USDA entry is dry, raw sorghum grain, which is uncooked and hard. Guideline F says a different state (raw vs cooked) is not substitutable. Using dry raw grain would require cooking it first, which changes the preparation method. The texture would also differ: canned sorghum is soft and tender, while the raw grain is hard and dry. A diner would notice the difference, so the match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is plain "couscous", which in a recipe is normally the dry, uncooked product bought from the store. The USDA entry is "Couscous, cooked", a different physical state. Guideline F rejects raw vs cooked as a state difference. Using cooked couscous would also change how the dish is prepared: dry couscous is hydrated or steamed as part of the recipe, and cooked couscous would skip that step. The weight would differ too, since dry couscous roughly triples in mass when cooked, so 150g of cooked couscous supplies far less dry grain than 150g of dry couscous. Condition 1 fails because the preparation changes, and condition 2 fails because the texture and moisture of the dish would differ.

The ingredient is malt syrup, a liquid sweetener made from sprouted barley. The USDA entry 'Syrups, malt' is the generic USDA category for malt syrup, so it names the same food. Condition 1: the syrup can be used in place of the ingredient as a liquid sweetener without changing preparation. Condition 2: the syrup is the same product type, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The leading '85g' is quantity and is ignored. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is lactose-free, nonfat (skim) milk, used as a liquid in the recipe. The USDA entry 'Milk, lactose free, fat free (skim)' describes the same product: lactose-free milk with the fat removed. Under guideline D, when the ingredient itself asks for a modified version (lactose-free, fat-free), the matching modified entry counts. The 300g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation, since both are liquid milk used the same way. Condition 2: the taste, texture and appearance should be the same, because it is the same product type with the same lactose and fat profile. Both conditions hold.

Step 1: The ingredient is frozen escarole, an uncooked leafy green that is thawed and then prepared or cooked as the recipe directs. The USDA match is 'Escarole, cooked', which is a different state. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a state difference that is not substitutable. Step 2: Using cooked escarole would skip or alter the cooking step. Cooked escarole is softer, wetter, darker and more compact than thawed escarole. If the dish cooks the greens further, the cooked entry would be overcooked and would change texture and appearance. If the dish uses them as a fresh-style component, the cooked entry would be noticeably different. Condition 1 fails because the preparation changes, and condition 2 likely fails because a diner would notice the softer, more cooked texture. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a shortening made from palm oil alone. The USDA entry is a household shortening made from a blend of hydrogenated soybean oil and palm oil. Guideline F says a different oil or fat is not substitutable, and a single ingredient is not substitutable for a blend containing it. The soybean component changes the fat composition, so the match fails the rule. Condition 1 (same use in preparation) would likely hold, but condition 2 (no detectable difference in taste, texture, or appearance) is not reliably met, since the fat sources differ. The quantity is ignored, as guideline A requires.

The ingredient is plain cottage cheese, with the leading weight (245g) being irrelevant under guideline A. The USDA entry, 'Cheese, cottage, creamed, large or small curd', is the standard default version of cottage cheese: creamed, with no added flavour, sweetener, or reduced-fat modification. Guideline D explicitly lists cottage cheese -> Cheese, cottage, creamed as a valid match. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same product and is used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food under the standard name. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain gelatin sheets (bloomed, so they would be dissolved into a liquid, set, or mixed into a recipe). The USDA match is 'Gelatin salad with vegetables', a prepared dish that contains gelatin plus vegetables and typically sugar and flavourings. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. It is also a finished product with added components, which guideline F rejects (a single ingredient vs a product containing it). Using it in place of gelatin sheets would add vegetables, flavour and possibly sweetness, and would change how the dish is prepared. A diner would notice the difference in taste and texture. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails too.

The ingredient is naan, a leavened flatbread. The USDA entry 'Bread, naan' names the same food with no added flavour, modification, or state descriptor, so it is the standard default version. The 65g quantity is ignored per the guidelines. Condition 1: naan can directly replace naan without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is the same bread used in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a sesame dressing, a sauce or condiment (typically a sesame-oil and soy or vinegar based dressing, often served cold on salads or noodles). The USDA match is Sesame chicken, a cooked dish of breaded and fried chicken pieces in a sweet sauce. Condition 1: the match is a prepared chicken dish, not a dressing; it cannot replace a dressing without changing preparation, since it is a protein entree with solid meat pieces, not a liquid condiment. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in appearance, texture (solid breaded chicken vs. pourable sauce) and taste (chicken dish vs. sesame dressing). It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a modified version of the same product. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is raw beef chuck, cubed. The USDA entry is 'Beef, chuck for stew, separable lean and fat, choice, raw', which is the same cut (chuck), sold in the stew-cube form, and uncooked. Cubing is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). 'Separable lean and fat' is the default way chuck is listed and sold when no trimming is specified, so it matches a plain 'beef chuck' ingredient (guideline D). 'Choice' is the standard retail grade. Condition 1: the chuck could replace the ingredient with the same preparation, since both are raw chuck cubes for stewing or braising. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same cut with the same fat content. Both conditions are met.

Jamun (Syzygium cumini) is the same fruit as Java-plum, also called jambolan, which is a regional/culinary name for it (guideline B). The USDA entry is 'raw', meaning uncooked fresh fruit, which matches the ingredient as bought. The 30g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the fruit could replace jamun without changing preparation, since no cooking method is implied. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, because it is the same food under another name. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw extra-lean ground turkey, an uncooked meat to be prepared in the recipe. The USDA entry is 'Turkey, ground, fat free, patties, broiled', which is a cooked product, formed into patties and broiled. Using it would change the cooking method, since the recipe would need raw meat cooked in the dish rather than pre-cooked patties. It also differs in state (raw vs cooked) and form (loose ground meat vs formed patties), which would affect texture and appearance. Guideline F states that raw vs cooked is a different state and not substitutable. Condition 1 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

Pine kernels are the seeds of pine trees and are commonly sold under the name pine nuts, so 'Pine nuts' is the same food under another name (guideline B). The quantity prefix '25g' is ignored (guideline A). The USDA entry is a plain, unmodified product with no added state or processing that would differ from what a shopper buys as pine kernels. Condition 1: pine nuts can be used in place of pine kernels without changing preparation, such as toasting or sprinkling. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since they are the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cooked ground turkey, with the leading weight (585g) being irrelevant per guideline A. The USDA match is 'Turkey, Ground, cooked', which is the same food in the same state (cooked, ground). Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since the dish would be prepared identically. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, as it is the same product. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is plain roti, a standard unleavened whole-wheat flatbread. The USDA entry 'Bread, chappatti or roti' is the same food under its regional name (chapati and roti are the same bread), so per guideline B it is a direct match. The quantity prefix '500g' is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the USDA food can replace the roti without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is the same product and needs no different handling. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned duck, which is a cooked, preserved product, typically packed in fat or its own juices. The USDA entry is raw duck meat, which is uncooked. Guideline F explicitly lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Substituting raw duck would change the cooking method, since the meat would need cooking before it could be used as canned duck is. The appearance, texture and flavour would also differ, and a diner would notice. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails too.

The ingredient is dark molasses, a liquid sweetener used as a single ingredient. The USDA entry 'Cookies, molasses' is a baked good (a finished cookie) that contains molasses as one component among flour, fat, sugar and other ingredients. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B), and it is not a modified version of molasses (guideline D). Guideline F rejects a single ingredient matched to a product containing it. Using a cookie in place of molasses would change the dish's preparation, flavour, texture and appearance, and a diner would notice a different food. Condition 1 and condition 2 both fail.

The ingredient is dried beechnuts, and the USDA entry is 'Nuts, beechnuts, dried', which describes the same food in the same state. The leading '20g' is quantity and is ignored. Using the USDA entry requires no change to preparation, since the dried nuts are used as bought, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'fresh shrimp cakes', a raw, formed shrimp product that is typically cooked by frying or steaming. The match is 'Shrimp, canned', which is pre-cooked and packed in liquid. Condition 1 fails: canned shrimp cannot stand in for raw formed cakes without changing preparation, since the cakes would need binding, shaping and cooking, and canned shrimp is already cooked. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (soft, canned, flaked versus a bound, cooked cake) and in appearance (no cake form, different colour and structure). Guideline F also rules out a raw versus cooked state difference. Quantity is ignored. Not substitutable.

Williams pear is the same variety as Bartlett pear. 'Williams' is the regional/trade name used in the UK and Europe (Williams Bon Chrétien), and Bartlett is the US name for it. Under guideline B, a regional name for the same food counts as the same food. The ingredient is 500g, and the quantity is ignored under guideline A. Condition 1: the pear can replace the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same fruit. The 'raw' descriptor matches fresh pears used as ingredients, and any knife work does not change the match. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is ground grass-fed beef, and the USDA entry is 'Beef, grass-fed, ground, raw', which is the same food with the same descriptors (grass-fed, ground, uncooked). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation, since both are raw ground beef. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the product is the same. The leading '400g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Ground meat is a standard raw form, so the match is exact under guideline B.

The ingredient is plain spaetzle, a fresh or dried egg noodle dumpling pasta. The USDA match is 'Beef with spaetzle or rice, vegetable, frozen meal', a prepared frozen dinner containing beef, vegetables, and spaetzle or rice. Condition 1: the match is a multi-component prepared meal, not the spaetzle alone. Substituting it would introduce beef, vegetables, and rice, and would change the dish entirely rather than just providing the noodle component. The dish would not be prepared the same way. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance because the beef and vegetables are added and the product is a frozen meal. Guideline F (a blend or product containing the ingredient is not a match for a single ingredient) applies. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is plain extra firm silken tofu, the standard default product. The USDA match is MORI-NU Lite Extra Firm silken tofu, which is a 'lite' version with reduced fat/calories. Guideline D treats 'lite' as a modification: a plain ingredient mapped to a modified version is not substitutable. The lite product is also a distinct branded product that is not what a shopper would normally buy under the plain name 'extra firm silken tofu', so the descriptor is not a normal-sale descriptor. Condition 1 (cooking method) is likely unaffected, but condition 2 may not hold: reduced-fat tofu can differ in texture and mouthfeel, and a diner could notice. Because the entry is a modified version rather than the default, it fails the match.

The ingredient is ground mung beans, meaning the dried legume already milled into a powder or flour. The USDA entry is whole dried mature mung bean seeds. Both are the same food, so the identity condition is met. However, grinding is a processing step that changes the physical form. Using whole seeds would require the cook to grind them first, which changes how the dish is prepared (condition 1 fails). Whole beans would also give a visibly coarser, different texture in the finished dish, which a diner would notice (condition 2 fails). Guideline F treats ground versus whole forms as a different state, and the guideline C exception for home grinding only covers meat and fish, not beans. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is walnut milk, a plant-based milk made from walnuts. The USDA match is oat milk, a different plant-based milk made from oats. Under condition 1, oat milk could be used in place of walnut milk without changing preparation, since both are liquid milk substitutes used in similar ways. However, condition 2 fails: walnut milk has a distinctly nutty flavour and a different protein and fat profile, and oat milk has a sweeter, cereal-like taste and different mouthfeel. A diner would likely notice the difference in flavour, especially in dishes where walnut milk is a prominent component. Oat milk is a different product from walnut milk, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and it is not a sibling of the same product type with an equivalent taste (guideline F, sibling variety with different taste, applies in spirit). Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh coconut meat, the white flesh of the coconut. The USDA entry 'Nuts, coconut meat, raw' is the same food in its uncooked state. Under guideline B, this is the same food under a different name. The quantity (50g) is ignored per guideline A, and 'optional' does not change the food itself. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are raw coconut meat used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same raw food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a specific product: Russian dressing, a sweet-tangy, orange-pink dressing typically based on ketchup or chili sauce with relish or paprika. Its fat-free form keeps that flavour profile. The USDA entry, 'Salad dressing, fat free, NFS', is a generic fat-free salad dressing with no stated flavour and no indication that it is Russian style. Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste and see a different dressing, since generic fat-free dressings differ in flavour and colour from Russian dressing. Guideline B does not apply because this is not the same food under another name, and the flavoured variety should not be treated as the generic default. Condition 1 is also doubtful, since the substitution changes the flavour of the dish. Because condition 2 is not met, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried coconut cream powder, used as a garnish. The USDA entry is raw coconut cream, the liquid expressed from grated coconut meat. The quantity (365g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 fails: a liquid cannot be used in place of a dry powder for a garnish without changing how the dish is prepared. Guideline F treats a different state (raw liquid vs processed dried powder) as non-substitutable. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would see and feel the difference, since a dry powder sprinkled as garnish looks and feels nothing like liquid coconut cream. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is frozen crab meat, thawed, which is a fresh-style crab meat. The USDA entry is canned blue crab, which is a different product state. Per guideline E, a thawed frozen product matches the frozen USDA entry of the same product, but this entry is canned, not frozen. Canned crab is typically packed in brine or water, is softer and more compacted, and has a different texture and flavour from thawed crab meat. A diner would likely notice the difference in texture and taste. Guideline F also rejects a different processed state (canned vs. fresh/frozen) when it changes the eating experience. The entry also specifies one species (blue crab), while the ingredient is unspecified crab meat. On the condition that the diner would not notice a difference, this fails.

Cassis berries are the French name for blackcurrants (Ribes nigrum). USDA 'Currants, european black, raw' is the same fruit, so this is the same food under a regional/culinary name (guideline B). The match is raw, and the 150g weight is ignored (guideline A). Using it in place of cassis berries would not change preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same species. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain beef pastrami, sliced, which a shopper would normally buy as regular, full-fat pastrami. The USDA entry is 'Pastrami, beef, 98% fat-free', a reduced-fat modified version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced/fat-free version is not a match, because the descriptor makes the product differ from what a shopper would normally buy under the plain name. Condition 2 also fails: a 98% fat-free pastrami is noticeably leaner and drier, so a diner could detect the difference in taste and texture. Sliced is only handling and does not change the match. Condition 1 might hold, since the same dish could be prepared with it, but both conditions must hold, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is chow chow relish, a pickled condiment made from chopped cabbage, green tomatoes, onions, peppers, mustard seed and vinegar, typically served cold as a topping or side. The USDA match, 'Chow fun noodles with vegetables, meatless', is a stir-fry-style rice noodle dish that is cooked, contains noodles, and has no pickled, vinegary, relish character. Condition 1 fails: it cannot be used in place of a relish without changing how the dish is prepared, since a cooked noodle dish is not a cold pickled condiment. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (sour, pickled, mustard-spiced versus savoury noodles), texture (chunky relish versus soft noodles) and appearance. The two products are not the same food under another name, so the guideline B exception does not apply.

The ingredient is sea scallop meat, which is the adductor muscle of a scallop, a shellfish from the bivalve family. The USDA match is 'Fish, sea bass, mixed species, raw', which is a finfish (bass). These are different animals from different taxonomic groups with distinct textures, flavours and appearances. Condition 1 fails: a sea bass fillet cannot be used in place of scallop meat without changing the preparation (scallops are typically seared whole, while bass fillets are cooked differently and would not be sliced or seared the same way). Condition 2 fails: a diner would readily notice the sweet, tender, almost creamy texture of scallop versus the flaky texture and flavour of sea bass. The quantity (130g) is ignored per the guidelines. This is not a regional name for the same food, so guideline B does not apply. It is not a substitutable match.

The ingredient is 'leek soup', a prepared, cooked liquid dish, not raw leek. The USDA match is 'Leeks, bulb and greens, root removed, raw', which is the uncooked vegetable. Condition 1 fails: raw leeks cannot stand in for soup without changing the preparation, since the dish would need cooking, liquid, and seasoning. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in texture, temperature, and appearance between a bowl of soup and raw leek pieces. This is the raw source versus a processed dish (guideline F), so it is not a same-food name variant (guideline B).

The ingredient is sour cherries (fresh or plain tart cherries, the fruit). The USDA match is 'Whiskey sour', which is a cocktail made from whiskey, lemon juice and sugar, not a fruit. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a processed or modified version of cherries. Condition 1 fails: using a whiskey sour cocktail in place of fruit would change how the dish is prepared (it is a liquid alcoholic drink, not a fruit to be added, chopped or cooked). Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice alcohol, citrus and a completely different texture and appearance. The quantity (40g) is irrelevant. Neither condition is met.

Thompson Seedless is a green (white) table grape variety. The USDA entry is 'Grapes, red, seedless, raw', a different colour and a sibling variety with a somewhat different flavour profile. Guideline F says a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable. Condition 1 is likely met, since the grapes would be served raw in the same way. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in appearance (green vs red skin) and in taste. The quantity (30g) is ignored per guideline A. Guideline B does not apply because this is a different variety, not the same food under another name. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'ham and cheese loaf', a processed deli-style meat loaf containing ham and cheese. The USDA entry 'Ham and cheese loaf or roll' names the same product with the same components (ham and cheese in a loaf form). Guideline B and C say that if the USDA entry names the same dish or product with the same components, it is a match. The leading quantity '100g' is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the loaf can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same product type (a 'roll' variant is a loaf-shaped form of the same product and is served the same way). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance between a ham and cheese loaf and a ham and cheese loaf or roll, as they are the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain '500g lamb shoulder', which is an uncooked raw meat. The USDA match is 'Lamb, shoulder, arm, separable lean and fat, trimmed to 1/4" fat, choice, cooked, roasted'. It is the same cut, but it is cooked and roasted. Under guideline F, raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using pre-roasted meat would change how the dish is prepared, since the meat would not be cooked in the recipe's method and could not be browned, braised or seared as intended. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, colour and flavour between raw-cooked meat and pre-roasted meat. The quantity (500g) is irrelevant under guideline A. Both conditions are not met, so the match is rejected.

The ingredient is ghee, a clarified butter. The USDA entry is 'Butter, Clarified butter (ghee)', which names the same product directly, so guideline B applies and it is the same food under the same name. Condition 1: ghee is used as a fat in cooking, and the USDA entry is the same fat, so no change to the cooking method is needed. Condition 2: the USDA entry is the same product with the same components (milk fat with water and milk solids removed), so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The 50g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain grits, and the USDA entry 'Grits, NFS' names the same food with no cooking state, preparation or added flavour. Under guideline B, a generic entry for the same food matches the plain ingredient. Under guideline E, an entry that names only the food is the generic food and matches the plain version. The quantity (100g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: grits can be used in place of grits with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh acorn squash, a winter squash. The USDA entry 'Squash, winter, acorn, raw' is the same food in its raw, uncooked state. The leading weight '390g' is decoration and is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since fresh acorn squash is normally prepared raw or cooked in the same ways. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same vegetable. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'american cheese' and the USDA entry is 'Cheese, American', which is the same food under the same name. The leading '265g' is only a quantity and is ignored. The USDA entry names no modified version (such as reduced-fat or sodium-reduced), so it matches the standard default product. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the same preparation, such as melting, layering, or slicing, without changing the method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product.

"Shrimp chips" (prawn crackers or krupuk) are a starch-based cracker containing shrimp, typically sold as uncooked dried discs that puff into a crisp snack when fried. "Shrimp, dried" is whole or pieces of dried shrimp meat. These are not the same food: one is a processed starch cracker and the other is a dried seafood product. Substituting dried shrimp would change how the dish is prepared, since the chips must be deep-fried to puff and dried shrimp would not expand. It would also change texture and appearance, because the diner would get chewy, salty shrimp pieces rather than light, crisp chips. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is lion's mane mushrooms (Hericium erinaceus), raw. The USDA match is maitake mushrooms (Grifola frondosa), raw. These are different mushroom species, not regional or trade names for the same food. Lion's mane has a shaggy, tooth-like, white appearance and a dense, seafood-like texture when cooked. Maitake has a frondy, layered, brown-grey appearance and a more earthy, woody flavour and chewier texture. A diner would likely notice the difference in appearance, texture and flavour, so condition 2 fails. Because the taste and texture differ, the match is not substitutable under guideline F (a different variety with a different taste). The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is refined peanut oil, which is peanut oil that has been refined to a neutral flavour and high smoke point. The USDA entry, 'Oil, peanut, salad or cooking', is the generic peanut oil used for cooking, and refined peanut oil is the standard form of that product sold for cooking. 'Refined' describes the normal processing of this product rather than a modified version, so it falls under the default-version rule (guideline D). Condition 1: the oil can replace the ingredient directly with no change to the cooking method, since both are used the same way for frying and sautéing. Condition 2: both are the same food with the same mild flavour and appearance, so a diner would not notice a difference. The quantity (60g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried bonito flakes (katsuobushi), a smoked, fermented, dried skipjack tuna product used for dashi and garnish, with a distinct smoky, umami flavour and a flaky, papery texture. The USDA match is 'Onions, dehydrated flakes', which is dehydrated onion, a different food entirely (a vegetable, not fish). Condition 1 fails: it cannot be used in place of bonito flakes without changing the dish's flavour base, since it would remove the fish-based umami and smoke and add onion sweetness and pungency. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice onion flavour instead of fish and smoke. The quantity is ignored per the guidelines. This is not the same food under another name, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a vanilla yogurt served with granola, so the dish has two components: yogurt and granola. The USDA match covers only the yogurt, specifically Greek vanilla lowfat yogurt. Under guideline D, vanilla yogurt is normally a low-fat product, so the lowfat descriptor is not a problem. The Greek style is a thicker, tangier variety, but the ingredient does not specify a style, so this point is minor. The decisive issue is the granola. Removing it changes the dish's texture (the crunch) and appearance (the visible granola pieces), and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 2 is not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is hubbard squash, a winter squash (Cucurbita maxima), typically sold whole and cooked as roasted or baked flesh. The USDA match is 'Squash, summer, casserole, with cheese sauce', a prepared casserole dish containing summer squash (a different species, Cucurbita pepo, e.g. zucchini/yellow squash) combined with a cheese sauce and other components. Condition 1: Hubbard squash is not the same food as summer squash; it is a different species and variety with a different texture and flavour profile. Substituting a prepared cheese-sauce casserole for a plain squash ingredient would fundamentally change the preparation: the dish would now contain cheese sauce and be a casserole rather than the squash used as a plain component. Condition 2: A diner would readily notice the cheese sauce, the summer squash flesh (softer, paler, with different flavour), and the casserole appearance. Neither condition is met. The quantity (20g) is ignored per the guidelines.

The ingredient is 500g of smoked bacon, which a recipe normally uses raw (uncooked) and then cooks. The USDA entry is 'Pork bacon, NS as to fresh, smoked or cured, cooked', so it is a cooked product. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using pre-cooked bacon changes the cooking method, since it would not render fat or crisp in the same way, and the same weight of cooked bacon yields much less meat. Condition 2 also likely fails: a diner would notice differences in texture (cooked bacon is already crisp or chewy in a different way) and appearance. The entry's 'NS as to smoked or cured' wording is generic and would not be the issue, but the cooked state alone makes it not substitutable.

The ingredient is pickled tripe, meaning tripe preserved in brine or vinegar, which gives it a sour, sharp flavour, a firmer texture and a different appearance. The USDA entry 'Tripe' is the plain, unpickled product, typically raw or simply cooked. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient becoming a version with added solution or additives as a modification, and guideline F says a different state (raw or cooked vs processed) is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because the plain tripe would need to be cooked, rinsed or otherwise treated differently to match a pickled dish. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the missing sourness and brine flavour. The match is not substitutable.

1. Identity: The ingredient is miso soup, a broth-based dish with miso paste, and the USDA entry 'Soup, miso or tofu' names the same dish. Nothing in the entry indicates a different product or a different soup. 2. State: The ingredient is frozen and then thawed. Guideline E says an entry with no state given is the generic food and matches thawed or plain versions. The USDA entry does not specify dehydrated, canned, or frozen, so it is the generic food. 3. Preparation: The ingredient is ready to eat after thawing, and the USDA soup is also served as a prepared soup, so the dish would not need a different cooking method. 4. Sensory: Miso soup that has been frozen and thawed should not differ visibly or in flavour from the generic miso soup entry, and a diner would not reasonably notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pepperoni, a cured, dry sausage. The USDA entry 'Pepperoni, NFS' names the same food with no modification, preparation, or added flavour, so it is the generic default version. Per guideline B, the same food under the same name matches. Condition 1: pepperoni can replace pepperoni without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is used in the same form. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. The 60g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked boneless turkey with no mention of skin. Smoking matches the USDA entry, and 'bone removed' matches 'boneless', so the state and cut agree. The USDA entry specifies 'with skin', which the ingredient does not ask for. Smoked boneless turkey is normally sold skinless (deli or smoked breast-style cuts), so the skin is an added component rather than the standard default. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version is not substitutable. Skin also changes the appearance and texture (colour, chewiness, fat content) in a way a diner could notice. Condition 2 is therefore not met.

The ingredient is smoked haddock. The USDA match is 'Fish, haddock, smoked', which is the same food in its smoked state. Guideline F states that plain vs smoked is a different state and not substitutable, but here the ingredient itself asks for the smoked version, so the matching smoked entry is the correct match (analogous to the rule that when the ingredient asks for the modified version, the matching entry is yes). Quantity (500g) is ignored. Smoked haddock is the same species and product as the USDA entry, with no added flavour or different cut. Cooking method is unchanged, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain tomato juice with no sodium qualifier. The USDA match is specifically 'Tomato juice, 100%, low sodium', a modified version. Guideline D says a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced/low sodium version is not substitutable, and the recipe does not ask for low sodium. Condition 2 also likely fails: the salt content of tomato juice is a taste component, so a diner could notice the lower-salt product. Condition 1 holds, since the juice could be used in the same way, but condition 2 does not, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is Spam specifically described as smoked, and sliced. Slicing is handling and does not change the match. The USDA entry is plain "Spam", which is the standard unsmoked luncheon meat. Under guideline F, plain versus smoked is a different state, not a same-food name variant. Smoking changes the flavour noticeably, so a diner would taste the difference. Guideline D also applies: when the ingredient asks for a modified version, only the matching modified entry qualifies, and this plain entry does not. Condition 2 therefore fails because taste would differ. Condition 1 is also questionable, since the smoked character is part of what the dish relies on.

The ingredient is 'artichoke dip' (the weight is ignored). The USDA match is 'Spinach and artichoke dip', which is a distinct product: it contains spinach as a major component in addition to artichoke. Under guideline B, this is not the same food under another name; it is a flavoured or component-modified variant of artichoke dip. Condition 1 is arguably met since it could be served in the same way, but condition 2 fails: a diner would taste the spinach and notice a difference in flavour, texture (spinach leaf pieces), and appearance (green flecks). Because the match adds a component the plain ingredient does not have, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a fresh artichoke, which by default means the globe artichoke (Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus), a flower bud. The USDA entry is Jerusalem artichoke (Helianthus tuberosus), a sunflower-family tuber. These are botanically and culinarily different foods, not regional or trade names for the same item (guideline B does not apply). Condition 1 fails: a cook would not prepare a tuber the same way as a flower bud, since the Jerusalem artichoke is typically peeled and treated as a root vegetable. Condition 2 fails: the taste (nutty, sweet, starchy vs. vegetal and slightly bitter), texture, and appearance differ, and a diner would notice. The weight is ignored per guideline A. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain jackfruit, with the leading 55g treated as decoration per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Jackfruit, raw' is the same food in its default uncooked form, which is the standard version a shopper would buy under the plain name (guidelines B and D). Nothing in the ingredient asks for a processed or modified form such as canned in brine or syrup, so no state change is implied. Condition 1: the raw fruit can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since any cooking the recipe applies is handled by the recipe itself. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference, because it is the same food in the same default state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is toasted raisin bread. The USDA entry 'Bread, raisin, enriched, toasted' is the same food (raisin bread) in the same state (toasted). The 'enriched' descriptor is the standard default for commercially sold raisin bread, not a modified version, so it does not count as a modification under guideline D. Condition 1: the match is already toasted, so it can replace the ingredient without any change to how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because both are toasted raisin bread of the same type. The quantity prefix is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain pork tenderloin, the standard default cut. The USDA match is a branded, peppercorn-flavoured pork tenderloin. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a flavoured version is not a match, and guideline G says a branded entry with an added flavour is also not a match. Condition 1 is not met: the flavoured product would be seasoned and likely pre-treated with added solution, so the cooking approach and expected result could change. Condition 2 is not met: a diner would taste pepper and other added flavouring and may see a peppercorn coating, which differs from plain pork tenderloin. The quantity (290g) is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is uncooked flatfish fillets. The USDA entry is 'Fish, flatfish (flounder and sole species), raw', which is the same food in raw form. Filleting is handling, not a change of state, and the 400g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the raw entry can replace raw fillets without changing the preparation, since the cooking method is the same. Condition 2: flounder and sole are the flatfish species normally sold as fillets, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain glutinous rice, a raw grain used as an ingredient. The USDA match is 'Cake made with glutinous rice', a finished baked or prepared dish containing rice along with other ingredients such as sugar, fat, eggs or flour. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B), and it is not a plain ingredient's standard version (guideline D). Substituting the cake would change the preparation entirely, since rice would have to be cooked or ground and combined with other components, and a diner would immediately notice a cake instead of rice in the dish (conditions 1 and 2 both fail). Quantity is irrelevant (guideline A).

The ingredient is 2% Greek yogurt with mixed berry flavour. The USDA entry is Greek yogurt, 2% fat, mixed berry blend, by Chobani. The leading 150g is ignored per guideline A. The product is the same food (Greek yogurt) with the same fat level (2%) and the same flavour (mixed berry), so it is the same product type under a brand name (guideline G). Flavoured yogurts are normally low fat (guideline D), and the ingredient itself asks for the 2% and mixed berry versions, so the matching entry is not a modification. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the dish with no change in preparation, since it is a yogurt used in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the fat level and flavour match. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is '200g ground veal'. The leading weight is ignored, so the question is whether ground veal matches 'Veal, ground, cooked, broiled'. Ground veal in a recipe is normally raw meat that will be cooked as part of the dish. The USDA entry is specifically cooked and broiled. Guideline F states that raw vs cooked is a different state and not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using pre-cooked, broiled veal would change how the dish is prepared, since it would not brown, bind, or cook through in the same way as raw meat. Condition 2 also fails: the cooked, broiled product differs in texture, colour, and flavour from raw ground veal as it appears in the finished dish. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is oaxaca cheese, shredded: a Mexican pulled-style cheese that is a semi-hard, stringy, melting cheese. The USDA match 'Head cheese' is a cold-cut/meat loaf product made from pork head meat and gelatinous stock, set in aspic and sliced. It is not a dairy cheese at all. Condition 1 fails: it cannot be used in place of shredded melting cheese without changing the dish entirely (it would not melt, would not string, and would add a meat product). Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance. Quantity and naming are irrelevant. Not the same food under another name, so not substitutable.

The ingredient is cube steak that has been breaded, so it includes a flour-and-crumb coating. The USDA entry 'Beef, steak, cube' is plain beef cube steak with no breading. Condition 1 fails: using the plain cut would skip the breading step, so the dish would be prepared differently (the coating would not be applied, and any breaded-frying or breading-dependent cooking would change). Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the missing crispy coating, which changes texture and appearance. The weight is decoration and is ignored. The beef cut itself matches, but the breading is a modification that changes preparation, texture and appearance, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a prepared salsa, a mixed dish made from pitanga and mango, and likely other components such as onion, herbs, and seasoning. The USDA match is only 'Pitanga (surinam-cherry), raw', a single raw fruit. Substituting it would omit the mango and the other salsa components, which changes the flavour, texture, and appearance of the dish. Under guideline F, a single ingredient is not substitutable for a blend or product that contains it. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would not match, and condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the missing mango and the other salsa ingredients. The quantity (250g) is ignored per guideline A.

1) The ingredient is a beef bouillon cube, which is a compressed form of dehydrated beef bouillon. The USDA entry is beef broth or bouillon in dry powder form, the same product type in a looser form. 2) Condition 1: In most recipes the cube is dissolved in water or added to a liquid, and the powder can be dissolved the same way with the same preparation steps. No cooking method changes. 3) Condition 2: Once dissolved, the cube and the powder give the same beef-flavoured stock. Diners would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The leading 15g is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a mix of two cuts: pork leg meat and spareribs. The USDA entry covers only one cut, fresh pork leg (ham) shank half, separable lean and fat, raw. Condition 1 fails: swapping in leg-only meat would change the composition of the dish, since the spareribs (bone, higher fat, different texture when cooked) would be missing. Guideline F rejects different cuts of meat and single items versus blends containing them. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would likely notice the absence of rib meat and bone, and the texture and appearance of the cooked dish would differ. The quantity is ignored under guideline A. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is sheep milk. The USDA entry is Milk, whole, which is cow's milk by default. Guideline B covers regional or trade names for the same food, but sheep milk and cow's milk are different foods from different animals, not alternate names. Condition 1 can be met, since milk can replace milk in most preparations. Condition 2 fails: sheep milk has a richer, higher-fat and higher-protein composition, a distinctly stronger flavour, and a denser texture, and a diner would likely notice the difference in taste and mouthfeel. The entry is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is imitation crab, chopped. The USDA entry is 'Crustaceans, crab, alaska king, imitation, made from surimi', which describes the same product type: imitation crab made from surimi. The 'Alaska king' label is USDA's naming convention for imitation crab sticks and does not indicate a different product. Chopping is knife work the recipe performs and does not change the match (guideline C). The entry names the same product with the same components, so the match is the same food under the standard descriptor (guideline C). Cooking method is unchanged, and the imitation crab looks and tastes the same as the ingredient as sold. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried tarragon, an herb sold dried (a dried herb, whole leaf). The USDA match is 'Gravy, chicken, dry', which is a powdered or granulated gravy mix made from chicken flavouring, starch, salt, fat and seasonings. It is a different food entirely, not the same food under another name, and it is not a dried herb. Condition 1 fails: it cannot replace dried tarragon without changing the dish, since it would add chicken flavour, salt, starch and fat and would alter how the dish is prepared and seasoned. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice a chicken-gravy flavour and different texture and colour in place of tarragon. The quantity (580g) is ignored per guideline A. Under guideline F, a different state or product (a blend containing other ingredients rather than the single herb) is not substitutable.

The ingredient is goat cheese packed in oil, and the USDA entry 'Cheese, goat' is plain goat cheese with no packing medium. Condition 1: the cheese itself is the same food, but the ingredient is preserved in oil. Guideline F lists a different packing medium as a non-substitute, and the oil is a distinct component that changes how the cheese is handled and used (it is drained or drizzled, and the oil may carry herbs or garlic). Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the oil's richer, greasier mouthfeel and added flavour, and the surface appearance differs. Since the packing medium changes flavour, texture and appearance, the match fails condition 2 and is not substitutable.

The ingredient is generic smoked sausage, which is normally a standard pork and/or beef smoked sausage at regular fat content. The USDA entry is a turkey, pork, and beef blend that is specifically low fat. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a low-fat modified version is not substitutable. Under guideline F, a blend of meats is not the same as the single-meat product a shopper would expect. Condition 2 also fails: the lower fat content and the turkey in the blend would change the texture and mouthfeel, and a diner could notice. The smoking matches, but the fat modification and meat blend do not, so the match fails.

Malabar spinach (Basella alba) and New Zealand spinach (Tetragonia tetragonioides) are different plant species, not regional names for the same food. They differ in leaf shape and texture, and Malabar spinach typically has reddish stems that New Zealand spinach lacks, so appearance differs. Their flavour and mucilaginous texture also differ somewhat. The shared 'spinach' name is misleading. Because this is a different species with a different taste and appearance, it is not the same food under another name. Condition 1 might be met, since both are leafy greens cooked similarly, but condition 2 fails because a diner could notice a difference in taste, texture and appearance. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is baked cheese snack crackers, a generic description of the baked cheese snack cracker category that Cheez-It exemplifies. The USDA entry, Crackers, cheese (Cheez-It), is that same product type under a brand name. Guideline B treats same food under another name as a match, and guideline G accepts a branded entry of the same plain product type. Using Cheez-Its in place of generic baked cheese snack crackers would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The quantity (55g) is ignored per guideline A.

Condition 1: The ingredient is drained canned pineapple, so the syrup is removed before use. The USDA entry is 'heavy syrup pack, solids and liquids', which includes the syrup. Using it would add the liquid back, so the dish would not be prepared the same way. Condition 2: A diner would likely notice the difference. Heavy syrup is much sweeter and wetter than drained fruit, which changes taste, texture, and moisture. Guideline F rejects a different packing medium (syrup vs juice vs water), and the entry's 'solids and liquids' wording explicitly includes the syrup that the ingredient removes. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is canned refried beans, and the USDA entry is canned refried beans in the traditional style, so they are the same food. The weight (200g) and the optional status are not relevant to the match. Warming is handling that the recipe does itself and does not change the match. Condition 1: the beans can be used in place of the ingredient with the same preparation, since they are warmed the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because 'traditional style' simply describes the standard canned refried bean product a shopper would buy under that name. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried orange juice powder, a dehydrated product with almost no water. The USDA match is orange juice frozen concentrate, undiluted, which is a liquid-based product with substantial water content. Condition 1: the match cannot be used in place of the powder without changing preparation. Substituting a wet, undiluted concentrate for a dry powder changes the moisture balance of the recipe, so it would require adjusting liquids and possibly other ingredients. Condition 2: the change in form (dry powder vs thick, watery concentrate) would alter texture and likely appearance, and the concentration per gram differs substantially, so the flavour intensity would change as well. Guideline F explicitly lists a different state (dried vs. not) as not substitutable. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is rice bran oil, a refined cooking oil pressed from rice bran. The USDA entry 'Rice bran, crude' is the raw bran material itself, not the oil. Guideline F states that the raw plant or source is not substitutable for the processed ingredient. Crude bran is a solid, fibrous, nutty-tasting material that cannot be used as a cooking fat, so it would change how the dish is prepared (it cannot be poured or used to fry) and would alter texture and flavour. A diner would notice the difference. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is 150g pork sausage, and the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Pork sausage', which names the same food with no added modifier, state, or processing descriptor. Under guideline B and D, a plain ingredient mapped to the standard default version is a match. Pork sausage is cooked the same way regardless of the match, and a diner would not perceive a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same food. Both conditions are satisfied.

The ingredient is cooked bacon, crumbled. The USDA entry is pork bacon, smoked or cured, cooked, which is the same food in the same cooked state. Crumbling is knife or handling work and does not change the match (guideline C). Bacon is normally smoked or cured, so that descriptor describes the standard product rather than a modification (guideline D). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is already cooked and can be crumbled. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same standard cooked bacon.

The ingredient is passion fruit juice, a liquid processed from the fruit. The USDA entry 'Passion fruit, raw' is the whole fruit, including rind, seeds and pulp. Guideline F says the raw plant or source is not substitutable for the processed ingredient. Condition 1 fails: using whole raw fruit in place of juice changes the preparation, since the juice would have to be extracted, strained of seeds and measured by volume or weight. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice seeds, pulp and texture where the dish expects a smooth liquid. The 85g quantity is ignored under guideline A. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 125g of mashed potatoes made with milk (the weight is ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry is 'Potato, mashed, from fresh, made with milk', which is the same dish: mashed potatoes prepared with milk, made from fresh potatoes. Condition 1: the entry can directly replace the ingredient with no change to preparation, since the dish is already mashed and milk-based. Condition 2: a diner would not perceive a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the USDA product is the same food under a standard name. The 'from fresh' descriptor reflects the standard way mashed potatoes are made, not a modification such as dehydrated flakes or frozen product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dry gin, a juniper-flavoured spirit. 'Dry' describes the standard London dry style, which is the default type of gin sold under the plain name, so it is not a modification (guideline D). The USDA entry 'Gin' is the generic spirit, which for practical purposes is the same product. Condition 1: gin can be used in place of dry gin with no change to preparation, since it is measured and mixed the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the generic entry is essentially the dry style. The quantity (30g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

Powdered malt syrup is a dried, concentrated malt extract, made by evaporating barley malt liquid. It is sweet, mostly sugars (maltose), and dissolves readily. Barley malt flour is finely ground malted barley grain. It is a flour with starch and enzymes, and it is far less sweet. It is a different product, not the same food under another name. Condition 1: swapping flour for syrup would change the dish's preparation, since the sugar content and moisture behaviour differ and the flour adds bulk and starch that the syrup does not. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in sweetness, flavour intensity, and texture. The match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is red wine vinegar (95g, quantity ignored). The USDA match is 'Cucumber salad made with cucumber and vinegar', which is a prepared dish containing cucumber, vinegar, and likely other components such as sugar or oil, rather than the vinegar itself. Condition 1 fails: you cannot use a cucumber salad in place of an ingredient in a recipe without changing the preparation, since it adds a major food component (cucumber) and is a finished dish. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste cucumber and would notice a different food, and the flavour and texture would differ from red wine vinegar alone. The match is a different food rather than a naming variant of the same product, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain turkey breast. The USDA entry 'Turkey, light meat, skin eaten' does describe breast meat ('light meat'), so the cut is broadly the same. However, the entry specifies that the skin is eaten. Turkey breast is normally bought and used as skinless meat in a recipe like this, so the skin-on version is a modified form of the plain ingredient (guideline D). Condition 1: substituting skin-on meat would change preparation, since the skin renders fat, browns and crisps differently, and it may need trimming or a different cooking approach. Condition 2: a diner would notice the skin's added fat, chewier or crisper texture, darker appearance and richer flavour. Both conditions are therefore not met. The entry is not substitutable.

The ingredient is canned corned beef, drained. The USDA entry 'Beef, cured, corned beef, canned' names the same product: canned, cured corned beef. Weight is decoration (guideline A). 'Drained' is handling that does not change the match (guideline C). Canned corned beef is normally sold in this form, so no modification descriptor applies (guideline D).
