Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

Baobab powder is a dried, ground pulp from the baobab fruit, with a tart, citrusy, slightly sweet flavour and an off-white to beige colour. The USDA entry is a sweetened chocolate beverage mix, made mainly of sugar, cocoa and milk solids, with a brown colour and chocolate flavour. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B), and it is not a plain or modified version of it. Using it would change the flavour (chocolate instead of tart fruit) and the appearance, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 may hold in a loose sense that powder could be stirred in, but condition 2 clearly fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is sweetened pomegranate juice, a juice product. The USDA entry is a pomegranate juice beverage at 40-50% juice, labelled 'light'. Guideline D treats sweetened and reduced/light versions as modifications, so the entry is not the default version of the plain ingredient. Guideline F also treats a blend or diluted product as different from the single ingredient. A beverage that is only 40-50% juice, with added water and sweetener, has a visibly different concentration and flavour intensity from sweetened pomegranate juice. Dishes that rely on the juice for colour, tartness or body would change. A diner would likely notice the thinner, less intense flavour. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable taste or appearance difference) both fail.

The ingredient is Honeycrisp apples, sliced. The USDA entry is Apples, honeycrisp, with skin, raw. Condition 1: the match is the same variety in the same raw state. Slicing is knife work the recipe does itself and does not change the match (Guideline C). The ingredient does not ask for peeling, so the USDA 'with skin' descriptor is consistent with it. The entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: the diner would taste the same Honeycrisp apple, with the same texture and appearance (skin on, as sold). No flavour, texture or appearance difference is introduced. Both conditions are met.

Pearl couscous is a toasted or plain semolina wheat pasta formed into small, uniform spheres, usually cooked by simmering in water or broth until chewy. 'Bulgur, cooked' is parboiled, cracked whole wheat kernels with irregular, grainy pieces and a softer, nuttier profile. The two are different foods: one is a shaped pasta, the other a cracked whole grain. Condition 1 fails in part because the preparation differs (pasta is typically simmered and drained, while bulgur is usually soaked or steamed to absorb liquid). Condition 2 also fails because a diner would see round, smooth, uniform pearls versus irregular grains and would notice a difference in chew and taste. Guideline B does not apply, since this is not a regional name for the same food.

The ingredient is fresh bitter melon, which is uncooked produce that a recipe would prepare itself. The USDA match is specifically 'cooked, boiled, drained, without salt,' so it is already prepared. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Using pre-boiled bitter melon would change the preparation: the recipe would skip or alter the cooking step, and texture would be softer and more tender. Diners could also notice the difference in texture and bitterness. The food itself is the same (bitter melon), but the state differs, so condition 1 (no change to how the dish is prepared) fails. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste or texture) is also doubtful. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain cornbread, and the USDA entry is cornbread made from a home recipe, which is the same food with the standard default preparation. The 100g quantity is decoration and is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since no cooking method, knife work or handling is altered. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the entry describes ordinary cornbread with no added flavour, modification or different state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sea scallops that are already steamed, and the USDA entry is bay and sea scallops, cooked, steamed. Both name the same food in the same state. The leading '220g' is quantity and is ignored. Using the USDA entry would not change how the dish is prepared, since the scallops are already cooked. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the match is the same steamed product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried whole egg, and the USDA entry 'Egg, whole, dried' is the same product under a standard name, so it is the same food (guideline B). Quantity is ignored (guideline A). Dried whole egg is a plain, default form of whole egg, not a modified or flavoured version (guideline D). Condition 1: the dried egg can replace the ingredient without changing the preparation, since it is used in the same way as the USDA product. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food in the same form. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pumpkin seed kernels (pepitas), which are raw or toasted hulled seeds of Cucurbita pepo. The USDA match is 'Pimento, canned', which is a red sweet pepper (Capsicum annuum) preserved in liquid. These are different foods: one is a seed, the other is a pepper fruit. Condition 1 fails because pimento cannot replace pumpkin seeds in a dish without changing its preparation, since pimento is a soft, wet, canned pepper and pumpkin seeds are dry, crunchy kernels used for toasting, grinding, or sprinkling. Condition 2 fails because a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste (sweet, vegetal pepper versus nutty seed), texture, and appearance (green-ish kernels versus red pepper pieces). Not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply.

The ingredient is pure beef tallow, a single rendered animal fat used for frying. The USDA entry is a heavy-duty frying shortening that blends beef tallow with cottonseed oil, and it is a food-service product. Guideline F rules out a single ingredient matched to a blend containing it (lard -> Shortening, lard and vegetable oil = no) and rules out industrial or food-service specialty fats matched to the home ingredient. Condition 2 also fails: the cottonseed component and the processed shortening base would change the flavour, mouthfeel and browning of fried food compared with pure beef tallow, and a diner could notice. Condition 1 is therefore not fully met either, since a different fat blend changes the frying characteristics. The quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is boneless beef chuck short ribs, a plain cut with no fat specification, so the default is the standard retail cut, which includes the surrounding fat (separable lean and fat). The USDA entry is the same cut (beef chuck, short ribs, boneless) and is raw, so the cut and state match. However, the entry is specified as 'trimmed to 0" fat', which is a modified, fat-free version of the cut rather than the default. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced or fat-free modified version is not a match. Fat content also affects how braised or seared short ribs cook and taste (moisture, richness, tenderness), so a diner could notice the difference. Condition 2 is not reliably met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is top round steak, a specific beef cut from the round primal. The USDA entry is eye of round steak, a different cut from the same primal. Top round is a larger muscle with a different grain and tenderness, and it is often cooked differently. Guideline F says a different cut of meat is not substitutable, even when the cuts look close. The USDA entry also specifies 0" fat trim and separable lean-and-fat, which describes the eye of round, not the top round. Because the cut differs, a diner could notice a difference in texture and the dish's preparation could change. Condition 1 and condition 2 are not both met.

The ingredient is hard cider, and the USDA match is literally 'Hard cider', so they are the same food. The quantity (60g) and the 'optional' label are decoration and do not affect the match. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is used the same way (added as a liquid). Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is powdered milk, which is dry milk powder used as a plain dairy ingredient. The USDA entry 'Milk, dry, whole, without added vitamin D' is the same product type in its plain, unfortified form. Condition 1: powdered milk is typically used by dissolving or mixing into recipes, and the whole dry milk entry can be used in the same way without changing the preparation. Condition 2: the match is the same food with no added flavour, additives or modification. The fat level of a whole versus nonfat powder is a minor possible difference, but the guidelines treat plain ingredients as matching their standard default version (milk -> Milk, whole). The entry is therefore substitutable, though a nonfat dry milk product could be the default in some markets.

The ingredient is dried egg noodles, which are wheat flour pasta made with egg. The USDA entry is somen, a very thin Japanese wheat noodle made from flour and salt, typically without egg. This is a different product, not the same food under another name. Somen is also much thinner than standard egg noodles, so cooking time, texture (softer, more delicate), and appearance would change. A diner would likely notice the difference in taste and texture. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) both fail.

The ingredient is a pear (Pyrus, a pome fruit). The USDA match is prickly pear, which is the fruit of Opuntia, a cactus. These are different species in different plant families, not regional or culinary names for the same food. Prickly pear has a distinct flavour, seed-filled texture, and a different appearance (spiny skin, magenta or green flesh) from a pear. A diner would clearly notice the difference. The quantity (250g) is irrelevant. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a combination of butternut squash and sage, so the dish's flavour depends on both components. The USDA match covers only butternut squash (frozen, unprepared) and contains no sage. Using it in place of the ingredient would drop the sage, which changes the flavour, and a diner would notice the missing herb. Condition 2 therefore fails. The frozen state would be acceptable on its own under guideline E, since freezing does not usually show in cooked squash, but that does not rescue the missing component. Condition 1 also fails: the match cannot replace the ingredient without changing what goes into the dish. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is pickled salsify, a salsify preserved in a vinegar-based brine, which gives it a sour, tangy flavour and a firm, acidic texture. The USDA match is salsify that has been boiled, drained and salted. It has no vinegar or pickling, so it tastes mild and earthy and has a softer texture. Substituting it would change the flavour and texture, and a diner would notice the difference. Under guideline F, a different state or processing (pickled vs cooked and salted) is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because the dish's preparation and flavour would change, and condition 2 fails because the taste and texture differ. The weight of 2g is ignored.

The ingredient is quail meat, skinned and boned, raw. The USDA entry 'Quail, meat only, raw' is the same food: quail meat with skin and bone removed, uncooked. 'Game quail' is a trade name for the same bird, so it counts as the same food under guideline B. 'Skinned and boned' is knife work and handling that the recipe does itself, and 'meat only' already describes that state, so it does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are raw quail meat. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since the meat is the same. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is canned tangerines packed in juice, drained. The USDA entry is Tangerines (mandarin oranges), canned, juice pack, drained. Tangerines and mandarin oranges are the same food under two names (guideline B). The packing medium matches: the ingredient is 'in juice' and the USDA entry is 'juice pack', so there is no packing-medium mismatch (guideline F). Both are drained, so the liquid is removed in either case. The 200g quantity is ignored (guideline A). The food is canned, not raw, but the ingredient is already canned and the USDA entry describes that same product, so the state matches. In use, a diner would not taste or see a difference, and the preparation would not change. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is amaranth leaves, a leafy green from the Amaranthus genus with a mild, spinach-like flavour and a softer texture. The USDA entry is coriander (cilantro) leaves, from the Coriandrum sativum plant, which has a distinct citrusy, soapy-bitter flavour. Guideline B covers regional names for the same food, but these are different plants, not alternative names. Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste the difference between cilantro and amaranth greens, so the dish's flavour would change. Chopping does not alter the match (guideline C), but the species mismatch is decisive.

The ingredient is dried apples, a processed form of Malus domestica (apple). The USDA entry 'Sugar-apples, (sweetsop), raw' refers to Annona squamosa, a different fruit in a different genus and family. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and it is not a form, cut, or preparation of apple. Condition 1 fails: it cannot replace dried apples without changing the dish, since it is a fresh, raw, custardy tropical fruit rather than a dried apple. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste a distinctly different fruit with different flavour, texture and appearance. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain pork sausage, crumbled, which is a raw or to-be-cooked meat product that the recipe would brown or cook. The USDA match is a sausage product already prepared in a tomato-based sauce. Using it would change the dish's flavour (tomato sauce added), appearance (sauced, not browned crumbles), and cooking method (it is already cooked and would not brown in the same way). The diner would notice the tomato sauce. The match is a modified or different product, not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well.

The ingredient is a cinnamon-flavoured oat cluster cereal, with no brand or honey mentioned. The USDA entry is a specific branded product, POST HONEY BUNCHES OF OATS with cinnamon, which is formulated with honey and carries its own recipe and coating. Guideline G says a branded entry with an added flavour or modification does not match, and the honey component is an added ingredient not implied by the ingredient name. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the cereal could be poured and eaten or used in the same way. Condition 2 is not clearly met: the honey-sweetened, brand-specific clusters would likely taste and look different from a generic cinnamon oat cluster, and a diner could notice the change. Because the USDA product is a different formulation rather than the same food under another name, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is tinned pilchards in tomato sauce, drained. The USDA entry is canned sardine (Pacific) in tomato sauce, drained solids with bone. Guideline B treats regional or trade names for the same food as matches. Pilchards and sardines are the same small clupeid fish, and pilchard is the common trade name for canned sardines in many markets (the Pacific sardine, Sardinops sagax, is itself sold as pilchard in parts of the world). The packing medium matches (tomato sauce), the state matches (canned, drained solids), and the 'with bone' descriptor fits canned pilchards, whose bones are softened during canning and typically eaten. The leading 150g is ignored per guideline A. Taste, texture and appearance should be essentially indistinguishable in the dish, so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is ricotta cheese, a fresh soft Italian whey cheese with a moist, grainy, mildly sweet and milky flavour. The USDA match is 'Imitation cheese', which is a cheese analogue made from vegetable oils, casein or other proteins, starches and additives rather than dairy cheese. Condition 1: it is not the same food under another name; it is a different product type with different ingredients, and substituting it would change the flavour, melt and texture behaviour in a ricotta-based preparation. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference in taste and mouthfeel, since imitation cheese lacks ricotta's characteristic fresh dairy flavour and curd texture. Under guideline F (different product, not the same food) and the rule that a diner would notice a different food, the match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is generic store-bought salsa, a ready-to-eat tomato-and-chile condiment. The USDA entry 'Sauce, salsa, ready-to-serve' is the same product under a standard name: a ready-to-serve jarred or refrigerated salsa. The quantity prefix (10g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient directly, since both are used as-is with no change to cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same kind of product. Both conditions hold.

1) Ingredient: strawberry Greek yogurt, with no fat level specified. Match: Yogurt, Greek, strawberry, nonfat. 2) Same food: both are strawberry-flavored Greek yogurt, so the product type is identical. 3) Preparation: it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to cooking method or handling. 4) Modification check: the nonfat descriptor could look like a modification, but guideline D says flavoured yogurts are typically sold low fat, and nonfat strawberry Greek yogurt is a normal retail version a shopper would buy under this name. The fat difference is a minor texture variation within the normal range for this product, not a different food. 5) Taste and appearance: strawberry flavour, colour and Greek tang are the same, so a diner would not reliably notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Pekin duck breast, raw, which is a cut of meat from the duck. The USDA match is 'Egg, duck, whole, fresh, raw', which is a duck egg. These are different foods entirely: one is muscle meat from the bird, the other is an egg. Guideline F explicitly rejects different cuts of meat and different source-versus-product distinctions, and this is an even larger difference (meat versus egg). Using a duck egg in place of duck breast would change the dish's preparation, texture, flavour and appearance, and a diner would immediately notice. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried watermelon seed kernels, and the USDA entry is 'Seeds, watermelon seed kernels, dried'. These are the same food under the same state (dried kernels), so the match is literal. Condition 1: the kernels can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since the same dried kernels are used. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. The 15g weight is decoration and is ignored. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is toasted marble rye bread. The USDA entry is 'Bread, marble rye and pumpernickel, toasted', which matches on preparation state (both toasted), so cooking method is not the issue. The problem is identity. The USDA entry is a combined entry covering two different breads, marble rye and pumpernickel, and does not describe marble rye alone. Pumpernickel is a sibling bread with a darker colour, a denser texture and a sweeter, more intense flavour. Under guideline F, a blend or product containing the ingredient, and a sibling variety with a different taste, are not substitutable. A diner could notice a difference in appearance and taste if the bread were pumpernickel-influenced rather than pure marble rye. Condition 2 is therefore not met.

The ingredient is canned black olives, drained. Canned black olives are commercially sold as canned ripe olives, so the USDA entry 'Olives, ripe, canned' names the same food in the same state. 'Drained' is handling the recipe does itself and does not change the match. The '(small-extra large)' descriptor is a standard size grade for how canned ripe olives are sold, not a flavour, packing, or processing modification. The leading '30g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the olives could be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same canned ripe olive. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned quail eggs, drained. The USDA entry 'Quail egg, canned' is the same food in the same state (canned), and the same product a shopper would buy under that name. 'Drained' is handling that does not change the match, and the weight is decoration. Condition 1: the canned quail eggs can be used directly in place of the USDA product without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same canned product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain pan dulce, meaning the standard version without added toppings. The USDA entry is pan dulce with a sugar topping. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version is not substitutable. The sugar topping is a visible, tasteable addition: a diner would see the crackly sugar crust and taste the sweetness, and it changes the appearance and texture of the bread. Condition 2 therefore fails. The dish's preparation may not change, but the diner would notice a different product, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is smoked sablefish, and the USDA entry is 'Fish, sablefish, smoked', which is the same food in the same state (smoked). The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Smoking is the defining state of the ingredient, so the match preserves it rather than changing it. Using the USDA product would not alter the cooking method, since smoked fish is served as is, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Melba rounds are thin, crisp, toasted bread rounds, and Melba toast is the same product, a thin, crisp, toasted bread slice. The difference is mainly the name and shape of the piece, not the food itself. Under guideline B, a regional or trade name for the same food counts as a match. Both are plain, standard, ready-to-serve versions with no added flavour, modification or different state. The same texture and taste carry over, and the dish is prepared the same way. The shape difference is minor for a crisp cracker-style base and does not change how the dish is made. The quantity is ignored under guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain bacon, which a shopper would normally buy as standard cured pork bacon. The USDA entry is 'Pork bacon, smoked or cured, reduced sodium, cooked'. Guideline D treats 'reduced sodium' as a modification, so a plain ingredient matched to a reduced-sodium version is not substitutable. Reduced sodium also lowers the saltiness, which a diner would taste, so condition 2 fails. The entry is also cooked, while bacon is normally used raw and cooked within the recipe, so it would change the preparation and the texture, which fails condition 1. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is fresh diced shallot, a raw bulb that is chopped at home. The USDA match is 'Shallots, freeze-dried', a processed product in which the shallot has been dehydrated. Under condition 1, freeze-dried shallot would not be used in place of fresh diced shallot without changing preparation: it must be rehydrated or added directly to a dish, which alters how it is handled and cooked, and it does not sauté or soften like fresh shallot. Under condition 2, a diner would notice the difference: freeze-dried pieces have a crisp, brittle, porous texture and a more concentrated, different flavour, while fresh shallot is moist, pungent and sweet when cooked. Per guideline F, fresh versus dried is a different state, so this is not a match. Knife work (dicing) does not change the match, but the freeze-drying does.

The ingredient is melted butterfat, which is the fat fraction of butter (milkfat). USDA 'Butter oil, anhydrous' is anhydrous milkfat, so it is essentially the same food under a different name (guideline B). Condition 1: it is a liquid fat that can be used in the same way as melted butterfat, with no change to the cooking method. Condition 2: anhydrous butter oil is standard, unbrowned milkfat with a mild butter flavour, so a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. The main caveat is that a browned or ghee-style product would differ, but the match is the plain anhydrous fat, which is what 'melted butterfat' describes. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is millet flour, a raw, ground form of the grain used as a dry ingredient in baking or batters. The USDA match is 'Millet, cooked', which is the whole grain after it has been boiled, so it is a different state (cooked vs raw) and a different form (whole grain vs ground flour). Using cooked millet in place of millet flour would change how the dish is prepared: it cannot be milled into flour, and it would not provide the dry, powdery structure a flour does in baking or thickening. A diner would notice a difference in texture and appearance, such as grainy pieces instead of a smooth batter or dough. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 also fails. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh (raw) pork tongue, which the recipe would prepare itself. The USDA entry is specifically 'cooked, braised', so it is a different state: raw versus cooked is explicitly listed as not substitutable. Using pre-braised tongue would also change the dish's preparation, since the recipe's own cooking step would be skipped or altered. A diner would likely notice the difference in texture and appearance from braised versus fresh tongue cooked as the recipe directs. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 is doubtful for the same reasons. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw pork heart, which the recipe will presumably cook as part of the dish. The USDA match is specifically 'cooked, braised' pork heart. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: substituting pre-braised meat would change the preparation, since the cook would have to skip or alter the cooking step, and the dish's method would change. Condition 2 also fails: braised heart has a different texture, colour and flavour from raw heart, and a diner could notice. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a plain beef stock cube, the standard default product. The USDA entry is bouillon cubes and granules specifically labeled 'low sodium', which is a modified version of the plain product. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a reduced-sodium version is not substitutable. The sodium reduction would also change the salt level and so the flavour of the dish, which a diner could notice. The entry also does not specify beef flavour, so it may not even be the same flavour profile. Condition 2 is not met, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is grapeseed oil, a fat used for cooking, frying, or dressings. The USDA match is grape juice, 100%, a fruit beverage. Condition 1: grape juice cannot replace an oil; it is aqueous, contains sugar, and would change the cooking method (it would steam or scorch rather than fry or coat) and the dish's preparation. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice a sweet, fruity, watery liquid in place of a neutral oil, changing taste, texture (no fat, so no richness or sheen), and appearance. Guideline F also rules out a different oil or fat, and grape juice is a different food entirely from grapeseed oil. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is a generic 'fruit yogurt' with no fat specification. The USDA match is 'Yogurt, nonfat milk, fruit', which is the same food (fruit-flavoured yogurt) with a fat-level descriptor. Guideline D says flavoured yogurts are typically low fat, so a fat descriptor on a fruit yogurt describes how the product is normally sold rather than a modification, and 'strawberry yogurt -> Yogurt, strawberry, low fat = yes' is the parallel case. Nonfat is a common retail version of fruit yogurt. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the same way, with no change to preparation, since it is eaten or mixed as yogurt. Condition 2: a diner would not reasonably notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance for an ordinary fruit yogurt, because the fat level is within the range shoppers normally buy under this name. Both conditions are met.

Condition 1: The ingredient is 100g of corn oil used for frying. The USDA entry is 80% fat stick margarine, which is a water-in-oil emulsion containing corn and soybean oils blended with water, salt, and likely milk solids or emulsifiers. Frying in margarine would change the cooking method: it has a lower smoke point, the water content causes spattering, and the milk solids brown and burn. Condition 1 fails. Condition 2: Margarine would impart a buttery or dairy flavour, change browning, and leave a different mouthfeel on fried food. A diner would likely notice. Guideline F applies: a single oil versus a blended, processed product containing it is not a match. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is dried pasilla pepper (the dried chilaca), a dark, wrinkled chile with a raisin-like, mildly smoky, cocoa-and-berry flavour and moderate heat. The USDA match is dried ancho, which is the dried poblano: sweeter, fruitier, milder, and with a different colour and texture. They are different chile varieties, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F says sibling varieties with a different taste are not substitutable. Condition 1 can be argued, since the chiles are both dried and could be rehydrated and blended in the same way. Condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice the difference in flavour and colour in a dish such as a mole or adobo sauce. The weight of 5g is irrelevant under guideline A. Because the taste differs, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried cranberry powder, a finely ground form of dried cranberries. The USDA entry is whole dried cranberries (sweetened, chewy pieces). Condition 1: using whole dried cranberries in place of a powder would change preparation. The fruit would need grinding, and it would not blend or disperse the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. A powder gives a fine, uniform, dusty or smooth texture and an even colour, while dried berry pieces are chewy and visibly distinct. Guideline F treats a different state of the same food (whole vs ground) as not substitutable, and the ground-at-home exception in guideline C applies only to meat and fish. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

Step 1: The ingredient is lemon-flavoured Greek yogurt, with no stated fat level. The USDA entry is Greek yogurt, nonfat, lemon blend, a branded product. The lemon flavour matches. Step 2: Guideline G says a branded entry of the same plain product type matches, and this is a lemon-flavoured product, not an added modification. Step 3: Guideline D says flavoured yogurts are typically low fat, so a fat-level descriptor describing how the product is normally sold is not a modification. Nonfat is within that low-fat range, so it does not alter the product a shopper would expect under this name. Step 4: Cooking method is unchanged, as a yogurt is used the same way. Taste, texture and appearance would be essentially the same: Greek style, lemon flavour, and a typical nonfat yogurt texture. A diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is generic 'hot sauce', which is most often a vinegar-based pepper sauce such as Tabasco-style. The USDA entry is 'Sauce, hot chile, sriracha', a specific variety that is thicker, sweeter, and garlicky, and it is made with sugar and garlic. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F rejects a sibling variety with a different taste. Substituting it would change the flavour and texture of the dish, and a diner would likely notice. Condition 2 fails. The 50g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is whole wheat sandwich bread, a standard commercial loaf. The USDA entry 'Bread, whole-wheat, commercially prepared' names the same food: whole wheat bread as sold in stores. Calling it 'sandwich bread' is a common name for the same product, not a modified version. Slicing or handling does not change the match (guideline C). The entry is the default commercial version, not a reduced, flavoured or specialty variant (guideline D). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is runny camembert, a soft-ripened cheese with a specific mild, earthy flavour and a creamy, spreadable-to-runny texture. The USDA entry 'Cheese sauce' is a processed product, typically made from cheese with milk, emulsifiers, starches or flour, and sometimes colourings. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1: swapping in cheese sauce would change preparation, since a whole runny cheese is cut, baked or spread in a way a sauce cannot be. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in flavour (processed, milder, less complex), texture (smooth and uniform rather than a rind-enclosed, bloomy, runny interior) and appearance (no rind, different form). Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable. The quantity (75g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is an unbranded 'honey clusters cereal with almonds', a honey-sweetened clustered cereal with almonds. The USDA entry is POST Honey Bunches of Oats with almonds, a branded product of the same type: a honey-coated clustered cereal with almonds. Guideline G treats a branded entry of the same plain product type as a match, and the ingredient does not specify a brand. Condition 1 holds because it can be used directly as a ready-to-eat cereal with no change to preparation. Condition 2 is a closer call, since different cereal brands can differ slightly in cluster size and sweetness. Applying guideline G, the same-type branded product counts as a match, so both conditions are judged to hold.

The ingredient is nonfat strawberry Greek yogurt. The USDA entry is Greek yogurt, nonfat, fruit on bottom, strawberry, by Chobani, which is the same product. Condition 1: the nonfat and strawberry descriptors match what the ingredient asks for, and 'fruit on bottom' is simply how strawberry Greek yogurt is normally sold, so the yogurt can be used directly without changing preparation. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. The brand name does not change the product type (guideline G). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the product is the same nonfat strawberry Greek yogurt. Both conditions are met.

1. Identity: The ingredient is chicken liver pate and the USDA entry is pate made from chicken liver. The food, its main components and its product type are the same, so this is the same food under a matching name. The quantity (250g) is ignored per guideline A.
2. Condition 1 (preparation): Pate is served as is, spread or sliced, with no cooking. Using the canned version requires no change to how the dish is prepared.
3. Condition 2 (diner perception): Canned chicken liver pate is a shelf-stable form of the same spread. Taste, texture and appearance are close enough that a diner would not reliably notice a difference. Pate is commonly sold in tins, so 'canned' describes a normal way of buying it, not a modification (guideline D).
4. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dry egg pasta, which is essentially dried egg noodles. The USDA entry 'Noodles, egg, dry, unenriched' is the same food: dry egg noodles made with egg and wheat flour. The leading '65g' is quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the dish is prepared the same way, since dry egg pasta is boiled or otherwise cooked like dry egg noodles, with no change in method. Condition 2: 'unenriched' means vitamins and minerals were not added back to the flour. That affects nutrition labelling, not taste, texture or appearance, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is plain shredded muenster cheese, which means the standard full-fat product. The USDA match is 'Cheese, Muenster, reduced fat', a modified version with lower fat content. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a reduced-fat version is not substitutable, and the recipe does not ask for reduced fat. Condition 1 is therefore not met as a like-for-like swap. Condition 2 also fails: reduced-fat cheese typically melts differently, has a firmer or drier texture, and a different flavour intensity, so a diner could notice the difference. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is fresh Dungeness crab meat. Retail fresh Dungeness crab meat is normally sold already cooked, picked from the shell, so the default form is cooked rather than raw. The USDA entry is the same food, Dungeness crab, in its cooked state. The 'moist heat' descriptor reflects the usual way Dungeness is cooked (boiling or steaming), not a modification. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since the meat is already cooked and needs no further cooking step. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because cooked Dungeness meat prepared by boiling or steaming is the standard product. The quantity (300g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is fresh spearmint leaves, an aromatic herb with a strong minty, menthol flavour. The USDA match is cos or romaine lettuce, raw, a mild leafy green with a crisp, watery texture and essentially no mint flavour. Condition 1: lettuce is not a culinary substitute for mint in a recipe; using it would change the dish's preparation intent, since the herb is the flavouring component. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the absence of mint flavour and aroma, and the appearance of the leaves differs in shape and colour. It is a different food, not a regional name or cut of the same plant, so guideline B does not apply. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is fresh horseradish root, grated. The USDA entry 'Horseradish' is the generic root entry with no processing state, so it is the same food. Grating is knife or handling work and does not change the match (guideline C). Per guideline E, an entry that names only the food matches fresh or plain versions. The entry does not name a prepared or jarred product such as creamed horseradish with vinegar, so no modified version is being matched. Quantity is ignored (guideline A). Preparation, flavour, texture and appearance are the same, so both conditions hold.

The ingredient is wild goose breast, and the USDA match is domesticated duck, meat only, raw. These are different species. Wild goose is a game bird with darker, gamier, more intense meat and a different fat profile and texture from domesticated duck. Condition 1 can be argued for a generic roast, but the match is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Condition 2 fails because a diner would likely notice the stronger flavour and the difference in texture and colour. Guideline F rejects near-identical items that differ in taste, and species differences of this kind qualify. Neither condition is clearly met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is long-grain rice listed by weight with no cooking state, so it is the dry grain as bought. The USDA match is 'Rice, white, long-grain, regular, enriched, cooked', which is the cooked product. Guideline F says raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Using cooked rice in place of dry rice would change how the dish is prepared (the rice would need cooking or would be absorbed differently), and the diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance. Condition 1 fails, and so does condition 2. The variety and type (long-grain white) match, but the state does not, so the match is rejected.

The ingredient is chicken hearts, a raw poultry offal product. The USDA match is 'Cereals ready-to-eat, QUAKER WHOLE HEARTS oat cereal', a breakfast cereal made from oats. These are entirely different foods: one is animal meat/offal, the other is a processed grain product. Condition 1 fails: chicken hearts cannot be used in place of oat cereal without changing how the dish is prepared (it would need to be cooked as meat, not as a cereal). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. The brand name 'Hearts' is a coincidental lexical overlap and does not make the foods the same. Guideline B (same food under another name) does not apply, and guideline F (different source/state) confirms rejection.

The ingredient is cashew oil, a pressed fat extracted from cashew nuts. The USDA match is 'Cashews, salted', which is the whole nut, roasted or raw, with added salt. These are different foods, not the same food under another name. Cashew oil is a liquid fat, while salted cashews are a solid nut snack. Using the nuts in place of the oil would change the dish's preparation (they cannot be poured or used as a cooking fat), its texture (solid pieces instead of liquid fat), and its flavour (added salt, and the nut itself rather than the extracted oil). A diner would notice the difference. Under guideline F, a different state of the source (oil versus the processed whole nut) is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is smoked goose liver pate. The USDA entry is 'Pate de foie gras, canned (goose liver pate), smoked', which names the same food: goose liver pate, smoked. Condition 1: the ingredient asks for the smoked version, so the smoked USDA entry matches it rather than being a modified substitute (guideline D). Pate is commonly sold canned or in similar packs, so 'canned' describes the normal packaging and does not change how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not be able to distinguish the taste, texture or appearance of a commercial smoked goose liver pate from this entry, since it is the same product type. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is ripe bananas, chopped. The USDA match is Bananas, overripe, raw. Condition 1 is about whether the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Chopping is handling the recipe does itself and does not change the match, but the match is a different ripeness stage. Condition 2 is about whether a diner would notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Overripe bananas are noticeably softer, sweeter, and browner than ripe bananas, and guideline F explicitly lists ripe vs overripe as not substitutable. Because the ripeness differs, a diner could notice the difference in flavour, sweetness, and appearance. Condition 2 is not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is frozen peas and carrots, an uncooked frozen vegetable mix that the recipe would normally cook or add in its frozen state. Guideline E treats frozen peas as matching the raw/fresh entry when freezing doesn't show and the food is normally cooked. The USDA match is 'cooked, boiled, drained, without salt', which is a different state. Guideline F explicitly lists raw vs cooked as not substitutable. Using a pre-boiled, drained product would change the preparation: the cook would no longer add the vegetables to the dish raw or frozen and cook them in it, and the texture would be softer and more uniform. Because the USDA entry describes a cooked state the ingredient does not have, the two conditions are not both met.

1. The ingredient is fresh luffa, the edible young fruit of the luffa gourd family (Luffa spp.), used as a vegetable in East and Southeast Asian cooking. 2. The USDA entry 'Gourd, dishcloth (towelgourd), raw' describes Luffa aegyptiaca, the same genus and a common edible luffa, also sold under the name towel gourd. 3. Under guideline B, a regional or trade name for the same food counts as a match, so this is the same food under another name. 4. The entry is raw, matching fresh produce; the recipe's own handling (peeling, cutting) does not change the match. 5. Cooking method is unchanged because both are prepared the same way as a raw gourd vegetable. 6. Taste, texture and appearance are expected to be the same because they are the same species; any cultivar variation is not a difference a diner would reliably detect in the dish. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried French lentils, a dried legume sold as lentils. The USDA entry 'Lentils, dry' is the generic dried lentil as bought, which matches the guideline that 'dry' legumes are the dried product itself. French (Puy-style) lentils are a variety of lentil rather than a different food, and the USDA entry names no specific variety, so it is the generic food. Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient with the same preparation (soaking or simmering, no change to method). Condition 2: the USDA entry does not specify a variety, so it does not assert a taste or texture that a diner would notice as different. A strict reader might argue Puy lentils differ from generic brown lentils, but the guidelines treat an unspecified generic entry as covering the food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain full-fat provolone, the standard default version of this cheese. The USDA match is 'Cheese, provolone, reduced fat', a modified lower-fat version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced-fat entry is not a match. The ingredient explicitly asks for full-fat, so the reduced-fat entry is the wrong version. Condition 2 also fails: reduced-fat provolone melts differently, is drier and firmer, and has a blander, less rich flavour, so a diner could notice the difference. Quantity is irrelevant. Condition 1 might pass in terms of preparation, but condition 2 does not, so the match is not substitutable.

Dancy is a named variety of tangerine, so the ingredient is literally a tangerine. The USDA entry 'Tangerine, raw' is the generic food with no variety or state specified, which guideline E treats as matching any fresh version of the food. Guideline F rejects sibling varieties with clearly different tastes (navel vs blood orange), but that applies when the USDA entry names a specific different variety. Here the USDA entry is the generic fruit, so it covers Dancy. Preparation is unchanged (raw, eaten as fruit), and a diner would not reasonably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance beyond normal tangerine variation. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'fresh whelks', which is the raw, uncooked mollusk as bought. The USDA match is 'Mollusks, whelk, unspecified, cooked, moist heat', which is a cooked product. Guideline F explicitly lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because the cooked entry would change how the dish is prepared: the recipe would need the whelks cooked at the point of use, or the dish's cooking sequence would change. Condition 2 also fails because cooked whelk differs in texture, firmness, and appearance from fresh raw whelk, and a diner could notice. The leading weight of 230g is ignored, and the species itself (whelk) matches, so the rejection rests only on the cooked state.

The ingredient is frog legs (200g; weight ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry is 'Frog legs', which names the same food with no state descriptor (no cooked/raw, frozen, or processing qualifier). Per guideline B and E, a USDA entry that names only the food with no state matches the generic food. Condition 1: frog legs could be used in place of frog legs without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried prunes, which are dried plums. The USDA entry 'Prune, dried' is the same food under a trade name, so it counts as literally the same product (guideline B). The quantity prefix '30g' is ignored (guideline A). Both are the dried form as bought, so no change of state applies. Using 'Prune, dried' would not change the preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Soy pulp is the same food as okara. Okara is the Japanese name for the fibrous pulp left after soy milk is made, and 'soy pulp' is its common English name. Under guideline B, same food under another name counts as a match. The USDA entry names the plain product with no added flavour, modification or cooking state, so it is the default version. Using okara in place of soy pulp does not change the preparation, and a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference because the two are the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is beef tallow, rendered beef fat. The USDA entry 'Fat, beef tallow' is the same food under a slightly different name. The weight (75g) is ignored per guideline A. Tallow is a single ingredient, not a blend, and the entry names no modified state such as hydrogenated or flavoured. Substituting it would not change the cooking method, flavour, texture, or appearance, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is bread and butter pickles, a sweet cucumber pickle. The USDA entry 'Pickles, cucumber, sweet' explicitly states that it includes bread and butter pickles, so it is the same food under the same name. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient, since both are pickled cucumbers used in the same form with no change to preparation. Condition 2: the sweet pickle entry covers bread and butter pickles, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The weight (15g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

Bottle gourd (Lagenaria siceraria) is the same vegetable as the white-flowered calabash gourd; 'bottle gourd' and 'calabash' are regional or culinary names for one food (guideline B). The USDA entry is 'raw', which matches a fresh ingredient, and the 30g quantity is ignored (guideline A). The match is the same food in the same state, so it could be substituted without changing preparation, taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions hold.

Gobo is the Japanese name for burdock root, so 'Burdock root, raw' is the same food under a regional or culinary name (guideline B). The USDA entry is raw, which is the state in which gobo is normally bought. Any cutting, shredding or peeling the recipe applies does not change the match (guideline C). The quantity is ignored (guideline A). Burdock root is sold fresh and is cooked or prepared in the same way as the USDA item, so the cooking method, flavour, texture and appearance are unchanged. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is lemon-infused vodka, a flavoured spirit: vodka with added lemon flavour. The USDA match is plain Vodka. Condition 1: Vodka could technically be used in the same preparation method (it is a liquid poured into a dish), so the method is unchanged. Condition 2: A diner would taste the difference. Lemon infusion adds a distinct citrus flavour and aroma, which is a flavour change. Per guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a flavoured/modified version is not substitutable, and guideline F treats a product with added flavouring as different from the base. Plain vodka would change the flavour of the dish, so condition 2 fails. The quantity (175g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is millet flour, a ground, processed form of millet. The USDA match is 'Millet, whole grain', the intact raw seed. Guideline F lists 'the raw plant/source vs the processed ingredient (cornstarch vs corn)' and 'whole vs ground' as not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: whole grain cannot replace flour without grinding it first, which changes how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 also fails: whole grains would give a visibly different texture and appearance in batters, doughs or baked goods. The match is not the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

Condition 1: The ingredient is imitation crab meat and the USDA entry is 'Imitation crab meat'. They are the same product, so it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to how the dish is prepared. The leading '300g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Condition 2: Since it is the same food, a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is blue cheese, crumbled. The USDA entry 'Cheese, Blue or Roquefort' is the same food under a standard name. Crumbling is knife or hand handling and does not change the match (guideline C). The quantity is decoration (guideline A). The entry is the plain default version, not a reduced-fat or modified product (guideline D). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since crumbled blue cheese is used directly in the dish. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cheese.

Fresh okara is the wet, moist soybean pulp left over from making soymilk or tofu. Soy flour, full-fat, raw is dry, finely ground whole soybean powder. These are different products in different states (fresh and wet versus dry and powdered). Using soy flour would change the dish's moisture, binding, and texture, since flour absorbs liquid and behaves differently from okara's crumbly, fibrous pulp. The flavour also differs, because raw soy flour tastes more beany and is denser. The cooking method would need adjusting, for example by adding liquid, so condition 1 fails. A diner would likely notice the different texture and mouthfeel, so condition 2 fails. This is a different state of the food, not the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 40g tempeh; the quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA match is simply 'Tempeh', which is the same food with no modifier, state, or processing descriptor. Tempeh is a fermented soybean cake; the plain USDA entry corresponds to the standard default product a shopper would buy under the name 'tempeh'. Using it in place of the ingredient requires no change in preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Condition 1: The ingredient is dragon fruit that was frozen and then thawed. The USDA entry 'Dragon fruit' names only the food, with no state (not frozen, dried, or canned), so under guideline E it is the generic food and matches fresh, thawed, or plain versions. Using it in place of thawed dragon fruit does not change how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: Thawed dragon fruit can be slightly softer and juicier than fresh, but the same flesh, flavour, and appearance remain. Guideline E treats the generic entry as matching thawed versions, so this difference is not one a diner would be expected to notice as a different food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'ground venison', a raw meat that the recipe will cook itself. The USDA match is 'Game meat, deer, ground, cooked, pan-broiled', which is already cooked and pan-broiled. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Using pre-cooked, pan-broiled meat would change how the dish is prepared (the meat would not brown or cook in the recipe) and could change texture and appearance. The quantity is ignored, and the species and cut are the same, but the state differs. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is sourdough bread, a yeasted, sour-fermented loaf that is baked and eaten as bread. The USDA match is 'Soup, tortilla', a prepared soup product made from tortilla pieces in a broth, which is a different food altogether. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B), so there is no identity match. Condition 1 fails: a soup product cannot stand in for bread without changing how the dish is prepared (it is not a baked, sliceable, or crumbable bread, and it would introduce broth and liquid). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste (no sourdough tang, different flavour profile), texture (soft or crisp tortilla pieces in liquid versus crumb and crust), and appearance. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is saffron, the dried stigmas of Crocus sativus, a distinct spice with a characteristic flavour, aroma, and vivid colour. The USDA match is turmeric, ground, which comes from the rhizome of Curcuma longa. These are different plant sources, not names for the same food, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1: turmeric could be used in cooking, but it is not a stand-in for saffron in preparation terms without changing the dish. Condition 2: saffron's floral, honey-like taste and its golden-orange colour differ from turmeric's earthy, bitter flavour and more yellow-orange tint; a diner would notice the difference in taste. Guideline F explicitly distinguishes different spices and states. Both conditions are therefore not met.

The ingredient is Oaxaca cheese, a Mexican semi-soft string cheese. The USDA entry 'Cheese, oaxaca, solid' is the same food under the same name, so the identity condition is met (guideline B). The ingredient is 500g, and the weight is ignored (guideline A). The ingredient is frozen and then thawed. Guideline E says frozen cheese for cooking matches the standard entry when freezing does not show, and this cheese is normally melted or mixed in cooking. The USDA entry has no frozen state, so it matches the thawed product. 'Solid' describes the normal form of the cheese and is not a modification (guideline D). Condition 1: the cheese can replace the ingredient without changing the preparation. Condition 2: once cooked, a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is blackcurrant, which is Ribes nigrum, the same species as the USDA entry 'Currants, european black, raw'. This is the same food under a regional name (guideline B). The weight '60g' is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). The USDA entry is raw, and the ingredient is a plain fresh fruit, so the raw match is the default version (guidelines C and D). Condition 1 holds: the fruit can be used in place of blackcurrant without changing preparation. Condition 2 holds: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same fruit.

The ingredient is beef heart, sliced, which is an animal organ meat (beef, heart). The USDA match is hearts of palm, raw, which is the edible shoot/core of palm trees, a plant vegetable. These are not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: beef heart would be cooked as meat (searing, braising, grilling), whereas hearts of palm is a plant product served raw or lightly cooked, so the preparation would change. Condition 2 fails: a diner would readily notice the difference in taste, texture (dense muscle versus crisp, fibrous palm), and appearance (dark red meat versus pale white cylinders). Sliced is knife work and does not change the match, and the quantity is ignored. Under guideline F, a different food source is not substitutable. Therefore neither condition is met.

The ingredient is fresh turkey sausage, a raw ground poultry sausage meant to be cooked before eating. The USDA match is 'Pickled sausage', which refers to a sausage product preserved in a pickling brine (typically a cured, pre-cooked, vinegar-brined product, often pork-based and sold shelf-stable or refrigerated). Condition 1: fresh turkey sausage would need to be cooked (pan-fried, grilled, etc.), while pickled sausage is already processed and is typically eaten as-is; using it would change the preparation method and the dish's flavour profile. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference: pickled sausage has a sharp vinegar tang, a firm, cured texture, and a different appearance and meat type (not turkey), versus fresh turkey sausage's mild, savoury, crumbly or juicy texture. It is not the same food under another name, and it is a processed/preserved state rather than the raw fresh product. Therefore it fails both conditions.

The ingredient is plain crab meat, picked over, which is the crab flesh itself with shell and cartilage removed. The USDA entry 'Crab salad' is a prepared dish containing crab mixed with mayonnaise or dressing and typically other components such as celery, onion, and seasonings. Using it would change the dish's flavour, texture, and appearance, and a diner would notice the added dressing and mix-ins. Knife or handling work like picking over does not change the match, but the added components are a different product, not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails because the dish could not be prepared the same way with a pre-dressed salad, and condition 2 fails because taste and texture would clearly differ.

The ingredient is dill seed and the USDA entry is 'Spices, dill seed', which is the same food. The quantity (1g) is ignored. Nothing in the ingredient suggests a modified or processed form, so the match is the standard default version. The spice is used in the same way, and a diner would not taste or see a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a mixture of two different foods: fresh sole and shrimp. The USDA entry covers only flatfish (flounder and sole species), raw, so it matches just the sole portion. Shrimp is a different food (crustacean, not fish) with a different taste, texture and appearance. Guideline F excludes a single ingredient standing in for a blend or product containing it. Using flatfish alone would change the dish's composition, so a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 (same preparation and composition) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture or appearance) both fail. The 'fresh' and 'raw' descriptors and the 200g quantity do not affect this.

The ingredient is 'chuck tender', a beef cut from the chuck (mock tender), with no cooking stated, so it is raw. The USDA entry is the same cut (chuck, mock tender steak, trimmed to 0" fat), so the cut identity matches. However, the entry is 'cooked, braised', and guideline F treats raw vs cooked as a different state. Substituting a pre-braised product would change the cooking method, since the raw meat would need to be cooked in the recipe, and the diner would see and taste a different product (already braised, with different texture and appearance). Condition 1 fails because the preparation would change, and condition 2 fails because the eaten result would differ. The 'separable lean and fat, trimmed' descriptor is also a minor point compared with the cooked state. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is sesame paste, a paste made from ground sesame seeds. The USDA entry 'Seeds, sesame butter, paste' is the same food under a different name (sesame seed paste, commonly sold as tahini), so guideline B applies. The quantity (5g) is ignored per guideline A. The entry is the plain, default product, with no added flavour, sweetener or modification, so guideline D is satisfied. Substituting it would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. One caveat: a toasted or Chinese-style sesame paste is darker and more strongly flavoured, which would be a different product. The ingredient is listed without that qualifier, so the default match stands.

The ingredient is 'toasted beechnuts', and the 10g quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Nuts, beechnuts, dried' describes the untoasted nut. Guideline F says plain vs toasted is a different state and is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because the match would skip the toasting step the recipe requires. Condition 2 fails because toasting deepens the flavour, darkens the colour and changes the crunch, so a diner would likely notice the difference. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is dried mole powder, a dehydrated concentrate that must be reconstituted or cooked with liquid before use. The USDA match is 'Mole sauce', a prepared, ready-to-use wet sauce. Condition 1 fails: substituting a prepared sauce for a dry powder changes the preparation, since the cook would no longer add water or stock to make the sauce and would have to adjust the liquid and simmering steps. Condition 2 also fails: the moisture content, concentration, and texture differ, so the final dish would have different consistency and flavour intensity. Under guideline F, a different state (dried versus prepared) is not substitutable. The quantity prefix is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain yellow mustard, a condiment made from mustard seed, vinegar, and turmeric. The USDA match is honey mustard dip, a flavoured product with honey and typically mayonnaise or oil as a base. Condition 2 fails: the dish would taste noticeably sweeter and different, and the colour and texture would differ. Condition 1 also fails, since honey mustard is a different product that a cook would not normally use as a direct swap for plain yellow mustard in basting. Guideline D rejects a plain ingredient mapped to a flavoured or modified version, and guideline F rejects a different product that merely looks close. The quantity and the 'for basting' note do not change this.

The ingredient is lemon, the citrus fruit. The USDA match is lemongrass (citronella), a tall tropical grass with a different plant family, appearance, and flavour profile. Guideline B covers same food under another name, but lemongrass is not a regional name for lemon. Lemongrass is a different food. Substituting it would change the flavour (citrusy-sour from lemon versus grassy-citrus from lemongrass) and the appearance (a fibrous stalk versus fruit flesh and juice). A diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable taste or appearance difference) both fail.

The ingredient is fresh stevia leaves, the whole raw plant. The USDA match is 'Sugar substitute, stevia, powder', a processed, concentrated extract sold as a sweetener. Guideline F rejects 'the raw plant/source vs the processed ingredient' and 'a different state: raw vs cooked, fresh vs dried.' Condition 1 fails: the powder cannot stand in for leaves without changing preparation. Using leaves means steeping or muddling a green herb, whereas the powder is added as a dry granular sweetener. Condition 2 also fails: the powder is far sweeter per gram, has a different flavour profile (the extract is often described as having a bitter or liquorice-like aftertaste), and looks like white powder rather than green leaves. A diner could notice the difference. Not substitutable.

Masa harina is a finely ground flour made from nixtamalized corn (treated with lime), used to make dough for tortillas, tamales and similar dishes. The USDA entry is blue cornmeal from Navajo blue corn, which is a coarser meal ground from untreated blue corn. Condition 1: the dough would not behave the same. Nixtamalization changes the starch and gives masa its binding and elastic texture, and cornmeal lacks that, so the preparation would change. Condition 2: the blue colour would be visible in the finished dish, and the flavour and texture would differ from masa-based foods. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain chicken skin, with no cooking state stated. The USDA entry is 'Chicken, broiler, rotisserie, BBQ, skin', which is cooked skin with a BBQ flavouring. Condition 1 fails: using rotisserie BBQ skin in place of plain skin would change the preparation, since the skin is already cooked and would not render or crisp the same way. Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste the BBQ flavour and see the cooked, browned appearance. Guideline F rejects matches that differ by cooked state or flavouring, and guideline D rejects a plain ingredient matched to a flavoured version. The weight is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is a hock (lower leg cut) of cured pork, which is what is commonly sold as a ham hock. The USDA entry 'Pork, ham hocks' names the same cut under its standard name, so it is the same food under another name (guideline B), not a different cut (guideline F). The entry has no preparation state in its name, so it is the generic food and covers the cured hock as bought. Preparation is unchanged, since a ham hock is cooked the same way as a cured pork hock in the same dish. Taste, texture and appearance are the same for the same cut. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a plain shredded Mexican cheese blend, which shoppers normally buy as a full-fat product (typically cheddar and Monterey Jack). The USDA entry is 'Cheese, Mexican, blend, reduced fat', which is a modified version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced-fat version is not a match. Condition 1: reduced-fat cheese melts, browns and sets differently, so the preparation and appearance of a dish (such as a melted topping or baked cheese) would change. Condition 2: diners would likely notice the drier, less creamy, less rich texture and milder flavour. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is plain 'almond milk', and the USDA entry 'Almond milk, NFS' is the generic almond milk entry with no further specification. Condition 1: almond milk can be used as-is in place of almond milk, with no change to cooking method. Condition 2: the entry names the same product with no added flavour, sweetening or modification, so no taste, texture or appearance difference is expected. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to the standard default version is a match. Both conditions hold.

A spiral ham is a whole, cooked (usually smoked or glazed) ham that is sliced in a continuous spiral. Prosciutto is a dry-cured, uncooked Italian ham sliced very thinly. Substituting prosciutto would change the dish's preparation: the spiral ham is typically heated through, while prosciutto is served uncooked. It would also change taste (salt-cured, air-dried, nutty versus smoky or sweet-glazed), texture (firm, dense and chewy versus silky and thin), and appearance (thin ribbons versus a spiral-cut joint). A diner would notice the difference, so neither condition is met. This is a different product, not the same food under another name.

The ingredient is dried pinto beans, which are uncooked and hard. The USDA match, 'Pinto beans, from dried, no added fat', describes pinto beans that have already been cooked from their dried state with no added fat. Guideline C treats 'mature seeds, raw' or 'dry' entries as the dried legume as bought, but this entry names a cooked preparation. Condition 1 fails: substituting cooked beans means the dish would skip the soaking and simmering that dried beans require, so the cooking method changes. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture and in how the beans are cooked into the dish. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as not substitutable. Therefore the match is not acceptable.

The ingredient is goose eggs and the USDA entry is 'Egg, goose, whole, fresh, raw', which is the same food. The weight '400g' is decoration and is ignored. The entry is raw and whole, and the ingredient is an uncooked egg, so handling or cooking in the recipe does not change the match. Using the same food in place of itself does not change the cooking method, flavour, texture or appearance, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked pollock, which is a smoked (processed) product. The USDA entry is plain pollock cooked by dry heat, with no smoking. Guideline F says plain vs smoked is a different state and not substitutable. A diner would taste the smoke flavour, and the match also has a different appearance and flavour profile. The USDA entry also notes it may contain added moisture-retaining additives, which is a further modification from the plain product. The flaking is handling and does not change the match. The quantity is ignored. Condition 2 fails because the smoky flavour would be noticed, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fried chicken, shredded. Shredding is knife work and does not change the match itself. The USDA entry is the same food: cooked, fried broiler/fryer chicken. The problem is the 'meat only' descriptor. Standard fried chicken includes skin and a crispy breaded or battered coating, and a shredded version carries those visible, crunchy pieces. The USDA entry has neither, so the match changes the texture and appearance a diner would notice. Condition 2 is not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'pea milk', a plant-based milk made by processing peas into a smooth, liquid beverage. The USDA match is 'Green peas, cooked, from restaurant', which is whole cooked legume vegetable. Condition 1 fails: pea milk cannot replace cooked peas in a recipe. It is a liquid, not a vegetable, so the preparation would change. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste and see a creamy, milky liquid versus whole cooked peas with a different texture and appearance. Guideline F covers this pattern (the raw plant/source versus the processed ingredient), so this is not a same-food name variant under guideline B. The leading '200g' and 'chilled' are ignored per guidelines A and C.

The ingredient is beef bouillon granules, a dry bouillon product with beef flavouring. The USDA entry is chicken broth or bouillon, dry, which is a different flavour base. Guideline B does not apply because this is not the same food under another name. Guideline F rules out a different product with a different flavour profile. Condition 1 is arguably met, since dry bouillon can be dissolved in the same way. Condition 2 fails: beef and chicken bouillon taste noticeably different, so a diner would notice the change in flavour. Both conditions must hold, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is chopped pimentos, which are sweet red peppers (Peppers, pimiento, canned or raw in the USDA sense). The match is Cheese, pasteurized process, pimento, a processed cheese product containing pimento pieces. Condition 1 fails: a processed cheese cannot replace chopped pimentos without changing the dish, since it adds dairy fat, cheese, emulsifiers and salt, and it would change the cooking method and the dish's structure. Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste cheese and notice a different texture and flavour. Guideline F rejects a single ingredient versus a product containing it. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is shelled squash seeds, which are generally hulled pumpkin/squash seeds, the same food sold as pepitas. Guideline B treats regional and trade names of the same food as matches. The USDA entry is 'Seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), raw'. The ingredient does not specify roasting, salting or seasoning, so the plain raw default applies (guideline D). Shelling is handling already reflected in the pepita form and does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the seeds can be used directly in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance between hulled squash seeds and raw pepitas. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is toasted almond oil, and the USDA match is plain almond oil. Guideline F lists 'plain vs toasted/smoked/roasted' as a different state that is not substitutable. Toasting adds a pronounced nutty, roasted flavour and aroma that a diner would notice, so condition 2 fails. The weight (25g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the oil could be used in the same way, but condition 2 is not, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain grapes (quantity of 55g is ignored per guideline A). The USDA match 'Grapes, raw' is literally the same food in its uncooked, default form. Condition 1: grapes can be used in place of grapes with no change in preparation, since no cooking method is involved and the match is the same raw fruit. Condition 2: a diner would detect no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is passion fruit juice, a plain juice with no stated modification. The USDA match is 'Passion fruit juice, 100%', which is the same food: the pure juice of passion fruit with no added sugar or other components. Quantity (480g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the juice could be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would taste the same passion fruit juice, with no visible or textural difference. The '100%' descriptor simply describes the standard plain juice as normally sold, so it is not a modification under guideline D. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain cottage cheese, which the guidelines treat as the standard default version (Cheese, cottage, creamed). The USDA match is a different product: it is lowfat (1% milkfat), which is a modified version of the plain food, and it is 'with vegetables', which is a flavoured or added-ingredient variant. Condition 1 fails because using it changes the dish's flavour and possibly its appearance, since visible vegetable pieces would be present. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would likely notice the vegetables and the different taste and texture. Quantity is ignored. Under guideline D and F, a plain food matched to a flavoured or modified entry is not substitutable.

The ingredient is stevia powder, and the USDA entry is 'Sugar substitute, stevia, powder', which names the same product type with the same form (powder). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient directly, since both are dry powders added in the same way, so the preparation does not change. Condition 2: the USDA entry is the generic stevia powder, not a flavoured, modified, or blended variant, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The quantity (1g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.
