Calamari is the culinary name for squid, which is the same food as the USDA entry 'Mollusks, squid, mixed species, raw'. The ingredient '65g calamari' is a plain, uncooked seafood item, and the USDA entry is the raw form, so no cooking-state mismatch applies. The leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is a generic mixed-species squid rather than a specific species, but calamari is commonly sold as mixed squid, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Condition 1 is met because the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 is met because the food is the same. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is Cornish game hen with the skin on. The USDA entry is Cornish game hen, meat only, raw, which explicitly excludes the skin. Condition 1: the dish would be prepared differently. Skin-on poultry is typically roasted or seared to render fat and crisp the skin, and meat-only flesh would not behave the same way or give the same result. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Skin contributes fat, flavour, a crisp or browned texture and visible appearance, and its absence changes all of these. Guideline D treats the ingredient asking for a specific version as the reference, so the meat-only entry is a modified version of what the ingredient specifies. Guideline F also rejects differences in cut or preparation that change the eaten product. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain 'honey mustard dressing', which shoppers normally buy as the standard full-fat version. The USDA match is 'Honey mustard dressing, light', a reduced-fat version. Under guideline D, 'light/lite' is a modification of the plain product, so it is not the default match. Condition 1 can be met in principle, since a dressing can be swapped in without changing preparation. Condition 2 fails: lower fat changes the mouthfeel, creaminess and flavour intensity, and a diner would likely notice. Because the match is a modified version of the plain product, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is green asparagus spears, 50g; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Asparagus, green, raw' is literally the same food: green asparagus in uncooked form. Spears are simply the usual way asparagus is sold, so no knife work or cut changes the match. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the recipe handling (trimming, cutting) is unaffected by the USDA entry being raw whole asparagus. Condition 2: a diner would see and taste the same green raw asparagus, with no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is plain chicken thigh, with no cooking state given, so the default is raw chicken thigh. The USDA entry is chicken thigh that is grilled, served with sauce, and eaten with skin. Condition 1 fails: substituting grilled, sauced chicken would change the preparation, since the dish would already be cooked and sauced rather than being cooked with the recipe's own method and seasonings. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the added grilling, the sauce flavour, and the browned appearance. The entry is a cooked, flavoured, modified version of a plain raw ingredient, and guideline F rejects differences in state and added flavour. The weight (115g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is beef ribeye, which in a recipe is normally bought and used raw. The USDA entry 'Beef, steak, ribeye, NS as to fat eaten' is a cooked-state entry, since USDA 'eaten' entries describe meat after cooking, with the fat-eaten status left unspecified. Condition 1 fails: substituting a cooked product for raw ribeye would change how the dish is prepared, because the meat would no longer need cooking as part of the recipe. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, colour and doneness. Raw vs cooked is a different state under guideline F, so the match is not substitutable. The 300g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is frozen pear slices that have been thawed. The USDA match is Pears, raw. Guideline E allows a frozen-then-thawed food to match the fresh entry only when it is normally cooked or mixed and freezing does not show. Pears are often eaten raw, and freezing and thawing visibly changes them: the flesh softens, becomes mushy, releases liquid, and can brown. Where the pear is served fresh, a diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance. Condition 1 (same preparation) is arguably met, since the recipe likely cooks or mixes the pear, but condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance) is not reliably met. The entry has no frozen or thawed state, and the match is only acceptable when freezing does not show, so it fails.

The ingredient is collards, a leafy green, and the USDA match is 'Collards, raw', which is the same food in its uncooked state. The quantity (100g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: collards could be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since the match is the same plant in the same raw state. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is literally the same food, raw, as the plain ingredient. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is farina, plus salt to taste. The USDA entry is farina (Cream of Wheat), which is the same food under its brand name, so the core ingredient matches. The 'enriched' descriptor is standard for farina sold in the US. The 'quick (1-3 minutes)' descriptor describes a cooking-time variant of the same product, sold under the same name, and it is still cooked the same way (simmered in liquid), so the preparation method does not change. Quick farina is finer and cooks faster, but it is the same product type, and the texture difference is small enough that a diner would not reliably notice it in a cooked dish. Salt is a seasoning added during cooking, not a food component that the USDA entry must cover, so its absence does not make the match unacceptable. Condition 1 is met. Condition 2 is likely met, since the cooked result is the same kind of farina dish. Overall both conditions hold.

The ingredient is cockles, sold in the shell, which is the same food as the USDA entry 'Cockles, raw'. Under the annotation guidelines, the 'raw' state matches because the ingredient is uncooked. Keeping the shell on or having the cook shuck it is handling, not a change of food, so 'in shell' does not change the match. The 500g quantity is ignored. Using the USDA entry in place of the ingredient would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference in the cockle meat. Both conditions are met.

Crisped rice is a puffed or toasted rice product, typically made by puffing rice grains under heat or pressure, often with sugar or malt. It is a dry, crisp, shelf-stable ingredient. 'Rice, fried, NFS' is a cooked dish, fried rice, a stir-fried preparation usually made with cooked rice, oil, egg and seasonings. It is not the same food under another name. Using it would change the dish's preparation, since it is a cooked, moist, savoury rice rather than a crisp puffed grain. Its taste, texture and appearance would also differ noticeably from crisped rice. Condition 1 fails and so does condition 2, so the match is not substitutable.

1. The ingredient is pickled morel mushrooms, a specific wild variety with a distinctive earthy, nutty flavour and a honeycomb texture. The USDA entry 'Mushrooms, pickled' is the generic pickled mushroom, usually cultivated button or similar mushrooms. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B). 2. Guideline F says a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable. A diner would likely notice the difference in flavour, texture and appearance between morels and standard pickled mushrooms. 3. Drained, pickled and the 50g quantity do not change this. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is soybean oil, and the USDA entry 'Oil, soybean, salad or cooking' is the standard retail soybean oil. 'Soy bean' and 'soybean' are the same food under another name (guideline B), and the entry is the plain default product, not a blend, modified version, or different oil (guidelines D and F). Quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would taste and see no difference, since it is the same oil. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh pork spleen, an organ meat (offal) that is a distinct food from any cut of pork muscle. The USDA match is 'Pork, cured, salt pork, raw', which is salt-cured fatback/belly-type pork fat, a different cut and product entirely. Guideline F states that a different cut of meat is not substitutable, and salt pork is also cured, which changes flavour and texture compared with fresh raw spleen. Condition 1 fails because salt pork would change the dish's preparation and flavour (it is fatty and salted, not organ tissue). Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. The quantity of 5g is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is bratwurst, and the USDA entry is 'Bratwurst', which is the same food under the same name. Guideline A says the 110g weight is ignored. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to its standard default version as a match. The USDA entry names no modified state, such as reduced fat or sodium, so it describes the standard product. Using it would not change the cooking method, since bratwurst is cooked the same way regardless of entry. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dry cranberry beans, which are the dried legume as bought. The USDA entry 'Beans, Dry, Cranberry (0% moisture)' is the same food: dried cranberry beans. Guideline C says 'dry' beans match the dried legume as bought. The '(0% moisture)' tag describes the dried state that dry beans already have, so it is a standard descriptor rather than a modification such as reduced sodium or added ingredients. Cooking method is unchanged, since both are soaked and cooked the same way, and a diner would see and taste the same bean. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 200g ground pork; the quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Pork, ground, raw' is the same food: ground pork in its raw, uncooked state, which is the plain default form a shopper would buy under the name 'ground pork' (guidelines B and D). Guideline E's frozen/thawed rules do not apply, and no cut, fat content, or processing differs. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation, since both are raw ground pork that the cook handles the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the product is identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain puffed wheat, a ready-to-eat puffed wheat cereal. The USDA entry is Cereals ready-to-eat, wheat, puffed, which is the same product. The only added descriptor is 'fortified', meaning vitamins and minerals were added. Ready-to-eat breakfast cereals are commonly fortified, so this describes how the product is normally sold rather than a modification that changes what a shopper would expect under the plain name (guideline D). Condition 1: it can replace the puffed wheat in a recipe with no change to preparation, since it is the same puffed cereal form. Condition 2: fortification adds nutrients but does not change taste, texture, or appearance in a way a diner would notice. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned skim milk. In practice, canned skim milk is evaporated skim milk, sold in cans as a fat-free product. The USDA entry 'Milk, evaporated, fat free (skim)' names the same product with the same components. The 'fat free (skim)' descriptor matches what the ingredient asks for, so it is not an unwanted modification under guideline D. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are canned, shelf-stable, liquid milk products used the same way. Condition 2: the taste, texture and appearance should match, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 150g mashed banana, which is raw, uncooked banana. Mashing is knife or handling work and does not change the match, and the weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry, 'Banana, baked', is a cooked product. Under guideline F, raw versus cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Baking also changes the banana's flavour (it becomes sweeter and more caramelised), its texture (softer and denser) and its appearance (browned, with a different colour). A diner would likely notice the difference, and the dish's preparation would change if baked banana replaced raw mashed banana. Condition 1 fails because the cooking method changes, and condition 2 fails because taste, texture and appearance differ. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is tangerine, a mandarin-type citrus fruit with a sweet-tart, acidic, citrus-aroma flavour and a segmented orange-coloured peel and flesh. The USDA match is Apricot, raw, a stone fruit with a different flavour profile (floral, mildly tart-sweet, no citrus notes), a smooth non-segmented flesh, and a different appearance (pale orange, fuzzy skin, pit). Apricots are not the same food under another name, and they are not a sibling variety of tangerine. Condition 1 fails because a cook would not use apricot in place of tangerine without changing the dish's preparation intent, and condition 2 fails because a diner would clearly notice citrus versus stone fruit in taste, texture and appearance. The quantity prefix is ignored.

The ingredient is plain cottage cheese, whose standard default in the guidelines is 'Cheese, cottage, creamed'. The USDA match is 'Cheese, cottage, lowfat, 2% milkfat', a reduced-fat version. Guideline D treats low-fat versions of a plain ingredient as a modification, so the match fails the same-food test. Condition 1 is met in that it could be swapped in without changing preparation. Condition 2 is not met: the lower milkfat content makes the cheese drier and less rich, and a diner could notice the difference in texture and mouthfeel. Because the match is a modified version rather than the standard default, it is not substitutable.

Ingredient is fontina cheese, used as an optional garnish; quantity is ignored per guideline A. USDA entry 'Cheese, fontina' is the same food under the same name, so it is the plain default version (guideline D). Freezing is not indicated and fontina is commonly sold fresh, so no frozen/thawed issue arises (guideline E). Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same cheese used as a garnish. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Anjou pear, a European pear cultivar (Pyrus communis), which is soft, buttery, and juicy when ripe. The USDA match, 'Pear, Asian, raw', is a different species (Pyrus pyrifolia/ussuriensis). Asian pears are round, crisp, and grainy, with a texture and flavour closer to an apple. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and it is not a sibling variety of the same kind. Condition 1: Asian pears can be used raw in many preparations, but a recipe built around Anjou pears would change in texture and sweetness, so the swap alters how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the crisp, granular texture and different flavour, and the appearance differs too. Guideline F rejects sibling varieties with different taste, so both conditions fail.

The ingredient is bagged microwave popcorn with butter flavour, and the USDA entry is microwave popcorn with regular (butter) flavour. These are the same product type, and the cooking method is the same: microwaved from the bag. The recipe does not specify an oil, so the 'made with palm oil' descriptor describes a common formulation of this product rather than a modification that conflicts with the ingredient. Under guideline D, a descriptor that reflects how the product is normally sold is not a modification. A diner would not expect a different taste, texture or appearance from the standard product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh pork jowl, a meat cut from the cheek area that contains both lean meat and fat layers. The USDA entry is pork backfat, raw, which is the pure subcutaneous fat layer from the back with little or no lean meat. Guideline F states that a different cut of meat is not substitutable. Backfat would change the dish's texture, flavour and appearance: it would render mostly fat, lacking the meat component that jowl provides. Condition 1 fails because the dish would be prepared differently (for example, the meat would not brown or cook the same way). Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in mouthfeel and taste. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A. Since neither condition is met, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is lima beans and corn with butter added. The USDA entry is the same dish: lima beans and corn, cooked, with fat added. Guideline C says that when the USDA entry names the same dish with the same components, it matches even if USDA adds a standard descriptor, and guideline D gives the parallel case of buttered peas and carrots matching 'Peas and carrots, cooked, fat added'. The entry's 'fat added' is the generic descriptor, so it covers the butter. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is already cooked and buttered. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. The leading 100g is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is whole coriander seeds, a single spice in its whole, dried seed form. The USDA match is 'Seasoning mix, dry, sazon, coriander & annatto', which is a multi-ingredient seasoning blend containing coriander plus annatto, and typically also salt, garlic, and other components. Under guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend containing it is not substitutable, and whole versus ground/processed spice is also a state difference. Using the blend would add annatto colouring and other flavours (salt, garlic, etc.), changing flavour and appearance (orange-red colour), and the diner would notice the difference. The quantity is irrelevant per guideline A. Conditions 1 and 2 are not met.

Condition 1: The ingredient is plain 'sliced deli ham' with no stated fat or additive requirements. The USDA entry is the same food type (sliced deli ham), so the cooking use would be the same. Condition 2: The entry is specified as '96% fat free, water added'. Guideline D treats fat-free and added-water (solution) descriptors as modifications when the ingredient asks for the plain default. Nothing in the ingredient calls for a fat-free or water-added ham, so the match is to a modified variant rather than the standard default. Some diners might also notice the difference in moisture and texture, and the leaner, water-added product is not what the plain name implies. Because the entry is a modified version of the plain ingredient, it fails the standard applied here.

The ingredient is 100g of mandarin orange segments, meaning whole fruit flesh in pieces. The USDA match is 100% freshly squeezed orange juice, a liquid processed product. Condition 1 fails: juice cannot replace segments without changing how the dish is prepared, since segments are solid pieces that would be added or arranged, while juice is a liquid. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance (no segment pieces, no fibrous or pulpy structure). The match is also a different food state (processed juice vs. the whole fruit) and a different citrus (orange vs. mandarin), which guideline F rules out. The quantity is ignored, as guideline A requires.

Winter melon is the common name for Benincasa hispida, the same plant listed in USDA as waxgourd (Chinese preserving melon), so this is the same food under a regional/trade name (guideline B). The ingredient is 'simmered', which is a cooked state, and the USDA entry is 'cooked, boiled, drained, without salt'. Simmering and boiling are both moist-heat cooking in water, so the cooking method is effectively the same and the match does not change how the dish is prepared (condition 1). The USDA entry adds no salt, flavouring or modification, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance (condition 2). The 10g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cold watermelon, cubed; the weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Watermelon, raw' is the same fruit in its uncooked state. Cubing and chilling are knife work and handling that do not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: watermelon can be used in place of itself with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would see and taste the same fruit; cubed raw watermelon matches the USDA raw entry in taste, texture and appearance. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is a chuck roast trimmed of visible fat. The USDA entry is chuck arm pot roast, which is a standard chuck roast cut, so it is the same cut and not a different one (guideline F does not apply). The entry is raw, which matches the uncooked meat implied by the ingredient. The trimming level differs slightly: 'trimmed to 1/8 inch fat' versus 'trimmed of visible fat'. Guideline C says trimming done in handling does not change the match, and the 1/8 inch trim is a close equivalent to removing visible fat. The 'choice' grade is a normal retail grade for this cut. Condition 1: the roast could be braised, roasted or stewed the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since the cut and lean-to-fat profile are essentially the same. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a plain frozen Cornish hen, thawed. Freezing does not change the match for a food that is normally cooked (guideline E), so the frozen/thawed state is not the issue. The USDA entry is the same species and product, but its descriptor 'meat only' specifies a skinless, boneless-style portion rather than the whole bird. A plain 'cornish hen' is normally sold as a whole bird with skin and bone, so 'meat only' is a modified form, not the standard default (guideline D). Using it would change the dish: a roasted or whole-prepared hen would lack skin, which affects appearance, moisture, browning and flavour, and the cook would need to change the preparation. Condition 1 (no change to preparation) and condition 2 (diner would not notice a difference in appearance and texture) are not both met.

The ingredient 'beet tops' is the leaves of the beet plant, which is the same food as 'beet greens' under a common culinary/regional name (guideline B). The ingredient is specified as cooked, and the USDA entry is 'Beet greens, cooked', so the cooking state matches (guideline C). The ingredient's weight is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). The match is a plain, default version with no added flavour, modification, or product difference (guideline D). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are cooked beet leaves. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same vegetable.

The ingredient is organic flax flakes, a single whole-food item used as a cereal-type ingredient. The USDA entry is a branded ready-to-eat breakfast cereal (Nature's Path Organic FLAX PLUS flakes), which is a multi-ingredient product made with flax alongside other grains, seeds, and sweeteners. Under guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend containing it is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because swapping in a prepared cereal changes what goes into the dish and may change how it is mixed or cooked. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would likely taste the added sweetness, other grains and seeds, and the toasted, crisp texture of the RTE cereal, which differ from plain flax flakes. The match is not the same food under another name, so it does not qualify under guideline B.

The ingredient is plain shredded mozzarella, the standard default version, which is typically whole milk or part-skim. The USDA match is 'Cheese, Mozzarella, nonfat or fat free', a modified version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a reduced or fat-free version is not substitutable. Condition 2 also fails in practice: fat-free mozzarella is noticeably firmer and more rubbery, melts and browns differently, and has a blander, less rich flavour, so a diner would likely notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. Condition 1 is also doubtful, since fat-free cheese often behaves differently when melted or baked. Neither condition is clearly met.

The ingredient is plain turnip greens, which are normally bought fresh and raw. The USDA match is canned turnip greens with no salt added, which is a processed, cooked product. Canning changes the greens' texture (they become soft and mushy), colour (they turn olive-brown), and flavour (they taste milder and more cooked). Guideline F says raw versus processed or cooked is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because a cook would not use canned greens where fresh ones are called for without changing the preparation. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the softer texture and different appearance. The 1g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain 'turkey bacon', which is the standard default product. The USDA match is 'Bacon, turkey, low sodium', a modified version with reduced sodium. Guideline D says a plain ingredient matched to a modified version (including reduced/low sodium) is not a match, and the ingredient does not ask for a low-sodium version. Condition 1 is therefore not cleanly met, since the product itself is different rather than just prepared differently. Condition 2 is also doubtful: turkey bacon is typically salted, so a low-sodium version would likely taste noticeably less salty and different. Both points lead to a non-substitutable result.

The ingredient is cumin seed, a spice (the dried seed of Cuminum cyminum) with a distinctive earthy, warm flavour. The USDA match is sesame seeds, a different plant species with a nutty, mild flavour and different appearance (sesame seeds are small, flat, and typically cream or white/black). Condition 1 fails: sesame seeds would not be used in place of cumin without changing the flavour profile of a dish that calls for cumin, and the cooking method would be altered by the need to toast or grind differently. Condition 2 fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste and appearance. The match is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is commercially prepared fish stock, bought ready-made. The USDA entry is fish stock prepared at home. Both are fish stock, so the broad food identity matches, but the USDA entry's descriptor ('home-prepared') marks a different product. Commercial stocks are typically made to a different formula, often with added salt, flavourings, or stabilisers, and at a different concentration, than home-made stock. Condition 1 is largely met, since stock is used the same way in either case. Condition 2 is doubtful: a diner could plausibly notice differences in saltiness, depth, or flavour intensity between the two. Because the USDA descriptor names a different production state rather than a trivial handling step, this is not a same-food-under-another-name match, and the two conditions are not clearly both met.

The ingredient is tahini, a sesame seed paste, stored and used at room temperature; the quantity (400g) is ignored. The USDA entry 'Tahini' is the same food under the same name, a plain product with no modifiers, flavourings, or added components. The 'room-temperature' qualifier is handling/storage and does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: tahini can be used directly in place of itself without any change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the identical product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pomegranate arils, the edible seed sacs of the fruit, eaten fresh and used as a garnish or fresh topping. The USDA match is pomegranate juice, 100%, a liquid processed product derived from the fruit. Condition 1: substituting juice for arils would change the preparation entirely, since arils are a whole-fruit, discrete, crunchy component added as a garnish, while juice is a liquid that cannot be sprinkled or scattered and would be mixed in or used as a base. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in texture (no crisp juicy pops) and appearance (no jewel-like seeds), and the dish would taste different. Per guideline F, the raw plant/source versus a processed ingredient (fruit versus juice) is not substitutable. The weight prefix is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is a pupusa filled with beans, and the USDA entry is 'Pupusa, with beans', which names the same dish with the same filling. The leading '250g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Because the food is literally the same, it could replace the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Chinese broccoli (gai lan, Brassica oleracea var. alboglabra), sold whole. That means the leafy stems, leaves and flowers together. The USDA entry is 'Broccoli, flower clusters, raw', which covers only the floral heads of standard broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica). Condition 1 fails: using only the florets changes what goes into the dish and discards the stems and leaves that are normally eaten. Condition 2 fails: gai lan is a different variety with thicker, crunchier stems, a more bitter and mustard-like flavour, and a different appearance, so a diner would notice. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. It is also a sibling variety with a different taste (F), and a partial part of the plant rather than the whole vegetable.

The ingredient is fresh mandarin segments. USDA 'Tangerines, (mandarin oranges), raw' explicitly names mandarin oranges as the same food, so it is the same food under a regional/trade name (guideline B). Weight is ignored (guideline A). 'Segments' is a knife-work/handling descriptor and does not change the match (guideline C). The entry is raw, matching fresh. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since they are the same fruit in the same fresh form. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned Fuji apple slices, drained. The USDA entry is raw apples without skin. Condition 1: the canned product is already cooked and processed, so using raw apple slices would change the preparation. Canned apple slices are heated during canning, which softens them, and they would need to be cooked or handled differently to match. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Canned apple is softer, more uniform and paler, and has a cooked flavour, while raw apple is firm, crisp and tart. Under guideline F, raw versus cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. The variety is also unspecified in the USDA entry, but the raw-versus-canned difference alone fails both conditions.

The ingredient 'shea oil' is oil pressed from shea nuts, and the USDA entry 'Oil, sheanut' is that same oil under its standard name, so it is the same food under another name (guideline B). The quantity prefix '100g' is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the oil can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is a liquid oil used the same way. Condition 2: the USDA entry names the same oil with no added flavour, modification, or processing state that would change taste, texture, or appearance, so a diner would not notice a difference. Neither the different-oil rule (F) nor the modified-version rule (D) applies, because the two names refer to the same product.

Condition 1: The ingredient is cinnamon bread that has been toasted, and the USDA entry is the same product in the same state (cinnamon bread, toasted). The toasting is requested by the ingredient, so the match is not a plain-to-toasted mismatch. Substituting the entry does not change the preparation. Condition 2: A diner would not taste, feel, or see a difference between toasted cinnamon bread and the same food under the USDA name. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is Concord grapes, a Vitis labrusca cultivar with a slaterich, sweet, foxy flavour and a thin, slip-skin. The USDA entry is muscadine grapes, a different species (Muscadinia rotundifolia) with a thick skin, a distinct musky flavour, and a different texture and appearance. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F rejects a sibling variety with a different taste. Condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice the musky flavour and thicker skin. Condition 1 is also doubtful, since the substitution changes the flavour profile of the dish. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is cooked pumpkin, unsalted. The USDA match is cooked, boiled, drained pumpkin prepared with salt. Condition 1 fails: the ingredient explicitly asks for no added salt, and the match has salt added, so it is a modified version rather than the plain food. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient mapped to a modified version such as added salt or reduced sodium as not matching. Condition 2 also fails: salt changes the flavour, and a diner tasting the dish could notice the difference. The food is the same pumpkin, but the salt makes the match unacceptable under these rules.

The ingredient is frozen chives, thawed, used in a recipe. The USDA match is freeze-dried chives. Condition 1: freeze-dried chives are a dehydrated, shelf-stable product, not a frozen-then-thawed fresh herb. Substituting them would change preparation: they must be rehydrated or used dry, and the quantity by weight would differ substantially because freeze-drying removes most of the water. Guideline F explicitly says a different state (fresh vs dried herb) is not substitutable. Condition 2: thawed frozen chives retain a fresh, green, moist appearance and a fresh onion-like flavour, whereas freeze-dried chives have a muted flavour, a different texture (brittle and crumbly), and a different colour and appearance when served. A diner would likely notice the difference. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is chapati, an unleavened flatbread. The USDA entry is 'Bread, chapati or roti, plain, commercially prepared', which names the same food under a regional name (guideline B). 'Plain' matches the default version, with no added flavour or modification (guideline D). 'Commercially prepared' describes how the product is sold rather than a modification that would change taste, texture or appearance. The chapati could be substituted without changing preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in a dish that uses a plain chapati.

The ingredient is Madras curry powder, a regional style of curry powder. The USDA entry is the generic 'Spices, curry powder', a ground spice blend. Both are the same product category: a ground, dry, pre-blended curry spice mix used the same way, with no change in cooking method. Madras is a regional name for a curry powder style, which guideline B treats as the same food under another name. Madras blends are typically hotter and redder, so a diner might notice a difference in heat and colour. However, this reflects variation in blend formulation within the same product type rather than a different food, and generic curry powder is a recognised equivalent. Condition 1 is met. Condition 2 is borderline, but the difference is in the standard range for curry powder blends rather than a different ingredient, so the match is judged acceptable.

The ingredient is fiddlehead ferns (the young fronds of ostrich fern, typically sold fresh). The USDA entry 'Fiddlehead ferns, raw' is the same food in its uncooked state. The leading '250g' is quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the match is the same raw food, so it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation (fiddleheads are normally cooked before eating, and raw/uncooked is the default for a plain ingredient). Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same food in the same state. Both conditions are met.

Hoisin sauce is a thick, sweet, fermented soybean-based condiment with garlic, sugar, and spices, giving it a sweet, savory, and slightly tangy profile. Worcestershire sauce is a thin, fermented liquid made from anchovies, vinegar, molasses, tamarind, and spices, with a sharp, salty, tangy flavour and no soybean base. Condition 1: Worcestershire is a thin liquid, while hoisin is a thick paste, so using it in place of hoisin would change the consistency of a glaze, marinade, or stir-fry sauce and alter how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste (no sweetness or soybean umami, added anchovy and vinegar sharpness) and in appearance (hoisin is dark brown and glossy and thick, Worcestershire is thin and brown). These are different products, not the same food under another name, and the match is not a modified version of the same product. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is 100g Virginia peanuts; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. Virginia peanuts are a market type/variety of peanut (large-kernel, commonly sold raw or roasted in the shell or shelled). The USDA entry 'Peanuts, virginia, raw' names the same food with the same state (raw, uncooked), so it is the same food under the same name (guideline B). Raw is the plain state as bought, and no cooking method or handling change is implied. Substituting it would not change preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is literally the same product in raw form. Both conditions are met.

Condition 1: The ingredient is Thousand Island dressing marketed for coleslaw. The USDA entry is plain Thousand Island dressing. Both are mayonnaise-and-condiment dressings used the same way, poured or mixed in cold, so the preparation method is unchanged. Condition 2: 'Coleslaw' here describes the intended use of the same dressing type, not a distinct flavour or modification, so the appearance and texture match. Coleslaw-branded versions can be somewhat sweeter, so a difference in taste is possible, but it is not a defining change to the product. Per guideline D, a descriptor that just reflects how the product is sold or used does not count as a modification. Both conditions are reasonably met.

The ingredient is ground beef sirloin, a raw minced meat. The USDA entry is 'Beef, steak, sirloin, lean only eaten', a whole steak cut whose 'eaten' descriptor indicates a cooked product. Condition 1 fails: ground meat is typically browned or crumbled in a dish, while a steak is a whole piece that would be cooked as a steak, so the preparation changes. Ground versus whole cut is also a different physical form, and the raw-versus-cooked state differs. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (crumbly versus whole-muscle chew) and appearance. Guideline F excludes a different cut of meat and a different state (raw vs cooked). Ground beef is not the same food as a sirloin steak, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is sesame flour, a ground powder made from sesame seeds. The USDA match, Chilchen (Red Berry Beverage) (Navajo), is a drink made from red berries, not a flour and not a sesame product. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B). It would change the dish's flavour, texture and appearance, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails because it cannot be used in place of sesame flour without changing preparation, and condition 2 fails because the taste and texture would differ noticeably.

The ingredient is a single cheese, fontina, which is melted as part of the recipe. The USDA entry 'Cheese fondue' is a prepared product, not the plain cheese. Typical cheese fondue is a blend of cheese with wine, starch (such as cornstarch or flour), and often garlic or kirsch. Under guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend or product containing it is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because the USDA product is already a cooked, thickened mixture, so using it would change the preparation: it cannot simply be melted in place of the cheese. Condition 2 also fails because the added wine, starch and seasonings alter flavour and texture, and a diner would likely notice the difference from melted fontina. The entry is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply.

The ingredient is baobab fruit pulp, a moist, fresh or raw fruit pulp. The USDA match is baobab powder, which is dried and ground. Guideline F lists a different state (raw vs dried) and processed vs source ingredient as not substitutable. Using powder in place of pulp would change the preparation: the powder would need to be hydrated or mixed in, and the 490g weight would not give the same moisture, consistency, or appearance. A diner could notice a different texture and appearance. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 likely fails too. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Not substitutable.

Moringa leaves are the leaves of Moringa oleifera, which is also called drumstick tree in South Asia, so 'Drumstick leaves' is the same food under a regional name (guideline B). The USDA entry is 'raw', which matches fresh leaves as an uncooked ingredient, and the weight is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the leaves can be used in place of moringa leaves with no change to preparation. Condition 2: they are the same plant, so a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

1) The ingredient is plain frozen blueberries, thawed; the 70g quantity is ignored. 2) The USDA entry is frozen blueberries, unsweetened. Frozen blueberries are normally sold unsweetened, so 'unsweetened' describes the standard product rather than a modification (guideline D). 3) Guideline E applies: frozen berries used in a dish are the frozen entry of the same product, and thawing does not change the match. 4) The parenthetical about USDA's Food Distribution Program is an administrative note and does not change the food. 5) Using the USDA frozen unsweetened blueberries would not change the cooking method, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is a specific sub-cut, the point (fattier, deckle-end) portion of the brisket. The USDA entry 'Beef, brisket' is the generic brisket, with no cut or fat-level specification. Guideline B's same-food allowance covers regional or trade names for the same item, not sub-cuts of meat. Guideline F explicitly says a different cut of meat is not substitutable. The point differs from the flat in fat content, marbling and texture after cooking, so a diner could plausibly notice the difference. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the same brisket-style cooking applies, but condition 2 is not reliably met. The weight (200g) is ignored per guideline A.

Condition 1 (same preparation): The ingredient is a fresh, raw, frenched rack of lamb. The USDA entry is the same cut (rib chop/rack roast, frenched, bone-in), raw and fresh, so it can be roasted or cooked in the same way with no change to method. The 'Australian, imported' origin and 'trimmed to 1/8" fat' descriptors reflect how this cut is commonly sold, and the trimming is consistent with a frenched rack, so they do not alter how it is cooked. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference): Origin labelling does not change the taste, texture or appearance of the meat for a diner, and the fat trim level is the normal state of a frenched rack. The 'separable lean and fat' entry is a standard USDA composition descriptor for this cut. Nothing here would be noticed by someone eating the dish. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a standard flavoured instant cinnamon oatmeal. The USDA entry is Quaker Instant Oatmeal, weight control, cinnamon. The brand match is fine, since Quaker is a common instant oatmeal brand (guideline G). The problem is the 'weight control' descriptor. That is a reformulated product line, not how instant cinnamon oatmeal is normally sold. Quaker's weight control variety is made with a different formulation (typically higher fibre, lower calorie, with oat bran and added fibre) and so differs in texture and taste. Guideline D treats a modified version of a plain ingredient as not substitutable. Condition 2 is also doubtful, because a diner could notice the denser, different texture and flavour. The 5g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions are not clearly met, so this is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw butternut squash that is cubed. Cubing is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). The USDA entry is cooked and baked, without salt. Guideline F says raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Using pre-baked squash would change how the dish is prepared, since the recipe would need the squash raw for roasting, sautéing or similar. The texture and appearance would also differ: raw cubes are firm, while baked squash is soft and mashable. A diner would likely notice the difference. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is plain lamb fat, with no state or cut specified. The USDA entry is raw external fat from lamb, the fat itself rather than a processed product such as rendered tallow or a blend. 'Australian, imported' is an origin descriptor for the same food, not a modification or a different cut. Raw external fat is the default form in which lamb fat is bought and used, and a diner would not perceive a difference in taste, texture or appearance. The weight (100g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'turkey wing' with no stated preparation, so the default is the raw meat as bought. The 225g weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA match is specifically cooked, with skin not eaten. Under guideline F, raw vs cooked is a different state and not substitutable. Using pre-cooked meat would change how the dish is prepared, since the recipe would need to cook the wing from raw. The skin-removal descriptor is also a modification the ingredient does not mention. Condition 1 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is agar agar powder, the dried gelling extract from red seaweed. The USDA entry 'Seaweed, agar, raw' names the same product, agar, so it is the same food under a common name (Guideline B). The 'raw' descriptor means uncooked, and the recipe's use of powder does not change the match (Guideline C). Condition 1: agar powder can be used in place of the USDA agar with the same preparation (hydrating and boiling to set). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in texture or taste, since both are the same gelling agar. The 'raw plant vs processed' rule (Guideline F) does not apply here because the USDA entry is itself the agar product, not the whole seaweed. Both conditions are met.

Semolina is milled, sifted durum wheat (the endosperm ground into coarse granules). The USDA entry 'Wheat, durum' refers to the whole durum wheat kernel as a raw grain. Guideline F says the raw source is not substitutable for the processed ingredient (cornstarch vs corn is the example given). Condition 1 fails: a whole grain cannot replace milled semolina without changing preparation. You would need to mill it first, and whole kernels would not behave like semolina in a dough, pudding, or couscous. Condition 2 also fails: the texture and appearance of whole kernels or bran-containing grain would differ from semolina flour. Semolina is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is basil pesto, a sauce made from basil, oil, nuts, cheese and garlic. The USDA entry 'Pesto sauce' is the generic pesto product, which is normally basil-based, so it is the same food under a general name (guideline B). The word 'fresh' describes how pesto is commonly sold (refrigerated) rather than a different state of the food, so it does not count as a modification (guideline D). The quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: pesto sauce can replace basil pesto in the same way, with no change to preparation, since both are used as-is, stirred into or spooned over a dish. Condition 2: a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because both are the same sauce type. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is low-sodium kimchi, and the USDA match is the plain 'Kimchi' entry. The core food is the same, so the question is whether the low-sodium modification changes it. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version is a no, and reduced/low sodium is listed explicitly. The USDA plain entry describes regular-sodium kimchi, which is how it is normally sold, so the descriptor 'low-sodium' is a real modification and not the standard default. Condition 1 holds: the kimchi could physically replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 fails: sodium content affects saltiness and flavour balance, and a diner could notice the difference in taste. Because the second condition is not met, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is tahini, a sesame seed paste made from ground toasted or raw hulled sesame seeds. The USDA match is fresh raw pork belly, an animal meat product. Condition 1 fails: pork belly cannot be used in place of tahini in any dish without fundamentally changing its preparation, since tahini is a paste used as a sauce or dressing base and would not be replaced by a raw cut of meat. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (nutty sesame versus pork), texture (smooth paste versus solid fatty meat), and appearance. This is a different food entirely, not a naming variant of the same food, and not a different cut of the same food. The quantity is irrelevant. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is hydrogenated babassu oil, a specific plant-derived fat. The USDA entry is an industrial palm kernel confection fat, which is a different source oil (palm kernel, not babassu) and is an industrial/food-service specialty fat. Guideline F says a different oil or fat is not substitutable, and industrial specialty fats are not substitutable for the home ingredient. Condition 1 fails because the swap changes the fat being used, not just its name. Condition 2 also likely fails, since a confection fat built to mimic cocoa butter may differ in melting profile, mouthfeel and flavour from hydrogenated babassu oil. Not the same food under another name, so not a match.

The ingredient is household vegetable shortening, and the USDA entry is 'Shortening, vegetable, household, composite', which names the same product. The leading '13g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the shortening can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to the cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product type. Both conditions are met.

Ingredient: nutritional yeast flakes, a deactivated yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) sold as a savoury, cheesy-flavoured seasoning ingredient, typically used as a sprinkle or mixed into sauces. USDA match: yeast extract spread, a dark, salty, concentrated paste made from autolysed yeast extract (similar to Marmite/Vegemite), typically spread on bread. Condition 1: Using yeast extract spread in place of flakes would change preparation: flakes are sprinkled or stirred in dry or into a sauce, while the spread is a viscous paste that must be dissolved or mixed in, and its salt content and concentration differ, so it cannot be used as a direct drop-in replacement without altering the method. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference: the spread gives a dark brown colour, intense salty-umami flavour and sticky paste texture, whereas nutritional yeast flakes are pale yellow, nutty and cheesy with a dry, flaky texture. Different product types (flake seasoning vs. concentrated extract paste) with different flavour, appearance and texture. Not the same food under another name, and the flavour and appearance differ. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is a beef tenderloin roast, cooked. The USDA entry is beef bottom round roast, separable lean and fat, trimmed to 0" fat, select, cooked, roasted. Tenderloin and bottom round are different cuts of beef with different tenderness, grain, and flavour. Guideline F explicitly says a different cut of meat is not substitutable. The USDA entry is also a round cut described as separable lean and fat, which differs from a tenderloin roast. Because the cut differs, the match would change the dish's texture and flavour, and a diner would likely notice. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh strawberries, sliced. The USDA match is frozen strawberries, sweetened, sliced. Guideline D treats 'sweetened' as a modification to a plain ingredient, so the match is not the default version. Guideline E allows frozen berries to match fresh only when they are normally cooked or mixed and freezing does not show. Sliced strawberries are often served fresh, where thawing softens the texture, releases liquid, and changes the appearance, and the added sugar changes the flavour. Condition 1 might be met, since the berries could be swapped in, but condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice the softer texture, extra sweetness and altered appearance. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a plain 155g chuck roast, which is a raw cut of beef that the recipe will cook. The USDA entry is 'Beef, chuck, arm pot roast, separable lean and fat, trimmed to 0" fat, select, cooked, braised', which is already cooked by braising and has all visible fat trimmed. Under guideline F, raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using pre-braised meat in place of a raw roast would change the cooking method, since the recipe's cooking step would be skipped or altered. Condition 2 also fails: the braised, fully trimmed meat would differ in texture, moisture, colour and appearance from a raw roast that is cooked within the dish, and a diner could notice. The entry matches the chuck cut, but the state and fat trimming make it a different product for this recipe.

The ingredient is a fresh whole turkey, meaning the whole bird with both light (breast) and dark (leg/thigh) meat. The USDA entry specifies only light meat, with meat and skin, raw. Guideline F treats a different cut of meat as not substitutable. Using light meat alone would change the dish's composition: dark meat is richer, moister and more fibrous, so a diner could notice a difference in taste and texture, and cooking times differ. The 'raw' and 'meat and skin' parts match, but the light-meat-only restriction is a different cut from the whole bird. Condition 2 therefore fails.

Hulled buckwheat kernels are buckwheat groats, the dehulled seed of the buckwheat plant. USDA's 'Buckwheat, whole grain' describes the same food: the whole hulled grain as sold, uncooked and dry. The name difference is a regional or trade naming variant, so the food is literally the same (guideline B). The weight '180g' is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1 is met because the grain can be used in place of the kernels with the same preparation, such as boiling or simmering. Condition 2 is met because a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same grain. The match is not a roasted (kasha) or flour product, so no state change applies.

The ingredient is fresh epazote leaves, an aromatic herb (Dysphania ambrosioides) with a distinctive resinous, medicinal flavour used in Mexican cooking. The USDA match is 'Spices, pepper, black', which is a dried, ground spice made from the peppercorn fruit of Piper nigrum. These are different plants and different food categories: epazote is a leafy herb, black pepper is a spice. Condition 1 fails: black pepper cannot be used in place of fresh epazote leaves without changing the dish's preparation and character, and it is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly taste the difference, since epazote's flavour is not peppery and the appearance of ground black pepper differs from green leaves. Guideline F also rules out a fresh herb being replaced by a different spice. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain dragon fruit (pitaya), with the quantity 130g being irrelevant per guideline A. The USDA match is 'Dragon fruit', which is the same food under the same name, with no processing state, cooking method, or modification indicated. Under guideline B, this is literally the same food. Dragon fruit is normally sold fresh and eaten raw, and the USDA entry describes the same raw fruit, so the preparation would not change. A diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is taro leaves (the greens, typically cooked and finely ground for dishes such as laing or palusami). The USDA match 'Taro, raw' refers to the corm (the starchy tuber), not the leaves. These are different parts of the plant with very different taste, texture, and nutritional profile: the corm is starchy and mild, while the leaves are fibrous, vegetal, and must be cooked to remove calcium oxalate irritants. Condition 1 fails because the leaves would be prepared differently (they require prolonged cooking and grinding, and the corm would not produce the same leafy purée). Condition 2 fails because a diner would clearly taste and see a difference, since the dish would be starchy and tuber-based rather than leafy and green. The guideline on 'raw plant/source vs processed' and 'different state' pattern applies here: a different edible part is not the same food under another name.

The ingredient is cooked gluten-free rice pasta. The USDA entry is 'Pasta, gluten-free, rice flour and rice bran extract, cooked, DE BOLES', which is cooked gluten-free rice pasta from a brand. Guideline G says a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. The '5g' quantity is ignored (guideline A). The 'cooked' state matches, so no cooking change is needed (guideline C). The rice bran extract is part of this product's normal formulation, not a flavour or modification that the ingredient excludes, and the ingredient itself asks for gluten-free rice pasta, which the entry describes (guideline D). Both conditions hold: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in a typical gluten-free rice pasta dish.

The ingredient is teff grain, a small tropical cereal grain from Ethiopia with a distinct nutty, slightly molasses-like flavour and very small round seeds. The USDA match is 'Wheat, durum', which is a different cereal species (Triticum durum) with a different flavour, grain size, texture when cooked, and gluten structure. Teff is not a regional name for durum wheat, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: teff cannot be swapped for durum wheat without changing how the dish is prepared (for example, teff injera is a fermented flatbread that durum wheat cannot replicate, and porridge or baking behaviour differs). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the flavour, texture and appearance of durum versus teff. The quantity is irrelevant per guideline A.

The ingredient is pickled chayote, a squash-type vegetable (Sechium edule) preserved in brine or vinegar. The USDA match is dill or kosher dill pickles made from cucumber. These are different foods, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Substitution would change the taste (cucumber and dill flavour versus chayote's mild, squash-like flavour), the texture (chayote is firmer and more fibrous and less crisp), and the appearance (pale chayote pieces versus green cucumber pickle slices). A diner would notice the difference, so condition 2 fails. Quantity is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is challah, a braided, egg-enriched bread typically made with eggs, oil, and sugar, giving it a rich, slightly sweet flavour, a soft and tender crumb, and a glossy golden crust. The USDA match is 'Bread, white, commercially prepared', a generic sandwich-style loaf. Condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice the difference in flavour (eggy, slightly sweet versus plain white), texture (denser, richer crumb versus standard commercial white), and appearance (braided, glossy crust versus a standard loaf). Challah is also not the same food under another name (guideline B), so there is no naming exception. Condition 1 is arguably met, since it could be used in the same way, but both conditions must hold. The match is not substitutable.

Winter melon (Benincasa hispida) is also commonly called wax gourd or Chinese preserving melon, so the USDA entry 'Waxgourd, (chinese preserving melon), raw' names the same food under a regional/culinary name (guideline B). The ingredient is fresh, and the USDA entry is raw, which is the same state. The quantity (85g) is ignored (guideline A). Using the raw wax gourd in place of fresh winter melon requires no change in preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance because it is the same vegetable. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is alfalfa sprouts. The USDA entry, 'Alfalfa seeds, sprouted, raw', is the same food: alfalfa sprouts are the sprouted seeds, and USDA's sprouted alfalfa entry is the standard record for them. Guideline B covers same-food matches under a different name. The entry is 'raw', and alfalfa sprouts are normally eaten raw, so the match carries no cooking-method or state change. Condition 1 holds: the sprouts could replace the USDA food without changing preparation. Condition 2 holds: a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference, since it is the same sprouts. The 25g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is canned bok choy, drained. Canning involves heat processing, so the food is cooked and preserved, not raw. The USDA match is 'Cabbage, bok choy, raw'. Condition 1: the match is not a plain substitute, because the dish is served with the drained canned product and the raw entry would change preparation (it would need to be cooked or otherwise prepared to match the softened canned vegetable). Guideline F explicitly lists raw vs cooked as not substitutable. Condition 2: canned bok choy is noticeably softer, more limp, and paler than raw bok choy, so a diner would likely notice the difference in texture and appearance. The leading '380g' and the 'for serving' note do not change this. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is plain bread crumbs (quantity ignored). The USDA entry 'Bread, crumbs, dry, grated, plain' is the standard dry, plain bread crumb product, which is the same food under USDA wording. Condition 1: dry grated plain crumbs can replace bread crumbs in any recipe (coating, binding, topping) without changing the preparation method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since plain dry crumbs are the default product. The entry is not flavoured, toasted, or seasoned, so none of the rejection criteria apply. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh amaranth leaves (the leafy greens of the amaranth plant, commonly used like spinach or callaloo). The USDA entry 'Amaranth leaves, raw' is the same food in its uncooked, fresh state. The quantity (270g) is ignored per guideline A. Fresh is the same as raw here, since 'raw' only means uncooked and no processing, cut, or preparation differs. Cooking method would be unchanged, and a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance because it is the same leaf. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is mustard seed, the whole dried seed of the mustard plant, used as a spice (whole spice, typically toasted or tempered in cooking or used in pickling). The USDA match is Honey mustard dip, a prepared condiment made from mustard, honey, vinegar or oil, and other ingredients. This is a different food: a prepared product containing mustard and sweeteners, not the raw seed. Condition 1 fails because it cannot replace whole seeds without changing preparation (you cannot temper or pickle with a creamy honey dip, and it would be added as a sauce, not a seed). Condition 2 fails because a diner would clearly taste sweetness, vinegar, and creaminess and see a paste rather than seeds. Per guideline F, a single whole spice is not substitutable for a processed blend or product containing it, and the raw source differs from the processed ingredient.

The ingredient is somen, a very thin, egg-free Japanese wheat noodle, frozen and thawed. The USDA entry 'Noodles, cooked' is a generic category that does not identify somen. Condition 1: somen is usually served chilled or in broth with a specific dipping sauce, and a generic cooked noodle could be prepared as a different noodle type, so the preparation may change. Condition 2: somen is much thinner than typical cooked noodles, has a smooth, firm, slightly slippery texture, and is usually made without egg, so a diner would likely notice a difference in texture, appearance and flavour. Because the match is a different noodle type rather than the same food under another name, it fails both conditions.

The ingredient is a mixture of kidney beans and brown rice, with the leading weight ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry names the same two components with no added flavour, modification, or cooking-state difference. Under guideline C, a USDA entry naming the same dish with the same components is a match. The entry has no state descriptor, so it is the generic food and matches the plain combination (guideline E). Using it in place of the ingredient would not change the preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sunflower seed oil, used for frying. The USDA entry is sunflower seed butter with salt added, which is a spread made by grinding sunflower seeds into a paste, not an oil. Condition 1 fails: using sunflower seed butter in place of oil for frying would change the preparation. It would not conduct heat or fry the same way, it would burn or leave solids, and it would not coat the food in the same manner. Condition 2 also fails: the diner would notice a paste-like, salty, nutty residue and different texture and flavour rather than a neutral oil. Guideline F explicitly rules out a different fat and a processed product versus the home ingredient. Not the same food under another name, so not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried mulberries, which are a processed, dehydrated form of the fruit. The USDA match is Mulberries, raw, which is fresh fruit. Guideline F states that a different state (raw vs dried) is not substitutable. Dehydration changes texture from soft and juicy to chewy and leathery, concentrates sugar and flavour, and alters appearance (darker, wrinkled). A diner would notice the difference, and the recipe would need rehydration or a different preparation. Condition 1 (use without changing preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance) both fail. The quantity is irrelevant.

The ingredient is pawpaw pulp that has been sweetened, so it is a modified version of the plain fruit. The USDA entry is raw, peeled, seeded pawpaw, which is unsweetened. Guideline D lists sweetened versions as modifications that do not match a plain ingredient. Condition 1 fails because the sweetening is an added ingredient, and the cook would have to add sugar to reproduce the dish. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would taste the difference between sweetened and unsweetened pulp. The 95g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain pork fat, the rendered or unrendered fat of the pig. The USDA entry is the separable fat from cured ham, which is a different cut of pork from a cured product. Guideline F rejects a different cut of meat, and guideline F's 'raw vs cooked / plain vs smoked or processed' principle applies to cured vs uncured. Condition 1: cured ham fat would not simply stand in for pork fat in a typical recipe without changing the dish, since curing salts and processing change how it behaves when rendered or cooked. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the cured, salty, ham-like flavour and possibly a different texture and colour. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is corn syrup, a specific glucose-based syrup with a neutral, mild sweetness. The USDA entry 'Syrup, NFS' (not further specified) is a generic category that could represent maple, cane, pancake, or other syrups. It is not literally the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 is arguably met, since a syrup could be used in the same way in cooking. Condition 2 fails: a diner could notice a difference in flavour if the generic syrup were maple or another distinctly flavoured syrup, and the sweetness, viscosity, and crystallisation behaviour may also differ. The match is not a confirmed equivalent, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is an unbaked graham cracker pie crust, a ready-made crust made from graham cracker crumbs, butter and sugar. The USDA entry 'Pie shell, graham cracker' names the same product with the same components. Per guideline C, an unbaked ready-made product matches its USDA product, and the 70g weight is decoration (A). Condition 1: the crust can be used directly in place of the ingredient with the same preparation (filling and bake as the recipe specifies). Condition 2: the USDA entry names no baked or unbaked state, so it does not signal a difference in taste, texture or appearance from the crust the recipe calls for. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is apricot preserves. The USDA entry 'Jams and preserves, apricot' names the same product, with 'preserves' explicitly included in the USDA label. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient in the same preparation, since no cooking method changes. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same apricot fruit spread. The 20g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is '145g chicory'. In UK and Commonwealth usage, 'chicory' without qualification usually means the blanched witloof head (Belgian endive), which is the same food as the USDA entry 'Chicory, witloof, raw'. The weight is decoration (guideline A). The entry is raw, so it is uncooked like the ingredient, and it needs no processing that changes the dish. Both are Cichorium intybus and share the same cut and appearance, so a diner would not reasonably notice a difference. Condition 1 holds because the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 holds for the same reason. The main ambiguity is that in US usage 'chicory' can mean leafy chicory or escarole greens, which differ in leaf form and bitterness. Without a qualifier, the witloof default is the most likely meaning, so the match is accepted.

The ingredient is spiced lentil pasta, a pasta made from lentil flour and seasoned with spices. The USDA match, 'Flavored pasta', is a generic flavoured wheat-based pasta with no mention of lentils. Condition 1: the preparation could be similar, since both are boiled pasta, so the cooking method does not clearly change. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference. Lentil pasta has a different base, a denser and firmer bite, and an earthy legume taste, while flavoured wheat pasta tastes and feels like wheat pasta. The USDA entry does not name the same food, so guideline B does not apply. Because the base ingredient differs and the taste and texture would change, the match fails condition 2.

The ingredient 'parmesan cream sauce' is a cream-based sauce flavoured with parmesan cheese. Alfredo sauce is the standard version of that same product: a cream and parmesan sauce, usually with butter and garlic. Under guideline B, a regional or culinary name for the same food counts as a match, and under guideline C, a USDA entry naming the same dish with the same core components is a match. Condition 1 holds because Alfredo can replace the sauce without changing preparation. Condition 2 is plausibly met because the taste, texture and appearance of a parmesan cream sauce and an Alfredo sauce are essentially the same; the main possible difference is the butter, which is a minor variation within the same sauce family. Both conditions are judged to hold.

The ingredient is 'dry curd cottage cheese', the unsalted, drained curd form of cottage cheese. The USDA entry 'Cheese, cottage, dry curd' names the same product under a standard descriptor. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same food and the leading '100g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is literally the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh jellyfish, sliced. The USDA match is Jellyfish, dried, salted. Under guideline F, 'a different state: raw vs cooked' and processed vs fresh are not substitutable. Fresh jellyfish is a raw, moist, crisp, translucent food, while dried salted jellyfish is a preserved product that must be rehydrated and desalted before use, has a very different texture (firm, crunchy, chewy), a salty and cured flavour, and a different appearance. Preparation would change (soaking/desalting required versus slicing and eating or light prep), and a diner would notice the difference. Guideline D/F on modified or preserved versions also points to rejection. Condition 1 fails because the dish's preparation would change, and condition 2 fails because taste, texture and appearance differ.

The ingredient 'pepper squash' is a regional or culinary name for acorn squash, which is a winter squash commonly sold under that name. Under guideline B, a regional or trade name for the same food counts as a match. The USDA entry 'Squash, winter, acorn, raw' is the plain, uncooked default for the fresh vegetable, which matches a plain ingredient with no stated preparation. The leading '15g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: acorn squash can be used in place of pepper squash without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because they are the same squash. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain rosemary, which in a recipe is normally the fresh herb. The USDA entry 'Rosemary, fresh' is the same food in the same state. The leading '200g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the fresh herb can be used in place of the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference, since it is the same fresh herb. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is crushed corn flakes, a breakfast cereal made from milled corn that is toasted or baked, often coated with sugar and malt, and used as a crumb coating. The USDA match is corn chips, a fried, salted corn snack. These are different products, not the same food under another name. Substituting corn chips would change the flavour (oil-fried, salty, savoury rather than toasted and mild), the texture (greasier, denser, different crunch), and the appearance (different colour and flake shape). A diner would likely notice the difference. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is cardoon, a vegetable sold in jars. Jarred cardoons are already blanched or cooked before preserving, so the cooked state of the USDA entry matches the ingredient's state. The USDA entry is the same food (cardoon) with a standard descriptor ('boiled, drained, with salt'). Jarred cardoons are commonly packed in brine, so the salt descriptor reflects how the product is normally sold. The ingredient is listed as drained, which removes most of the packing liquid, so the packing medium should not show. Cooking method is unchanged, and texture and appearance should be close to the USDA cooked, drained cardoon. Condition 1 is met. For condition 2, a diner would likely not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, though residual brine or acid from the jar could slightly alter flavour, so this is a judgement call. On balance the match is acceptable.

The ingredient is firm silken tofu, and the USDA entry is MORI-NU Tofu, silken, firm. This is the same plain product type under a brand name, which guideline G treats as a match. Condition 1: firm silken tofu can be used directly in place of the ingredient, with the same preparation (blending, cubing, or crumbling) and no change in cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the product is the same firm silken style. The weight prefix (150g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chilled somen noodles, a thin Japanese wheat noodle that is boiled and served cold, typically with a dipping sauce. The USDA match is 'Noodle pudding', a baked or cooked dish made from egg noodles, cottage or cream cheese, sugar, eggs and often raisins or fruit, usually served as a casserole or dessert. Condition 1: Substituting noodle pudding for somen would fundamentally change the preparation. Somen is boiled, chilled and served as a noodle component, whereas noodle pudding is a baked, bound egg-and-dairy dish; the cooking method and role in the dish would be altered. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. Noodle pudding is sweet, custard-like and dense, while chilled somen are plain, firm, slippery strands. These are different foods, not the same food under another name, so the match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is smoked queso anejo, a specific product in which smoking adds a distinct smoky flavour and aroma. The USDA entry, 'Queso Anejo, aged Mexican cheese', describes the plain, unsmoked cheese. Guideline F lists 'plain vs smoked' as a different state that is not substitutable.
