Condition 1 is arguably met, since the cheese could be grated or crumbled in the same way. Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste the absence of smoke, which changes the flavour of the dish. Because the flavour difference is noticeable, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is canned Thompson seedless grapes packed in water. The USDA entry is canned Thompson seedless grapes in water pack, so the food and packing medium match. The weight is decoration and is ignored. 'Solids and liquids' is USDA's standard way of describing the whole canned product, and a diner would not taste or see a difference from the same water-packed grapes. Condition 1 is met because the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 is met because taste, texture and appearance are the same. Both conditions hold.

Celery salt is a seasoning blend, mainly sodium chloride combined with ground celery seed. The USDA entry 'Celery, cooked, as ingredient' is the cooked vegetable stalk, not a salt or seasoning. Using cooked celery in place of celery salt would change the flavour, since it would add no salinity and would not provide the concentrated savoury-seasoning taste. It would also change the dish's texture and appearance, and a diner would notice the difference. This is a different state (cooked vegetable vs. seasoning blend) and a blend vs. single-ingredient mismatch, so it fails both conditions.

The ingredient is refined palm oil, which is pressed from the fleshy mesocarp of the palm fruit and is high in palmitic acid. The USDA match is palm kernel oil, which is pressed from the seed kernel and is a lauric-type fat with a very different fatty acid profile, melting behaviour and flavour. Guideline F says a different oil is not substitutable, even when the two look close. Palm kernel oil is a sibling oil, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Using it would change the fat's melting point, texture and mouthfeel, and it would not be a neutral swap. Condition 1 (no change to preparation) and condition 2 (no detectable difference in taste or texture) are therefore not both met. The 45g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is a whole-wheat dinner roll (a wheat-flour yeast roll, typically made with whole wheat flour). The USDA entry 'Rolls, dinner, rye' is a dinner roll made with rye flour. Condition 1: a rye roll could physically replace a whole-wheat roll in a dish without changing preparation, since both are ready-made dinner rolls. Condition 2: rye flour gives a distinctly different flavour (earthy, sour, caraway-like notes often present) and a denser, darker crumb and appearance than whole-wheat flour. A diner would likely notice the difference in taste and appearance. Under the guidelines, a different flour is explicitly not substitutable (bread flour vs cake flour is given as an example; rye vs whole wheat is the same category of distinct grain flour with a different taste). Therefore the match fails condition 2.

The ingredient is 'carp fillets', which in a recipe is raw fish to be cooked as part of the dish. The USDA match is 'Fish, carp, cooked, dry heat', which is already cooked. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Using pre-cooked carp would change how the dish is prepared, since the fish would not be cooked during the recipe, and the texture and appearance would differ from raw fillets going through the cooking process. The weight is ignored per guideline A, and carp is the same species, so the mismatch is only in state (raw vs cooked by dry heat). Condition 1 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a frozen mixture of two different vegetables, pearl onions and peas. The USDA entry is only frozen chopped onions, which contains no peas. Under the guidelines, a single ingredient does not substitute for a blend that contains it (F). Condition 1 fails because replacing the mix with chopped onions alone would change the dish's composition. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the missing peas and the chopped rather than whole pearl onion shape. The quantity is ignored (A).

Piñon nuts are pine nuts, the same food under a regional name (guideline B). The USDA entry 'Nuts, pine nuts, dried' describes shelled pine nuts as normally bought, so no state or modification differs from what a shopper would buy under the plain name (guidelines C and D). The quantity (75g) is ignored (guideline A). Cooking method is unchanged because the nuts are used the same way, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 100g of chopped dates. The leading weight is ignored per guideline A. Dates are normally bought dried and pitted, and the USDA entry 'Date' names the same fruit with no modifying state, so it matches the generic food. Chopping is knife work that does not change the match (guideline C). Using the USDA date in place of chopped dates would not change the preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since the fruit is the same and only the cut differs. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a combination of two foods, hot dogs and sauerkraut, so it is a mixture. The USDA entry 'Hot dog, beef' covers only the hot dogs and contains no sauerkraut. Under guideline F, a single ingredient does not substitute for a blend that contains it. Condition 1 fails because using only the hot dog would omit a major component, which changes the dish's preparation and composition. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would clearly notice the absence of sauerkraut in taste, texture and appearance. The quantity and 'drained' wording do not change this.

The ingredient is dried tilapia, shredded, which is a preserved, dehydrated product with a dense, brittle texture and a concentrated, savoury flavour. The USDA match is 'Fish, tilapia, raw', which is fresh, uncooked fillet with moisture and a soft, flaky texture. Condition 1 fails: raw fish cannot be substituted for dried fish without changing how the dish is prepared. Dried fish typically needs no cooking or is used as a seasoning, while raw fish must be cooked and would also need rehydration or other handling. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in taste (dried, salted, intensified flavour), texture (dry, shredded, crisp versus moist and flaky), and appearance. The guidelines treat raw vs. dried states as different foods (rule F), so this is not a same-food-under-another-name case (rule B).

The ingredient is 'rice crackers' and the USDA match is 'Rice crackers', which is literally the same food. The leading '100g' is quantity and is ignored per the guidelines. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is the same product with no cooking or handling change. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is beef bologna, and the USDA entry 'Bologna, beef' names the same product: a beef bologna sausage. Per guideline B, the same food under another name counts as a match. The weight (150g) is ignored per guideline A. The entry names no modified state such as reduced fat or sodium, so guideline D does not reject it. Cooking method, flavour, texture and appearance are unchanged, since the diner would be eating the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain shredded chicken tenders, with no breading mentioned. The USDA entry is 'Chicken breast tenders, breaded, uncooked', which is a coated product. Breading changes the appearance, texture and flavour of the chicken, and a diner would notice the coating once the meat is shredded and cooked into the dish. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version is not substitutable. The USDA entry is also uncooked, while shredded chicken in a dish is normally cooked, which adds a further mismatch in preparation. Condition 2 fails, and the breading means the match would change the dish's texture and appearance, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a frozen wholemeal (whole wheat) flatbread. The USDA entry is chapati or roti, whole wheat, commercially prepared, frozen. Wholemeal is the British term for whole wheat, so the grain matches. Chapati and roti are unleavened whole wheat flatbreads, so the food is essentially the same product under a regional name, which guideline B covers. The entry is also frozen and commercially prepared, matching the ingredient's frozen state (guideline E). Nothing in the USDA entry suggests a modified version such as added fats, sweetening or flavouring. Condition 1 holds: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 holds: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance between a frozen whole wheat flatbread and a frozen whole wheat chapati/roti. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is double-acting baking powder, a standard leavening product. The USDA entry is the same product type, specifically the double-acting form, and names its common acid system, sodium aluminum sulfate, which is the typical composition of double-acting baking powder. Guideline D treats a descriptor that reflects how the product is normally sold as not a modification. Baking powder is used in the same way (mixed into dry ingredients, activated by moisture and heat), so the preparation method does not change. In a baked product, a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the leavening action is the same. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is swordfish steak, a specific species of large predatory fish with firm, dense, meaty flesh and a mild, slightly sweet flavour. The USDA match is Atlantic farmed salmon, raw. Salmon and swordfish are different species, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1: salmon is a fatty, flaky fish with a distinct oily texture; cooking swordfish steak (grilling, searing, broiling) and salmon fillet would differ in handling, cooking time, and doneness expectations, so the preparation would change. Condition 2: a diner would readily notice the difference in flavour (salmon is richer and more oily, swordfish milder and meatier), texture (swordfish is firmer and steak-like, salmon flakes more readily), and appearance (swordfish is pale ivory to light pink, salmon is orange-pink with visible fat lines). Guideline F also treats a different species with a different taste as not substitutable. Both conditions fail, so the match is not acceptable.

The ingredient is a specific cut, duck breast, which is the lean, light meat of the bird and is typically cooked medium-rare with the skin scored or rendered. The USDA entry 'Duck, domesticated, meat only, raw' is the generic meat of the whole bird, mixing breast with darker, tougher leg and thigh meat, and excludes skin. Guideline E allows frozen-then-thawed meat to match fresh meat when freezing does not show, but guideline F says a different cut of meat is not substitutable. Using mixed whole-bird meat would change the texture (leg meat is firmer and needs longer cooking) and the flavour and appearance of a breast-based dish, and it would drop the skin that duck breast usually carries. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (diner would notice) are therefore not met.

The ingredient is fenugreek seed, a dried aromatic spice seed used whole or ground in curries and spice blends, contributing a distinctive bitter, maple-like flavour. The USDA match is 'Liver, paste or pate', a meat product (animal organ spread). These are not the same food under different names, and they are entirely different categories (spice seed vs animal offal product). Using liver pate in place of fenugreek would change the flavour, texture and appearance of the dish completely, and a diner would immediately notice. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) both fail.

The ingredient is young kohlrabi, peeled and sliced, which is simply kohlrabi (the bulb of the same vegetable) prepared with standard knife work and peeling. The USDA entry 'Kohlrabi, raw' is the same food in uncooked form. Per the guidelines, peeling and slicing do not change the match, and the quantity (495g) is ignored. Youth/size of the bulb is the same vegetable, not a sibling variety. Substituting raw kohlrabi keeps the preparation the same and a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is fresh sliced rose apple (Syzygium species, also called wax apple or jambu), a different fruit from the apple (Malus domestica). The USDA match is dried apple, which is Malus domestica in dehydrated form. Rose apple is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. The match also fails on state: fresh versus dried (guideline F). Dried apple is chewy, concentrated and sweet, while fresh rose apple is crisp, watery and mildly floral. A diner would notice the texture and flavour difference, and the dish would not be prepared the same way. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well.

The ingredient is a canned ham hock, a specific cut (the lower leg/shank portion, typically sold with bone and connective tissue). The USDA match is 'Ham, chopped, canned', a processed, finely chopped or formed ham product. Guideline F says a different cut of meat is not substitutable. Using chopped canned ham would also change texture and appearance: a hock gives whole pieces of meat, gelatinous connective tissue and a bone-derived richness, while chopped ham gives uniform small pieces. Cooking method and dish appearance would change, and a diner would likely notice the difference. Drained weight and knife work do not bridge this gap. The two conditions are not both met.

The ingredient is pork sirloin, a lean cut from the hip/loin area of the pig. The USDA match is pork belly, raw, a fatty cut from the underside of the pig. Per guideline F, a different cut of meat is not substitutable, even though both are pork. Substituting belly for sirloin would change the fat content, texture, and cooking behaviour (belly renders fat and becomes tender with long cooking, whereas sirloin is lean and dries out if overcooked), and a diner would notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails. The weight is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is wild rice cooked with butter. The USDA entry 'Rice, wild, 100%, cooked, fat added' is the same food (100% wild rice, cooked) with the same added-fat component. The '100%' descriptor confirms it is pure wild rice, not a blend. The USDA 'fat added' wording is the standard descriptor for rice cooked with a fat, as in guideline C's buttered peas example, so it names the same dish with the same components. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are cooked wild rice finished with fat. Condition 2: a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the fat is a minor component and the rice is the same. Both conditions are met.

Hoshigaki is the Japanese name for dried persimmon, made by peeling, air-drying and kneading the fruit. The USDA entry 'Persimmon, dried' is the same food under a generic name, so it passes the same-food-under-another-name test (guideline B). Condition 1: the match needs no change to preparation, since the ingredient is used as a dried fruit in the same way. Condition 2: the USDA entry is the plain default dried persimmon (guideline D), and a diner would not reliably taste or see a difference. Hoshigaki's natural sugar bloom and soft chewy texture are variations within the same product type, not a different food. Quantity is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned turkey, drained. The USDA entry 'Turkey, canned' names the same food in the same packed form. 'Drained' is handling that removes packing liquid and does not change the match (guideline C). The entry is the standard default version with no modifier such as low sodium or flavoured (guideline D). Using it in place of the ingredient would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Condition on the sodium part is met: the ingredient asks for reduced-salt, and the USDA entry is lower sodium. The problem is the meat. 'Italian sausage' with no meat named defaults to pork, and the USDA entry is chicken or turkey. Under guideline F, a different meat changes the product's flavour, fat profile and appearance. Chicken or turkey Italian sausage is paler, leaner and tastes noticeably different, so a diner would likely notice. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

Condition 1 (same cooking method/preparation): The ingredient is a smoked, boneless turkey drumstick. The USDA entry is smoked, cooked, bone removed, so the smoking state and boneless preparation match. Smoked turkey drumstick is normally sold already cooked, so the 'cooked' descriptor is the standard form and does not change how the dish is prepared. The 100g quantity is ignored per guideline A. The ingredient does not specify skin, so the USDA 'with skin' descriptor is the default for a smoked drumstick and is not a modification. Condition 2 (diner would not notice a difference): Smoked, cooked, boneless turkey drumstick meat would taste and feel the same as the USDA entry. The skin detail is not specified in the ingredient, so no visible difference can be assumed. Both conditions are met.

The USDA entry is plain fried tofu prepared with calcium sulfate, with no seasoning or glaze. The ingredient is fried tofu finished with a sweet soy glaze. The glaze changes the flavour (sweet and savoury, not neutral) and the appearance (darker, sticky surface), so condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference. The cooking step also differs, since the glaze is applied or cooked onto the tofu, so condition 1 is not met either. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to a flavoured or modified version as not substitutable, and the sweet soy glaze is exactly that kind of added flavour. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is green plantain. Green plantain is an unripe plantain, which is the same food as the USDA entry 'Plantains, underripe, raw'. The only difference is the name, so guideline B applies. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since both are raw, unripe plantain. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because both describe the same unripe fruit. The leading '400g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is turkey bologna, and the USDA entry is 'Bologna, turkey', which is the same food under a reversed name. The 305g quantity is decoration and is ignored. Condition 1: turkey bologna can be used in place of itself with no change to preparation, since it is used the same way (sliced, diced, or cooked as the recipe directs). Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the USDA entry describes the same product with no added modification, flavour, or cut. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain margarine, the standard fat product. The USDA match is a light, reduced-fat margarine-like spread (SMART BALANCE Light Buttery Spread). Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a 'light' or reduced-fat version is a modification, so it fails. Condition 1: a spread with much lower fat and higher water content would change how a dish behaves in cooking and baking, such as browning, texture, and structure. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice a difference in richness, texture, and mouthfeel, especially in baked goods or sauteed dishes. Both conditions fail. The quantity (30g) is irrelevant.

The ingredient is goat meat, and the USDA entry is 'Game meat, goat, raw', which is the same food under a category-style name. The weight is decoration and is ignored. The entry is raw, which matches fresh goat meat as bought. Condition 1: goat meat can replace the USDA goat meat without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same meat in the same raw state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient 'salsa roja' is Spanish for 'red salsa', so the USDA entry 'Salsa, red' names the same food under a translated name (guideline B). The weight '75g' is ignored (guideline A). The USDA entry has no modifier such as low-sodium, reduced-fat, or frozen, so it is the plain default version (guideline D). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the same way, serving it as a condiment or mixing it in with no change to preparation. Condition 2: the USDA entry is the generic red salsa, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance beyond normal recipe-to-recipe variation in homemade versus commercial salsa. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is an all-beef hot dog, and the USDA match is a turkey hot dog. The quantity is irrelevant. Condition 1 is arguably met, since a turkey hot dog could be cooked and served in the same way. Condition 2 fails: turkey and beef have clearly different flavour, texture, fat content and appearance, and a diner would notice the difference. Turkey hot dogs are a different product from beef hot dogs, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Per guideline F, a different meat source is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a frozen raw ribeye steak, which is the same cut of beef. The USDA entry is the same cut, so the food identity matches and the frozen state would not show after thawing (guideline E). The problem is the state. USDA's 'lean and fat eaten' wording describes the edible portion as it is served, which is normally cooked, not raw. Cooking the raw steak versus using a cooked-state entry would change appearance, texture and flavour. The entry names no raw state, so it cannot be treated as the raw steak. Because the match appears to describe a cooked product, it would alter the preparation and be noticeable to a diner, so it fails both conditions. This reading rests on the usual meaning of 'eaten' in USDA naming; if the entry were raw, the answer would change.

1. The ingredient is fresh durian, a single fruit with no modification, cooking, or processing stated. The USDA entry 'Durian, raw or frozen' explicitly includes raw durian, which is the same food as fresh durian. The 'raw or frozen' wording covers the fresh state, so this is not a frozen-only match. 2. Condition 1: the raw entry can replace fresh durian without changing preparation, since no cooking or handling step is implied. 3. Condition 2: a diner eating raw durian would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the entry describes the same raw fruit. The frozen option is an alternative that is also listed, but it does not change the match, since the raw state the ingredient calls for is included. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is toasted, unsalted white bread. The USDA entry is white bread, commercially prepared, toasted, low sodium, no salt. Guideline D says a plain ingredient matched to a modified entry is normally a no, but here the ingredient itself asks for the unsalted version, so the matching no-salt entry counts. Weight '10g' is ignored (guideline A). The toasted state matches, so there is no cooking-method or state mismatch. The 'low sodium no salt' descriptor describes the same unsalted product, so the food is the same. Condition 1 holds: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 holds: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance between unsalted toasted white bread and this entry, since it contains no added salt in either case. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh marjoram leaves. The USDA match is dried marjoram. Guideline F explicitly lists fresh vs dried herb as a state difference that is not substitutable. Drying concentrates and changes the flavour, and the leaves differ in texture and appearance (dried leaves are brittle and greyish-green, while fresh leaves are soft and bright green). Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in flavour and appearance. The 12g quantity is irrelevant under guideline A. Condition 1 may hold in a loose sense, but both conditions must be met.

The ingredient is raw croaker fillets, which are uncooked fish to be cooked as the recipe directs. The USDA entry is croaker that is already cooked, breaded and fried. Condition 1 fails: using pre-fried, breaded fish would change the cooking method, since the recipe would be prepared with a finished product instead of raw fillets. Condition 2 also fails: the breading, the fried coating, the oil absorbed during frying, and the altered texture and appearance would all be noticeable. Under guideline F, raw versus cooked is a different state, and the breaded/fried preparation adds further differences. The ignored quantity (250g) does not affect this.

The ingredient is plain sliced American cheese, the standard full-fat product. The USDA match is 'Cheese, American, reduced fat', which is a modified version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a reduced/low-fat version is not substitutable. Reduced-fat American cheese has a different fat content, which changes its melt, mouthfeel, and flavour, so a diner could notice the difference. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste or texture) are both at risk, and guideline D settles it: not substitutable.

West Indian cherry is a regional name for the acerola (Malpighia emarginata), so the USDA entry 'Acerola, (west indian cherry), raw' is literally the same fruit under another name. The USDA entry is raw, which matches the unspecified fresh fruit in the recipe. The quantity prefix '200g' is decoration and is ignored. Because it is the same food, it can be used without changing preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plant-based mayonnaise, an eggless mayonnaise made with plant-based emulsifiers and oils. The USDA entry, 'Vegan mayonnaise', names the same product under a different label. Plant-based and vegan mayonnaise are the same food, so this is a same-food-different-name match (guideline B). The quantity (15g) is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any dish without changing preparation, since both are used as a spread, dressing or binder in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because they are the same product category with the same sensory profile. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is soft margarine, a plain product with no specified oil blend, brand, or fat content. The USDA entry is a tub margarine at 80% fat, which is the standard fat level for soft tub margarine, and it is a soft spread, the same product type. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. The oil blend (canola, palm, palm kernel) is simply how this brand is made, and the ingredient does not ask for any particular oil, so guideline F's different-oil rule does not apply. Condition 1: it can replace soft margarine in the same preparation without changing the method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since soft tub margarine varies by brand in exactly this way. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked bratwurst, and the USDA entry is Bratwurst, beef and pork, smoked. Both name the same product in the same state (smoked), so the processing state does not differ. The ingredient does not specify meat composition, so the USDA beef-and-pork blend is the standard default version of bratwurst. Condition 1: the sausage can be used directly in place of the ingredient, and the cooking method (reheating, frying, grilling, or slicing) stays the same. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the product is the same smoked bratwurst. The weight is ignored per the guidelines. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh swimming crab meat, which in trade usage refers to Portunus-genus swimming crabs (e.g., blue swimmer or Asian swimming crab). The USDA entry is Crustaceans, crab, blue, raw, which is Callinectes sapidus, the North American blue crab. These are related swimming crabs in the same family, but they are different species, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F treats a sibling variety with a different taste as not substitutable. Blue crab and Portunus crabs differ in meat sweetness, firmness and flavour, which a diner could plausibly notice. The USDA entry also describes a raw whole crab rather than picked meat, which adds a further mismatch in form. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste or texture) is therefore not reliably met, so the match is not substitutable.

1. The ingredient is extra firm tofu. The match is Vitasoy USA Azumaya Firm Tofu, a branded firm tofu. It is the same food type (soy curd) but a different firmness grade. 2. Extra firm tofu is pressed to lower water content, so it is denser, holds its shape under frying, cubing, or stir-frying, and has a chewier, less crumbly bite. Firm tofu is softer and more likely to break apart or absorb more liquid in the same preparation. 3. Condition 1: substituting firm tofu can change how the dish is handled, such as needing gentler stirring, longer pressing, or different cooking to keep cubes intact. Condition 2: a diner could plausibly notice the softer texture and looser crumb, so the two products differ in texture, which the guidelines treat as a substantive difference. 4. Because the texture difference is noticeable and can change preparation, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried mackerel, which is preserved by salting and then air- or sun-drying, giving a hard, dehydrated, low-moisture product. The USDA match, 'Fish, mackerel, salted', describes a salted fish that is not dried, so it keeps a much higher moisture content and a softer, moister texture. Condition 1 fails: dried fish is typically rehydrated, shredded, pounded, or fried before use, and a moist salted fillet would change the preparation. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (chewy and dense versus moist and flaky) and in concentrated, savoury flavour. Guideline F treats different preservation states as non-substitutable, as with fresh versus dried herbs, so the match is rejected.

The ingredient is stewed gooseberries, which are gooseberries (Ribes genus) that have been cooked, usually with sugar, so they are soft and sweetened. The USDA match is Groundcherries (cape gooseberries or poha), raw. Cape gooseberries and poha are Physalis species, a different plant family from the true gooseberry, so this is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). The match is also raw, while the ingredient is stewed, which is a cooking-state difference (guideline F). Using raw Physalis in place of stewed gooseberries would change the preparation, the flavour (tart and tropical rather than stewed gooseberry), the texture (firm and whole rather than soft), and the appearance (small golden husked fruit rather than stewed green or red berries). A diner would notice the difference. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is goose fat, an animal fat used for cooking (roasting, frying, confit). The USDA match is 'Flour, soy, full-fat', which is a soybean flour product, not a fat at all. Condition 1 fails: using soy flour in place of goose fat would change how the dish is prepared (it cannot provide fat for frying or roasting, and would alter the cooking medium and the structure of the dish). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in flavour (no poultry richness), texture (flour versus fat), and appearance. Per guideline F, a different fat or a processed ingredient from a different source is not substitutable. The match therefore fails both conditions.

The ingredient is tempeh that has been fried, so it is crisp, browned, and has absorbed oil. The USDA entry 'Tempeh, cooked' is the generic cooked form, usually steamed or simmered, with no frying. Condition 1 fails: using the plain cooked tempeh would change the preparation, because the dish would need frying added. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (soft versus crisp), appearance (no golden browning), and flavour (no fried or oil character). Guideline F treats a different state of preparation as a non-match, so this is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a cooked eye of round roast, sliced. The USDA entry is the same cut (eye of round roast, beef round), cooked and roasted. Slicing is knife work and does not change the match. The entry's 'trimmed to 0" fat, select' descriptor is a trim level, and a plain 'eye of round roast' is normally sold with little external fat, so this is the default version rather than a modified one. The cooking state matches, so the dish would not be prepared differently. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance between the lean-trimmed USDA roast and a typical eye of round roast. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain cocoa powder, sold dry. The USDA entry 'Cocoa powder, not reconstituted' names the same food in its dry, as-bought state. 'Not reconstituted' only confirms it is the dry powder rather than a prepared drink or mix, which is how cocoa powder is normally sold. The entry carries no modifier such as sweetened, flavoured, or reduced-fat, so it is the standard default version (Guideline D). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not detect a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

Pinyon nuts are the edible seeds of pinyon pines, which belong to the pine genus, and they are commonly sold and labelled as pine nuts. This makes the USDA entry 'Nuts, pine nuts, dried' the same food under a regional/trade name (guideline B). The 'dried' descriptor matches how pine nuts are normally sold as shelled, dried kernels, so it is the standard default product. Grinding is handling done at home and does not change the match (guideline C). The weight '16g' is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the nuts can replace the ingredient in the same preparation without changing the method. Condition 2: pinyon and other pine nuts share a similar mild, rich, buttery flavour and soft texture, and once ground they would look and taste essentially the same to a diner. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 500g fresh ground pork; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Pork, fresh, ground, raw' is the same food: fresh (not cured or cooked) ground pork in its raw state. Guideline C notes that 'raw' means uncooked and that grinding is handling, so 'ground' and 'raw' fit the recipe's uncooked fresh ground pork. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation, since it is the same product. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

Step 1: Identify the ingredient. Orange roughy is a deep-sea fish (Hoplostethus atlanticus), not a regional or trade name for Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua), so guideline B does not apply. The match is a different species. Step 2: Check condition 1, preparation. Both are white fish fillets that could be cooked the same way, so preparation alone would not block substitution. Step 3: Check condition 2, taste and texture. Orange roughy has a softer, moister, more delicate flake and a richer, oilier mouthfeel than cod, and its flavour is distinct. A diner familiar with either fish would plausibly notice the difference. Guideline F rejects sibling varieties with different taste, and a different species of fish with a noticeably different texture falls under the same logic. Step 4: Condition 2 is not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is green goddess dressing, and the USDA entry is 'Salad dressing, green goddess, regular', which names the same product. The leading '250g' is only a quantity and is ignored. 'Regular' is the standard default version rather than a modified one (such as reduced-fat or light), so it matches the plain product a shopper would buy. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the same way, with no change to preparation, since it is the same dressing used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product type. Both conditions are met.

Boiler onions are small whole onions, usually white, sold as a size grade for boiling or pickling rather than a different species or variety. The USDA entry 'Onions, white, raw' is the same food. The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Raw means uncooked, and the recipe's own handling (peeling, boiling) does not change the match. Both conditions hold: the match can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance.

Step 1: The leading '30g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). The ingredient is a canned diet shake, a ready-to-drink meal-replacement shake. The USDA entry is a ready-to-drink nutritional shake, branded Slim-Fast, which is a canned diet shake brand. Step 2: Condition 1 is met. A ready-to-drink shake can be added to a dish in the same way as a canned diet shake, with no change to cooking method or preparation. Step 3: Condition 2 is met on the guideline's terms. The ingredient does not specify a flavour or brand, so the USDA entry is the same plain product type (a branded ready-to-drink diet/protein shake), which guideline G treats as a match. Flavour varies between brands, but the ingredient does not name one, so no specific difference is indicated. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is plain provolone cheese, the standard full-fat default. The USDA match is 'Cheese, provolone, reduced fat', which is a modified version. Guideline D says a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced/low-fat version is not substitutable, because the modification is not how provolone is normally sold. Condition 1 is arguably met, since it could be melted or sliced in the same way. Condition 2 fails: reduced-fat cheese typically has a firmer, drier texture, less melt, and a milder, less rich flavour, which a diner could notice. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is semolina flour, which is milled durum wheat semolina. The USDA entry 'Flour, semolina, fine' is the same product: semolina flour, with 'fine' describing a standard grind that a shopper would normally buy under the plain name. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to its standard default version as a match. The ingredient does not specify a coarse grind, so no modification is being asked for. Guideline F rejects different flours such as bread versus cake flour, but this is a grind descriptor on the same flour type, not a different flour. Cooking method is unchanged (it is used the same way in any recipe), and a diner would not notice a difference in taste or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cassava flour, and the USDA entry 'Flour, cassava' names the same product under a slightly different word order. Condition 1: cassava flour can replace the USDA food directly, since it is the same plain flour and the dish is prepared the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. The quantity (50g) is irrelevant. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'ground pumpkin seeds', meaning the seeds have been reduced to a meal or powder. The USDA entry is 'Seeds, pumpkin and squash seed kernels, dried', which describes whole dried kernels. Condition 1: Guideline C lists grinding at home as an allowed handling step only for meat or fish, so it does not carry over to seeds. Using whole kernels where ground seeds are called for would change how the dish is prepared (it would need grinding, or would not blend or coat the same way). Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance, since whole kernels show as distinct pieces while ground seeds give a fine, uniform meal. Guideline F also treats whole versus ground as a different state. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is pork tail, and the USDA entry is 'Pork, fresh, variety meats and by-products, tail, raw', which is the same food, named by its anatomical cut. Under guideline B, a literal same-food match counts. The quantity (235g) is ignored per guideline A. The entry is raw, which matches a plain uncooked ingredient, and any knife work or handling in the recipe does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same raw cut. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is hazelnut oil, a specific pressed oil used for serving. The USDA match is 'Hazelnuts', which is the whole nut itself, not an oil. Under guideline F, a different oil or fat is not substitutable, and the raw source versus processed ingredient is also a mismatch (the raw plant/source vs the processed ingredient). Condition 1 fails: a whole nut cannot be used in place of a drizzled oil for serving without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (a liquid oil versus solid nut pieces) and in taste/appearance. The quantity (35g) is ignored per guideline A.

Ingredient: plain low-fat yogurt, 250g (quantity ignored per guideline A). USDA match: 'Yogurt, plain, low fat'. Condition 1: the USDA entry is the same food with the same modification (low fat) and the same plain flavour, so it can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation method. Condition 2: a diner would not perceive a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the product is literally the same plain low-fat yogurt. The ingredient explicitly asks for the low-fat version, so the matching low-fat entry is correct per guideline D. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Monterey Jack cheese, a dairy cheese made from cow's milk. The USDA entry is 'Fish, mackerel, jack, canned, drained solids', which is jack mackerel, a fish. These are not the same food under another name, and the match fails condition 1: a fish cannot be used in place of cheese without changing the dish's preparation, since melting, grating or slicing behaviour and the whole cooking method would differ. It also fails condition 2: a diner would immediately notice fish instead of cheese in flavour, texture and appearance. The shared word 'jack' is coincidental and does not indicate the same food. Guideline B does not apply because this is not a regional or trade name for cheese. Guideline F's principle that a different food is not substitutable applies here.

The ingredient is unsweetened almond milk. The USDA match is 'Almond milk, sweetened'. Guideline D states that a plain ingredient mapped to a modified version (sweetened/unsweetened) is not a match, and sweetened/unsweetened is explicitly listed as a modification. Condition 1: substituting sweetened almond milk for unsweetened would change the dish's flavour, since added sugar would be present in a savoury or unsweetened preparation, and it could affect cooking behaviour in sauces or batters. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the added sweetness in taste. Therefore neither condition is reliably satisfied, and the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is unsalted butter, a dairy fat made from churned cream with a rich, smooth, mild flavour and a spreadable, melting texture. The USDA match is feta cheese, a brined, crumbly, salty, tangy sheep's or goat's milk cheese. Condition 1: butter cannot be replaced by feta without changing how the dish is prepared. Butter is used for creaming, melting, sautéing, and emulsifying; feta does not melt or emulsify into fat in the same way and would be a solid crumbly addition rather than a fat. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste (salty, sharp, tangy versus neutral and sweet-creamy), texture (crumbly versus smooth/melting), and appearance. The entry is a different food entirely, not a name variant or a processing form of butter, so guideline B does not apply. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

Ingredient is almond butter, a plain ground almond spread. USDA entry is 'Almond butter' with no modifier, so it is the same plain product under the same name. Quantity (5g) is ignored per guideline A. Preparation: a spread used as-is in a recipe, so no change in cooking method. Taste, texture and appearance match the default product, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'pickled fish' and the USDA entry is 'Fish, pickled'. These name the same food with the same state (pickled, not raw or cooked), so the match is literal, not a different product. The weight '150g' is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match is the same food, so it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: because it is the same pickled fish, a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sriracha, a chili-garlic hot sauce. The USDA entry 'Sauce, hot chile, sriracha, TUONG OT SRIRACHA' is a branded sriracha, the same plain product type. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product counts as a match, and the entry adds no extra flavour or modification. The 120g weight is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Used in place of sriracha, it would not change preparation, and a diner would not taste a difference, since it is the same condiment. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh cockles, a bivalve mollusc. The USDA entry is 'Cockles, raw (Alaska Native)', which is the same food. 'Fresh' corresponds to 'raw' (uncooked), and the '(Alaska Native)' qualifier is a source or regional designation for the same species rather than a processing change or modified version. The weight (200g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the cockles could be used directly in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not detect a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same food in the same raw state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a combination of two components: cavatappi (dried pasta) and marinara sauce. The USDA entry covers only the sauce, 'Sauce, pasta, spaghetti/marinara, ready-to-serve', and has no pasta component. Condition 1 fails because using only the sauce would omit the pasta, so the dish would not be prepared the same way. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the missing pasta. The quantity (25g) is ignored per guideline A. Because the match covers only one of the two components, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a mixture of two foods, dates and walnuts, chopped. The USDA match, 'Dates, medjool', covers only the dates. Condition 1 fails: using dates alone would omit the walnuts, so the dish would be prepared with a different set of ingredients. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the missing walnut texture, crunch and flavour. Per guideline F, a single ingredient does not substitute for a blend or combination containing it. The 100g quantity and the 'chopped' handling are irrelevant to this mismatch.

The ingredient is grilled hot dog buns, meaning the bread rolls only. The USDA entry is a prepared sandwich: a beef hot dog served on a white bun. It contains a meat component the ingredient does not include, so it is a different food rather than the same food under another name. Using it would add a beef frank to the dish, which a diner would notice, so condition 2 fails. It also cannot be used in place of plain buns without changing the dish's contents, so condition 1 fails. The 'grilled' preparation is not reflected in the entry either. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 400g egg noodle (a dried or fresh pasta made with egg, cooked in boiling water as a starch component). The USDA match is 'Noodle pudding', which is a baked or set dessert dish typically made from cooked noodles combined with eggs, sugar, dairy, and often raisins or fruit, then baked. Condition 1 fails: egg noodles are a plain pasta boiled and served or stir-fried, whereas the match is a composed sweet dish that is baked, so using it in place of egg noodles would fundamentally change how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would readily notice a sweet, custard-like baked pudding instead of plain noodles in taste, texture, and appearance. The match is a different food product, not a naming variant of egg noodles, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'pork bones', meaning bones themselves, typically used for stock or braising. The USDA entry is a specific cut, pork loin backribs, bone-in, lean only. It is not the same food under another name. It is a meat cut with the fat trimmed away, so it carries less fat, collagen and marrow than typical pork bones, and it is a different cut from whatever the bones would come from. Guideline F says a different cut of meat is not substitutable. In a dish where the bones are simmered for stock or flavour, a diner would likely notice a difference in richness, body and taste. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) are not both met. The quantity is ignored, per guideline A.

The ingredient is raw squid, sliced (the slicing is knife work and does not change the match). The USDA entry 'Rice with squid, Puerto Rican style' is a prepared dish containing rice, sofrito, and other ingredients, not squid as a standalone food. Condition 1 fails: using this dish in place of sliced squid would change the preparation, since the squid would be cooked with rice and seasonings rather than used as a raw/prepared squid ingredient. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice rice and seasoning in place of plain squid, altering taste, texture and appearance. This is a blend/composite dish versus a single ingredient, which the guidelines explicitly reject.

The ingredient is plain whipping cream. In most markets it is a 30-36% milkfat cream sold under the name 'whipping cream', which is what USDA's 'Cream, fluid, light whipping' describes. The USDA entry is the standard default version of the same product, with no added flavour, modification or different state. Whipping cream and light whipping cream are used the same way: they are whipped, poured, or folded in without changing the method. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable. The 75g quantity is ignored per the guidelines.

The ingredient is 75g of d'Anjou pears with skin on. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. D'Anjou is a pear cultivar, and the USDA entry 'Pear, Anjou, green, with skin, raw' is the same variety, described with the standard descriptor of its colour (green), which is how Anjou pears are normally sold. 'Skin on' matches 'with skin'. Raw is correct for fresh pears used in a dish, and no cooking method change is implied. Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same variety with skin intact. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh passion fruit, the whole raw fruit with pulp, seeds, and a tart, concentrated flavour. The USDA match is passion fruit nectar, a processed beverage made from the fruit pulp diluted with water and typically sweetened. Condition 1 fails: nectar cannot replace whole fruit in a recipe without changing its preparation, since the fruit's seeds, pulp, and structure are gone and the liquid adds volume and sugar. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (no seeds or pulp), concentration of flavour, and sweetness. This is a raw food versus a processed product, which guideline F rules out. The weight is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is canned peas and carrots, drained. The USDA entry is canned peas and carrots, regular pack, solids and liquids, which is the same dish with the same components. Draining is handling that the recipe does itself, so under guideline C it does not change the match. Regular pack is the standard default for canned vegetables, so no modified version is involved. The 'solids and liquids' wording describes the whole can as USDA records it, and the drained ingredient is just the solids. Using the drained solids in place of the entry would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is queso fresco, crumbled (50g; quantity ignored). The USDA entry 'Cheese, queso fresco, solid' is the same food under the same name. Crumbling is handling done by the recipe and does not change the match (guideline C). Queso fresco is a fresh cheese normally bought and used in crumbled form, so the USDA entry describes the same default product. 'Solid' is a standard descriptor for a block/cheese form and does not indicate a modified version. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient without altering preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same cheese. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain radish (quantity 245g is ignored). The USDA match is 'Radish', which is the generic raw radish entry, the same food under the same name. Radish matches the plain ingredient with the standard default preparation. Condition 1: radishes can be used in place of radishes without any change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same vegetable. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cornmeal mush prepared without added fat, and the USDA entry is 'Cornmeal mush, no added fat', which names the same dish with the same no-added-fat qualifier. Condition 1: the match is the same food, so it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: since it is the same food with the same preparation, a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The 400g quantity is ignored per the guidelines. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a smoked lamb rack, which is lamb that has been smoked. The USDA entry is raw lamb rack (New Zealand, partly frenched, lean only), with no smoking. Guideline F states that plain versus smoked is a different state and not substitutable. Smoking changes the flavour and appearance (smoke aroma, darker surface, different taste), and a diner would notice the difference. Quantity and the frenching/trimming descriptors do not change the verdict, since the decisive mismatch is the smoked versus raw state. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is oven-roasted chicken white meat, which is chicken breast meat that has been cooked by roasting. The USDA entry is 'Chicken, broilers or fryers, breast, meat only, cooked, roasted', which is the same food: broiler/fryer chicken breast, meat only (no skin), cooked by roasting. The leading '100g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the match is already roasted and cooked, so it can replace the ingredient without changing the preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not detect a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since both are roasted white meat. Both conditions are met.

Step 1: The ingredient is plain 'ground turkey' with no lean ratio specified. The USDA match is raw ground turkey at 85% lean / 15% fat, which is a standard default ground turkey product that shoppers commonly buy under that name. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to the standard default version as a match. Step 2: Ground turkey is prepared the same way (browned, crumbled, mixed, or formed) regardless of the fat ratio within the common range, and the 85/15 product is the usual version, so the diner would not expect a visibly or texturally different dish. The quantity (245g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain pork rinds, which are fried or puffed pork skin snacks. The USDA entry 'Snacks, pork skins, plain' describes the same food under a common alternate name (pork skins = pork rinds), with no added flavour or modification. Condition 1: it can be substituted without changing preparation, since it is the same product whether crushed for breading or eaten as is. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. The 300g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is frozen yellow summer squash that has been cooked. The USDA entry is frozen, cooked summer squash, yellow or green, with no added fat. Yellow summer squash is one of the summer squashes the entry explicitly covers, so the food is the same. Condition 1: the match is frozen and cooked like the ingredient, so it can replace it without changing the preparation. The 'no added fat' descriptor reflects the plain cooked default, since the ingredient names no added fat, so it is not a modification under guideline D. Condition 2: yellow and green summer squash are closely similar in taste, texture and appearance once cooked, and the entry names yellow explicitly, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 25g brown butter (butter cooked until its milk solids brown, giving a nutty, toasted flavour). The USDA match is Lemon-butter sauce, a prepared sauce made from butter with added lemon juice (and typically other seasonings), so it is a different product with an added flavouring. Condition 1: substituting it would change the preparation, since brown butter is made by cooking butter in the pan, whereas lemon-butter sauce is a ready-made flavoured product that adds acidity and citrus. Condition 2: a diner would taste the lemon and lack the toasted, nutty brown-butter flavour, and the sauce's appearance and texture also differ. Per guideline F (a different state or flavoured/modified product is not equivalent) and D (flavoured versions are not the plain default), neither condition is met. The weight is irrelevant (guideline A).

The ingredient is frozen lima beans that have been thawed, with no cooking method specified. Guideline E maps a thawed frozen product to the frozen USDA entry of the same product. The match 'Lima beans, from frozen' is the same food in its frozen form. 'No added fat' describes the USDA preparation default for this product (cooked and drained with no fat added), not a modified version like reduced-sodium or low-fat. Lima beans are normally cooked within a recipe, so the thawed beans would be prepared the same way, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient 'cow brain' is beef brain, the same food under a different name, so guideline B applies. The USDA entry 'Beef, variety meats and by-products, brain, raw' is the raw beef brain. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same raw tissue and the recipe handling is unchanged. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. The 125g weight is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 100g of rockfish fillets, which is a raw, uncooked ingredient that the recipe will cook itself. The USDA match is 'Fish, rockfish, Pacific, mixed species, cooked, dry heat', so it describes an already-cooked product. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Using the cooked entry would change how the dish is prepared, since the fish would already be cooked, and a diner would notice differences in texture and appearance. Condition 1 fails, so the match is not substitutable. The species (Pacific rockfish, mixed species) is a reasonable match, and the leading weight is ignored per guideline A, but the cooked state alone is disqualifying.

The ingredient 'rose apple' is the same fruit as the USDA entry 'Rose-apples, raw'; the USDA name is the literal name of the food. The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A. The entry is raw, and the recipe is not known to involve any cooking or processing that would make it differ, so the default raw version applies. Neither the preparation method, flavour, texture, nor appearance would change, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

1. The ingredient is generic chocolate puffed cereal, a crisp, puffed-grain cereal with cocoa flavour. The USDA entry, COCOA PEBBLES by POST, is a branded chocolate-flavoured puffed rice cereal, which is the same product type. 2. Guideline G says a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. Cocoa Pebbles is not a modified or added-flavour version of a plain item, because chocolate puffed cereal is itself the flavoured product. 3. Condition 1: it can be used directly with no change to preparation, since both are eaten or mixed as ready-to-eat cereal. 4. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in the general taste, crunch, or appearance. Minor brand-level variation exists, but the guidelines treat the branded same-type product as equivalent. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh (raw) scallops, which are uncooked and will be cooked as part of the recipe. The USDA match is 'Scallops, grilled', a cooked product. Per guideline F, raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Using grilled scallops would change the cooking method, since they are already cooked, and the diner would notice a difference in texture, flavour and appearance (char, firmness, colour). The quantity is ignored. Condition 1 fails because the preparation changes, and condition 2 fails because taste and texture differ.

The ingredient is gouda cheese, a semi-hard Dutch cheese with a richer, sweeter, nuttier flavour that deepens with age. The USDA match is edam, a different Dutch cheese with a milder, saltier, less buttery taste, a firmer texture, and typically lower fat content. They are not the same food under another name. Condition 1: edam can be grated or sliced in the same way, but swapping it changes the cheese itself. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the milder flavour and different melt and appearance, especially with the red-wax or yellow-rind distinctions. Since the two are sibling varieties with different taste, this is not substitutable under guideline F.

The ingredient is cooked king crab, and the USDA entry is Alaska king crab, cooked by moist heat. Alaska king crab is the species sold as king crab, so this is the same food under a standard name (guideline B). The ingredient is already cooked, and the USDA entry is cooked, so the match does not require a different preparation (condition 1). Moist-heat cooking is how king crab is normally cooked and sold, so a diner should not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance (condition 2). The quantity is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chuck steak, a cut from the beef chuck. The USDA entry 'Beef, steak, chuck' names the same cut. Guideline B treats the same food under another name as a match, and guideline C says handling such as trimming does not change the match. The quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match is the same cut, so it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cut. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is cream cheese, a soft, smooth, high-fat, tangy fresh cheese. The USDA match is ricotta, a different cheese. Condition 1: ricotta is not normally used as a drop-in for cream cheese without changing the preparation. Recipes that rely on cream cheese, such as cheesecake, frosting or dips, usually need it beaten or whipped to a smooth, dense consistency, and ricotta is wetter and grainier, so it would need draining, blending or other adjustments. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice. Ricotta has a grainy, curd-like texture, lower fat, and a milder, less tangy flavour, and the appearance and mouthfeel of the finished dish would differ. The ingredient is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply, and the difference is not a trivial modifier as in guideline D. The quantity (795g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is smoked pork link sausage, and the USDA entry is 'Sausage, smoked link sausage, pork', which describes the same product: a smoked link sausage made from pork. The weight prefix is ignored. Smoking is present in both, so it is not a modification that changes the food. The entry is the standard default version, not a reduced, flavoured, or otherwise modified product. Cooking method is unaffected, since the sausage is prepared the same way either way. A diner would not taste, feel, or see a difference, because it is the same food under a near-identical name.

The ingredient is fiddlehead ferns that were frozen and then thawed. The USDA entry is the same food in the same state: frozen fiddlehead ferns, unprepared. Under guideline E, a frozen product that is thawed matches the frozen USDA entry of the same product. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the entry is unprepared and fiddleheads are normally cooked, so the recipe's handling is unchanged. Condition 2: freezing and thawing do not change the taste, texture, or appearance in a way a diner would notice in a cooked dish. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is simmered beef tongue, which is beef tongue cooked by simmering. The USDA entry is 'Beef, variety meats and by-products, tongue, cooked, simmered', which is the same food in the same state (cooked by simmering). The leading '185g' is quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing the preparation, since it is already simmered and needs no further cooking. Condition 2: the diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food prepared the same way. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chicken liver pâté, a smooth, spreadable product that is usually puréed and enriched with fat such as butter or cream. The USDA entry is 'Livers, chicken, chopped, with eggs and onion', which describes a coarser, chunkier chopped-liver preparation with visible hard-boiled egg and onion pieces. These are different products, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. The match fails condition 1, because using chopped liver in place of pâté changes the preparation: it is not a smooth spread and would not behave the same when served or spread. It also fails condition 2, because a diner would notice the coarser texture and the egg and onion flavour. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is black bean sauce, bottled: a condiment made from fermented black soybeans, with garlic, sugar, salt, and other seasonings, typically in a sauce or paste form. The USDA match is Lentils, dry, which is a whole dried pulse. Condition 1: Lentils cannot replace a bottled sauce without changing the preparation. The sauce is a seasoning added as a liquid or paste, while lentils are a solid legume that would need cooking and would not provide the sauce's liquid consistency or function. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference. Black bean sauce has a salty, savoury, fermented, umami flavour and a glossy, dark, saucy texture. Dry lentils would give a starchy, earthy, bland flavour and a firm, granular texture. The food is also a fermented soybean product, not a lentil, so this is not the same food under another name. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is plain salted butter, quantity ignored. The USDA entry 'Butter, salted' is the same food under the same name, the standard default version of salted butter. Cooking method is unchanged, since butter is used the same way. Taste, texture and appearance are the same, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried epazote, an herb with a distinctive flavour (often described as medicinal, pungent, citrus-camphor notes) and is a different species from oregano. The USDA match is 'Spices, oregano, dried', which is a different herb with a different flavour profile. Condition 1 concerns whether it could replace the ingredient without changing preparation; dried oregano can be added at the same stage as dried epazote, so the cooking method is not necessarily altered. However, condition 2 requires that a diner would not notice a difference in taste. Epazote and oregano taste clearly different, so a diner would likely notice. Guideline F also states that a different state (dried vs fresh herb) or different food is not substitutable, and epazote is not the same food as oregano under another name (guideline B does not apply, since these are distinct herbs, not regional names for the same plant). Therefore the match fails condition 2 and is not substitutable.

The ingredient is lion's mane mushroom, sliced. The USDA entry is 'Mushroom, lion's mane', which is the same food with no cooking or processing state listed, so it is the generic food. Under guideline B it is the same food. Slicing is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the mushroom can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same fresh mushroom. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same mushroom in the same state. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a combination of two different foods, snapper and shrimp. The USDA entry covers only one of them, mixed-species snapper fish, cooked by dry heat. It contains no shrimp, so it is not the same food as the ingredient. Condition 1 fails: substituting it would drop one of the two components, changing the dish's composition and preparation. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the shrimp was missing and that the dish's seafood content differed. The quantity and the cooked state do not change this conclusion.

The ingredient is fresh raw oysters, weighed at 150g; the leading quantity is ignored. The USDA match 'Oysters, fried' is a cooked, breaded and deep-fried product. Condition 1 fails: substituting fried oysters for fresh oysters changes the cooking method, since fresh oysters would be used raw, poached, baked or otherwise prepared, not fried in batter. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture (crisp coating versus soft flesh) and appearance. Guideline F rules out a raw versus cooked state difference, so this is not a same-food-under-another-name case under guideline B.

Quantity (5g) is ignored. The ingredient is vanilla coconut yogurt, a plant-based yogurt made from coconut. The USDA entry is vanilla yogurt made from dairy milk, specifically low fat. It is not the same food under another name. Condition 1: it could physically replace the ingredient in the same preparation, but the base changes from coconut to dairy, which is a different product, not a regional or trade name for the same thing. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference. Coconut yogurt has a distinct coconut flavour, a different mouthfeel and a different tang profile from dairy yogurt, and it can look different in colour and set. Since the base ingredient differs, the match fails both conditions, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a maple brown sugar flavoured oat cereal. The USDA entry is Quaker Maple Brown Sugar LIFE Cereal, a branded ready-to-eat cereal with the same maple brown sugar flavour. Guideline G treats a branded entry of the same product type as a match, and guideline D says a flavoured entry matches when the ingredient itself asks for that flavour. The weight prefix (100g) is ignored per guideline A. Both substitution conditions hold: the cereal can be used directly with no change to preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The one uncertainty is whether the base grain blend matches the generic 'oat cereal', but the product is the same flavoured ready-to-eat cereal, so I treat it as a match.

The ingredient is canned butter beans (large lima beans) combined with creamed corn. The USDA entry is canned succotash made from corn and lima beans, specifically with cream-style corn. Butter beans are the same food as lima beans, so the components match. Canned succotash with cream-style corn is the same dish, and the canned product is used as-is with no change to preparation, so condition 1 holds. Canned lima beans and cream-style corn would look, feel and taste the same to a diner, so condition 2 holds. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cooked spaghetti squash, 115g (quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry is 'Spaghetti squash, cooked', which is the same food in the same state (cooked), with no added components, flavouring, or modification. Condition 1: the match can directly replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are already cooked and the recipe handling is unaffected. Condition 2: a diner would not perceive any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food in the same cooked state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 450g of peeled shallot bulbs with the root removed, which is a plain raw shallot prepared for cooking. The USDA entry 'Shallots, bulb, peeled, root removed, raw' describes the same food with the same preparation (peeled, root removed) and the same state (raw). Per guideline A the quantity is ignored, and per guideline C the handling descriptors (peeled, root removed) do not change the match. The food is literally the same, so condition 1 is met: the shallots can be used in place of the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 is also met: a diner would not taste, feel or see any difference between these identical raw shallot bulbs. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is almond milk, a beverage made by blending almonds with water and straining. The USDA match is almond oil, which is a pressed fat extracted from almonds. These are different foods: one is a water-based drink and the other is a pure lipid oil. Condition 1 fails because almond oil cannot be used in place of almond milk in a recipe without changing the liquid base, moisture, and how the dish is prepared (it would not dissolve or emulsify the same way and would add pure fat instead of liquid and protein). Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in taste, mouthfeel, and appearance, since almond oil lacks the milky body and flavour of almond milk. Ignoring the 5g quantity, as the guidelines require, does not change this. This is not a same-food-by-another-name case; it is a different product derived from the same source, which falls under the 'raw source vs processed ingredient' and 'different fat' exclusions.

The ingredient 'chuck tender' is a beef cut from the chuck (a beef muscle, often cooked as a steak or roast and known as mock tender). The USDA entry 'Chicken tenders or strips, NFS' is poultry, specifically the chicken breast tender strip. These are different animals and different cuts, not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails: a cook would not substitute chicken tenders for beef chuck tender without changing the dish's preparation, since the beef would be cooked and seasoned differently and the chicken would be cooked to a different doneness. Condition 2 fails: a diner would clearly notice beef versus chicken in flavour, texture (beef muscle fibre versus chicken strip), and appearance. Guideline F explicitly rules out a different cut of meat, and this is a different species entirely. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain 'crab' with the leading weight ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Crab' names only the food with no processing state, so it is the generic food. Under guideline B and E, a generic entry matches a plain ingredient, and crab can be used in place of crab without changing preparation. The match is the same food, so diners would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cashew nut oil, specified as unsalted. The USDA entry is cashew nuts that are oil roasted with salt added. Guideline D says a plain ingredient matched to a modified version (here, salt added, which is the opposite of the unsalted specification) is not substitutable. The ingredient asks explicitly for the unsalted version, so the salted entry differs in a way a diner would taste. The entry also describes whole nuts that were oil roasted, not a plain cashew nut oil, which is a difference in processed state (guideline F). The quantity is irrelevant. Condition 2 fails because the salt would be noticeable in taste, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is hard-boiled eggs, which are whole eggs cooked in the shell and peeled. The USDA entry 'Egg, whole, cooked, hard-boiled' is the same food in the same state. The weight is decoration (guideline A). 'Sliced' is knife work the recipe does itself and does not change the match (guideline C). Hard-boiled eggs are normally sold and used as such, so there is no modification or different cooking method. The diner would see and taste the same sliced hard-boiled egg whichever source is used. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is mole verde, a green Mexican mole made mainly from tomatillos, pepitas (pumpkin seeds), herbs and green chiles. The USDA entry 'Mole sauce' is a generic entry, and the standard mole it describes is typically mole poblano, a brown sauce built on dried chiles and chocolate. Condition 1: the match is a different variety of sauce, so it would not simply stand in for mole verde without changing the dish's flavour profile. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Mole verde is bright green and tangy/herbaceous, while a standard brown mole is dark, rich and chocolatey, so both taste and appearance differ. Under guideline F, a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable. The quantity (10g) is ignored. Neither condition is met.
