The match is not the same food under another name, and it is not a plain or standard version of the ingredient. Neither condition is met, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is prunes, which are dried plums. The USDA entry 'Prune, dried' names the same food, so it is the same product under a near-identical name (guideline B). Nothing in the recipe is listed as changing preparation. The match is the dried fruit as bought, not a cooked, modified, or different-variety product, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The ingredient is a plain, shredded Mexican blend cheese, which a shopper would normally buy as full-fat. The USDA match is 'Cheese, Mexican blend, reduced fat', a modified version. The ingredient is fat-free ground turkey, and the USDA entry is 'Turkey, ground, fat free, raw', which is the same product in the same raw state. The 150g quantity is ignored per guideline A. The ingredient is goat milk, a dairy liquid used as a milk. The USDA match is just 'Goat', which refers to the animal as a food source (goat meat), not goat milk. This is a different food, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Milk is not an acceptable substitute for meat in any recipe, so the dish's preparation, flavour, texture and appearance would all change. Condition 1 and condition 2 both fail. Okara is the wet, fibrous soy pulp left over after soymilk is made. It is a processed byproduct, not a whole bean. The dish would also differ in texture and appearance, since whole cooked beans are firm and intact, while okara is soft and granular. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well.

The ingredient is vodka sauce, a creamy tomato-based pasta sauce flavoured with vodka, cream, and typically garlic and herbs. The ingredient is plain vanilla yogurt. The USDA entry is vanilla yogurt, low fat, fortified with vitamin D. The ingredient is fresh cranberry beans, a shelling bean (Phaseolus vulgaris, also called borlotti in some regions) eaten as a legume. The ingredient 'Ethiopian sourdough flatbread' describes a fermented, sour, flat bread from Ethiopia. Injera is exactly that: a sourdough-fermented Ethiopian flatbread with a spongy surface. The ingredient is bluefish fillet, which is the same fish sold as a cut. The USDA entry 'Fish, bluefish, raw' is the same species in its uncooked form. The ingredient is frozen enoki mushrooms: a thin, long-stemmed, raw-style mushroom usually eaten fresh or quickly cooked, with a crisp, delicate texture and a fine appearance. The ingredient is venison, which is deer meat. The USDA entry is raw beef chuck for stew, separable lean and fat. Venison is very lean with a distinct gamey flavour and a finer, denser texture, and it is typically cooked differently (often marinated or cooked to rare or medium-rare). Condition 1 (no change in preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste or texture) both fail.

The ingredient is fresh plain pancakes. The USDA entry is plain pancakes in the frozen state. The ingredient also explicitly specifies 'fresh', which signals the intended state. Condition 1 is doubtful because a frozen product would need reheating, changing the preparation. Condition 2 fails because a diner would likely notice the texture difference. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fennel bulb, trimmed, with a 4g quantity that is ignored per guideline A. The parenthetical 'optional' does not change the food identity. The ingredient is ripe pear, 220g (quantity ignored per guideline A). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the ripeness state is the same generic fruit as the plain 'pear' entry. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh eel, a fish. The USDA match is raw chicken broiler/fryer meat. The ingredient is smoked sturgeon. The USDA entry is 'Fish, sturgeon, mixed species, smoked', which is the same food in the same smoked state. The ingredient is a plain hazelnut spread. The USDA match is a chocolate hazelnut spread, which adds cocoa and chocolate flavour and changes the colour and sweetness profile. Step 1: Identify the food. The ingredient is nettle tops, which are the same plant as USDA's Stinging Nettles. The parenthetical '(Northern Plains Indians)' is a regional/cultural attribution for the same food, not a different product, so it does not make it a different food (guideline B).

Step 3: Condition 1 (cooking method). Blanched nettles could be used in place of parboiled nettles without changing how the dish is prepared, since the recipe would still receive nettles that have already been briefly boiled.

Step 4: Condition 2 (sensory). Blanching and parboiling produce the same degree of wilting, colour setting and tenderness, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance.

Step 5: The quantity (145g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pork sirloin tip roast, boneless, which is a pork cut. The USDA match is beef round tip, separable lean and fat, raw, which is a beef cut from the round primal. The ingredient is plain fresh strawberries, quantity ignored. The USDA entry 'Strawberries, raw' is the same food in its raw, uncooked state, which is the default fresh form. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since no cooking method or handling is altered by the match. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the food is the same fresh strawberry. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is thousand island dressing, reduced fat, and the weight (75g) is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Salad dressing, thousand island dressing, reduced fat'. Condition 1: the reduced-fat dressing can directly replace the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: the same product would have the same taste, texture and appearance, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh sheep milk, a liquid dairy product from a different animal species than cow milk. The USDA entry 'Milk, malted' is a processed product: a dried or powdered milk blend containing malted barley and wheat flour, with a distinct malty flavour. Condition 2 fails because the malted flavour, colour and texture would be noticeable to a diner. This is not the same food under another name, and it is not a default version of milk. Guideline F applies: a processed ingredient is not the plain source product. The quantity is irrelevant.

The ingredient is 325g of ground chicken leg meat, and the USDA entry is raw chicken broiler/fryer leg meat only. The leading weight is ignored per guideline A. Both are raw, with no cooking method, added ingredients, or flavour difference. The entry is the same food in its cut, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance once the dish is prepared with ground meat. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is hazelnut, meaning the whole nut (a raw/plain food item). The USDA match is 'Oil, hazelnut', which is a refined fat extracted from hazelnuts, not the nut itself. Condition 1: substituting hazelnut oil for hazelnuts would change the preparation, since a nut is chopped, toasted, or added whole, whereas oil is poured or measured as a liquid fat; it is a different processed ingredient (guideline F: the raw source vs the processed ingredient). Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in texture (crunch versus liquid fat) and appearance. Both conditions fail, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain soy milk, with no sweetness specified. The USDA match is 'Soy milk, sweetened', which is a sweetened modified version. The quantity (220g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions cannot be assumed to hold, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried pollock, a white fish (Theragra/Pollachius species) sold dried and salted or unsalted. The USDA match is Lentils, dry, a legume. Condition 2 fails because a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. Per guideline F (different source/state, not the same food under another name), this is not substitutable. The weight is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain endive, sold as the fresh vegetable. The USDA entry 'Endive, raw' is the same food in its uncooked state, which is the default form a shopper would buy. Fresh endive and the USDA raw endive share the same taste, texture and appearance, so a diner would not notice a difference, and condition 2 holds.

The ingredient is 100g salted egg yolk, meaning whole yolks that have been cured or salted, giving a moist, firm, savoury, salty product. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in saltiness, flavour, and the firm, sandy-to-creamy texture of cured yolk versus dry powder. Per guideline F (different state: dried vs. cured/processed) and D (salted is a modified version of a plain ingredient), this is not a substitutable match.

The ingredient is plain cassava, the starchy root vegetable. The USDA entry 'Cassava, raw' is the same food in its uncooked, default form. Condition 1: cassava root can be used in place of itself without changing preparation, since any cooking or handling in the recipe applies equally to both. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the food is identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is rice bran oil, and the USDA entry is 'Oil, rice bran', which is the same food under a slightly different name (guideline B). The leading '30g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the oil can directly replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is used the same way in cooking. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same oil. Both conditions are met.

1. The ingredient is cotija cheese powder, a dehydrated, finely ground form of cotija. The USDA entry is Cheese, mexican, queso cotija, which is the standard solid (crumbly block) cheese. 2. Guideline F treats a different state (dried or processed versus the plain product) as not substitutable, and this is the same food in a different processed form rather than a different name for the same product. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is whole quail, which in a recipe is normally the raw bird that the dish will cook. The USDA match is 'Quail, cooked', which is already cooked. The ingredient is sweet pickles, chopped. Chopping is knife work the recipe does itself and does not change the food (guideline C). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chicken stock, a liquid broth made by simmering chicken bones/meat with water and aromatics, used here as a serving liquid. The ingredient is generic 'almond milk' with no sweetness specified. The USDA entry is specifically 'unsweetened, plain, refrigerated'. The ingredient is an unsalted almond spread, which is essentially almond butter under another name. The ingredient is turkey heart that has been simmered, so it is already cooked. The USDA entry is 'Turkey, all classes, heart, cooked, simmered', which is the same food in the same cooked state. The ingredient is ready-made mole sauce, and the USDA entry is simply 'Mole sauce', which is the same food with no added modification, state, or branded variant. The ingredient is fluid buffalo milk. The USDA entry, "Milk, indian buffalo, fluid," describes the same food: fluid milk from buffalo, with the regional name 'Indian buffalo' used for it. The ingredient is Italian dressing, which is a herbed vinegar-and-oil dressing flavoured with ingredients such as oregano, basil and garlic. The ingredient is reduced-fat feta, a modified version of feta. The USDA entry is 'Cheese, feta, whole milk, crumbled', which is the full-fat version. The ingredient is sepia, which is the common culinary name for cuttlefish. The ingredient is a dried mixture of squid and shrimp, which is an uncooked, dehydrated product that the recipe would presumably rehydrate or cook. The ingredient is frozen amaranth leaves (Amaranthus, a leafy green), thawed. The USDA match is canned grape leaves (Vitis leaves, typically brined and packed in a jar). These are different plants, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline E covers frozen-versus-fresh differences within the same food, not a change of species. Using canned, brined grape leaves in place of amaranth leaves would change the flavour (briny and tangy versus mild and earthy), the texture (soft, pickled-like versus tender-cooked greens), and the appearance (leaf shape and colour differ). The preparation would also change: canned grape leaves are already cooked and brined and would need rinsing and different handling. A diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is cooked oat bran that has been cooled. The USDA entry is 'Oat bran, cooked', which is the same food in the same state (cooked). Cooling is handling that does not change the match (guideline C: chilled and room-temperature handling do not alter the match). The 75g quantity is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the cooked oat bran could replace the cooled cooked oat bran without changing preparation, since the only difference is temperature, which the recipe itself handles. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cooked food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is European-style unsweetened cocoa powder, meaning alkalized (Dutch-process) cocoa. The USDA entry is Cocoa, dry powder, unsweetened, HERSHEY'S European Style Cocoa, which is the same product type under a brand name. Guideline G says a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. Guideline D says that when the ingredient itself asks for a specific version, the matching entry for that version counts, so the European-style descriptor is satisfied rather than being a modification. The quantity (300g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the cocoa powder can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: the diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same kind of alkalized unsweetened cocoa powder. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 95% lean ground beef, a plain raw ground beef product sold at the standard lean level. The USDA entry 'Beef, ground, 95% lean meat / 5% fat, raw' describes the same product: ground beef at 95% lean, uncooked. The leading weight '525g' is decoration and ignored. Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is the same raw ground beef and would be cooked identically. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the cut, fat ratio and state are the same. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'dried tri-tip strips', which is a dried, cured meat product (jerky-style). The USDA match is raw beef, bottom sirloin tri-tip roast, separable lean and fat, trimmed to 0" fat, select grade. Guideline F lists 'a different state: raw vs cooked' and processed vs raw as non-substitutable. Dried strips have been dehydrated, typically seasoned or cured, and have a chewy, concentrated texture and flavour. Raw tri-tip is fresh whole muscle meat that would need cooking, which would change the dish's preparation method, texture, and appearance. A diner would notice the difference. Ignoring the 125g quantity and the cut match (both are tri-tip), the state difference alone fails both conditions.

1. The ingredient '75g pork and beans' refers to the common canned product of the same name: navy or haricot beans baked in a tomato-based sauce with pork. The leading weight is ignored per guideline A. 2. The USDA entry 'Beans, baked, canned, with pork' describes the same canned product: beans with pork in a sauce. Guideline B and D treat the same food under another name, or the standard default version, as a match. 3. Condition 1: the canned product is used as-is, so it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. 4. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product type. The USDA entry is the standard canned version, not a modified one, so no flavour or texture change applies. Both conditions are met.

Celeriac (celery root) is a distinct root vegetable, Apium graveolens var. rapaceum, with a dense, starchy, bulbous texture and a milder, nutty flavour. Celery, raw refers to the leafy stalk (Apium graveolens var. dulce), which is crisp, fibrous, watery and has a stronger, more bitter, distinctly 'green' taste. This is not a regional or trade name for the same food, nor a cut or inner part of the same vegetable. Using celery stalks in place of celeriac would change the dish's texture (crisp versus dense and firm), flavour, and appearance (stalk slices versus cubed or grated root), and a diner would notice. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) both fail.

Camembert is a soft-ripened, surface-mold cheese with a bloomy white rind, a dense buttery interior, and a rich, earthy flavour. The USDA match is creamed cottage cheese, a fresh unripened curd cheese with a mild, tangy taste and a moist, lumpy texture. Condition 1 fails: camembert is typically served whole, baked, or sliced, and cottage cheese cannot take its place in those preparations without changing the dish. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in flavour, texture (smooth and runny-centred versus curdy), and appearance (rind versus loose curds). These are different cheese types, not the same food under another name, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient 'chowchow' is a pickled relish (typically chopped cabbage, green tomatoes, peppers, onions, and mustard in a vinegar-sugar brine). The USDA match 'Bread, white' is a baked wheat flour product. They are different foods, not the same food under another name. Using bread in place of chowchow would change the dish's flavour (sour, tangy, spiced versus neutral bread), texture (crunchy, wet vegetable pieces versus soft crumb), and appearance (visible vegetable relish versus plain bread). A diner would immediately notice. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) both fail. The quantity is irrelevant.

The ingredient is avocado, mashed. The USDA entry, 'Avocados, raw, all commercial varieties', is the same food in its generic raw form. Mashing is knife or handling work and does not change the match (guideline C). The 450g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the raw avocado can replace mashed avocado without changing preparation, since the recipe does the mashing itself. Condition 2: once mashed, the flesh of any commercial avocado variety looks, tastes and feels the same to a diner, and the entry is the generic all-varieties entry, so no noticeable difference arises. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a generic chocolate-flavoured crisp cereal, which is a chocolate-flavoured puffed or crisped rice-type cereal. The USDA entry is a specific branded product, QUAKER MOTHER'S COCOA BUMPERS, which is a different named cereal with its own shape (bumpy puffs), texture and recipe. It is not literally the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Under guideline G, a branded entry counts only when it is the same plain product type without added modification. Here the ingredient is already a chocolate-flavoured cereal, and the match is a distinct chocolate-flavoured sibling with a different shape and taste profile. Condition 1 could be met by swapping the bag in, but condition 2 likely fails: a diner would probably notice the different puff shape and flavour and appearance in the finished dish. Therefore it is not substitutable.

1. Identity: 'Turkey, light meat' is the breast meat of the bird, so it is the same food as roasted turkey breast. 2. Preparation: both are roasted, so the cooking state matches. 3. Skin: 'skin not eaten' describes the meat with the skin removed or left off the plate, which is how roasted turkey breast is normally served. It is a standard USDA descriptor rather than a modification (guideline C). 4. Quantity is ignored (guideline A). 5. Sensory check: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance between roasted turkey breast and roasted light-meat turkey without skin. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried jellyfish, an animal food (a marine invertebrate, cnidarian) that is cured and dried, then typically rehydrated and used in salads or cold dishes with a chewy, crunchy texture and a mild briny taste. The USDA match is 'Spices, basil, dried', a dried herb (Ocimum basilicum leaves). Condition 1 fails: basil cannot stand in for jellyfish in any preparation, and it is not even a protein or seafood, so it would change how the dish is prepared (rehydration, cutting, seasoning method). Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (herbal, sweet-peppery versus briny, neutral seafood), texture (leafy, crumbly versus chewy, gelatinous), and appearance (green flecks versus translucent pale strips). This is not the same food under another name, and it is a different category entirely, so guideline B does not apply. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is pork rind, a common name for pork skin that has been fried or puffed and is eaten as a snack or used as a crumb. The USDA entry 'Pork skin rinds' names the same food under a different name, which counts as the same food per guideline B. Crushing is handling done by the recipe and does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: 'Pork skin rinds' can replace crushed pork rind without changing the preparation, since crushing is the only step and it is applied to the matched food. Condition 2: a diner would taste and see the same fried pork skin, with no difference in flavour, texture category, or appearance once crushed. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried chervil (a dried herb). The USDA match is 'Spices, chervil, dried', which is the same food: dried chervil. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Guideline F states that fresh vs dried herb is a different state, but here both sides are dried, so that distinction does not apply. Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same dried herb. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Fuji apple slices (raw, sliced apple of the Fuji variety). The USDA match is Sugar-apples (sweetsop), raw, which is a tropical fruit (Annona squamosa) of a completely different genus and family from the apple (Malus domestica). It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F rules out a sibling variety with different taste; this is an entirely different fruit with a custardy, sweet, granular flesh and seeds, unlike the crisp, firm, tart-sweet apple. Substituting it would change the flavour, texture and appearance of the dish, and a diner would notice. Slicing does not change the match (guideline C), but the species itself is wrong. Condition 1 fails in that the dish's preparation would be altered by a different fruit with different handling, and condition 2 fails because taste, texture and appearance all differ. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is pork belly, and the USDA entry 'Pork, fresh, belly, raw' is the same food: fresh, uncooked pork belly. The quantity (150g) is ignored per guideline A. The entry is the plain default version with no added flavour, curing, or modification, so it meets guideline D. Condition 1 holds: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the same raw cut is used and the cook method is unchanged. Condition 2 holds: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cut of meat.

Chicken flats (also called wingettes) are the middle section of the chicken wing, sold under a regional/trade name. Under guideline B, this is the same food as the USDA wing entry under another name. The USDA entry is the wing as raw meat. Preparing flats by removing bone and skin is handling comparable to trimming, which guideline C says does not change the match. The cut is the same wing meat, not a different part of the bird like breast or thigh. Cooking method is unchanged (the same fried, baked or grilled wing preparation), and a diner would not notice a difference in taste or texture. Weight is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient 'celery salt' is a seasoned blend: salt combined with ground celery seed. The USDA entry 'Salt, table, iodized' is plain sodium chloride with iodine added and no celery seed. Under guideline F, a single ingredient is not substitutable for a blend that contains it. The celery flavour is clearly perceptible, so a diner would notice the difference in taste. The quantity is irrelevant (guideline A). Both conditions fail: the dish would taste different, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is cashew oil, a distinct tree-nut oil with a mild, buttery, slightly sweet flavour. The USDA match is walnut oil, a different oil with a pronounced nutty, somewhat bitter flavour and different fatty acid profile. Guideline F explicitly states that a different oil is not substitutable, even when the oils look close. Condition 1 (same use in preparation) might loosely hold for a neutral-fat role, but condition 2 fails because a diner would likely notice the walnut flavour versus cashew's milder taste. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is pawpaw that has been peeled and seeded. The USDA entry is 'Pawpaw, peeled, seeded, raw', which is the same food with the same preparation state. Peeling and seeding are knife work the recipe performs, and per guideline C they do not change the match. The quantity (400g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions hold: the entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is semolina pasta, i.e. dry pasta made from durum wheat semolina. The USDA match is millet flour, which is a flour milled from millet, a different grain entirely (not wheat, not gluten-containing, different taste and texture). Condition 1: millet flour cannot replace semolina pasta in preparation; pasta is a formed, boiled product, and millet flour cannot be shaped and cooked into pasta in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance. Ignoring the quantity, this is a different food, not the same food under another name, and it is not a processed or modified version of the same product. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is spinach dip, a prepared dip. The USDA entry 'Spinach dip, regular' names the same product with no modification or added flavour. Per guideline D, the plain/default version of an ingredient matches the standard USDA entry. The quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A. Using the USDA entry would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same food under the same name. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a frenched, bone-in lamb rack, a rib rack roast. The USDA entry describes the same cut: lamb rib chop/rack roast, frenched, bone-in, raw. The weight (370g) is ignored per guideline A. The entry's 'Australian, imported' origin is a sourcing detail the ingredient does not specify, so it does not change the food. The 'trimmed to 1/8" fat' and 'separable lean and fat' descriptors reflect standard trimming and handling, which guideline C says does not alter the match. Condition 1: the rack can be used in place of the USDA cut without changing the preparation (same roasting or searing, same frenching and bone-in presentation). Condition 2: the same cut, raw, with similar fat cap and lean-to-fat ratio, would look and taste essentially the same on the plate. No modification, state change, or different cut is involved. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is toasted wheat bran cereal, and the USDA entry is Kretschmer Toasted Wheat Bran, a ready-to-eat cereal of the same name and product type. The toasted state is in both descriptions, so it is not a mismatch (guideline F concerns plain vs toasted only when the ingredient is plain). The Sun Country and Kretschmer names are brand and distributor labels for the same product type (guideline G). The quantity prefix is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the cereal could be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same toasted wheat bran cereal. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain corn flour, a finely ground dried corn product (masa-style or cornmeal-type flour depending on region, but generally a plain ground corn product). The USDA match is a barbecue-flavor extruded corn-based snack chip made with enriched masa flour. Condition 1: Corn flour would be used as a raw dry ingredient in baking, thickening, or coating; a barbecue-flavored extruded snack chip is a finished, seasoned, fried or extruded product and cannot replace corn flour without changing the preparation entirely. Condition 2: Diners would clearly notice the difference: the match carries barbecue seasoning, oil content, extruded crunchy texture, and is a snack food rather than a neutral flour. Per guideline F, a processed product containing the ingredient (and a flavoured one) is not the same as the plain ingredient, and guideline D rejects flavoured versions of plain ingredients. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a combination of two foods: navy beans and diced ham. The USDA entry is only cooked navy beans, boiled without salt, with no ham. Condition 1 fails: the match cannot replace the ingredient without changing the dish, because the ham component is absent and would have to be added or handled separately. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the missing diced ham in taste, texture and appearance. Under guideline F, a single ingredient does not match a combination that contains it. The 5g quantity is ignored per guideline A and does not affect the result.

The ingredient is freeze-dried chives, a dehydrated product. The USDA match is 'Chives, raw', which is fresh, uncooked herb. Guideline F lists 'a different state: raw vs cooked, fresh vs dried herb' as not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because freeze-dried chives are rehydrated or used directly, and fresh chives are added differently, with different moisture and handling. Condition 2 also fails because freeze-dried chives have a more concentrated, muted flavour, a crisper texture, and a different appearance from fresh green chives. The match is not the same food in a different name, so the answer is no.

The ingredient is great northern beans, a dried legume sold as bought, with the quantity (15g) ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Beans, great northern, mature seeds, raw' is the same food. Per guideline C, 'mature seeds, raw' for beans is the dried legume as bought, so it is the same product and not a cooked or processed state. The trailing note 'Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program' is an administrative descriptor, not a product modification. Condition 1: the beans can be used in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same bean in the same state. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is Asian pear (Pyrus pyrifolia), a distinct pear type with a crisp, juicy, apple-like texture and a different sweetness profile. The USDA match is Red Anjou (Pyrus communis), a European pear with a soft, buttery texture. Asian pear is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Substituting Anjou would change the eating texture from crisp to soft, which a diner would notice, and it would alter the flavour. Guideline F treats a sibling variety with a different taste as not substitutable. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

Pork fillet is the UK/Australian name for the pork tenderloin, the same cut sold under a regional name (guideline B). The USDA entry 'Pork, loin, tenderloin, boneless, raw' is the raw, boneless tenderloin, so it matches the uncooked ingredient. Condition 1: the match is the same cut, so it can be used without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same meat. Both conditions hold, and the 150g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is dried apples that are sulfured and uncooked, weighing 100 g; the weight is decoration and is ignored. The USDA entry 'Apples, dried, sulfured, uncooked' names the same product with the same state: dried, sulfured, and raw/uncooked. Under guideline D, dried apple is normally sold sulfured, so the sulfured descriptor does not count as a modification. Substituting it changes neither the preparation nor the dish, since it is the same food with the same processing. A diner would not taste, feel or see a difference.

The ingredient is longan puree, a processed, blended form of the fruit with a smooth, uniform texture. The USDA match is 'Longans, raw', which is the whole fresh fruit with flesh, skin and seeds. Condition 1 fails: using whole raw longans in place of puree would require blending or pureeing, which changes how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance, since the puree is smooth while whole longans have a distinct flesh and seed. Guideline F rejects a raw source versus a processed ingredient, so this is not a substitutable match.

Condition 1: The ingredient is quinoa pasta, a dry pasta that is normally cooked as part of the dish. The USDA entry is pasta already cooked, so using it would change the preparation: the dry pasta would not be boiled, and the cooked pasta would be added at a different stage. Guideline F treats raw/dry versus cooked as a different state, so this fails. Condition 2: The USDA entry is a blend of corn flour and quinoa flour, not the single-ingredient quinoa pasta implied by the ingredient. Guideline F says a single ingredient versus a blend is not substitutable. Corn-based pasta also differs in texture and flavour from quinoa-based pasta, and a diner could notice this. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is coconut sugar, a sugar made from coconut palm sap with a caramel-like, molasses-like flavour and granular texture. The USDA entry 'Coconut, packaged' refers to packaged coconut meat, typically shredded or flaked and usually sweetened. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F rules out a different sugar: swapping in a coconut meat product would change the sweetness source, flavour, texture and appearance of the dish. Condition 1 fails because the item cannot replace the sugar without changing preparation: it cannot dissolve or caramelise like a sugar. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in taste and texture. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is plain bran flakes, a breakfast cereal. The USDA entry 'Cereal, bran flakes, plain' names the same product in its plain form, with no added flavour, sweetener or modification. Under guideline B and D, a plain ingredient matched to the standard plain version is a match. The 70g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: bran flakes can be used directly in place of the same product without changing preparation, whether eaten dry, with milk, or used in a recipe. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same cereal. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a smoked turkey frankfurter, a poultry sausage. The USDA entry 'Frankfurter, meat' is the generic frankfurter, which is conventionally made from beef or pork or a blend, not turkey. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B). Condition 1: the dish could be prepared the same way, since both are cooked sausages, so the preparation method is unchanged. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference. Turkey frankfurters have a leaner, milder, distinctly poultry flavour and a different texture and colour from beef or pork frankfurters, so the substitution is detectable. Because condition 2 fails, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw chicken leg and thigh skin, which the cook will prepare (typically rendering, roasting, or frying) as part of the recipe. The USDA entry is cooked, braised skin. Guideline F says raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Using pre-braised skin would skip the cook's own cooking step and change the dish's texture, fat rendering, colour, and flavour. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would change. Condition 2 also fails because the skin would look and feel different, with braised flavour and softened texture that a diner could notice. The cut (drumstick and thigh skin) matches, but the cooking state does not.

The ingredient is canned figs packed in light syrup. The USDA entry is canned figs packed in water, with solids and liquids. The shared food is the same, so condition 1 is only partly met on identity, but the packing medium differs. Guideline F says a different packing medium (in syrup vs water pack) is not substitutable. The sweetened syrup changes the taste and mouthfeel of the figs, and a diner would notice the sweeter, more syrupy flavour. Because the medium differs, the match fails on flavour, so condition 2 is not met either.

The ingredient is toasted onion bread, a specific bread product with toasted state. The USDA match is 'Bread, onion, toasted', which is onion bread in toasted form. Quantity (250g) is ignored. Condition 1: the match is the same food (onion bread) in the same toasted state, so it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same toasted onion bread. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is green olives (a cured fruit of Olea europaea, typically brined and sold in jars or cans). The USDA match is 'Green beans, raw', which is a different food entirely (Phaseolus vulgaris pod vegetable). They are not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1: green beans cannot replace olives in a dish without changing its preparation, since olives are a cured, brined, ready-to-eat fruit and green beans are a raw vegetable needing cooking. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (salty, briny, tangy versus grassy and mild), texture (soft, fleshy versus crisp), and appearance. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is beef tripe, a raw cut of beef variety meat (honeycomb or other stomach tripe). The USDA entry is 'Beef, variety meats and by-products, tripe, raw', which is the same food, raw tripe, as bought. The quantity (145g) is ignored per guideline A. Freezing and handling are not relevant since no state change is specified beyond raw. Condition 1: the raw tripe can be used directly in place of the ingredient without changing the preparation. Condition 2: the diner would not notice any difference, since it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is palm kernel oil, and the USDA entry 'Vegetable oil, palm kernel' is the same oil under a different name, so guideline B applies. The 5g quantity is ignored (guideline A). The ingredient is listed as melted, so it is used in liquid form, and the USDA entry is the oil itself with no added components or modification. Condition 1: the oil can replace the ingredient without changing the preparation, since melting is the recipe's own handling and does not alter the match. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same oil. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain corn puff cereal, the standard unsweetened puffed-corn product used in recipes. The USDA match is Malt-O-Meal Corn Bursts, a branded, sweetened puffed-corn cereal. Guideline G says a branded entry with an added flavour or modification is not a match, and guideline D treats sweetened versions of a plain ingredient as a modification. Condition 1 is therefore questionable: the sweetened product would change the dish's flavour. Condition 2 also fails, because a diner would taste the added sugar and notice the difference, especially in savoury or coating uses. The two products are not the same food, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a 10g mixture of mustard oil and sunflower oil, i.e. a blend containing two oils. The USDA match is sunflower oil alone. Per guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend containing it is not substitutable, and a different oil is not substitutable. Mustard oil has a distinct pungent flavour that would change the taste of the dish, so the match would alter flavour and a diner could notice the difference. The quantity is irrelevant (guideline A). Both conditions are not met.

Step 1: The ingredient is halibut fillet, which is the same food as the USDA entry 'Fish, halibut, Atlantic and Pacific, raw'. The quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A. Step 2: The ingredient is frozen and thawed. Per guideline E, frozen fish that is normally cooked does not match only when the thawed form visibly differs where served fresh. Halibut fillets are normally cooked after thawing, and freezing does not visibly change them, so the raw entry matches. Step 3: Condition 1 holds: raw halibut can replace thawed halibut fillets without changing the preparation method. Condition 2 holds: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance once the fish is cooked, since the ingredient is simply the thawed form of the same fish.

The ingredient is cooked, roasted lamb rib. The USDA entry is lamb rib, cooked and roasted, which is the same cut in the same state. The method and the dish are unchanged. Guideline A says to ignore the 160g quantity. The entry adds the standard descriptors 'separable lean and fat', 'trimmed to 1/8 inch fat' and 'choice' grade. Guideline D treats such descriptors as normal retail presentation, not modifications, because the ingredient does not ask for a leaner or fattier version. The fat trim level is the usual default for retail lamb, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Condition 1 (same cut, same cooked state, same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) are both met.

The ingredient is plain margarine, which is normally a full-fat stick or tub product used for baking, frying and spreading. The USDA match is a branded 'margarine-like spread' labelled 'Super Light without saturated fat', which is a reduced-fat, low-fat-type product. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified or lite version is not substitutable, and this product is clearly a lite spread rather than the standard default. Condition 1 fails: its high water content and lower fat level change how it behaves in cooking, such as in creaming, baking, sautéing or pastry, so the preparation would be altered. Condition 2 also fails: the lower fat and higher water content would change the texture, richness and appearance of the finished dish, and a diner could notice the difference. Because both conditions are not met, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fine semolina, a milled durum wheat product. The USDA entry 'Flour, semolina, fine' describes the same product under a standard naming convention, so it is the same food under another name (guideline B). Using it requires no change in cooking method, and it is the default form of the ingredient as sold, so it matches (guideline D). The quantity is ignored (guideline A). Taste, texture and appearance are the same, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh swordfish steak, and the USDA entry is raw swordfish. It is the same food in its plain, uncooked state. A steak is a cut of swordfish, which the guidelines treat as the same food. Quantity is ignored. Raw matches fresh, and the USDA entry names no modification, preservation, or added ingredient. Condition 1: the fish can be prepared the same way (grilled, seared, or baked) with no change in method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same raw fish.

The ingredient is rice noodles, which are made from rice flour and water and are usually soaked or briefly boiled. The USDA entry is egg noodles, which are made from wheat flour and egg and are normally boiled. These are different foods, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails because the preparation changes: rice noodles are often soaked rather than boiled, and swapping in egg noodles would change the cooking method and the dish's character. Condition 2 also fails: egg noodles are yellow, have a wheat-and-egg flavour and a chewier, springier texture, while rice noodles are white, translucent when cooked, soft and neutral in flavour. A diner would notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain dried (desiccated) coconut, unsweetened: a dry, finely shredded product. The USDA entry is 'Nuts, coconut meat, dried (desiccated), creamed', which is a different product. 'Creamed' coconut is a compressed, paste-like form with a much higher fat content and a moist, dense texture, not the loose shreds or flakes of desiccated coconut. Condition 1 fails: using creamed coconut in place of dry shredded coconut would change how the dish is prepared (it cannot be measured or sprinkled the same way and would need liquid or fat adjustments). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture and mouthfeel, and the dish's appearance would differ. Under guideline F, a different processed state is not substitutable, and the creamed product is not the same food as the plain dried ingredient.

The ingredient is ripe papaya, cubed. The USDA entry is Papaya, raw. Guideline A says the weight is ignored. Guideline B: this is literally the same fruit. Guideline C: cubing is knife work that the recipe itself performs and does not change the match, and 'raw' means uncooked fresh fruit, which is what the recipe calls for. Ripeness is not specified in the USDA entry, which is the generic food, so it matches a ripe papaya (guideline F's ripeness rule applies to a different ripeness entry, not a generic one). Condition 1: the papaya can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same fruit in the same form. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cinnamon-spice instant oatmeal, and the USDA entry is Quaker Instant Oatmeal, Cinnamon-Spice, dry, which names the same product with the same components. The quantity (5g) is ignored per guideline A. The entry is dry, which matches the ingredient as bought. Guideline B and G cover same-product and branded matches, and guideline F's flavour and modification rules do not apply because the flavour is what the ingredient asks for. Condition 1: the dry product can replace the ingredient with the same preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same product.

The ingredient is lard, and the USDA entry is simply 'Lard', which is the same food with no modifiers, blends, or processing descriptors. The quantity (100g) is ignored per guideline A. 'Melted' describes handling the lard before use, which does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the lard can be used in place of the melted lard without changing how the dish is prepared, since melting is the same step. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same fat. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is veal bratwurst, and the USDA entry is pork bratwurst, which is a different meat. Veal and pork differ noticeably in flavour, texture and fat profile, so a diner would likely notice the difference, failing condition 2. The USDA entry is also cooked, while the ingredient is an uncooked sausage that would need cooking, so the preparation would change, failing condition 1. Guideline F treats a different cut or type of meat as non-substitutable, and this is a different animal species, so it is not a same-food name variant under guideline B.

The ingredient is dried oregano, an herb (Lamiaceae family, aromatic leaves used as a seasoning). The USDA match is 'Bulgur, dry', which is a cracked whole-wheat grain product, a cereal with a starchy, mild, nutty flavour and a chewy texture. These are entirely different foods: one is a dried aromatic herb, the other a cereal grain. Condition 1 fails: bulgur cannot be used in place of oregano without changing the dish, since it would add bulk and starch rather than herbal seasoning. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in flavour (earthy, peppery herbal oregano versus bland grain) and texture (chewy grain pieces versus dry leaf fragments). The quantity and the 'dried' descriptor do not make them the same food, and this is not a naming variant of the same item. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain cottage cheese, the standard default product, which guideline D would match to 'Cheese, cottage, creamed'. The USDA match, 'Cheese, cottage, with vegetables', is a variant with added vegetables. That is an added component, not the same food under another name. It changes the taste, which would be noticeable, and the appearance, since vegetable pieces are visible. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient mapped to a flavoured or modified version as not substitutable. Condition 1 is met, since the product could be swapped in without changing the preparation, but condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the vegetables and the altered flavour.

The ingredient is reduced-fat (2%) lactose-free milk, a specific modified milk product. The USDA entry 'Milk, lactose free, reduced fat (2%)' describes the same product: lactose-free milk at 2% fat. Quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A. The ingredient explicitly requests the lactose-free and reduced-fat versions, so the matching modified entry counts as a match per guideline D. Condition 1: it can replace the milk directly with no change to preparation (same liquid, same handling, same heating behaviour). Condition 2: lactose-free 2% milk has the same taste, texture, and appearance as the ingredient, since it is the same product; a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh Granny Smith apple that the recipe juices itself. The USDA match is commercially produced 100% apple juice, which is a processed product, not the same food. Condition 1: a cook could pour in store-bought apple juice, but that changes how the dish is prepared because the juice is not made from the specified variety, and the recipe's juicing step is skipped. Condition 2: Granny Smith juice is noticeably tart and sharp. Commercial 100% apple juice is typically a blend of sweeter varieties, often pasteurised and sometimes from concentrate, with a milder, sweeter flavour and a different colour and clarity. A diner would likely notice the difference. Guideline F rules out both a sibling variety with a different taste and the raw source versus a processed ingredient. Both conditions fail, so this is not substitutable.

The ingredient is kielbasa that is fully cooked and pan-fried. The USDA entry is 'Kielbasa, fully cooked, pan-fried', which names the same food in the same state and preparation. The leading '165g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the USDA food can replace the ingredient without changing the preparation, because it is already pan-fried and fully cooked, matching the recipe's stated state. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product prepared the same way. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh Gala apple, sliced, which is raw fruit. Sliced is handling only and does not change the match. The USDA entry 'Apple, baked' is a cooked product. Under guideline F, raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: baking changes the preparation, so the dish would not be prepared the same way. Condition 2 also fails: baked apple is softer, sweeter, and browned or collapsed compared with raw sliced apple, so a diner would notice. Gala is a variety, and the USDA entry names no variety, but the raw/cooked difference alone is decisive.

The ingredient is salted mung bean noodles, which are glass or cellophane noodles made from mung bean starch. They are a processed noodle product with a slippery, translucent, chewy texture. The USDA entry is whole mung bean seeds, cooked and boiled with salt, so it is a legume, not a noodle. This is the raw source versus a processed ingredient, which guideline F excludes. Substituting whole cooked beans would change the dish's texture and appearance: the beans are opaque, firm and bean-shaped, while the noodles are translucent and strand-like. A diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails because the dish would be prepared differently, since noodles are soaked and used as strands rather than cooked beans. Condition 2 also fails because taste, texture and appearance all differ. The salt in the USDA entry does not offset these differences. The quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is smoked turkey breast with lemon pepper seasoning. The USDA entry is smoked turkey breast with lemon pepper flavour, so the state (smoked, cooked) and the seasoning both match. Guideline F rejects plain vs smoked, but here both sides are smoked, so that does not apply. Guideline D treats added flavour as a modification, but the ingredient itself asks for the lemon pepper flavour, so the flavoured entry matches. The '97% fat-free' descriptor is a possible concern because fat-free is a modified-product descriptor. However, turkey breast is naturally very lean, and the lean deli-style version is how this product is normally sold, so guideline D's exception applies. A diner would not notice a meaningful difference in taste, texture or appearance. Cooking method is unchanged, since it is an already-smoked, ready-to-eat meat. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is queso asadero, reduced fat. The USDA entry 'Cheese, mexican, queso asadero' is the same cheese type, so the food identity matches. However, the ingredient specifies a reduced-fat version, and the USDA entry names no reduced-fat or low-fat descriptor, so it represents the standard full-fat product. Under guideline D, a plain product matched to a modified version is not a match, and when the ingredient asks for a modified version, only the matching modified entry qualifies. Condition 1: a full-fat cheese could replace it in preparation, but would change melt behaviour and richness. Condition 2: a diner could plausibly notice the higher fat content in mouthfeel, creaminess and how the cheese melts and browns. Because the fat-level difference alters texture and flavour, the match fails condition 2.

The ingredient is fresh mussels, scrubbed. Scrubbing is preparation handling that does not change the food, and the 250g quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry "Mussels" names only the food with no state (no cooked, dried or processed descriptor), so per guideline E it is the generic food and matches fresh mussels. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since mussels are cleaned and then cooked as the recipe directs. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is gooseberries (quantity 95g is ignored). The USDA match is 'Gooseberries, raw', which is the same food under the same name, in its plain uncooked state. Condition 1: gooseberries can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same fresh fruit. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a dry savory gravy mix, a powder that is prepared by whisking with liquid and cooking. The USDA match is a ready-made beef gravy (HEINZ Home Style), a finished liquid product that needs no preparation. Condition 1 fails: using the ready gravy in place of the dry mix would change the preparation, since the cook would skip the mixing and thickening steps and would have a different volume of liquid from 310g of dry powder. Condition 2 also fails: the ready gravy is a specific beef-flavoured product, while the ingredient is an unspecified savory mix. Its consistency, appearance and flavour when made would differ from a mix-based gravy. Because the match alters both preparation and the final product, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is self-rising flour, a wheat flour with added leavening (baking powder) and salt. The USDA match is self-rising cornmeal, made from corn rather than wheat. Guideline F states that a different flour is not substitutable, and guideline B does not apply because this is a different food, not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails: the cornmeal would change the dish's preparation and structure, since wheat gluten is absent and cornmeal behaves differently in batters and doughs. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the coarser, grittier texture, the yellow or white corn flavour, and the altered appearance of baked goods. Both conditions are unmet, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient names two different foods: morel mushrooms and shallots. The USDA entry 'Mushrooms, raw' covers only the mushroom part and says nothing about shallots, so it cannot stand in for the whole ingredient. Condition 1 fails because replacing the ingredient would drop the shallots entirely. Morels are also a distinct variety with a much stronger, earthier flavour and a honeycomb texture that generic cultivated mushrooms (white button, cremini) do not have, so a diner would notice the difference. Condition 2 fails as well. The quantity (350g) is ignored per the guidelines. The match is not substitutable.

Agen prunes are dried European plums (Prune d'Agen), which is what 'prune' means as a dried product. USDA 'Prune, dried' is the generic dried prune, so this is the same food under a regional/trade name (guideline B). 'Pitted' is handling and does not change the match (guideline C). The ingredient is plain dried prunes with no modification, so it matches the standard default (guideline D). Agen is the classic prune variety, so there is no sibling-variety taste difference that a diner would notice (guideline F). Cooking method, flavour, texture and appearance are unchanged. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is sesame paste (tahini), a smooth paste made by grinding sesame seeds, usually hulled and sometimes toasted, with added oil in some cases. The USDA entry is whole, dried sesame seeds. Condition 1: whole seeds cannot replace a paste without changing preparation. Tahini must be ground, blended, or stirred into dressings, sauces, or batters, and whole seeds would not blend into a smooth paste. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Whole seeds give a crunchy, granular texture and a different appearance, and the flavour differs from the concentrated, oily, often toasted paste. Guideline F treats the raw source versus the processed ingredient, and whole versus ground, as non-substitutable. Gram quantity is ignored. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is beef heart, cubed; the 100g quantity and the 'optional' label are ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is beef heart, raw. Cubing is knife work that does not change the match (guideline C), so the entry is the same food in the same uncooked state. The 'New Zealand, imported' descriptor only identifies the country of origin and does not alter the product, so it is not a modification (guideline G/D). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is raw beef heart that would be cubed in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same cut of the same meat, differing only in origin.

The ingredient is raw sweet potato (a root vegetable, the plain food). The USDA match is 'Restaurant, Chinese, lemon chicken', a prepared composite dish made primarily of battered, fried chicken in a sweet lemon sauce. Condition 1: substituting this for sweet potato would change the entire preparation: it is a cooked, multi-component meat dish, not a vegetable that could be used in its place; the cooking method and dish composition would be altered. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (citrus-sweet sauce, chicken meat), texture (fried batter, meat) and appearance. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw sunflower kernels. The USDA entry 'Seeds, sunflower seed, kernel, raw' is the same food, described with USDA's standard naming. The leading '105g' is quantity and is ignored. 'Raw' matches the ingredient's raw state, and no cooking method or preparation changes. Condition 1 is met because the entry can be used directly in place of the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 is met because a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product.

The ingredient is dried mackerel fillets, a preserved, dehydrated (and typically salted or cured) fish product. The USDA entry is Atlantic mackerel that has been cooked by dry heat, which is a fresh cooked product. Condition 1 fails: using cooked, dry-heat mackerel in place of dried mackerel changes the preparation, since the dried product is a different state and would not be prepared in the same way. Guideline F says a different state (dried vs cooked) is not substitutable. Condition 2 also fails: dried mackerel has a firmer, chewier texture, a concentrated, saltier flavour, and a different appearance from moist cooked mackerel, and a diner would notice. The 'optional' label and the 250g quantity are irrelevant (guideline A). Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is raw lamb liver. The USDA entry 'Lamb, variety meats and by-products, liver, raw' is raw lamb liver, the same food under the standard USDA naming. The quantity (100g) is ignored per guideline A. Raw matches raw, and no cooking method, flavour, texture, or appearance would change, so a diner would not notice a difference. Condition 1 and condition 2 are both met.

The ingredient is dried tart cherries, which are dehydrated, shrivelled, chewy and sweet-tart in concentrated flavour. The USDA match is Cherries, frozen, which is a fresh-style fruit that is water-filled, soft and juicy when thawed. Guideline F says a different state (dried vs fresh/frozen) is not substitutable. Using frozen cherries would change the texture from chewy to juicy and soft, change the flavour concentration, and change the appearance from dried, dark pieces to whole or halved cherries. A diner would notice the difference, and the preparation would also change, since dried fruit is often rehydrated or added to batters and baked goods in ways that fresh/frozen fruit would not replicate. The quantity (380g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is garland chrysanthemum (shungiku), a leafy green in the Chrysanthemum genus, Chrysanthemum coronarium, also called Japanese/edible chrysanthemum greens. The USDA entry 'Chrysanthemum, garland, raw' is the same plant under its common English name, so it is the same food under another name (guideline B). The 150g weight is irrelevant (guideline A). The entry is 'raw', which matches fresh leaves as bought; the recipe's handling such as cutting or blanching does not change the match (guideline C). No cooking method, flavour, texture, or appearance difference is introduced by the match itself, and it is the plain fresh vegetable rather than a modified or processed product (guidelines D and F). Both conditions are met.

Condition 1: The ingredient is roasted turkey with no stated cut, and the USDA entry is roasted turkey (light and dark meat). Both are cooked by roasting, so the dish would be prepared the same way. The unspecified cut means the generic light-and-dark mix fits. The 400g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2: Light and dark meat is the normal form in which roasted turkey is served, so a diner would not reasonably expect a different taste, texture, or appearance. The skin-eaten descriptor is a standard way roasted turkey is sold and eaten, and the ingredient does not ask for skinless meat, so it does not count as a modification (guideline D). Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is plum sauce, a ready-to-serve condiment used for serving. The USDA entry 'Sauce, plum, ready-to-serve' names the same product type, with no added flavour or modification and no cooking step implied. The quantity (10g) and the 'optional, for serving' note do not change the match. Using the USDA product would not alter how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not taste or see a difference, since it is the same condiment. Both conditions are met.

Condition 1 (method): 'oven-baked' is a form of roasting, so the cooking method matches 'cooked, roasted'. The problem is the cut. The ingredient is 'chicken back pieces' with no qualifier, so the default version is bone-in pieces, usually with skin. The USDA entry is 'meat only', which means the bone and skin are removed. Serving bone-in back pieces versus stripped meat changes the dish's appearance (bones, browned skin) and texture (skin and bone-in cooking), and it changes the fat content. Under the guidelines, a plain ingredient matched to a modified or different-cut version is not a match, and a different cut is not substitutable. Condition 2 (diner would not notice): a diner would notice the absence of bones and skin in a dish that is served as back pieces. Neither condition is clearly met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is thick plain yogurt, a set, spoonable product. The USDA entry 'Yogurt, liquid' describes a thinner, pourable yogurt, usually a drinkable style, not the thick plain product. Condition 1: using it in place of thick yogurt would change how the dish is prepared, because it won't hold body, dollop, or fold in the same way, and a thin base can alter the cooking outcome. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in texture and mouthfeel. It is not the same food under another name (no regional or trade-name equivalence), and the 'liquid' state is a different product form, not a modifier applied to the plain yogurt. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient 'spaetzle' is a soft, chewy, egg-based German noodle or dumpling that is boiled or pan-fried. The USDA match, saltine crackers, is a dry, crisp, baked, salted wheat cracker. Condition 1 fails: crackers cannot be used in place of spaetzle without changing preparation. Boiling or frying a cracker would not produce a noodle-like dish, and crackers do not hydrate into a comparable dumpling. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in texture (chewy versus crisp), taste (eggy and savoury versus salty and baked), and appearance (noodle-like shape versus flat squares). This is a different food, not a regional or culinary name for the same product, so guideline B does not apply. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is cream of tartar (potassium bitartrate), a leavening acid and stabilizer used in baking and meringues, sold as a fine white powder. The USDA match is Cream of wheat, NFS, a breakfast cereal made from milled wheat semolina/farina. These are entirely different foods: cream of tartar is a pure chemical acid salt, while cream of wheat is a grain product. A name similarity ('cream of') does not make them the same food. Substituting cream of wheat would change the chemistry of the dish (no acidification, no stabilization of egg whites, altered leavening), would add starch and gluten, and would change texture and taste. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails too, since a diner would notice a difference in taste and texture.

The ingredient is canned lobster meat, drained. Canned lobster is a cooked, processed product, and the drained weight is decoration per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Crustaceans, lobster, northern, raw', which is uncooked whole or fresh lobster. Guideline F rejects a raw vs cooked state difference. Canned lobster has been cooked and packed, so its texture is firmer and more fibrous, its colour is pinkish-white rather than translucent raw flesh, and its flavour is different. Raw lobster would also require cooking, which changes the dish's preparation. Condition 1 fails because using raw lobster would change how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is American cheese slices. The USDA entry 'Cheese, American' is the generic American cheese product, which is the same food as the sliced product sold under the plain name. Slicing is handling that does not change the match (guideline C). The entry has no modifier such as reduced fat, low sodium, or flavoured, so it is the standard default version (guideline D). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the same preparation, since it melts and is used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product type. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is quinoa flour, which is finely ground quinoa seed. The USDA match is 'Quinoa, uncooked', which refers to the whole, intact seeds. Condition 1: the recipe's preparation would change. Flour is used for baking or thickening and would need to be milled or blended from the whole grain, which is not the same as substituting the seeds directly. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Whole seeds give a grainy, crunchy texture and visible seeds, while flour gives a fine, powdery texture that changes the crumb, appearance, and mouthfeel of the dish. This is a state difference (whole grain vs ground), similar to whole spice vs ground spice, and guideline F treats the raw source versus the processed ingredient as non-substitutable. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is plain Swiss cheese that has been melted. The USDA entry 'Cheese fondue' is a prepared dish, not the cheese itself. Standard fondue is made by melting Swiss-type cheese with wine, often with garlic, kirsch and a starch thickener, so it is a composed product with added components. Condition 1 fails: the match is not simply melted Swiss cheese, so it cannot stand in for the ingredient without changing the preparation (it would need wine, starch and seasonings added, or the dish would be a different one). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would likely notice the wine or kirsch flavour, garlic, and the different texture from starch thickening compared with plain melted Swiss. Guideline F rejects blends and products that contain the ingredient alongside other components, and the 100g quantity is ignored.

The ingredient is diced lamb heart, an organ meat (offal) from the lamb. The USDA match is 'Lamb or mutton loaf', which is a processed, cooked, ground meat loaf product, likely containing ground lamb and other ingredients. Condition 1: Substituting a loaf for diced raw or cooked heart would change the preparation; heart is a distinct organ cut that is diced and cooked as chunks, whereas a loaf is a formed, processed meat product. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference in texture (firm muscular heart pieces versus a uniform, soft, ground-meat loaf), appearance (heart's distinctive dense, fibrous cut surface versus loaf), and flavour (organ meat flavour versus seasoned loaf). Ignoring quantity, the match is a different food product (a processed loaf rather than heart offal), so it is not the same food under another name. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is reduced-sodium beef stock, a modified version of beef stock. The USDA entry, 'Soup, stock, beef, home-prepared', is the plain default version and does not indicate reduced sodium. Under guideline D, a plain entry does not substitute for a modified one; the match would need to be a reduced-sodium entry to count. Condition 1 is not clearly met in terms of product identity, and condition 2 fails because the sodium content, and therefore the saltiness and flavour balance of the finished dish, could differ from what the recipe intends. The match is the plain product, not the reduced-sodium one, so it is not substitutable.

The recipe ingredient is arrowroot as used in cooking, which is almost always arrowroot starch/powder, a refined thickener. The USDA entry 'Arrowroot, raw' describes the raw tuber/root of the plant. Per guideline F, the raw plant source is not substitutable for the processed ingredient. Using raw tuber in place of starch powder would change preparation (it cannot dissolve and thicken the same way, and would need peeling, grating, or cooking) and would change texture and appearance in the finished dish, so a diner would notice. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 also fails.

Hubbard squash is a variety of winter squash, and the USDA entry 'Winter squash, raw' is the generic category that includes hubbard, along with butternut, acorn and others. Guideline B treats the same food under another name as a match, and guideline E treats a USDA entry that names only the food, with no state, as the generic food. The ingredient is raw and the weight is ignored per guideline A. Hubbard is a sibling variety with a somewhat denser, sweeter flesh, but the generic entry is not a specific variety, so it covers the ingredient. Cooking method is unchanged (it is still a raw winter squash to be prepared the same way), and a diner would not reliably detect the difference from generic winter squash. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Roquefort cheese. The USDA entry 'Cheese, Blue or Roquefort' names the same food, so it is the same product under the same name (guideline B). The 'broiled until bubbly' phrase describes what the recipe does to the cheese, not a different state of the food, so it does not change the match (guideline C). The 150g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the USDA cheese can be broiled in the same way without changing the preparation. Condition 2: a diner would see and taste the same cheese, with no visible or flavour difference from the entry's food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dry roasted walnuts that are salted. The USDA entry is walnuts, dry roasted, with salt added. Both describe the same food with the same processing: walnuts, dry roasted, and salted. The leading '9g' is quantity and is ignored. The preparation state (dry roasted) matches, and the salt addition matches the 'salted' descriptor, so the item would not change the dish's preparation, flavour, texture or appearance. A diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh (raw) milkfish fillets, which the recipe will presumably cook itself. The USDA match is milkfish cooked by dry heat, so it is already cooked. Condition 1 fails: substituting a pre-cooked product would change how the dish is prepared, since the cooking step would be skipped or altered. Condition 2 also fails: the cooked fish would differ in texture and appearance from raw fillets once the dish is made. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. The quantity (100g) is irrelevant.

The ingredient is half and half, a dairy product (a blend of milk and cream, roughly 10-18% milkfat). The USDA match is raw fresh pork leg (ham) shank half, separable lean only. This is a meat cut, not a dairy product. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a modified or branded version of half and half. Condition 1 fails: pork cannot replace half and half in a recipe without changing how the dish is prepared (it would need to be cooked as meat, and cream cannot be substituted by raw pork). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice a difference in taste, texture, and appearance. The quantity (370g) is irrelevant. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh pork belly. The USDA entry 'Pork, belly' names the same cut. The leading '300g' is quantity and is ignored. 'Sliced' is knife work, which does not change the match under guideline C. Condition 1: the entry is the same cut, so it can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same meat cut and sliced pork belly is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is round steak, ground, which is top round steak ground at home. The USDA entry is top round steak from the same round cut, raw, Choice grade, trimmed to 0" fat. Guideline C says grinding at home for meat does not change the match, so the cut and state are the same food under the ingredient's name. The ingredient does not specify a fat level, so the trimmed entry does not conflict with it. The quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are raw round beef and the grinding is done as part of handling. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same muscle, in the same raw state, with no added fat. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is 200g gouda, sliced. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Sliced is knife work and does not change the match (C). The USDA entry 'Cheese, gouda' is the same food with no modification, state, or blend descriptor, so it is the standard default version (D). Condition 1: gouda can be used in place of gouda, sliced, with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same cheese. Both conditions hold.

Step 1: The ingredient is plain Greek yogurt, the standard default with no fat level specified. The weight (365g) is ignored per guideline A.
