Step 2: The USDA entry is Greek yogurt made with low fat milk, plain. It is the same food, but it carries a fat-level descriptor. Guideline D treats low/reduced-fat versions of a plain ingredient as a modification, so the match is not the default version. The exception for descriptors that are normal for a product applies to flavoured yogurts, frozen yogurt, parfaits and buttermilk, not to plain Greek yogurt, which is sold at several fat levels. Step 3: Condition 1 is met, since it could be used in the same preparation. Condition 2 is doubtful. Low-fat Greek yogurt is noticeably less rich and creamy than full-fat, and a diner in a dish where the yogurt is central, such as a dip, sauce or dressing, could notice the difference in mouthfeel and flavour. Because the entry adds a fat-level modification and the texture difference could be detected, the match fails.

The ingredient is hamachi, which is Japanese amberjack (Seriola quinqueradiata) sold under the yellowtail name. It is a specific fish, and the recipe gives no cooking state, so it is treated as raw, as hamachi is usually eaten raw as sashimi or crudo. The USDA entry is 'Fish, yellowtail, mixed species, cooked, dry heat', which is a cooked product from mixed species. Condition 1 fails: substituting a cooked product would change how the dish is prepared, since raw fish cannot be replaced with cooked fish without changing the dish. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, flavour and appearance between cooked and raw hamachi. Raw vs cooked is a state difference that makes the match non-substitutable, and the 'mixed species' wording adds a further mismatch with a single specific fish.

The ingredient is bulk pork sausage, meaning raw, unlinked sausage meat sold loose. The USDA entry 'Pork sausage' names the same food with no state or modification, so it is the generic food. Under guideline E, a generic entry matches fresh or plain versions. Bulk sausage is simply pork sausage sold without casings, so the same food is used and the dish is prepared the same way (crumbled and browned or mixed into a recipe). Condition 1 is met: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 is met: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product. The quantity (370g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is romano cheese powder, a dried, powdered, hard grating cheese used as a seasoning or dry coating. The USDA match is 'Cheese sauce', a prepared, moist, emulsified product usually made from processed cheese, milk, fat, and emulsifiers. Condition 1: Substituting a sauce for a dry powder would change preparation. A powder is sprinkled or mixed in dry, while a sauce is a liquid that would alter moisture, binding, and cooking method. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference. Cheese sauce has a smooth, wet, creamy texture and different appearance, and its flavour profile (processed, emulsified, milder) differs from a dry aged romano powder. It is also not the same food under another name, and the match is a different product state and type. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is 'lean ground beef', which in common usage means ground beef with a high lean-to-fat ratio, most often sold as 90% lean / 10% fat. The USDA entry 'Beef, ground, 90% lean meat / 10% fat, raw' is that same standard product, uncooked. The '200g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can be used directly with no change to preparation, since the raw ground beef is handled and cooked the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because this is the same product under a more specific name. The fat percentage is the default for lean ground beef, not a modified version (guideline D). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is puffed wheat, a whole-grain cereal product that has been puffed into light, crisp pieces and is usually eaten dry or as a crunchy addition. The USDA match, Cream of wheat, NFS, is a milled farina from wheat that is cooked into a soft porridge. Condition 1 fails: puffed wheat cannot replace cream of wheat without changing the preparation, since puffed wheat is added dry or as a crunchy element while cream of wheat must be cooked with liquid. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (crisp and airy versus smooth and creamy) and appearance (distinct puffed kernels versus a fine porridge). These are different products, not the same food under another name. The quantity is ignored per the guidelines.

The ingredient is plain clam juice, the liquid from clams, which is a savoury, briny seafood broth. The USDA entry is clam and tomato juice, a blend in which tomato juice is a major component. Under guideline F, a blend or product containing the ingredient is not the same as the single ingredient. Condition 1 is arguably met only loosely, since a cook could pour it in, but condition 2 fails. Tomato adds acidity, sweetness, a red colour and a distinctly tomato flavour, so a diner would likely notice the difference in taste and appearance. The entry is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is a naval orange, which is the common misspelling or variant name for the navel orange. The USDA entry 'Oranges, raw, navels' names the same variety. 'Sectioned' describes knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). The quantity is ignored (guideline A). The food is the same and is served raw, so cooking method, flavour, texture and appearance are unchanged. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sliced salami. The USDA entry 'Salami, NFS' is the same food under a generic name. The 'sliced' descriptor is handling that does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: salami can be used directly in place of sliced salami without changing preparation, since the dish would be prepared the same way. Condition 2: the entry is the generic food with no added flavour, modification or cooking state, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chicken frankfurters, a plain processed sausage product. The USDA entry 'Frankfurter, chicken' names the same product with the same main component. The leading '150g' is quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: a chicken frankfurter can replace another chicken frankfurter without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is cooked the same way (sliced, heated, or grilled). Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the USDA entry describes the same plain product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a blend of acai berry and banana. The USDA match is baby food of banana with mixed berries, strained. Condition 1: the match is a different product with different components. Acai is not one of the 'mixed berries' in a generic baby-food blend, and the match is a commercial pre-packaged baby food rather than a home-blended fruit mix. Condition 2: a diner would taste the difference. Acai has a distinctive earthy, berry-like flavour that a mixed-berry baby food would not reproduce, and the product's specific sweetness and flavour profile would differ. Guideline F rules out a sibling or different variety with a different taste, and a different product with different components. The match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is cooked farina that has been salted. The USDA entry is enriched farina cooked with water and salted, so it is the same food in the same state (cooked, salted). The enriched designation is the standard default for farina sold in most markets and does not change taste, texture or appearance. Cooking method is already complete, so the match requires no alteration to how the dish is prepared. The 10g quantity is ignored per the guidelines. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is flax oil, cold pressed. The USDA entry is 'Oil, flaxseed, cold pressed', which is the same product under a different name (flaxseed oil is flax oil). Both are the same cold-pressed oil, with no added flavour, modification, or different state. The weight '100g' is decoration and is ignored. Condition 1: the oil can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same oil. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain fruit yogurt. Guideline D treats flavoured yogurts as normally low fat, so the 'lowfat' descriptor is not a problem. The USDA entry, however, specifies 'with low calorie sweetener.' Standard fruit yogurt is sweetened with sugar, so this is a modified version (sweetener changed), which guideline D lists as a modification. Condition 1 is arguably met, since it could be swapped in without changing preparation. Condition 2 fails: the substitution of a low-calorie sweetener for sugar changes the taste, and a diner would likely notice the sweetness profile differs. Quantity (5g) is ignored per guideline A. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is skinless chicken breast, which is the light meat of a chicken with skin removed. The USDA entry is light meat from a roasting chicken, meat only (no skin or bone), raw. Light meat is the breast and tenderloin, so this is the same cut and the same food, just described under a different name. Freshly raw meat from a roasting bird and a standard chicken breast are not visibly or texturally different once cooked, so the dish would be prepared the same way and a diner would not notice. The entry is not a different cut (it is light meat, not thigh or drumstick), and it is raw, matching the ingredient. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried blueberries. The USDA match is raw cranberries. These are different fruits, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Blueberries are sweet and mild, while cranberries are very tart, so the flavour would change. The match is also raw, while the ingredient is dried (guideline F: raw vs dried is a different state). Dried blueberries are soft and chewy, while raw cranberries are firm and juicy, so the texture and appearance would also differ. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

Cashew nut paste is ground cashews, and cashew butter is also ground cashews, so they are essentially the same food under different names (guideline B). The ingredient does not specify raw or roasted, so the default version of each applies (guideline D), and the match is not a modified or flavoured product. Neither entry adds a different oil, sugar, or flavouring. Quantity is ignored (guideline A). Cashew paste and cashew butter are interchangeable in preparation, since both are used by stirring or blending into sauces and doughs. Any difference in oil separation or wetness is minor and would not be noticed in the finished dish. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain smoked ham, the standard default product. The USDA entry is a modified version: 'extra lean' (reduced fat) and 'low sodium' (reduced sodium). Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a reduced-fat or reduced-sodium version is not the same product, and the ingredient does not ask for that modified version. Condition 2 also fails in practice: a diner could notice the lower salt and leaner texture and flavour compared with regular smoked ham. Because the match fails the product-identity test and would likely be noticeable in taste and texture, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is soft silken tofu. The USDA match is Mori-Nu silken tofu, extra firm. Both are silken tofu, so the food type is the same, but the texture grade differs. Condition 1: extra firm silken tofu is denser and holds its shape better, so using it in place of soft silken tofu would change how the dish is prepared (for example, it would not blend or fold in the same way and would behave differently in a soft-textured dish). Condition 2: a diner would notice the firmer, denser texture compared with soft silken tofu. The guidelines reject matches that change texture, and this one does. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is roasted unsalted sunflower seeds. The USDA match is pumpkin and squash seeds, roasted without salt. These are different foods (different seed species), not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Pumpkin seeds are flatter, green-tinted and have a different flavour and crunch from sunflower seeds, so a diner would likely notice the difference in taste and appearance. The roasting and lack of salt do match, but the species difference alone means condition 2 fails. Guideline F also treats a different food as non-substitutable. Neither condition is fully met.

The ingredient is black walnut pieces, a different species from the English/Persian walnuts usually represented by the USDA 'Walnuts' entries. Black walnuts have a much stronger, distinctive flavour, so this is a sibling variety with a different taste (guideline F), not the same food under another name (guideline B). The USDA match is also honey roasted, which adds honey sweetness and coating. Guideline F lists plain vs roasted as a different state, and guideline D treats flavoured versions as modifications. A diner would notice the sweet honey coating and the different walnut flavour, and the dish's flavour would change. Condition 2 fails, and the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw pork butt (Boston butt), a fresh uncooked cut. The USDA match is 'Pork, fresh, shoulder, (Boston butt), blade (steaks), separable lean only, cooked, braised', so it is the same cut but in a cooked, braised state. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. The entry also describes a braised product, so using it would mean the dish is not prepared as intended: the recipe's pork would already be cooked, changing the cooking method, texture and appearance. Also, the entry is lean-only, while 'pork butt' normally includes fat. Condition 1 fails because the cooking method would change, and condition 2 fails because a diner would notice braised, cooked pork where raw pork was expected. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain half and half, a standard dairy product of roughly 10-18% milkfat (a mix of cream and milk). The USDA match is 'Cream, half and half, fat free', a modified version with the fat removed. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a reduced or fat-free version is not a match. Condition 1 fails: the fat-free product would change the dish's richness and how it behaves when heated, whipped, or emulsified. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the thinner mouthfeel, lack of richness, and different behaviour in sauces and coffee. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is pickled beetroot slices taken from a jar. The USDA entry is pickled beets, canned, with solids and liquids. Condition 1: the match is the same food (beetroot, pickled), and the jar versus can packaging does not change how the dish is prepared. The 'solids and liquids' wording covers the pickling brine that jarred pickled beets normally come in, so no extra step is needed. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference, since the pickled beet slices and their brine are the same product. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain Greek yogurt with no fat specification, so the default version is a plain, full-fat-range product. The USDA entry is specifically nonfat (fat-free). Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a fat-free/reduced-fat version is a modification, so it is not the standard default. Guideline D's 'normally low fat' exception covers flavoured yogurts, frozen yogurt, parfaits and buttermilk, not plain Greek yogurt, so it does not apply. Condition 1: nonfat yogurt can often stand in for yogurt, but the change in fat content alters the dish's richness and how it behaves in cooking, such as when it is heated or baked. Condition 2: nonfat Greek yogurt is noticeably tangier, thinner-tasting and less creamy than whole or 2% versions, so a diner could notice the difference in taste and mouthfeel. Both conditions are not clearly met, so this is not substitutable.

Chestnut meal is ground dried chestnuts, the same product that is sold as chestnut flour. Under guideline B, regional and trade names for the same food count as a match, so 'Flour, chestnut' is the same food under another name. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the same preparation, since it is used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same ground chestnut product. Both conditions are met, and the 100g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

Condition 1: The ingredient is plain barbecue sauce, used as a sauce or glaze. KC Masterpiece Original is a branded barbecue sauce, the standard default version of that product type. Swapping it in does not change how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: The original KC Masterpiece is a common, standard barbecue sauce, so a diner would not expect a flavour or texture distinct from a generic barbecue sauce. Guideline G treats a branded entry of the same plain product type as a match, and the entry has no added flavour or modification. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is powdered soy creamer, a dry powder. The USDA match is liquid coffee creamer, a different physical form with a different water content and packaging. Swapping a liquid for a powder changes how the dish is prepared: the liquid adds moisture and volume, so the recipe's dry-to-wet balance and mixing steps would change, which fails condition 1. The match also doesn't reflect the soy base of the ingredient; typical USDA liquid coffee creamers are dairy or non-dairy oil-based products with different flavour and mouthfeel, so a diner could notice a difference in taste and texture, which fails condition 2. Guideline F (a different state, such as dry versus liquid, is not substitutable) applies directly. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is marble rye and pumpernickel bread, toasted. The USDA entry is Bread, marble rye and pumpernickel, toasted, which names the same product in the same state. The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the bread can be used in place of this ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since both are toasted. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same bread in the same toasted state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a mixture of two foods: cashew nuts and dried cranberries, chopped. The USDA match covers only cashew nuts, dry roasted, without salt added. Condition 1 fails: the match omits the dried cranberries entirely, so it cannot replace the ingredient without changing the dish's composition. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the missing dried fruit in taste (sweet-tart), texture (chewy) and appearance (red pieces). Guideline F rejects a single ingredient standing in for a blend containing it. The 'dry roasted' state is a further, separate mismatch, since the ingredient does not specify roasting. The chopped handling does not affect the result, and the 6g quantity is ignored.

The ingredient is plain hazelnuts, and the USDA entry is 'Hazelnuts', the same food with no added state, flavour, or processing. Under guideline A the 75g quantity is ignored. Under guideline D a plain ingredient matches the standard default entry. Hazelnuts are typically used whole, chopped, or ground in cooking and baking, and the USDA entry does not change that. Nothing in the entry alters the cooking method, flavour, texture, or appearance, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is turkey bone: the skeletal part of the bird, typically used for stock or broth and discarded or left in the dish. The USDA entry 'Turkey, NFS' is generic edible turkey meat with no specified part or state. These are not literally the same food, and guideline F rejects a different cut or part of the same animal. Using meat in place of bone would change the preparation: bones are simmered for flavour and collagen and are not eaten, while meat would be cooked and served as meat, so the dish's flavour, texture and composition would change. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well because a diner would notice that meat was present where bone was intended. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is a 50/50 blend of milk and cream. USDA 'Cream, fluid, half and half' is a standard commercial product made by blending milk and cream, so it is essentially the same food under a different name, not a modified or different product. It is a plain fluid dairy product with no added flavour, sweetener, or reduction. Its fat content (about 10.5-18%) falls within the range a 50/50 milk-cream mix would produce, depending on the cream used. Condition 1 holds: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 is reasonably met: the taste, texture, and appearance would be essentially the same in the dish, with at most a minor difference in richness that a diner would be unlikely to notice.

The ingredient is a generic 'pupusa' with no filling specified. The USDA entry 'Pupusa, meat' is a specific filled variant. Pupusas are commonly sold with cheese (queso), bean (frijol), mixed (revueltas), or meat fillings, so the plain name does not imply meat. Condition 1: the preparation is broadly similar (masa shell, griddled), so the cooking method is not obviously altered. Condition 2: if the recipe's pupusa were cheese or bean, a diner would taste a different filling, and the meat variant adds a flavour and texture not specified by the ingredient. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a modified or flavoured version is not a match. Because the filling is a defining component and the ingredient does not ask for meat, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw beef stew meat, cubed (guideline C: cubing does not change the match, so the question is what food is being bought). The USDA entry 'Stew, beef' is a prepared dish, a beef stew with gravy and usually vegetables, not the raw meat cut. Condition 1 fails: using a prepared stew in place of raw stew meat would change the preparation, since the meat would already be cooked and mixed with other components. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in flavour, texture and appearance, and the stew would carry extra vegetables and gravy. This is a product containing the meat rather than the meat itself (guideline F), and it is not the same food under another name (guideline B). Not substitutable.

The ingredient is a liquid egg substitute. The USDA entry is an egg substitute in liquid or frozen form, labelled fat free. Condition 1: the match is the same kind of product, so it can replace the ingredient in the same recipe steps (beating, mixing, cooking) without changing preparation. Condition 2: egg substitutes are normally sold fat free, since they are built from egg whites with additives and no yolk fat, so the 'fat free' descriptor describes the standard product rather than a modified version (Guideline D). Liquid egg substitute and its fat-free USDA counterpart look, cook and taste essentially the same, so a diner would not notice a difference. The quantity is ignored (Guideline A).

Ingredient is 190g blackberries, a plain fresh fruit used as a recipe component. USDA entry 'Blackberries, raw' is the same food in its uncooked, default form. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Blackberries are normally sold fresh and used raw or cooked in recipes, so the raw entry matches the standard default version (guideline D). No cooking method change, flavour, texture or appearance difference is implied by the match itself; a diner would not notice a difference between fresh blackberries and the raw USDA entry. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried coconut, normally sold as desiccated or shredded coconut meat with its fat intact. The USDA entry 'Flour, coconut' is coconut flour, a defatted product milled from dried coconut meat. Condition 1: coconut flour cannot replace shredded or desiccated coconut without changing the preparation. Its very different moisture absorption would alter batter or dough, and it cannot provide the chewy shreds called for in most uses. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Coconut flour is a fine, powdery, low-fat material with a much weaker flavour and a different texture, while dried coconut is visibly flaky or shredded and richer in taste. Under guideline F, a different flour or a processed form of the food is not substitutable, so both conditions fail.

The ingredient is 'unpolished rice flour', which is flour milled from unpolished rice, meaning rice that retains its bran layer. That is the same food as brown rice, so 'Rice flour, brown' is the same product under another name (guideline B). Cooking method is unchanged, since both are used as flour in the same way. Flavour, texture and appearance should also match, because the bran is retained in both, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plantain, and the USDA entry is 'Plantain, raw', which is the same food in the same uncooked state. The quantity (350g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: plantain can be used in place of itself without changing preparation, since the raw entry matches the raw ingredient and any knife work or handling does not alter the match. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain cashew butter, and the USDA entry is 'Cashew butter', which is the same food under the same name. The leading '100g' is quantity and is ignored. The parenthetical '(for drizzling)' describes how it is used, not a modification of the product, so the cooking method stays the same. The USDA entry names no modified state such as sweetened, salted-reduced, or flavoured. Diners would not taste or see a difference between the ingredient and the match. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain Monterey Jack, a single cheese. The USDA entry 'Cheese, Colby Jack' is a blend of Colby and Monterey Jack cheeses, usually sold as a marbled orange-and-white product. Under guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend containing it is not substitutable. Condition 2 also fails: the marbled orange colouring is visible in the dish, and Colby adds a milder, slightly sharper and more tangy flavour than plain Monterey Jack, so a diner could notice the difference in appearance and taste. Condition 1 is not the deciding issue, since the cheese could be grated or melted the same way. The quantity is ignored.

The ingredient is generic fruit juice concentrate, a plain 100% juice product, usually a single-fruit or mixed-juice concentrate with no added sweeteners or flavours. The USDA match is 'Fruit punch juice drink, frozen concentrate', a flavoured blended drink. Under the guidelines it counts as a modified/flavoured version (guideline D) and a blend rather than the plain product (guideline F). Its flavour profile, sweetness and acidity would differ from a plain juice concentrate, and it is a juice drink rather than juice. Condition 2 would likely fail, since a diner could notice the different taste. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Because the flavour difference is substantive, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is low-fat raisin granola, and the USDA entry is Quaker Low Fat 100% Natural Granola with Raisins. Both name the same product with the same components: granola, low fat, and raisins. Guideline D says that when the ingredient itself asks for the modified version (low fat), the matching modified entry counts as a match. Guideline G says a branded entry of the same plain product type matches, and the Quaker brand here is the same product type with no extra flavour. The quantity (17g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the granola can directly replace the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since it is the same low-fat raisin granola. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is acerola juice concentrate, unsweetened. The USDA entry is acerola juice, raw, which is the fresh, unprocessed, not-concentrated juice. Concentrate is a processed state of the juice, with water removed, so it is not the same product as raw juice. Guideline F treats a different state and the raw source versus processed ingredient as non-matches. Condition 1 fails: 250g of concentrate contains far more acerola solids than 250g of raw juice, so swapping them changes the recipe's flavour, sweetness, acidity and the amount of liquid. The dish would have to be reformulated, for example by reconstituting or adding more juice, which changes preparation. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would likely notice a difference in intensity of flavour and possibly in body or appearance. The 'unsweetened' descriptor is consistent with raw juice, but it does not address the concentration difference. Both conditions are not met.

Condition 1: The ingredient is vanilla yogurt, a flavoured yogurt. The USDA entry is yogurt with low-fat milk and flavours other than fruit, which covers vanilla. Flavoured yogurts are normally sold low fat (guideline D), so this is the standard product a shopper would buy under this name. It can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: Vanilla flavouring, yogurt texture and appearance all match. The low-fat milk base is the normal form of this product and does not produce a noticeable difference in taste or texture for a diner. Both conditions hold. The 15g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is raw serrano chile, sliced (a single vegetable; the slicing is knife work and does not change the match). The USDA entry is 'Peppers and onions, cooked, no added fat', a cooked mixed dish of peppers and onions. It is not the same food as raw serrano chile: it adds onions, is cooked, and is a blend rather than a single ingredient. Condition 1 fails because using it would change the dish's preparation (cooked and combined with onions rather than raw sliced chile). Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the added onion flavour, the softer cooked texture, and the different appearance. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is fresh rosemary sprigs used as a garnish. The USDA match is 'Spices, pepper, black', which is a different food entirely: black peppercorns/ground black pepper, a different plant and flavour profile from rosemary (an herb, Rosmarinus officinalis). Condition 1 fails: substituting black pepper for a rosemary garnish would change the dish's flavour and the garnish's appearance (green sprig versus dark ground/peppercorn specks), so the preparation changes. Condition 2 fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste (peppery versus resinous herbal) and appearance. The quantity of 1g is ignored per the guidelines and does not affect the result. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply.

The ingredient is fenugreek sprouts, a specific sprout variety with a distinctive slightly bitter, maple-like flavour and a particular appearance. The USDA entry 'Sprouts, NFS' is a generic 'not further specified' category covering sprouts of any seed type, such as mung bean, alfalfa or radish. It does not name fenugreek, so it is not the same food under another name (guideline B). Condition 1 (same preparation) might hold, since sprouts are handled similarly, but condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice a different sprout's flavour and texture. Sprout varieties are sibling products with different tastes (guideline F), so the match is not substitutable. The 290g quantity is ignored (guideline A).

The ingredient is 'queso dip', a smooth, typically processed or melting cheese dip, usually eaten warm or melted. The USDA match 'Queso Fresco' is a fresh, crumbly, unmelted Mexican cheese. Condition 1 fails: queso fresco would not melt into a dip, so swapping it in would change how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (smooth and creamy versus crumbly), flavour (mild dairy and processed-cheese dip versus fresh, salty cheese) and appearance. The quantity is ignored per guideline A, and the names are not the same food under different labels (guideline B). Queso dip is not the plain cheese, so this is not a standard-default match (guideline D). It is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a blend of two different berries: loganberries and raspberries, frozen. The USDA entry covers only loganberries, frozen. Guideline F says a single ingredient versus a blend containing it is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because the dish would not be made with a single berry type. Condition 2 also fails because loganberries and raspberries differ in flavour (loganberries are tarter and more pronounced) and in colour and seed character, so a diner could notice the difference. The frozen state itself is acceptable under guideline E, but that does not address the missing raspberries. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is macadamia nuts, with the 15g quantity being irrelevant per guideline A. The USDA match is 'Macadamia nuts' with no state descriptor, which by guideline E is the generic food and matches fresh or plain versions. Condition 1: macadamia nuts can be used directly in place of macadamia nuts with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is farro, cooked, which is an ancient wheat (Triticum species) with a chewy texture and nutty flavour. The USDA match is pearled barley, cooked, which is a different grain (Hordeum vulgare). This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Both are chewy, whole-grain-style cooked grains, so they could occupy a similar place in a dish, which partly meets condition 1. However, barley has a different flavour profile, a different starch and gluten structure, and a different visual appearance (pearled barley is pale and smoother), so a diner would likely notice a difference in taste and texture. Guideline F rejects different plant sources and sibling products with different taste, and this pairing fits that pattern. Condition 2 is not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain pumpkin, and the USDA entry is 'Pumpkin, raw', which is the same food in its uncooked state. The leading '35g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the raw pumpkin can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the ingredient is not specified as cooked, canned, or processed. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same raw vegetable. Both conditions are met.

Toor dal is split, dehulled pigeon peas (red gram dal), a processed form sold as a distinct product. The USDA entry is whole dried mature pigeon peas with their seed coats intact. Condition 1: Whole peas need a much longer soak and cook time, and they do not break down the way split dal does, so cooking the dish with them would change its preparation. Condition 2: Cooked dal is typically smooth, soft and yellow-orange, with broken split halves and no visible skins. Whole pigeon peas keep their shape and hulls, so a diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance. Guideline C covers whole dried legumes as bought, but toor dal is not sold in that form, so the match does not hold. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is smoked squid rings, 115g (quantity ignored). The USDA match is squid, mixed species, cooked, fried. Condition 1: the match is cooked and fried, whereas the ingredient is smoked squid, which is a preserved, ready-to-eat product that is not fried. Using fried squid would change the preparation (it is already cooked and deep-fried, not smoked), so the dish's method would be altered. Guideline F states that plain vs smoked and raw/cooked states are not interchangeable. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference, since smoked squid has a smoky flavour, a chewier, drier texture and a darker, browned appearance, while fried squid has a crisp batter or coating and an oily, fried flavour. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is nonfat strawberry-flavored milk. The USDA entry is Strawberry milk, fat free (skim). 'Nonfat' and 'fat free' are the same fat level, and both entries describe strawberry-flavored milk, so the flavour and fat content match. The ingredient itself asks for the flavoured, low-fat version, so the matching flavoured entry is correct under guideline D. The weight prefix is ignored (A). Condition 1: the milk can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since both are skim-based strawberry milk. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is outside skirt steak, raw. The USDA entry is the same cut (outside skirt, plate steak, boneless), raw and uncooked. The 'trimmed to 0" fat' descriptor describes fat trimming, which the guidelines treat as knife work or handling (like 'trimmed') that does not change the match. 'All grades' is the standard default for this cut. The cooking method is unchanged, since the steak is cooked the same way either way. Visually and in taste, the difference between a lightly trimmed and a fully trimmed skirt steak is minor, and it does not make the diner eat a different food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain ricotta cheese, frozen and then thawed. The USDA entry 'Cheese, ricotta, whole milk' is the same food. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to its standard default version as a match, and whole milk is the usual default for ricotta since the ingredient names no fat level. Guideline E says frozen cheese for cooking matches the fresh entry when freezing does not show, and ricotta is normally mixed or cooked, so thawed ricotta is acceptable. The ingredient does not state a modified version such as part-skim, so no modification applies. Condition 1 holds because the match can be used directly without changing preparation. Condition 2 holds because thawed ricotta used in a dish should not be noticeably different in taste, texture or appearance from whole milk ricotta.

The ingredient is plain dried egg white powder. The USDA entry is dried egg white that is 'stabilized' and 'glucose reduced'. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version with added additives or treatment is not substitutable. Stabilized dried egg white contains added stabilizers and has had glucose removed, which is a processing change, not the default form of the plain product. Under guideline F, specialty processed or food-service ingredients differ from the home ingredient. The stabilizers also change whipping and foaming behaviour, so a dish made with meringue-style or whipped preparations could differ in texture and stability. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in texture or appearance) are not reliably met, so the match is not substitutable.

1. Identity: 'Hot sauce' is a pepper-based condiment, and the USDA entry 'Sauce, ready-to-serve, pepper or hot' describes that same product category under a formal name, so it is the same food under another name (guideline B). 2. Modification: the entry is the generic, ready-to-serve default and carries no flavour, reduced-sodium, or other modifying descriptor that would make it differ from a shopper's normal hot sauce (guidelines D and G). 3. Quantity is ignored (guideline A). 4. Condition 1: the match can be used directly in place of hot sauce without changing preparation, since it is a ready-to-serve condiment added the same way. 5. Condition 2: the generic entry reflects the standard product, so a diner would not reasonably perceive a difference in taste, texture, or appearance attributable to the substitution. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is '25g cherry', a fresh cherry fruit (the weight is decoration per guideline A). The USDA match is 'Soy sauce', a fermented liquid condiment made from soybeans, wheat, and brine. Condition 1: Soy sauce is not the same food as cherry under any regional or culinary name (guideline B does not apply), and substituting it would change the dish's preparation, since cherries are a fruit added for sweetness, tartness, or texture while soy sauce is a salty, savoury liquid. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste (salty, umami versus sweet-tart fruit) and in appearance and texture (liquid condiment versus whole fruit). Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is plain frozen English muffins, thawed, which is a bread product. The USDA match is 'Egg sandwich on English muffin', a composite dish that includes egg, and usually cheese and possibly meat, on top of the muffin. Condition 1 fails: using the egg sandwich in place of the muffins would add egg and other fillings, changing how the dish is prepared and what the recipe contains. Condition 2 fails: a diner would clearly notice the presence of egg and other filling, so the eating experience differs. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and it is a prepared dish rather than the ingredient itself (guideline F, different state and composition). The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a plain bagel. The 200g is only a quantity and is ignored. Splitting is knife work or handling, which does not change the match (guideline C). The USDA entry 'Bagel' names the same food with no modifying state, flavour, or preparation, so it is the generic default version (guideline D). Condition 1: a bagel can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since the split is done by hand either way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is red leaf lettuce, a raw leafy green used fresh. The USDA match is 'Lettuce, cooked', which is a different state of the same food. Condition 1 fails: cooking changes the preparation, since raw lettuce is typically used in salads, wraps or as a garnish, and substituting cooked lettuce would change how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference, because cooked lettuce is wilted, softened, darker and has a different texture, flavour and appearance. Per guideline F, raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is high oleic canola oil, unhydrogenated, a liquid oil used as a plain cooking fat. The USDA entry is industrial canola oil that is partially hydrogenated and labelled for deep fat frying. Condition 1 fails: partially hydrogenated oil is a different processed fat from unhydrogenated high oleic oil. It is also an industrial, food-service specialty fat, which guideline F excludes from matching the home ingredient, and its intended use is deep frying, so it is not a straightforward swap for the recipe's preparation. Condition 2 also fails: partial hydrogenation changes the fat's solid fraction, melting behaviour, mouthfeel and flavour stability, and it contains trans fatty acids, so a diner could notice differences in texture and taste. The quantity (20g) is irrelevant. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

"Queensland nuts" is a regional/trade name for macadamia nuts (Macadamia integrifolia and related species, native to Queensland, Australia). Under guideline B, a regional name for the same food counts as the same food. The USDA entry "Nuts, macadamia nuts, raw" is the uncooked nut, and the recipe does not state any cooking or processing that would change it. The weight prefix "35g" is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the raw macadamia nut can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same nut. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a crispy rolled tortilla (a taquito) filled with seasoned pork. The USDA entry 'Taquito, beef or pork' names the same dish with the same components: a crispy rolled tortilla with a meat filling, and pork is one of its listed options. Under guideline B and C, a USDA entry that names the same dish with the same components is a match. Preparation method is unchanged because both are fried or baked rolled taquitos, and the tortilla, shape, and crispy texture are the same. The entry is a general 'beef or pork' category, so its filling may be an average of both meats rather than pure pork, which could be slightly noticeable. However, pork is explicitly included in the entry, and the guidelines treat the same named dish as a match. Condition 1 is met. Condition 2 is reasonably met, since the taste and appearance of a pork taquito fall within the entry's stated scope.

The ingredient is queso fresco, a fresh, moist, crumbly cheese normally used uncooked as a garnish. The USDA match is queso asadero, a semi-soft, mild melting cheese made for melting in quesadillas and similar dishes. They are different cheeses, not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails: asadero would not be crumbled or sprinkled the way queso fresco is, so the preparation changes. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (smooth and stretchy versus crumbly) and in how the garnish looks and melts or holds its shape. The 40g quantity is ignored.

The ingredient is dried bok choy flakes, a dehydrated product. The USDA match is raw, fresh bok choy. Guideline F states that a different state (raw vs processed, fresh vs dried) is not substitutable. Using fresh bok choy in place of dried flakes would change the preparation (the flakes would need rehydrating or the recipe would need adjusting for moisture and volume), and the dish would differ in texture and appearance because fresh leaves are crisp and moist while dried flakes are brittle and concentrated. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well, since a diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance. The match is not substitutable.

1. The ingredient is canned French lentils (a Puy-type variety), drained. The leading weight and the drained handling step are ignored per guidelines A and C. 2. The USDA entry 'Lentils, from canned' matches the canned form, and that part is correct. 3. The USDA entry names no variety, so it is the generic lentil. French lentils are a specific variety that holds its shape and has a firmer, more peppery flavour. Generic canned lentils are often brown or green types that soften more and taste milder. Under guideline F, a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable. 4. Condition 1 (same preparation) is arguably met because both are canned and used the same way. Condition 2 is not reliably met, since a diner could notice the softer texture and different flavour of a generic lentil in place of French lentils. The match fails on the variety difference.

The ingredient is prickly pear, the fruit of the Opuntia cactus. The USDA match is pear nectar, a processed beverage made from true pears (Pyrus). These are different foods, not regional names for the same food, so guideline B does not apply. Pear nectar is also a liquid, sweetened and processed product, while prickly pear is a raw whole fruit. Using it would change the dish's flavour, texture and appearance, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well.

Pearl onions are a small-sized cultivar of the common onion (Allium cepa), so the USDA entry names the same food. The ingredient is a frozen product that has been thawed, and guideline E says a thawed frozen product matches the frozen USDA entry of the same product, so 'Onions, frozen, whole' fits the state. 'Unprepared' describes the raw, unpeeled state, but the thawed pearl onions are already peeled, and peeling does not change the match under guideline C. Condition 1: the onions can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to the cooking method, since both are cooked or mixed in the same way. Condition 2: freezing is not visible once the onions are cooked or mixed into a dish. The remaining difference is size, since pearl onions are smaller, but this is the same food sold in a smaller form, and a diner would not normally taste a difference between them in a cooked dish. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is generic dried persimmons with no variety specified. The USDA entry is the dried form of the same fruit (Japanese persimmon, dried), and dried Japanese persimmons are the common dried persimmon sold in shops. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matches the standard default version. The quantity (300g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the entry is the same dried product, so it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since the dried fruit is the same product. Any variety difference is not specified by the ingredient, so it does not count against the match. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain green leaf lettuce, raw or wilted (the recipe wilts it). The USDA entry 'Lettuce, wilted, with bacon dressing' is a prepared dish: wilted lettuce tossed in a bacon dressing. Condition 1: the match would add a bacon dressing, which changes the preparation. Plain wilted lettuce would be dressed with nothing or a simple seasoning, so the dish's preparation changes. Condition 2: a diner would taste bacon fat, vinegar, and sugar-type dressing flavour, which is a clear flavour difference, and the appearance would also differ with bacon bits and dressing. Under guideline F/D, this is a plain ingredient mapped to a flavoured/modified version, which is not substitutable. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is parsnips (fresh root vegetable, quantity irrelevant). The USDA entry 'Parsnips, raw' is literally the same food in its uncooked, whole fresh state. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since peeling, chopping or cooking is handled by the recipe, not the match. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same raw vegetable. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is welsh onion (Allium fistulosum), a green, scallion-type onion sold as chopped green stems. The USDA entry is frozen chopped onion, which is the bulb onion (Allium cepa). These are different species, not regional names for the same food, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline B's scallion example maps to 'Onions, spring', not to a bulb onion. Condition 2 also fails: bulb onion is sharper, sweeter when cooked, and paler, with a different texture and appearance from welsh onion greens, so a diner would likely notice the difference. Freezing does not explain the gap (guideline E), since the underlying food differs. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is soy nut butter, a spread made from roasted or raw soybeans (soy nuts) ground into a paste, with a distinct legume/soy flavour and a smooth, thick texture. The USDA match is 'Cookie, butter or sugar, with fruit and/or nuts', which is a baked cookie product containing fruit and/or nuts. Condition 1: a cookie is a baked product, not a spread or paste; it cannot be used in place of soy nut butter without changing how the dish is prepared (the soy nut butter would have to be a baked-in ingredient, but the match is an entire finished cookie with flour, sugar, fat and leavening, so substituting it would fundamentally change the recipe). Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (sweet baked biscuit flavour versus soy paste), texture (crumbly/baked versus smooth paste), and appearance. Not the same food under another name, and it is a different product type entirely. Neither condition is met.

1) Same food: the ingredient is frozen pineapple juice concentrate, and the USDA entry is pineapple juice, frozen concentrate, so the product type matches. 2) Frozen and thawed: guideline E says a frozen product that is thawed matches the frozen USDA entry of the same product, so the 'frozen' state is correct. 3) 'Undiluted' matches concentrate as bought, not reconstituted juice. 4) 'Unsweetened' is a descriptor that could be read as a modification under guideline D. However, frozen pineapple juice concentrate is normally sold unsweetened with no added sugar, so the descriptor reflects the standard product rather than a modified version (the exception in D). 5) Cooking method is unchanged: a thawed concentrate is used the same way. 6) Taste, texture and appearance should match the standard product, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

Southern peas is a regional name for cowpeas, and blackeye is one of the most common southern pea varieties. The USDA entry is for immature cowpea seeds (blackeyes), frozen and unprepared, which matches frozen southern peas as bought. Guideline E treats frozen peas that are normally cooked as matching the USDA entry, since freezing does not show in the finished dish. Cooking method stays the same: the peas are simply cooked from frozen. Any variety difference among southern peas (crowder, cream) is minor and would not be noticed in a cooked dish. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a wheat bagel. The USDA entry 'Bagel, wheat' describes the same food under a near-identical name, so it is the same product rather than a sibling or modified version. The leading '200g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: a wheat bagel can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is unsalted roasted Queensland nuts. Queensland nut is a regional name for the macadamia, so this is the same food under another name (guideline B). The USDA entry is macadamia nuts, which is the same food. The ingredient is roasted and unsalted; the USDA entry is dry roasted and without salt added. Dry roasting is the ordinary way macadamias are roasted, so the roasted state matches and the unsalted state matches. Quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the nuts can be used in place of each other with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is pork tenderloin specifically flavoured teriyaki, so the same cut (pork tenderloin) with a teriyaki flavour is the requested version. The USDA entry is the same cut, pork tenderloin, prepared with a teriyaki flavour. Under guideline D, when the ingredient itself asks for the flavoured version, the matching flavoured entry counts. Guideline G's rule against branded flavoured entries applies to plain ingredients, not to ingredients that name the flavour. Cooking method is unchanged (it is still a pork tenderloin to be cooked as the recipe directs). The flavour matches the teriyaki the recipe calls for, so a diner would not expect any difference in taste, texture, or appearance from the teriyaki-flavoured cut. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked haddock, flaked. Smoking is a processing step that gives the fish a distinct smoky flavour, colour and firmer texture. The USDA match, 'Fish, haddock, fried', is haddock that has been cooked by frying, with a breaded or crisp coating and added fat. Condition 1 fails: using fried haddock would change the preparation, since the recipe calls for smoked fish to be flaked, and a fried product would not be a direct substitute for it. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the absence of smoke and notice the crisp, fried exterior. Guideline F rejects a 'plain vs smoked' or 'raw/cooked vs processed' state difference, and this pairing differs on both counts. Flaking does not change the match. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is generic raw fresh pork sausage with no stated seasoning. The USDA entry is a specific variety, Italian sausage, mild, which is seasoned with fennel and other Italian spices. Condition 1: the match is raw pork sausage, so cooking method would generally carry over. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference in flavour, since mild Italian sausage has a distinct fennel-forward taste that plain fresh pork sausage (for example, breakfast-style) does not. Because the ingredient does not specify Italian seasoning, the Italian variety is a flavoured sibling rather than the plain default, and the flavour change is noticeable. Condition 2 is not met.

The ingredient is strawberry powder, which is a fruit-based powder made from actual strawberries. The USDA entry is a strawberry-flavor beverage mix, a powdered drink product that is sweetened and flavored, typically containing sugar, citric acid, and artificial or natural flavorings, with little or no fruit. Under guideline F, a blend or product with added components is not the same as the single ingredient, and under guideline D, a flavored or sweetened version of a plain product is a modification, not the default. Condition 1 is doubtful because the beverage mix would change the sweetness, acidity and flavour balance of the dish and may not behave the same in the recipe. Condition 2 fails because a diner would likely taste the added sugar and artificial-style flavour compared with true strawberry powder. Guideline B does not apply because the two are not the same food under another name. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried shrimp, rehydrated in water. That is a dehydrated, typically salted and intensely flavoured product, which is then softened by soaking. The USDA match, 'Shrimp, canned', is a cooked, canned product packed in brine. Condition 1 fails: using canned shrimp would skip the drying and rehydration step, so the preparation changes. Under guideline F, a different state (dried versus canned/cooked) is not substitutable. Condition 2 also fails: canned shrimp lacks the concentrated, savoury, slightly chewy character of rehydrated dried shrimp, and a diner would likely notice the difference in flavour and texture. The quantity (75g) is ignored, as guideline A requires.

The ingredient is whole sorghum grain, rinsed before use. The USDA entry is 'Sorghum, whole grain, white, dry, raw', which is the same food: uncooked whole sorghum grain as bought. Rinsing is handling that does not change the match (guideline C), and the weight is decoration (guideline A). 'Dry, raw' describes the uncooked dried grain, the same state as the ingredient. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the grain is cooked the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same grain. Both conditions are met.

Pomegranate seeds are the arils, the edible inner part of the pomegranate fruit. The USDA entry 'Pomegranate, raw' describes the same fruit, and its edible portion is the arils, with the peel and membranes treated as refuse. Under guideline B, an inner part of the same food counts as the same food. The quantity (75g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the arils are simply separated from the fruit as they would be for the seeds. Condition 2: the taste, texture and appearance of the arils are the same, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain yogurt, with no fat level specified, so the standard default is the regular (whole milk) product. The USDA match is 'Yogurt, low fat milk, plain', which is a reduced-fat version. Guideline D treats low-fat as a modification of a plain ingredient, and the exemption for normally low-fat products covers flavoured yogurts, frozen yogurt, parfaits and buttermilk, not plain yogurt. Condition 2 also fails: low-fat plain yogurt is thinner, tangier and less rich, so a diner could notice the difference in taste and texture, especially in a dish where the yogurt is a prominent component. Condition 1 may hold for simple substitution, but since condition 2 fails, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried jujube, while the USDA match is Jujube, raw. Both refer to the same fruit, so the food identity matches. However, guideline F says a different state (raw vs dried) is not substitutable. Dried jujubes are wrinkled, chewy, and much sweeter and more concentrated in flavour, while raw jujubes are crisp, juicy, and apple-like. Using raw fruit would change the texture, sweetness, and appearance, and would also change the preparation (dried fruit is typically rehydrated, simmered, or chewed as is, while raw fruit would not be prepared that way). A diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 (no change in preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance) both fail.

The ingredient is conch meat, which comes from marine sea snails (gastropods). The USDA entry is clam meat, which comes from bivalves. These are different animals, not regional or trade names for the same food, so guideline B does not apply. Conch is typically firmer and chewier than clam, and its flavour is distinct. In dishes such as conch fritters, ceviche or stew, a diner would likely notice the difference in texture and taste. Condition 1 (same preparation) may be met, but condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste or texture) is not. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

Alfredo sauce is a cream-and-butter sauce flavoured with Parmesan (and usually garlic and seasonings). The USDA entry, 'Sauce, cheese, ready-to-serve', describes a shelf-stable or ready-to-serve cheese sauce, typically a processed cheese sauce of the nacho type. These are different foods, not the same food under another name. Condition 2 fails: the sauce's flavour, texture and appearance differ, and a diner would likely notice a sharper, processed-cheese taste in place of creamy garlic-Parmesan alfredo. Condition 1 is also doubtful, since a processed cheese sauce behaves differently in cooking and in the finished dish. The 25g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is sweetened pitanga preserves, a processed fruit product (jam/preserve) made by cooking pitanga fruit with sugar. The USDA match is raw pitanga (surinam cherry), an uncooked whole fruit. Condition 1: Preserves cannot be used in place of raw fruit without changing preparation; the fruit must be cooked and sweetened with sugar to form a spread, so the dish's preparation would change (a spreadable, cooked, sugared product versus whole raw fruit). Condition 2: A diner would clearly notice the difference in taste (added sweetness, cooked flavour), texture (soft, gel-like or spreadable versus firm fresh fruit) and appearance. Per guideline F, raw vs processed and sweetened vs unsweetened are not substitutable. The match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is stew meat, which is beef stew meat, typically cut from chuck or similar cuts and sold as cubes for stewing. The USDA entry 'Beef, stew meat' names the same product directly. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation, since it is the same food under the same name. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. The quantity (150g) is ignored per guideline A. The match is the same food under the same name, so it is substitutable.

The ingredient is canned tuna packed in water, drained. The USDA entry is light tuna canned in oil, drained solids. Condition 1 (same preparation): the dish would be prepared the same way, but the match is a different packing medium. Guideline F explicitly says a different packing medium (e.g. in syrup vs juice, or water vs oil) is not substitutable. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference): oil-packed tuna is noticeably richer, moister and more mellow in flavour and texture than water-packed tuna, and a diner could notice the difference. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain 'sage', which in a recipe is normally the fresh herb (the leaves), and the weight is given in grams, which is typical for fresh herbs. The match is 'Spices, sage, ground', a dried, ground spice. Guideline F explicitly says fresh vs dried herb and whole vs ground spice are different states and not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using ground dried sage changes preparation, since fresh leaves are typically chopped, fried or layered, while ground powder is mixed in. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in flavour intensity, texture and appearance (no visible leaves, different dried-spice taste). The quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is round steak, a cut from the round primal of beef. The USDA entry 'Beef, steak, round' names the same cut of beef, with no added state such as cooked, marinated, or seasoned. Quantity is irrelevant. The match is the plain, standard version of the same food, so the cooking method, flavour, texture, and appearance are unchanged. A diner would not notice a difference, so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a generic orange-flavored drink that is fortified (the fortification is part of what the recipe asks for). The USDA entry is a fruit juice drink with added calcium, branded as Sunny D, which is itself an orange-flavored drink fortified with calcium. Per guideline D, when the ingredient asks for a fortified version, the matching modified entry counts. Per guideline G, a branded entry of the same product type is acceptable. The entry does not add any flavour beyond the orange profile the ingredient describes. Condition 1: the drink could be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are ready-to-drink liquids used the same way. Condition 2: the taste, texture and appearance are those of an orange-flavored fortified drink, so a diner would not reasonably notice a difference attributable to the match. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain 'fruit yogurt', which a shopper would normally buy as fruit-flavoured yogurt. The USDA entry is 'Yogurt, fruit, low fat'. Guideline D says fruit and flavoured yogurts are typically low fat, so the 'low fat' descriptor reflects how the product is normally sold and is not a modification. The '9 g protein/8 oz' phrase is a nutritional label descriptor for the same product type. Condition 1: it can directly replace fruit yogurt in any recipe without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product type. The leading '200g' is only quantity and is ignored. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dry roasted cashews, unsalted. The USDA entry is cashew nuts, dry roasted, without salt added, which is the same food in the same state: dry roasted and unsalted. The quantity prefix (2g) is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient with no change in preparation, since both are used as-is. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the roasting state and salt content are identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain 'cottage cheese', whose standard default is full-fat creamed cottage cheese. The USDA match is 'Cheese, cottage, lowfat, 1% milkfat, no sodium added', which is a modified version: it is low-fat and has no added sodium. Guideline D says a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced-fat or low-sodium version is not a match, because the product differs from what a shopper would normally buy under the plain name. Condition 1 is therefore questionable: the swap alters the product rather than just the handling. Condition 2 also fails in practice, since 1% milkfat cottage cheese is noticeably less rich and creamy than creamed cottage cheese, and a diner could notice the difference in texture and flavour. The quantity (100g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is corn relish, a ready-made condiment of chopped corn, peppers, onion, vinegar, sugar and spices. The USDA entry 'Relish, corn' names the same product with the same components, so it is the same food under the same name (guideline B and D). Substituting it changes no preparation step, since it is a condiment used as-is. The weight (75g) and the '(optional)' note are decoration (guideline A). A diner would not taste, see or feel a difference between the two, because they are the same product type. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh jicama (a root vegetable, also called yambean, Pachyrhizus). The USDA entry 'Yambean (jicama), raw' is literally the same food under its alternate common name, which guideline B treats as a match. The quantity (500g) is ignored per guideline A. The entry is raw, which matches 'fresh' jicama as normally bought and used; any peeling or cubing in the recipe is handling that does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: jicama can be used in place of itself with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference, since it is the identical food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 70g plantain, meaning the raw/cooked fruit used as a starchy vegetable in cooking (e.g., fried, boiled, or baked). The USDA match is Plantain chips, a snack product that is thinly sliced, fried or baked, and salted/seasoned. Condition 1 fails: plantain chips are a processed, already-fried snack and cannot replace a whole plantain without changing how the dish is prepared (the plantain would need to be cooked, sliced, or mashed rather than used as a crisp snack). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice a difference in texture (crisp and dry versus soft and starchy) and flavour (salted, fried snack versus sweet-starchy fruit). This is the raw plant versus a processed product, which falls under the 'raw source vs processed ingredient' pattern and is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried tofu (dried bean curd, a soy product that is pressed and dehydrated, typically firm and chewy, used in braises, stir-fries, and soups). The USDA match is cooked white rice with no added fat, a starchy grain with a soft, moist texture and neutral flavour. Condition 1 fails: substituting cooked rice for dried tofu would change the dish's preparation, since tofu is a protein component that is rehydrated or braised, while rice is a starch that is cooked separately and would not play the same role. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would readily notice the difference in taste, texture (chewy protein versus soft grain), and appearance. These are different foods, not the same food under another name, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is yellowtail, ground. The USDA entry is 'Fish, yellowtail, mixed species, raw', which is the same fish under the generic USDA name. Guideline C says grinding at home for fish does not change the match, and 'raw' means uncooked, which is what the recipe needs. Condition 1: the entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is raw and can be ground the same way. Condition 2: it is the same species group with no added flavour, modification or processing, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. The 'mixed species' wording reflects USDA's generic yellowtail entry rather than a different product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is panko breadcrumbs: a processed, toasted/dried bread product with a light, crisp, flaky texture, used as a coating. The USDA match is Lentils, dry, which is a dried legume (mature seeds). These are not the same food under another name, and lentils are not a processed form of bread. Condition 1 fails: lentils cannot replace panko as a coating or binder without changing preparation, since they would not form a crisp crust and would require cooking first. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would readily notice small firm legumes instead of crisp breadcrumb coating in taste, texture and appearance. Not substitutable.

1. Same food: the ingredient is egg white, and the USDA entry is raw egg white, so it is the same food. The quantity (340g) is ignored per guideline A.
2. Fresh vs frozen/pasteurized: guideline E says a frozen product matches the fresh/raw entry when the food is normally cooked or mixed and freezing does not show. Egg whites are normally cooked, baked, or whipped, so thawed frozen whites would not visibly differ in the finished dish.
3. Pasteurization: this is a processing step, not a flavour, texture, or appearance change a diner would notice in a cooked or whipped dish. The main practical difference is that pasteurized whites may whip slightly differently, but this is not a difference in how the dish is prepared or how it looks or tastes to a diner.
4. Condition 1 (same preparation): separated, thawed whites are used the same way as fresh whites, so the cooking method does not change.
5. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference): a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance.
Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain soy milk with no sweetness specified. The USDA match is 'Soy milk, sweetened, plain, refrigerated', so the match carries a 'sweetened' modifier. Guideline D lists sweetened/unsweetened as modifications when the plain ingredient maps to a modified version, and the exception for descriptors that are normally how a product is sold does not clearly apply, since unsweetened soy milk is a common default. Sweetness would change flavour in savoury dishes and be noticeable in sweet ones, so condition 2 (no noticeable taste difference) fails. The other elements (plain, refrigerated, liquid) are compatible, but the sweetening alters flavour, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a Mexican melting cheese sold in string style. Oaxaca is the classic string-style Mexican melting cheese, so the USDA entry names the same food under a regional/culinary name (guideline B). The 65g quantity is ignored (A). Shredded or pulled string-style cheese is a handling form of the same cheese, so the cooking method is unchanged: it melts the same way in the same dish (condition 1). Taste, texture and appearance should match because it is the same product, so a diner would not notice a difference (condition 2). The entry is plain, with no added flavour or modification (D), so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is crumbled cotija cheese, a dry, salty, aged Mexican cheese that crumbles firmly and has a sharp, savoury flavour. The USDA match is feta, a brined cheese that is moister, softer and tangier. Cotija is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Feta is a different cheese variety with a different taste and texture. Guideline F rejects sibling varieties with different taste, and a diner would likely notice the difference in moisture, sharpness and saltiness. Although feta is a common stand-in, it fails condition 2, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is ground brisket, a meat product typically ground from brisket with its fat retained, so it is fattier and juicier when cooked. The USDA entry is brisket flat half, separable lean only, trimmed to 1/8" fat, raw. That is a lean, trimmed whole cut, not a ground product. Grinding at home does not change the match under guideline E, but the lean-only, trimmed, flat-half specification means it is a different product from typical ground brisket in fat content and cut. Guideline F says a different cut of meat is not substitutable. The fat difference would change the texture, moisture and flavour of the cooked dish, such as a burger or meatball, and a diner would likely notice. Conditions 1 and 2 are not both met.

The ingredient is plain Greek yogurt, a strained, thick, high-protein yogurt sold under that name in its standard default form. The USDA match is 'Yogurt, plain, nonfat', which is a fat-free version of regular (unstrained) plain yogurt. Condition 1: Greek yogurt is typically used as-is in cooking and dips, so swapping in a looser, unstrained yogurt would change how thick sauces, dips or baked goods set. Condition 2: the texture is noticeably thinner and wetter than strained Greek yogurt, and the fat-free descriptor changes the mouthfeel and richness. Per guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a fat-free/modified entry is not substitutable. Both conditions fail, so the match is rejected.

The ingredient is turkey pastrami, and the USDA entry is 'Pastrami, turkey', which names the same product under a different word order. The quantity (150g) is irrelevant. No cooking method is implied that would differ, and the product is the same cured, smoked turkey breast deli meat, so a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is turkey bacon, chopped, which is a turkey-based meat product. The USDA match is 'Bacon bits', a dried, shelf-stable, pork-based product with a crumbly, hard texture. Turkey bacon is not the same food as bacon bits, so guideline B does not apply. Chopping is knife work and does not change the match, but the underlying food differs. Condition 1 fails because bacon bits are used as a dried topping and cannot stand in for chopped turkey bacon, which is cooked into the dish, without changing its preparation. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in flavour (pork versus turkey, dried and smoky-sweet versus meaty) and in texture (dry and brittle versus soft and chewy). Not substitutable.

The ingredient is frozen peas and carrots with butter added. The USDA entry, 'Peas and carrots, frozen, cooked, fat added', names the same product with the same components: peas and carrots, frozen, with fat added. Guideline C says that buttered peas and carrots matches 'Peas and carrots, cooked, fat added'. The 'cooked' descriptor is standard for frozen vegetables sold ready to heat, and guideline E says frozen peas match when freezing does not show. The quantity (310g) is ignored per guideline A. The dish would be prepared the same way with either food, and a diner would not taste or see a difference, so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw lobster tail meat. The USDA match is raw blue crab, which is a different crustacean species. It is not the same food under another name (unlike prawns/shrimp or littleneck clams), so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1: the cooking method could stay the same, but the dish would be prepared with a different animal. Condition 2: lobster and blue crab differ in flavour, sweetness, and fibre texture, and a diner would likely notice the difference. Guideline F warns against substituting closely related items with different taste, and this is such a case. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.
