The ingredient 'tart green apple' is most commonly Granny Smith, the standard tart green apple sold in shops. The USDA entry is 'Apples, raw, granny smith, with skin', a raw fresh apple with the same taste, texture and appearance. The 100g quantity is ignored per guideline A. The 'Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program' text is only an administrative note and does not change the food. The ingredient does not ask for peeling, so 'with skin' is the normal default. Guideline F's sibling-variety rule (e.g., Fuji vs Granny Smith) does not apply, because 'tart green' identifies Granny Smith rather than a different variety. Condition 1 holds (same raw apple, same preparation). Condition 2 holds (a diner would not notice a difference).

The ingredient is '30g currant' (the dried fruit, typically Zante or dried currants, a small dried grape-like fruit with a tart, sweet flavour). The USDA match is 'Wheat bran', which is the outer layer of the wheat kernel, a fibrous, dry, bland cereal byproduct. Condition 1: Wheat bran cannot be used in place of currants without changing the dish: currants supply sweetness, moisture, chewiness and fruit flavour, while bran is dry, gritty and bland, so the preparation (e.g. baking, soaking, or folding into batter) would change. Condition 2: A diner would readily notice the difference in taste (no fruit sweetness or tartness), texture (no chewy fruit pieces) and appearance (no dark dried-fruit specks). The entry is not the same food under another name, and it is not a cut or variant of currants. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is '30g sweet rice', a plain raw grain (glutinous rice). The quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA match, 'Rice, sweet, cooked with honey', differs in two ways. First, it is cooked, while the ingredient is an uncooked dry grain, so using it would change the cooking method, which fails condition 1. Second, it has honey added, which changes flavour and sweetness, and a diner would notice this, which fails condition 2. Guideline F rules out raw versus cooked and a flavoured or modified version of a plain food. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is teff flour, a flour milled from teff grain (a small cereal grain). The USDA entry is Injera, Ethiopian bread, which is a fermented flatbread made from a batter that is typically predominantly teff flour, cooked on a griddle into a spongy sheet. Condition 1: Teff flour is an ingredient used to make injera, but injera is a finished, cooked bread product, not a flour. Substituting injera for teff flour would require the flour to be fermented, mixed into a batter and cooked into flatbread, which changes the entire preparation method; you cannot use it as a flour in a recipe that calls for 50g of flour. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference in texture and appearance (a spongy, sour, fermented flatbread versus a dry flour powder in the dish). Guideline F also says the raw source versus a processed product is not substitutable. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is a turkey drumstick with skin on, listed as a raw recipe input that the dish will cook. The USDA match is 'Turkey, drumstick, cooked, skin eaten', which is already cooked. Guideline F states that raw versus cooked is a different state and not substitutable. Using the cooked entry would skip the cooking step the recipe requires, so it would change how the dish is prepared (condition 1 fails). A diner would also notice the difference in texture and flavour, since the meat would already be roasted or braised before it reaches the dish (condition 2 fails). The skin and drumstick cut match, but the state does not, so the match is rejected.

The ingredient is plain shredded mozzarella, the standard full-fat version a shopper buys under that name. The USDA entry is 'Cheese, mozzarella, nonfat', a modified fat-free version. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient mapping to a fat-free/reduced-fat version as a modification, so it fails the same-food test. Condition 1 also fails: nonfat mozzarella melts, browns and stretches differently from full-fat, so cooking results change. Condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice a firmer, rubberier texture and less richness, and the appearance when melted differs. The quantity prefix is ignored. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient 'chinese leaves' is the common UK/Australian name for Chinese cabbage, which is the same food as Cabbage, chinese (pe-tsai), raw. Per guideline B, regional and culinary names for the same food count as the same food. The quantity prefix '100g' is ignored per guideline A. The ingredient is a plain fresh vegetable with no stated modification, and the USDA entry is the raw, uncooked form, which matches the default raw state implied by the ingredient. Any knife work does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same vegetable under a different name.

The ingredient is prosciutto, a dry-cured, thinly sliced Italian ham that is typically eaten raw. The USDA entry "Ham, prosciutto" names the same food directly, so it is the same product under the same name. Quantity (250g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: prosciutto can be used in place of itself with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw flank steak, sliced, which is a single beef cut. The USDA match is a prepared fast-food product, a Taco Bell soft taco containing a tortilla, steak, and other fillings and sauces. Condition 1 fails: the taco cannot replace raw flank steak in a recipe without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is already assembled, cooked, and seasoned, and it is not a raw meat cut. Condition 2 fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in texture, flavour, and appearance, because a tortilla, cheese, and sauce are present and the steak is not the same plain cooked-as-needed meat. Guideline F also applies: a single ingredient is not substitutable for a blended or composite product containing it. Quantity is ignored, and the 'steak' wording does not make the composite product the same food.

The ingredient is plain turkey sausage, which shoppers normally buy as a standard product. The USDA entry is a different product in three ways. First, it is 'reduced fat', a modified version of the plain food, and guideline D treats plain-to-modified as not a match. Second, it is 'brown and serve', a pre-cooked product, while the plain ingredient is typically bought raw and cooked in the recipe, so the cooking method would change. Third, the reduced fat content and pre-cooked texture would likely be noticeable in taste, texture and browning. Condition 1 (same preparation) fails, and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) is doubtful, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw turkey gizzards, weight 200g (quantity ignored). The USDA entry is 'Turkey, gizzard, all classes, raw', which is the same food: raw turkey gizzards, with 'all classes' simply denoting that the entry covers all turkey age/sex classes as sold. Both the cooking method and the dish's appearance, taste and texture would be unchanged, since the food is identical and in the same raw state. Under the guidelines, a plain ingredient mapped to its standard raw USDA entry is a match. Condition 1 is met, and condition 2 is met because a diner would notice no difference.

The ingredient is strawberry-flavoured Greek yogurt. The USDA entry is Greek yogurt, nonfat, with strawberry fruit on the bottom, from a branded product. Condition 1: the match is the same food, Greek yogurt with strawberry, and the recipe can use it in the same way with no change in preparation. Strawberry Greek yogurt is normally sold as a low-fat or nonfat product, so the nonfat descriptor reflects the standard retail version under guideline D and is not a modification. The branded entry matches a plain product type, and the ingredient itself asks for the flavoured version, so the flavoured entry matches under guideline G. The fruit-on-bottom layout is a packaging presentation, not a different food. Condition 2: a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. The main possible difference is the fat level, but nonfat is the usual form of this product, so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is saltine crackers with unsalted tops, a standard product. The USDA entry is 'Crackers, saltines, unsalted tops (includes oyster, soda, soup)', which names the same product with the same descriptor. The quantity prefix is ignored per guideline A. The parenthetical lists related cracker types that USDA groups under this entry, but the entry itself is the same food. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is used as the same crushed or whole cracker. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product type with the same salt treatment. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried blueberries, and the USDA entry is 'Blueberries, dried'. These are the same food with no added state or modifier in either name, so the match is literal. Quantity (320g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: dried blueberries can be used directly in place of the USDA dried blueberries with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the product is the same dried fruit. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw lamb breast, which the recipe will cook itself. The USDA entry is cooked, braised lamb breast, lean meat only, separable. Guideline F says raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Using a pre-braised product would change the cooking method, since the dish would no longer be cooked from raw, and the diner would notice a different texture and appearance. The 'lean only' qualifier also removes the fat that lamb breast normally carries, which changes taste and texture. Condition 1 fails because the preparation changes. Condition 2 fails because the diner would notice a different texture, appearance and flavour. The 300g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is pheasant, a game bird meat (raw or unspecified preparation). The USDA match is cooked white rice with no added fat, a grain product. Condition 1 fails: rice cannot replace pheasant in a recipe without fundamentally changing the dish's preparation, since pheasant would be cooked as meat (roasted, braised, pan-seared) while rice is a starch side that is cooked by boiling or steaming. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance between poultry meat and plain white rice. The quantity (80g) is irrelevant. This is a different food entirely, not the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is sunflower seeds (a seed, typically raw or roasted, eaten as a snack or used in baking and salads). The USDA match is 'Couscous, dry', which is a granular pasta product made from semolina/wheat flour. These are different foods: couscous is a wheat-based pasta, while sunflower seeds are oilseeds. Condition 1 fails: couscous cannot be used in place of sunflower seeds without changing the preparation (it would need hydrating and would not provide seeds for crunch or roasting). Condition 2 fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance (nutty, crunchy seed versus soft, bland grain). The quantity is ignored per the guidelines. This is not the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

1. The ingredient is a pork chop, which is a cut from the loin. The USDA entry is top loin chops, so the cut matches and is not a different cut such as belly or shoulder. 2. The ingredient is frozen and thawed. Guideline E says frozen meat matches the fresh/raw entry when freezing does not show in the finished dish, and a thawed chop cooked in a recipe looks and tastes the same as a fresh one. 3. The ingredient does not specify bone-in or boneless, so the standard default applies. The USDA entry is the standard way to describe a plain pork chop, with 'separable lean and fat' being the normal retail descriptor. 4. Cooking method is unchanged: the chop is still raw pork chop meat, so it can be cooked the same way. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is plain Greek yogurt with no fat level specified, so the standard default is a regular full-fat plain Greek yogurt. The USDA match is specifically 'nonfat', which is a fat-free modified version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a fat-free/reduced version is not substitutable. Condition 1 is arguably met, since nonfat Greek yogurt could be swapped in without changing the preparation method. Condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice the difference, because nonfat Greek yogurt is typically thinner, tangier, and less creamy than full-fat, which affects taste, texture, and mouthfeel. Both conditions must hold, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is chokecherries (Prunus virginiana), pitted. The USDA match is sour red cherries, raw (Prunus cerasus). These are different species, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Chokecherries are far more astringent and bitter than sour cherries, and their flavour and mouthfeel differ noticeably. Under guideline F, a different variety with a different taste is not substitutable. Pitting and the 500g quantity do not change this. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in taste, and chokecherry-based dishes would not taste the same with sour cherries.

The ingredient is raw wild rabbit. The USDA entry 'Game meat, rabbit, wild, raw' is the same food: wild rabbit, uncooked. The 30g quantity is decoration and is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are raw wild rabbit meat. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the food is the same raw wild rabbit. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a flour tortilla, and the USDA entry 'Tortilla, flour' names the same food under the same name. The leading '150g' is quantity and is ignored. The USDA entry has no modifying descriptor such as reduced fat, sodium, or flavouring, so it is the standard default version. It could be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is unsalted rice crackers, made from rice flour and typically crisp, light, and mild in flavour. The USDA match is 'Crackers, wheat', which is made from wheat flour and has a different base grain, a different flavour profile, and a different texture and appearance. Guideline F treats a different flour as a different ingredient, and the diner would notice the change in taste and texture. The match also does not account for the unsalted specification, since wheat crackers are normally salted. The two conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is caesar dressing, a condiment (an emulsion of oil, egg, lemon, garlic, anchovy, and cheese). The USDA match is a prepared Caesar salad made with romaine, croutons, and cheese, explicitly without dressing. Condition 1 fails: the match is a whole salad, not the dressing, so it cannot replace the dressing in a recipe without changing the dish. Adding the salad would bring lettuce, croutons, and cheese, and would not supply the creamy, savory, acidic dressing component. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the absence of dressing in taste, texture (the coating and moisture), and appearance. The entry is a different food from the ingredient, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is cuttlefish ink, the dark fluid from the ink sac, used as a black colouring and flavouring garnish. The USDA entry is the cooked flesh of cuttlefish, prepared by moist heat. Condition 1 fails: the ink is a separate part of the animal, not the meat, and it is not cooked as a garnish, so the match would change how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 fails: the flesh is pale and firm, while the ink is dark, glossy and briny, so a diner would clearly see and taste the difference. The quantity (400g) is ignored. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a powdered (dehydrated) egg substitute, which must be reconstituted with water before use. The USDA match is a liquid or frozen fat-free egg substitute, already hydrated, and used directly. Substituting it means skipping the reconstitution step and adding liquid in a different amount, so the cooking preparation changes. Guideline F treats a different state (dried vs. fresh/liquid) as not substitutable. Powdered egg products also often contain starches, gums, or other additives that differ from the liquid product, so the texture and flavour of the finished dish could differ. The quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 fails because the preparation changes, so the match is not substitutable.

1. Quantity (15g) is ignored per guideline A. 2. 'Chile negro' is a regional/culinary name in Mexican cooking for the dried chilaca chile, which is the same food sold as dried pasilla. Guideline B says regional names count as the same food. 3. The USDA entry 'Peppers, pasilla, dried' is the dried form, matching the dried ingredient, so no change of state. 4. Condition 1: the dried pepper can be used in place of the dried chile negro with the same preparation (rehydrating, toasting, blending into sauces). Condition 2: the taste, texture and appearance are the same because they are the same pepper under another name. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is reduced-fat milk, which the recipe explicitly requests in its lower-fat version. The USDA entry is 'Milk, reduced fat, fluid, 2% milkfat', which is the same food. The added vitamin A and vitamin D are standard fortification in US fluid milk and are how shoppers normally buy it, so they are not a meaningful modification. The quantity (570g) is ignored. Cooking method is unchanged because it is still fluid milk at the same fat level. Taste, texture and appearance are not noticeably different from reduced-fat milk, since the fat content matches and the vitamins do not change flavour or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pork fat, which is a raw fat used in cooking. The USDA entry is 'Pork, fresh, separable fat, cooked', which describes fat that has already been cooked. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Using pre-cooked fat would change how the dish is prepared: it would not render, melt, or brown the same way in the pan, and its texture and appearance would differ. The entry is the same food type, so the only mismatch is the cooked state. That mismatch is enough to fail both conditions, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is '540g ground chorizo', a raw ground sausage that a recipe would normally cook as part of the dish. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA match is specifically 'cooked, pan-fried', which is a different state from raw (guideline F: raw vs cooked is not substitutable). Condition 1 fails: using pre-cooked, pan-fried chorizo would change how the dish is prepared, because the meat would no longer need to be rendered and browned in the recipe, and the fat rendering and browning would differ. Condition 2 also fails: the pre-cooked product would differ in texture, moisture, fat content and appearance, and a diner could notice. Since the ingredient is plain (unspecified as cooked), its default is raw, so the cooked USDA entry does not match.

The ingredient is corn tortillas (soft, unfried flatbread) cut into strips. The USDA match is tortilla chips, plain, which are fried or baked corn tortilla pieces that are crisp, shelf-stable and seasoned with salt. They are a different processed state, not the same food under another name. Substituting chips would change the preparation: strips meant to be fried, simmered or softened in a dish would instead be added already crisp, and the cooking method would change. The diner would also notice the difference in texture (crisp versus soft or softened), flavour (fried corn and salt versus plain masa) and appearance. Both conditions fail, so this is not substitutable.

The ingredient is pork skin (the skin of a pig, a meat by-product). The USDA match is 'Plum, black, with skin, raw', which is a fruit (black plum with its skin). These are entirely different foods from different kingdoms of the food supply: one is animal tissue, the other a stone fruit. Condition 1 fails: using plum skin in place of pork skin would change the dish's preparation (pork skin is typically rendered, fried into crackling, or gelatinous when simmered, while plum skin would not behave this way). Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance. The guideline on 'the raw plant/source vs processed ingredient' and the general principle that a different food is not substitutable apply. The quantity (400g) is irrelevant. No naming or regional-synonym rule applies, since 'pork skin' and 'black plum' are not the same food under another name.

The ingredient is salsa verde, a Mexican-style sauce made from tomatillos, chilies, onion, garlic, cilantro, lime, and other seasonings, typically served raw or cooked as a condiment. The USDA match is Salsify, cooked, which is a root vegetable (a taproot in the daisy family) prepared by boiling or steaming. These are not the same food under another name, and salsify is not a component of salsa verde. Condition 1 fails: substituting cooked salsify for salsa verde would change the dish's preparation, since a sauce or condiment would be replaced by a plain cooked root vegetable. Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (tangy, herbaceous, spicy sauce versus mild, slightly sweet, earthy vegetable), texture (liquid or chunky sauce versus firm cooked root), and appearance (green sauce versus pale vegetable pieces). Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain fresh pineapple, quantity ignored. The USDA entry 'Pineapple, raw' is the same food in its uncooked, default form. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since any knife work or handling (chopped, cubed, etc.) does not alter the match under the guidelines. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same fruit in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a 25g blend of tapioca flour and almond flour, so it contains two different flours. The USDA entry 'Flour, almond' covers only one of those components. Under guideline F, a single ingredient does not match a blend or product that contains it. Substituting almond flour alone would drop the tapioca flour, which changes the flour's texture (tapioca adds starch and chew and lightens crumb) and the dish's structure and appearance, so a diner could notice. Condition 1 (preparation unchanged) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture or appearance) are not both met. The leading '25g' is ignored per guideline A.

Condition 1: The ingredient is fresh eggplant, cubed. The USDA match is Eggplant, raw. Eggplant is the same food, and cubing is knife work that the recipe itself performs, so it does not change the match (guideline C). Using the raw eggplant in place of fresh cubed eggplant does not alter how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: Fresh eggplant and raw eggplant are the same product in the same state, so a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met, and the quantity prefix is ignored (guideline A).

The ingredient is plain quick oats, and the USDA entry is a branded quick oats product (QUAKER Quick Oats) in its dry, uncooked form, so the food type and state match. The 'with Iron' descriptor is an added nutrient, but it is how this product is normally sold in the US rather than a flavour, texture or processing change. Under guideline D, a descriptor that reflects normal retail sale is not a modification. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. Cooking method is unchanged, and a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference from iron fortification. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient 'desiccated coconut' is the same product as the USDA entry 'Nuts, coconut meat, dried (desiccated)'; the name matches directly (guideline B). The USDA entry adds 'not sweetened', which is a modifier (guideline D). The ingredient is plain and does not request a sweetened version, and plain desiccated coconut is normally sold unsweetened, so the descriptor describes the standard default. The quantity (20g) is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since dried shredded coconut is used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same dried, shredded coconut meat. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is real king crab meat (a shellfish from Lithodidae family), shelled and minced. The USDA match is imitation crab meat, which is a surimi product made from fish paste (typically pollock or other white fish), starch, egg white, sugar, flavourings and colouring. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F rejects a product that is a blend or processed form versus the raw source; imitation crab is a processed, formulated product differing in ingredients from the crustacean. Condition 1: substituting imitation crab would change the dish's base ingredient and likely its preparation behaviour (surimi is pre-cooked and has a different moisture and binding profile when minced). Condition 2: a diner would readily notice the difference in taste (sweeter, fish-paste flavour rather than sweet shellfish), texture (fibrous, springy, uniform versus natural flaked crab) and appearance. Both conditions fail, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is toasted rice bran, which has been heat-treated to develop a nutty flavour, a darker colour and a drier, crisper texture. The USDA match, 'Rice bran, crude', is the raw, untoasted product. Guideline F says plain versus toasted is a different state and not substitutable. Using crude bran in place of toasted would change the flavour and appearance of the dish, and a diner would likely notice the difference. Condition 1 fails because the cooking step that produces toasted bran is skipped. Condition 2 also fails because the taste and colour would differ.

The ingredient is lentil pasta, made from lentil flour, which gives it a distinct earthy flavour, a different colour (often green, brown or red), and a different texture from wheat-based pasta. The USDA entry 'Pasta, whole grain, cooked' is wheat-based whole grain pasta. Condition 1: it could be swapped in mechanically, since both are cooked pasta, so cooking method would be unchanged. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance, especially the colour and earthy flavour of lentil pasta. This is a different food made from a different base ingredient, not the same food under another name (guideline B), so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 30g wheat bran; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Wheat bran' is literally the same food under the same name, with no cooking state, modification, or processing descriptor that would differ from what a shopper buys as wheat bran. Condition 1: wheat bran can be used directly in place of wheat bran with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the identical product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is potato starch, a processed starch extracted from potatoes (the raw plant source processed into a powder). The USDA match is 'Potato, baked, NFS', which is a whole cooked potato vegetable. Under guideline F, the raw plant/source vs the processed ingredient is not substitutable (analogous to cornstarch vs corn). Condition 1 fails: potato starch is a fine white powder used as a thickener or binder, and a baked potato cannot be used in its place without changing how the dish is prepared (it would not dissolve, thicken, or bind in the same way). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice chunks of baked potato versus a smooth thickened texture. The quantity (100g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is clarified butter, which is butter with the water and milk solids removed. The USDA entry is 'Butter, Clarified butter (ghee)', which names the same product under its common alternate name. Ghee is a form of clarified butter, so this is the same food under another name (guideline B). The leading '13g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing the preparation, since it is used in the same way for frying, sauteing or finishing. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Ghee is typically cooked a little longer, which can add a slightly nuttier note, but the USDA entry describes the same clarified product, so this is not a different food for annotation purposes. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain burdock root, boiled and drained, with no mention of salt. The USDA entry is the same food in the same cooked, boiled, drained state, but it is specified 'with salt'. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a version with added solution or additives is a modification, not the default. Added salt also changes the flavour, which fails condition 2 because a diner could taste the difference. Cooking method and state match, so the only issue is the added salt, but that is enough to fail both conditions as the rules are written.

The ingredient is a salted buttery spread sold in a tub, which is a vegetable oil and butter blend, a margarine-type product. The USDA entry is 'Margarine-like, vegetable oil-butter spread, tub, with salt', which describes the same product type with the same components: vegetable oil and butter, in tub form, salted. The 'with salt' descriptor matches the ingredient's 'salted', and this is the normal version of the product rather than a modified one, so guideline D does not reject it. The 15g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: it can directly replace the spread with no change to preparation, since it is a spread used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not detect a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same kind of product.

The ingredient is a raw Golden Delicious apple, sliced. Slicing is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C), so the relevant comparison is raw apple versus 'Apple, baked'. Baked apple is a cooked product. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using baked apple in place of raw sliced apple changes the preparation, since the apple would already be cooked and softened rather than raw. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, flavour and appearance, because baked apple is soft, caramelised and often browned, while raw apple is firm, crisp and bright. The variety difference is not the issue. The cooking state is what makes this a non-match.

The ingredient is pancake syrup, a table syrup blend sold for pouring over pancakes. The USDA entry 'Syrups, table blends, pancake' names the same product under its standard USDA name, so it is the same food under another name (guideline B). Condition 1: it can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is poured or measured the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product type. The 200g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is apple walnut oatmeal, and the USDA entry is Quaker Real Medleys apple walnut oatmeal, dry. Both describe the same product: apple walnut flavoured oatmeal, sold dry and uncooked. The weight prefix (25g) is ignored per guideline A. The branded entry is the same plain product type with the same flavour, so guideline G applies and it is not a modified version. The 'dry' state matches the uncooked ingredient, and the apple and walnut components are the same, so the dish would be prepared the same way and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance.

The ingredient is karela, which is bitter gourd, the same vegetable as the USDA entry 'Balsam-pear (bitter gourd)' under a regional name (guideline B). The state also matches. The ingredient is boiled and salted, and the USDA entry is 'pods, cooked, boiled, drained, with salt', so both describe a boiled, salted product. Draining is ordinary handling that does not change the result. The 15g weight is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same food in the same boiled and salted state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried whipping cream powder, a dehydrated, shelf-stable product that must be reconstituted with water before use. The USDA match is 'Cream, fluid, light whipping', a liquid dairy cream with a different water content and fat concentration. Condition 1 fails: substituting the fluid cream for the powder would change preparation, since the powder would no longer be measured dry and would need no added liquid, and the fluid cream would add moisture and volume the recipe did not expect. Condition 2 also fails: the dish's texture, consistency and richness would likely differ, and a diner could notice. Per guideline F, a different state (dried vs fluid) is not substitutable. The quantity (75g) is ignored.

Condition 1: The ingredient is a pesto sauce, and the USDA entry is also a pesto sauce, so it could be used in place of the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: The ingredient is a frozen product that is thawed. Guideline E says a frozen product should match the frozen USDA entry of the same product, and the shelf-stable entry is a different processing state. Frozen pesto cubes are typically fresh-style pesto, which is brighter and greener in colour and flavour, with a softer texture. Shelf-stable jarred pesto is pasteurised or preserved, typically darker and more uniform, with a different flavour and texture. A diner could notice this difference in a dish where the pesto is a visible or flavour-forward component. Condition 2 is not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is Dutch-process cocoa powder, which by definition is cocoa treated with alkali to reduce acidity. The USDA entry 'Cocoa, dry powder, hi-fat or breakfast, processed with alkali' is the same product: alkali-processed cocoa powder at the standard high-fat level (about 20-22% fat) that is normally sold as Dutch-process. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the same recipe steps. It is a dry powder used the same way, with no change to method. Condition 2: the alkali treatment gives the same darker colour, milder acidity and smoother flavour, and the standard fat level is what a shopper would normally buy under this name, so a diner would not notice a difference. The 'hi-fat' descriptor describes the normal form of this product rather than a modification, so guideline D does not apply. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is toasted quinoa flour: quinoa that has been ground into flour and then toasted. The USDA match is 'Quinoa, uncooked', which is the raw whole grain. Condition 1 fails: whole raw seeds cannot replace flour without changing preparation, since they would need grinding and toasting, and they would not behave the same in batters or doughs. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice whole grains versus a toasted flour in texture and especially in the nutty, roasted flavour that toasting produces. Guideline F rules out both a raw versus processed state and plain versus toasted, and the source grain versus its processed form is also a mismatch. The entry is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is store-bought blueberry muffins, which is the same food as the USDA entry 'Muffins, blueberry, commercially prepared'. Store-bought is the same as commercially prepared, and the parenthetical about mini-muffins only broadens the entry to include smaller muffins, which are still blueberry muffins. The quantity (400g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the muffins can be used as-is in place of the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since no cooking method is implied. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the USDA entry describes the same commercially made blueberry muffin. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cooked ground pork. The USDA entry 'Pork, fresh, ground, cooked' is the same food in the same state: fresh pork, ground, and cooked. The leading '150g' is only a quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are cooked ground pork and no cooking method or handling is altered. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product in the same cooked state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'spicy cocktail sauce', a flavoured variant of cocktail sauce. The USDA entry 'Cocktail sauce' is the plain, default version. Under guideline D, a plain product matched to a flavoured or modified version is not substitutable. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the sauce could be used in the same way. Condition 2 fails: the added heat changes the taste, and a diner would notice the difference. The 25g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Because condition 2 is not met, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is toasted whole wheat raisin bread, 20g; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Bread, whole wheat, with raisins, toasted' names the same product with the same components: whole wheat bread, raisins, and toasting. Toasting is a state present in both, so it is not a difference (guideline F's 'plain vs toasted' applies only when one side is plain). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are already toasted. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the product is the same bread in the same toasted state. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is plain soy milk with no sweetness or other qualifier. The USDA match is specifically 'unsweetened, plain, shelf stable'. Guideline D treats sweetened/unsweetened as a modification, so a plain ingredient matched to an unsweetened entry is not the standard default version. Substituting unsweetened soy milk for an unspecified soy milk could change the sweetness of the dish, which a diner could notice, so condition 2 is not reliably met. The 'shelf stable' descriptor only describes packaging and would not be a problem on its own. The 'unsweetened' modifier is the deciding factor, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is palm kernel shortening, a solid, typically hydrogenated or fractionated fat that is melted for use. The USDA entry, 'Vegetable oil, palm kernel', is a liquid oil. Guideline F says a different fat is not substitutable. Condition 1: the melted shortening could be poured in where the oil would go, so the method might not change. Condition 2: shortening and oil differ in fat composition and behaviour. Shortening sets solid when chilled and affects crumb, tenderness, and mouthfeel in baked goods, while the oil stays liquid, so a diner could notice a difference in texture. Shortening is also a specialty fat rather than the plain oil. Since the entry is a different fat rather than the same food under another name, the match fails condition 2.

The ingredient is rice wine, a liquid fermented seasoning or beverage (such as Shaoxing or mirin). The USDA match is 'Rice, cooked, NFS', which is a solid cooked grain. Condition 1 fails: a liquid cannot replace cooked rice in a recipe without changing how the dish is prepared, since it would alter the moisture, cooking method, and role of the ingredient. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste (no wine or fermented flavour), texture (a solid grain instead of a liquid), and appearance. The quantity (75g) is ignored per the guidelines. This is a different food, not the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is strawberry banana Greek yogurt, and the USDA entry is Yogurt, Greek, 2% fat, strawberry banana, CHOBANI. Condition 1: the match is the same food (Greek yogurt with strawberry banana flavour), with no change to cooking method. The weight is ignored per guideline A. The entry is branded, but it is the same plain product type, so guideline G allows it. Condition 2: the ingredient does not specify a fat level. Flavoured yogurts are normally sold low fat (guideline D), and 2% is a typical fat level for flavoured Greek yogurt, so a diner would not expect a different fat content. The flavour, texture (Greek style) and appearance match. Neither condition fails, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is capon meat with skin, a raw whole-bird cut. The USDA entry 'Chicken, capons, meat and skin, raw' is the same food: capon, meat and skin, uncooked. The leading '400g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Nothing in the ingredient suggests a modified, cooked, or processed form, so the USDA entry matches the default version (guideline D). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the same preparation, since both are raw capon with skin. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product.

The ingredient is a combined mix of dark corn syrup and brown sugar. The USDA entry is a table blend of corn syrup and refiner's sugar, which is a different product. Brown sugar gets its colour and molasses flavour from the molasses it retains, and dark corn syrup is coloured and flavoured with caramel, so a refined sugar blend would be paler and milder. Its appearance and taste would differ, so condition 2 fails. Guideline F also rules out a different sugar or syrup, and the USDA entry is a blend with no molasses. The quantity is ignored. Because the taste and appearance would change, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is sweetened canned coconut cream, and the USDA entry is 'Coconut cream, canned, sweetened', which is the same product with the same sweetened state. Guideline D says that when the ingredient itself asks for the modified version, the matching modified entry counts as a match, so sweetened maps to sweetened. The 250g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation, since both are canned, sweetened coconut cream used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food with the same sweetness. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is 300g Italian mortadella, a cured, emulsified pork luncheon meat. The USDA entry is 'Italian sandwich on wheat', a prepared sandwich made with bread and multiple fillings. Condition 1 fails: a sandwich cannot replace the meat in a recipe without changing how the dish is prepared, since it contains bread, cheese, vegetables and condiments, and it is not a meat ingredient. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. The entry is a different food, not the same food under another name, and it is not a plain form of the meat. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is 'smoked bacon', which is sold raw (uncooked) and is cooked as part of the recipe. The USDA match, 'Pork bacon, smoked or cured, cooked', is a cooked product. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Using pre-cooked bacon would change the preparation: it would not render fat or crisp in the pan the way raw bacon does, and the texture and appearance of the finished dish would differ. The leading '455g' is ignored per guideline A. The smoked/cured descriptor itself matches, so the only mismatch is the cooked state, but that mismatch is decisive under the rules. Condition 1 fails because the cooking method changes, and condition 2 likely fails because texture and appearance would differ.

1. The ingredient is 'pickled ginger', and the USDA entry is 'Ginger root, pickled'. This is the same food under the same name, so guideline B applies. The leading '100g' is decoration (guideline A). 2. Pickled ginger is normally sold pickled in vinegar, usually sweetened, so the USDA entry describes the standard form a shopper would buy under the plain name (guideline D). It is not a modified version. 3. Substituting one for the other needs no change to preparation. Both are used as a ready-to-eat condiment, typically served as-is with sushi. 4. The USDA entry names no state or variant that would change taste, texture or appearance, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh rhubarb, diced (400g). The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Diced is knife work that does not change the match (guideline C). The USDA entry 'Rhubarb, raw' is the same food in its uncooked, fresh state, which is exactly what the recipe calls for. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the diced rhubarb is handled by the cook. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the food is the same raw rhubarb. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cheese ravioli served with marinara sauce, so it is a composite dish: pasta, cheese filling, and tomato-based sauce. The USDA entry is cheese-filled ravioli with no sauce, so it covers only part of the ingredient. Condition 1 fails: using the sauceless entry would change how the dish is prepared and served, because the marinara component would be missing, and the cook would have to add it separately. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the absence of tomato sauce in taste, moisture and appearance. Ignoring the 10g quantity, the match is incomplete, not the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is celeriac, a root vegetable, prepared by peeling and grating. The USDA entry is 'Celeriac, raw', which is the same food in its uncooked state. Peeling and grating are knife work and handling the recipe does itself, so they do not change the match (Guideline C). The weight of 300g is decoration (Guideline A). Condition 1: the raw celeriac can be peeled and grated in exactly the same way, so the preparation is unchanged. Condition 2: a diner would see and taste the same grated raw celeriac, with no difference in flavour, texture or appearance. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is fried vegetable dumplings. The USDA entry is fried wonton, dumpling or pot sticker with no meat, which is the same food category: a fried dumpling with a non-meat filling. The entry is a generic description of that product, so it names the same dish with the same key components. Cooking method matches (fried), and the no-meat filling is consistent with 'veggie'. The leading '30g' is quantity and is ignored. Filling details can vary between dumpling products, but the USDA entry covers that range, and a diner would not reasonably expect a different food from a fried vegetable dumpling. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cream cheese spread, a spreadable cream cheese product with a mild, tangy flavour. The USDA entry is a processed cheese spread made from a Swiss cheese base. It is not the same food under another name. Its flavour is distinctly Swiss (nutty, sweeter), not the tangy taste of cream cheese, so a diner would notice the difference. Its texture is also that of a processed cheese spread, not a cream cheese. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable. The 150g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is arrowroot powder, a processed starch extracted from the arrowroot tuber and used as a thickener. The USDA entry 'Arrowroot, raw' describes the raw tuber/root vegetable, not the refined starch. Guideline F explicitly states that the raw plant/source is not substitutable for the processed ingredient (e.g., cornstarch vs corn). The raw tuber cannot be used in place of the powder without changing the preparation: it would need grating, cooking, and would not thicken a sauce or give the same texture or appearance. A diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 and condition 2 both fail.

1. The ingredient is fresh pork tenderloin with a peppercorn coating or seasoning. The USDA entry is a branded, peppercorn-flavoured Hormel Always Tender product. Both are pork tenderloin, so the cut matches. 2. The entry is a flavoured version, and the ingredient does ask for peppercorn, so the flavour itself is a fair match. 3. The 'Always Tender' name indicates a product enhanced with added solution, which guideline D treats as a modification (added solution/additives). The ingredient does not ask for an enhanced or injected product. Injected solution changes texture, juiciness, and saltiness in ways a diner could notice. 4. Condition 1 (same preparation) is plausibly met, but condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste or texture) is not, because the added solution is an unrequested modification. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is sauerkraut juice alone, the brine liquid. The USDA entry is canned sauerkraut including both solids and liquid. Condition 1: using the full product in place of juice would add shredded cabbage pieces, changing the dish's texture and preparation, so the method is altered. Condition 2: a diner would notice the solid shreds and the different texture and appearance. The entry is the whole product, not the juice component, so it does not meet either condition.

The ingredient is 'turkey sausage, sliced'. The weight is decoration and sliced is knife work, so both are ignored. The question is the state of the sausage. The USDA entry is 'Sausage, turkey, fresh, raw', which is uncooked. Turkey sausage sold as a sliceable product is usually pre-cooked or smoked, and recipes that call for sliced sausage typically add it ready to eat or to brown. Guideline F says raw vs cooked is a different state and not substitutable. Using raw sausage would require cooking it through, which changes the preparation method, and the final texture and appearance would differ from a cooked or smoked slice. Condition 1 therefore fails, and condition 2 likely fails as well, since a diner would notice raw, pale, or undercooked-looking sausage versus a cooked slice.

The ingredient is raw mature fava beans (dried mature seeds, as bought). The USDA entry 'Broadbeans (fava beans), mature seeds, raw' is literally the same food under a regional/culinary name (fava bean = broad bean), and 'mature seeds, raw' describes the dried legume as sold. Quantity is ignored. Condition 1: the same food can be used in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: no difference in taste, texture, or appearance would be noticed, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is ground savory, a dried herb. The USDA entry 'Spices, savory, ground' is the same food under a different name: savoury is the British spelling of savory, and the 'spice' label is just USDA's category for the dried, ground product. Both are ground and dried, so there is no state difference (guideline F's whole-vs-ground and fresh-vs-dried concerns do not apply). The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would taste and see the same ground savory, so there is no detectable difference. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is dried tarragon, crumbled. The USDA match is 'Spices, tarragon, dried', which is the same food: dried tarragon leaves. Crumbling is handling done at home and does not change the match (guideline C). The quantity is irrelevant (guideline A). Guideline F explicitly says a fresh vs dried herb or whole vs ground spice difference is not substitutable, but here both are dried, so the state matches. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same dried herb. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain poppy seeds, the whole dried seed used in cooking. The USDA entry 'Spices, poppy seed' is the same food. 'Spices' is only the USDA category label, not a different state, cut, or modified version. Condition 1: the seeds can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel, or see a difference, since it is the same seed. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried, salted squid, a preserved product that is typically rehydrated or cooked from a dry, salty state. The USDA entry is squid, mixed species, cooked, fried, a ready-cooked product with a battered or fried exterior. Condition 1 fails: using fried squid would change the preparation, since the dish would need no rehydration and would not use the dried-and-salted form. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice a difference in texture (crisp fried coating and tender cooked flesh versus the chewy, dense, salty texture of dried squid) and in flavour (salt-cured and dried versus fried). Guideline F treats a different state (dried/salted versus cooked) as not substitutable, so the match is rejected.

The ingredient is wild boar shoulder, a fresh meat cut from a wild boar. The USDA entry is 'Wild rice, raw', which is a grain (seeds of an aquatic grass, Zizania). These are not the same food under another name, and the match fails on the raw source versus processed/different food identity. Condition 1 fails: wild rice cannot replace boar shoulder in a dish without changing preparation entirely, since one is a meat requiring searing or braising and the other is a grain requiring boiling. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice a difference in taste, texture and appearance. The quantity (40g) is ignored per guideline A. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw porterhouse steak, and the USDA entry is the same cut: beef short loin porterhouse steak, raw. The extra descriptors ('separable lean and fat', 'trimmed to 1/8" fat', 'all grades') describe the standard retail trim and grade range for this cut, which is how a porterhouse steak is normally sold. Guideline C says trimming does not change the match, and the ingredient specifies no grade or fat level that would conflict. Condition 1: the steak can be cooked in the same way (grilled, pan-seared, etc.) without changing the preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same raw cut with the same standard trim. Both conditions are met.

Cane syrup is a thick, concentrated sweetener made by boiling down cane juice until it becomes a dark, sticky syrup. The USDA entry 'Sugar cane beverage' is a drink made from sugar cane juice, which is thin, watery, and far less concentrated. It is not the same food under another name. Using it in place of cane syrup would change the dish's sweetness, flavour, viscosity, and texture, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would change (the liquid would not bind, thicken, or glaze as the syrup does). Condition 2 also fails. The quantity is ignored, per guideline A.

The ingredient is a dry beef bouillon cube, a concentrated solid that the cook dissolves in water as part of the recipe. The USDA entry is 'Soup, beef broth or bouillon, powder, prepared with water', which is already the reconstituted liquid soup. Condition 1 fails: using the prepared liquid in place of the dry cube changes how the dish is prepared. The cook would have to omit or adjust the water the recipe expects, and the 5g of dry solid would become a large volume of liquid, altering the dish's moisture and concentration. Guideline F also rules this out: dry versus prepared is a different state, similar to whole versus ground spice. Condition 2 is also doubtful, since the dish's liquid content and seasoning strength would differ. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Because the dry cube and the prepared liquid are different states and the substitution changes preparation, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is salted mackerel, and the USDA entry is 'Fish, mackerel, salted'. These describe the same food: mackerel that has been salt-cured, which is how it is normally sold under that name. The weight prefix '100g' is decoration and is ignored. Condition 1: the salted mackerel can replace the USDA food without changing preparation, since it is the same product and needs no further processing. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the USDA entry describes the same salted product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is active dry yeast, a plain baking ingredient. The USDA entry 'Leavening agents, yeast, baker's, active dry' is literally the same product under a USDA name. Guideline A says to ignore the 2g quantity. Guideline B says same food under another name counts. Condition 1: active dry yeast can be used in place of itself with no change to preparation. Condition 2: the diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is turkey merguez, a spiced, seasoned sausage made from ground turkey (or turkey meat) with paprika, cumin, harissa-style spices, and typically casing. The USDA entry 'Turkey, neck' refers to the neck portion of the bird, a bony cut of dark meat with skin and connective tissue, sold as a whole neck and not as a ground or seasoned sausage product. Condition 1: Merguez is cooked by grilling, pan-frying or broiling as a formed sausage; turkey neck is a bone-in cut that requires long braising or stewing to become tender, so the preparation method would have to change. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference: the spicing, the sausage texture, the absence of bone and the appearance of a formed link would all differ. This is a different food (a different cut and product form), not a naming variant of merguez, so it is not substitutable under the cut-of-meat and state rules.

The 'Nutritional powder mix' label is a generic USDA category, and the entry names no added flavour or modification (such as chocolate or vanilla), so it is not treated as a modified version. Step 2: It is used as a powder in the same way, with no change to cooking method. Brand-to-brand differences in taste or texture are the normal variation between products of the same type, which a diner would not attribute to a substitution. The main risk is that the 'powder mix' wording implies additives, but nothing in the entry specifies them. On balance, it is substitutable.

The ingredient is plain 'chocolate milk', whose default version is a standard sweetened chocolate milk. The USDA match is 'Milk, chocolate, lowfat, reduced sugar', which is the same food but with a modified formulation: reduced sugar. Guideline D says a plain ingredient matched to a modified version (reduced/low/sweetened variants) is not substitutable, and the ingredient does not ask for reduced sugar. Condition 1 (preparation) would likely be met, since the milk can be used in place of chocolate milk. Condition 2 fails: a diner could plausibly notice the lower sweetness and different taste, and the lowfat base may also change mouthfeel compared with the standard product. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is gin, a distilled spirit (alcoholic beverage) used as a liquid component. The USDA match is 'Gin fizz', which is a cocktail: a mixed drink made from gin, lemon or lime juice, sugar, and carbonated water (soda), often with egg white. Condition 1: gin cannot be swapped for a finished gin fizz without changing the preparation. Using a gin fizz in place of gin would add citrus, sugar, and carbonation, and would require the recipe to be restructured around a pre-mixed cocktail rather than an alcohol component. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in taste (sweet, citrus, effervescent flavour versus the neat spirit's juniper and botanical profile) and in texture (carbonation, possible foam). Since the match is a different, mixed product containing additional components, it is not the same food under another name, and it fails both conditions.

The ingredient is raw beef stew meat, an uncooked cut of beef (usually chuck) sold in cubes for braising or stewing. The USDA match, 'Beef stew, canned entree', is a fully prepared, cooked, canned dish containing beef plus vegetables and gravy. Condition 1 fails: using it would skip the browning and braising the recipe calls for, so the cooking method changes. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, appearance, and flavour, since the canned product is already cooked, has a sauce, and has added vegetables. This is a prepared dish, not the same food under another name, and the guidelines reject raw vs cooked and processed vs plain.

Ox tongue is beef tongue, the same food under a different name (guideline B). The quantity prefix '400g' is ignored (guideline A). The USDA entry is 'Beef, variety meats and by-products, tongue, raw', which is the uncooked, default form of the same cut, so it matches the plain ingredient (guideline C/D). Using it changes neither the cooking method nor the flavour, texture or appearance of the dish, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

Button mushrooms are the same food as white mushrooms (Agaricus bisporus); 'button' is a common trade name for the small young form, which fits guideline B. The USDA entry 'Mushrooms, white, raw' is the uncooked form, which matches the ingredient's raw state. 'Ground' is preparation done at home, like chopping, and per guideline C it does not change the match. Condition 1: the same mushroom can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not perceive a difference, since the food is identical and grinding is part of the recipe's own handling. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is 'fresh turnip', which refers to the root vegetable (Brassica rapa, the bulb). The USDA entry 'Turnip greens, raw' is the leafy green top of the same plant, a different edible part with a different taste (more bitter, peppery), texture, and appearance. Guideline B covers the same food under another name or a cut of the same vegetable, but turnip greens are not the root under another name. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the leaves in place of the root. The weight is ignored per guideline A. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is horseradish sauce, a prepared condiment made from grated horseradish root combined with vinegar, sugar, salt and usually a creamy or oil-based dressing. The USDA match 'Horseradish' is the plant root itself (raw or prepared root without the sauce base). Condition 1 fails because the root cannot stand in for a creamy, sauced condiment without changing the dish's preparation. The root is the raw source and the sauce is a processed, multi-component product, which guideline F rules out. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would taste the sharp, raw root without the sweetness, acidity and creaminess of the sauce, and would notice the difference in texture and appearance. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried bay leaves, a whole dried spice leaf. The USDA entry 'Spices, bay leaf' is the generic dried bay leaf spice, with no fresh, ground, or processed state named. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient directly, with the same handling (added whole to a dish, removed before serving). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since it is the same dried leaf in the same form. The quantity is ignored per the guidelines. The entry is the plain default version of the same food, so it matches.

The ingredient is cooked perch, flaked. The USDA entry is Fish, perch, mixed species, cooked, dry heat, which is the same food in the same cooked state. The ingredient names only 'perch' with no species, so the mixed-species generic entry is the standard default version. Flaking is handling done by the cook and does not change the match (guideline C). Cooking method is dry heat, which is the default way cooked fish is prepared, so the dish's preparation would not change. Taste, texture and appearance of cooked, flaked perch would match the USDA entry, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is salted butter, a dairy fat containing about 80% milk fat, water, milk solids, and added salt, and it is softened for use. The USDA match is shortening, a fat of vegetable or animal origin with no water, milk solids, or salt, and it is not dairy. Guideline F says a different fat is not substitutable. Condition 1 is not met: swapping shortening for butter changes the fat, and the recipe's creaming or spreading behaviour would differ. Condition 2 is also not met: a diner would notice the loss of butter flavour and the salt, and the texture and colour of baked or spread products would differ. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is canned tuna packed in oil, drained, with no species or salt specification. The USDA entry is white tuna (typically albacore), canned in oil, without salt, drained solids. Two differences matter. First, the species: white albacore is a different tuna from the light tuna (usually skipjack) that a shopper normally gets under the plain name 'canned tuna in oil'. Guideline F treats sibling products with different taste and appearance as non-substitutable, and white tuna is paler and firmer. Second, 'without salt' is a modified version of a product normally sold with added salt. Guideline D says a plain ingredient mapped to a modified version is not a match, and the salt difference is noticeable in flavour. Both conditions fail: the swap would change flavour and appearance, and a diner could notice the difference.

The ingredient is plain Gouda cheese, cubed, a single raw dairy product. The USDA match 'Cheese fondue' is a prepared dish made from melted cheese combined with wine, starch, and seasonings, and it is not the same food as Gouda. Condition 1 fails: substituting fondue would change how the dish is prepared, since the recipe calls for solid cubes of cheese that are added as they are, while fondue is already melted and mixed with other ingredients. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (solid cubes versus a smooth melted sauce) and in flavour (wine, garlic and seasonings in fondue that Gouda does not contain). Because the match fails both conditions, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is bison round steak, raw. The USDA entry is buffalo (bison) top round steak, raw, from the Shoshone Bannock source. Bison and buffalo are the same animal under different names, so the species matches (guideline B). Round steak is a steak cut from the round primal, and top round is a subprimal within that same primal, so this is not a different cut in the sense of guideline F, which concerns different primals such as brisket versus chuck. Top round is also the most common retail form of round steak. The 'free range' and 'Shoshone Bannock' descriptors describe how the bison was raised and sourced, which is how bison is normally sold, so they are not modifications that change taste or texture. The entry is raw, matching the raw ingredient, and the weight is ignored per guideline A. Cooking method is unchanged, and a diner would not reasonably detect a difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is 'shrimp cakes', a formed patty or cake of minced or chopped shrimp, usually bound and then fried or steamed. The USDA entry 'Shrimp toast' is a different dish: a paste of shrimp spread over a slice of bread and deep-fried. Condition 1 fails because substituting it would change the preparation: a shrimp cake is formed and cooked on its own, while shrimp toast needs bread and a spreading step. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would notice the difference in texture, since shrimp toast has a bread base and a crisp crust, and in appearance, since it is a slice rather than a cake. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B), and it is not a plain-to-standard match (guideline D). Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is plain 'sliced deli chicken' with no mention of sodium level, so the standard default product applies, which is regular-sodium deli chicken. The USDA entry is 'Chicken, prepackaged or deli, luncheon meat, reduced sodium'. Under guideline D, reducing sodium is a modification, and a plain ingredient matched to a modified version is not substitutable. The sodium reduction changes the salt level, so a diner could plausibly notice the difference in flavour. The cut, form and state (sliced, deli, luncheon meat, cooked) otherwise align, so the mismatch rests entirely on the reduced-sodium descriptor. Condition 2 is therefore not reliably met.

Quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A. 'Pork fillet' is the British/Australian trade name for pork tenderloin, the same cut of the same meat, so guideline B applies and it is the same food under another name. The USDA entry 'Pork, tenderloin' names only the food with no processing state, so it is the generic food and matches fresh or plain preparations (guideline E). Using it does not change the cooking method, flavour, texture or appearance, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a specific flavoured dressing: green goddess, made with herbs (typically parsley, chives, tarragon), anchovy or garlic, and a creamy base. The USDA entry 'Salad dressing, light, NFS' is a generic, unflavoured light dressing. The 'light' descriptor matches, but the green goddess flavour is absent from the USDA entry. Condition 1 is about substitution in the dish, and a diner would taste the difference in herbs and seasoning, so condition 2 fails. Under guideline D, a plain or generic product should not be treated as a flavoured variant, so this is not a match.

The ingredient is smoked turkey kielbasa, meaning the sausage is made from turkey alone. The USDA entry is Kielbasa, Polish, turkey and beef, smoked, which is a blend of turkey and beef. Guideline F says a single ingredient versus a blend containing it is not substitutable. The beef content changes the flavour, fat profile, texture and appearance compared with an all-turkey sausage, and a diner could notice the difference. The smoked state and Polish kielbasa style do match, but the meat composition does not. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is pecan butter, a spread made by grinding pecans into a smooth paste, often with added oil or salt. The USDA match, 'Pecans, NFS', is the whole nut in its generic form. Condition 1 fails: a spread cannot replace whole or chopped nuts without changing how the dish is prepared, because a paste cannot be measured, folded, or spread the way the nut is. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (smooth paste vs. solid pieces) and in taste or fat content from any added oil. Guideline F rules out a raw source versus its processed form, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is vodka at 80 proof (40% ABV). The USDA entry, 'Alcoholic beverage, distilled, vodka, 80 proof', is the same product with the same strength, so it is the same food under the same name. The leading weight (195g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient in the same preparation, since it is the same liquid added the same way. Condition 2: a diner would detect no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same spirit at the same proof. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fennel seed, a whole dried spice (seeds of Foeniculum vulgare) used as a flavouring. The USDA match is a raw mild Italian pork sausage, a meat product containing pork, seasonings, and typically fennel, but it is a single composite food, not the spice itself. Condition 1: fennel seed cannot be substituted for a sausage; they are different foods with different roles. The sausage would replace the meat component of a dish, changing the preparation entirely (it would be a meat ingredient rather than a seasoning, and it adds pork, fat, and moisture). Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice a different food, with pork texture and fat content instead of crunchy or aromatic seed flavour. The guideline on single ingredients versus products containing them (F) and the raw source versus processed product applies. Quantity is ignored. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is egg noodles, a wheat-flour and egg pasta product that is typically boiled or stir-fried and has a soft, chewy, yellow, eggy texture. The USDA match is rice noodles, dry, which is made from rice flour with no egg, has a different flavour (neutral and milder, lacking egg richness), a different texture (more brittle and translucent when cooked, often softer or more delicate), and a different appearance (white or translucent versus yellow). It is a different food product, not a naming variant of the same food. Condition 1 could be argued as possible since both are noodles boiled or stir-fried, but preparation timing and handling differ (rice noodles need soaking or shorter cooking). Condition 2 clearly fails because a diner would notice the colour, the eggy flavour and the texture difference. Quantity is ignored per the guidelines.

The ingredient is kippered herring roe, which is cured and smoked. The USDA entry is plain Pacific herring eggs with no smoking or curing. Under guideline F, plain vs smoked is a different state, so the match changes the flavour and appearance of the dish. A diner would taste smoke and notice the difference in texture and colour. Condition 1 (same preparation) fails, and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste or appearance) also fails. The quantity and the 'Alaska Native' label do not affect the result.

The ingredient is plain 'oat milk' with no stated sweetness. The USDA entry is specifically 'unsweetened, plain, refrigerated'. Guideline D treats sweetened/unsweetened as a modification, so a plain ingredient matched to an unsweetened version is not the standard default. Sweetness is a taste difference a diner could notice, and it can change the flavour of the dish. Condition 1 might hold, since the preparation is the same, but condition 2 fails because the taste may differ. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is pork butt (pork shoulder), a raw pork cut. The USDA entry is beef bottom sirloin butt (tri-tip), lean only, cooked and roasted. Under the guidelines, a different species is a different food, and a different cut of meat is explicitly not substitutable (F). The entry is also cooked while the ingredient is raw, which is a different state (F). Swapping in beef would change the flavour, texture, fat content and appearance, and a diner would notice the difference, so both conditions fail.

The ingredient is dehydrated papaya, and the USDA entry is Papaya, dried. 'Dehydrated' and 'dried' are the same processing state and name the same food, so this is the same food under another name (guideline B). The USDA entry has no modifier such as sweetened, sulfured or in syrup that would make it differ from the plain product a shopper buys under this name (guideline D). The 395g weight is ignored (guideline A). Using the dried papaya in place of dehydrated papaya would not change the preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain garlic powder, a dried, ground spice. The USDA entry 'Spices, garlic powder' is the same product under the standard USDA name. It is not a blend, a modified version, or a different state. Guideline B treats the same food under another name as a match, and guideline A says the 3g quantity is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient in the same preparation without changing the method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product.

The ingredient is sweetened dried peaches, a dehydrated fruit that is sold and used as a dried product. The USDA match is 'Peaches, dried, sulfured, stewed, with added sugar', which is a dried fruit that has been rehydrated and cooked (stewed). Sulfuring and added sugar match the ingredient's typical form, so those descriptors are acceptable. The problem is 'stewed'. That is a different processed state, cooked and moist, versus a dried, chewy fruit. Condition 1 fails: putting stewed peaches where dried peaches are called for changes the preparation, since the fruit would not hold its shape, dry texture, or chewiness in baked goods, trail mixes, or similar uses, and would add liquid. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice soft, moist, stewed fruit versus leathery dried pieces in texture and appearance. Guideline F lists dried versus cooked states as not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried cranberries, and the USDA entry is 'Cranberries, dried', which is the same food under the same name. The leading '25g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). The USDA entry names no modification such as added flavour, reduced sugar, or a packing medium, so there is no modified-version issue (guideline D). Dried cranberries are a plain dried fruit that can be used directly in place of the USDA entry without changing preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Condition 1: The ingredient is grilled beef loin. The USDA entry is beef loin (top loin), cooked and grilled, so the cooking method matches and the dish would be prepared the same way. The ingredient does not specify a sub-cut, so top loin is a reasonable default within the loin category. The USDA descriptor 'trimmed to 1/8" fat' is the standard retail trim, not a modification. Condition 2: Grilled top loin with standard trim is what a diner would expect from grilled beef loin, so taste, texture and appearance would not reveal a difference.
