The main risk is that 'loin' could be read as tenderloin, which would be a different cut, but the ingredient does not say that. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is parboiled rice, a grain that is partly cooked under pressure and then dried, used as a cooking ingredient that is boiled or steamed into a side dish or added to a recipe. The USDA match is rice crackers, a baked or fried, puffed, seasoned snack product. Condition 1 fails: rice crackers cannot replace parboiled rice in a recipe without changing how the dish is prepared, since they cannot be cooked as a grain and would not absorb liquid or form the same cooked grain. Condition 2 fails: the texture (firm, separate grains versus a crisp, brittle cracker), flavour, and appearance would all differ and a diner would clearly notice. This is a different food product, not a naming variant of the same food, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is honey roasted cereal clusters, a generic honey-roasted oat cluster cereal. The USDA entry is POST Honey Bunches of Oats, honey roasted, a branded ready-to-eat cereal of the same product type with the same flavour (honey roasted). Per guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches, and the honey roasted descriptor matches the ingredient rather than adding a modification. Condition 1: it can be used directly in place of the cereal clusters with no change to preparation, since it is an uncooked ready-to-eat product. Condition 2: it has the same honey roasted flavour, clustered oat texture and appearance, so a diner would not reasonably notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dry corkscrew pasta, a shape of ordinary dry wheat pasta. The USDA entry 'Pasta, dry, enriched' is the generic dry enriched pasta, which covers pasta of any shape. Under guideline B, a regional or shape name for the same food counts as the same food, and under guideline D, a plain ingredient matches the standard default version. Condition 1 holds: dry pasta is cooked in the same way whatever its shape, so the preparation does not change. Condition 2 holds: the USDA entry describes the same enriched durum-wheat dry pasta, with the same taste and texture. The only difference is shape, which the generic entry does not specify and which a diner would not treat as a different food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is egg powder that has been reconstituted with water, so it is dehydrated whole egg returned to a liquid state. The USDA entry is whole egg, raw, frozen, pasteurized, which is the same food in liquid form. Condition 1: the reconstituted powder is handled like liquid egg, so it can replace pasteurized whole egg without changing preparation (whisking, mixing, baking or scrambling). Frozen liquid egg is thawed and used the same way. Condition 2: rehydrated whole egg powder and pasteurized liquid whole egg are very close in taste, texture and appearance once cooked or mixed, and a diner would not notice a difference. The main caveat is that the powder is a processed form and may carry a slight dried-egg flavour, but that difference is minor in mixed or cooked dishes. Both conditions hold, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient 'turnip tops' is the leafy green of the turnip plant, which is the same food as 'turnip greens' under a regional/culinary name (guideline B). The USDA entry 'Turnip greens, raw' is the uncooked leaves, matching the ingredient as bought, and the weight prefix is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are cooked or used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same leafy vegetable.

Fine semolina is milled durum wheat, a wheat product with a pale golden colour, a nutty wheat flavour, and a specific gluten structure. The USDA entry is yellow cornmeal (corn flour), a different grain with a distinct corn flavour, a grittier texture, and a more saturated yellow colour. Guideline F says a different flour is not substitutable, and this is a different grain altogether. Changing semolina to cornmeal would alter the dish's flavour, texture and appearance, and a diner would notice (for example in pasta, gnocchi, or puddings). The quantity is irrelevant. Condition 1 and condition 2 both fail.

The ingredient is Quaker oat bran, a plain branded oat bran product. The USDA entry is the same product: 'Cereals, QUAKER, Oat Bran, QUAKER/MOTHER'S Oat Bran, dry'. It is dry, uncooked oat bran with no added flavour, sweetener, or modification. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Per guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type is a match. The 250g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

1. The ingredient is generic 'hot pepper sauce', a plain condiment product type. 2. The USDA entry 'Sauce, ready-to-serve, pepper, TABASCO' is a branded pepper sauce, which is the same plain product type. 3. Guideline G says a branded entry of the same plain product type counts as a match. It has no added flavour or modification that the plain ingredient lacks, and the 'ready-to-serve' descriptor just reflects how the sauce is normally sold. 4. Quantity (15g) is ignored per guideline A. 5. Used in place of the ingredient, the preparation does not change, and it is the same kind of condiment. Brand flavour differences are a limitation, but the guidelines treat branded entries of the plain type as substitutable.

The ingredient is 'extra-lean ground turkey'. In US retail, 'extra-lean' ground turkey is conventionally the 93% lean / 7% fat product, so it is the same food under a descriptive name, as in guideline B. The USDA entry is 'Turkey, ground, 93% lean, 7% fat, raw', which is uncooked, matching the plain raw ingredient. The leading '200g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the 93/7 ground turkey can replace the extra-lean ground turkey in the same recipe with the same preparation, since both are raw ground turkey of the same fat content. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the fat content is the same. Both conditions are met.

Cream of coconut is a sweetened coconut product by definition, so the ingredient itself calls for the sweetened version. Guideline D says that when the ingredient asks for a modified version, the matching modified USDA entry counts. 'Nuts, coconut cream, canned, sweetened' is the closest USDA match: same base food (coconut cream), canned, and sweetened. Cream of coconut is thicker and sweeter than plain coconut cream and contains stabilizers, so some difference in sweetness and texture is possible. The USDA entry is the nearest available category, and the remaining gap is a matter of degree rather than a different food. Applying guideline D consistently, it is treated as an acceptable match, though this is a judgment call.

The ingredient is plain cranberry juice. The USDA entry is 'Cranberry juice cocktail, bottled', which is a sweetened blend. Cranberry juice cocktail typically contains added sugar and roughly 25-30% juice, while plain cranberry juice is essentially undiluted and tart. Guideline D treats sweetened versions of a plain ingredient as a modification, so this is not the same food under another name. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the added sweetness, which changes flavour, and the cocktail's flavour profile differs from the tart juice. Condition 1 is therefore also questionable, since a recipe calling for unsweetened juice would have its sugar balance altered. Both conditions are not met.

1) Ingredient: 45g whole grain oat cereal. The weight is ignored per guideline A. The ingredient is a plain, generic whole grain oat ready-to-eat cereal with no flavour, sweetening or other modification specified. 2) USDA entry: Cereals ready-to-eat, QUAKER WHOLE HEARTS oat cereal. This is a branded whole grain oat ready-to-eat cereal, the same basic product type as the ingredient, and it is not a flavoured or reduced/modified variant. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. 3) Condition 1 (substitutable without changing preparation): the product is eaten or used as a ready-to-eat oat cereal in the same way, so no change to cooking or handling is needed. Met. 4) Condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture or appearance): both are toasted whole grain oat cereal pieces. Brand-specific recipe details could differ slightly, but the category match is the intended standard, and a diner would not reasonably notice a change in the basic product. Met. Both conditions are satisfied.

The ingredient is Japanese-style soy sauce, which is shoyu: a soy sauce brewed from soybeans and wheat. The USDA entry is 'Soy sauce made from soy and wheat (shoyu)', which names the same product under its Japanese name. Under guideline B, this is the same food under another name. The 140g weight is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation, since it is used the same way as a liquid seasoning. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is salted egg yolk, a savoury product preserved with salt. The USDA entry is egg yolk that is sugared, meaning it has added sugar, a sweet product typically used in desserts. Sugar and salt are different additives that change flavour, so a diner would taste the difference. Under guideline D, a plain or savoury ingredient mapped to a sweetened version is not a match, and guideline F rules out a different additive or treatment. Condition 2 fails because taste would differ, and the swap would also change the dish's flavour profile. Condition 1 fails too, since the sweet yolk would not work where salted yolk is used as a savoury component. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is brewed green tea, and the USDA entry is 'Beverages, tea, green, brewed, regular', which is the same food: regular brewed green tea. The '75g' quantity is decoration and is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are already-brewed green tea used as a liquid. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same beverage. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is rose apple (Syzygium jambos, family Myrtaceae), which is a different fruit from the true apple (Malus domestica). The USDA match is Gala apple, a Malus cultivar. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Rose apples have a mild, floral, watery, crisp flesh and a bell-like shape with a pink-red skin, while Gala apples are sweet-tart, dense and crisp, with a different flavour and appearance. A diner would notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance, so condition 2 fails. Since the match is not the same food, it cannot be substituted without changing the dish's flavour and texture.

The ingredient is canned southern peas, which are the same food as cowpeas (blackeyes, crowder, southern peas), so this is a same-food-different-name match under guideline B. The quantity (25g) is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is canned and plain, matching the ingredient's canned form. Draining is handling that does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the peas can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same legume in the same canned form. Both conditions are met.

Fontina is a semi-soft Italian cow's milk cheese with a mild, nutty, buttery flavour and a smooth, creamy melt. Provolone is a pasta filata cheese, firmer, with a sharper, tangier flavour and a different melting behaviour. They are different cheeses, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Condition 1 is not clearly met, because the swap can change how the dish melts and binds. Condition 2 fails, because a diner would likely notice the sharper, tangier taste and different texture. Guideline F treats different varieties with different tastes as not substitutable.

The ingredient is instant cream of wheat in its dry state, and the USDA entry is Cereals, CREAM OF WHEAT, instant, dry. These are the same product under the same name, with the same form (instant) and state (dry). Under guideline B, the same food under another name counts as a match. The 250g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are used dry in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 200g ground veal; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA match is 'Veal, ground', which is the same food under the same name, with no added modification or state descriptor that would differ from a shopper's normal purchase. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since ground veal is used the same way in any recipe. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is creamy soy nut butter, a spread made from roasted soy nuts. The USDA entry 'Soy nut butter' names the same product under the same name. The weight prefix '12g' is decoration and is ignored. 'Creamy' describes the default smooth texture of soy nut butter, which is the standard form of the product, so the USDA generic entry matches without a modified version. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient in the same preparation, with no change in cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food and the generic entry covers the standard creamy spread. Both conditions are met.

1. The ingredient is peppercorn dressing, a commercial salad dressing flavoured with peppercorns. The USDA entry is 'Salad dressing, peppercorn dressing, commercial, regular', which names the same product with the same components. Under guideline B, it is the same food under the same name. Under guideline G, it is a plain product type rather than a modified or flavour-added version. The leading '30g' quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is used as a dressing in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product type. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient 'custard apple' is an Annona fruit, but the name is used for several species. In many markets it means cherimoya, atemoya, or bullock's heart (Annona cherimola, Annona x atemoya, or Annona reticulata). The USDA entry 'Sugar-apples, (sweetsop), raw' is Annona squamosa, a different species. Guideline B covers the same food under another name, but these are distinct fruits, not regional names for one food. Guideline F treats a sibling variety with a different taste as not substitutable. Sugar apple has a grainier, more granular flesh, a different sweetness and aroma profile, and more numerous large seeds than custard apple. A diner would likely notice the difference in taste and texture. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable. The answer depends on which fruit the recipe means by 'custard apple'; if the recipe's region uses the name for sugar apple, the answer would change.

The ingredient is cashew nuts, and the USDA entry is 'Cashews, NFS' (not further specified). This is the same food under a standard name, with no added state, flavour, or processing that would change preparation. 'NFS' means the entry is generic, so it covers cashews as normally bought and used in cooking. Quantity is ignored. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same nut. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain corn flour, a raw ground milled ingredient used as a base for cooking. The USDA entry is 'Corn flour patty or tart, fried', a prepared, fried food product made from corn flour, not the flour itself. Using it in place of corn flour would change the dish: it is already cooked and shaped, so it cannot be used as a flour in the same preparation. A diner would notice the difference in form, texture and appearance. Under guideline F, the raw source ingredient is not interchangeable with a processed or prepared product. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well.

The ingredient is tempeh, a fermented soybean cake made from whole cooked soybeans bound with a fungal culture. The USDA match is firm tofu, a curd made from soy milk coagulated with calcium sulfate. These are different foods. Tempeh has a nutty, earthy, mushroom-like flavour from fermentation and a chewy, grainy texture with visible whole soybeans. Firm tofu is bland, smooth-textured and uniform in appearance. Substituting tofu would change the flavour, texture and appearance of the dish, and a diner would likely notice. Tofu and tempeh are not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is fresh epazote, an herb. The USDA entry 'Epazote, raw' is the same food in its uncooked, fresh state. The quantity (75g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation, since both are fresh raw herb. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same herb in the same state. Both conditions are met.

Dried kombu is a thick brown kelp (Laminaria/Saccharina), used mainly to make dashi and simmered dishes. The USDA entry 'Seaweed, laver, raw' describes laver, a thin red alga (Porphyra, the source of nori), usually eaten raw or toasted. These are different species, not regional names for the same food. Laver is also raw and fresh, while kombu is dried, so the state differs (guideline F). Condition 1 fails: using laver in place of kombu would change the dish's preparation, since kombu is typically steeped for stock and laver is not. Condition 2 fails: the flavour (kombu's strong glutamate umami versus laver's milder, sweeter taste) and texture (thick, tough, and gelatinous when simmered versus thin and delicate) would be noticed. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is rice vermicelli, dried: a thin noodle made from rice flour and water, cooked by boiling or soaking before use, with a long thread-like texture. The USDA match is Cream of rice, which is a finely ground, cooked-to-porridge cereal made from milled rice (rice granules/flour), typically sold as a hot breakfast cereal. It is not a noodle and is not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails: it cannot replace rice vermicelli in a dish without changing preparation, since rice vermicelli is boiled or soaked as noodles, while cream of rice is cooked into a porridge-like mush or used as a flour-like ingredient. Condition 2 also fails: diners would immediately notice a difference in texture (long, springy strands vs. smooth, mushy cereal) and appearance. The guideline on processed ingredients (cornstarch vs corn) and different state/product forms supports rejection.

The ingredient is ground mace. The USDA match is 'Spices, mace, ground', which is the same food with the same state (ground spice). Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: mace can be used in place of ground mace without changing preparation at all. Condition 2: a diner would detect no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is literally the same spice in the same form. Guideline F's 'whole vs ground spice' distinction does not apply because both are ground. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh potato gnocchi, a plain ready-to-cook product, and the weight is decoration. The USDA entry 'Gnocchi, potato' names only the food with no state descriptor (no dried, frozen, or cooked qualifier), so under guideline E it is the generic food and covers fresh gnocchi. Condition 1: fresh potato gnocchi is normally boiled or pan-cooked until it floats, and the same handling applies to the generic gnocchi entry, so the preparation does not change. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the entry is the same potato dumpling. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is neufchatel, a soft, spreadable cheese that is lower in fat than cream cheese. The USDA entry 'Cheese, neufchatel' names the same food under the same name, so it is the same product rather than a modified version. The 90g leading weight is decoration and is ignored. Neufchatel is normally sold and used in this form, so there is no preparation change, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is buckwheat flour, a ground, milled product made from buckwheat groats. The USDA match is buckwheat groats, which are the whole hulled kernels (raw or cooked), not flour. Under guideline F, the raw plant/source versus the processed ingredient are not substitutable (e.g., cornstarch vs corn). Using groats in place of flour would change how the dish is prepared: flour is incorporated into batter or dough and produces a smooth, cohesive texture, while whole or cracked groats remain as discrete grains with a chewy, nubbly texture and different appearance. A diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance. Condition 1 (no change in preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) both fail. The quantity (100g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is apricot kernel oil, a pressed plant oil with a distinctive nutty, marzipan-like flavour, used as a cooking or dressing oil. The USDA match is 'Babyfood, juice, orange and apricot', which is a fruit juice blend for infants (orange and apricot fruit juice). It is not an oil at all; it is an aqueous, sugary fruit product containing no fat from kernels. Condition 1 fails: it cannot replace an oil in cooking or dressings without changing how the dish is prepared (liquid fruit juice would not fry, emulsify, or coat the way oil does, and would introduce water and sugar). Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (fruity sweetness versus nutty oil), texture (watery versus oily/mouthcoating), and appearance. Per guideline F, a different fat or oil is not substitutable, and this entry is far from even the same category. Quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is sautéed shallots, meaning the shallots have been cooked in fat until softened and often lightly browned. The USDA match is 'Shallots, raw', which is uncooked. Under condition 1, substituting raw shallots would change how the dish is prepared, since the cook would need to sauté them. Under condition 2, a diner would notice the difference: raw shallots are crisp and sharp, while sautéed shallots are soft, sweeter, mellower in flavour, and golden in colour. Guideline F explicitly treats raw versus cooked as not substitutable. The shallot identity matches, but the cooking state does not, so the match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is ketchup, a plain condiment, and the USDA entry 'Ketchup' is the same food under the same name. The weight (30g) is ignored per guideline A. 'Room-temperature' describes how the product is handled before use, not a modification of the product, so it does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: ketchup can replace this ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the food is the same product served at a different temperature. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sweet bean sauce, a fermented soybean-based condiment (typically made from yellow soybean paste, sugar, and flour or starch) with a thick, sweet, savoury flavour and dark brown colour. The USDA match is rice crackers, a dry, crisp, baked or fried puffed rice snack. These are not the same food under another name, and they are not a plausible substitute: rice crackers contain no soybean paste, have a completely different flavour profile (bland or lightly salted versus sweet and umami-rich), a dry crisp texture instead of a viscous sauce, and a different appearance. Using rice crackers in place of sweet bean sauce would change how the dish is prepared (it is a liquid to be stirred, spread or simmered, not a snack to be crushed or layered) and a diner would immediately notice the difference. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well.

The ingredient is toasted sprouted wheat bread. The USDA entry, 'Bread, wheat, sprouted, toasted', names the same product in the same state. Sprouted wheat matches sprouted wheat, and toasted matches toasted. The leading '30g' is quantity and is ignored. Guideline F rejects plain-versus-toasted mismatches, but here both sides are toasted, so no state difference exists. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without any change to preparation, since it is already toasted. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food in the same state.

The ingredient is shallot (quantity 50g is ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry 'Shallots, raw' is literally the same food, uncooked, in its standard form. Shallots are not sold in a different cut or processed state here, and no preparation difference is implied by the raw entry. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since any knife work (chopping, slicing) does not alter the match per guideline C. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same raw shallot. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is lean pork shank meat, cubed. The USDA entry is fresh pork from the leg (ham), shank half, separable lean only, raw. Both describe the same cut: the shank is the lower part of the leg, and the entry is lean-only and uncooked, matching 'lean' and 'raw'. Cubing is knife work done at home and does not change the match (guideline C), and the weight is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same cut of pork in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain Swiss cheese, the standard default product. The USDA match is 'Cheese, Swiss, reduced sodium', a modified version with lower sodium. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient becoming a reduced-sodium version as a modification, not a match. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the cheese could be used in the same preparation. Condition 2 fails: reduced-sodium Swiss cheese has less salt, so its taste differs, and a diner could notice. The ingredient does not ask for the reduced-sodium version, so the modified entry does not qualify.

The ingredient is quinoa flour (or quinoa meal), a finely ground dry product used as a flour in baking or cooking. The USDA entry 'Quinoa, NS as to fat' is the whole quinoa grain, generally listed as cooked, with the fat state unspecified. Condition 1: swapping whole quinoa for quinoa flour would change the preparation, since the grain would need cooking and would not perform as a flour in batters, doughs or thickening. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in texture (whole grain pieces versus a fine powder) and in how the dish is built. Flour versus whole grain is a different physical form, which guideline F treats as a different state, so the match fails on both conditions.

The ingredient is sardines packed in oil and drained. The USDA entry is Atlantic sardine canned in oil, drained solids, with bone. Both describe the same food in the same state: canned, oil-packed, and drained. The ingredient does not specify a species, so the Atlantic entry is a reasonable default. The 'with bone' descriptor reflects how canned sardines are normally sold, since the bones are softened and eaten, and it is not a modification. Under the guidelines, the gram weight is ignored and drained solids match a drained ingredient. Condition 1: the match could replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same canned sardine product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a mixture of two fruits, strawberries and rhubarb, diced. The USDA match is 'Rhubarb, raw', which covers only one of the two components. Guideline F says a single ingredient is not substitutable for a blend or product containing it. Condition 1 fails because the dish would lose the strawberries it calls for, which changes the composition and preparation. Condition 2 fails because a diner would taste the difference: rhubarb alone is very tart, while the strawberry component adds sweetness and a different flavour and colour. The 150g quantity and the 'diced' knife work do not change this, per guidelines A and C.

The ingredient is sliced liverwurst. The USDA entry is Oscar Mayer Braunschweiger Liver Sausage, sliced. Braunschweiger is a regional variety of liver sausage, and in the US market it is commonly sold and used interchangeably with liverwurst. Under guideline B, a regional or trade name for the same food counts as a match. Guideline G also applies: a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. Condition 1: the sliced product can be used in place of sliced liverwurst with no change in preparation, since both are ready-to-eat sliced deli sausages. Condition 2: liverwurst varies widely between brands in smokiness, spicing and texture, so a diner would not reliably notice a difference. Braunschweiger is not a modified, flavoured or reduced version, and 'sliced' is handling that does not change the match. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is light cream, and the USDA entry 'Cream, light' is the same product under a nearly identical name. Light cream is the standard default version of that dairy product, so guideline D applies and no modification is involved. The weight (210g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: light cream can replace this entry directly without changing preparation, since both are used the same way (pouring, whipping, cooking, or adding to sauces). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the two are the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain chicken tender strips, which are raw chicken meat to be cooked in the recipe. The USDA match is a cooked, breaded, fried restaurant platter from Applebee's, which is a prepared dish, not the raw meat. Using it would skip the cooking the recipe requires, so condition 1 fails. It is also breaded and fried, with a different texture and appearance, and a diner would notice the difference, so condition 2 fails. The quantity is ignored per the guidelines. Not substitutable.

1) Identity: the ingredient and the USDA entry are the same food, fresh fava beans, raw. 2) Form: the USDA entry is 'in pod', while the ingredient is already shelled. Shelling is handling the recipe does itself, comparable to shucking, which guideline C says does not change the match. The pod is inedible packaging, and the diner eats only the beans either way. 3) Quantity is ignored per guideline A. 4) Condition 1: the cook shells the pods, which is the same prep the recipe already assumes, so the preparation is unchanged. Condition 2: once shelled, the beans are identical in taste, texture and appearance. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a buttery spread, a fat product used as a butter or margarine substitute, typically made from vegetable oils with water and sometimes milk solids. The USDA match is pasteurized process American cheese spread, a processed dairy product made from cheese, emulsifiers and salts. These are different foods. Condition 1 fails: in a recipe the buttery spread would be used for fat in cooking, baking or spreading, and the cheese spread would add cheese flavour, salt and a different melt and emulsion behaviour, changing preparation and results. Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste the sharp, cheesy flavour and notice the different texture and colour. Guideline F rejects a different fat for a fat, and a single ingredient versus a processed product differs in state. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is the same cut (porterhouse steak, raw), so the cut itself matches. The USDA entry differs in two ways. First, the grade: the ingredient specifies choice grade, but the entry is select. Choice has noticeably more intramuscular marbling, which affects juiciness, tenderness and flavour when cooked, so a diner could plausibly notice. Second, the trim: the entry is trimmed to 1/8" fat, while the ingredient names no trimming, so it is a modified version of a plain cut. Because the grade and trim change flavour and texture, condition 2 fails, and the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain fresh coconut cream, a savoury-neutral cream made from fresh coconut. The USDA entry is canned coconut cream that is sweetened. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a sweetened version is a modification and does not count as a match. Guideline F also treats fresh versus processed/canned as a different state. Adding sugar changes the flavour, and a diner would likely notice the sweetness in a savoury dish. Condition 2 therefore fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is roasted peanuts ground at home into a paste: a single ingredient, unsalted by default, with no added fat, sugar or stabilisers. The USDA match is commercial 'Peanut butter, smooth style, with salt', a processed product containing peanuts plus added salt and typically other additives such as sugar, oil or stabilisers. Under guideline F, a single ingredient is not substitutable for a blend or product containing it, and the processed product is not the same as the raw/roasted source. Under guideline D, the plain ingredient mapped to a modified version ('with salt') does not count as a match. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would likely taste the added salt and may notice a different texture and flavour from commercial peanut butter. Quantity is ignored, as instructed. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is chicken ham, a processed chicken meat product sliced or cubed as a meat for a dish. The USDA match is 'Ham salad spread', which is a mayonnaise-based spread containing chopped ham (or ham pieces) mixed with pickle relish, mayonnaise-type dressing, and seasonings. Condition 1: substituting a creamy, dressed spread for a solid meat ingredient would change how the dish is prepared, since the spread is already seasoned and emulsified and cannot be used as a meat component in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice a difference in texture (creamy, spreadable versus firm meat pieces) and flavour (added mayonnaise, relish and seasonings). The match is also not the same food under another name; it is a prepared composite product. Therefore, the match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is saffron threads, crushed. The USDA entry 'Spices, saffron' is the same spice with no processing state given. Crushing is hand handling, which guideline C says does not change the match. Crushed threads are still threads, not a ground powder, so the whole-versus-ground distinction in guideline F does not apply. Condition 1: saffron could replace the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same spice. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is garlic naan, which is naan flavoured with garlic (typically with garlic and butter or herbs on top). The USDA entry is plain naan, commercially prepared and refrigerated. Condition 1: the preparation could be swapped, since both are ready-made flatbreads, so this part is arguably met. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference, because garlic naan has a distinct garlic flavour and appearance (garlic and herb topping) that plain naan lacks. Guideline D treats a plain product versus a flavoured version as a modification, so this is not a match. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is iceberg lettuce that has been braised, so it is already a cooked product. The USDA entry 'Lettuce, cooked' matches the cooked state, so the cooking state is not a mismatch. The entry does not name a variety, so it is the generic lettuce food, which covers iceberg (guideline B and E). Using cooked lettuce in place of braised iceberg would not change how the dish is prepared, since the braising step is part of the recipe and the USDA entry describes the same cooked state. Iceberg is a mild-flavoured variety, and once braised, a diner would not reliably detect a difference in taste, texture or appearance between it and other cooked lettuce. Condition 1 and condition 2 are both met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is raw minced venison, a single meat ingredient that the recipe will cook as part of the dish. The USDA entry is 'Meat loaf made with venison/deer', a prepared, already-cooked product that combines venison with other components such as binders, seasonings and usually egg or bread crumbs. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B), and it is not a plain ingredient's standard version (guideline D). Condition 1 fails: using a finished meatloaf in place of minced raw venison changes how the dish is prepared, because the cook would have to drop the cooking step and the added binders and seasonings would change the dish. Condition 2 would also likely fail, since a diner would taste the added seasonings and see the loaf's cooked, bound texture rather than loose minced meat. Guideline F also rejects a single ingredient matched to a blend or product containing it. Because condition 1 is not met, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw veal top round, with the leading weight ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Veal, leg (top round), separable lean only, raw', which is the same cut (top round) in the same state (raw). The 'separable lean only' descriptor reflects how top round is normally sold as a trimmed cut, so it is the standard default rather than a modified version (guideline D). Under guideline F, the concern would be a different cut, and this is not one. Cooking method, flavour, texture and appearance are unchanged, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is mango nectar, canned. The USDA entry is 'Mango nectar, canned', which is the same product under the same name. The leading '75g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Canned mango nectar is normally sold as that product, so the match is the default version rather than a modified one. Nothing about the dish's preparation, flavour, texture or appearance would change, and a diner would not be able to tell the difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh fava beans in their pods, which is the same food as the USDA entry 'Beans, fava, in pod, raw'. Condition 1: the USDA entry is the raw, unshelled form, so it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. The leading '30g' is only a quantity and is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2: a diner would see the same fava beans in pods, with no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is porridge made with milk and butter. Porridge is oatmeal cooked in liquid, so the USDA entry 'Oatmeal, regular or quick, made with milk, fat added' names the same dish with the same components: oats, milk, and added fat (butter fits the 'fat added' descriptor). Per guideline C, USDA adding its standard descriptor does not make it a different dish. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are cooked oatmeal made with milk and fat. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because both are the same cooked oat porridge with milk and fat. The 10g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is fresh beech mushrooms, trimmed. Trimming is knife work that does not change the food (guideline C). The USDA entry "Mushroom, beech" names the same food under its common name, so it is the same food under another name (guideline B). The entry carries no cooked, dried, canned or flavoured state, so it matches the plain fresh product (guidelines D and E). Quantity is ignored (guideline A). Substituting it would not change preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried oysters, a dehydrated, shelf-stable product that is typically rehydrated or soaked before use and has a concentrated, chewy texture and intense umami flavour. The USDA match is 'Oysters, steamed', a freshly cooked, moist, soft product. Condition 1 fails: dried oysters must be rehydrated and usually cooked differently, so swapping in steamed oysters changes how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (chewy versus soft) and flavour (concentrated dried umami versus fresh steamed). Per guideline F, a different state (dried versus cooked) is not substitutable, and the entry is not the same food under another name.

Kombu is a kelp, so the species identity is close to 'Seaweed, kelp, raw'. However, kombu as sold for cooking is dried, and the USDA entry is for raw, fresh kelp. Under the guidelines, a dried product is a different state from the raw entry, as with fresh versus dried herbs. Condition 1 fails because dried kombu must be rehydrated or simmered (for example, for dashi), while raw kelp would be handled and cooked differently. Condition 2 also fails: dried and fresh kelp differ noticeably in texture, flavour intensity and appearance. The quantity and the 'optional' label are ignored. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'water crackers', a plain, unsalted-topping cracker made from flour, water and salt. The USDA entry 'Crackers, water' names the same product under a standard descriptor. The 760g weight is decoration and is ignored (Guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient in the same way, with no change to preparation, since both are ready-to-eat crackers used as-is. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product type. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is apple butter, a spread made from cooked-down apples. The USDA entry 'Fruit butters, apple' names the same product under a standard descriptor, so it is the same food under the same name (guideline B). Apple butter is normally sold sweetened and spiced, so that is the default version a shopper would buy under the plain name, not a modified version (guideline D). The weight (100g) is ignored (guideline A). Using the USDA entry changes no preparation step, and a diner would not taste or see a difference because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is grapeseed oil (20g, quantity ignored). The USDA match is 'Oil, grapeseed', which is the same food under the same name. Condition 1: grapeseed oil can be used directly in place of grapeseed oil with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the identical product. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is refined soya oil. 'Soya' is the regional name for soybean, so this is the same food under another name (guideline B). The USDA entry 'Oil, vegetable, soybean, refined' names the same product with the same processing state, refined. Guideline A says to ignore the 5g quantity. Condition 1: the oil can be used in place of the ingredient without changing the preparation method, since it is the same oil used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same refined soybean oil. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a hard-boiled egg, meaning the egg has been cooked in its shell, so its texture, appearance, and state are those of a cooked egg. The USDA match is 'Egg, whole, raw', which is uncooked. Guideline F states that raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because a raw egg cannot replace a hard-boiled egg without changing how the dish is prepared (the egg would need to be boiled, which alters the preparation). Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference: a raw egg has a liquid yolk and runny white and would look and feel different from a firm, hard-boiled egg. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is sea cucumber, a marine echinoderm (an animal), sliced and used as a seafood ingredient. The USDA entry is 'Cucumber salad made with cucumber and vinegar', a prepared vegetable salad. These are not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. The name overlap is coincidental. Substituting the salad would change the main ingredient, and a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture (crisp vegetable vs. gelatinous sea cucumber), and appearance. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails.

Dried wakame is a brown kelp (Undaria pinnatifida) that is rehydrated and eaten as a tender, slightly slippery vegetable, typically in soups, salads, or miso dishes. The USDA entry 'Seaweed, agar, dried' refers to agar, a gelling agent extracted from red algae (Gelidium and Gracilaria). These are different species and different products. Agar is a polysaccharide used for setting gels and is not eaten as a vegetable. Using it in place of wakame would change the dish's texture, flavour, and appearance, and a diner would notice. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Because it is a different food and not a regional or trade name for the same one (guideline B), and the state and function differ, the match fails both conditions.

Piment d'Espelette is a specific PDO chili pepper, sold dried and usually ground, with a mild, fruity, slightly smoky flavour. The USDA entry 'Chili with meat' is a prepared dish (chili con carne) containing meat, beans, tomatoes and spices. It is not the same food under another name, and it is a blend or composed product rather than a single ingredient. Using it would change the dish's preparation, since the chili pepper would be replaced by a cooked stew, and the flavour, texture and appearance would also change, with meat and beans present. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is refried beans, and the USDA entry is 'Refried beans', which is the same food under the same name. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient directly with no change to preparation, since refried beans are used as they are, and the 235g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is raw pork loin, a specific cut of pork meat. The USDA match is 'Sausage and peppers, no sauce', which is a prepared dish combining sausage (a processed, seasoned ground meat product, typically pork or other meats) with peppers. This is a different food: a blended, seasoned, processed product that contains peppers and sausage casing/fat, not a plain pork loin cut. Condition 1 fails: substituting it would change the preparation, since pork loin is a whole muscle cut cooked as such, whereas sausage and peppers is a composed product. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (ground/sausage texture vs. whole muscle), flavour (seasoning, fennel/spices, peppers), and appearance. Per guideline F, a different cut or product containing the meat plus other ingredients is not substitutable. Quantity is ignored.

The ingredient is shiitake mushroom caps, weight given as 35g (quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry 'Mushrooms, shiitake, raw' is the same food: shiitake mushrooms in raw, uncooked form. Caps are simply the cap portion of the mushroom, a cut of the same food, and guideline B and C indicate that the inner part or a cut of the same vegetable counts as the same thing, and that knife work or trimming does not change the match. Condition 1: the raw shiitake can be used in place of the caps without changing preparation, since any cooking would be done by the recipe in both cases. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the caps are shiitake flesh in the same raw state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is whole wheat pita bread, a plain bread product made from whole wheat flour. The USDA entry 'Bread, pita, wheat or cracked wheat' describes a pita made with wheat flour, which is the whole wheat pita category. Substituting it does not change how the dish is prepared: it is still a ready-to-eat pita used in the same way. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same type of wheat pita product. The quantity (290g) is ignored per guideline A. The match is the same food under a standard product name, so it is substitutable.

The ingredient is a corn and pepper relish, a prepared condiment mixing corn kernels with diced peppers, typically in a vinegar/brine dressing with sugar, salt and spices, and sold drained. The USDA match 'Corn, raw' is only plain uncooked sweet corn. Condition 1: substituting raw corn would change the dish, since the relish contributes pepper pieces, pickling liquid acidity, sweetness and seasoning; it is not a like-for-like swap for a prepared product. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in taste (no tang, no pepper flavour, no seasoning) and in appearance and texture (no peppers, no marinated character). Per guideline F, a single ingredient versus a product containing it, and a raw source versus a processed ingredient, are not substitutable. The match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is chicken giblet powder, a dried and ground processed product. The USDA entry is raw chicken broiler or fryer giblets, which are fresh, uncooked, whole organ meats. Condition 1: the raw giblets cannot replace the powder without changing preparation. Powder dissolves, disperses and concentrates flavour in ways that whole raw giblets do not, so the dish would need to be rebuilt around chopping, simmering or grinding. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in texture, appearance and concentrated savoury flavour. Guideline F rejects a raw source versus a processed ingredient, and a different state (raw versus dried and ground). Guideline C allows home grinding of raw meat, but powdered giblets are a dehydrated product that cannot be produced by home knife work. The quantity (200g) is ignored. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is cauliflower florets (Brassica oleracea, Botrytis group): white, dense, mild-flavoured curds with a different texture and appearance. The USDA match is broccoli, raw (Brassica oleracea, Italica group): green flowering heads with stalks, a distinct sharper, more vegetal taste and visibly different florets. Condition 1 is not met in a strict sense only if cooking would change; here, substituting broccoli for cauliflower changes the colour and flavour of the dish and is a different vegetable, not a naming variant (guideline B does not apply because these are sibling vegetables, not the same food under another name). Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice green rather than white florets and a different taste and texture. Per guideline F (sibling varieties with different taste are not substitutable), this is not a match.

The ingredient is smoked turkey with no stated cut, skin status, or meat type. The match is the same food (smoked turkey, light or dark meat) and the smoked state matches, so the core product is correct. The deciding difference is 'skin eaten'. Standard retail smoked turkey (deli breast, smoked sliced turkey) is normally sold skinless, so the skin modifier is not how a shopper would normally buy the plain product. Skin changes appearance (visible browned skin) and texture (chewier, fattier bite), and a diner would plausibly notice it. Light/dark mix is acceptable as generic turkey meat, and the 250g quantity is ignored. Because the skin-on descriptor alters appearance and texture relative to the default product, condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is dried cherries, and the USDA entry is Cherries, dried, which is the same food in the same state. Quantity (100g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is the same dried product used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the product is identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a chocolate hazelnut spread specifically labelled 'reduced sugar'. The USDA entry 'Chocolate hazelnut spread' is the standard default product, which contains the usual sugar level. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version is a no, and the reverse is also a mismatch: the ingredient asks for the reduced-sugar version, and the USDA entry does not describe one. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the spread could be swapped in without changing preparation. Condition 2 fails: a reduced-sugar spread is noticeably less sweet and can differ in texture, so a diner could taste the difference. The quantity (30g) is ignored, per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain 'cream', whose standard default in recipes is heavy or whipping cream (roughly 36% milkfat). The USDA match 'Cream, light' is a lower-fat product (about 18-30% milkfat). Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified or lower-fat version does not count. Condition 1: light cream would not whip the same way and would behave differently in sauces, custards, or reductions, so the preparation could change. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice a difference in richness, mouthfeel, and body, especially in whipped or cream-based dishes. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

1. The ingredient is 'blueberry muffin cereal', a generic ready-to-eat cereal with a blueberry muffin flavour. The leading '145g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). 2. The USDA entry is 'Cereals ready-to-eat, MALT-O-MEAL, Blueberry MUFFIN TOPS Cereal'. It is a branded blueberry muffin-flavoured ready-to-eat cereal, the same product type the ingredient asks for. The flavour is the one requested, so it is not a modification (guideline D). Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. 3. Condition 1: the cereal is eaten as is, so it can directly replace the ingredient without changing preparation. 4. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance because the ingredient is specified only by type. Blueberry muffin cereals from other makers vary somewhat, but this entry is a genuine example of the named product type, so it is an acceptable match.

The ingredient is a canned smoked chicken pate. The USDA entry is a smoked pate de foie gras made from goose liver. These are different source animals and different products: chicken pate versus a goose liver (foie gras) pate. Foie gras pate is far richer, smoother and more distinctly flavoured than a chicken pate, and it is typically priced and served as a luxury product. A diner would likely notice the difference in taste and texture. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and the match is not a plain-to-standard equivalent. Condition 1 might be met in a loose sense, since both are spreadable pates, but condition 2 fails because the flavour, texture and identity of the meat differ. Under guideline F, different meat sources are not substitutable.

The ingredient is shelled Brazil nuts, weight is ignored. The USDA entry 'Brazil nuts' is the same food with no state descriptor, which under guideline E matches the generic food, including plain/shelled forms. Brazil nuts are normally sold shelled, so 'shelled' is only handling and does not change the match. Substituting one for the other would not change preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sorghum flour, a finely ground processed product. The USDA match is sorghum grain, the whole uncooked kernel. Guideline F rejects a raw source versus its processed form, and a whole-versus-ground difference is also a state change. Using whole grains in place of flour would require milling or cooking and would change texture and appearance, so condition 1 fails. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice whole kernels rather than a flour-based batter or dough. This is not the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

Ingredient is plain fresh grapefruit, 200g; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Grapefruit, raw' is the same food in its uncooked, fresh state, which is the standard default version (guideline D). Grapefruit is eaten or used raw in most preparations, so no cooking method change is implied. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same fruit in the same raw state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a smoked tomato salsa, and the USDA entry is a generic red salsa. Condition 1: the quantity is ignored, and the preparation is a condition-free swap in form, since both are salsas used as condiments. Condition 2: the ingredient specifies smoking, which adds a distinct smoky flavour and often a darker, roasted appearance. Guideline F states that plain vs smoked/roasted is a different state and not substitutable. A diner would likely notice the smoky taste compared with a standard red salsa. Condition 2 therefore fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is wild duck breast that has been smoked. The USDA entry is raw wild duck breast, meat only, with no smoking. Both the cut and the species match, so the food itself is the same. However, guideline F says plain vs smoked is a different state and not substitutable. Smoking changes flavour, colour and texture, so a diner would notice the difference, and the dish's preparation would also differ, since the smoked product is not cooked or prepared the same way as raw meat. Condition 2 fails because taste and appearance would visibly differ. The quantity (175g) is ignored per guideline A. Because the match is raw rather than smoked, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 150g of cooked lean ground turkey, crumbled. The USDA entry is ground turkey at 93% lean / 7% fat, pan-broiled crumbles. Lean ground turkey is commonly sold as 93% lean, so the raw food is the same. Both entries are in the cooked, crumbled state the recipe asks for, and pan-broiling is a way of cooking the meat, not an added flavouring or treatment. Using the USDA entry would not change how the dish is prepared, since the cook would add the same cooked crumbled turkey. The taste, texture and appearance of pan-broiled crumbles match cooked crumbled lean ground turkey, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh fava beans (Vicia faba), a broad bean sold shelled for its inner seeds. The USDA match is 'Beans, snap, green, raw', which is the whole immature pod of a common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) eaten as a vegetable. These are different foods, not regional or culinary names for the same thing (guideline B). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference, since fava beans are starchy, firm, and mealy with a distinct flavour, while snap beans are crisp, tender, and grassy, and the appearance also differs (shelled seeds versus whole pods). Because the food itself differs, the match is not substitutable under either condition.

The ingredient is fenugreek paste from a jar, a prepared condiment made by grinding fenugreek seed and adding liquid, and often other ingredients such as vinegar, salt, or oil. The USDA match, 'Spices, fenugreek seed', is the dried spice seed itself. Under guideline F, a single dry spice is not interchangeable with a processed or prepared form of it, and whole or ground spice differs from a paste. Using dry seed in place of paste would change how the dish is prepared: the seed would need grinding and hydrating, and it would lack the paste's moisture and any added ingredients. The flavour and texture would also differ, so a diner could notice. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 likely fails as well.

The ingredient is pumpkin seeds (Cucurbita seeds), roasted. The USDA match is watermelon seed kernels (Citrullus seeds), dried. These are different foods from different plants, with different flavour and appearance. Pumpkin seeds are green, flat and oval, while watermelon seed kernels are small, pale and pointed. The ingredient is also roasted, while the match is dried and unroasted. Guideline F rules out a different state (plain vs roasted), and the seeds themselves are not the same food, so they are not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Using watermelon kernels would change flavour, texture and appearance, and a diner would notice. Quantity is ignored.

The ingredient is salted duck egg, a cured product whose defining feature is salt-curing in brine, which gives it a strong salty flavour, a firmer and oilier texture, and a distinctive vivid orange yolk. The USDA entry 'Duck egg, cooked' is a plain, unsalted, cooked whole duck egg. Condition 1: using the plain cooked egg would change how the dish is prepared, because the curing step that produces the salted egg's characteristic flavour and texture is absent. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in taste (no salinity or cured flavour) and texture (plain set egg rather than the dense, sandy salted yolk). Per guideline D, a plain product matched to a modified (salted/cured) version is not substitutable. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is a cooked mixture of peas and corn. The USDA entry is 'Peas and corn, cooked, no added fat', which names the same two components in the same cooked state. The 'no added fat' descriptor is the standard plain preparation for cooked vegetables and does not change the food. The leading '80g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is already cooked and needs no further handling. Condition 2: a diner would see and taste the same cooked peas and corn, with no difference in flavour, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is rhubarb, a fresh tart stalk vegetable (the quantity 275g is ignored). The USDA match is 'Mock chicken legs', a processed meat analogue, typically made from textured vegetable protein or wheat gluten and sold as a meat substitute product. Condition 1: rhubarb is not the same food under another name and is not a cut or variant of it, so the match is not a valid stand-in. Substituting mock chicken legs would require different preparation (rhubarb is stewed, baked into pies, or made into compotes, whereas mock chicken is a savoury protein product typically cooked by frying, baking or simmering), so the cooking method and dish would change. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (sour, fruity versus savoury meaty), texture (fibrous, stalky versus meat-like), and appearance (red-pink stalks versus processed meat analogue). Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is plain 'chili sauce'. In the USDA database, 'Tomato chili sauce' is the standard default version of that product, which is what a shopper normally buys under that name (American-style chili sauce is tomato-based). The quantity (150g) is ignored. The match is not a modified, flavoured, reduced or differently processed version, and it is not a different food. Substituting it would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met, with the caveat that a non-tomato chili sauce such as Thai sweet chili sauce would be a different product.

The ingredient is fennel bulb, which has a distinct anise/licorice flavour, a crisp-but-fibrous texture, and a bulbous white-and-green appearance. The USDA match is celery, raw, a different vegetable with a grassy, savoury flavour and different appearance. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), so it is not a regional or culinary synonym. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the absence of the anise flavour and the change in appearance. Condition 1 is also doubtful, since fennel is typically used for its aniseed flavour, which celery cannot replicate. The weight (5g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is head cheese, a cold-cut/terrine made from pig head meat and gelatinous stock, set in aspic and typically sliced and served cold. The USDA match is Cheese, paneer, a fresh unaged dairy curd made from milk, typically pressed into blocks and often cooked (fried or grilled). Condition 1: paneer is not the same food under another name and is not a cut or variant of head cheese; substituting it would change the dish entirely, since head cheese is a meat product and paneer is a dairy product, and the preparation (cold slicing of a meat terrine versus cooking a curd) would not be preserved. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (pork and gelatin versus mild milky curd), texture (firm meat and jelly versus soft, squeaky curd), and appearance (marbled meat in aspic versus white block). Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is yellow dragon fruit (yellow pitaya, Selenicereus megalanthus), a distinct variety within the dragon fruit group. The USDA entry 'Dragon fruit' is the generic food, not a regional or trade name for the same thing. Yellow dragon fruit is a sibling variety, which guideline F treats as non-substitutable when the taste differs. It is generally sweeter and more mildly flavoured than the common red- or white-fleshed dragon fruit, and its yellow skin is a visible appearance difference. Condition 1 (same preparation) can be met, but condition 2 (diner would not notice a difference in taste or appearance) is not reliably met, so the match fails.

The ingredient is high oleic sunflower oil, used for frying. The USDA entry, 'Oil, sunflower, high oleic (70% and over)', is the same product under its standard name. The leading '6g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the oil can replace the ingredient in frying without changing the cooking method, since it is the same oil used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the fat is identical. The entry is not a different oil (guideline F), a modified version, or a processed source. Both conditions hold.

Condition 1 (preparation): The ingredient is a milk-based protein powder used as a dry ingredient. The USDA entry is a milk-based protein powder, so it can be added in the same way without changing the cooking method. Condition 2 (sensory): The ingredient names no flavour, brand or additive, so it is the generic product type. Muscle Milk is a branded milk-based protein powder, and guideline G treats a branded entry of the same plain product type as a match. Brand and flavour differences between protein powders exist, but the ingredient does not specify any, so a diner would not expect a particular taste or texture that the substitute would contradict. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw beef tongue. The USDA entry is raw beef tongue from New Zealand, a country-of-origin label on the same product. Condition 1: the tongue can be used in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation, since it is the same raw cut. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the meat is the same food. Country of origin is not a modification such as added flavour, reduced fat, or a different cut. The quantity prefix is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is roasted safflower seeds. The USDA match is safflower seed kernels, dried, which is an unroasted, raw-style entry. Condition 1: substituting raw kernels for roasted seeds would skip the roasting step, so the preparation changes. Condition 2: roasting alters flavour (nutty, toasted), texture (crisper, drier), and appearance (colour darkens), so a diner would likely notice. Guideline F explicitly lists plain vs toasted/roasted as a different state, not substitutable. The quantity is ignored, and the match is otherwise the same seed.

The ingredient is black bean sauce, a condiment typically made from fermented black soybeans, garlic, and seasonings, sold under that name. The USDA entry is literally 'Black bean sauce', the same food under the same name. The quantity (50g) is ignored per guideline A. The product is not a different cut, oil, variety, or processed source; there is no modification, cooking state, or blend that differs from the plain product a shopper would buy. Preparation would not change, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

1. Ignore the leading '265g' quantity, per guideline A. 2. The ingredient is 'chicken legs, skin on'. In common culinary usage, 'chicken legs' most often means drumsticks, and the USDA entry is specifically the drumstick, so it is the same food under a common name (guideline B). Skin-on matches 'meat and skin', and 'raw' matches an uncooked ingredient. 3. Condition 1: the drumstick can replace the chicken legs without changing the preparation, since the cooking method for a raw skin-on leg piece is the same. 4. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the same cut is being served. 5. Residual ambiguity: if 'chicken legs' were read as leg quarters (thigh plus drumstick), this would be a different cut under guideline F. The plain-language reading points to drumsticks, so I treat it as a match.

The ingredient is pesto genovese, the traditional basil pesto from Genoa (basil, pine nuts, garlic, hard cheese, olive oil). The USDA entry 'Pesto sauce' is the generic, unmodified pesto product. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to its standard default version is a match, and genovese is the default style of pesto. Condition 1: pesto is used the same way (as a sauce, spread, or stirred in), so the preparation does not change. Condition 2: the generic pesto sauce is basil-based with the same core components, so a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Minor recipe variation between commercial pestos does not make the generic entry a different food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is tamari, a Japanese soy sauce made from fermented soybeans, typically wheat-free, with a rich, savoury, umami flavour and a liquid form. The USDA match is sesame oil, salad or cooking, which is an oil pressed from sesame seeds with a nutty flavour. These are different foods: tamari is a fermented soy-based condiment, while sesame oil is a fat. Using sesame oil in place of tamari would change the flavour profile entirely (salty, umami, fermented versus nutty, fatty) and would also change the dish's liquid and seasoning behaviour in preparation. A diner would readily notice the difference. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well. Not the same food under another name, and not a substitute under the guidelines.

The ingredient is 55g baobab powder. The leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA match is 'Baobab powder', which is the same food under the same name. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same powder used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'sapote fruit', a general term covering several unrelated fruits (mamey sapote, white sapote, black sapote). The USDA entry 'Mammy-apple, (mamey), raw' is Mammea americana, the mammee apple, which is a different species and family from the sapotes. The shared 'mamey' name is a source of confusion, but it does not make them the same food. Guideline B (same food under another name) does not apply, since this is a different fruit rather than a regional name for the same one. Its flavour and texture also differ from sapote fruit, so a diner would likely notice the change, and the match fails condition 2. Under guideline F, a different variety or species with a different taste is not substitutable. The quantity is irrelevant.

The ingredient is a T-bone steak, which is the same food as the USDA entry 'Beef, steak, T-bone, NS as to fat eaten'. The 150g weight is decoration and is ignored (A). The 1-inch thickness describes the cut's size, not a different product, so it does not change the match. The USDA entry names no cooking state or modification, so it is the generic food and matches the plain steak (B, E). Fat content is 'NS as to fat eaten', meaning unspecified, so it does not conflict with a standard T-bone. Using this entry would not change how the steak is prepared, and a diner would not taste a difference from the same cut of beef. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain turkey back meat with no mention of added solution. The USDA entry is turkey back meat, meat only, raw, but specifically 'with added solution,' meaning it has been injected or brined. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a version 'with added solution/additives' is a modified version and does not count as a match. Condition 1: the added solution means the cook would need to account for extra salt and moisture, so preparation may need adjusting, and the wet brine can change how the meat browns and cooks. Condition 2: the added solution changes taste (saltier, seasoned) and texture (plumper, moister, more spongy), which a diner could notice. Turkey back meat is normally sold without added solution, so the descriptor is not the standard way this product is bought. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is a shredded Mexican cheese blend, typically a meltable mix such as Monterey Jack, cheddar and queso quesadilla, used for melting in dishes like quesadillas, nachos and enchiladas. The USDA match, queso cotija, is a hard, dry, crumbly, salty aged cheese that does not melt in the way shredded blends do. Condition 1 fails: swapping in cotija changes how the dish behaves in cooking, since it would not melt into a stretchy, fused layer. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, meltiness, flavour (sharper and saltier) and appearance. The match is a single specific cheese, not the blend, and it is a different product with a different function. Under the guidelines, a different product with a different state and function is not substitutable, so both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is a frozen mix of peas and onions with no stated preparation, so it is normally used raw from the freezer and cooked as part of the dish. The USDA entry is specifically 'cooked, boiled, drained'. Condition 1 fails: substituting an already-boiled product changes how the dish is prepared, because the cooking step would be skipped or the vegetables would be doubly cooked. Condition 2 is also doubtful: boiled vegetables would be softer and less vivid than frozen peas and onions cooked in the dish. Raw/unprepared versus cooked is a state difference that the guidelines treat as non-substitutable, so the match fails.

1. The ingredient is tomato puree, a canned tomato product. The USDA entry is 'Tomato products, canned, puree', the same food. The '5g' quantity is ignored per guideline A.
2. Condition 1 (same preparation): tomato puree can be used directly in place of the USDA puree without changing the cooking method.
3. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference): the USDA entry is the standard canned tomato puree. Its 'without salt added' wording is the plain product descriptor, not a flavour or texture modification, and a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance.
4. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh turkey heart, a raw poultry offal. The USDA entry 'Turkey, all classes, heart, raw' is the same food (turkey heart) in raw form. The quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A. Fresh is the default state for raw, so 'raw' matches fresh. Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same raw food and any cooking method applies equally. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, as the food is identical. Both conditions are met.

Ingredient is 100g ground veal, raw. USDA match is 'Veal, ground, raw', which is the same food with the same state (raw, ground). The leading weight is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since both are raw ground veal. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is literally the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is crushed pineapple, a pulpy, fruit-bit product with texture, typically canned in its own juice or syrup. The USDA match is pineapple juice, a liquid with no fruit pulp or pieces. Condition 1: swapping juice for crushed pineapple would change how the dish is prepared. It adds liquid where the recipe expects solid, fibrous fruit, and it would alter moisture and binding, so the preparation changes. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance, since the pulp and chunks disappear and the dish takes on a thinner, juice-like consistency. The guidelines treat the raw plant versus processed-product distinction and different-state matches as non-substitutable, and juice is a different product form from crushed fruit. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

Step 1: Identify the ingredient. 'Smoked Swiss cheese sausage' is a smoked sausage containing Swiss cheese. The leading '500g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Step 2: Identify the USDA entry. 'Swisswurst, pork and beef, with swiss cheese, smoked' is a smoked Swiss-style sausage with Swiss cheese, which is the same food under a regional/trade name (guideline B). The 'pork and beef' component is USDA's standard composition for this product, not a modification. Step 3: Condition 1 (preparation).
