The entry is already smoked and ready to eat or cook as the recipe specifies, so it can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Step 4: Condition 2 (sensory). It has the same smoked flavour, cheese inclusions, and sausage texture and appearance, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is kumquat leaves, the foliage of the plant. The USDA match, 'Kumquat, raw', is the fruit. These are different plant parts with different flavour profiles: the leaves are aromatic and herbal with a bitter, green note, while the fruit is sweet-tart. Condition 1 fails because the leaves cannot be swapped for the fruit without changing the dish's flavour and structure, since the fruit is not a leaf and would not be prepared the same way. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the taste and appearance difference. This is not a regional or trade name for the same food, so guideline B does not apply. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is sweet corn relish, a condiment whose main component is corn kernels, usually with bell pepper, onion, vinegar and sugar. The USDA match, 'Pickle relish, sweet', is a cucumber-based relish. Guideline B does not apply because these are different foods, not the same food under another name. Guideline F rejects a different food or product type that shares a general category. Substituting one for the other would change the flavour, since corn relish is sweet with a corn-forward taste and cucumber relish is a tangy pickle flavour. It would also change the appearance and texture, because corn kernels are visible and cucumber dice look different. A diner would notice the difference. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is enchilada sauce, a condiment-style sauce used to coat or flavour dishes. The USDA match 'Enchilada, NFS' names the dish itself, a filled, rolled tortilla. These are different foods, not the same food under another name. Using a whole enchilada in place of a measured amount of sauce would change how the dish is prepared (the sauce would not coat or flavour the dish in the same way), and a diner would notice a different food and different taste and texture. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails. The quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is a smoked turkey wing. Smoked turkey wings are normally sold as the bone-in wing with skin, and the recipe does not say the bone was removed. The USDA entry is smoked, cooked, with skin, bone removed, so the smoking, cooking state and skin match. The difference is the bone. Removing the bone changes how the wing is handled and cooked: bones add flavour and body to stocks and braises, and a bone-in wing looks and eats differently from a boneless one. Under guideline D, the plain ingredient maps to its standard default version, which is bone-in, so the bone-removed entry is a modified version. A diner could also notice the absence of the bone and its effect on texture and flavour. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) are therefore not both met. The quantity and the word 'divided' are irrelevant.

The ingredient is plain naan bread, the standard default version. The USDA entry is naan made with whole wheat flour, commercially prepared and refrigerated. Whole wheat is a modification of the plain product, and guideline D treats a plain ingredient mapped to a modified version as not a match. Guideline F also rules out a different flour. Condition 2 fails as well: whole wheat naan is visibly darker, has a coarser texture and a nuttier flavour, so a diner would likely notice the difference. The quantity (395g) is ignored. The refrigerated state is ordinary packaging and does not change the match. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is explicitly fresh apricot halves. The USDA match is canned apricots, packed in water, without skin, with solids and liquids. Canning heat-processes the fruit, so it is a cooked, processed state rather than raw fresh fruit (guideline F: raw vs cooked and fresh vs processed are not interchangeable). Canned apricots are noticeably softer, more uniformly coloured, and carry a liquid packing medium, which changes texture and appearance. The 'solids and liquids' entry also means the liquid is part of the product, which a recipe would handle differently from fresh halves. Condition 1 is not met because using canned fruit would change how the fruit is handled and how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 is not met because a diner would likely notice softer texture and different appearance and flavour. The 'halved' descriptor is knife work and does not matter here, but the state difference does. Guideline E does not apply because the match is canned, not frozen or thawed.

The ingredient is ampalaya (bitter gourd) leaves. The USDA entry is bitter gourd leafy tips, raw. Ampalaya leaves are typically sold and used as the tender young leaves and shoots, which is what 'leafy tips' describes, so this is the same food under a regional or trade description (guideline B). The 230g weight is ignored (guideline A). The 'raw' state is the uncooked plant, which matches the fresh leaves the recipe uses (guideline C). Condition 1: the leafy tips could replace the leaves in the same preparation, such as sautéing or boiling in Filipino dishes, without changing the method. Condition 2: both carry the same characteristic bitterness and leafy green appearance. Any difference from a slightly higher share of tender stem is minor and would not be noticed by a diner. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried agar, a gelling agent derived from red seaweed. The USDA entry 'Seaweed, agar, dried' is the same food in the same state (dried). Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Used in place of the ingredient, it requires no change to preparation: it is hydrated and boiled the same way. A diner would not taste or see a difference, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is natural (plain, unflavoured) yoghurt. Yoghurt and yogurt are the same food under regional spelling, so the name difference does not matter. The USDA entry is 'Yogurt, NS as to type of milk, plain', which is the plain, unflavoured product with the milk type unspecified. That is the standard default version, so it is not a modified entry such as low-fat, sweetened, or flavoured. The quantity (250g) is ignored. Condition 1: it can replace the yoghurt in a recipe without changing preparation, since yoghurt is used as-is, stirred, or dolloped. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same plain yoghurt. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried egg noodles, uncooked, and the '50g' is decoration per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Noodles, egg, dry, enriched' is the same product: dry egg noodles in their standard enriched form, which is how they are normally sold. Condition 1: the noodles can be used directly in place of the ingredient with the same preparation, boiled from dry. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, since 'enriched' is the standard commercial form and not a flavour or modification. Both conditions hold.

Condition 1: The ingredient is dry roasted mixed nuts with peanuts, salted. The USDA entry is mixed nuts, dry roasted, with peanuts, salt added. Both describe the same product in the same state (dry roasted, not raw or oil roasted), with the same components (mixed nuts including peanuts) and the same salting. 'Chosen Roaster' is a brand/trade name on a plain product of the same type, which guideline G accepts. The quantity (10g) is ignored per guideline A. Preparation would not change. Condition 2: Taste, texture and appearance should match, since the USDA entry describes the same dry-roasted, salted, peanut-containing mix. A diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is toasted barley bread, and the USDA entry is 'Bread, barley, toasted'. Both name the same product in the same state (toasted), so the match is literal and not a different state. The leading '360g' is quantity and is ignored. Guideline F's 'plain vs toasted' rule applies only when the ingredient is plain and the entry is toasted, or vice versa; here both are toasted. Condition 1: the bread can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since no further toasting or handling is implied. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same toasted barley bread. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is charentais melon, a small French cantaloupe-type muskmelon with orange flesh, a netted rind, and a strong, perfumed aroma. The USDA match is honeydew, raw, a different melon type with pale green flesh, a smooth rind, and a milder, less fragrant taste. Charentais is not the same food under another name (guideline B), and honeydew is a sibling melon with a different taste (guideline F). Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the green flesh instead of orange and the different flavour and aroma. Condition 1 is also not met, since the substitution changes the dish's flavour and appearance. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain ketchup, the standard default version. The USDA match is 'Ketchup, reduced sodium', a modified version. Guideline D lists reduced sodium explicitly as a modification, so a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced-sodium entry is not a match. Condition 2 also fails: reduced-sodium ketchup has less salt, so a diner could notice the difference in taste. Condition 1 is not the issue, since the product could be used in the same way, but the taste change means both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is plain 'shortening' that the recipe specifies for frostings. The USDA entry is 'Shortening, special purpose for cakes and frostings, soybean (hydrogenated)', a specialty bakery fat. The default home shortening would be a general vegetable shortening, so this is a modified or specialty version rather than the plain product. Guideline F rejects industrial or food-service specialty fats in place of the home ingredient, and a different fat is not substitutable. The specific fat source (soybean, hydrogenated) and the special-purpose formulation, which is usually built with emulsifiers for aeration and creaming, could also change frosting texture and mouthfeel. Condition 1 (same preparation) may hold, but condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste or texture) is doubtful. The 'for frostings' wording makes the match arguable, but the specialty-fat rule takes precedence, so the match is rejected.

The ingredient is coconut water, the thin clear liquid from inside young coconuts. The USDA match is coconut cream, canned, sweetened, a thick, rich, sugared emulsion of coconut meat and fat. These are different foods: coconut water is a low-fat, lightly sweet, watery liquid, while canned sweetened coconut cream is a dense, high-fat, heavily sweetened product. Condition 1 fails because substituting it would change the liquid volume, consistency and the way the dish comes together (it cannot be poured or used as a thin liquid base without changing the recipe). Condition 2 also fails because a diner would clearly notice the richer, thicker texture, the added fat and the much stronger sweetness and flavour. The quantity is irrelevant. Coconut water is not the same food as coconut cream under another name, and the sweetened, canned cream is a modified product, so it is not a match.

The ingredient is fresh chestnuts. The USDA match is 'Nuts, chestnuts, chinese, dried', which is a dehydrated product. Condition 1 fails: dried chestnuts must be rehydrated or softened before use, and fresh chestnuts are typically roasted, boiled, or peeled, so the preparation changes. Condition 2 also fails: dried chestnuts have a denser, chewier, drier texture and a more concentrated flavour, and a diner would notice the difference. Per guideline F, a different state (fresh vs dried) is not substitutable. The weight '30g' is ignored.

The ingredient is açaí juice, made from the açaí berry (Euterpe oleracea), which has an earthy, chocolatey-berry flavour and a thick, dark purple appearance. The USDA entry is cranberry juice, 100%, a different fruit with a sharp, tart flavour and a lighter red colour. Guideline B does not apply because these are different foods, not regional or trade names for the same one. Condition 1 might be met in a loose sense, since both are juices used as a liquid, but condition 2 fails: a diner would clearly taste the difference between açaí and cranberry, and the colour would also differ. Guideline F (a different variety or source with a different taste) supports rejection. The 150g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is sweetened condensed milk: milk reduced by evaporation and heavily sweetened with sugar, giving a thick, very sweet, caramel-like product. The USDA match is plain whole milk, an unsweetened liquid with a different water content and no added sugar. Condition 1 fails: substituting whole milk for sweetened condensed milk would change the dish's preparation (it lacks the thickness and sweetness the recipe relies on, and would not set or caramelise the same way). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the much lower sweetness, thinner texture and different flavour. Under guideline D, sweetened is a modification of plain milk, so this is not a match. The quantity (200g) is ignored.

The ingredient is beef tallow, rendered beef fat. The USDA entry 'Fat, beef tallow' is the same food under the same name, so it is literally the same product (guideline B). The 30g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Using the USDA entry would not change how the dish is prepared, since it is the same fat used the same way (condition 1). A diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance because the food is identical (condition 2). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cold brew coffee, which is made by steeping coarse grounds in cold water for many hours. The USDA entry is coffee brewed hot with tap water. Chilling alone would not change the match under guideline C, but cold brew is a distinct extraction method, not just chilled hot-brewed coffee. Cold extraction produces a noticeably different flavour: lower acidity, less bitterness, a smoother and sweeter profile, and different aromatic compounds. Condition 1 can be met in the sense that a liquid coffee could be swapped in, but condition 2 fails because a diner would likely notice the difference in taste. Guideline F also treats a different state or processing as a non-match, and this is a different preparation of the same beverage. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'mole', a Mexican sauce, and the USDA entry is 'Mole sauce', which names the same dish with no added modifier. The 200g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to its standard default entry counts as a match. Mole has no separate plain-versus-modified variants in the USDA listing, so the generic entry is the default version. Used in the same way, it would not change the preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh raw beef liver, sliced (the quantity and slicing are ignored per the guidelines). The USDA entry is canned liver pate, a processed, spreadable product that is cooked, emulsified and typically blended with fat, seasonings and other ingredients. Condition 1 fails: pate cannot be used in place of sliced fresh liver without changing how the dish is prepared, since liver is normally pan-fried or grilled as slices, while pate is served cold or spread. Condition 2 fails: a diner would readily notice the difference in texture (firm slices versus smooth paste), appearance, and flavour from the added ingredients. This is the raw/fresh source versus a processed product, which the guidelines treat as not substitutable.

The ingredient is whole grain spelt flour, and the USDA entry 'Flour, spelt, whole grain' is the same product under a standard name. The leading '30g' is quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the flour can replace the ingredient directly with no change in preparation. Condition 2: it is the same food, so a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cooked pigeon peas with salt. The USDA entry is pigeon peas (red gram), mature seeds, cooked, boiled, with salt. Pigeon peas and red gram are the same food under different names (guideline B). The entry is cooked, which matches the ingredient's cooked state, and it is salted, which matches the ingredient's salting. Neither is a modified version. The 8g quantity is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match could replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same cooked, salted pigeon pea. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is hot dog bun crumbs, a processed, dried, crumbed form of bread used as a coating or topping. The USDA entry is the whole hot dog bun, a soft, intact roll. Condition 1: the whole bun cannot be used in place of crumbs without first crumbing it, and that step changes the preparation the recipe calls for. Unlike chopping or rinsing, crumbing converts the food into a different product form. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference. Crumbs give a dry, granular, even coating that browns and crisps differently from a soft roll. Because the match is the source bread rather than the crumb product, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is red seedless grapes, weight is decoration (guideline A). The USDA entry 'Grapes, red, seedless, raw' is literally the same food: red seedless grapes, uncooked. Guideline B and C support a match; no cooking method change is implied, and raw fresh grapes would not be noticed as different. Condition 1 (can be used in place without changing preparation) is met, and condition 2 (no visible or taste difference) is met since the match is the same fresh product.

The ingredient is drumstick leaf powder, a dried and ground form of the leaves of the moringa (drumstick) tree. The USDA match is 'Drumstick pods, raw', which refers to the fresh, uncooked seed pods of the same tree. Leaves and pods are different plant parts with different flavour, texture and appearance. The pods are also raw and fresh, while the ingredient is a dried, ground powder. Condition 1 fails because a powder cannot be used in place of whole raw pods without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. The quantity (220g) is ignored, per guideline A.

The ingredient is whole wheat focaccia, and the USDA match is plain Italian focaccia. The USDA entry names the same dish, so the food type matches. However, the ingredient specifies whole wheat flour, while the match is made with the standard (refined) flour. Guideline F says a different flour is not substitutable. Whole wheat focaccia is darker, denser, has a nuttier, more bran-like flavour, and a coarser crumb, so a diner would notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is vegan aioli, a garlic-flavoured, egg-free emulsified sauce. The USDA match is regular mayonnaise, which is made with egg yolk and has no added garlic. Condition 1 (usable in place without changing preparation) is largely met, since both are spreadable emulsified condiments. Condition 2 fails on two counts. First, aioli is a flavoured version of mayonnaise, and the plain entry lacks the garlic flavour, so a diner would taste a difference (guideline D: a flavoured or modified version is not the plain match). Second, the match contains egg while the ingredient is explicitly vegan, so the diner would be eating something different, not merely a similar sauce. Either difference alone makes it non-substitutable.

The ingredient is 'smoked sausage', a smoked link sausage, which is commonly made from pork (e.g., kielbasa-style). The USDA entry 'Sausage, smoked link sausage, pork' describes the same food: a smoked link sausage made from pork. The 210g quantity is ignored per guideline A. The 'smoked' descriptor is part of the ingredient's own name, so it does not create a state mismatch as it would for plain versus smoked meat (guideline F). Condition 1: the sausage can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is sliced or cooked the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product type. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is hazelnut oil, and the USDA entry is 'Oil, hazelnut', which is the same product under a standard name. The leading '50g' is quantity and is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the oil can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to the preparation, since it is an oil used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same oil. No modification, blend, or different oil type is involved. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried shiitake mushrooms. The USDA entry 'Mushrooms, shiitake, dried' is the same food in the same state (dried), so no cooking method change is needed. Rehydrating dried shiitake is the normal preparation for the ingredient as bought, and the USDA entry describes that same product. The 150g weight is decoration per guideline A. Both conditions hold: the match can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance.

The ingredient is dry rice paper sheets, cut into strips. The USDA entry is simply 'Rice paper', the same product with no added state, flavour, or modification. Cutting into strips is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). Dry is the normal state in which rice paper is sold, so the USDA entry matches it (guideline E: a name-only entry is the generic food). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried corn syrup solids, a dry powdered form of corn syrup used to add sweetness and body without moisture. The USDA match, 'Syrups, corn, dark', is a liquid syrup with added caramel colour and a molasses-like flavour. Condition 1 fails: the powder cannot replace the liquid without changing the recipe's moisture, method, and how the ingredient is handled. Using a liquid syrup would also change the dry-ingredient balance. Condition 2 fails: 'dark' corn syrup carries a distinct molasses-like flavour and darker colour that a diner would likely notice. Guideline F rules out a different state (dry solids vs liquid syrup) and a flavoured or coloured variant. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is lox, a cured salmon sold thinly sliced. The USDA entry is 'Fish, salmon, chinook, smoked, (lox), regular', which names lox explicitly, so it is the same food under its standard name. Per guideline B, that is a match. Guideline C says knife work such as 'thinly sliced' does not change the match. The entry is the regular, default version, not a reduced-sodium or other modified product (guideline D). Swapping it in would not change the cooking method, since lox is normally served cold and unheated. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain crayfish, and the USDA entry is raw crayfish (mixed species, farmed). It is the same food, so it is the standard default version. The quantity (200g) is ignored. The ingredient does not specify wild or farmed, so farmed is an acceptable default. Mixed species does not change taste or texture for a typical crayfish dish. Cooking method is unchanged because both are raw, and the eater would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient asks for unsalted pita chips, while the USDA entry is salted pita chips. Under guideline D, a plain product matched to a modified version (here, salted, with added sodium) is not a match, and the 'unsalted' specification is a deliberate request for the non-salted version. Condition 1: the chips could physically replace each other in preparation, since the cooking and handling are the same. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in taste, because salt is a clearly perceptible flavour and the salted chips would taste noticeably different from unsalted ones. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

Step 1: The ingredient 'Japanese rice wine' is the English name for sake, the fermented rice beverage of Japan, so the USDA entry 'Alcoholic beverage, rice (sake)' names the same food under another name (guideline B). Step 2: The quantity (945g) is ignored (guideline A). Step 3: Condition 1 is met, since sake can replace it as a liquid in the same preparation without changing the cooking method. Step 4: Condition 2 is met, because sake is the same product, so a diner would not detect a difference in taste, texture or appearance. The main caveat is that 'Japanese rice wine' is sometimes used loosely for mirin, a sweeter cooking rice wine. The entry is not mirin, but the ingredient's wording most literally describes sake, so the match holds.

The ingredient is honeycomb pork tripe, which is the reticulum (second stomach) of a pig. The USDA entry is beef tripe from New Zealand, which is the stomach of a cow. These are different animals, so this is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Condition 1: a cook could physically swap beef tripe for pork tripe and cook it the same way, but the dish would not be the same product. Condition 2: pork and beef tripe differ in flavour, texture, and fat content, and a diner could plausibly notice the difference. Guideline F treats a different cut of meat as non-substitutable, and a different species is a stronger difference than a different cut. The match fails on the second condition, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is tomato concentrate (a cooked-down, evaporated tomato paste or puree) diluted with water. The match is Tomato juice, 100%, a ready-to-drink product that is not concentrated. Condition 1: Using juice in place of diluted concentrate would change the preparation. The diluted concentrate has a more intense, cooked, concentrated tomato flavour and a thicker body, and the amount of water needed to reach a juice-like state is not known. Juice would be used at a different strength and with different body, so the recipe's dilution step would no longer be reproduced. Condition 2: A diner would likely notice the difference in flavour depth and mouthfeel, since concentrate has been reduced and juice has not. Concentrate is a different state of the product (concentrated and cooked down) from juice, which is a different product in its own right, so this is not the same food under another name. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is a chicken frankfurter, a ready-made sausage. The USDA entry 'Frankfurter, chicken' names the same product with the same main component (chicken), so it is the same food under the same name. The weight (500g) is ignored per guideline A. Because it is the same product, it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation (condition 1), and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance (condition 2). No modified version, different cut, or processed-state mismatch is indicated.

The ingredient is pig's tongue, which is pork tongue, the same food the USDA entry describes. The USDA entry is 'Pork, fresh, variety meats and by-products, tongue, raw'. Pig's tongue is literally the same product, so this is a same-food-under-another-name match (guideline B). The weight (110g) is ignored (guideline A). The entry is raw, which matches uncooked pig's tongue, and any preparation the recipe does itself does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the match can replace pig's tongue without changing preparation, since it is the same cut of the same animal. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried persimmon, sold as slices. The USDA entry 'Persimmon, dried' is the same food in the same dried state. Slicing is handling that does not change the match (guideline C), and the entry names no modification, additive, or different variety. Using the USDA dried persimmon in place of dried persimmon slices would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is whole-wheat pasta in its dry, uncooked form, weighed at 75g. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Pasta, whole-wheat, dry' is the same food under the same state (dry, uncooked), so it is the same product rather than a different food. The parenthetical about the USDA Food Distribution Program is an administrative note about the entry's origin and does not describe a different product, preparation, or ingredient. Condition 1: the dry pasta can replace the ingredient with no change to cooking method, since both are boiled the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is oil roasted pecan halves with no salt added. The USDA entry is 'Nuts, pecans, oil roasted, without salt added', which is the same food with the same processing and the same salt status. Halving is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). The quantity prefix is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the USDA pecans can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference, since the nut type, oil roasting and lack of added salt are identical. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is dehydrated apple pieces, which is the same food as dried apple under a different name, so guideline B applies. The USDA entry 'Apple, dried' is the standard dried apple product. Dried apple is normally sold sulfured, so any sulfur treatment is the default rather than a modification (guideline D). The quantity is irrelevant (guideline A). Using dried apple in place of dehydrated apple pieces does not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Croissant crumbs are simply croissants that have been crushed into small pieces, so they are the same food in a different physical form. Crushing is handling the recipe does itself, similar to the guideline that ground-at-home or chopped preparations do not change the match. Condition 1: a whole croissant can be crushed into crumbs for use as a topping or coating without changing the cooking method. Condition 2: once crushed, the crumbs are still baked croissant with the same flavour, butter content and golden colour, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste or appearance. The USDA entry 'Croissant' names the same product, and its baked state matches croissant crumbs.

The ingredient is Chinese broccoli (gai lan, Brassica oleracea var. alboglabra) florets, the flowering heads with leaves and tender stems. The USDA entry is broccoli (var. italica) stalks only. Chinese broccoli is a distinct vegetable, not just a regional name for common broccoli, so guideline B does not apply. The USDA entry is also a different part of the plant: stalks rather than florets. Stalks are thicker, paler, and more fibrous, so they would change the texture and appearance of a dish that calls for florets, and a diner would likely notice. The match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is diced pork kidney, an organ meat from a pig. The USDA match 'Kidney beans with meat' is a canned or prepared dish of red kidney beans, typically in a sauce with pork or beef pieces. These are different foods: one is an animal organ, the other is a legume-based prepared dish. Condition 1 fails because using kidney beans in place of pork kidney would change the dish entirely (the protein source, the cooking method and the preparation would not match a recipe built around offal). Condition 2 also fails because a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance between organ meat and beans in sauce. The name overlap ('kidney') is coincidental and does not indicate the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply.

The ingredient is acorn squash, a distinct winter squash variety. The USDA match is butternut squash, raw, which is a sibling variety. Guideline F states that a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable. Acorn squash has a dark green, ridged skin, a yellow-orange flesh that is often more fibrous and watery, and a milder, less sweet flavour. Butternut has a tan skin, smooth flesh, and a sweeter, nuttier taste. A diner would notice the difference in appearance and flavour, and the cut and cooking may also differ. Condition 2 is not met, so the match is not substitutable. The quantity is ignored per guideline A, and raw versus cooked is not the issue here.

The ingredient is 2% fat Greek yogurt with coconut, which is the product the USDA entry describes: 'Yogurt, Greek, 2% fat, coconut blend, CHOBANI'. The quantity (400g) is ignored per guideline A. The coconut flavour is part of the ingredient itself, so the flavoured entry matches rather than being a modification (guideline D). The Chobani brand is a branded entry of the same product type (guideline G). Condition 1: the yogurt can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same product type with the same fat level and flavour. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is prickly pear (the fruit of the Opuntia cactus, sweet and mildly flavoured, with a distinctive taste and seed-filled texture). The USDA match is olive oil for salad or cooking, which is a fat/oil. It is not the same food under another name and is not a processed or modified version of prickly pear. Condition 1 fails: substituting olive oil would change how the dish is prepared, since the fruit would be missing and an oil added in its place. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. Quantity is irrelevant, so the 10g weight does not change the result.

The ingredient is purslane, and the USDA entry is 'Purslane, raw', which is the same plant with no added processing or state change. The weight (345g) is decoration and is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: purslane can be used in place of itself with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same raw food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is buttermilk, a liquid dairy product (chilled, optional). The USDA match is 'Pancakes, buttermilk, prepared from recipe', a cooked baked good. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B), and it is not a processed form of buttermilk (guideline F). Condition 1 fails: using pancakes in place of buttermilk would change the preparation entirely, since a liquid ingredient cannot be replaced by a finished cooked dish. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice a different texture, appearance and flavour. The 'chilled' and 'optional' wording does not affect the food identity (guideline C). Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is clam juice, a liquid broth or stock made from clams. The USDA match is 'Clams, steamed or boiled', which is the cooked clam meat itself. These are different foods. Clam juice is a liquid used for flavour and moisture, while steamed clams are solid shellfish. Substituting the meat for the juice would change the dish's liquid content, texture and flavour, and a diner would notice. Guideline B does not apply, since this is not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would change, and condition 2 fails because taste and texture would differ.

The ingredient is powdered half and half, a dehydrated dairy product that must be reconstituted with water before use. The USDA entry 'Cream, half and half' is the liquid, fresh dairy product. Condition 1 fails: using liquid half and half in place of the powder changes preparation, since the powder would have to be reconstituted and the liquid would have to be used without that step, and the recipe's moisture and liquid balance would shift. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would likely notice differences in texture, mouthfeel, and flavour, because powdered half and half is a different product from liquid cream. Per guideline F, a different state (dried vs fresh/liquid) is not substitutable. The quantity in grams is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is potato bread that has been toasted. The USDA entry 'Bread, potato, toasted' is the same product in the same state. Guideline F rejects plain versus toasted only when the two sides differ, and here both are toasted. Toasting is the stated preparation of the ingredient, so the match does not alter the cooking method or the dish. Condition 1 is met: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 is met: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same toasted potato bread. The 85g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain smoked link sausage with no specified meat or formulation. The USDA entry is a specific formulation, pork and beef with nonfat dry milk added. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to a modified version, including one 'with added solution/additives', as not substitutable. Nonfat dry milk is an added ingredient that can subtly change the texture and flavour of the cooked sausage, so a diner could plausibly notice. Condition 2 is not clearly met, so the match fails.

The ingredient is seasoned rice crackers, a rice-based snack with added seasoning (for example soy or savoury flavouring). The USDA entry 'Crackers, rice and nuts' is a different product: it is a rice-and-nut cracker, so it contains nuts that the ingredient does not. Under the guidelines, a blend or product containing an extra component is not the same as the single ingredient (F), and a flavoured or modified version of a plain item does not match the plain item (D). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would likely notice the nut flavour and possibly the texture and appearance difference. Condition 1 might be met if the cracker were swapped for cooking, but the dish would taste different, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is asadero cheese, shredded. The USDA entry 'Queso Asadero' is the same cheese under its Spanish name, which guideline B treats as the same food. Shredding is knife or handling work and does not change the match (guideline C). The 360g weight and the '(optional)' note are decoration and do not affect the match (guideline A). Using the USDA cheese in place of the ingredient requires no change to preparation. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried shad, a preserved product that is typically salted or dried and must be rehydrated or cooked differently. The USDA entry is 'Fish, shad, american, raw', which is fresh, uncooked fish. Guideline F lists raw vs processed/dried states as a non-match, and the same logic applies to fresh vs dried herbs. The quantity (400g) and the bone-in descriptor do not change this. Condition 1 fails because dried fish would need soaking or a different cooking method than fresh raw fish. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would notice the difference in texture, appearance, and flavour between dried and fresh shad.

The ingredient is cooked somen noodles, a Japanese wheat noodle, served cooked. The USDA entry 'Noodles, japanese, somen, cooked' is the same food under the same state (cooked). Weight prefix is ignored per guideline A. The match is the same food with the same preparation state, so it could be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Farina is a milled wheat product, and Cream of Wheat is a branded farina. The instant variety of farina is the same product as the USDA entry 'Cereals, CREAM OF WHEAT, instant, dry'. Guideline B treats regional, culinary, and trade names of the same food as matches, and guideline G accepts a branded entry of the same plain product type. The USDA entry is dry and uncooked, which matches farina as bought, and it adds no flavouring or modification. Using it would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is iceberg lettuce. The USDA entry 'Lettuce, iceberg, raw' is the same food in its uncooked form. The quantity (30g) is ignored per guideline A. 'Chilled' describes handling and storage, which guideline C says does not change the match. Condition 1: the lettuce can replace the ingredient in the same preparation, since no cooking method is involved. Condition 2: a diner would see and taste the same iceberg lettuce, with no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain blue cheese (250g; the quantity is ignored). The USDA entry 'Cheese, blue' is the same food under its standard name, with no modifier such as reduced fat, sodium, or added flavour. Blue cheese is normally sold and used as is, so the match is the standard default version. It can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a generic electrolyte sport beverage. The USDA entry is a sports drink, a branded example of the same product type (guideline G: a branded entry of the same plain product type = yes). It does not specify a flavour, sweetener variant or modified version, so it is not a modified product (guideline D). Condition 1: a sports drink can be poured or added in place of an electrolyte sport beverage without changing any preparation step. Condition 2: both are the same category of flavoured, sweetened, electrolyte-containing drink, so a diner would not reasonably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance attributable to the category. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried feijoa, a different fruit from papaya. Feijoa has a distinct aromatic, tart-sweet flavour, while papaya is mild and sweet. The ingredient is also dried, so it is dehydrated and chewy, whereas the USDA entry is raw, fresh, soft fruit. Using papaya would change the flavour, texture and appearance of the dish, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 (same food under another name) is not met, and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) fails.

The ingredient is quince. The USDA entry 'Quinces, raw' is the same fruit in its uncooked state. The weight '200g' is decoration and is ignored. 'Peeled' is knife/handling work, which per guideline C does not change the match. The fruit is a plain, unmodified product, so no modified-version issue arises. Condition 1: the quince can replace the ingredient as an optional garnish without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would see and taste the same raw quince, peeled or not, so nothing noticeable differs. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is baked beans (navy or haricot beans in a sweet tomato and molasses sauce), heated. The USDA entry is chili with beans in a microwavable bowl, which is a different dish: chili has a spiced, chili-pepper-based sauce, often with meat, and is not the same product as baked beans. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in flavour (smoky, spicy chili versus sweet, tomato-molasses baked beans) and in appearance and texture (chunks of meat and chili sauce versus beans in a thick sauce). The match is not the same food under another name, and the difference is not a trivial descriptor, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is spiny lobster, and the USDA entry is Crustaceans, spiny lobster, mixed species, raw. These are the same food: the USDA entry is the spiny lobster species group, and the ingredient names no cooking or processing state, so it is presumed raw like the match. The leading 230g is decoration and is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same raw food and the recipe handles it the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the food is the same species group in the same raw state. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is walleye fillets, already cooked. The USDA entry is the same fish (walleye) in the same cooked state. The only extra detail is the cooking method, 'dry heat'. The ingredient does not specify a method, so a cooked walleye fillet is the standard default for this item. Using the dry-heat entry does not change how the dish is prepared, because the fish is already cooked and needs no further cooking step (condition 1). The species, state and cooked texture match, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance (condition 2). The quantity (250g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is dried Monterey Jack powder, a dehydrated, powdered form of the cheese. The USDA entry 'Cheese, monterey' is the standard solid cheese. Guideline F rejects a different state (dried vs fresh/solid). Substituting the block cheese would change the dish's preparation: the powder dissolves, disperses, or blends in a way that solid cheese does not, and the ingredient cannot be swapped without altering the mix's texture and concentration. A diner would also notice differences in texture and appearance, and the flavour would be more concentrated in the powder. The match is the same cheese in a different state, not the same food under another name, so it fails both conditions.

The ingredient is a refried bean spread, essentially refried beans in spreadable form. The USDA entry is 'Bean dip, made with refried beans', a prepared dip that uses refried beans as a base. Refried beans are not the same food as a bean dip. The dip is a blended product that typically adds seasonings and other components, and its additives are not specified in the entry. Under guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend containing it is not substitutable. Condition 1 (same preparation) may hold, since both are spread or dip onto food, but condition 2 is doubtful: a diner could plausibly notice differences in flavour and texture from the added components and the dip's form. The match is therefore not reliably substitutable.

The ingredient is reduced-sodium smoked bacon, presented as a raw ingredient to be cooked as part of the recipe. The USDA entry matches on reduced sodium (guideline D: a modified ingredient matches the modified entry) and on the generic 'NS as to fresh, smoked or cured' wording, which covers smoked bacon. However, the USDA entry is 'cooked', while the ingredient is an uncooked product. Under guideline F, raw vs cooked is a different state, not a handling difference. Using pre-cooked bacon would change the preparation: the diner would not get the rendering, crisping and fat release that come from cooking raw bacon in the dish, and the texture and appearance would differ. Condition 1 therefore fails, and condition 2 likely fails for the same reason. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is mint chutney, a specific flavoured variety (green, herbal, mint-based). The USDA entry 'Chutney' is the generic category, which covers many types, such as fruit or tomato chutneys, that are not mint-flavoured. This is not the same food under another name (rule B), and the generic entry does not match a flavoured version of the product (rule D). Swapping in a different chutney would change the flavour and appearance of the dish, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is generic powdered creamer, a non-dairy cream substitute sold in its regular form. The USDA entry is 'Cream substitute, powdered, light', which is the same product category but with the 'light' descriptor. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version (here reduced-fat) is not the standard default, and 'light' does not describe how powdered creamer is normally sold. Condition 1 is met, since the product could be swapped in without changing preparation. Condition 2 is not clearly met: a reduced-fat version would likely give a thinner, less rich mouthfeel and a slightly different taste in coffee or the dish, which a diner could notice. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is hydrolyzed soy protein, a dry protein ingredient used as a protein source or flavour enhancer. The USDA entry is soy sauce made from hydrolyzed vegetable protein, a finished liquid condiment. These are different foods, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F rejects a raw or processed source versus a product made from it, and a single ingredient versus a product containing it. Condition 1 fails: soy sauce is a liquid, so using it for 17g of dry protein would change the recipe's moisture, liquid balance and method. Condition 2 also fails: soy sauce adds a salty, savoury, dark-coloured flavour and appearance that a diner would notice. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a pickled egg (whole chicken egg preserved in brine/vinegar, typically with a sour, tangy flavour and a firm, translucent-to-yellow appearance), quartered. The USDA match is 'Egg substitute, powder', a dried, powdered egg-replacement product made from egg white and other ingredients, which must be reconstituted before use. Condition 1: Using powdered egg substitute would require reconstitution and cooking/handling changes; it cannot replace a ready-to-eat quartered pickled egg without altering how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference: no pickled/vinegar flavour, different texture (firm solid white and yolk versus a powder-derived product), and different appearance (no quartered whole-egg look). It is also a different food state (processed powder substitute versus whole egg, pickled). Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is smoked cisco, and the USDA entry is Fish, cisco, smoked. It is the same food, with the same smoked state, so no preparation or flavour difference arises. The 120g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Guideline F's 'plain vs smoked' rule applies only when the ingredient is plain and the match is smoked, which is not the case here. Both conditions hold: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

Almond paste is a processed product made from ground almonds with a large amount of sugar, giving it a smooth, dense, sweet texture. The USDA entry is whole almonds, lightly salted, which are a nut sold whole and salted. Condition 1 fails: whole almonds cannot replace almond paste in a recipe without changing its preparation, since the paste must be ground, mixed, or rolled and whole nuts do not bind or sweeten the way the paste does. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the added sugar and salt and notice the difference in texture. Guideline F applies, since the raw source (almonds) is not the processed ingredient (almond paste). The quantity is ignored, as Guideline A requires.

The ingredient is cream of rice cooked in salted water. The USDA entry is 'Cereals, CREAM OF RICE, cooked with water, with salt', which is the same food (cream of rice) in the same state (cooked) prepared the same way (water plus salt). The leading '12g' is quantity and is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match needs no change to how the dish is prepared, because the cooking method (cooking in salted water) is identical. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference between cream of rice cooked in salted water and the USDA's cream of rice cooked with water and salt. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is corned beef brisket, a brined and cured product, usually sold cooked and sliced. The USDA entry is raw, fresh beef brisket flat half, choice grade, with no curing. Corned beef is made from brisket, but it has been cured in salt, nitrite and spices, which changes its flavour, pink colour and texture. Using raw brisket would require brining and cooking, which alters the preparation, and a diner would notice the difference in taste and appearance. Guideline F rules out a different state (raw vs processed/cured), so condition 1 and condition 2 both fail.

The ingredient is a banana nut whole grain cereal, with the 80g quantity ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry, POST GREAT GRAINS Banana Nut Crunch, is a branded ready-to-eat cereal of that same type: banana nut flavour, whole grain, and a crunch format. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches, and the banana nut flavour is part of the ingredient's own description, not an added modification. Cooking method is unchanged because both are eaten as cereal. Taste, texture and appearance should be close enough that a diner would not reasonably notice a difference between this brand and a generic banana nut whole grain cereal. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 15g of dry chicken bouillon cubes, a concentrated seasoning that is dissolved in water during cooking. The USDA entry is a prepared soup: chicken broth or bouillon made up with water, already in liquid form. Condition 1: the match would change how the dish is prepared. The cubes are added as a dry, concentrated solid, so swapping in a ready liquid broth would add a different volume of liquid and alter the dissolving step, and the 15g quantity of prepared broth contains far less seasoning solids than 15g of cubes. Per guideline F, a different state (dry concentrate vs. prepared liquid) is not substitutable. Condition 2: the dish's saltiness and flavour intensity and its liquid balance would differ, and a diner could notice a weaker or more diluted flavour. Because condition 1 fails, and condition 2 is also doubtful, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried longan, and the USDA entry is 'Longans, dried', which is the same food under the same state. The quantity is irrelevant. Dried longan is the product as normally bought, so using the USDA entry would not change the preparation. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because they are the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a plain honey mustard dressing, which is normally sold as a regular, full-fat product. The USDA match is specifically the fat-free version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced or fat-free modified version is not a match. Fat-free dressings also use different formulation (added thickeners, gums and sweeteners, and no oil), so the texture, mouthfeel and flavour differ from the regular dressing. Condition 1 is not met because swapping in a different formulation changes how the dressing behaves in the dish, and condition 2 is not met because a diner would likely notice the thinner, less rich texture and altered flavour. The quantity (200g) is irrelevant.

The ingredient is pickled tabasco peppers, a specific pepper cultivar (Capsicum frutescens) with its own heat level and flavour profile. The USDA entry 'Peppers, hot, pickled' is a generic hot-pepper entry, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Tabasco is a sibling variety with a different taste, which guideline F treats as not substitutable. Condition 1 is arguably met since the pickled pepper could be swapped in without changing preparation. Condition 2 likely fails: a diner could notice a difference in heat, sharpness and flavour, because the generic entry may reflect different varieties such as jalapeno or cherry peppers. Since the flavour difference would be noticeable, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is bottom round steak, braised, with fat trimmed. The USDA entry is bottom round steak, braised, trimmed to 0" fat, so it is the same cut in the same cooked state. Trimming is handling that the recipe already does, so it does not change the match (Guideline C). The 'choice' grade is a standard default for a plain beef cut, and 'separable lean and fat' describes the cut's composition, with trimming to 0" fat matching 'fat trimmed'. The quantity is ignored (Guideline A). Condition 1: the braised steak can replace the ingredient without changing the preparation, since both are already cooked and braised. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cut prepared the same way with the same fat content. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is plain 'sour cherries', which most recipes take as fresh. The USDA match is canned sour cherries in light syrup, including the liquid. Condition 1: canned fruit cannot be swapped in without changing the preparation. The recipe would need draining, the added syrup changes the liquid balance, and the fruit is already cooked and softened, so the handling differs. Condition 2: a diner would notice. Canned cherries are softer, less firm, and carry a sweet syrupy flavour that fresh sour cherries lack, and they look different. Guideline F rules out a different state (fresh vs processed) and a different packing medium (light syrup). Guideline D's point that canned fruit is normally in syrup does not apply, because the plain ingredient is fresh fruit, not canned fruit. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is smoked cheddar, sliced. The USDA match is Cheese, cheddar, sharp, sliced. Condition 1: Sliced is a knife-work descriptor that does not change the match, so the form is compatible. Sharp cheddar is a flavour/age variety, but the key issue is the smoked treatment. Guideline F states that a plain ingredient versus a smoked, toasted or roasted version is a different state and not substitutable. Smoking changes the flavour and appearance (darker surface, smoky aroma and taste), so a diner would notice. The USDA entry is plain sharp cheddar with no smoke, so it would alter flavour. Condition 2 therefore fails as well: a diner would taste the smoky difference. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is yellow squash, which in US retail usually means straightneck or crookneck summer squash. The USDA match is 'Squash, summer, scallop, raw', which refers to scallop or patty pan squash. Both are summer squash, but they are distinct varieties rather than the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1: the raw match could be swapped in and cooked the same way, since both are soft-fleshed summer squash. Condition 2: scallop squash has a flattened, disc-shaped body with scalloped edges, while yellow squash is elongated or curved. A diner would notice the difference in appearance when the squash is sliced or served, and the flavour and texture are also not identical. Guideline F covers sibling varieties that differ in taste or appearance. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is prunes, which are dried plums. The USDA entry 'Plums, dried (prunes), uncooked' names prunes explicitly, so it is the same food under its standard name (guideline B). The ingredient is already the dried product, so the match's dried state is the same as what a shopper buys. The entry is 'uncooked', which matches the plain ingredient, and the 75g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace prunes in the recipe without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same fruit. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is amaranth flour, and the USDA entry is 'Flour, amaranth', which is the same plain product under the same name. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the recipe without changing preparation, since it is used by weight in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same flour. The 150g quantity is irrelevant. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is warm flour tortillas, a thin unleavened flatbread made from wheat flour, fat, water and salt, typically soft and pliable. The USDA match is bread stuffing, a seasoned, dry or moist crumb mixture usually made from bread cubes or crumbs with herbs, celery, onion and fat. Condition 1: Stuffing is a loose, seasoned crumb product, not a flatbread sheet or wrap. Using it in place of tortillas would change how the dish is prepared (it cannot be folded, rolled, or warmed as a wrap or used to scoop), so the preparation changes. Condition 2: A diner would readily notice the difference in texture (soft, pliable, chewy flatbread versus crumbly, seasoned stuffing), flavour (plain wheat versus herbed, savoury stuffing seasoning) and appearance. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is queso fresco, a fresh, crumbly, mildly salty Mexican cheese; the leading weight (90g) is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Queso Fresco' is the same named product, so it is literally the same food (guideline B). Queso fresco is a plain, standard product, and the USDA entry names no modification such as reduced fat or sodium, so it is the default version (guideline D). Using it does not change how the dish is prepared, since it is used as a crumbled or sprinkled cheese, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain savoy cabbage, shredded, which is a single raw vegetable. The USDA entry 'Cabbage salad, NFS' is a prepared salad, which is typically coleslaw-style shredded cabbage tossed with dressing (mayonnaise or vinegar-based, often with carrot, sugar, and seasoning). Condition 1: Using it in place of plain shredded cabbage would change the dish's preparation, since the dressing and other components are added and the cabbage is no longer just a raw ingredient to be handled in the recipe. Condition 2: A diner would notice the taste (dressed, seasoned, sweet or tangy), texture (softened or wilted by dressing), and appearance (coated, with added components). Guideline F rejects a single ingredient matched to a product containing it, and the rule that a plain ingredient mapped to a modified version is not a match also applies. The entry is not the same food under another name. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is individually wrapped yellow cheese slices, which in practice are American-style process cheese slices (sold as 'singles'). The USDA entry is 'Cheese, pasteurized process cheese food or product, American, singles', which describes that same product type under the standard USDA name. Condition 1: the entry can replace the ingredient without any change to preparation, since both are used the same way (sliced, melted, layered, eaten as-is). Condition 2: the USDA entry describes the default product a shopper buys under this name, so flavour, texture and appearance would match and a diner would not notice a difference. The quantity (50g) is ignored per the guidelines. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is palm kernel oil, a specific fat derived from the kernel of the palm fruit, which is distinct from palm oil (derived from the fruit pulp) and from other oils. The USDA match is microwave popcorn, a finished snack product that is flavoured (butter flavour) and made with palm oil. Condition 1 fails: the match is not a fat that could be used in place of palm kernel oil in preparing a dish; it is a finished popcorn product, and a fat swap would not be a like-for-like substitution in cooking. It also differs in kind: the match is a blend of popcorn, flavouring and fat, not a single oil, and per guideline F, a single ingredient vs a product containing it is not substitutable. Additionally, palm oil is a different fat from palm kernel oil (different fatty acid profile, taste and melting behaviour), which is a further mismatch under guideline F. Condition 2 also fails: a diner eating popcorn would certainly notice a difference from eating a plain fat, and the flavour and texture of the product would change. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is a fresh pork loin chop, which is a cut from the loin. The USDA entry is 'Pork, fresh, loin, top loin (chops), boneless, separable lean and fat, raw', which names the same cut (top loin chops), in fresh, uncooked form. The 'boneless' and 'separable lean and fat' descriptors reflect how this cut is normally sold and do not alter the food. The ingredient does not specify bone-in, so the standard boneless default applies. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient with the same cooking method, since it is the same raw chop. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cut with the usual fat content. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is soft white wheat, a grain sold as whole wheat kernels. The USDA entry 'Wheat, soft white' names the same food with the same descriptor, so it is the same product rather than a sibling variety. The weight (300g) is ignored per guideline A. Both are uncooked dry grain, so the cooking method is unchanged (condition 1). The match is the identical food under the same name, so a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance (condition 2). Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is dried peach, and the USDA entry 'Peach, dried' is the same food under a near-identical name, so it is the same product rather than a sibling, modified, or differently processed version. Guideline B and the dried-fruit example in guideline D (dried peaches -> Peaches, dehydrated, sulfured) support a match. Condition 1: the entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are dried peach pieces used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same dried peach. The leading '130g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a plain baguette, a French bread loaf. The USDA entry 'Bread, french or vienna' names the same product family: lean, crusty, yeasted French-style bread, which is what a baguette is. Under guideline B, this is the same food under a regional or culinary name, and under guideline D a plain ingredient maps to its standard default version. The parenthetical 'includes sourdough' widens the entry to cover sourdough variants, but it does not make the entry a different product. Condition 1: a baguette can be substituted without changing preparation, since it is used as bread in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance between a baguette and french/vienna bread, since they are essentially the same bread type. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cooked peas and carrots (a plain cooked mixed vegetable side). The USDA entry 'Peas and carrots, cooked, NS as to form' is the same food with the same components, cooked, with no added fat, sauce or flavouring specified. Quantity (30g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are already cooked and need no further cooking method change. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, as it is the same cooked product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is allspice, a whole or ground spice (Pimenta dioica berries) used for flavouring. The USDA match is white bread, commercially prepared, a baked bread product. These are entirely different foods: allspice is a spice with a pungent, warm, clove-cinnamon-like flavour, while white bread is a starch-based baked good. Condition 1 fails: bread cannot replace allspice in a recipe without changing how the dish is prepared, since it adds bulk, texture and structure instead of spice. Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice the absence of allspice flavour and the presence of bread texture and appearance. Guideline F (whole vs ground spice, and different foods generally) and the general rule that a different food is not substitutable both apply. The quantity of 30g is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is cannellini beans, and the USDA entry is the same food: cannellini beans in dry form. Under guideline C, 'dry' for beans is the dried legume as bought, and the quantity is ignored. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient as its standard default version, and the dried bean is the plain form of this legume. Condition 1 is met on the assumption that the recipe uses the bean as the plain ingredient; if the recipe expected canned beans, soaking and cooking would be needed, which would change preparation. Condition 2 is met because the same bean, once cooked, has the same taste, texture and appearance. Both conditions hold under the annotation rules, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is boneless duck breast, which in ordinary cooking means domestic duck (e.g., Pekin or Muscovy). The USDA entry is wild duck breast, meat only, raw. Guideline B covers regional or trade names for the same food, but wild duck is a different food from domestic duck, not a different name for it. Wild duck is typically smaller, leaner, darker, and firmer, with a noticeably gamier, stronger flavour than farmed duck. Guideline F says a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable. Condition 1 might hold, since the cut is the same and it could be cooked the same way. Condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice the stronger flavour, the darker and firmer texture, and the richer colour. Because the second condition is not met, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is yellow summer squash, a distinct cultivar of summer squash. The USDA match is zucchini, a different summer squash variety with green skin. Guideline B treats regional names for the same food as equivalent (for example, courgette and zucchini), but yellow summer squash and zucchini are sold as separate varieties, not as one food under two names. Guideline F says a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable. Yellow squash is typically a little sweeter and more delicate, and its yellow skin is visible in the finished dish. Condition 1 is likely met, since the same knife work and cooking method would apply. Condition 2 fails because a diner could see the yellow skin and flesh and would likely notice a difference in appearance and some difference in taste. Both conditions must hold, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a plain 'soy protein concentrate' with no production method specified. The USDA entry names one specific processing route, acid washing, which is a sibling variant of the concentrate. Soy protein concentrates are made by acid wash, alcohol wash, or water/heat treatment, and these routes differ in flavour, solubility, and binding or texture. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to a modified or specially processed version as not substitutable, and guideline F treats a different processing state as a different food. The entry is the same general product category, but it is a specific processed variant that may change how the dish tastes or behaves, and the diner could notice the difference. Condition 2 is therefore not reliably met.

Moringa oleifera pods are the same food as drumstick pods. 'Drumstick' is a common regional name for the moringa pod, so under guideline B this is a same-food, different-name match. The USDA entry 'Drumstick pods, raw' is the uncooked pod, which is the plain form of the ingredient, so no state change applies (guideline C). The leading '30g' quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the pods can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same pod. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a smoked vodka sauce. The USDA entry is a standard vodka sauce with tomatoes and cream, with no smoking mentioned. Condition 1 (no change in preparation) is arguably met, since both are sauces used the same way. Condition 2 fails: smoking adds a distinct smoky flavour and aroma that a diner would notice. Guideline F explicitly says plain vs smoked is a different state and not substitutable. The quantity (150g) is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is fresh pork trotters (pig feet). The USDA entry is pickled pork hocks, which differs on two counts. First, it is a different cut: hocks are the leg joint above the foot, while trotters are the foot itself. Second, it is a cured, brined product with a salty, tangy flavour, unlike fresh trotters. Condition 1 fails because the dish would be prepared differently. Its brining and salting would change the cooking method and seasoning, and it would not be a straight swap. Condition 2 fails because a diner would taste the cured, pickled flavour and see different cut and texture. Per guideline F, a different cut of meat and a processed or cured state are not substitutable.

The ingredient is a generic buttery round snack cracker, the style of cracker Ritz represents. The USDA entry 'Crackers, butter (Ritz)' is a buttery round snack cracker, so it is the same product type under a brand name. Guideline G treats a branded entry of the same plain product type as a match. Condition 1: the crackers can be used as-is, eaten or crumbled, with no change to cooking method. Condition 2: a buttery round cracker of this type would not show a noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance from the Ritz-style entry. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is minced shrimp, meaning raw or cooked shrimp flesh that has been chopped or ground at home. Under guideline C, the knife work does not change the food. The USDA entry 'Shrimp, cake or patty' is a formed, processed product that typically contains binders, fillers, seasonings and often breading, so it is not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails: using a pre-formed patty in place of minced shrimp changes preparation, since the patty already has a shape, binders and seasoning and would not be handled as loose minced meat. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the added binders and seasonings and notice a firmer, more uniform, processed texture rather than minced shrimp. Guideline F (single ingredient vs product containing it) applies. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is papaya (a fruit, typically eaten raw, sweet, orange-fleshed with a distinct musky flavour and soft texture). The USDA match is Green beans, raw, which is a different vegetable entirely (legume pod, crisp, grassy/vegetal flavour, green colour). Condition 1 fails: green beans cannot replace papaya without changing the dish's preparation, since papaya is used as a fruit (fresh, in salads, smoothies, desserts) and green beans would be a vegetable cooked or served differently. Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (sweet vs grassy), texture (soft flesh vs crisp pod) and appearance (orange flesh vs green pods). Not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is venison steak, a plain cut of venison. The USDA entry 'Venison, steak' names the same food and cut with no state descriptor (no raw/cooked, frozen, or processed qualifier), so it is the generic food. Under guideline E, a generic entry with no state matches fresh or plain versions. The leading '200g' is decoration (guideline A). Cooking method is unchanged, since the same steak is prepared the same way, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance because it is the same meat and cut.

The ingredient is unsweetened soy milk, which is the plain, unsweetened product. The USDA match is 'Soy milk, sweetened', which is a sweetened version. Guideline D treats sweetened versus unsweetened as a modification, and a plain-to-sweetened swap is not acceptable. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the milk could be poured into the same dish, but the sweetener changes the flavour. Condition 2 fails because a diner would likely taste the added sugar, particularly in savoury dishes or in sauces and batters where unsweetened milk is expected. The ingredient requests the unsweetened version and the match is the sweetened one, so the entry does not match.

1. The ingredient is an annatto-coriander seasoning packet, a dry blend whose named components are annatto and coriander. The USDA entry is a dry seasoning mix named for the same two components (coriander and annatto), so it names the same product type with the same listed components. 2. Both are dry, ready-to-use seasoning blends, so the cooking method would not change: the packet is added to the dish the same way. 3. Taste and appearance: annatto gives colour and coriander gives flavour in both, so a diner would not expect a visible or flavour difference. The USDA sazon category may carry additional standard sazon ingredients such as salt, cumin, or garlic. Since the packet's own description names only annatto and coriander, this uncertainty is noted, but the USDA entry is the same product type with the same named components, so it is treated as an acceptable match. 4. Quantity (10g) is ignored per the guidelines. Both conditions are met.

Condition 1: The ingredient is mole sauce that has been frozen and thawed. The USDA entry 'Mole sauce' names the same dish with no state descriptor (not dried, not canned, not cooked-vs-raw specific), so it is the generic food. Mole is normally served as a prepared sauce, so it can be used in its place without changing the preparation. Condition 2: Mole is a mixed sauce, and freezing and thawing it does not visibly or noticeably change its taste, texture, or appearance in the dish. A diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met, consistent with guideline E (frozen-then-thawed matches the plain entry when freezing does not show).

1) Ingredient: toasted baguette slices. It is a French bread, already toasted, cut into slices. 2) USDA entry: 'Bread, french or vienna, toasted', which covers French-style breads in toasted form. Baguette is a French bread, so this is the same food category, and the toasted state matches. 3) Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation.
