Slices are handled as the recipe requires, and cutting does not change the match (guideline C). 4) Condition 2: a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance between toasted baguette and toasted French/Vienna bread. The entry's explicit 'includes sourdough' wording shows USDA treats the entry as a broad French-bread category, not a single sibling variety with a distinct taste. The residual difference (crust and crumb density between baguette and other French or Vienna loaves) is minor and within the category. Both conditions are met.

Ingredient: red leaf lettuce, used as an optional garnish. USDA match: 'Lettuce, red leaf, raw'. Condition 1: The match is literally the same food (red leaf lettuce), raw, which is how a garnish would normally be used. Substituting it would not change how the dish is prepared; the quantity (40g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2: A diner would see and taste the same red leaf lettuce; no cooking, flavour change, or processing difference is implied. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a boneless pork chop, which is a cut from the pork loin. The USDA entry is 'Pork, fresh, loin, center loin (chops), boneless, separable lean and fat, raw', which describes the same cut: boneless center loin chops, uncooked. The 'separable lean and fat' descriptor only reflects that the chop is sold with its fat, which is the normal way a boneless pork chop is bought, so it is not a modification. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is raw and the same cut, so any cooking method used for a boneless pork chop applies unchanged. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same cut from the same primal. Both conditions are met. The 115g weight is decoration and is ignored.

1. The ingredient is the generic 'chili pepper' with no colour, variety or state specified. The USDA entry 'Peppers, hot chili, red, raw' is the same food (a raw hot chili pepper), so it matches the plain, default version. 2. The 'red' descriptor does not modify the product; it describes the ripeness and colour of a standard fresh chili that is sold as chili pepper. Since the ingredient does not ask for green or any other variety, the red raw entry is the default match. 3. Cooking method is unchanged: it is raw in both cases, and knife work such as chopping does not alter the match. 4. Flavour and appearance would be essentially the same for the typical unspecified chili pepper. Condition 1 and condition 2 are both met.

The ingredient is plain smoked pepperoni, the standard dry sausage. The USDA entry is a modified version, 'Pepperoni, reduced sodium'. Per guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a reduced-sodium version is not a match, because the recipe does not ask for reduced sodium. Condition 2 also fails: reduced-sodium pepperoni tastes noticeably less salty and can differ in flavour and texture from the regular product. The quantity prefix is ignored. The match therefore fails both conditions.

The ingredient is veal sweetbreads, which come from calves. The USDA match is lamb sweetbread from New Zealand, which comes from sheep. These are different animal species, so this is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Guideline F treats different meat sources as not interchangeable, and the match is raw, so the cooking state is the same. Condition 1 can be argued, since both are offal cooked the same way, but condition 2 fails. Veal sweetbreads are noticeably milder and more delicate, while lamb sweetbreads have a richer, gamier flavour and a different texture, and a diner would likely notice the difference. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain fermented napa cabbage, a single vegetable ingredient. The USDA match 'Cabbage, kimchi' is a seasoned prepared dish. Standard kimchi contains chili powder, garlic, ginger, scallions, and fish sauce or salted seafood, so it is a blend rather than the plain fermented cabbage (guideline F: single ingredient vs. a product containing it). Using kimchi would change the flavour (spicy, savoury, pungent) and appearance (red from chili), and a diner would notice. Condition 2 fails, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain evaporated milk, whose standard default is whole (full-fat) evaporated milk. The USDA match is 'Milk, evaporated, fat free (skim)', a modified low/fat-free version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a fat-free or reduced-fat version is not substitutable. Condition 1: swapping in skim evaporated milk in most recipes can work mechanically, since the cooking method stays the same. Condition 2: the lower fat content changes mouthfeel, creaminess, and richness, especially in custards, sauces, and desserts, so a diner could notice a difference in texture and flavour. Since the match alters the texture and taste of the dish, it fails condition 2.

The ingredient is shredded wheat and bran cereal, a plain ready-to-eat cereal type. The USDA entry, POST Shredded Wheat n' Bran (spoon-size), is a branded version of that same product type with no added flavour or modification. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. Condition 1: the cereal can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: the spoon-size form is the standard way this product is sold, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The 100g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient 'spring onions' is a regional/culinary name for the same vegetable that USDA lists as 'Onions, spring or scallions (includes tops and bulb), raw'. Per guideline B, regional names for the same food count as the same food (scallion -> Onions, spring). The quantity (300g) is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is raw, and the spring onions would be used raw or with only knife work (trimming, chopping), which per guideline C does not change the match. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'Pancake syrup' and the USDA match is 'Pancake syrup', which is the same named product, so it is the literal same food. The 50g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the syrup can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw beef liver. The USDA entry is raw beef liver from New Zealand, a country-of-origin variant of the same food. The quantity (250g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the liver can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are raw and the same cut of the same organ. Condition 2: origin does not change the taste, texture, or appearance of raw beef liver in a way a diner would notice. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried goat milk, a powder. The USDA match is fluid goat milk with added vitamin D, a liquid. Per guideline F, a different physical state (dried vs fluid) is not substitutable. Using fluid milk in place of powder adds a large amount of water and changes the dry-to-wet ratio, so the dish's preparation would change (the recipe would need adjusting for liquid, and the dry ingredients' hydration and texture would differ). The vitamin D fortification is an added modification under guideline D, which further separates it from the plain product. Condition 1 fails because the preparation changes. Condition 2 also likely fails because the texture and moisture of the dish would differ. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain white bread slices used as a garnish, which is normally served untoasted (or prepared as the recipe directs from plain slices). The USDA match is 'Bread, white, toasted', which is a different state. Guideline F explicitly lists 'plain vs toasted' as not substitutable. Toasting changes colour, crispness, and texture, so a diner could notice the difference in appearance and mouthfeel. Also, using toasted bread would alter the preparation (the recipe would need toasting to be applied to plain slices). Condition 1 fails because the preparation changes, and condition 2 fails because taste, texture, and appearance differ. The quantity (150g) is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is canned peas and onions, and the USDA entry is canned peas and onions, so it is the same food under the same name. The USDA wording 'canned, solids and liquids' describes the product as it is normally sold in cans, with its packing liquid, and the ingredient does not ask for drained or solids-only. Neither a different cooking method nor a different flavour, texture or appearance is implied, so the dish would be prepared the same way. Under the guidelines, a canned product matched to its canned USDA entry is the standard default version, and the leading 100g is ignored. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh veal tongue. The USDA entry is veal tongue, raw. It is the same food, and 'raw' matches 'fresh' because the ingredient is uncooked. The weight is decoration and is ignored. 'Variety meats and by-products' is only the USDA category label and does not change the product. Condition 1: the same cooking method applies, since the tongue is simply prepared as the recipe directs. Condition 2: a diner would see and taste the same veal tongue, so there is no difference in taste, texture or appearance.

The ingredient is 200g cold chocolate milk, a flavoured milk beverage. The USDA match is 'Bread, white, commercially prepared', which is a baked bread product, a completely different food category. Condition 1 fails: chocolate milk cannot be substituted for bread without changing the dish's preparation (it is a liquid, not a baked solid, and cannot be used as a bread product). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice a difference in taste, texture and appearance between chocolate milk and white bread. The match is not the same food under another name, and no guideline supports accepting it.

The ingredient is custard apple, and the USDA entry is literally named 'Custard-apple, (bullock's-heart), raw'. The USDA entry uses the same common name, with bullock's-heart as a regional alias, so this is the same food under another name (guideline B). The entry is raw, which matches a fresh, unprocessed fruit. The leading '30g' is only quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Nothing in the ingredient implies cooking, processing, or a modified version, so the dish would be prepared the same way. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance between the same fruit and its USDA entry. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sweet pickle slices (cucumbers pickled in a sweet brine, served cold, crisp and tangy-sweet). The USDA match 'Pickles, fried' is a breaded and deep-fried product, a different preparation. Condition 1: substituting fried pickles would change the dish's preparation, since the pickles would need to be fried, breaded and cooked rather than used as a raw pickled condiment or ingredient. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference; fried pickles have a crunchy battered coating, hot greasy texture, and altered flavour versus a sweet, vinegary, crisp pickle slice. The match is not the same food under another name, and it differs in state (fried vs pickled raw product). Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is a fruit and cream flavour instant oatmeal, sold dry as packaged. The USDA entry is the same product: Quaker Instant Oatmeal, fruit and cream variety, dry. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient directly, since both are the same dry packaged product and the 200g weight is ignored per guideline A. The 'dry' descriptor matches the product as bought (guideline C). Guideline G treats a branded entry of the same product type as a match, and this is the same flavour variety, not a modified version. Condition 2: the diner would taste, texture and see the same oatmeal, because it is the same variety. No difference in taste, texture or appearance is expected. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is whole egg that has already been cooked, with no specific cooking method stated. The USDA entry is 'Egg, whole, cooked, NS as to cooking method', which is the same food in the same state (cooked whole egg), with the cooking method left unspecified. Under the guidelines, a plain ingredient matched to its standard default version is a match, and the quantity prefix '250g' is ignored. Condition 1: the entry is already cooked whole egg, so it can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: the ingredient does not specify a cooking method, so a cooked whole egg of the generic type is indistinguishable in taste, texture and appearance from the entry as the recipe describes it. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is beef tripe, which is the edible stomach lining of cattle (a variety meat, typically sold pre-cleaned and often pre-cooked or blanched). The USDA match is beef tenderloin steak, raw, a different cut of muscle meat from the loin. Guideline F explicitly states that a different cut of meat is not substitutable. Tripe has a distinctive rubbery, spongy texture and a different flavour and appearance from tenderloin, and it is normally prepared by long simmering or specific cleaning, so the cooking method would change and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails. The quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is wild-caught catfish fillets, with no species specified. The USDA entry is specifically farmed channel catfish, raw. Condition 1: the cooking method would not change, since both are raw catfish fillets, so the preparation could stay the same. Condition 2: wild and farmed catfish differ in taste and texture. Farmed catfish is typically milder and fattier, with a more consistent texture. Wild catfish usually has a leaner, firmer flesh and a more pronounced, sometimes earthy flavour. A diner could plausibly notice the difference, and the ingredient explicitly specifies wild-caught while the match explicitly specifies farmed. Because the sourcing is a stated attribute that changes flavour and texture, the match is not a same-food equivalent under guideline F (a different variety/sourcing with a different taste is not substitutable). Condition 2 is not met.

The ingredient is smoked chicken meat (a whole-cut or piece of poultry), frozen and then thawed. The USDA entry is a sausage product made from a blend of chicken, beef and pork, skinless and smoked. Under guideline F, a single ingredient is not substitutable for a blend or product containing it. The sausage is also a processed, emulsified or ground product, so the texture would differ from solid smoked chicken. Condition 1 fails because the dish would be prepared differently, since sausage is not a drop-in for chicken pieces. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the change in texture, appearance and flavour, including the added beef and pork. The frozen/thawed state (guideline E) does not change this conclusion.

The ingredient is cured corned beef brisket, and the USDA entry is also cured corned beef brisket, so the base food is the same. Two details prevent a clear match. First, the ingredient asks for 'lean' brisket, but the USDA entry does not specify lean and is the default cut with its usual fat. Fat content visibly and texturally changes the sliced meat, and the entry is not the lean-specific version the recipe requests. Second, the ingredient gives no cooking state, and commercial corned beef brisket is often sold raw and cooked in the recipe. The entry is specifically 'cooked', so if the recipe expects raw cured brisket, the preparation would change. Because the lean specification is not met and the cooking state is uncertain, a diner could notice a difference in texture and appearance, so condition 2 is not reliably satisfied.

The ingredient is smoked beef tenderloin, a cured and smoked product. The USDA entry is raw beef tenderloin steak, trimmed, with no smoking. The cut matches (tenderloin), but guideline F explicitly says a plain item is not substitutable for a smoked one (plain vs smoked). Smoking changes flavour, colour and texture, so a diner would notice. Condition 1 fails because the dish's preparation would change, and condition 2 fails because the taste and appearance differ. The 365g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is basil pesto sauce. The USDA entry is a branded ready-to-serve basil pesto sauce, which is the same food under a brand name. Guideline G accepts a branded entry of the same plain product type. The 'ready-to-serve' descriptor just describes how pesto is normally sold, not a modification such as reduced fat or added flavour. Condition 1: the pesto could replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same basil pesto. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is toasted white bread, and the USDA entry is 'Bread, white, toasted', which is the same food with the same processing state. The leading '355g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Guideline F says plain bread is not interchangeable with toasted bread, but here the ingredient itself specifies toasted, so the matching toasted entry is the correct version (the same logic as guideline D). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the bread is already toasted and needs no further cooking. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same toasted white bread.

The ingredient is fresh cannellini beans (white kidney beans, Phaseolus vulgaris, a sibling cultivar of the common bean). The USDA match is 'Kidney beans, NFS', which is a generic kidney bean entry (typically red kidney beans, a different variety with a darker colour, thicker skin, and a different flavour and texture). Cannellini beans are a distinct variety with a creamy, delicate interior and a pale appearance; a diner would notice the red/dark colour of kidney beans in the dish and the different texture and taste. Per guideline F, a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable. The 'fresh' state is also not clearly matched by the NFS entry, though the main issue is the variety difference in appearance and flavour. Condition 1 might be met by simple swapping in preparation, but condition 2 fails because appearance and taste would differ noticeably.

The ingredient is hydrolyzed soy protein, which is soy protein that has been broken down by enzymatic or acid hydrolysis into peptides and amino acids. The USDA match is soy protein isolate, which is intact, non-hydrolyzed protein. These are different processed states of the same source, so under guideline F (raw source vs processed ingredient, different state) they are not the same food. Condition 1: hydrolysis changes solubility, dispersibility and how the protein behaves in liquids and heat, so substituting isolate would alter how the dish is prepared (for example, it may not dissolve or disperse the same way, and it lacks the hydrolysate's functional behaviour). Condition 2: hydrolyzed soy protein contributes a distinct savoury or umami flavour and a different mouthfeel, and isolate would change taste and texture, which a diner could notice. Guideline D also treats a plain ingredient mapped to a modified version as a non-match. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is pork rinds, which are the fried or puffed crispy pork skin snack (or pork rind used as a crunchy topping/coating). The USDA match is 'Pork, cured, salt pork, raw', which is raw cured fatback/salt pork, a fatty cut of pork belly/back fat that is salt-cured and uncooked. This is not the same food: pork rinds are the skin, typically cooked/fried or puffed to a crisp, light, airy texture, while salt pork is raw, dense, fatty cured meat. Substituting would change the texture (crunchy vs. fatty and dense), the preparation (it would need cooking/frying to resemble pork rinds), and the flavour and appearance. A diner would notice the difference. Per guideline F, a different cut/product and raw vs. processed state are not substitutable. Quantity is ignored.

The ingredient is a Valencia orange, a fruit and a specific sweet orange variety. The USDA match, 'Orange Blossom', does not name the fruit. An orange blossom is the flower of the orange tree, or a flower-derived product, not the edible fruit. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Even treating it as a different orange product, it would be a different food with a different flavour, texture and appearance. Condition 1 fails because the fruit cannot be swapped for a blossom without changing the dish. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice eating a flower product instead of orange segments or juice. The leading '75g' weight is ignored per guideline A.

Ingredient is 100g ground chicken, a plain raw ground chicken product. USDA match is 'Chicken, ground', which is the generic ground chicken entry (no cooking state or modification stated, so it matches the raw/default ground chicken). Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: ground chicken can be used in place of ground chicken with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain chestnuts, weight ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Chestnuts', the same food with the same name and no added state, processing, or flavour descriptor. Under guideline E, an entry naming only the food is the generic food and matches fresh or plain versions. Guideline B confirms the same food under the same name is a match. Chestnuts can be used in place of the ingredient without any change in preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is rye bread, and the USDA entry is 'Bread, rye'. These name the same food under the same plain product type, with no added flavour, modification, or state change. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since bread is used in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. The 100g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dry oat bran, which is uncooked and used as a dry ingredient in a recipe. The USDA entry is 'Oat bran cereal, cooked', which is already cooked and prepared as a hot cereal. Condition 1 fails: substituting cooked oat bran for dry oat bran changes how the dish is prepared, since the cooking step would be skipped or altered, and the added moisture would change the batter or dough. Condition 2 also fails: the cooked product has a different texture, moisture and appearance from the dry grain, and a diner could notice the difference. Guideline F explicitly lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable.

The ingredient is beet greens (the leafy tops of Beta vulgaris, a leafy green in the chard/spinach family), chopped. The USDA match is green peas, raw, which are the immature seeds of Pisum sativum, a legume. These are different foods, not regional names for the same item, and not an inner part or cut of the same vegetable. Condition 1 fails: beet greens are cooked as a leafy green (sauteed, braised, wilted), whereas green peas would be cooked as a pod-seed legume with a different method and timing, and the dish would be prepared differently. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would readily notice the difference in flavour (earthy, slightly bitter greens versus sweet, starchy peas), texture (tender leaves and stems versus firm, round seeds), and appearance (dark leafy strands versus small green spheres). Chopping does not alter the match. Therefore neither condition is met.

Textured soy protein is the dry, dehydrated product that is commonly sold as textured vegetable protein (TVP), made from defatted soy flour or concentrate. The USDA entry 'Textured vegetable protein, dry' names the same product under a trade or regional name, so under guideline B it is the same food. Condition 1: it is dry, so it can be rehydrated and cooked in the same way with no change to the preparation method. Condition 2: the dish would taste and feel the same, since both are the same dehydrated soy product, and no visible or textural difference would be expected. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh dinner rolls, a plain bread product. The USDA entry 'Rolls, dinner, wheat' names the same product type (dinner rolls) and carries no preparation, modification, or additive descriptor beyond the standard wheat-flour base that dinner rolls normally use. Guideline B and D treat the same food under the same name, in its default version, as a match. The 75g weight is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the roll can replace the ingredient in the dish with no change to preparation, since it is a ready-to-serve roll with no cooking step introduced. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same kind of roll in its standard form. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is 100g of frozen ground bison that has been thawed. The USDA entry is 'Bison, ground, raw', which is the same food (ground bison) in its uncooked state. Per guideline E, frozen meat that is normally cooked and whose freezing is not visible matches the fresh/raw entry; the thawed state does not change how the meat is cooked or how it looks or tastes once cooked. The leading quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the raw ground bison can be used in place of thawed ground bison with the same preparation (browning, forming patties, etc.). Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the freezing and thawing are not discernible in the cooked dish. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chowchow relish, drained. The USDA entry is chowchow pickle with cauliflower, onion and mustard, sweet, which is the same food under a more specific name. Chowchow is a relish of cauliflower, onion and mustard seed in a pickling brine, and the standard American version is commonly sweet, so the 'sweet' descriptor reflects how the product is normally sold rather than a modification. 'Drained' is handling that does not change the match. The quantity (105g) is ignored. The dish would not be prepared differently, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance.

The ingredient is roast beef, meaning cooked, roasted beef, which is commonly made from round cuts such as tip round, top round, or eye of round. The USDA entry is cooked, roasted tip round beef, so it names the same product (roasted beef) with the same components. The 'trimmed to 0" fat' and 'separable lean and fat' wording describes trimming, which is handling rather than a different food, and roast beef strips are typically lean. Condition 1: the match could replace the ingredient with no change to preparation, since both are already cooked and roasted and need only cutting into strips. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because both are cooked, roasted beef with similar lean appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is wasabi powder, a dry ground product that is normally mixed with water to form a paste before use. The USDA match is wasabi paste, a ready-to-use prepared condiment. Condition 1: substituting paste for powder changes preparation, because the cook would skip the mixing step, and the amounts would not translate directly since paste is wet and contains different proportions of ingredients. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice differences in texture (smooth paste versus a powder-derived mixture), moisture and potentially flavour intensity and additives. Guideline F lists a different state (dried or ground versus prepared) as not substitutable. The quantity prefix is ignored. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is uncooked dinner roll dough, a raw, unbaked yeast dough that would be shaped and baked as part of the dish. The USDA entry 'Rolls, dinner, sweet' describes finished, baked sweet rolls. Condition 1 fails: substituting baked rolls for raw dough changes the preparation, because the dough would not rise or bake. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice baked, sweet rolls in place of raw dough, since the texture, appearance and flavour differ (sweet versus plain dough). The entry is not the same food under another name, and it is not a raw or unbaked form of the product.

The ingredient is plain chicken wings, which are a raw, unseasoned meat. The USDA entry is 'Chicken wings with hot sauce, from precooked'. Condition 1 fails: the match is precooked, so using it would skip the raw cooking the recipe requires, which changes the preparation. Condition 2 also fails: the hot sauce changes the flavour and appearance, and a diner would notice the seasoning and the cooked, sauced exterior. Guideline F rejects raw vs cooked states, and guideline D rejects a plain ingredient mapped to a flavoured version. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh mangosteen, a raw whole fruit. The USDA match is canned mangosteen in syrup pack, a processed product. Condition 1: canned fruit cannot be used in place of fresh fruit without changing preparation. Fresh mangosteen is eaten raw, while the canned version is already cooked or preserved and arrives in liquid, so the handling and use differ. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. The syrup pack adds sweetness, and canning softens the flesh and changes its texture and appearance. Guideline F rules out a different state (raw vs processed) and a different packing medium (syrup pack). The quantity (20g) is irrelevant under guideline A. Neither condition is met.

Napa cabbage is the common culinary name for Chinese cabbage (Brassica rapa, Pekinensis group). The USDA entry 'Cabbage, chinese (pe-tsai), raw' is the same food under a regional/trade name, so guideline B applies. Pe-tsai is the barrel-shaped Chinese cabbage type sold under the same name in most markets. The 'raw' descriptor matches an uncooked ingredient, and the 30g weight is ignored per guideline A. Using it in place of napa cabbage would not change preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Poori is a deep-fried, puffed Indian flatbread, and 'puri' is the same food under an alternate spelling/name, so this is the same food under another name (guideline B). The weight '30g' is ignored (guideline A). The USDA entry names the same product with no modifying state or flavour, so it matches the plain default version (guideline D). Using it in the dish would not change preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is '400g pork and beef sausage'; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Pork and beef sausage', which names the same food with the same components (pork and beef), so it is literally the same product under the same name (guideline B and C/D: the entry names the same product with the same components). No cooking method is implied that the USDA entry would alter, and no modified version (reduced fat, flavoured, etc.) is specified in either the ingredient or the entry. Condition 1: it could replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is añejo cheese, an aged Mexican cheese. The USDA entry 'Queso Anejo, aged Mexican cheese' is the same food under its Spanish name, so under guideline B it is the same product. The quantity (150g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match is the same product, so it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation (grating, crumbling, or sprinkling work the same way). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cheese. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is leftover fajita meat, which is cooked fajita meat that has already been seasoned and prepared. The USDA entry 'Fajita, beef or pork' names the same prepared dish. The ingredient does not specify the protein, so the entry's beef-or-pork scope covers it. Using it in place of the leftovers would not change how the dish is prepared, because it is already cooked and only needs reheating or assembling. The fajita preparation and seasoning are the same in both. Condition 1 is met. For condition 2, a diner would not see a difference in appearance or texture between the leftovers and the USDA fajita meat, since both are the same seasoned fajita preparation. The one unresolved point is whether a diner would taste a beef-versus-pork difference, but the leftover meat's protein is unspecified, so the match is treated as the same dish. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is babassu nut oil, a single plant-derived oil pressed from babassu palm kernels. The USDA entry 'Oil, babassu' names the same product under a shortened name, so it is the same food (guideline B). Condition 1: the oil can be used directly in place of the ingredient at the same weight with no change to preparation, since it is the same fat with the same handling. Condition 2: because it is the same oil, a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The leading '15g' is quantity decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chicken heart that has been simmered. The USDA entry is chicken heart, all classes, cooked, simmered, which is the same food with the same preparation. The weight prefix is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing the preparation, since both are already simmered. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the match describes the same simmered chicken heart. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is 'spoon-size original shredded wheat'. The USDA entry is 'Cereals ready-to-eat, POST, Shredded Wheat, original spoon-size', which names the same product: original spoon-size shredded wheat cereal. The leading '200g' is only a quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches, and the entry adds no flavour or modification. Condition 1: the cereal can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same original spoon-size biscuit. Both conditions are met.

The USDA entry is raw, boneless choice ribeye steak, which matches the cut of beef. The ingredient is specified as smoked, so it is a processed state of the same cut. Guideline F says a different state, including plain versus smoked, is not substitutable. Smoking adds a distinct smoky flavour, changes the colour and surface appearance, and alters the texture of the meat. A diner would notice the difference in taste, so condition 2 fails. Using raw ribeye would also change the preparation, since the smoking step is skipped, so condition 1 fails too. The quantity (500g) is ignored per guideline A.

Canned bamboo shoots come from the young shoots of bamboo grass. Palm hearts come from the inner core of palm trees. These are different plants, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). They also differ in flavour and texture: bamboo shoots are crisper, with a slightly bitter, earthy taste, while palm hearts are softer, milder, and more tender. A diner would likely notice the difference in texture and flavour, and the two are not interchangeable in dishes such as stir-fries where bamboo shoots are typically used. Condition 2 therefore fails, and the match is not substitutable. The 115g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is boysenberry syrup, a liquid topping used for drizzling. The USDA entry is the whole canned boysenberry fruit packed in heavy syrup, so the product is the fruit plus its packing liquid, not the syrup on its own. Substituting it would put whole or pieces of fruit on the dish where a smooth syrup was intended, changing appearance and texture, which fails condition 2. Condition 1 also fails: a drizzle would have to be reworked, for example by blending or straining the canned fruit, which changes how the dish is prepared. The canned heavy syrup is also a sweetened packing medium, not the same product as a boysenberry-flavoured syrup. Not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply.

Step 1: The ingredient is turnips, specifically Japanese turnips (kabu, Brassica rapa), which are a culinary name for the same vegetable. The USDA entry is pickled turnip, the same food in a preserved state. Guideline B treats regional and culinary names as the same food. Step 2: The 50g weight is ignored (Guideline A). Pickled turnip is served cold as a condiment or side in both cases, so the preparation does not change. Step 3: The main risk is flavour. Japanese pickled turnips are often sweet-soy or salt-pickled, while the USDA entry is a generic pickled turnip whose seasoning is unspecified. This is a seasoning-style difference rather than a different food or cut, and the entry does not name a modified or flavoured product. Given the guidelines' treatment of culinary names as the same food, both conditions are judged to be met, with some uncertainty about seasoning.

The ingredient is dried peaches, a dehydrated, chewy fruit. The USDA match is 'Babyfood, fruit, peaches, junior', a finely pureed, wet, cooked baby food product. Condition 1 fails: using a puree in place of dried fruit changes the preparation. The moisture, sugar concentration and texture differ, so a dish using dried peaches would not be prepared the same way. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice a smooth, wet puree where chewy dried pieces are expected. Guideline F rejects different states (dried vs cooked/processed). The correct match would be a dried or dehydrated peach entry, not baby food. Quantity is ignored.

The ingredient is welsh onion (Allium fistulosum, also called Japanese bunching onion or negi), sliced; the quantity is ignored. The USDA match is 'Welsh rarebit', which is a cheese-based dish made from melted cheese, often with beer, mustard and seasonings, served on toast. It is not a vegetable and is not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails: using a cheese dish in place of sliced onion would change the dish entirely, since the preparation and components would not match. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. The match is a different food, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is prune puree, a dark, sweet, sticky puree made from dried plums. The USDA match is raspberry puree, seedless, a different fruit. Condition 1 fails: swapping raspberry for prune changes the preparation's flavour base, and the sugar, acidity and fruit profile differ. Condition 2 also fails: raspberry puree is bright red and tart, while prune puree is dark brown-purple and deeply sweet, so a diner would notice the difference in taste and appearance. Guideline B does not apply, since prune and raspberry are not the same food under another name. Guideline F rules out a different food that is not a sibling variety of the same fruit. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is tilapia, baked (250g; quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry is 'Fish, tilapia, baked or broiled', which is the same food in the same cooked state, prepared by the same method (baking). Condition 1: the match is the baked tilapia itself, so it can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the entry describes the same baked fish. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is fried gyoza, a Japanese pot sticker: a pan-fried dumpling with a thin wheat wrapper and a savoury filling. The USDA entry 'Wonton, dumpling or pot sticker, fried' names pot stickers directly, so gyoza are the same food under a regional/culinary name (guideline B). The 'fried' state matches, since gyoza are normally pan-fried, so the cooking state is the same as bought (guideline C). The entry is generic for dumplings and pot stickers, so filling and seasoning differences between gyoza and a generic fried dumpling fall within the same category and are not a different food. Condition 1 is met: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 is reasonably met: a diner would not expect a visible or textural difference between a fried gyoza and a fried pot sticker in this category. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is frozen artichokes. The USDA entry is Artichokes (globe or french), frozen, unprepared, which is the same food in the same frozen state. Under guideline B, this is the same food. Under guideline E, a frozen product matches the frozen USDA entry of the same product. The quantity (75g) is ignored per guideline A. The word 'unprepared' describes the product as sold without added preparation, which is consistent with a plain frozen artichoke ingredient and does not introduce a modification such as marinated or seasoned. Condition 1: the entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are used the same way after thawing or cooking. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food in the same frozen form.

The ingredient is cuttlefish that has been simmered, so it is a cooked, moist-heat preparation of cuttlefish. The USDA entry is 'Mollusks, cuttlefish, mixed species, cooked, moist heat', which is the same food in the same cooked state, prepared by the same moist-heat method. Simmering is a moist-heat cooking method, so the preparation is not altered. Condition 1 is met: the match can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 is met: cuttlefish cooked by moist heat matches the simmered product in taste, texture and appearance. The '95g' quantity and the '(optional)' label are not relevant to the match under guideline A. The match is therefore substitutable.

The ingredient is cracked wheat bread that has been toasted. The USDA entry is 'Bread, wheat or cracked wheat, toasted', which names the same product (wheat or cracked wheat bread) in the same state (toasted). Guideline F warns against a toasted match for an untoasted ingredient, but here both are toasted, so the states agree. The quantity prefix '90g' is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are already toasted bread. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel, or see a difference between cracked wheat toasted bread and the USDA wheat/cracked wheat toasted bread. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is chicken broth cubes, the dry bouillon cubes used to make broth. The USDA entry 'Soup, chicken broth cubes, dry' describes the same dry product under a near-identical name. Condition 1: the cubes can be swapped in directly, since the dish is prepared the same way (dissolved or crumbled into the recipe). Condition 2: the diner would taste the same chicken-broth flavour and see the same result, because it is the same product type. The leading '65g' is quantity and is ignored. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sweet cherries, and the USDA entry 'Cherries, sweet, raw' is the same food in its uncooked, fresh form. The quantity (260g) is ignored per guideline A. Sweet cherries are the standard default variety named in the entry, so there is no sibling variety, modified product, or processed state involved. Condition 1: the cherries could be used directly in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since no cooking method is implied by the ingredient and raw fresh cherries are the default. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is literally the same fruit in the same raw state. Both conditions are met.

Condition 1: The ingredient is plain safflower seeds, used as a dry seed ingredient. The USDA entry is dried safflower seed kernels. Under guideline B, this is the same food under a trade or culinary name. Under guideline D, the plain ingredient maps to the standard default version, and dried is the normal state in which safflower seeds are sold. Guideline C says handling does not change the match, and the leading weight is ignored (A). Substituting the entry would not change how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: Safflower seeds sold for cooking are typically the kernels, so a diner would not expect a different taste, texture, or appearance. The kernel descriptor describes how the seed is normally sold rather than a modified product (guideline D). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pistachio nuts, finely ground. The USDA entry is 'Pistachio nuts, unsalted', which is the same food. Grinding is knife or processing work done at home and does not change the match (guideline C). The ingredient does not specify salted or flavoured, so the plain unsalted default is the standard version (guideline D). Using the unsalted nut in place of the ground pistachio does not change the preparation method. A diner would not taste or see a difference from the nut itself, so both conditions hold. The 25g quantity is ignored (guideline A).

The ingredient 'dried poha flakes' refers to flattened, parboiled rice flakes (beaten rice), a dried cereal product used in Indian cooking. The USDA entry 'Groundcherries, (cape-gooseberries or poha), raw' refers to the fruit Physalis peruviana, which is also called 'poha' in some regions. The shared name is a coincidence of nomenclature, not the same food. Condition 1 fails: a fruit cannot replace dried rice flakes without changing how the dish is prepared (the flakes are soaked or cooked as a grain, the fruit is raw). Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice a tart, juicy berry instead of starchy, dry rice flakes in taste, texture and appearance. Guideline B (same food under another name) does not apply, because these are different foods.

The ingredient is toasted oat bran cereal, sold as a ready-to-eat cereal. The USDA entry is a branded ready-to-eat cereal explicitly named Toasted Oat Bran cereal, so it is the same product type under a brand name (guideline G: branded entry of the same plain product = yes). The 'toasted' descriptor matches the USDA name rather than differing from it, so guideline F's toasted-vs-plain distinction does not apply. The leading 300g is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the cereal can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same ready-to-eat product. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance because it is the same toasted oat bran cereal. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is light cream (a dairy cream with roughly 18-30% milkfat, used for pouring, sauces and enriching dishes). The USDA match is Duck sauce, a sweet-and-sour condiment typically made from apricot or plum, sugar, vinegar and seasonings. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a modified or processed version of cream. Condition 1 fails: using duck sauce in place of light cream would change the preparation, since cream is emulsified into sauces or whipped and poured, whereas duck sauce is a sweet fruit condiment that would make the dish sweet and tangy. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly taste the sweet-sour fruit flavour and notice a very different colour and texture. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is smoked pork shoulder, a ready-to-eat product that has been smoked, which is a cooked/processed state. The USDA entry is 'Pork, cured, shoulder, blade roll, separable lean and fat, unheated', which is an uncooked cured product. Guideline F treats raw vs cooked and plain vs smoked as different states, so this is not the same food. Condition 1 fails: using the raw cured entry would change the preparation, because the meat would need cooking and would not arrive smoked. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, appearance and smoky flavour. The USDA entry does not specify smoking, and 'unheated' signals it is not the cooked product. The quantity (310g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain whole wheat bread, toasted. The USDA entry is whole wheat bread with raisins, toasted. Guideline B does not apply because this is not the same food under another name. The raisin version adds an ingredient that changes the flavour, sweetness, texture and appearance. A diner would notice the raisins, so condition 2 fails. Guideline D also treats added flavouring or additions as a modification, not the default version. Condition 1 is met, since the preparation (toasting) is the same, but condition 2 is not, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is palm kernel shortening, a processed fat derived from palm kernel oil, used in baking and frying; chilling is handling and does not change the match. The USDA match is Hearts of palm, raw, which is the edible inner shoot of a palm tree, a vegetable with a crisp, watery texture and mild flavour. It is not the same food, and it is not a fat. Condition 1 fails: it cannot replace a solid fat in a dish without changing preparation (creaming, shortening pastry or frying behaviour would be lost). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. This is the raw plant source versus a processed fat, which the guidelines explicitly treat as non-substitutable.

The ingredient is farmer's cheese, drained. The USDA entry is 'Cottage cheese, farmer's', which names the same product: farmer's cheese is a dry-curd cheese that the USDA lists under the farmer's cheese name. The quantity (225g) is ignored per guideline A. 'Drained' is knife-work-style handling that does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are used in the same way as a fresh curd cheese. Condition 2: the same product under the same name should not show a taste, texture, or appearance difference in the finished dish. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is banana pepper, a mild, sweet-tangy pepper. The USDA match is jalapeño, a different pepper variety with noticeably more heat and a grassier, more vegetal flavour. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B), so it is not a regional or trade-name equivalent. Guideline F rejects sibling varieties with a different taste. A diner would likely notice the much greater heat and different flavour, so condition 2 fails. Condition 1 is arguably met since they are both fresh peppers used similarly, but both conditions must hold. The quantity is ignored (guideline A).

The ingredient is fresh duck eggs, beaten. The USDA entry 'Egg, duck, whole, fresh, raw' is the same food in the same state. 'Fresh' matches the fresh descriptor. 'Beaten' is handling done by the recipe and does not change the match (guideline C). The 100g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the raw whole duck egg can be used in place of the beaten duck egg without changing preparation, since the cook beats it. Condition 2: the diner would taste and see the same duck egg, so no difference in taste, texture or appearance arises. Both conditions are met.

Cornmeal is ground dried corn (whole or degermed endosperm meal), a standard baking and cooking ingredient. The USDA entry 'Corn bran, crude' is the outer pericarp layer separated during milling, a different milling fraction with a different composition, texture, and flavour. It is not the same food under another name. Using bran in place of cornmeal would change the dish's texture (coarse, fibrous, bran-heavy), flavour, and appearance, and a diner would notice. Condition 1 and condition 2 both fail.

The ingredient is fructose powder, a pure dry sugar. The USDA entry, 'Sweeteners, tabletop, fructose, dry, powder', describes the same product: dry powdered fructose sold as a tabletop sweetener. The 'tabletop' descriptor reflects how fructose powder is normally sold, not a modification. The quantity (5g) is ignored. Condition 1: the powder can replace the ingredient directly with no change to preparation, since both are dry powders measured and mixed the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because both are the same sugar in powder form. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked dungeness crab, a specific smoked, raw-sold crab product. The USDA match is 'Crab, canned', which is a cooked, canned crab product in a packing medium, typically a different species mix (often blue or snow crab) and processed state. Guideline F states that a plain versus smoked/processed state is not substitutable, and a different state (canned/cooked vs smoked) changes flavour and texture. Guideline B does not apply because canned crab is not literally the same food as smoked dungeness crab. A diner would notice the smoky flavour and different texture and appearance. Therefore the match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is dried apricots. The USDA match is dried figs, uncooked. These are different fruits with different flavours (apricot is tart and bright, fig is sweet and musky), different textures (figs have many small crunchy seeds, apricots are smooth), and different appearance (figs are darker and more irregular in shape, apricots are orange). Guideline B does not apply because this is not the same food under another name, and guideline F rules out sibling or different varieties with distinct taste. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in flavour, texture and appearance. Condition 1 is also doubtful, since swapping figs for apricots would change the dish's flavour. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a smoked lamb chop, while the USDA entry 'Lamb, chop' is the plain, unsmoked meat. Condition 1: the smoked product is cured and smoked, which changes how it is prepared and is not a plain chop that can be cooked the same way without altering the dish. Condition 2: a diner would notice the smoky flavour, and the smoking also changes the colour and texture of the meat. Guideline F explicitly lists 'plain vs toasted/smoked/roasted' as a state difference that is not substitutable. The quantity (250g) is irrelevant under guideline A. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is steel-cut oats in uncooked form, which is the dried grain as bought. The USDA entry 'Oats, whole grain, steel cut' is the same food under the same name, with no cooking, flavouring, or processing modification. The 'uncooked' qualifier describes the default dry state that the USDA entry also represents, and the weight is decoration per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same dry grain that gets cooked in the recipe. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the cooked result is identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sun-dried tomato halves, which are tomatoes (Solanum lycopersicum), dried and typically packed in oil or sold dry. The USDA match is 'Peppers, hot chile, sun-dried', which is a different vegetable (hot chile peppers, Capsicum). This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Swapping them would change the flavour from sweet, tangy tomato to hot, pungent chile, and diners would notice the difference. Quantity and knife-work descriptors do not change this. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is cooked butter beans (a legume, Phaseolus lunatus/limensis, typically sold canned or cooked). The USDA match 'Butter, NFS' refers to dairy butter, a fat made from cream. Condition 1: Butter cannot replace cooked beans in a dish; it is a different food entirely, and substituting it would change the cooking method and the dish's basic composition. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance (creamy fat versus starchy legume). The name overlap ('butter') is coincidental; the entries are not the same food under another name. Neither condition is met.

1. The ingredient is a generic peanut butter crunch cereal, and the USDA entry is a branded peanut butter crunch cereal (Quaker Cap'n Crunch's Peanut Butter Crunch). The product type is the same: a ready-to-eat peanut butter flavoured crunch cereal. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. The flavour in the ingredient name is not an added modification, since the USDA entry carries the same flavour. 2. Method: the cereal is eaten ready-to-eat with no cooking, so the preparation is unchanged. 3. Taste, texture and appearance: the cereal is the same kind of product with the same peanut butter crunch flavour and shape, so a diner would not reasonably notice a difference between the two. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is scallion (green onion), with the quantity (50g) ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Green onion, (scallion), bulb and greens, root removed, raw', which explicitly names scallion as the same food. Per guideline B, scallion and green onion are the same food under regional/culinary names, and the USDA entry includes the bulb and greens, the standard way scallions are sold. The 'root removed' descriptor reflects normal trimming and does not change the product, and 'raw' matches a plain fresh ingredient. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the scallion with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same vegetable in the same raw state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is snapper fish, and the USDA entry 'Fish, snapper' names the same food with no added state, preparation, or modification. Under guideline B it is the same food. Guideline E says a generic entry with no state matches fresh or plain versions of the food. The 300g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Snapper can be used in the same preparation without changing the cooking method, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the food is the same species.

Senbei are Japanese rice crackers, so the USDA entry 'Crackers, rice' names the same general food under a regional name (guideline B). The USDA entry has no flavour, cut or preparation descriptor, so it is the generic rice cracker. It can be used in the same way, as a crushed or whole crisp, without changing preparation. Senbei vary in seasoning (plain, soy-glazed, seaweed-wrapped), so a diner could notice a difference if the dish relies on a specific style. Without that specified, the generic rice cracker matches the plain default, and the texture and appearance are closely comparable.

The ingredient is a frozen mix of sweetcorn and butter beans. Butter beans are the same food as lima beans (the large lima variety, sold under a regional name), so the USDA entry 'Succotash, (corn and limas)' names the same two components. The USDA entry is frozen and unprepared, which matches the frozen ingredient as bought, and 'unprepared' means uncooked, as the ingredient is. Freezing does not visibly alter corn or lima beans in a cooked dish, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. The quantity (20g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked chicken liver. The USDA entry is chicken liver, all classes, cooked, simmered, which is unsmoked and cooked by simmering. Condition 1 fails: the entry is a plain simmered product, and the recipe's smoked product would need a different preparation (smoking) that the match does not provide. Condition 2 also fails: smoking adds a distinct smoky flavour and colour that a diner would notice. Under guideline F, plain vs smoked is a different state and not substitutable. The quantity is ignored, per guideline A.

The ingredient is whole grain farro, meaning the unpearled grain with its bran intact. The USDA entry is pearled farro, which has had the bran and part of the outer layer removed. Guideline B does not apply because these are not the same food under different names. Guideline F rejects a processed or refined form in place of the source product, and the ingredient explicitly asks for whole grain. Condition 1 fails because pearled farro cooks considerably faster, so the preparation would change (cooking time and likely water ratio). Condition 2 also fails: pearled farro is more tender, less chewy, and lighter in colour and appearance, and a diner could notice the difference in texture and bite. The quantity (190g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain tofu with no stated style, firmness, or coagulant. The USDA entry is 'Tofu, raw, regular, prepared with calcium sulfate', which is the standard default tofu. Calcium sulfate is the most common coagulant used in regular tofu, so this describes how the product is normally made rather than a modified version (unlike 'calcium reduced' or 'reduced sodium'). Condition 1: it is raw, as tofu is used, and can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the 30g quantity is ignored. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because this is the ordinary tofu people buy under the plain name. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh tomato puree, a raw, uncooked puree made from fresh tomatoes. The USDA match is canned tomato puree with salt added, so it is a processed, cooked, canned product with added salt. Guideline F rejects a different state (raw vs cooked/processed), and guideline D treats a plain ingredient turned into a modified version (salt added) as not a match. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would likely notice the difference, since canned puree tastes cooked and salted and lacks the brighter, fresher flavour of fresh puree. The 2g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 might pass for use in a sauce, but condition 2 does not, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is walnut oil, and the USDA entry 'Walnut oil' is the same food. 'Cold-pressed' describes the extraction method, which is how walnut oil is normally produced and sold, so it does not turn the food into a different product (guideline D: plain ingredient to standard default version). The quantity prefix is ignored (guideline A). Using the USDA walnut oil would not change how the dish is prepared, since both are used as an oil. Any taste difference from the pressing method is a minor variation within the same food, not a different food, so a diner would not reasonably notice a different product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pomegranate juice reconstituted from concentrate. The USDA entry is pomegranate juice from concentrate, so the food and its state match. The only extra descriptor is 'shelf-stable', which describes the common retail packaging of juice rather than a flavour, sweetening, or other modification. Shelf-stable juice is the normal form a shopper buys under this name, so per guideline D it is not a meaningful modification. Quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the recipe with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not taste or see a difference, since it is the same juice product. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is sunflower seeds still in the shell, a raw whole-seed form. The USDA entry is sunflower seed kernels, meaning the shells are removed, and the kernels are oil roasted, meaning they have been cooked. Using the kernels would change how the dish is prepared, since the shells would not need to be removed or handled. Oil roasting is a different processing state from raw (guideline F: plain vs roasted is not substitutable), which changes flavour, texture, and colour. A diner would also notice shelled, roasted kernels versus whole in-shell seeds. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is 50g chokecherries, with no preparation or state specified, so it is the default raw fruit. The USDA entry is 'Chokecherries, raw, pitted (Shoshone Bannock)'. 'Raw' matches uncooked fruit. 'Pitted' describes handling (stone removal), which guideline C says does not change the match. The '(Shoshone Bannock)' label names a regional/traditional chokecherry type rather than a different food, so under guideline B it is the same fruit under a regional name, not a sibling variety with a different taste (guideline F). The quantity is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions hold: the fruit could be used without changing preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance.

The ingredient is strawberry Greek yogurt, with the 985g quantity ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is Yogurt, Greek, strawberry, lowfat. Condition 1: the match is the same product type (Greek yogurt with strawberry flavouring), so it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: per guideline D, flavoured yogurts are typically sold as low fat, so 'lowfat' describes how this product is normally bought rather than a modification. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned imitation crab meat, which is surimi: a processed fish paste, usually from pollock or other white fish, formed and flavoured to resemble crab. The USDA entry 'Crab, canned' is real crab meat from crustaceans. These are different foods, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Condition 1: the substitution would not change the preparation method, so the dish could in principle be made the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Surimi has a springier, more uniform, fibrous texture, a sweeter and milder flavour, and a bright orange-pink surface, while real crab has a flakier texture, a distinct briny flavour and an off-white to pale appearance. Guideline F also rejects a processed ingredient matched to its raw source. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'strong white flour', the UK name for high-protein white bread flour (about 12-13% protein). The USDA entry 'Wheat flour, white, bread, enriched' is the bread flour product, so it is the same food under a regional name (guideline B). The quantity (330g) is ignored (guideline A). Enriched is the standard default for white flour sold in shops, so it is not a modification (guideline D). Bread flour is the same product as strong white flour, so the 'different flour' exclusion in guideline F does not apply. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing the method (same mixing, kneading and proving). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient 'slaw dressing' is a dressing for coleslaw, which is the same food as the USDA entry 'Salad dressing, coleslaw'. The quantity prefix (25g) is ignored. Condition 1: the USDA item is the same product, so it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: since it is the same product, a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. The entry adds no flavour or processing modification beyond what a coleslaw dressing normally is. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is spaghetti squash, a distinct cultivar whose flesh separates into stringy strands when cooked and is pale yellow. The USDA entry is butternut squash, a different variety with dense, sweet, orange flesh. This is a sibling variety, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Cooking spaghetti squash to create strands, or serving it as a noodle substitute, would not work with butternut, so condition 1 fails. A diner would notice the dense, orange, sweeter flesh instead of pale, stringy strands, so condition 2 fails too. Quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is spaghetti sauce, a condiment-style tomato-based sauce used on pasta. The USDA entry is a complete frozen entree of spaghetti with meat sauce, which contains pasta and meat as well as sauce. Under guideline F, a single ingredient is not substitutable for a blend or product that contains it. Condition 1 fails: using the entree in place of the sauce would add pasta and meat and change how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the extra pasta, meat chunks and different composition. The entry is a prepared dish, not the sauce itself, so it is not the same food under another name.

The ingredient is plain 'spaghetti sauce', which means the standard default version a shopper would buy under that name. The USDA match is 'Spaghetti sauce, fat free', a modified version with the fat removed. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a fat-free or low-fat version is not substitutable. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the sauce could be heated and served the same way. Condition 2 fails: removing fat from a tomato-based sauce typically changes its mouthfeel, richness and flavour, and a diner could notice the difference. The quantity is irrelevant (guideline A).

The ingredient is bacon fat, rendered fat from cured, smoked pork belly. The USDA match is Lard, which is rendered pork fat without the curing and smoking. Guideline F says a different fat is not substitutable, and bacon fat is a distinct fat product. Condition 1 is arguably met, since lard could be used in the same cooking steps. Condition 2 fails: bacon fat carries smoky, salty, cured-meat flavour from the bacon, which a diner would likely notice in the finished dish. Both conditions must hold, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried bean sauce granules, a processed fermented-soybean seasoning (a dried, instant form of yellow bean sauce) that is salty and savoury. The USDA match, 'Beans, NFS', is a generic, unspecified bean, most likely a whole legume. Using whole beans in place of the granules would change the dish's flavour, since the seasoning would be missing, and its texture and appearance, since it would be whole beans rather than a dissolved or dispersed sauce. This is the raw or plain legume versus a processed ingredient, the same pattern as the source-versus-processed rule in guideline F. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is plain pork sausage links, which a shopper would normally buy as the standard full-fat product. The USDA entry is specifically 'reduced fat' pork sausage. Under guideline D, reduced fat is a modification of a plain ingredient, not the default version, and reduced-fat sausage is not what people normally buy under the plain name. Condition 2 also fails: reduced-fat sausage has noticeably different texture, juiciness, and cooking behaviour (less fat renders out, so it can dry out or brown differently), so a diner could notice the difference. The entry is the same food type, but the modified fat content makes it a different product, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a creamy Roquefort dressing, a standard commercial salad dressing made with Roquefort (blue) cheese. The USDA entry is 'Salad dressing, blue or roquefort cheese dressing, commercial, regular', which names the same product with the same components. 'Creamy' describes the normal texture of this dressing, not a modified version, and the 'regular' descriptor matches the default commercial product. The leading '200g' is quantity and is ignored. Used in place of the ingredient, it would not change preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance.

The ingredient is blue cheese dressing, a creamy dressing made with blue cheese. The USDA entry 'Blue or roquefort cheese dressing' names the same product type. Roquefort is a variety of blue cheese, so this is the same dish under a regional or culinary name (guideline B). The USDA wording adds no unexpected modifier such as low fat, reduced sodium or flavoured. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is used as a dressing or dip in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because both are creamy, white-to-pale dressings with blue-cheese flavour. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a generic milk-based protein powder, such as unflavoured whey or casein. The USDA entry is a branded sports nutrition powder mix (Muscle Milk), which is a blend. It contains added sugars or sweeteners, flavourings, fats, vitamins and minerals, so it is not the same food under another name. Condition 1: it could physically replace the powder in a recipe without changing the preparation. Condition 2: the added flavour and sweetness would likely change the taste and possibly the texture of the dish, and a diner could notice. Per guideline G, a branded entry with added flavour or modification is not a match, and per guideline F, a blend or product containing the ingredient is not substitutable. Both conditions are not reliably met.

The ingredient is strawberry yogurt, a dairy product made from milk cultures. The USDA match is SILK Strawberry soy yogurt, a plant-based product made from soy milk. Under guideline B this is not the same food under another name, and it is not a modified version of the dairy product either. It is a different base ingredient. Condition 1 (substitution without changing preparation) could technically hold, since both are spoonable yogurts used the same way. Condition 2 fails: soy yogurt has a distinct soy flavour and a different texture and mouthfeel from dairy yogurt, and a diner would likely notice the difference. Guideline G's brand rule covers branded versions of the same product type, and soy yogurt is not the same product type as dairy yogurt. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is cream of wheat, a hot cereal made from the endosperm of wheat (finely milled farina, typically cooked into porridge). The USDA match is wheat bran, which is the outer layer of the wheat kernel, a different part of the grain with a coarse, fibrous, nutty texture and a different flavour profile. It is not the same food under another name (Guideline B), and it is not a modified version of the same product (Guideline D). Condition 1 fails: cream of wheat is cooked as a smooth porridge or used as a thickener/binder, while bran would be added as a coarse fibrous material that changes the cooking outcome, so the preparation would be altered. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the coarse, gritty, bran texture and the different taste compared with smooth cream of wheat. Per Guideline F, a different part of the processed grain is not substitutable. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is generic 'protein powder', which in cooking typically means a whey, casein, soy, or pea protein powder, usually flavoured or unflavoured, sold as a supplement ingredient. The USDA entry 'Nutritional powder mix, protein, light, NFS' is a nutritional drink or shake mix powder: a blended product that contains protein plus other components such as carbohydrates, sweeteners, flavourings, and possibly vitamins and minerals, and it is 'light' (a modified, reduced-calorie style) and not sold as a single-ingredient protein. Condition 1: It could be used in place of protein powder in a sense, but it is a multi-component, reduced-calorie blend rather than a pure protein ingredient, so it would change the composition and likely the sweetness, flavour, and how the mix dissolves or behaves in cooking. Condition 2: A diner would likely notice differences in taste and texture, since the blend's flavour and sweetness profile and its added ingredients differ from a plain protein powder. Under guideline F, a blend or product containing the ingredient, and a modified version ('light'), do not count as the same food. Therefore neither condition is clearly met, and the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is toasted challah bread, and the USDA entry is 'Bread, egg, Challah, toasted'. Both name the same food (challah) in the same state (toasted). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the bread is already toasted and needs no further cooking. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the match describes the same toasted challah. The weight prefix is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is dill seed, the dried mature seed of the dill plant. The USDA match is 'Spices, dill weed, dried', which is the dried leaves and stems. These are different parts of the plant with noticeably different flavour profiles: dill seed is more pungent, warm and slightly bitter, while dill weed is milder and grassy. Their appearance also differs (small brown seeds versus green-flecked leaf fragments). Substituting one for the other would change the taste and appearance of the dish, so condition 2 fails. Condition 1 is also unlikely to hold, since a cook would not treat them as interchangeable without changing the recipe's flavour. Guideline B does not apply because these are not the same food under different names. Under guideline F, a different state or different product of the same plant is not substitutable.

The ingredient is an unbranded cinnamon toast cereal, a sugared, cinnamon-flavoured toast-shaped ready-to-eat cereal. The USDA entry, Malt-O-Meal Cinnamon Toasters, is a ready-to-eat cereal in the same cinnamon-toast product type, sold as a branded equivalent. Guideline G treats a branded entry of the same plain product type as a match, and the ingredient names no brand or modification. Quantity is ignored (A). Cooking method is unaffected because both are eaten dry or in milk. Taste, texture and appearance are the same product category, so the diner would not expect a different food. Minor brand-to-brand variation in shape and sweetness is inherent to any unbranded cereal name, so the entry is an acceptable match under the same-type rule.

The ingredient is plain sauerkraut, and the USDA entry is 'Sauerkraut', the same food under the same name. The leading weight (65g) is ignored per guideline A. Plain sauerkraut is normally bought as a fermented, drained product, which is the standard default version, so no modification applies.
