Condition 1: sauerkraut can replace sauerkraut with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a dry thousand island dressing mix, a powdered seasoning blend that is normally combined with a base such as mayonnaise, sour cream or yogurt before use. The USDA entry is a ready-to-use, fat-free liquid salad dressing. Condition 1 fails: using the finished dressing in place of the dry mix would change how the dish is prepared, because the mix's seasonings would have to be incorporated into a base rather than added as a finished product. Condition 2 also fails: the dry mix is a single seasoning blend in a different state from the prepared, fat-free dressing, and the fat-free version differs from a standard thousand island dressing in flavour and texture. Under guideline F, a different state and a blend versus a finished product are not substitutable, and guideline D treats fat-free as a modification. The entry is therefore not an acceptable match.

The ingredient, cream of rice, is a plain milled rice cereal (a dry, ground grain product used to make porridge). The USDA entry, 'Fish and rice with cream sauce', is a prepared composite dish containing fish, rice and a cream sauce. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a modified version of cream of rice. Condition 1 fails: using the dish in place of cream of rice would change the preparation, since the cereal would need cooking into porridge and the fish and sauce would be added. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice fish and cream sauce in place of a smooth rice cereal. The quantity prefix is irrelevant. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is baked beans (typically navy or haricot beans in a sweet tomato-based sauce), mashed. The USDA match is refried beans, canned, fat-free, which are pinto or similar beans mashed and seasoned, with no tomato sauce and no sugar. Condition 1: the match is a different product, not the same food under another name, so it cannot simply replace the ingredient. Baked beans are a ready-to-eat sauced product, and refried beans are a different bean-based product, so the preparation would change. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Baked beans are sweet and tomato-flavoured with a saucy appearance, while refried beans are savoury, earthy and thicker in texture. The 'fat-free' descriptor is also a modification of the typical product (guideline D). Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is pork ear, an edible cut made of skin and cartilage that is cooked and eaten for its chewy, gelatinous texture. The USDA entry is pork backfat, raw, which is a layer of fat from beneath the skin. These are different tissues and not the same food under another name. Replacing ear with backfat would change the texture from chewy cartilage to soft, fatty meat, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture or appearance) both fail.

The ingredient is durian, and the USDA entry is 'Durian, raw or frozen', which is the same food. The quantity (70g) is ignored per guideline A. The entry covers both raw and frozen durian, so whether the ingredient is fresh or thawed does not matter (guideline E). Using it would not change the preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fennel seeds, a whole spice. The USDA entry 'Spices, fennel seed' names the same food with no modification, preparation, or blend. Under the guidelines, a plain ingredient matched to the standard entry for the same food counts as a match. The 10g quantity is ignored. Swapping one for the other would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not taste or see a difference. The entry does not indicate ground or toasted seeds, so it is the default whole seed.

The ingredient is fresh red seedless grapes, which are raw fruit. The USDA match is canned Thompson seedless grapes packed in water, with solids and liquids. Canned fruit is a processed state, not the fresh fruit, and the guidelines treat a different state and packing medium as non-substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using canned grapes changes preparation, since they are already cooked or processed, come with packing liquid, and cannot be used as fresh fruit in the same way (for example, for garnish or raw eating). Condition 2 also fails: canned grapes are softer, have a different texture, a more uniform appearance, and a distinctly different taste from fresh grapes, and a diner would likely notice. The variety (Thompson seedless) is the same type, so the failure comes from the canned, water-packed state rather than the grape identity.

The ingredient is oyster sauce, a condiment made from oyster extract, sugar, salt, and thickeners (often with soy sauce or caramel), giving a thick, sweet-savoury, dark brown sauce. The USDA match 'Mushroom, oyster' is the fresh edible fungus (Pleurotus ostreatus), a vegetable with no sauce form, no oyster extract, and a totally different taste and texture. It is not the same food under another name, nor a cut or form of it. Using mushrooms in place of oyster sauce would change flavour (umami and sweetness), texture (solid vegetable vs liquid sauce), and appearance (no glossy brown sauce), and a diner would notice. Condition 1 fails because the sauce cannot be substituted by a raw mushroom without changing the preparation, and condition 2 fails because the taste and appearance differ. Therefore it is not substitutable.

Bing is a named variety of sweet cherry, and it is a dark red sweet cherry. The USDA entry 'Cherries, sweet, dark red, raw' is the generic raw category that includes Bing. Guideline F rejects a sibling variety with a different taste, such as Fuji versus Granny Smith. Here the USDA entry covers the variety itself, not a different sibling, so the variety-name check does not apply. The weight (150g) is ignored per guideline A. Preparation is unchanged: both are raw, fresh cherries eaten or used as-is. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the USDA category is the same fruit type. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is soybean oil, a refined fat extracted from soybeans. The USDA match is 'Soybeans, mature seeds, raw', which is the whole dried legume (the bean itself), not the oil. Under guideline F, the raw plant/source versus the processed ingredient is not substitutable (for example, cornstarch versus corn). Condition 1 fails: you cannot use whole raw soybeans in place of liquid oil for frying, dressing, or baking without changing how the dish is prepared, since the beans are solid, must be cooked, and do not provide fat for cooking. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice whole beans instead of oil in taste, texture, and appearance. The 65g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is hemp seed butter, a processed spread made by grinding hulled hemp seeds into a smooth paste, usually with oil added. The USDA entry is 'Seeds, hemp seed, hulled', which is the whole, dry, unprocessed seed kernel. Condition 1 fails: the whole seeds cannot stand in for a spread without changing preparation, since they would need grinding and an oil or paste base. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice whole crunchy seeds rather than a smooth, spreadable paste. Per guideline F, the raw source differs from the processed ingredient, so this is not a match. The 6g quantity is irrelevant.

The ingredient is plain granulated sugar (sucrose in its standard refined, granulated form). The USDA entry 'Sugars, granulated' is the same food under its standard name: granulated sugar is the default product a shopper buys under that name. The quantity (70g) is ignored per guideline A. Substituting it into a recipe would not change the method, and the taste, texture, and appearance of the dish would be unchanged, since it is the same product. No modification, blend, or different sugar type (such as brown, powdered, or raw) is indicated. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned peas and carrots, with no mention of butter, oil, or fat. The USDA entry is 'Peas and carrots, canned, cooked, fat added', which is a modified version. Guideline D says a plain ingredient matched to a modified version is not substitutable, and the 'fat added' descriptor is not how canned peas and carrots are normally sold. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would likely taste added fat and see a glossier, different appearance. The guideline C example (buttered peas and carrots matching 'fat added') applies only when the recipe itself asks for the buttered version, which this ingredient does not. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is fresh green seedless grapes. The USDA match is canned Thompson seedless grapes in water pack, including the liquid. Thompson seedless is the variety behind most green seedless grapes, so the cultivar alone is not the problem. The problem is the state. Canning cooks and softens the fruit, so the canned grapes have a softer, mushier texture and a different appearance from fresh ones, and the packing liquid adds a different moisture profile. Guideline F lists a different state (raw vs processed) and a different packing medium as non-substitutable, and a diner would notice eating canned grapes in place of fresh. Condition 2 fails, and the swap would also change how the dish is prepared, since fresh grapes are usually cut or used whole and canned ones are not handled the same way. Condition 1 is also not met.

The ingredient is plain parmesan, and the USDA entry 'Cheese, parmesan, hard' is the same food under its standard USDA name. Per guideline B, this is the same food, so it is substitutable. Quantity (300g) is ignored per guideline A. No cooking method changes, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the USDA entry describes the same hard grating cheese. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is shrimp cakes, a shrimp-based cake or patty. The USDA entry 'Shrimp, cake or patty' names the same product type with the same core component (shrimp formed into a cake), so it is the same food under a matching name (guideline B and C). The quantity prefix is ignored (guideline A). Since the ingredient is a plain version of the product, the USDA entry is its standard default form, not a modified one (guideline D). The entry is generic and does not specify a modified state such as reduced-sodium or flavoured. Condition 1: the match can stand in for the ingredient in the same recipe without changing how it is prepared, since both are shrimp cakes to be cooked as the recipe directs. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same kind of product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sunflower seed oil. The USDA match is 'Oil, sunflower', which is the same food under a generic name; sunflower oil is the default sunflower-derived cooking oil and the entry names no modification or blend. Per guideline A the 9g quantity is ignored. Condition 1: the oil can be used in place of sunflower seed oil with no change in preparation. Condition 2: diners would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same oil. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is anise seeds, a whole spice with a distinct licorice-like flavour. The USDA entry is breadfruit seeds, boiled, which is a different food altogether: a starchy, starch-based seed from the breadfruit tree, with a bland, chestnut-like taste and a soft, starchy texture. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: breadfruit seeds cannot stand in for anise seeds in a recipe without changing how the dish is prepared, since the anise seeds are used for their aromatic flavour and the breadfruit seeds are boiled starch. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the absence of anise flavour and the different texture. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a specific cut, boneless duck breast, which is a single muscle portion with no bone. The USDA entry 'Duck, Peking' names a duck breed (Pekin), and its entries cover the whole bird or its mixed parts, not the breast alone. Guideline F treats a different cut of meat as not substitutable. Using a whole-bird entry would mean including dark meat, bone, and skin in different proportions, which changes the cut and the preparation: a boneless breast is seared or roasted as a single portion, while a whole-duck entry implies carving or cutting from a carcass. The entry is the same species and breed, but not the same cut, so it fails condition 1 and likely condition 2 as well.

The ingredient is fish sauce, a fermented condiment made from anchovies or other fish, salt, and water, with a strong savoury, umami-rich flavour and a thin liquid texture. The USDA match is 'Fish, catfish, NFS', which is the raw flesh of catfish, a whole food with no fermentation, no salt-brine liquid, and no sauce properties. Condition 1 fails: catfish cannot be used in place of fish sauce without changing the preparation, since it is a solid protein, not a seasoning liquid, and it would not function as a condiment or flavouring. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste (mild fish flesh vs. intense fermented umami) and texture (solid vs. liquid). The quantity (10g) is ignored per guideline A, and this is not a same-food-under-another-name case per guideline B, nor a plain-to-modified variant. It is the raw source food versus a processed, fermented ingredient, which falls under guideline F.

The ingredient is canned sirloin, which is a cooked, processed, shelf-stable product that has been drained. The USDA match is raw top sirloin steak, which is uncooked fresh meat. Condition 1: Substituting raw steak would change the preparation, since canned meat is already cooked and typically flaked or shredded, while raw steak would need to be cooked first, which alters the dish's method and timing. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference in texture (firm, moist, flaked canned meat versus a seared or cooked steak), appearance, and likely flavour (canned processing and added salt or liquid). Guideline F rejects raw vs cooked and processed vs raw as different states. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is pork skin, an animal byproduct (raw pork skin, typically rind). The USDA match is 'Potatoes, flesh and skin, raw', which is a vegetable (potato tuber with skin). These are different foods from entirely different sources: animal connective tissue/skin versus a plant tuber. Condition 1 fails: potato skin cannot replace pork skin in any dish without changing the preparation (pork skin is rendered, fried into cracklings, or gelatinous-cooked, whereas potato would be boiled, baked or fried as a vegetable). Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture (crisp, gelatinous, fatty pork rind vs starchy potato), and appearance. Per guideline F, this is a different source/state, and the match is not a naming variant of the same food (guideline B does not apply). The quantity (230g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is cube steak, a beef cut (top round or similar) that is mechanically tenderized and pressed into a thin cutlet. The USDA match is a dry powdered/cube bouillon soup product, which is a seasoning-based processed food, not a meat cut. Condition 1 fails: it cannot be used in place of cube steak in a dish without changing preparation, since it is not a meat that can be breaded and pan-fried or braised. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in texture (no meat fibers) and appearance. This is a different food entirely, not a naming variant of the same product, so it is not a match under guideline B or F.

The ingredient is sautéed peppers and onions, which are cooked in fat. The USDA entry 'Peppers and onions, cooked, fat added' names the same dish with the same components (peppers and onions) in the same state (cooked with added fat). The gram weight is ignored per guideline A. Sautéing is a cooked-with-fat preparation, so the USDA descriptor matches the method rather than altering it. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, and the entry could replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is red enchilada sauce, and the USDA entry is 'Enchilada sauce, red', which names the same product with no added state, modification, or preparation descriptor. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient directly, since it is the same sauce used in the same way, with no change to cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. The quantity prefix and the word 'optional' do not affect the food match (guideline A). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned mandarin oranges, drained. The USDA entry is 'Tangerines (mandarin oranges), canned, juice pack, drained'. Mandarins and tangerines are the same food under different names, and the USDA entry explicitly labels itself as mandarin oranges, so the food identity matches (guideline B). The ingredient does not specify a packing medium. Canned mandarins are normally sold in light syrup or juice (guideline D), so a juice-pack entry describes a normal version of the product rather than a modification. The packing medium is a concern under guideline F, but the recipe does not call for syrup, and once drained, the fruit's sweetness, texture and appearance should differ little from juice-packed segments. Preparation is unchanged: the fruit is drained in both cases. Both conditions are met, though the match is less certain if the recipe relies on syrup sweetness.

Sapodilla (Manilkara zapota) and mamey sapote (Pouteria sapota) are different fruits from different plant genera. Their names are similar, but they are not the same food under another name. Sapodilla has brown skin and a sweet, brown-sugar or pear-like flesh. Mamey has a reddish-orange flesh with a distinct flavour often described as sweet potato, pumpkin or almond-like. Using mamey would change the flavour and appearance of the dish, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 and condition 2 both fail.

The ingredient is endive, a leafy vegetable (chicory family) eaten raw or cooked. The USDA match is 'Spices, pepper, black', which is a dried spice made from peppercorns. These are not the same food under another name, and the match is not a regional or culinary synonym for endive. Condition 1 fails: black pepper cannot replace endive without changing the dish's preparation, since endive would be omitted or entirely replaced by a seasoning. Condition 2 fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance, as pepper would add pungent heat and no leafy vegetable body is present. The quantity (2g) is ignored per guideline A.

Straw mushrooms (Volvariella volvacea) are a different species from shiitake (Lentinula edodes). They are small, oval, and usually sold canned or fresh in a different form, with a milder, slightly earthy, distinctive flavour and a softer texture. Shiitake is a larger, meatier mushroom with a stronger, smoky-umami taste and a firmer, chewier texture. The USDA entry is raw shiitake, a sibling species with a different taste, texture and appearance, so it is not the same food under another name. Guideline F rules out sibling varieties with different taste. A diner would notice the difference in flavour, texture and appearance, so both conditions fail.

The ingredient is imitation crab meat, a surimi-based product. The USDA entry is the same product type: imitation crab made from surimi. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient directly, since both are the same ready-to-eat surimi product and need no change in preparation. Condition 2: the USDA entry's 'alaska king' label is the species name commonly used for imitation crab sticks and flakes, so it does not describe a different product. Taste, texture and appearance should match the ingredient, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is butter-flavored instant grits, and the USDA entry is Quaker Instant Grits, Butter flavor, dry. Condition 1: the match is the same product in the same dry state, so it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation (the quantity is ignored per guideline A). Guideline D says a flavoured entry does not match a plain ingredient, but here the ingredient itself asks for the butter-flavored version, so the matching flavoured entry counts. The Quaker brand is acceptable because it is the same plain product type (guideline G). Condition 2: a diner would taste butter flavour and see the same dry grits in both cases, so no difference would be noticed. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a goose egg, an entire egg from a goose. The USDA match is goose liver, raw, which is an organ meat from the same animal species but a completely different food. Using liver in place of an egg would change how the dish is prepared: eggs bind, leaven, emulsify and coat, while liver is a meat that must be cooked and processed differently. Diners would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. Quantity (75g) is ignored per the guidelines. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is chard, a leafy green. The USDA entry 'Chard, raw' is the same food in its uncooked, default form. The quantity (420g) is ignored per guideline A. Using the USDA entry in place of the ingredient requires no change to preparation, since knife work or washing does not alter the match (guideline C). Chard sold plainly is the standard raw product, so no modification or state difference applies (guideline D). A diner would see and taste the same leaves, so neither condition is violated. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is asadero cheese, a specific Mexican melting cheese, used melted. The USDA match is 'Cheese sauce', a prepared product made from processed cheese with water, emulsifiers, and other additives. Condition 1: Swapping in cheese sauce changes the composition of the dish. It is a different product with a different consistency and a shelf-stable, emulsified character, not the same food. The 'melted' state of the ingredient does not make the sauce equivalent. Condition 2: A diner would likely notice the difference in flavour (sauce-style, processed, typically milder and saltier) and texture (smooth, emulsified, pourable versus the stringy, fresh melt of asadero). Guideline F also applies: a processed product with added ingredients is not the same as the plain cheese. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is ground turmeric, a dried spice in powdered form. The USDA match is 'Spices, turmeric, ground', which is the same food under the same name. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Ground turmeric is the standard default form of the spice, so no processing or state difference exists between the ingredient and the match. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance because the product is identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 1% low-fat milk, which is a specific modified milk product, and the USDA entry 'Milk, low fat (1%)' is the same product under its standard name. Condition 1: the milk can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation method, since both are liquid milk at the same fat level. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the entry describes the same 1% fat milk. The 200g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Because the ingredient itself asks for the low-fat version and the USDA entry is the matching low-fat version, guideline D gives a match. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is frozen turnip greens and turnips, with the leading weight ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Turnip greens and turnips, frozen, unprepared', which names the same two components (turnip greens and turnips) in the same frozen state. Per guideline E, a frozen product matches the frozen USDA entry of the same product. 'Unprepared' simply means uncooked and untrimmed, which is compatible with an ingredient that the recipe will prepare itself. Cooking method, flavour, texture and appearance are not altered by the match, and a diner would not distinguish the two. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a New York strip steak, raw. The USDA entry, 'Beef, short loin (NY strip steak), raw', names the same cut explicitly, so it is the same food under another name. The leading '510g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Both raw, so the cooking method is unchanged, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient lists two components: fish tofu and whiting fillets. The USDA match, 'Fish, whiting, NFS', covers only the whiting fillets. Fish tofu is a distinct processed product, a pressed fish-paste block, not raw whiting, so the match omits one of the two components. Guideline F rejects a single ingredient standing in for a blend or product that contains it. Replacing the dish's fish tofu with plain whiting would change its texture (firm, pressed, springy versus flaky fillet), and a diner would notice the difference. The 250g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is canned tomato sauce with salt, the standard salted version. The USDA match is the 'no salt added' version, which is a sodium-modified product. Under guideline D, a reduced or no-salt-added version is a modification, not the default, so it does not match. Condition 1: the dish could be prepared the same way, so the cooking method is unchanged. Condition 2 fails: the salt level differs, so a diner would likely notice a difference in taste, since the no-salt version tastes flatter and less seasoned. Both conditions must hold, so the match is not substitutable. The 5g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is pickled lamb tongue, meaning the tongue has been cured or brined in a pickling solution, which changes its flavour (salty, tangy, seasoned), texture (firmer, cured), and colour. The USDA match is 'Lamb, variety meats and by-products, tongue, raw', which is fresh, uncooked, unseasoned tongue. Substituting raw tongue would require the dish to be brined or seasoned, which changes preparation. A diner would also notice the difference in taste and texture. Guideline F rejects a different state, such as raw versus processed, and guideline D rejects a plain item for a modified version. Condition 1 and condition 2 both fail.

The ingredient is malabar spinach (Basella alba), a leafy vine green that is a different plant from true spinach (Spinacia oleracea) and is not the same food under another name. The USDA match, 'Spinach dip, regular', is a prepared, mixed dip product, not a raw or cooked leafy vegetable. Using it would change the preparation: the chopped leaves would be replaced by a creamy, seasoned dip. Diners would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is raisin wheat bread that has been toasted. The USDA entry is wheat or cracked wheat bread with raisins, also toasted. Both the base product (wheat bread) and the added component (raisins) match. The toasted state also matches, so the rule against plain-versus-toasted mismatches does not apply. The leading weight (150g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is already toasted and needs no further cooking. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel, or see a difference between the two, because they describe the same toasted raisin wheat bread.

The ingredient is dried pasilla pepper. The USDA entry is 'Peppers, pasilla, dried', which is the same food in the same state. The quantity (5g) is ignored per guideline A. 'Stemmed' is knife or handling work that does not change the match (guideline C). Dried is the state the recipe specifies, and the USDA entry is also dried, so cooking method, flavour, texture and appearance are unchanged. A diner would not notice a difference.

The ingredient is radish slices used as an optional garnish. Quantity (60g) is ignored per guideline A. The USDA match is 'Radish', the generic raw food. Radish slices are simply a knife-cut form of raw radish, which guideline C says does not change the match. Using whole raw radish in place of sliced radish does not change how the dish is prepared (it is still sliced at home or served as a garnish), and a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance beyond the slicing itself, which the recipe handles. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fish stock (a seafood-based broth). The USDA match is beef stock, home-prepared. Condition 1: Substituting beef stock for fish stock would change the flavour base of the dish; fish stock is a distinct product from beef stock, and they are not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Using beef stock would alter the dish's flavour profile, which violates the criteria. Condition 2: A diner would likely notice the difference in taste, since beef and fish stocks have clearly distinct flavours and aromas, and beef stock is also darker in colour. Guideline F treats different-source products as not interchangeable. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

Glass noodles are the same food as cellophane noodles (also called long rice), which are made from mung bean starch. The USDA entry 'Noodles, chinese, cellophane or long rice (mung beans), dehydrated' names the same product under its alternative names. 'Dehydrated' describes the dry packaged noodles as normally bought, which is how glass noodles are sold. Condition 1: the dry noodles can be used directly, with the same soaking or boiling preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is king oyster mushrooms, a fresh edible fungus (Pleurotus eryngii), with a firm, meaty texture and mild umami flavour. The USDA match is BURGER KING, Chicken Strips, a fast-food breaded and fried chicken product. Condition 1: this is a different food entirely, not a name variant or a cut of the same food, so it cannot replace the mushrooms without changing the dish's preparation; it would be a breaded poultry product rather than a vegetable. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (poultry and breading versus mushroom), texture (crispy coated meat versus dense fungal flesh) and appearance. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is coconut water, the liquid from inside young coconuts. The USDA entry 'Nuts, coconut water (liquid from coconuts)' describes the same food under a USDA category label ('Nuts' is the food-group heading for coconut products). Guideline B says same food under another name counts as a match. The USDA entry names no modification, flavouring, or added sweetener, so it is the plain default version. The quantity (500g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since it is the same liquid. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is salted fish fillets, a cured product whose defining traits are high salt content, firmer and drier texture, and a preserved flavour. It typically needs soaking or desalting before cooking. The USDA match is haddock, steamed: a fresh, cooked, unsalted fish. Condition 1 fails because using steamed haddock would change the preparation, since the salted fish would normally be desalted and cooked differently, and the steamed fish cannot be salted in the same way. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the much saltier, more concentrated, firmer-textured flavour of cured fish versus plain steamed haddock. This is a different state (cured vs cooked fresh) and a different product, so it is not substitutable under guideline F.

The ingredient is plain 'currants' in a metric weight, which in recipe usage means dried currants (the standard baking form, as with raisins and sultanas). The USDA entry 'Currants, dried' is the same food in its default form. Condition 1: dried currants can replace the ingredient in baking or cooking without changing the method, since the recipe would be handled the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the product is the same dried fruit. The weight is ignored per the guidelines. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain canned tomato puree, the standard default product. The USDA entry 'Tomato, puree, canned' is the same food under the same name, with no added flavour, modification, or different state. Quantity (400g) is ignored per guideline A. Using the USDA match would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chicken bologna, a processed sliced luncheon meat made from finely emulsified chicken meat with seasonings, binders, curing agents, and typically smoked and cooked. The USDA match is 'Chicken, feet, boiled', which is a different food entirely: the feet of the bird, a bone-and-skin-heavy cut, boiled and not emulsified or processed into a sausage-style product. Condition 1 fails: it cannot be used in place of bologna without changing how the dish is prepared, since bologna is sliced for sandwiches or cubed, while feet must be boiled, deboned and picked. Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in texture (smooth, firm, sliceable emulsion versus gelatinous skin and cartilage), flavour (cured, seasoned, smoky versus plain boiled), and appearance. This is not the same food under another name, and it is not a cut of the same food in the sense of guideline B; it is a different product of the chicken, comparable to the case of a different cut of meat or a processed product versus its raw source (guideline F).

The ingredient is 250g king oyster mushrooms; the weight is decoration per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Mushroom, king oyster' is literally the same food under the same name (king oyster mushroom), with no stated cooking state, so it corresponds to the generic fresh food. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since the mushrooms would be cleaned, sliced and cooked the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same mushroom. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain molasses, and the USDA entry is 'Molasses', the generic food with no modifying state. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to the standard default version is substitutable. The 300g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Molasses can be used in place of itself without changing preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is reduced-fat pecan butter, a nut butter made from pecans. The USDA match is peanut butter, reduced fat. Condition 1 (same food / could be used in its place without changing preparation): peanut butter and pecan butter are different foods; a peanut is a legume, while pecans are tree nuts. Guideline F states a different source/variety with a different taste is not substitutable, and guideline B only allows substitution when it is literally the same food under another name, which it is not. Condition 2 (diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance): pecan butter has a distinctly different buttery, sweeter, more mellow flavour compared with peanut butter's roasted legume taste, so a diner would notice. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a mixture of two nuts: oil-roasted peanuts and oil-roasted cashews. The USDA match covers only one of them, oil-roasted Virginia peanuts without salt. Guideline F rejects a single ingredient standing in for a blend that contains it. Using only peanuts would drop the cashews, so the dish would change in flavour (cashews are sweeter and milder than peanuts), texture (cashews are softer and creamier) and appearance (cashew pieces are paler and differently shaped). A diner would notice the difference. The 'without salt' descriptor is also a minor difference from a plain roasted nut mix. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable. The 10g quantity is ignored, per guideline A.

The USDA entry 'Passion-fruit juice, purple, raw' is the same fruit juice, so the food identity matches. The recipe ingredient, however, is juice simmered down to a syrup, which is a cooked, reduced, concentrated product. Guideline F rejects a raw-vs-cooked state difference. Condition 1 fails: substituting raw juice would change the preparation, because the reduction step would no longer produce the syrup. Condition 2 also fails: raw juice is thinner, more dilute and tarter than a reduced syrup, and a diner would notice the difference in flavour, sweetness, viscosity and appearance. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is low-sodium tomato and vegetable juice. The USDA entry is 'Tomato and vegetable juice, 100%, low sodium', which is the same product with the same components. The ingredient itself asks for the low-sodium version, so the matching low-sodium entry is the correct match (guideline D). The quantity prefix '100g' is decoration (guideline A). Condition 1: the juice can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the USDA entry describes the same 100% tomato and vegetable juice with the same sodium level. Both conditions are met.

The base food is the same: 'Olives, black' matches black olives, and 'sliced' is knife work that does not change the match (guideline C). The ingredient, however, is 'roasted with garlic'. Guideline F says a plain versus roasted state is not substitutable, and guideline D treats added flavouring as a modification. Roasting alters the olives' texture, colour and flavour, and the garlic adds a flavour a diner would notice. The USDA entry is plain black olives with no roasting or garlic. Condition 1 is not met because the match would not reproduce the roasting step, and condition 2 is not met because a diner would notice the missing garlic-roasted flavour and appearance.

The ingredient is plain 'corn syrup', and the USDA entry is 'Syrups, corn, light', which is the standard light corn syrup. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matches its standard default version, and light corn syrup is the usual default when a recipe simply says 'corn syrup'. The 'light' descriptor reflects how this product is normally sold, not a modification such as reduced or sweetened. It is the same food with the same use and handling, so the cooking method does not change. Dark corn syrup would differ in flavour, but the plain name does not call for it. Condition 1 (same use, same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture or appearance) are both met.

The ingredient is jarred curry paste, a concentrated spice-and-aromatic paste (often with oil, chilli, garlic, and lemongrass) that the cook fries or blooms and then builds a dish around. The USDA entry is 'Curry sauce', a ready-made, thinner, liquid sauce. This is not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails: substituting a liquid sauce for a paste changes the preparation, because the cook would need to omit or reduce added liquid and could not bloom the paste in the same way. Condition 2 also fails: the dish would taste different, since the sauce is more diluted, usually has different seasoning balance, and the result would have a different texture and consistency. Because both conditions must hold, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw chicken drumsticks. The USDA match is grilled chicken drumstick with sauce, skin eaten. Condition 1 fails: the match is cooked, and the ingredient is raw, so it cannot be used in place of the raw meat without changing how the dish is prepared. It also adds sauce and implies skin is eaten, which changes flavour and appearance. Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste the sauce and see grill marks, so the food would be noticeably different. Guideline F rejects raw vs cooked and processed or flavoured variants, and the same cut of meat does not offset that. The quantity prefix is ignored. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is dried spearmint, and the USDA entry is Spearmint, dried. It is the same herb in the same state (dried), so the match is literal. Condition 1: the dried herb can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the recipe handles dried spearmint the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel, or see a difference, because the product is the same. The 90g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fermented tofu (furu/doufu ru, a cured, salty, funky fermented bean curd used as a condiment). The USDA entry is 'Mayonnaise, made with tofu', which is a creamy emulsified spread/dressing made by blending tofu with oil, vinegar or lemon juice and seasoning. Condition 1: fermented tofu is a cube of pressed, fermented, brined soybean curd used as a seasoning, typically added in small amounts or mashed into sauces; mayonnaise-tofu is a different product in form and role, and it cannot be used in its place without changing how the dish is prepared, since the fermentation, salt, and characteristic texture of the cube would be lost. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste (sharp, funky, fermented, salty flavour versus mild, creamy, eggy/oily mayonnaise flavour) and in texture and appearance (firm cube or paste versus smooth emulsion). The product is a different food, not the same food under another name, so neither condition is met.

The ingredient is fresh (raw) pompano fillet, which is the same fish as the USDA food, so the species is not in question. The USDA entry, however, is 'Fish, pompano, fried', a cooked and breaded product. Guideline F rules out raw vs cooked as a different state. Condition 1 fails: a raw fillet cannot be used in place of fried fish without changing how the dish is prepared, since the cook would have to fry it. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, appearance and flavour between raw fillet and fried pompano. The weight (585g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is canned white hominy, and the USDA entry is 'Hominy, canned, white', which is the same food. The leading '50g' is quantity and is ignored. Canned hominy is normally sold in water or brine, and the USDA canned entry is the standard default for that product, so no modified preparation is implied. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since both are canned white hominy ready to heat or add. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the product is the same. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient 'garbanzo beans' is a regional name for chickpeas, which guideline B treats as the same food. The quantity (30g) is ignored per guideline A. The ingredient does not state a cooked or canned form, so the default reading is the dried legume as bought. USDA's 'Chickpeas (garbanzo beans, bengal gram), mature seeds, raw' is the dried legume in its uncooked state, matching guideline C. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same food and any soaking or cooking would be identical. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is literally the same food under another name. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cider vinegar, and the USDA entry is 'Vinegar, cider', which is the same food under the standard name. The 105g quantity is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Used in place of the ingredient, it would not change the preparation method. Diners would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain soybean oil. The USDA entry is soy oil, which is the same base oil, but it is labelled as an industrial, refined product for woks and light frying. Guideline F states that industrial or food-service specialty fats and ingredients are not substitutable for the home ingredient, and the entry's own label marks it as a food-service specialty product with a different intended use and likely different formulation. Condition 1 is therefore not clearly met, since the USDA product is designed for a specific industrial frying context rather than being the plain home ingredient. Because the entry is a specialty industrial variant rather than the standard default oil, it fails the substitution test under the guidelines even though the underlying oil is the same.

The ingredient is cooked pork tongue, braised, with the weight as irrelevant decoration (guideline A). The USDA entry is Pork, fresh, variety meats and by-products, tongue, cooked, braised, which is the same food (pork tongue) in the same state (cooked, braised). Both the cooking method and the product match, so the dish would not change in preparation. The USDA 'fresh' descriptor is the standard way pork tongue is listed and does not alter the product as eaten (guideline D and E). A diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance because the food is the same braised pork tongue. Both conditions are met.

Hoja santa (Piper auritum) is a large, fresh Mexican herb with a distinctive anise, sassafras-like, and peppery flavour. It is not the same food as spearmint under another name. Spearmint is a different plant (Mentha spicata) with a menthol-minty flavour. The USDA entry is also dried, while the ingredient is a fresh leaf used as a wrapping or flavouring. Condition 1 fails: using dried spearmint would change the dish's flavour and possibly its preparation, since hoja santa leaves are typically used whole as wrappers for steaming or grilling, and dried mint cannot do that. Condition 2 fails: a diner would clearly notice the minty flavour instead of the anise-like hoja santa flavour. The 400g quantity is ignored under guideline A.

The ingredient is plain barley flour, ground from whole or pearled barley grain. The USDA entry is barley malt flour, which is made from malted (sprouted and kilned) barley. Malting changes the grain's chemistry: it develops sugars and enzymes and gives a sweet, malty flavour. This is a different processed product, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Guideline F rules out a different flour and a processed ingredient in place of the plain source. Using malt flour would change the flavour and browning of baked goods, and a diner could notice the difference. Condition 2 is not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is '15g sage', which refers to the culinary herb sage (fresh or dried leaves, Salvia officinalis). The USDA match is 'Sage Valley, Gluten Free Vanilla Sandwich Cookies', a branded sandwich cookie product containing flour, sugar, vegetable oil and vanilla flavouring. Condition 1: the cookie cannot be used in place of the herb; it is a completely different food with a different role in a dish, and substituting it would change the preparation (it would be sweet, baked, and not an herbal seasoning). Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice a sweet vanilla cookie instead of savoury sage in taste, texture and appearance. The match name shares only the word 'Sage' as a brand name, which is not the same food. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is roasted turkey breast, which is light meat from the breast. The USDA entry is 'Turkey, whole, light meat, meat and skin, cooked, roasted', so it is light meat from a whole bird with the skin included. Condition 1: the recipe could use either in the same preparation method, since both are cooked roasted turkey, so the cooking method does not change. Condition 2: the skin adds fat, a crisp or chewy texture, and a browner, more varied appearance, and a diner could notice this. The skin also means the product is not the same as plain roasted breast meat. Guideline F treats different cuts and different states as non-substitutable, and the skin-on entry is effectively a different product for appearance and texture. Because the second condition fails, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is smoked sturgeon, flaked. The USDA entry is sturgeon, mixed species, smoked, so the food (sturgeon) and the state (smoked) both match. The ingredient does not name a species, so the mixed-species entry is the generic sturgeon product a shopper would buy under that name. 'Flaked' is handling that does not change the match (guideline C). The 120g weight is ignored (guideline A). Cooking method is unchanged, since the food is already smoked and ready to eat. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance from the USDA product's named state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'fish sticks', a ready-made breaded fish product. The USDA entry 'Fish, stick' names the same product under a slightly different wording, so it is the same food under another name (guideline B). The leading '300g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). The entry carries no cooking-state or modification descriptor such as reduced fat, sodium, or 'frozen' versus 'cooked', so it is the generic default version of the product (guideline D). The fish-stick product is normally bought and prepared in the same way, so the cooking method stays the same. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is lemon pepper seasoning, a spice blend of ground black pepper, lemon peel/zest, salt and often other seasonings. The USDA match is lemon pie filling, a sweetened, thickened dessert filling made from lemon juice, sugar, starch and eggs/butter. Condition 1: lemon pie filling is a sweet, wet, thickened product, and cannot be used in place of a dry savoury seasoning rub without changing how the dish is prepared (it would not sprinkle or season, and would add moisture and sugar). Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (sweet dessert flavour instead of peppery savoury citrus), texture (gloopy versus dry granular) and appearance. Both conditions fail, so it is not substitutable. The quantity is irrelevant.

The ingredient is a roasted, bone-in pork rib roast. The USDA entry is pork fresh center rib roast, bone-in, cooked, roasted, so the cut (rib roast), the bone-in state, and the cooked-roasted state all match. The 200g quantity is ignored per guideline A. 'Separable lean and fat' is the standard USDA analytical descriptor for how the meat is itemised, not a modification of the food, so the diner would eat the same roast with the same fat and lean portions. Cooking method is already done in both, so the dish is prepared the same way. Taste, texture and appearance should be indistinguishable. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is frozen melon balls that have been thawed. The USDA entry 'Melon balls, frozen' is the same product in the same state. Guideline E says a frozen product that is thawed matches the frozen USDA entry of the same product (e.g. frozen mango chunks, thawed -> Mango, frozen). Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since the thawed ingredient is the same as the frozen entry. Condition 2: the same food in the same frozen-then-thawed state, so no taste, texture, or appearance difference beyond what the ingredient itself already has. The leading '100g' is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions are met.

Apple purée is a smooth puree of apples, and 'Applesauce, regular' is the standard default USDA entry for that same product, so it is the same food under a different name (guideline B). The leading '100g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: applesauce can replace apple purée in a recipe without changing how the dish is prepared, since both are used as ready-to-use smooth apple puree. Condition 2: the regular applesauce entry is the plain default version, not a flavoured, low-sugar, or otherwise modified product (guideline D), so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw wheat flakes, a plain grain product that is normally cooked (for example in porridge, muesli, or baking) before eating. The USDA entry 'Cereal, wheat flakes' is a processed ready-to-eat cereal, typically precooked and toasted or otherwise processed for eating dry or with milk. Condition 1 fails: substituting the ready-to-eat cereal would change how the dish is prepared, since it would not be cooked as raw flakes would be and would not add the same texture when cooked. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would likely notice the difference in texture, crispness, flavour, and appearance. This is a processed product rather than the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply, and guideline F (raw vs processed/cooked state) points to a non-match.

The ingredient is plain fat-free milk, which is nonfat milk. The USDA entry is 'Milk, fluid, nonfat, calcium fortified', and its parenthetical explicitly names it as 'fat free or skim', so it is the same product under another name. Guideline D says a fat-free ingredient matches the modified nonfat entry because the ingredient itself asks for that version. The calcium fortification is a standard descriptor of how fat-free milk is normally sold in retail, not an unusual modification. Condition 1: it can be used directly in place of fat-free milk with no change to preparation. Condition 2: calcium fortification does not change taste, texture, or appearance, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain blueberries specified as unsweetened. The USDA match is 'Blueberries, frozen, sweetened', which carries added sugar. Guideline D classes sweetened versus unsweetened as a modification, so a plain or unsweetened ingredient mapped to a sweetened entry is not a match. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the added sweetness, and the syrupy sweetened fruit would change flavour and texture in the dish. The frozen state is not the problem, since frozen berries for baking can match under guideline E. The sweetening is what breaks the match. Condition 1 may hold for a baking use, but both conditions must be met, so the match fails.

The ingredient is freeze-dried açaí powder, a fruit powder made from dehydrated açaí berries, used as an optional addition to a recipe. The USDA match is 'Avocado, for use on a sandwich', which is a different fruit (Persea americana, a fleshy green fruit with a buttery, mild flavour and creamy texture) and is not a processed or dried product. Açaí is a dark purple berry from a palm; avocado is not a sibling variety or a cut of the same food, so guideline B (same food under another name) does not apply. Condition 1 fails: avocado cannot be substituted for freeze-dried açaí powder without changing the preparation, since the powder is a dry, fine ingredient and avocado is a fresh, soft, oily fruit that would not dissolve or disperse the same way. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in colour (deep purple vs pale green), flavour (tart, berry-like vs mild and buttery), and texture. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'kelp' with no preparation state given, and the USDA entry 'Seaweed, kelp, raw' is the same food in its plain, uncooked form. Per guideline A the 60g quantity is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace kelp without changing how the dish is prepared, since no cooking method is implied. Condition 2: with no specified state, a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance from the plain raw kelp the entry describes. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is salt pork, a cured cut of fatback or belly pork that is salted and fatty. The USDA match, 'Salt, table', is sodium chloride, a seasoning with no pork, fat or meat content. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. It fails condition 1, because using salt in place of salt pork would change the dish's preparation, since the pork fat is rendered and contributes cooking fat and substance. It also fails condition 2, because diners would notice the absence of pork fat, meat texture and savoury richness. The 5g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is ground lamb fat, meaning pure lamb fat (essentially 100% fat). The USDA entry is ground lamb at 85% lean / 15% fat, a blended meat product that is mostly lean muscle tissue. Condition 1 fails: using 85/15 ground lamb where lamb fat is called for changes the dish's fat content, how it renders and browns, and its moisture and mouthfeel. Substituting it would also change the dish's flavour, since the lean meat would dominate instead of the fat. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, richness, and appearance, because the substitute is mostly lean meat rather than fat. Per guideline F, a single ingredient is not substitutable for a blend or product containing it, and the match is also a different state of the food. The quantity (100g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain mozzarella cheese, which the standard default version of the product. The USDA match is 'Cheese, mozzarella, low sodium', a modified version with reduced sodium. Guideline D says a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced/low sodium version is not substitutable. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the cheese could be used in the same preparation. Condition 2 fails because reduced sodium lowers the salt level, so a diner would likely notice a difference in taste. The descriptor is not how mozzarella is normally sold, so it does not fall under the exception for normally modified products.

The ingredient is 400g peach, a plain fresh peach. The USDA match is 'Peach, raw', which is the same fruit in its uncooked, default state. The leading weight is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the peach could replace the ingredient in any preparation without changing the method, since no cooking or handling is implied beyond normal knife work (guideline C). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the entry is the same food in its standard raw form, with no variety, ripeness, or processing differences specified. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fried tofu, and the USDA entry 'Tofu, fried' names the same food under the same name. Fried tofu is normally sold as a fried product, so the USDA entry describes the product as a shopper would buy it. Nothing in the entry, such as a flavouring, modification, or different cooking state, changes it. The 40g quantity is ignored per the guidelines. Using the USDA entry in place of the ingredient would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain popcorn, the default unflavoured popped snack. The USDA entry is microwave popcorn, plain, light. Condition 1 (same preparation): the entry is a microwave-popped product that is sold ready-packaged with added oil and salt. Plain popcorn is normally popped at home or air-popped, so the match changes the preparation method. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference): 'light' denotes a reduced-fat, reduced-calorie modification (guideline D: 'lite' is a modification of the plain product). The reduced fat and the bagged-oil coating would change the taste, mouthfeel and greasiness compared with plain popcorn. A diner could notice this difference. Both conditions are not met, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is poultry seasoning, a spice blend typically made from ground sage, thyme, marjoram, rosemary, and black pepper, with the sometimes-added nutmeg or ginger. The USDA match is 'Seasoning mix, dry, chili, original', which is a chili seasoning blend built around chili powder, cumin, oregano, garlic, and salt. These are different spice blends with different dominant flavour profiles: poultry seasoning is herbal and savoury, while chili seasoning is smoky, cumin-forward and spicy. Condition 1 fails in the sense that the match is a different product, and it would alter the dish's flavour profile, so it cannot be used without changing the dish. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would notice the taste difference (chili/cumin flavour instead of sage/thyme). It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a modified default version of poultry seasoning. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a generic solid vegetable fat, which in home cooking is usually a general-purpose hydrogenated shortening. The USDA entry is a specialty shortening for cakes and frostings, made from soybean oil and formulated with emulsifiers and other additives to give a particular whipping and creaming performance. Guideline F treats a different fat, and industrial or food-service specialty fats, as not substitutable for the home ingredient. The source oil is also specified (soybean) where the ingredient is unspecified, and the formulation differs. Condition 1: it could often be swapped into a cake or frosting mechanically, but the specialty formulation may change the batter or frosting behaviour. Condition 2: a diner could plausibly notice a difference in the texture or mouthfeel of a frosting or cake made with a cake-and-frosting specialty shortening versus a general solid vegetable fat. Because the entry is a specialty fat rather than the plain default, the match fails.

The ingredient is fresh cod fillet, which is raw cod sold as a fillet. The USDA entry is raw Pacific cod, the same food under a more specific species and origin name. Guideline B treats the same food under another name as a match, and the 'Pacific' designation is a regional variant of cod, not a different cut, flavour, or state. The parenthetical 'may have been previously frozen' does not matter here: per guideline E, freezing does not show in a fish that is normally cooked and is commonly sold previously frozen. Filleting is handling the recipe does itself and does not change the match. The 395g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Cooking method, taste, texture and appearance would be unchanged, so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sliced almonds, a specific tree nut sold as almond slices. The USDA match is 'Nuts, pecans', which is a different nut species. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), so the first step of the check is whether the swap is literal. It is not. Pecans and almonds differ in flavour: pecans are richer and more buttery, while almonds are milder and more bitter-sweet. They also differ in shape and appearance. Sliced almonds are thin, pale, oval slivers, while pecans are irregular, darker, and brownish with a distinct wrinkled surface. Toasting or baking would also yield different flavours and colours. A diner would likely notice the change in taste and appearance, so neither condition is met. Knife work such as slicing does not change this, and guideline F treats sibling or different foods as non-substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh beef brisket. The USDA entry 'Beef, brisket' names the same cut with no cooking state or added components, so it is the generic food and matches fresh. The 200g weight is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: brisket can be used in place of brisket without changing the preparation. Condition 2: diners would not notice a difference, since it is the same cut. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chicken sausage. The USDA entry, 'Turkey or chicken sausage', is a category that explicitly includes chicken sausage as one of its two named types, so the ingredient is literally one of the foods the entry covers. Condition 1: chicken sausage can be used in place of the ingredient without changing the preparation, since it is cooked and handled the same way. Condition 2: a chicken sausage that falls under this entry is the same product, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. The one caveat is that the entry could describe turkey sausage, which tastes leaner and milder. That is a sibling variety within the entry, not the ingredient itself, so it does not disqualify the match. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is okra cooked without salt. The USDA entry is okra cooked, boiled, drained, with salt. It is the same food and the same cooking method, so the cooking method and appearance would not change. However, the entry adds salt, which the ingredient explicitly excludes. Salt changes the flavour, and a diner would likely taste the difference. Under guideline D, the ingredient asks for the unsalted version and the match is the modified salted version, so it does not qualify. Condition 2 fails because taste would differ.

The ingredient is plain semolina pasta, a single food served as a side or garnish. The USDA match, 'Pasta with sauce, NFS', is a prepared dish that includes a sauce. Condition 1: substituting it would change the preparation, because the pasta would arrive already sauced rather than plain. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in flavour and appearance, since the sauce adds flavour, moisture and colour. The match is not the same food under another name, and it is not the default version of the plain ingredient. Both conditions fail, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is grapeseed oil, used for frying. The USDA match is sunflower oil. Guideline F explicitly states that a different oil is not substitutable (sunflower oil vs canola oil is given as an example). Grapeseed oil and sunflower oil are distinct oils with different fatty acid profiles, smoke points, and subtly different flavour and mouthfeel. Condition 1 (same preparation) could be arguably met since both are neutral frying oils, but condition 2 fails: a diner could potentially notice a difference in flavour or texture from the oil, and the guideline requires a different oil to be rejected. The quantity (100g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is canned walleye, drained: a precooked product packed in water or brine, then drained. The USDA entry is walleye cooked by dry heat (baked, broiled or similar), a fresh-cooked preparation with no canned or packed-medium state. Both are cooked, so the raw/cooked rule does not decide it, but the preparation and product state differ. Canned walleye is moister, softer and flakier, and often carries a brined, processed taste. Dry-heat cooked fillets have a firmer, drier, browned texture and a different flavour. A diner would likely notice the difference in texture and taste, and the dish would not be prepared the same way, since canned fish is typically used flaked or mashed without further cooking. Under the packing-medium and processed-state rules, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is Jerusalem artichokes, a root tuber (Helianthus tuberosus) that is a different plant from globe artichoke and is not a vegetable used in a prepared dip. The USDA match 'Spinach and artichoke dip' is a prepared, mixed product containing spinach, cheese, mayonnaise or sour cream, and globe artichoke hearts. Condition 1 fails: it is a composite ready-made dip, not a raw tuber that could be prepared in place of Jerusalem artichokes, and using it would change the dish's preparation entirely. Condition 2 fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance, since the dip is creamy and contains spinach and cheese, whereas Jerusalem artichokes are crisp or starchy root vegetables. Per guideline F, a blend or product containing the food is not a match for a single ingredient. The name overlap ('artichoke') is misleading, since globe artichoke and Jerusalem artichoke are not the same food.

The ingredient is 460g scallops, which are the real shellfish (typically sea scallops or bay scallops, raw). The USDA match is 'Mollusks, scallop, mixed species, imitation, made from surimi', which is an imitation product made from fish paste (surimi), not a mollusk. Under guideline F, a different food source and processed product is not the same food; this is analogous to the raw source vs processed ingredient. Condition 1: Imitation scallops could in principle be cooked in similar ways (searing, sauteing), but the surimi product is pre-cooked, has a different structure, and is not equivalent for preparation (e.g., searing a raw scallop to a golden crust differs from heating a pre-cooked surimi piece). Condition 2: Diners would readily notice the difference in taste (fish paste vs sweet shellfish), texture (springy, fibrous vs tender), and appearance (uniform, dyed surface vs natural scallop). Neither condition is fully met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is turkey fat (the fat itself, rendered or raw fat from the bird) cut into strips. The USDA entry is ground turkey meat, 93% lean / 7% fat, raw, which is a lean-meat product containing mostly muscle tissue with a small fat fraction. Condition 1: Using 93/7 ground turkey in place of turkey fat strips would change the preparation: the ingredient is a fat to be cut into strips (for rendering, larding, or similar), whereas the match is a ground meat that cannot be cut into strips and has very different fat-to-protein composition. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference in texture (ground meat versus firm fat strips), appearance, and flavour, since turkey fat contributes richness and mouthfeel that lean-dominant ground meat does not. Guideline F also rules out a different cut or a different fat source. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is plain boiled lotus root, with the weight treated as decoration (guideline A). The USDA entry is the same food in the same cooked state (cooked, boiled, drained), so the food identity and cooking state match. The difference is the USDA descriptor 'with salt'. The ingredient does not specify salted preparation, so the match is a plain-to-modified version. Guideline D treats 'with added solution/additives' as a modification that is not substitutable. The added salt also changes the taste of the boiled root, so a diner could notice it. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the same boiling step could be used, but condition 2 fails because the salt changes the flavour.

The ingredient is 70g white peach, a fresh stone fruit (white-fleshed peach variety). The USDA match is White beans, from canned, no added fat, a legume (Phaseolus/Vigna-type bean) packed in liquid. These are entirely different foods: one is a sweet fruit, the other a savoury pulse. Condition 1 fails: a white bean cannot be used in place of a peach without changing how the dish is prepared (a peach is eaten raw or baked as fruit, while canned beans are a cooked legume). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (sweet, floral fruit vs bland starchy bean), texture (juicy flesh vs soft mealy bean) and appearance. The name overlap ('white') is coincidental and does not make them the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Guideline F also rules out substitution between different processed/source states and distinct foods. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fermented fish, shredded (a raw/processed fish product used as a condiment or seasoning ingredient, e.g. in Southeast Asian or Chinese cooking). The USDA match is 'Fish curry', a prepared dish containing fish simmered in a spiced curry sauce with other components such as coconut milk, oil, and spices. Condition 1: Using fish curry in place of shredded fermented fish would change the preparation entirely, since the fermented fish is an added ingredient that is not cooked into a sauce; a prepared curry is a different dish and cannot stand in for an ingredient. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference in flavour (pungent fermented funk versus a spiced curry sauce), texture (shredded dried/fermented fish versus a saucy curry), and appearance. The entry names a different dish with different components, not the same food under another name. Therefore neither condition is met.

The ingredient is toasted wheat germ, and the USDA entry is wheat germ, toasted, plain. Both name the same food in the same state (toasted), so the USDA entry is the same product rather than a different state. The 'Cereals ready-to-eat' prefix is just USDA's category label for the item and does not change what the food is. Condition 1: the toasted wheat germ can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since the cook would add the same product in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same toasted wheat germ. The 'plain' descriptor in the USDA name is the standard unflavoured version, not a modification, and the ingredient does not ask for any flavoured or modified variant. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a steamed Chinese bun, which is a steamed, yeast-leavened wheat-flour bun, generally plain and white. The USDA entry 'Bao bun' names the same category of food under a common English name: a Chinese steamed bun. Under guideline B, regional or culinary names for the same food count. The entry has no modifiers (no filling, no sweetening, no fat or state descriptor), so it is the generic food rather than a modified version. Cooking method is the same, since both are steamed and not altered by the substitution. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance between a plain steamed Chinese bun and a bao bun of the same type. The main residual uncertainty is whether the USDA bao bun is a filled variety, which would be a difference in the dish, but the entry does not indicate a filling, so the match holds.

The ingredient is plain 'tapioca' and the USDA entry is 'Tapioca, pearl, dry', which is the standard dry product sold under the name tapioca (guideline D: plain ingredient to standard default version). The entry names the same food in its dry, as-bought state, so it is the same food under the same name (guideline B). The weight is decoration (guideline A). The main uncertainty is that 'tapioca' can also mean tapioca flour or starch, which would be prepared differently from pearls. Nothing in the ingredient text points to that form, so the default pearl interpretation applies. Under that reading, the match does not alter the cooking method, flavour, texture or appearance of the dish, so both conditions hold.

The ingredient is plain pecans, and the USDA entry 'Nuts, pecans' is the same food with no added state, flavour, or processing descriptor. Under guideline B, the same food under the same name matches. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to the standard default version is substitutable. The 25g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Using pecans in place of the USDA pecans would not change preparation, taste, texture, or appearance, so both conditions hold.

The ingredient is 'long beans and rice', a mixed ingredient containing two components: long beans (yardlong beans, a vegetable) and rice. The USDA entry covers only cooked long-grain white rice with salt, with no beans. Condition 1 fails: using plain rice would drop one of the two components named in the ingredient, so the dish's preparation would not match. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the absence of the long beans in taste, texture and appearance. Guideline F rejects a single ingredient standing in for a blend or combination that contains it. The leading '10g' quantity is ignored per guideline A and does not affect the outcome.

The ingredient is grapefruit sections packed in juice. The USDA entry is grapefruit sections, canned, juice pack, with solids and liquids included. The packing medium matches: juice pack is juice, so there is no syrup-versus-juice mismatch (guideline F). The 'solids and liquids' wording describes the whole as-packed contents, which is how a recipe using canned grapefruit with its juice would be prepared. Canned fruit is normally sold in juice or syrup (guideline D), so the descriptor is not a modification. The entry is the same food in the same canned state, so a cook could use it without changing the preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain unsweetened cocoa powder. The USDA entry 'Cocoa powder, not reconstituted' is the standard dry cocoa powder as bought, which is unsweetened by default; sweetened products are listed separately as cocoa mixes. 'Not reconstituted' only describes the dry form, not a modification, and it is the form a home cook uses. The leading weight is ignored. Condition 1: the powder is used the same way with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same product.

The ingredient is 'herring fillets' with no cooking state stated, so it is the plain, typically raw fish as bought. The USDA entry is specifically 'cooked, dry heat'. Guideline F treats raw versus cooked as a different state, so the match would change the preparation: the recipe would need to cook the fish, and a diner would notice the texture and appearance differ from raw fillets. Condition 1 (no change to preparation) fails, and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance) is also not met. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is tamarind pulp, unsweetened: a concentrated, unsweetened paste from the fruit. The USDA match is canned tamarind nectar, a diluted beverage that is typically sweetened with sugar. Condition 1 fails: nectar is a liquid drink, not a concentrated pulp, so it would change how the dish is prepared (volume, moisture, and the amount of sweetener would all shift). Condition 2 also fails: the added sugar and thinner consistency would change the flavour and texture. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a sweetened or modified version is not a match. The two are not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), so the match is rejected.
