The ingredient is 200g pheasant breast, which by default is raw meat that the recipe will cook. The USDA entry is 'Pheasant, cooked', so the states differ: raw versus cooked. Guideline F lists raw versus cooked as a non-substitutable state difference. Using pre-cooked meat would change the cooking method, since it would not be cooked through the recipe, and the texture and appearance would differ from raw breast that is cooked in the dish. The entry is also not specific to the breast cut. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would change, and condition 2 fails because the diner could notice the difference in texture and doneness. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is frozen apple juice concentrate, thawed and served as is. The USDA entry is ready-to-drink apple juice, canned or bottled, unsweetened, with added ascorbic acid. Condition 1 fails: concentrate is a different product from single-strength juice. It is roughly 3 to 4 times more concentrated, so using ready-to-drink juice would change the quantity of solids and sugar per serving and alter how the dish is prepared (for example, the dilution or reduction step would no longer apply). The added ascorbic acid is also an additive, so the entry is a modified version of plain apple juice (guideline D). Condition 2 fails too: a diner would notice the much thinner, less intense flavour and different mouthfeel compared with thawed concentrate. The 150g weight is ignored per guideline A. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'liquid egg', which in standard usage means a liquid whole-egg product (yolk and white combined), the default version of the plain name. The USDA match is 'Egg, white, raw, fresh', which contains only the albumen. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to a different modified version as not substitutable, and guideline F rejects a different state or component. Condition 2 also fails: egg white is clear and lacks the yolk's yellow colour, richness, and flavour, so a diner garnished with it would notice the difference in appearance and taste. The 'for garnish' note does not change the component. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried figs, chopped. The USDA entry 'Figs, dried, uncooked' is the same food in its dried, uncooked state, so the state matches. Chopping is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). Quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the figs can be used directly in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same dried fig. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a braised chuck tender, which is the same cut as USDA's 'chuck, mock tender steak' (mock tender is the trade name for chuck tender). The USDA entry is also braised, so the cooking state matches and the dish would not be prepared differently. Grade and trimming are handling or default descriptors rather than a different food: the recipe does not specify fat content, and the entry is the standard braised version of this cut. Taste, texture and appearance would match a braised chuck tender, so both conditions hold.

The ingredient is plain, unspecified 'crackers' and the USDA entry is the generic 'Crackers, NFS', which is the same food under its most general name. Per guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to the standard default version is a match. The leading '200g' is only quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the generic entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the recipe does not specify a cracker type that would require different handling. Condition 2: because the ingredient itself names no particular variety, flavour or style, a diner would not expect a specific cracker and so would not notice a difference from the generic version. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is lamb kidney, an organ meat with a strong, distinctive flavour and a different texture from muscle meat. The USDA match is 'Lamb, ground, raw', which is ground muscle meat from lamb cuts such as shoulder or leg. Mincing kidney at home does not change the food into ground lamb, so this is not the same food under another name (guideline B). Kidney is a different food from ground lamb, not a different cut of the same meat, but the principle in guideline F applies: a diner would notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is bay scallops, a mollusk (sea scallop family, small-sized). The USDA match is 'Spices, bay leaf', which is a dried herb/spice from the bay laurel tree. These are entirely different foods: one is a shellfish and the other is a dried aromatic leaf. Condition 1 fails: bay leaf cannot be used in place of scallops without changing the dish entirely, since the preparation (searing, poaching, etc.) would have to change to a completely different food. Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance. The quantity (5g) is irrelevant per guideline A. No naming or regional equivalence applies (guideline B), and the spice entry is not a processed or cooked version of the same food (guideline F). Not substitutable.

The ingredient is a fresh (raw, uncooked) T-bone steak. The USDA entry is cooked, broiled meat, so the match changes the state of the food. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a non-substitutable difference, and a cook would have to apply heat in a different way to use it, which changes the preparation. The USDA entry is also 'separable lean only, trimmed to 0" fat', which describes the lean muscle with all fat removed, while a fresh T-bone steak as bought includes fat and the strip and tenderloin sections. Because the match is cooked rather than raw and is lean-only rather than the steak as sold, it fails condition 1 (it cannot replace the raw steak without changing how the dish is prepared) and condition 2 (diners would notice the difference in texture, appearance and juiciness of cooked trimmed lean meat versus a raw steak).

The ingredient is plain, unsweetened bran flakes. The USDA entry is 'Cereal, bran flakes, flavored', which is a modified version. Guideline D treats flavoured and sweetened versions as modifications of a plain ingredient, and the ingredient specifically asks for unsweetened. Flavoured bran flakes are typically sweetened (sugar, malt, or flavouring), so a diner would taste the difference, and the flavour of the dish would change. Condition 2 fails. Condition 1 is also doubtful, since the sweetness changes the flavour profile of the dish. The quantity (75g) is irrelevant under guideline A. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is a whole red delicious apple, eaten raw as a snack (200g is quantity, ignored). The USDA match is apple juice, 100%, a liquid beverage made by pressing and processing apples. Condition 1: Apple juice cannot replace a snacking apple without changing the dish; the apple is eaten whole as a solid fruit, while the juice is a liquid, so the preparation changes entirely. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice a liquid instead of a crisp, solid fruit, with clear differences in texture, appearance and eating experience. Guideline F explicitly excludes the raw plant/source versus a processed ingredient, and a state difference (solid whole fruit vs juice). Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is plain cottage cheese, which the default USDA entry 'Cheese, cottage, creamed' represents. The match is 'Cheese, cottage, lowfat, 1% milkfat, lactose reduced', which is a modified version: it is lowfat (1% milkfat) and lactose reduced. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a reduced/low-fat or lactose-reduced version is not a match. The descriptors are not how cottage cheese is normally sold under the plain name, since standard cottage cheese is typically creamed rather than 1% lactose-reduced. Condition 1 is arguably met, as the product could be swapped in without changing preparation. Condition 2 is not met: 1% lowfat cottage cheese has a drier, less creamy texture and a different mouthfeel than creamed cottage cheese, and lactose reduction can make it taste slightly sweeter, so a diner could notice the difference. Both conditions must hold, so the match fails.

The ingredient is '25g buttermilk dressing and crumbled blue cheese', which is a composite: a creamy buttermilk-based dressing mixed with crumbled blue cheese. The USDA match is plain 'Buttermilk', which is only the liquid dairy product. Condition 1: Swapping in plain buttermilk would drop the blue cheese entirely and replace a seasoned, emulsified dressing (with oil, herbs, seasoning, and the blue cheese pieces) with a thin cultured liquid. The dish's preparation would change because the dressing's components and its role as a dressing or topping would not be reproduced. Condition 2: A diner would notice the absence of blue cheese crumbles (visible white/blue flecks, sharp funky flavour), the lack of dressing seasoning and body, and the thin liquid texture versus a thick dressing. The match is therefore a single component of a multi-component ingredient, which the guidelines treat as not substitutable (a single ingredient vs. a blend or product containing it). Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is foraged wild raspberries, and the USDA entry is wild raspberries from a regional food composition source. This is the same food, so guideline B applies. 'Foraged' describes how the berries were gathered, not a different product. The USDA entry names no cooked, dried, sweetened, or processed state, so it matches the fresh berries. Condition 1: the berries can replace the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: the wild berries are the same food, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is cane syrup, a plain sweetener made by boiling sugarcane juice. The USDA entry 'Syrup, Cane' names the same food under a slightly different word order, so it is the same product (guideline B). The leading '250g' is only quantity and is ignored (guideline A). 'Warm' is handling the recipe performs and does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the syrup can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would taste and see the same syrup, with no difference in flavour, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh sage leaves. The USDA match is 'Spices, rosemary, dried', which is a different herb (rosemary rather than sage) and in dried form rather than fresh. Under guideline F, a fresh herb vs a dried herb is a different state and not substitutable, and rosemary and sage are different herbs with distinct flavour profiles. Substituting dried rosemary for fresh sage would change the flavour of the dish, and a diner would likely notice the difference in taste and appearance (dried leaves vs fresh green sage). Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is dried coconut flour, sold packaged. The USDA entry 'Flour, coconut' names the same product under the same name. The quantity (40g) and the word 'packaged' describe how it is bought and do not change the food. Coconut flour is a single ingredient with no added flavour, sugar, or modification, so it is the standard default version. Swapping one for the other would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is toasted, salted sunflower seeds. The USDA entry is 'Seeds, sunflower seed kernels, toasted, with salt added', which is the same food in the same state (toasted) with the same modification (salted). Guideline F rejects plain vs toasted, but here both are toasted, so that does not apply. Guideline D treats salted as the default for this product, and the entry names the same product with the same components. The weight '10g' is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel, or see any difference.

The ingredient is turkey liver, a raw organ meat from turkey. The USDA match is 'Roast beef spread', a processed, spreadable product made from roast beef (typically with added ingredients, emulsified into a paste). Condition 1: Turkey liver is raw offal that would be cooked (sauteed, pan-fried, etc.); roast beef spread is a ready-to-eat, pre-processed spread that cannot be cooked in place of liver without changing the dish entirely. It is a different food (different species, different organ/cut, and a processed blend rather than a single raw ingredient), so the preparation would change. Condition 2: A diner would readily notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance between liver and a beef spread. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is Spanish peanuts, chopped. The USDA entry 'Peanuts, spanish, raw' is the same food. Chopping is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). The ingredient does not state roasted, salted or otherwise processed, so the raw default applies. Spanish peanuts are a recognised variety of the same nut, and the match is the same food, not a sibling variety with a different taste. Condition 1: the raw nuts can replace the chopped ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance beyond the chopping that the recipe already specifies. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh chives, and the USDA entry is Chives, raw. Fresh chives are the uncooked herb as bought, so 'raw' matches the fresh state. The 150g weight is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions hold: the entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same herb in the same state.

The ingredient is imitation crab (surimi-based seafood analogue, typically made from processed fish paste such as pollock, with starch, egg white, sugar, and crab flavouring, and often sold as flaked or stick-shaped cooked product). The USDA match is imitation cheese, a dairy-based product made from milk proteins and fats. These are entirely different foods: one is a seafood-based surimi product, the other is a cheese analogue. Imitation cheese is not the same food under another name, and it would not be used in place of imitation crab without changing the dish's preparation, flavour, texture, and appearance. A diner would immediately notice cheese instead of crab-flavoured fish paste. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is buckwheat noodles, cooked. The USDA entry is 'Noodles, japanese, soba, cooked'. Soba is the Japanese name for buckwheat noodles, so this is the same food under a culinary/regional name (guideline B). The entry is cooked, matching the ingredient's cooked state, and the leading weight is ignored (guideline A). Using soba in place of buckwheat noodles requires no change in preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since they are the same product type. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain cherries, which are a raw fruit. The USDA entry is Cherry pie filling, a processed, cooked product that contains sugar, starch thickener, and often added flavourings and colouring. Guideline F rules out a raw food being replaced by a processed or cooked version (raw vs cooked; the raw source vs the processed ingredient). Using pie filling would change the dish's sweetness, texture (thickened, syrupy), and appearance (glossy, gel-like), so a diner would notice. Condition 1 (no change in preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance) both fail.

The ingredient is plain rice flour. The USDA entry 'Rice flour, white, unenriched' is the same food, the standard default version of plain rice flour, with only the usual USDA descriptors (white, unenriched) added. Rice flour is not a different cut, oil, or sugar, and it is not a modified, flavoured, or processed variant. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since unenriched white rice flour is the ordinary product sold under the plain name. The quantity (100g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

Condition 1 (same preparation): The ingredient is a roast, and the USDA entry is also a roast raw, so the cooking method would not change. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference): The USDA entry is a specific cut, eye of round, while the ingredient names only a generic 'roast' with no cut. Guideline F says a different cut of meat is not substitutable, and nothing in the ingredient confirms it is eye of round. The source also differs: the ingredient says 'wild' elk, while the USDA entry is 'free range' elk from a specific producer (Shoshone Bannock). Wild and ranched elk can differ in flavour and texture, and a diner could notice. Because the cut is unverified and the sourcing differs, the two conditions are not clearly met.

The ingredient is a plain, uncooked pork shank, which the recipe would prepare itself. The USDA match is 'Pork, fresh, leg (ham), shank half, separable lean only, cooked, roasted'. Condition 1 fails: the match is already cooked and roasted, so using it would change the cooking method. Guideline F says a raw vs cooked difference is not substitutable, and a plain ingredient replaced by a roasted item changes how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 also fails: the roasted, cooked meat would differ in texture, appearance and flavour from raw shank that is braised or otherwise cooked in the dish. The match also covers only the separable lean, which further changes the cut compared with a whole shank. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is salt-brined fiddlehead ferns, a preserved and seasoned product. The USDA match is raw fiddlehead ferns, which are uncooked and unseasoned. Brining adds salt and changes flavour, and it can also change texture. Guideline F rejects a different state (raw vs processed), and guideline D rejects a plain item matched to a modified version with added solution. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the salt and notice the difference. The quantity (5g) is ignored per guideline A. The ferns are the same vegetable, but the brined state changes taste and handling, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is coconut yogurt, a fermented, creamy, dairy-free yogurt made from coconut milk with a tangy flavour and thick, spoonable texture. The USDA match is Oil, avocado, which is a pressed fat with no fermentation, no tang, no protein or water-based creaminess, and a liquid pourable texture at room temperature. Condition 1 fails: using avocado oil in place of coconut yogurt would change how the dish is prepared (it cannot be spooned, dolloped, whisked into a creamy base, or fermented-tangy flavoured in the same way). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste (no tang, oily flavour), texture (oily rather than thick and creamy), and appearance. The quantity (15g) is ignored per the guidelines. Coconut yogurt and avocado oil are different foods, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply.

The ingredient is breadfruit flour, a processed, dried and ground product. The USDA match is raw breadfruit seeds, which is the raw source material in whole, uncooked form. Guideline F rules out a raw source versus a processed ingredient. Condition 1 fails: raw seeds cannot replace flour without changing preparation. They would need cooking and grinding, and they cannot be mixed into a batter or dough the way flour can. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance, since whole cooked seed pieces are not flour. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is whole milk ricotta cheese; the leading weight (155g) is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Cheese, ricotta, whole milk' names the same product with the same components (whole milk ricotta). Under guideline B and D, this is the same food under the same name, and the plain ingredient maps to the standard default version with no modification such as reduced fat or added additives. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation, since it is the same cheese. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance because the product is identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is oat bran bread that has already been toasted. The USDA entry is 'Bread, oat bran, toasted', which names the same food in the same state. Guideline F rejects plain vs toasted mismatches, but here both sides are toasted, so the state matches. The quantity prefix (195g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match is the same product in the same prepared state, so it can be used without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference, since both are toasted oat bran bread. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a milk-based protein powder in its light version. The USDA entry is 'Nutritional powder mix, light (Muscle Milk)', a light milk-protein powder mix of the same product type. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. The ingredient itself asks for the light version, so the light entry matches under guideline D. Condition 1 holds: the powder can be used in the same way without changing the preparation method. Condition 2 is less certain. Muscle Milk is typically sold flavoured and sweetened, and the ingredient does not specify a flavour, so a diner could notice a difference in taste depending on the recipe. Given the ingredient's unspecified flavour and the product-type match, I judge it acceptable, but the flavour question is the main risk.

The ingredient is plain cooked pork sausage, the standard default version. The USDA match is 'Pork sausage, reduced sodium, cooked', a modified version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a reduced-sodium version is not substitutable, since the descriptor changes the product from what a shopper would normally buy under the plain name. Condition 1 (same preparation) is likely met because both are cooked sausage. Condition 2 is not met: reduced sodium lowers salt, so a diner could plausibly notice a flavour difference. The match therefore fails.

The ingredient is cake flour, a wheat flour with low protein content milled from soft wheat. The USDA match is a cake made with glutinous rice, which is a finished baked product, not a flour, and its main component is glutinous (sticky) rice flour rather than wheat flour. Condition 1 fails: using this entry would mean replacing a flour with a finished cake, which changes the entire preparation method and dish structure. Condition 2 also fails: the diner would clearly notice a different taste, texture (sticky, chewy rice versus a tender wheat crumb), and appearance. Per guideline F, a different flour is not substitutable, and this match is even further removed since it is a different product altogether. The quantity (80g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is pork tenderloin, ground. Guideline C says ground-at-home meat does not change the match, so 'ground' is handling and not a difference in food. The USDA entry is the same cut (pork loin, tenderloin) in raw form, so it is the same food and not a different cut (Guideline F). The entry's 'separable lean and fat' descriptor is the standard way tenderloin is listed, and the ingredient does not ask for a lean-only version. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient in the same preparation, since raw ground tenderloin is cooked the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same cut of pork in raw form. Both conditions are met.

1. Identity: The ingredient is grated coconut meat, which is the same food as USDA 'Coconut, fresh' (raw coconut meat). Grating is knife or handling work and does not change the match (guideline C).
2. Frozen/thawed: Under guideline E, a frozen item matches the fresh entry when it is normally cooked or mixed and freezing does not visibly change it. Frozen grated coconut is commonly used in curries, desserts, and baking, where freezing and thawing are not evident.
3. Condition 1 (preparation): Fresh grated coconut can be used in place of thawed frozen grated coconut with no change to the cooking method.
4. Condition 2 (sensory): Thawed grated coconut may be slightly moister, but the difference in taste, texture, and appearance is minor and would not be noticed in a typical dish.
5. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is store-bought puri, a small unleavened Indian flatbread that is normally deep-fried, which makes it puff up, become crisp, and turn golden and blistered. The USDA match is 'Bread, paratha', a layered flatbread that is cooked on a griddle with fat, giving it a flaky, layered, softer texture. These are different breads, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: a cook using paratha in place of puri would not fry it to puff it, so the preparation changes. Condition 2 also fails: the puffed, crisp texture of puri and the flaky, layered texture of paratha would be noticeable to a diner. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is plain white hominy grits, sold dry. The USDA entry is Quaker hominy grits, white, regular, dry. That is the same product type (white hominy grits, dry) under a brand name, which guideline G treats as a match. 'Regular' describes the standard product rather than a modified version, and 'dry' matches the ingredient as bought. The 200g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient with no change in preparation, since both are cooked the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is unsalted Valencia peanuts, which are plain and unroasted. The USDA entry is Peanuts, valencia, oil-roasted, with salt. The variety matches, since both are Valencia. The two differences are the processing and the seasoning. Oil-roasting changes flavour, aroma, colour and crunch, and guideline F lists plain vs roasted as not substitutable. Added salt is also a flavour change a diner would notice, and the ingredient specifically asks for unsalted. Condition 1 fails because the USDA product is a processed, roasted, salted version, not the same raw food, and it would alter how the dish is prepared and seasoned. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would taste the roasting and salt. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is guava juice, a liquid beverage/juice made from guava fruit with water and typically sugar or no added sugar. The USDA match is guava paste, a thick, dense, sweetened concentrated fruit paste (solid, gel-like, often very high in sugar). Condition 1: guava paste cannot be used in place of guava juice without changing preparation. Juice is a liquid that can be mixed, poured, or reduced into sauces, marinades, or drinks; paste is a solid that would need to be diluted, melted, or whisked with water to approximate juice, which alters how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference in texture (thick and sticky versus thin and liquid) and likely in sweetness intensity and appearance. This is a different state and form of the food (processed concentrate paste versus juice), not the same food under another name. Neither condition is met, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is rye flour, a specific flour made from rye grain. The USDA match is 'Flour, barley', made from barley grain. These are different cereal grains with different protein and gluten characteristics, different flavour (rye has a distinctive earthy, sour note; barley is milder), and different baking behaviour (rye doughs are stickier and denser, with different crumb and rise). This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F explicitly states that a different flour is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because swapping barley flour for rye flour would change the dough handling and results. Condition 2 fails because a diner would likely notice the difference in flavour, texture and crumb. The quantity (50g) is irrelevant per guideline A.

The ingredient is Medjool dates, a specific soft, large, caramel-flavoured variety. The USDA match is Deglet Noor dates, a different cultivar that is firmer, drier, less sweet and smaller. Both are dates, but guideline F rejects sibling varieties with a different taste. Condition 2 fails because a diner would likely notice the firmer texture and milder, less caramel-like flavour, especially in a dish where dates are a main component. The match is therefore not substitutable.

Yellow pickerel is a regional trade name for walleye (Sander vitreus), the same fish that USDA lists as 'Fish, pike, walleye, raw'. The USDA entry is the raw form, which matches the ingredient's 'raw' state. 'Fillets' describes a cut and does not change the match, and the 300g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Because it is the same species under another name, the dish would be prepared the same way and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is miso paste, a fermented soybean paste. The USDA entry 'Miso' is the same food under the same name, with no added flavour, modification, or processing state that differs from a shopper's normal purchase. 'Softened' is handling that does not change the match (guideline C). The quantity is ignored (guideline A). Using the USDA miso in place of miso paste does not change the preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a sesame dressing, a prepared condiment typically made from tahini or sesame paste blended with oil, vinegar or lemon juice, sweeteners and seasonings. The USDA match is 'Sesame seeds', which is the raw whole seed. Condition 1: seeds cannot be used in place of a liquid dressing without changing the preparation; a dressing is poured or emulsified, while seeds would be sprinkled or ground, so the method changes. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (no acidity, oil, salt, or sweetness), texture (dry and crunchy versus smooth and liquid) and appearance. Not the same food under another name, and it is not a plain ingredient matching its default version. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is toasted raisin bread, and the USDA entry 'Bread, raisin, toasted' is the same food in the same state. Raisin bread is the food, and toasted is the state, so both match. Guideline F rejects a plain-vs-toasted mismatch, but here both sides are toasted, so that rule does not apply. The 100g weight is decoration (guideline A). Condition 1: the bread can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is already toasted and needs no further cooking. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product in the same toasted state.

The ingredient is plain buttermilk, used for thinning. The USDA entry 'Milk, buttermilk, fluid, whole' is the same food, so the name matches. The issue is the fat descriptor. Under guideline D, buttermilk is normally sold as low fat, so the default version is low fat. The 'whole' entry is therefore a modified version relative to what a shopper would buy under the plain name, which the guidelines treat as not substitutable. Condition 1 (same preparation) holds, since thinning works the same way. Condition 2 is doubtful because a diner could notice the richer, heavier fat content in the thinned dish. Applying the rule consistently, the match fails.

The ingredient is dry chicken bouillon, a dehydrated seasoning-stock product sold as granules or cubes. The USDA entry, 'Soup, chicken broth or bouillon, dry', describes the same product category: dry chicken bouillon. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient directly in the same way (dissolved or added as a dry seasoning) without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: the dry form is the same product, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The quantity (10g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is clam juice, a liquid broth or stock made from clams, used for flavour in liquid-based preparations. The USDA entry 'Clams, canned' is the shellfish meat, packed with its liquid. These are different foods: a liquid flavouring versus solid clam meat. Using canned clams would add solid pieces of seafood, changing the dish's texture and appearance and its liquid base. Clam juice is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F rejects matches where the processed ingredient differs from its raw or source form. The match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is uncooked gnocchi, a dough-based dumpling made mainly from potato, flour, egg and often cheese. The USDA entry is baked potato with the peel eaten, which is a cooked whole vegetable. Condition 1 fails: baked potato is already cooked, so it cannot replace raw gnocchi that must be boiled or pan-fried. Gnocchi also contain flour and egg, so the USDA entry is not the same product. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (soft, dense, pillowy dumpling versus fluffy flesh with skin) and appearance. Guideline F also rules out a raw/uncooked versus cooked state difference, and the entry is not a named gnocchi product. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is butter beans, a legume (large Lima beans), drained as they come from a can or jar. The USDA match is 'Butter, without salt', a dairy fat made from cream. These are not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. The word 'butter' in the name is a coincidence and does not make them the same product. Condition 1 fails: butter cannot replace drained beans without changing the dish, since it would alter its ingredients, cooking method, and structure. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice a dairy fat in place of beans in taste, texture, and appearance. Not substitutable.

1) The ingredient is '30g toasted oat cereal'; the quantity is decoration per guideline A. 2) 'Toasted oat cereal' describes a ready-to-eat oat cereal that is toasted, which is the defining form of Cheerios (the original, unflavoured oat-based toasted cereal). 3) The USDA entry 'Cereals ready-to-eat, GENERAL MILLS, CHEERIOS' is a branded entry of the same plain product type, which guideline G accepts. It is not a flavoured or modified variant (not honey nut, not frosted). 4) Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient in the same way, since no cooking step changes. 5) Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the product is the same type of toasted oat cereal. Both conditions are met.

1) The ingredient is fresh lamb fat, diced. 'Diced' is knife work and does not change the match. 'Fresh' corresponds to 'raw', which is the USDA state. 2) The USDA entry is 'Lamb, New Zealand, imported, subcutaneous fat, raw'. Subcutaneous fat is the layer of fat under the skin, which is the fat normally sold and rendered as lamb fat, so it is the same food rather than a different cut. Rule F's cut distinction (for example, pork belly vs pork loin) does not apply, because both describe the same lamb fat. 3) 'New Zealand, imported' is a country-of-origin specification, not a modification or processing state. A shopper buying lamb fat would not normally be restricted to a specific origin, and origin does not visibly change the raw fat. 4) Cooking method, flavour, texture and appearance would be unchanged. A diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is radicchio, a red-leaved chicory, and the USDA entry is Radicchio, raw, which is literally the same food in its uncooked state. The quantity (30g) is decoration and is ignored. Condition 1: radicchio used in a dish would be prepared the same way (washed, torn or chopped), so the USDA raw entry can stand in without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same raw vegetable. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus). The USDA match is breadfruit (Artocarpus altilis), a related but distinct species. The two are not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. They differ in taste and texture: breadfruit is starchy and bread-like when cooked, while jackfruit is sweet when ripe and fibrous and meat-like when young and unripe. A diner would notice the difference in flavour and texture, and the dish's preparation could change, so condition 1 and condition 2 both fail. The weight (150g) is ignored per guideline A.

Condition 1 (same food, same preparation): Lulo is the common name for naranjilla, so this is the same fruit. The ingredient is frozen pulp that is thawed, and the USDA entry is the frozen form of the same pulp, which matches under guideline E. Both are used the same way in a dish. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference): The ingredient does not specify sweetness, but the USDA entry is specifically 'unsweetened'. Guideline D treats sweetened/unsweetened as a modification when the plain ingredient does not ask for it. Commercial frozen lulo pulp is often sweetened, so a diner could notice a difference in taste. The match is the right fruit and form, but the unsweetened descriptor is a modification the ingredient does not call for, so it fails condition 2.

The ingredient is pumpernickel bread that has been toasted. The USDA entry is plain pumpernickel bread, which is the same food but untoasted. Guideline F lists 'plain vs toasted' as a state difference that is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because the dish would need an extra toasting step, which changes the preparation. Condition 2 also fails because toasting changes the crust colour, crispness, flavour (Maillard browning), and texture, so a diner could notice the difference. The weight is ignored per guideline A. Because the toasting state differs, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is cooked beans and tomatoes, with no fat, seasoning, or other modification specified. The USDA entry is 'Beans and tomatoes, no added fat', which names the same dish with the same two components. The 'no added fat' descriptor is the standard default for a plain cooked beans-and-tomatoes preparation, not a modified version like reduced-sodium or sweetened, so it falls under the guidance that standard descriptors still match. Condition 1: it could replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since both are cooked and ready to add. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the entry describes the same cooked beans and tomatoes without added fat, which is how such a dish is normally made. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cream of coconut, a sweetened, thick coconut product, which is cooked down. The USDA entry is a prepared pudding made from a dry mix with 2% milk. Condition 1: The match is a starch-thickened, milk-based dessert, not a coconut product. Swapping it in would change the preparation, since the recipe calls for cooking down a coconut product and the pudding is already a finished, gelled dish. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference. The pudding adds dairy flavour, a starch-set texture and a different sweetness and mouthfeel. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a plain or standard version of cream of coconut. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is 'cardoni, fresh', which is cardoon, a vegetable also known as cardoni in Italian and cardoon in English. The USDA entry 'Cardoon, raw' is the same food under a regional or culinary name (guideline B). The leading '100g' is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). 'Fresh' corresponds to 'raw', meaning uncooked (guideline C). Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same uncooked vegetable. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the identical food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is turmeric powder, which is ground turmeric. The USDA entry 'Spices, turmeric, ground' is the same food under a standard name, so it is the same product rather than a different state or blend. The leading '15g' quantity and the word 'optional' are ignored per the guidelines. Condition 1: the spice can replace the ingredient in the same way, with the same preparation (added as a ground powder). Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, colour or texture, because it is the same ground turmeric. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is coleslaw dressing, specifically the reduced-fat version. The USDA entry 'Salad Dressing, coleslaw, reduced fat' is the same product type with the same modification. The quantity (30g) is ignored per guideline A. Under guideline D, when the ingredient asks for a reduced-fat version, the matching reduced-fat entry is a match. Used in place of the ingredient, it would not change preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same food under the same name.

The ingredient is unsalted boiled Brussels sprouts, drained. The USDA entry is cooked, boiled, drained Brussels sprouts with salt. Otherwise these are the same food prepared the same way, so the cooking method matches (condition 1 is not the problem). The difference is the salt. The ingredient explicitly asks for an unsalted version, and the USDA entry is the salted version, which is a modified form of the plain product. Guideline D treats a salted/unsalted difference as a modification, not as the same default product. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the added salt in the sprouts, so the dish's flavour would change. Because the match changes flavour and the ingredient specifies unsalted, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is high oleic canola oil, a specific variety of canola oil with a different fatty acid profile (higher oleic, lower linolenic). The USDA entry is plain canola oil, the standard default. Under guideline D, the ingredient asks for a modified version and the match is the plain version, so it fails. Guideline F also treats a sibling variety or a different oil as not substitutable. Condition 1 (same preparation) is met, since the oil can be used in the same way. Condition 2 is doubtful: high oleic oil is more heat-stable and can have a slightly different flavour and mouthfeel, and the guideline treats these as distinct products. The match is therefore not substitutable.

1. The quantity (100g) is decorative and is ignored. 2. The ingredient is plain 'ground pork', with no lean or fat specification, so it is the generic default. The USDA entry is 'Pork, ground, 84% lean / 16% fat, raw', which is the same food in raw, uncooked form. 3. The 84/16 ratio is a standard, commonly sold lean level of ground pork, not a modified product such as a reduced-fat or processed version. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is ground raw pork that cooks the same way. Condition 2: the difference from other common ground pork ratios is small enough that a diner would not reliably notice a change in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sweet gherkins, which are small cucumbers pickled in a sweet brine. The USDA entry is 'Pickles, cucumber, sweet', which covers sweet pickled cucumbers and explicitly includes bread and butter pickles, a close sibling. Per guideline B, a gherkin is a small pickled cucumber, so this is the same food under a different name. Per guideline D, the ingredient asks for the sweet version, so the sweet-pickle entry matches it rather than being a modified version. The 5g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the pickles can be used directly in place of sweet gherkins with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since both are sweet pickled cucumbers. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is buckwheat groats, a whole-grain seed (kasha when toasted, or raw groats). The USDA match is Cheese, parmesan, shredded, a dairy product. Condition 1: Buckwheat cannot be replaced by shredded parmesan without changing the dish's preparation. Buckwheat is cooked by simmering in water or toasting, as a grain, while parmesan is a shredded aged cheese used as a topping or ingredient and would not behave as a grain (no cooking to a fluffy, separate texture). The food is a different food group entirely, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (nutty, earthy grain versus salty, savoury cheese), texture (grainy, chewy seed versus dry, crumbly or melted cheese) and appearance. Neither condition is met.

Asadero is a Mexican melting cheese, a mild, buttery, pale cheese in the Oaxaca/Monterey Jack family. Colby is a separate American cheese, a mild cheddar relative with a softer, more open texture and a different flavour profile. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 can be argued, since shredded colby could physically replace shredded asadero in a melted dish. Condition 2 fails: colby has a different flavour (more cheddar-like and slightly sweet) and a different melt and stretch in dishes such as quesadillas or queso fundido, which a diner could notice. Guideline F treats a different variety with a different taste as not substitutable, so this is not a match.

The ingredient is baked pita chips, a wheat-flour bread product usually seasoned lightly or plain and baked. The USDA match is plain tortilla chips, which are made from corn masa and are typically fried. Condition 1 is not met: the match is a different food product made from a different base, and swapping it would change the dish's flavour (corn versus wheat) and how the chip is prepared (fried versus baked). Condition 2 is also not met: a diner would notice the corn flavour, the different texture, and the different appearance of tortilla chips compared with pita chips. The quantity is ignored, and this is not a same-food naming match. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw tilapia fillets, 500g; the quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA match 'Fish, tilapia, fried' describes tilapia that has been cooked by frying. Condition 1: substituting fried tilapia for raw fillets would change the preparation, since the dish would have to be cooked by frying rather than by whatever method the recipe uses for raw fish. Guideline F explicitly says raw vs cooked is a different state and not substitutable. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in texture, appearance (breaded/golden exterior, oil absorption) and flavour between fried and raw/plain fillets. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain tapioca starch, a single processed starch used as a thickener or binder. The USDA entry is a dry pudding mix, a blended product that typically contains sugar, flavourings, and often milk solids, and it is meant to be cooked with milk into a pudding. Condition 1 fails: using it in place of starch would change the preparation, since it would add sweetness and other ingredients and would not thicken the same way. Condition 2 fails: the added sugar and flavour would change the taste, and the dish would be sweetened or flavoured differently. This is a blend versus a single ingredient, a different state (processed starch versus a sweetened pudding mix), so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a processed, breaded, pre-formed fish stick product. The USDA match 'Fish, NFS' is a generic, unspecified fish with no breading, forming, or cooked state. Condition 1 fails: using plain fish would require breading and shaping, which changes how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the missing breaded coating and different texture and appearance. The match is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. The weight is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is pork kidneys, trimmed, and the USDA entry is raw pork kidneys from the variety meats and by-products category. It is the same food. The leading '500g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). 'Trimmed' is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). The USDA entry is raw, which matches the uncooked ingredient. Cooking method is unchanged, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance because the food is identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh, raw red seedless grapes. The USDA entry is canned Thompson seedless grapes packed in heavy syrup, with solids and liquids. Condition 1: canned grapes are a processed state, not the fresh fruit, and the heavy syrup packing medium adds liquid and sugar. Using them in place of fresh grapes would change the preparation: the grapes would need draining, and the syrup would enter the dish. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Canned grapes are softer, sweeter, and have a different texture and appearance from fresh grapes. The guideline that canned fruit is normally in syrup explains why the entry is a real product, but it does not make it equivalent to fresh grapes. Guideline F rejects a different packing medium and a different state (raw vs processed). Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is snapper, a specific reef fish (Lutjanidae family). The USDA match is Atlantic cod, a different species (Gadidae family). This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Snapper and cod differ in flavour (snapper is typically sweeter and more delicate), in flesh texture and firmness, and in appearance (snapper has pink-red skin and a different flake structure). A diner would likely notice the difference, and cooking methods that suit snapper may not suit cod in the same way. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable. The weight prefix and the 'raw' state are irrelevant to this conclusion.

The ingredient is glutinous rice flour (sweet rice flour, made from glutinous/sticky rice). The USDA entry 'Flour, rice, glutinous' names the same product under a standard descriptor. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient with no change to the preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same flour. The weight (400g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is hemp seeds with the hull intact (unhulled). The USDA entry is hulled hemp seed, meaning the hard outer shell has been removed. Condition 1: the match is not a same-food-under-another-name case like the examples in guideline B. Hulling is a processing step, not knife work or handling of the kind listed in guideline C, so it changes the product itself. Condition 2: a diner would notice. Unhulled seeds are darker, firmer and crunchier, with a more fibrous, earthy bite. Hulled hearts are softer, paler and milder. The difference is visible and textural. Guideline F also rejects a different processed state of the same source. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain carp, a fish sold fresh or raw by default. The USDA entry 'Fish, carp' names only the food with no cooking state, so it is the generic food and matches the fresh/raw default. The 250g weight is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace carp without changing preparation, since the recipe handles carp as a raw fish. Condition 2: the same species, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is suet, the hard fat from around beef kidneys and loins, which is the food the USDA entry describes. The quantity (465g) is ignored per guideline A. 'Finely chopped' is knife work and does not change the match per guideline C. The USDA entry 'Beef, variety meats and by-products, suet, raw' is the same food in raw form, which is how suet is normally bought for cooking. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the same preparation, such as rendering or mixing into a pudding or pastry. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same fat in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dehydrated minced onion. The USDA entry is dehydrated onion flakes. Both are the same food (dried onion) in the same processed state (dehydrated), differing only in the cut or piece size. Guideline B says a cut of the same food sold as the same thing counts as a match, and the quantity prefix is ignored under guideline A. Condition 1: flakes can be used in place of minced dried onion with the same preparation, since both are rehydrated or added directly to the dish in the same way. Condition 2: the difference in piece size is slight and once cooked or rehydrated, a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is ground ham, and the USDA entry 'Ham, ground' describes the same food under the same name. The leading '200g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Ground ham is a standard product, and the USDA entry is the ground form of the same ham, so it can be used directly without changing the recipe's preparation. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same product in the same form. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is goose liver, trimmed, and the USDA entry is 'Goose, liver, raw'. This is the same food. The 150g quantity is ignored per guideline A. 'Trimmed' is knife work and does not change the match per guideline C. The entry is raw, which matches the fresh ingredient as it would be used in cooking. Using the USDA entry would not change the preparation method, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Masa harina is corn flour that has been nixtamalized (treated with lime) and finely ground, which is the product USDA describes as 'Corn flour, masa'. The 'enriched, white' descriptor matches the standard US-sold masa harina (for example, enriched Maseca-style products), so it is the default version a shopper would buy under the plain name, not a modified one. It is not a different flour (guideline F) or a different state; it is the same food under its standard name (guideline B). The dish would be prepared the same way and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is lamb breast, a cut of lamb meat (fatty, richly flavoured, typically braised, roasted or grilled). The USDA match is turkey breast, sliced, prepackaged, a different meat species with a leaner, milder flavour, different texture and colour, and it is a processed deli-style product. Per guideline F, a different cut or type of meat is not substitutable. Using turkey would change the flavour, texture and appearance of the dish, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 (same preparation without changing method) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture or appearance) both fail.

The ingredient is raw Pacific cod, which is a fresh, uncooked fish. The USDA match is 'Fish, cod, baked or broiled, coated', a cooked product with a coating. Condition 1 fails: the match is already cooked, so using it would change how the dish is prepared (the cook would no longer cook the fish themselves), and the coating adds a step that is not part of the recipe. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, appearance and flavour, since the coating and pre-cooked state are visible and tasted. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a state difference that is not substitutable, and added coating is a modification of the plain fish. Cod species (Pacific vs Atlantic) is not the issue here, so the match fails on preparation state and coating.

The ingredient is ground chicken gizzards, an organ meat (giblet) with a distinctly denser, chewier texture and a stronger, more livery flavour than muscle meat. The USDA entry 'Chicken, ground, raw' is ground chicken meat, typically from breast or thigh muscle. Condition 1: the dish could be prepared the same way, so the cooking method is not altered. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference in taste and texture between gizzard and standard ground chicken. Guideline F treats a different cut of meat as not substitutable. The 400g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Because condition 2 fails, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain 'cheese crackers' with no sodium qualifier. The USDA entry is 'Crackers, cheese, low sodium', a modified version. Guideline D says a plain ingredient matched to a modified version (including low sodium) is not substitutable, and the ingredient does not ask for low sodium. Condition 1 is about the same food, and it is the same product type, but the sodium modification is a formulation change. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would likely notice the reduced salt, since cheese crackers' flavour depends heavily on salt. The quantity (300g) and the '(divided)' note do not affect the match.

The ingredient is 200g steamed scallops, meaning scallop meat that has been steamed as the cooked preparation. The USDA entry 'Scallops, steamed or boiled' is the same food in the same state (steamed scallops). Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient without changing the preparation, since the food is already steamed and the match is the steamed product. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same steamed scallop. The weight is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sunflower oil, and the USDA match is 'Sunflower oil', which is literally the same food with the same name. The quantity (45g) is ignored per guideline A. Using sunflower oil in place of sunflower oil does not change the cooking method, flavour, texture, or appearance, and a diner would not notice any difference. Both substitutability conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried maitake mushrooms (Grifola frondosa). The USDA match is dried shiitake mushrooms (Lentinula edodes). These are different mushroom species, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1: a cook could in principle rehydrate and use either in the same way, so preparation might not change. Condition 2: maitake and shiitake differ in flavour (maitake is earthier and more peppery, shiitake is smokier and meatier), in texture (maitake has a firmer, frillier, more branching structure), and in appearance (maitake clusters look distinct from shiitake caps). A diner would likely notice the difference. Per guideline F, a different variety with a different taste is not substitutable. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is roasted walnut oil, a cooking oil pressed from walnuts and typically sold as a finishing oil with a distinct toasted, nutty flavour. The USDA match is 'Nuts, walnuts, dry roasted, with salt added', which is a whole-nut snack food, not an oil. Condition 1: the walnut oil is a liquid fat used for drizzling or cooking, while the match is a solid, salted roasted nut that cannot replace an oil in preparation without changing how the dish is made (no liquid fat, different cooking behaviour, adds crunchy solids and salt). Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in texture (crunchy pieces versus smooth oil) and taste (added salt, whole nut pieces) and appearance. This is a different form of the food (oil versus whole nut), so it is not substitutable under guideline F (single ingredient in a different state/product form, and the roasted/salted state differs). Quantity is ignored.

The ingredient is raw beef liver, 400g; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Liver, beef' is the same food under a generic name with no state given. Per guideline E, an entry that names only the food matches fresh or plain versions of it, so it counts as the raw form. Condition 1: beef liver can be used directly in place of 'Liver, beef' with no change to preparation, since the match is the same food and no cooking method is implied. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same organ meat. No modified, cooked, processed or different-cut version is involved. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh marjoram sprigs used for garnish. The USDA match is 'Long Island iced tea', a mixed alcoholic cocktail containing spirits, sweetener, citrus and cola-type flavouring. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a component of the herb. Condition 1 fails: it cannot be used in place of fresh herb sprigs for garnish without changing the preparation entirely, since it is a liquid beverage rather than a plant material. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, appearance and form. Per guideline F, a blend or product is not substitutable for a single raw ingredient, and a diner would clearly notice eating a cocktail instead of herb sprigs. The quantity is irrelevant.

The ingredient is 'valencia peanuts' with no preparation stated, so it is the plain nut, most likely raw. The USDA match is 'Peanuts, valencia, oil-roasted, without salt', a roasted and oil-processed product. Guideline F lists plain versus roasted as a state difference that makes items non-substitutable. Condition 1 fails because using oil-roasted nuts changes the preparation: the dish would need to be made with a roasted ingredient, and roasting is a cooking step the recipe does not call for. Condition 2 fails because roasting changes the flavour (toasted and nutty versus raw and mild), the crunch and texture, and the colour, and a diner would likely notice. The quantity (5g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is plain sunflower butter. The USDA entry is sunflower seed butter, the same product under its standard name. The only descriptor is 'with salt added', which is not a modification here: commercial sunflower seed butter is normally sold salted, so a shopper would expect this product under the plain name (guideline D). The quantity (3g) is ignored (guideline A). Cooking method is unchanged, since it is a spread used as-is. Flavour differences from the typical salted product are negligible, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a soft flour tortilla, the standard ready-to-eat wrap-style flour tortilla. The USDA entry is a flour tortilla in the 'ready-to-bake or -fry' category, a distinct product type intended to be baked or fried into shells, chips or tostadas. Condition 1: the match would change how the dish is prepared. A recipe calling for soft tortillas as wraps or for warming would need baking or frying instead, so the cooking method changes. Condition 2: these products are typically firmer and less pliable than soft wraps, and a diner would likely notice the different texture and appearance once cooked. The USDA name does not describe the same product with the same handling. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain guacamole, frozen and thawed, with no mention of tomatoes. The USDA entry is 'Guacamole with tomatoes', a variant that adds tomato pieces. Condition 1: the match is the same general food and could be swapped in, so the preparation would not change. Condition 2: tomato pieces would be visible in appearance and noticeable in taste and texture, so a diner would detect the difference. Under guideline D and F, a plain ingredient mapped to a flavoured or modified version is not substitutable. The thawing is a minor point, since the frozen-versus-fresh issue is secondary to the added tomatoes. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a standard creamy Italian dressing, which is the default full-fat version. The USDA match is 'Creamy Italian dressing, light', which is a reduced-fat version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version (light/reduced-fat) is not a match. Condition 1 is also unmet in practice: the dish would be prepared the same way, but the swap changes the dressing's composition. Condition 2 fails because reduced fat lowers mouthfeel and richness, and a diner could notice the difference in taste and texture. Both conditions are not satisfied, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is red wine vinegar, a sharp, clear-to-ruby vinegar made from red wine. The USDA match is balsamic vinegar, which is made from cooked grape must, aged, and is sweeter, thicker, and dark brown. Condition 1: balsamic could be swapped in mechanically, but it would change the dish's flavour profile, since it is sweeter and more complex with a different acidity character. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference in taste, and the dark colour would change the appearance of a dressing, sauce, or marinade. Balsamic and red wine vinegar are distinct products, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is basil pesto, a plain product type: a sauce of basil, oil, cheese, nuts and garlic. The USDA entry is a branded pesto with basil, ready-to-serve and refrigerated. Per guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches, and the brand name adds no flavour modification. Ready-to-serve and refrigerated are how basil pesto is normally sold, so they do not count as modifications (guideline D). The 5g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the pesto could replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is used as-is. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance for the same basil pesto. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is green mango (raw, unripe mango) used for chutney. The USDA match is 'Chutney', which is a prepared condiment made from fruit, vinegar, sugar, and spices, usually cooked. Condition 1: Substituting chutney for raw green mango would change the preparation entirely; the mango is an ingredient being cooked into chutney, while the match is already the finished condiment. This is not a same-food-under-another-name case, and the cooking method and dish composition would change. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance, since chutney contains sugar, spices and vinegar and is not raw green mango. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is puffed oat cereal, a plain puffed-grain product. The USDA entry is Barbara's Puffins Original, a branded puffed oat cereal in its original, unflavoured form. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. Puffins are not a flavoured or modified version, so they are not excluded. Condition 1: Puffins can replace puffed oat cereal in the same way, with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since both are light, crisp, puffed oat cereals. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is uncooked turkey bacon, which the recipe will prepare itself. The USDA match is turkey bacon that has already been microwaved, so it is a cooked product. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Using pre-cooked bacon would also change the cooking method, since the dish would no longer cook the bacon from raw, and it would alter texture and appearance (microwaved bacon is crisped or shrunken differently and has a different fat rendering). Condition 1 fails because the preparation changes, and condition 2 fails because a diner could notice the difference in texture and appearance. The quantity (250g) is ignored.

The ingredient is onion powder, a dried, ground spice made from dehydrated onion, with a pungent, savoury allium flavour. The USDA match is chocolate beverage powder, dry mix, not reconstituted, which is a sweetened cocoa-based product containing sugar, cocoa, and often milk solids and emulsifiers. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a sibling variety or a different state of onion. Condition 1 fails: substituting it would change the flavour profile and the dish's preparation (cocoa and sugar in place of onion seasoning). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly taste chocolate instead of onion, and the colour and texture of the seasoning would differ. The quantity is irrelevant per guideline A.

The ingredient is fresh cod liver, a fish organ. The USDA match is goose liver, raw, from a poultry bird. These are different animals and different species, so this is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Cod liver has a distinct flavour, is oily and fishy, and has a different texture and colour than goose liver. A diner would notice the difference, and the dish would taste noticeably different. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is plain cranberries, and the USDA entry is 'Cranberries, raw', which is the same food in its standard uncooked form. The quantity (30g) is ignored per guideline A. Plain ingredient to the standard default version matches (guideline D). Substituting the entry would not change preparation, since the cranberries are used as bought, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is turkey pastrami, diced. The USDA entry 'Pastrami, turkey' is the same food. The quantity (495g) and the word 'optional' do not affect the match. Dicing is knife work and does not change the product (guideline C). Using the USDA entry would not alter the cooking method, since the pastrami is used the same way. A diner would not taste, texture or see a difference, because it is the same cured turkey product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chocolate milk, and the USDA entry is 'Chocolate milk drink', which is the same product under a near-identical name. The ingredient's quantity (75g) is ignored per guideline A. Chocolate milk is the plain ingredient here, so the flavoured-milk modification rule in D does not apply: the ingredient itself asks for the chocolate version, and the USDA entry is that version. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is a liquid drink that is used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same kind of chocolate-flavoured milk drink. Both conditions are met.

Fish sauce is a fermented, salted condiment made from fish (usually anchovies), with a strong umami flavour and a liquid form. The USDA entry 'Fish, NFS' is a generic, not-further-specified fish food, which is the raw or cooked flesh of a fish. Using it in place of fish sauce would change the flavour profile entirely, since the dish would lose the fermented, salty, umami character and gain no liquid seasoning. Guideline F treats the raw source versus the processed ingredient as non-substitutable (e.g., gelatin powder vs pork skin), and fish sauce is clearly a processed product derived from fish. Condition 1 fails because the cooking method and preparation would not stay the same: the sauce is a liquid seasoning added to the dish, not a protein. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would notice the difference in taste and texture. The quantity (20g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is sliced lunch ham, which is a deli luncheon meat sold in slices. The USDA entry 'Ham, prepackaged or deli, luncheon meat' names the same product type. Sliced is handling that does not change the match (guideline C), and the quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient in the same preparation, since it is the same product used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same deli ham. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is semolina, the milled endosperm of durum wheat. The USDA entry 'Semolina, unenriched' is the same food. The 'unenriched' label refers only to whether vitamins and minerals were added back after milling. It does not change the flavour, texture, or appearance, and a diner would not notice it. 'Fine' describes the grind, and the USDA entry does not specify a grind, so it is the generic food; fine semolina is still semolina. The same cooking method applies: it is used the same way in pasta, couscous, cakes, or porridge. Condition 1 (same preparation) is met. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance) is met. Enrichment is not one of the modifications listed in guideline D (reduced, low, sweetened, added solution, flavoured), and it has no sensory effect. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is quinoa flour, and the USDA entry 'Flour, quinoa' names the same product under a standard descriptor order. Condition 1: quinoa flour can directly replace this entry without changing preparation, since it is the same food and the weight is irrelevant. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the product is identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is green curry paste, a spiced Thai seasoning blend of green chilies, lemongrass, galangal, garlic, shallot, kaffir lime, coriander, cumin and shrimp paste, with a savory, herbal, spicy flavour. The USDA match is 'Bean paste, sweetened', a sweetened paste made from cooked, mashed sweet red beans (anko-type). Condition 1: Bean paste could be spooned into a recipe in place of curry paste, but it would not fulfil the same role; the dish's preparation (frying the paste in coconut cream, for example) would produce a sweet bean dish rather than a curry. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference: the flavour would be sweet and earthy instead of hot, aromatic and savoury, and the colour and texture would differ from a green curry. Not the same food under another name, and the sweetened bean paste is a different product with a different flavour profile. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is thousand island dressing, a creamy mayonnaise-based condiment with tomato/ketchup, pickle relish and seasonings. The USDA match 'Long Island iced tea' is a cocktail made from rum, vodka, gin, tequila, triple sec, sour mix and cola. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a dressing or a condiment. Condition 1 fails: it cannot be used in place of the dressing without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is a liquid alcoholic beverage with no emulsified creamy base. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. Quantity is ignored per the guidelines. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is pickled eggs, drained. The USDA entry 'Egg, whole, pickled' is the same food: whole chicken eggs preserved in pickling brine. 'Drained' is handling that removes excess brine and does not change the product's identity, so it does not affect the match. The quantity (40g) is ignored per the guidelines. Condition 1: the entry can directly replace the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same pickled egg product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is frozen blackberries. The USDA entry is frozen loganberries. Loganberries are a separate hybrid berry (a cross of raspberry and blackberry), not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 is met in a narrow sense, since both are frozen berries used the same way in cooking. Condition 2 is not met: loganberries have a tarter, distinctly different flavour from blackberries and a reddish-purple rather than near-black appearance, so a diner could notice the difference. Guideline F rejects sibling varieties with different taste, and this is analogous. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is ground pork at 84% lean (about 16% fat). The USDA entry is ground pork at 96% lean (about 4% fat), raw. Both are raw ground pork, so the food itself is the same. The ingredient specifies its lean percentage, though, and the USDA entry differs by 12 percentage points in fat. Condition 1: the fat difference changes how the dish behaves. Higher-fat ground pork renders more fat during cooking, so pan behaviour, browning, and moisture differ, and the recipe's cooking method may need adjusting for the leaner meat. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference in juiciness, mouthfeel, and richness, especially in dishes like burgers, sausages, or meatballs where fat content is central. Because the lean percentage is part of what the ingredient specifies and the gap is large enough to affect texture and flavour, the match fails condition 2 and is not substitutable.

The ingredient is palm kernel oil, a distinct saturated tropical fat with a high saturated fat content, firm at room temperature and with a characteristic flavour and melting profile. The USDA match is sunflower oil, a liquid, highly unsaturated vegetable oil with a neutral flavour. Guideline F explicitly states that a different oil or fat is not substitutable (for example, sunflower oil vs canola oil). Swapping palm kernel oil for sunflower oil would change texture (it would no longer set firm or give the same solidity in fats, confectionery or baked goods), and it would change how the fat behaves in preparation. The quantity of 50g is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 (same preparation without changing method) fails, and condition 2 (diner would notice a difference in texture and mouthfeel) also fails. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is tamari, a soy sauce traditionally brewed with little or no wheat, which gives it a richer, less sharp flavour. The USDA match, shoyu, is a soy sauce made from soy and wheat, which is the standard Japanese style with a different flavour profile. Tamari is not literally the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. The match fails condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference in flavour, and anyone avoiding wheat would notice the presence of wheat. Substituting shoyu for tamari would also change the flavour of the dish, so condition 1 is not cleanly met either. This is a different product with a different taste, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain brown rice, the standard grain. The USDA entry is 'Rice, brown, with gravy, no added fat', a prepared dish that includes gravy.
