Condition 1 fails: using it would change the dish's preparation, since the gravy is already cooked in and the rice is no longer a plain grain to be cooked separately. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste and see the gravy, which changes flavour and appearance. This is a different product (a rice dish with sauce), not the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

Condition 1 (same preparation): Turkey pepperoni and beef-and-pork pepperoni are both sliced, ready-to-eat cured sausages, so they could be used in the same way without changing the preparation. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference): The meat source differs. Turkey pepperoni is leaner, has a milder and different flavour, a different texture and fat profile, and a different colour and appearance from beef-and-pork pepperoni. A diner would likely notice the difference in taste and texture. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Because the second condition fails, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is toasted welsh onion. Welsh onion (Allium fistulosum, a scallion-type onion) is a different plant from the common bulb onion. Under guideline B it is not a regional name for the bulb onion, though it is close to scallion, which maps to Onions, spring. The USDA match 'Onions, raw' is the bulb onion, so the food itself differs. The ingredient is also toasted, and guideline F rejects plain versus toasted, so the match changes the preparation state. Raw bulb onion would not be toasted in the dish, and a diner would notice the difference in flavour, texture and appearance. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails. The quantity (480g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is whipping cream, a dairy product high in milkfat (roughly 30-36%) that is whipped to create aeration and used for toppings, fillings and sauces. The USDA match is Cream of wheat, NFS, which is a breakfast cereal made from milled wheat (semolina/farina) that is cooked in water or milk into a porridge. These are not the same food under another name and are not in the same category. Cream of wheat contains no milkfat and cannot be whipped into a foam. Substituting it would change the preparation method (whipping is impossible; it would be cooked as a porridge instead of being used as a cream), and it would change flavour (cereal grain versus rich dairy), texture (thick starchy paste versus light, fluid or whipped cream) and appearance. A diner would clearly notice the difference. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is plain smooth peanut butter, the standard default product. The USDA match is 'Peanut butter, smooth, reduced fat', a modified version with lower fat content. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced-fat version is not a match, and reduced-fat is not how smooth peanut butter is normally sold. Condition 1 is arguably met since it could physically be spread or stirred in the same way, but condition 2 fails: reduced-fat peanut butter typically has a different texture, is often thinner or has added ingredients, and a diner could notice the difference in taste and mouthfeel. Quantity (10g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is a whole turkey with the skin on, and no cooking state is given, so it is the raw default. The USDA entry 'Turkey, whole, skin (light and dark), raw' is the same food: a whole turkey with skin, covering both light and dark meat, uncooked. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the same whole bird with skin is roasted or otherwise cooked the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the product is the same whole bird with skin. The 250g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is fresh kohlrabi, which is raw and used as an uncooked vegetable. The USDA match is 'Kohlrabi, cooked', which is the same food in a different state. Guideline F explicitly lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Substituting cooked kohlrabi would change the dish's preparation, since the vegetable would already be cooked. A diner would also notice the difference in texture (softer, less crisp) and flavour (milder, sweeter after cooking). Condition 1 and condition 2 both fail, so the match is not substitutable.

Panko breadcrumbs are Japanese-style coarse, flaky breadcrumbs made from wheat bread (crustless), used as a crispy coating for frying or baking. The USDA match is vermicelli made from soybeans, a thin noodle-like pasta/starch product made from soy flour or soy protein, not bread. Condition 1: substituting soybean vermicelli for panko would change preparation (it is not a crumb and would not form a crisp breaded coating; it would need different handling or would not bind/coat the same way). Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference in texture (noodle strands versus crisp crumbs) and appearance. It is a different food entirely, not a naming variant of panko, so guideline B does not apply. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is fresh chorizo, which is raw sausage that must be cooked before eating. The USDA entry is 'Sausage, pork, chorizo, link or ground, cooked, pan-fried', which is already cooked. Guideline F says raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Using pre-cooked chorizo would change the preparation: it could not be cooked in the dish as raw meat would be, and it would change the texture, browning and fat rendering. The weight (170g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 fails because the dish's cooking method would change, and condition 2 fails because the appearance and texture of the cooked sausage would differ from raw chorizo as it cooks. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is bottom round steak, raw, a specific beef cut. The USDA entry is top round steak, boneless, trimmed to 0" fat, choice, raw. Top round and bottom round are different primal cuts (both from the round, but from different muscles). Guideline F says a different cut of meat is not substitutable, and the two differ in texture and tenderness, so a diner could notice. The USDA entry also specifies trimming to 0" fat, which is a further modification from the plain ingredient. The quantity (550g) is irrelevant. Condition 2 fails because texture would likely differ, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is orange juice that has been simmered down until syrupy, so it is a reduced, concentrated, cooked product. The USDA match is raw orange juice, which is uncooked and unconcentrated. Under condition 1, substituting raw juice would change how the dish is prepared, because the cook would have to simmer it down to reach the syrupy state. Under condition 2, a diner would likely notice the difference: raw juice is thinner, less sweet and more tart, and it lacks the glossy, viscous texture of a reduction. Guideline F lists raw versus cooked and the processed versus the source as non-substitutable states, and the reduction is a change of state. Because the match fails both conditions, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is beef head cheese, a cooked, pressed and gelled meat product made from cow head meat set in its own aspic and typically eaten cold and sliced. The USDA entry 'Beef, cow head' is the raw cut of cow head meat, not the processed product. Guideline F rejects a raw source versus the processed ingredient, and the same logic applies here. Condition 1 fails because using raw cow head would require cooking and shaping it into a set, sliced product, which changes the preparation. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in texture, gelled appearance and flavour between a pressed, set head cheese and plain cooked or raw head meat. Quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is gouda cheese (a semi-hard Dutch cheese, sold as a block for eating or cooking). The USDA match is 'Cheese souffle', which is a prepared baked dish made from eggs, milk/white sauce, and cheese, cooked and puffed into a light, airy form. Condition 1: Gouda cannot be substituted for in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Gouda is a raw cheese component that would be melted, grated, or cubed into a recipe, whereas the souffle is a finished baked dish with a different composition (eggs, base sauce, leavening by whipped egg whites). Using a souffle in place of gouda would fundamentally change what the dish is and how it is prepared. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice a difference in taste, texture (soft, airy, custard-like versus firm, sliceable or meltable cheese), and appearance. Gouda is not the same food as cheese souffle, and this is not a regional or trade-name variant. The match therefore fails both conditions.

The ingredient is a sliced beef frankfurter. The USDA entry 'Frankfurter, meat' is the generic frankfurter entry, which covers the same product type: a cooked, cured, smoked sausage sold as a frankfurter. The 'sliced' descriptor is handling and does not change the match (guideline C). The USDA entry does not specify beef, so it is the standard default version of the product, which fits guideline D. Condition 1: the frankfurter can be used in place of a beef frankfurter with the same preparation (heating, slicing, serving). Condition 2: the appearance, texture and general flavour are the same; any difference between a beef-only and a mixed-meat frankfurter is minor and would not reliably be noticed by a diner. Both conditions are met, so it is substitutable.

The ingredient is uncooked rock lobster tails. In common culinary and trade usage, 'rock lobster' refers to spiny lobsters (genera such as Palinurus and Jasus), and rock lobster tails are the tail meat of those animals. The USDA entry 'Crustaceans, spiny lobster, mixed species, raw' is the same food under a regional/trade name, so the match is literal (guideline B). The entry is raw, which matches the 'uncooked' wording, and tail handling or portioning does not change the match (guideline C). It is not a modified, processed, or blended product. Because it is the same food, the dish would be prepared the same way, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is diced ham, which is normally a cooked, wet-cured ham sold in cubes. The USDA match is prosciutto, a dry-cured, air-dried, uncooked ham. Condition 1: swapping prosciutto for diced cooked ham changes the preparation. Prosciutto is typically used thinly sliced or as a raw garnish, and it would not be diced and cooked the way ham is in most recipes. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Prosciutto has a dense, chewy, intensely salty and savoury flavour, and it is a different product from cooked ham. This is a different processing state (dry-cured raw vs cooked), so it is not the same food under another name. Condition 1 and condition 2 both fail.

The ingredient is plain peanut butter (quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA match is 'Peanut butter, reduced sodium', a modified version with sodium reduced. Guideline D states that a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced/low sodium modified version is not a match, since the ingredient does not ask for the reduced sodium version. Condition 1 (same preparation) would hold since it is spread/used identically, but condition 2 fails: reduced-sodium peanut butter tastes measurably less salty than standard peanut butter, so a diner could notice the difference in flavour. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fonio flour, a finely milled product made from fonio grain. The USDA entry is the raw whole grain. Guideline F says the raw source and the processed ingredient are not substitutable, with cornstarch vs corn as the example. The grinding that makes flour is not knife work or handling of the kind the guidelines exempt, so it changes the form of the food. Using whole grain in place of flour would change preparation: it cannot be mixed, sifted, or used as a flour in batters or doughs without milling. A diner would also notice the difference in texture and appearance. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is straw mushroom powder, a dried and ground product made from Volvariella volvacea. The USDA match is raw white button mushrooms (Agaricus bisporus), a different species. Straw mushrooms are not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F rules out a different state (dried and ground powder vs raw fresh) and a different variety with a different taste. Using fresh white mushrooms would change the dish: the diner would taste a different mushroom flavour, the texture would differ, and the powder could not be reproduced from raw slices. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would change, and condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the different flavour and appearance. The quantity (205g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is bone marrow (the soft tissue inside bones, a distinct edible food with a rich, fatty, buttery texture when cooked). The USDA match, 'Beef, neck bones', is the bone itself, typically with meat and connective tissue attached, and is a different food: the marrow is not the bone or the neck meat. Condition 1 fails: using neck bones would not replicate the dish's preparation, since the marrow would not be present as a soft, spreadable or sliceable component. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture and flavour, as bone marrow is a soft, rich, fatty element while neck bones are hard bone with tough meat and cartilage. The quantity (110g) is ignored. Since the match is a different food, not the same food under another name, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw pollock fillets, and the USDA match is cooked pollock. Guideline F says raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because a recipe calling for raw fillets would need to cook them, and cooked pollock cannot be used in their place without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 also fails, since cooked fish differs in texture and appearance from raw fish, and a diner would notice. The 210g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is 'Santa Maria steak, lean'. Santa Maria style beef is traditionally cut from the bottom sirloin tri-tip, so the USDA entry (Beef, bottom sirloin, tri-tip roast) names the same cut under a different label. 'Roast' versus 'steak' is a sales-form difference, not a different cut. The USDA entry is raw, which matches an uncooked ingredient, and 'separable lean only, trimmed to 0" fat' matches the 'lean' descriptor. Condition 1: the same cut can be cooked by the same Santa Maria method, so preparation is unchanged. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference, because it is the same muscle with the same lean trim. Both conditions are met. The main uncertainty is whether 'Santa Maria steak' is meant as tri-tip or as top sirloin; the tri-tip reading is the standard one.

1. The ingredient is 'ground buffalo'. In US grocery and culinary usage, 'buffalo' on a meat label almost always means American bison, so the USDA entry 'Game meat, bison, ground, raw' names the same food under a regional/trade name (guideline B). Water buffalo is the only reading that would differ, and it is not the usual meaning of this label. 2. Ground raw meat matches raw ground meat with no cooking or handling change, so the preparation stays the same (condition 1). 3. Bison and buffalo are the same meat, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance (condition 2). 4. The 150g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pickled monkfish, a fish (Lophius) that is pickled or marinated. The USDA match is Pork, pickled pork hocks, which is a pork cut (pig trotter/leg section) cured in brine. These are different foods from different animals and different species, so they are not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Condition 1 fails: substituting pork hocks for monkfish would change the protein source and the dish's preparation, as a fish dish would be replaced by a pork dish. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture (bone and gelatinous pork skin versus flaky fish), and appearance. The quantity (200g) is irrelevant per guideline A. Per guideline F, a different cut or source of meat is not substitutable.

The ingredient is pistachio kernels, which are shelled pistachio nuts. The USDA entry 'Nuts, pistachio nuts, raw' is the same food in its raw, unprocessed state. The quantity (10g) is ignored per guideline A. Pistachio kernels are normally sold raw or ready to use, and the USDA entry is the standard default version, so it matches the plain ingredient. Condition 1: the nuts can be used directly in place of the kernels without changing preparation, since both are raw shelled pistachios. Condition 2: a diner would see and taste the same nut; no flavour, texture or appearance change arises from substitution. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a codfish fillet, which is cod sold as a fillet, presumably uncooked and in its default form. The USDA entry 'Fish, cod, Atlantic, raw' is the same food (Atlantic cod) in its standard uncooked state. The 140g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Cutting the fish into a fillet is handling, which does not change the match per guideline C. Condition 1: the raw cod could replace a raw cod fillet without changing the preparation method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same species in the same raw state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a maple-flavored corn syrup. Pancake syrup is typically corn syrup with maple flavoring, so it is the same product type with the same flavor profile the recipe asks for. Under guideline D, when the ingredient itself calls for a flavored version, the matching flavored entry counts. Both can be used the same way with no change to preparation (condition 1). The main possible difference is the 'dark' descriptor, which can mean a slightly deeper molasses or caramel note, and pancake syrup is often a lighter amber. That difference is small and unlikely to be noticed in a finished dish, and the two products look similar (condition 2). On balance both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plum sauce, a prepared condiment typically made from plums cooked with sugar, vinegar, chilies, garlic and spices, with a thick, sweet-sour, glossy texture. The USDA match is Carissa (natal-plum), raw, which is the uncooked fruit of a different plant (Carissa macrocarpa, a sour, tart berry-like fruit). Condition 1 fails: the raw fruit cannot be used in place of a sauce without changing preparation, since it would need cooking, sweetening, seasoning and saucing. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice a raw, unseasoned fruit instead of a sweet-savoury sauce in taste, texture and appearance. Guideline F applies, since raw source material is not the processed ingredient. Quantity is irrelevant.

The ingredient is plain dried pear. The USDA entry is 'Pears, dried, sulfured, uncooked', which is the same food (dried pear) with the standard processing descriptor. Under guideline D, sulfuring is how dried fruit such as apricots, apples and peaches is normally sold, so it does not count as a modification. 'Uncooked' describes the dried fruit as bought, which is the state the ingredient assumes. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace dried pear in the same preparation without changing the method. Condition 2: a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since sulfured dried pears are the typical commercial product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is horseradish cream, a creamy condiment made by combining grated horseradish with cream or a cream-based dressing, plus vinegar, sugar and salt. The USDA entry 'Sauce, horseradish' is the generic prepared horseradish sauce, which is typically sharper and more vinegar-based and has a thinner, less dairy-rich texture. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 might be met, since both are used as cold condiments without any change to preparation. Condition 2 fails: horseradish cream is milder, creamier and paler, and a diner would likely notice a difference in taste, texture and appearance. Because the match changes flavour and texture, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is sliced braunschweiger, a smoked liver sausage. The USDA entry is Oscar Mayer Braunschweiger Liver Sausage, sliced, which is the same product. Under guideline C, 'sliced' is handling that does not change the match. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches, and nothing in the entry adds a flavour or modification. Condition 1 holds: it can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2 also holds: a diner would taste and see the same liver sausage, with no difference in flavour, texture or appearance. The 200g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is high oleic sunflower oil, which is a specific variety of sunflower oil with a fatty acid profile high in monounsaturated oleic acid. The USDA match is sunflower oil with less than 60% linoleic acid, which is the standard, lower-oleic type. Under guideline F, a different oil is not substitutable, even when the two look close. The two oils differ in fatty acid composition, which affects smoke point, oxidative stability and, slightly, flavour and mouthfeel. The USDA entry is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 is therefore not clearly met, since the swap changes the oil itself, and condition 2 is at risk because flavour and performance can differ. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is seasoned diced turkey (the quantity 255g is ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry 'Turkey, diced, light and dark meat, seasoned' names the same product: diced turkey meat with seasoning. Condition 1: the diced turkey could replace the ingredient in the recipe without changing preparation, since both are the same seasoned diced meat; any cooking would proceed identically. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, as the USDA entry describes the same seasoned, diced product (light and dark meat is the standard mix for diced turkey). The seasoning is the same descriptor the ingredient itself asks for, so it is not a modification (guideline D). Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is fava beans, shelled, which are fresh or raw legume seeds (broad beans). The USDA match is olive oil, a liquid fat that is a completely different food from a legume. Condition 1 fails: olive oil cannot be used in place of fava beans without changing the dish entirely, since the beans would be omitted and an oil added in their place. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. The quantity prefix (30g) is irrelevant. This is not a same-food-under-another-name case, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is boiled mustard spinach that was salted during cooking, then drained. The USDA entry is the same food, cooked and boiled, drained, but explicitly without salt. Condition 1 (same preparation): the cooking method is the same, but the ingredient specifies salting while the match does not, so the preparation differs by one step. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference): salt is a flavour component, and a diner would taste the difference between salted and unsalted greens. Guideline D treats a salted/unsalted difference as a modification, so the match is not the default version of the ingredient. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a plain artichoke, and the quantity (140g) is decoration under guideline A. The USDA entry 'Artichoke' names only the food with no processing state, so it is the generic food and matches the fresh vegetable (guideline E). Condition 1: the match can replace the artichoke with no change in preparation, since it is the same vegetable. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is fresh huckleberries. The USDA entry is 'Huckleberries, raw (Alaska Native)', which is the same food in its uncooked state. 'Rinsed and dried' is handling that does not change the match (guideline C), and the leading '400g' is quantity, which is ignored (guideline A). The '(Alaska Native)' label identifies a traditional-harvest source and does not indicate a processed, sweetened, or otherwise modified product. Used in place of the ingredient, the match would not change the preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is baking soda (sodium bicarbonate), a leavening agent and pure chemical compound used in cooking. The USDA match is 'Soft drink, cream soda', a sweetened, flavoured carbonated beverage containing water, sugar or sweeteners, flavourings, and carbon dioxide. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a modified version of baking soda. Condition 1 fails: cream soda cannot be used in place of baking soda without changing the preparation. Baking soda provides alkalinity and chemical leavening; a liquid soft drink would add liquid, sugar, and flavour, and would not produce the same rise or reaction. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice sweetness, vanilla-like flavour, and altered texture and colour. The quantity (6g) is ignored per guideline A. Since both conditions are not met, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw ground turkey (460g), which the recipe will presumably cook as part of the dish. The USDA match is 'Turkey, Ground, cooked', which is a different state. Guideline F explicitly lists raw vs cooked as a non-substitutable difference. Condition 1 fails: using pre-cooked turkey would change the preparation, since raw meat must be browned or cooked through in the recipe, while cooked turkey would be added already done and would not undergo that step. Condition 2 also fails: the cooked product would differ in texture and appearance, being firmer, drier and more crumbly, and the final dish would taste and look different. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. The same food under another name rule (B) does not apply, since this is the same meat in a different state rather than a different name.

The ingredient is sake, a Japanese rice wine made by fermenting rice. The USDA match is Cheese, feta, a cheese made from sheep's or goat's milk brined in whiskey-free salt water. These are entirely different foods: one is an alcoholic fermented rice beverage and the other is a dairy product. Condition 1 fails because feta cannot replace sake without changing the dish's preparation (sake is a liquid used for cooking or deglazing, while feta is a solid cheese). Condition 2 also fails because a diner would clearly notice a difference in taste, texture, and appearance. Guideline B (same food under another name) does not apply, and no regional or trade name links the two. The quantity prefix is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient 'Chinese preserved bean curd' is fermented tofu, commonly called furu or fuyu in Chinese cooking. The USDA entry 'Tofu, salted and fermented (fuyu)' names the same food under its Chinese name, which is the same-food-under-another-name case in guideline B. The leading '45g' is quantity and is ignored (A). Both the ingredient and the USDA entry are the standard salted, fermented cubes sold in brine, so the cooking method, flavour, texture and appearance stay the same, and a diner would not notice a difference. The generic ingredient name does not specify red (nanru) or white varieties, so the default version applies. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain egg powder, which is dried whole egg, a single ingredient. The USDA entry 'Egg substitute, powder' is a manufactured product, usually built from egg whites plus added starches, gums, and other additives, and it is not the same food. Under guideline F, a single ingredient versus a product containing it, or a processed/modified version, is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because the formulation differs, so the product would not behave the same in the recipe. Condition 2 also likely fails: the added components and missing yolk fat would alter flavour, texture, and colour in baked or cooked dishes, and a diner could notice. The match is rejected.

The ingredient is 200g of whole buttermilk, and the quantity is ignored per guideline A. 'Whole' here describes the buttermilk as normally sold, not a modification. The USDA entry 'Milk, buttermilk, fluid, whole' is the same food under the standard name. Guideline D notes that buttermilk is typically low fat, so the 'fluid, whole' descriptor matches how buttermilk is normally bought and does not signal a modified version. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, see, or feel a difference, since it is the same product.

The ingredient is walnut oil, a specific nut oil with a distinct strong, nutty flavour and aroma. The USDA match is almond oil, a different oil with a milder, sweeter, marzipan-like flavour. Guideline F explicitly states that a different oil is not substitutable even when it looks close (e.g., sunflower oil vs canola oil). Condition 1 (same preparation method) could arguably be met since both are liquid fats used in the same way, but condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice the absence of walnut oil's characteristic flavour. Walnut oil and almond oil are not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). The weight prefix is ignored per guideline A. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain cream cheese, which by default means regular full-fat cream cheese. The USDA entry is 'Cheese, cream, low fat', a modified version. Guideline D treats a plain-to-low-fat change as a modification that makes the match not substitutable. 'Softened' is handling and does not change the match. Low-fat cream cheese also differs in texture (firmer, less creamy, sometimes watery or gummy) and in richness of flavour, which a diner could notice. Condition 2 is therefore not met, and the match fails on both conditions.

The ingredient is dry cream of wheat, an uncooked cereal product bought as a dry grain. The USDA entry describes cream of wheat that has already been cooked with water on the stove-top, so it is the prepared dish rather than the dry ingredient. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using the cooked entry in place of dry cereal would skip the cooking step the recipe requires, so the preparation changes. The entry also specifies a 1-minute cook-time variety, which adds a further product difference. Condition 2 also fails in practice, since a diner would notice a difference in texture and consistency between dry-cooked and pre-cooked cereal. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is plain unsweetened applesauce. The USDA entry is 'Applesauce, unsweetened', which is the same product with the same descriptor. Guideline A says to ignore the 100g quantity. Guideline D treats the unsweetened version as the matching entry when the ingredient itself asks for it. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any dish with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product.

The ingredient is smoked turnip greens, a fresh leafy vegetable that has been smoked. The USDA match is canned turnip greens, solids and liquids, which is a preserved product packed in liquid and cooked during canning. Condition 1: Using canned greens in place of smoked fresh greens would change preparation, since the canned product is already cooked and comes in a packing liquid, and it lacks the smoking step. Smoking is a state change under guideline F (plain vs smoked), and the raw/cooked and canned vs fresh distinction is also a different state. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference in flavour (the smoky taste would be absent and canned turnip greens have a distinctly softer, cooked texture and a different appearance with liquid). Therefore neither condition is met.

The ingredient is chestnut flour, and the USDA entry is 'Flour, chestnut', which names the same product under a different word order. Quantity (150g) is ignored. Condition 1: chestnut flour can directly replace this entry without changing the preparation, since it is the same ground chestnut product used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food and no modification, blend, or state change is indicated. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is tamarind paste, a processed paste made from the pulp of tamarind pods, with a distinctly sour, tangy, and sweet-tart flavour and a thick, sticky texture. The USDA match is Watermelon, raw, which is a sweet, watery fruit from a completely different plant family. Condition 1 fails: watermelon cannot be used in place of tamarind paste in a recipe such as a chutney, curry, or sauce without changing how the dish is prepared, since it contributes no sourness, no paste consistency, and no acidity. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste (sweet and mild versus sour and tangy), texture (juicy and watery versus dense paste), and appearance. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and it is not a cut or variant of the same product. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is smoked sablefish (black cod), a fatty, rich, buttery fish. The USDA match is smoked haddock, a different species with a lean, flaky texture and milder flavour. Guideline B does not apply because these are not the same food under different names. Guideline F rejects a different variety with a different taste. Condition 1 might be met because both are smoked fillets used the same way, but condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the richer, oilier texture and the different flavour. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain pâté de foie gras, a standard goose liver pâté. The USDA entry is canned goose liver pâté that is smoked. Guideline F explicitly lists 'plain vs toasted/smoked/roasted' as a state difference that makes items not substitutable, and guideline D treats a plain-to-modified version as a no. Smoking adds a distinct smoky flavour that a diner would notice, so condition 2 fails. Condition 1 may hold since the dish could be prepared the same way, but both conditions must be met. The 100g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is regular evaporated milk, the standard canned, unsweetened, concentrated milk sold under that plain name. The USDA entry 'Milk, evaporated, whole' is the same food under a formal name: evaporated milk is normally made from whole milk. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to its standard default version as a match, and nothing in the ingredient asks for a modified version such as skim, sweetened, or fortified. The 200g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 holds because it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 holds because a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is peanut oil, a refined or unrefined oil pressed from peanuts. The USDA entry 'Oil, peanut' is the same food under its generic name, with no modifier, blend, or processing descriptor that changes it. Guideline B and D treat a plain ingredient matching the standard default product as a match. Condition 1: peanut oil can be used directly in place of the same oil with no change in cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same oil. The quantity (5g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dry beef bouillon, a powdered beef-flavoured stock base used for seasoning and flavouring. The USDA entry, 'Soup, beef broth or bouillon, powder, dry', is the same product in the same dry powder form. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient directly, since both are dry powdered beef bouillon added to the dish in the same way, with no change to cooking method. Condition 2: the diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product type. The 15g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 50g hazelnuts, which in cooking means the common hazelnut (Corylus avellana). The USDA entry, 'Hazelnuts, beaked (Northern Plains Indians)', is a different species (Corylus cornuta), a wild North American shrub whose nuts are smaller and have a different flavour and texture. The 50g quantity is ignored per guideline A. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B), so it is a sibling variety with a different taste (guideline F). Condition 2 fails because a diner would likely notice a difference in taste and size. Condition 1 is not clearly met either, because the nut's appearance and yield would differ. Not substitutable.

Step 1: The ingredient is 'bretzel sticks, salted'. 'Bretzel' is the German word for pretzel, and sticks are a shape of the same baked snack, so this is the same food under another name (guideline B). The 300g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Step 2: The USDA entry 'Pretzels, hard, plain, salted' is the standard default version: a hard, plain, salted pretzel with no added flavour or modification (guideline D). Pretzel sticks are typically a hard pretzel product, so the match is the plain standard version. Step 3: Condition 1: a hard salted pretzel can be used in place of salted pretzel sticks without changing how the dish is prepared, since both are used as a crunchy, salted snack or garnish. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste or texture. The only difference is shape, and the USDA entry does not specify shape, so it covers the generic product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a plain tomato and vegetable juice with no sodium specification. The USDA entry is the low-sodium version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version (reduced/low sodium) is not a match, because the ingredient does not ask for that modification. The sodium difference also changes taste: a low-sodium juice is noticeably less salty than a standard tomato and vegetable juice, so a diner would likely notice. Condition 1 is arguably met since the juice could be poured or used in place of the ingredient, but condition 2 fails because the taste differs. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is plain bacon (a raw or cured pork belly slice, typically sold as strips and cooked before eating). The USDA match is 'Bacon bits', which is a processed, pre-cooked, dried, crumbled bacon product, typically shelf-stable and sold as a topping. Condition 1: Bacon bits cannot be used in place of bacon strips without changing preparation. Bacon must be cooked from raw as strips, rendering fat and crisping, whereas bacon bits are already cooked, dehydrated, and crumbled, so they cannot be fried or laid in a dish the same way; cooking method and yield change. Condition 2: A diner would notice differences in texture (crisp, meaty strips versus brittle, dry crumbles), appearance (strips versus small bits), and likely flavour intensity and fat content. Bacon bits are a different product form (processed topping) rather than the same food under another name. Guideline F also treats processed or state-differing products as non-substitutable. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is gold kiwi fruit (Actinidia chinensis, yellow-fleshed). The USDA match is green kiwifruit (Actinidia deliciosa), peeled and raw. Peeling is handling, so it does not change the match. However, gold and green kiwi are sibling varieties, not the same food under another name. Gold kiwi is typically sweeter, with a more tropical flavour and less tartness, and its flesh is yellow rather than green. Guideline F lists a sibling variety with a different taste as not substitutable. A diner would notice the yellow colour and the different flavour, so condition 2 fails. Condition 1 also fails because the variety changes the dish's flavour and appearance.

The ingredient is alfalfa sprouts (fresh, rinsed vegetable sprouts). The USDA match is 'Sugar substitute, liquid, NFS', a sweetener product. These are entirely different foods: one is a raw sprouted vegetable, the other is a liquid sugar replacement. Condition 1 fails: a sugar substitute cannot be used in place of alfalfa sprouts without changing the dish entirely, since it would add sweetness and a liquid form where a crisp, mild sprout is expected. Condition 2 fails: a diner would readily notice the difference in taste (sweet vs. grassy/mild), texture (crisp sprouts vs. liquid) and appearance. No guideline makes these the same food, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is sliced American cheese, which in the US is almost always pasteurized process American cheese sold in slices. The USDA entry, 'Cheese, pasteurized process, American, without added vitamin D', describes that same product. Slicing is handling that does not change the match (guideline C). The 'without added vitamin D' descriptor is the standard default for this product, not a modification (guideline D). Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with the same preparation, since it melts and is handled the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because vitamin D fortification does not affect these. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh ground veal, 310g (quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA match is 'Veal, ground, raw', which is literally the same food: ground veal in its raw, uncooked state. 'Fresh' describes the raw state and 'ground' matches the USDA descriptor directly. Guideline C notes that 'ground at home' for meat does not change the match, and there is no cooking method, flavour, texture, or appearance difference between the two. Condition 1 holds: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 holds: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is kiwi fruit, and the USDA match is 'Kiwi fruit, raw', which is the same food under the same name with no processing or modification. The 300g quantity is decoration and is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the fruit can be used directly in place of the ingredient without any change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the identical raw fruit. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh, raw serrano pepper, diced. Dicing is knife work and does not change the match. The USDA entry is 'Peppers, hot, cooked', which describes a cooked product. Guideline F explicitly says raw vs cooked is a different state and not substitutable. Cooking would soften the pepper's texture, change its appearance, and mellow its sharp, fresh flavour, so a diner would notice. Condition 1 fails because using cooked peppers would change how the dish is prepared (the pepper would already be cooked, which alters the process). Condition 2 also fails because the taste and texture differ. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is fonio grain, rinsed. The USDA entry is Fonio, grain, dry, raw, which is the same food in its uncooked, dry state. Rinsing is handling that does not change the match (guideline C), and the 200g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the grain can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the same dry grain is used. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is napa cabbage, which is the same food as USDA's Chinese cabbage (pe-tsai), so the names match under guideline B. The ingredient is boiled and salted. The USDA entry is 'cooked, boiled, drained, with salt', which matches both the cooking state and the salting. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the USDA match is the same food in the same prepared state, so it can replace the ingredient without changing the preparation. Condition 2: boiled, salted Chinese cabbage would look, feel and taste the same to a diner as boiled, salted napa cabbage. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a raw turkey neck, weight 355g (quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry 'Turkey, neck' names the same cut with no cooking state or modification, so it is the generic food and matches fresh or plain versions (guideline E). It is the same food with the same cut, so no change in cooking method is needed. A diner would not notice a difference between the two. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain beer, and the USDA entry is 'Beer', which is the same food under the same name with no modifier such as light, non-alcoholic, or flavoured. The leading '75g' is quantity and is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: beer can replace beer without changing the preparation method. Condition 2: the diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned navy beans, drained. The USDA entry is 'Beans, navy, mature seeds, canned', which is the same food in the same state. Draining is handling the recipe does itself and does not change the match (guideline C). The leading '75g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Canned beans are the standard default form of navy beans, so this is the plain product, not a modified version (guideline D). Substituting the USDA canned entry would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is the same cut, beef shank crosscuts, and 'trimmed' is handling that does not by itself change the match. The USDA entry, however, specifies 'separable lean only', which is a leaner, modified version of the cut. Plain shank crosscuts are normally sold with the bone, seam fat and connective tissue, and trimmed of excess fat rather than reduced to lean meat alone. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced-fat or lean-only version is not a match. Cooking would also differ: the lean-only meat lacks the marrow, collagen and fat that give braised shank its texture and richness, so a diner would likely notice. Condition 2 fails, and the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is whole wheat sandwich bread slices that are browned. The USDA entry is wheat bread, toasted. Browning bread is essentially toasting it, so the cooking state matches: the recipe's browned state is what the toasted entry describes, not a modification (Guideline F's plain-vs-toasted rule applies when the ingredient is untoasted). The base food is the same type: wheat bread, the standard sandwich-slice form, and the USDA name covers wheat bread generally. Cracked wheat is a minor descriptor in the USDA name and does not change the bread type a shopper would expect under 'wheat' sandwich bread. Condition 1: toasted wheat bread can replace browned wheat bread without changing the preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the browning is equivalent to toasting. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is high oleic canola oil, a plain retail cooking oil. The USDA entry is 'Oil, industrial, canola, high oleic', which is a food-service/industrial specialty version of the same oil. Guideline F states that industrial or food-service specialty fats are not substitutable for the home ingredient. Guideline B (same food under another name) does not rescue it, because the 'industrial' descriptor marks a different product category rather than a regional or trade name for the same item. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the oil could be used in the same way, but the guideline-defined distinction between industrial and home fats means the match fails the standard for substitutability.

The ingredient is hubbard squash, cut into cubes. The USDA entry is 'Squash, winter, hubbard, raw', which is the same food in its uncooked state. Cubing is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). The quantity is ignored (guideline A). Nothing in the recipe is described as cooked or processed, so the raw entry fits. Condition 1: the raw squash can be used directly in place of the cubed hubbard squash without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since it is the same squash in the same form.

The ingredient is parboiled brown rice, dry. The USDA entry is 'Rice, brown, parboiled, dry' from UNCLE BEN'S, which is the same product under a brand name. Guideline G says a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. The quantity prefix (250g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the rice can be used directly in place of the ingredient, and it is cooked the same way (parboiled brown rice is cooked as dry rice), so the preparation does not change. Condition 2: it is the same dry parboiled brown rice, so taste, texture and appearance are the same and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a smoked olive tapenade. The USDA match is plain 'Olive tapenade'. Guideline F states that plain versus smoked is a different state and is not substitutable. Smoking changes the flavour profile noticeably, so a diner would taste the difference. The quantity prefix (30g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2 fails because taste would differ, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is canned roast beef, a shelf-stable, pre-cooked product that is typically moist, soft, and often shredded or chunked, and it is drained before use. The USDA match is deli-style roast beef, a refrigerated, prepackaged product sliced into firm, thin pieces. Both are cooked beef, but they are different products. The canned version is a different processing and packing format with a softer, more tender texture and a different appearance. Substituting deli slices would change the texture and appearance of the dish, and a diner would likely notice the difference. Quantity is ignored. Condition 1 (no change to preparation) is doubtful because the sliced deli product would not behave like drained canned meat in most recipes, and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance) fails. Under guideline F, a different processed state or packing is not a substitute.

The ingredient is cardoon, a vegetable in the artichoke family, sold fresh and uncooked. The USDA entry 'Cardoon, raw' is the same food in its uncooked state. The leading '390g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: cardoon can be used in place of itself with no change to preparation, since the 'raw' descriptor matches the uncooked ingredient. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same vegetable. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh pineapple, cubed, which is the raw fruit with only knife work applied. The USDA match is canned pineapple packed in syrup. Guideline B does not apply because this is not the same food under another name; it is a processed form of it. Guideline F rejects a different state (raw vs processed) and a different packing medium. Canned pineapple in syrup is also softer, sweeter, and has a different texture and appearance from fresh cubes, so a diner would likely notice. Condition 1 can be met in a loose sense, since the fruit could be substituted, but condition 2 fails because taste and texture differ noticeably. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is English muffin rounds that have been split (halved), which is handling and does not change the food. The USDA entry is English muffins, plain, enriched, which is the standard default version of the same product. The 'without calcium propionate' wording is a preservative variant that a shopper would not normally distinguish, and the 'includes sourdough' note only indicates the entry covers sourdough muffins, not a different product. Quantity is ignored per the guidelines. Used in place of the ingredient, the muffins would be prepared the same way and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is '100g whole duck', meaning a whole raw duck (the quantity is ignored per guideline A). The USDA match 'Sauce, duck, ready-to-serve' is a prepared sauce, not the meat itself. It is a different food product (a sauce, a processed condiment-type item) rather than the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: using a duck sauce in place of whole duck would change how the dish is prepared, since the meat would not be cooked or present. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. This is comparable to the raw source versus a processed ingredient pattern in guideline F. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is a combined item: breakfast sausage plus sweet red peppers. The quantity prefix is ignored per guideline A. The USDA match, 'Peppers, sweet, red, raw', covers only the peppers and omits the breakfast sausage entirely. Under guideline F, a single ingredient is not substitutable for a blend or product that contains it. Condition 1 fails because using only raw peppers would drop the sausage and change how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 fails because a diner would clearly notice the missing pork sausage in taste, texture and appearance. Both conditions must hold, so the match is not substitutable.

Papadums and papad are the same food under different names, so the identity condition is met. The problem is the state. A 500g papadums purchase is normally the dry, uncooked wafer, which the cook then fries or dry-roasts as the recipe directs. The USDA entry is 'grilled or broiled', meaning it is already cooked. Using it would skip the cooking step the recipe calls for, which fails condition 1. It would also change the texture and appearance: the grilled product is browned and blistered, while the dry wafer puffs and crisps when cooked in the recipe's own way, so a diner could notice a difference, which fails condition 2. Because the entry is a cooked state rather than the dry product as bought, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is custard apple (Annona species, also called sugar apple or cherimoya-type fruit), which is a different fruit from the apple (Malus domestica). The USDA entry is dried sulfured apple. Guideline B covers regional or trade names for the same food, but custard apple is not a regional name for apple. Dried custard apple has a creamy, sweet, tropical flavour and a soft, custardy texture, while sulfured dried apple is tart-to-sweet, firmer and chewier, with a different appearance. A diner would notice the difference, so condition 2 fails. Condition 1 also fails, since the flavour change alters the dish. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain vegetable shortening, a solid household baking fat. The USDA entry is 'Shortening, household', the standard home shortening made from soybean and cottonseed oils, which is what a shopper normally buys under that name. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to its standard default version as a match. The ingredient does not specify an oil, so the oil blend in the entry is not a modification. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Used in place of the ingredient, it is the same type of fat with the same handling (creaming, rubbing in, melting) and would not change the dish's texture, flavour or appearance in a way a diner would notice. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain asparagus (quantity irrelevant). The USDA entry 'Asparagus, raw' is the same food in its uncooked, default form, with no added processing or modification. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since raw asparagus is the plain form a cook would buy and prepare. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is powdered sugar (confectioners' sugar), and the USDA entry 'Sugars, powdered' is the same product under its database name. Using it requires no change to preparation, and it has the same taste, texture and appearance. The quantity is irrelevant. The only possible concern is the cornstarch anti-caking agent in commercial powdered sugar, but the USDA generic entry covers the standard commercial product, and a diner would not notice the difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain matzo with no sodium qualifier. The USDA entry is 'Crackers, matzo, reduced sodium', a modified version. Guideline D lists reduced sodium as a modification, so a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced-sodium entry is not a match. The recipe does not ask for a low-sodium product, and reduced sodium can change the taste of a plain cracker, so a diner could notice the difference. The descriptor is not how matzo is normally sold under the plain name, so it is not a neutral descriptor either. Condition 2 is not reliably met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient 'sesame paste' is the same food as tahini, which is commonly sold and labelled as sesame butter. The USDA entry 'Sesame butter, creamy' names that same product with no added flavour, sweetener, or modification, so it is the same food under another name (guideline B). The leading '30g' quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the paste with no change to preparation, since both are spooned or stirred in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because both are smooth, creamy sesame pastes. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chickpea flour (besan), a flour milled from dried chickpeas (legume, Cicer arietinum). The USDA match is wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, bleached, a different flour made from a different plant source (wheat). Under guideline F, a different flour is not substitutable (e.g., bread flour vs cake flour). Condition 1 fails: replacing chickpea flour with wheat flour changes the dish's preparation, since chickpea flour is gluten-free, does not form the same gluten structure, and is often used in batters, socca, or pakoras where it behaves differently. Condition 2 also fails: chickpea flour has a distinct nutty, earthy flavour and yellowish colour, and a diner would notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. The 'sifted' descriptor and the 150g quantity do not change this (guidelines A and C).

The ingredient is fresh, raw borage leaves. The USDA match is borage leaves that have been cooked by boiling and drained. Condition 1 fails: the match is a cooked product, so it would change how the dish is prepared. Raw versus cooked is a different state, and the guidelines do not treat it as the same food. Condition 2 also fails: boiling changes the leaves' texture (they soften and wilt), and their flavour and appearance also change, so a diner would notice. Both conditions are unmet, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain egg yolk that has been frozen and thawed. The USDA entry is the same food, raw egg yolk, in its frozen form, and it is pasteurized, which is how frozen egg yolk is normally sold. Under guideline E, a frozen product that is thawed matches the frozen USDA entry of the same product. Condition 1: the yolk can replace the ingredient directly with no change to cooking method, since both are raw yolk used in the same way after thawing. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because pasteurization and freezing do not change the yolk in a way that shows in the finished dish. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is 400g of Jack cheese in block form. Jack cheese is commonly known as monterey jack in the US, so this is the same food under a different name (guideline B). The USDA entry 'Cheese, monterey jack, solid' is the plain, standard default version of that cheese, sold as a block, so no modification is implied (guideline D). The quantity is irrelevant (guideline A). Condition 1: it can be used in place of the block Jack cheese without changing preparation, since it is the same solid cheese for slicing, shredding, or melting. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked goose liver pate, and the USDA entry is 'Pate, goose liver, smoked, canned'. Both name the same food (goose liver pate) in the same state (smoked). The only extra descriptor is 'canned', which is a packaging form the ingredient does not specify. Pate is commonly sold in tins, so this does not change the dish's preparation. The quantity prefix is ignored. Condition 1 is met because the entry can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 is met because a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance between the two products.

The ingredient is ground capon meat. The USDA entry, 'Chicken, capons, giblets, raw', describes giblets (typically heart, liver and gizzard), not the muscle meat of the bird. Guideline F rejects a different cut or part of the same animal, since it changes flavour and texture. Giblets, especially liver, have a distinctly different taste, texture and appearance from ground meat. Cooking would also change: ground meat is typically browned or formed into patties, while giblets are usually simmered or chopped for stock. A diner would notice the difference, so condition 2 fails, and condition 1 fails as well because the preparation would have to change. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is 'queso seco', meaning dry cheese. It is a salty, aged, crumbly garnish cheese such as cotija or queso añejo. The USDA match is 'Queso Fresco', a fresh, moist, mild cheese. Condition 1: the names refer to different cheeses, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Fresh and aged/dry cheeses are different states, which guideline F treats as non-substitutable. Condition 2: a diner would taste the difference, since fresh queso is milder and less salty, and would notice the softer, moister texture compared with a dry, aged crumble. Both conditions are not met. The quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is dried bonito flakes (katsuobushi), a smoked, fermented, dried skipjack tuna product used for dashi and as a topping, providing a distinctive smoky, umami flavour and a flaky, papery texture. The USDA match is 'Cereal, corn flakes, plain', a ready-to-eat breakfast cereal made from milled corn, toasted and sweetened-style grain flakes with no fish, no smoke, and no umami. Condition 1 fails: corn flakes cannot be used in place of bonito flakes in dashi or as a garnish without changing the preparation (they would not extract stock, and would not be prepared the same way). Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice the absence of fish flavour and the different texture and appearance. This is not a same-food-under-another-name case (guideline B) and is a completely different food category, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain non-fat vanilla yogurt (3g, quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry 'Yogurt, vanilla, non-fat' names the same product with the same components: vanilla-flavoured yogurt that is non-fat. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient with no change in preparation, since both are used as-is in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food under the same description. Per guideline D, the fat-free descriptor matches what a shopper would normally buy under this name, and a flavoured yogurt is typically low fat, so no modification penalty applies. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is wild boar, a wild pig, which is a distinct meat with a strong, rich, pork-like flavour and a firmer, fattier texture. The USDA match is wild rabbit, a different animal with lean, mild, delicate meat. Rabbit is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), so the match is a different species. Substituting it would change the flavour, texture and fat content, and a diner would likely notice the difference. Condition 2 fails, and condition 1 is also doubtful because the cooking method and seasoning would often need to change for rabbit. The match is not substitutable.

The USDA entry 'Flour, coconut' is the plain, untoasted coconut flour. The ingredient is the same food, so the food identity matches. However, the recipe specifies 'toasted until golden', which is a processing step the user must perform. Using the untoasted match would skip that step, so the preparation changes (condition 1 fails). Toasting also changes flavour (nutty, roasted) and colour (golden versus pale), so a diner would notice the difference (condition 2 fails). Guideline F explicitly lists 'plain vs toasted' as a different state that is not substitutable. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is cantaloupe melon, quantity 200g is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Melons, cantaloupe, raw' is literally the same food under the same name, with no cooking, modification, or processing descriptor. Raw is the expected state for cantaloupe as an ingredient, and the weight is irrelevant. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same fruit. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a generic cheddar-flavoured snack cracker. The USDA entry 'Crackers, cheese (Goldfish)' names a cheese snack cracker, and Goldfish are a cheddar cheese snack cracker, so it is the same product type under a brand name (guideline G). Condition 1: the match is a ready-to-eat cheese cracker that can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: the eater would not notice a difference in taste or texture, because it is the same kind of product. The only visible difference is the fish shape, which is a brand-specific feature and does not make the food a different type. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a beef and pork sausage, and the USDA entry is pork and beef sausage. Both name the same product with the same two meats; only the order of the meats in the name differs, which is not a difference in the food itself. The USDA entry names no cooking state or modification, so it is the generic sausage a shopper would normally buy under this name. Condition 1: the sausage can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the quantity is ignored and the product type is the same. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the product is the same blend of the same meats. Both conditions are met.

1) Quantity (140g) is ignored per guideline A. 2) Red yautia is a colour variety of yautia (Xanthosoma), the same species as the generic 'Yautia (tannier)' entry, so it is the same food under a regional or varietal name (guideline B). 3) The USDA entry names no state or processing (raw is implied by the 'raw' label), so it matches the generic food (guideline E). 4) Cooking method is unchanged: both are peeled, boiled, fried or mashed the same way. 5) Taste and texture are very close among yautia cultivars, and the diner would not reliably notice a difference in a cooked dish. The main risk is a sibling-variety flavour difference (guideline F), but the colour variant is not a distinct sibling with a clearly different taste. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'Canola Harvest soft spread', a named margarine product. The USDA entry is 'Margarine, 80% fat, tub, CANOLA HARVEST Soft Spread', which is the same branded product, with the USDA adding its standard descriptors (80% fat, tub, ingredient list). The '8g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the same spread can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is used the same way (spread, melt, or mix). Condition 2: because it is the same product, a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The USDA's 80% fat tub descriptor is how this product is normally sold, not a modification. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is minced pork (ground pork, raw, quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry 'Pork, fresh, ground, raw' is the same food: fresh raw ground pork. Minced is the culinary name for ground meat (guideline B and C: handling such as grinding/mincing does not change the match). It is the default version, not a modified or blended product, and not a different cut, since ground pork is a generic form of pork. Substituting it would not change how the dish is prepared (raw, same cooking method), and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a frozen blue cheese dressing, a prepared product. Its main components are a creamy base (typically mayonnaise, oil, sour cream or buttermilk, plus vinegar and seasonings) with blue cheese crumbles. The USDA match, 'Cheese, blue', is the single plain ingredient alone. Condition 1: substituting plain blue cheese for a pourable dressing would change how the dish is prepared, because the dressing's liquid, emulsified texture and added fats and acids would be missing, and it would need to be thinned, emulsified or mixed differently. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in texture (crumbly solid versus smooth, creamy, pourable dressing) and in flavour (no tang, oil or other dressing components). Guideline F applies: a single ingredient versus a blend or product containing it is not substitutable. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is beef bouillon sold canned and condensed. The USDA entry is 'Soup, beef broth bouillon and consomme, canned, condensed', which is the same product under a slightly different name, so it is the same food (guideline B). The 10g quantity is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match is the same canned condensed beef bouillon, so it can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: since it is the same product, a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is corn cooking oil, a plain edible corn oil used for cooking. The USDA entry 'Oil, corn' is the same food under a standard name, since corn oil is the default product a shopper buys under that name. The 6g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: corn oil can replace corn cooking oil in any preparation without changing the method, because they are the same fat. Condition 2: a diner would not detect a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the oils are identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pita pockets, which is pita bread in its standard form. The USDA entry 'Bread, pita, white, enriched' names the same product type with the standard default composition (white flour, enriched), so it is the same food under a common name (guideline B) and the plain default version (guideline D). Condition 1: pita pockets can be used in place of the USDA pita bread without changing how the dish is prepared, since the bread is the same kind and form (pocket pita, not a modified or flavoured version). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the match is the same product. The quantity (250g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

1. The ingredient is vanilla-flavoured Greek yogurt. The USDA entry is Greek yogurt, vanilla flavour, from Chobani. The flavour and product type match, and a branded entry of the same product type is acceptable (Guideline G). The 12g quantity is ignored (Guideline A).
2. The only difference is the 'nonfat' descriptor. The ingredient does not specify a fat level. Flavoured yogurts are typically sold low fat, and vanilla Greek yogurt is commonly sold nonfat, so 'nonfat' describes how this product is normally sold rather than a modification (Guideline D).
3. Cooking method is unchanged, since both are yogurt used as-is. Taste, texture and appearance are essentially the same for a vanilla Greek yogurt, so a diner would not reasonably notice a difference.
4. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is spinach dip, a specific flavoured dip whose defining component is spinach, typically green in colour and with a spinach-herb taste. The USDA match is 'Vegetable dip, regular', a generic vegetable-flavoured dip, which is not the same product. It is a different flavour profile and likely a different appearance (not green, no visible spinach). Condition 1 could arguably be met since both are dips used the same way, but condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in flavour and appearance. Under guideline D and F, a flavoured variant is not the plain or default version, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is parboiled rice: whole rice grains that have been partially cooked under pressure before milling, so they keep their shape and a firm, separate-grain texture when cooked. The USDA match, cream of rice, is a finely ground rice product that cooks into a smooth porridge. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Substituting it would change the cooking method, since it is simmered into a porridge rather than cooked to separate grains, and a diner would notice the smooth, creamy texture instead of distinct grains. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails too.

The ingredient is canned mackerel, drained, which is the same food as the USDA entry 'Fish, mackerel, canned'. The quantity prefix is ignored, and 'drained' is handling that does not change the product's identity. The USDA entry is the generic canned mackerel with no added flavour, modification, or different state. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are canned fish used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same canned mackerel. Both conditions are met.

Condensed milk is a sweetened, concentrated, viscous dairy product (roughly 40% added sugar). The USDA entry is dry whole milk powder with added vitamin D, an unsweetened, dehydrated product. Condition 1 fails: dry milk powder cannot replace a syrupy liquid without reconstitution and added sugar, which changes how the dish is prepared (for example, it would not make a thick, sweet filling or caramel-type base). Condition 2 also fails: the sweetness, thickness, and mouthfeel of condensed milk would be noticeably different. This is a different state (dried vs. concentrated liquid) and a sweetened vs. unsweetened version, so it is not the same food and is not substitutable.

The ingredient is Cornish game hens, which are young domestic chickens (a Cornish chicken cross) and are poultry. The USDA match is 'Game meat, deer, raw', which is venison, a different animal and a different meat category. Venison is dark, lean and strongly flavoured, with a different texture and fat profile from chicken. Swapping it in would change the flavour, texture and appearance of the dish, and a diner would notice. The quantity (75g) is irrelevant. This is not the same food under another name, so it fails both conditions.

The ingredient is plain ground pork, cooked and crumbled. The USDA entry is ground pork, 72% lean / 28% fat, cooked, in crumbles, which is the same food in the same state. The 72/28 ratio is the standard USDA default for ground pork, so it counts as the default version rather than a modified one (guideline D). The 'cooked' and 'crumbled' descriptors match the recipe's own preparation, and the 105g weight is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing the preparation, since it is already cooked and crumbled. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, as the fat-ratio variation within ground pork is minor and the crumbled cooked form looks and eats the same. Both conditions hold.

Pork crackling is pork skin, usually with a layer of fat still attached, roasted or fried until crisp and dense. 'Pork skin rinds' in USDA refers to pork skin that has been fried or puffed into a light, airy snack. Both are cooked pork skin, but the processing differs. Crackling is prepared by roasting the skin of a joint, which yields a dense, layered, glassy texture and often retains some fat. Rinds are typically puffed and hollow, with a lighter, more brittle texture and no fat layer. Substituting rinds for crackling would change the texture and appearance of the dish, and a diner would likely notice the difference. Condition 1 (no change to preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance) are not both met.

The ingredient is a pork rib roast, but the USDA entry is for beef rib eye steak/roast, bone-in. These are different species, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Guideline F states that a different cut of meat is not substitutable, and beef and pork are even more distinct. Using beef would change the flavour, texture, colour, and cooking behaviour (beef rib roast is typically cooked to a different doneness and has different fat and muscle characteristics), and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails because the cooking method and dish would change, and condition 2 fails because taste and appearance would differ. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw jalapeno pepper, and the USDA match is Peppers, jalapeno, raw, which is the same food with the same state (raw, uncooked). The leading weight of 10g is decoration and is ignored per guideline A. No cooking method is implied, and the match is the literal same vegetable, so the dish would not change in preparation, flavour, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is whey protein powder, a single concentrated protein ingredient. The USDA entry is 'Nutritional powder mix, whey based, NFS', a generic category of nutritional or meal-replacement mixes that are whey-based but typically contain added carbohydrates, fats, sweeteners, flavourings, vitamins and minerals. It is not literally the same food, so guideline B does not apply. Under guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend or product containing it is not substitutable.
