The ingredient is artichoke dip, and the USDA entry is 'Artichoke dip', which is the same product under the same name. The quantity (100g) is ignored per guideline A. 'Chilled' describes storage temperature, not a change in the food, so it does not alter the match per guideline C. Condition 1: the dip can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same dip. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried plums (prunes). The USDA match is Bulgur, dry, which is a cracked wheat grain product, a completely different food from dried plums. Condition 1 fails: bulgur cannot replace dried plums in a recipe without changing the dish's preparation, since it is a grain requiring soaking or cooking, whereas dried plums are a fruit used as is or rehydrated. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would readily notice the difference in taste (mild nutty wheat versus sweet, tart fruit), texture, and appearance. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'light sesame dressing' and the USDA entry is 'Sesame dressing, light'. These name the same product with the same descriptor, only reordered. The leading '25g' is quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the light sesame dressing can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is a dressing used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product type with the same 'light' (reduced-fat) modifier the ingredient asks for. Guideline D says a matching modified entry is a match when the ingredient itself asks for that version. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is flax seeds, and the USDA entry 'Seeds, flaxseed' is the same food under the standard name (flaxseed is flax seed). The leading '10g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. No cooking method, flavour, texture, or appearance differs, and no modified, processed, or cooked state is implied. Under guideline B, the same food under another name is substitutable, and both conditions hold.

The ingredient is beef heart, and the USDA entry is 'Beef, variety meats and by-products, heart, raw', which is the same food in its raw form. The quantity (250g) is ignored per guideline A. Beef heart is normally cooked from raw, and the USDA entry is the raw product as bought, so the match needs no change in cooking method. Nothing in the entry indicates a different cut, a processed state, or a modified version. A diner would not be able to tell the difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is buffalo milk (the dairy product from water buffalo). The USDA entry is buffalo meat: top round steak, raw, from free-range buffalo (Shoshone Bannock). These are entirely different foods: one is a liquid dairy product, the other is raw muscle meat. Condition 1 fails: a dairy milk cannot be substituted with a raw steak without changing how the dish is prepared, since the steak would require cooking, cutting and would not act as a liquid. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. The shared word 'buffalo' is only a source-animal overlap, not the same food, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F (different state and raw source vs processed ingredient) also supports rejection. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is 200g pomegranate juice, a plain liquid juice. The USDA entry 'Pomegranate juice, bottled' is the same food under its standard product name, with no added flavour, sweetener, or modified state indicated. Ignoring the quantity as instructed, the match is the same plain product. Condition 1: it can be used directly in place of the juice without changing the preparation method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same juice sold in bottles. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is ranch dressing and the USDA match is 'Ranch dressing', which is the same food under the same name. The quantity (150g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since no cooking method is involved. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is scallion greens (the green tops of scallions/green onions), 75g; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Onions, spring or scallions (includes tops and bulb), raw' is the same food under a regional/culinary name (scallion -> Onions, spring, guideline B). The entry includes the bulb as well as the tops, but the ingredient is specifically the greens; this is a part-of-the-same-vegetable difference rather than a different food, and the greens are the dominant portion of a scallion's edible green-and-white stalk. Guideline B covers cuts/inner parts of the same vegetable sold as the same thing, and the cut here is a sub-portion of the same raw plant. Condition 1: the greens can be used in place of the whole scallion with no change in preparation (same raw handling, chopping, garnishing). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the bulb is the same mild flavour and texture as the greens, only slightly more pungent at the base. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable. Under guideline C, 'raw' is uncooked and the knife work does not change the match.

The ingredient is 400g pork fat, a plain, uncooked animal fat. The USDA entry 'Pork, fresh, separable fat, raw' is the raw fat that can be separated from pork carcass and cuts, which is the same food under a more formal name. Guideline B treats the same food under another name as a match. The entry is raw, which matches the plain fresh ingredient, and it is not a modified or processed product such as lard or rendered fat. Condition 1: it can be used in place of pork fat without changing preparation, since both are raw pork fat handled the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the food is the same fat. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is millet, a grain, and the USDA entry is the same grain in raw form. Millet is normally cooked before eating, so the question is whether the frozen-then-thawed state changes anything. Freezing does not visibly or texturally alter raw dry millet, so a thawed portion behaves like the raw grain. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the same preparation (cooking the millet as usual) without changing the method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance in the cooked dish. Both conditions hold, consistent with guideline E for frozen items that are normally cooked and where freezing does not show.

The ingredient is 500g nectarine, a fresh raw stone fruit. The USDA match is 'Pancakes, plain, prepared from recipe', a cooked flour-based baked product. Condition 1: pancakes are not the same food as nectarines and cannot replace them in a recipe without fundamentally changing the dish's preparation; the nectarine would be removed or the dish would be a different preparation entirely. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance between fruit and plain pancakes. The match is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and it is a different product category (guideline F-style difference of state and source). Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is canned loquats packed in syrup, then drained. The USDA entry is dried apples, sulfured, uncooked. These are different fruits, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Canned loquat is a canned, syrup-packed fruit that is soft and moist. Dried sulfured apple is a dehydrated, chewy, tart product. Substituting one for the other would change texture, moisture, sweetness and appearance, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails too.

The ingredient is mole sauce, specified as reduced sodium. The USDA match is plain 'Mole sauce', with no sodium modification. Under guideline D, when the ingredient asks for a modified version (reduced sodium), the plain entry is not the matching modified entry. Reduced-sodium versions have lower salt, so a diner could notice a difference in taste. Condition 2 is not met, so the match is not substitutable. The 25g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is raw ground bison (250g, quantity ignored). The USDA match is 'Bison, ground, grass-fed, cooked', so the state differs: raw versus cooked. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a state difference that makes items non-substitutable. Using pre-cooked meat would change how the dish is prepared, since the cook would have to skip or shorten browning and the timing of the dish would change. The diner would also likely notice differences in texture and appearance. Grass-fed is an additional specification that may differ in flavour from standard bison. Condition 1 fails because the preparation changes, and condition 2 is likely to fail because texture and appearance would differ. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain Swiss cheese, shredded, with no request for a reduced-sodium version. The USDA match is 'Cheese, Swiss, reduced sodium', a modified version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a reduced-sodium entry is not substitutable. Shredding is handling and does not change the match. The reduced sodium changes flavour: Swiss cheese tastes saltier and more savoury at standard levels, so a diner could notice the difference. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a plain, jarred spaghetti sauce, which is the standard default product with normal sodium content. The USDA entry specifically describes a low-sodium version. Guideline D says a plain ingredient matched to a reduced or low sodium version is not substitutable, because the modification changes taste. A diner would likely notice the reduced saltiness, and the sauce's flavour would differ. The entry is otherwise the same product type (spaghetti/marinara, ready-to-serve), but the low-sodium modifier fails condition 2 and changes the flavour. Condition 1 is satisfied in that it could replace the sauce in preparation, but the taste difference means the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain 'sun-dried tomatoes', which is the same food as the USDA 'Tomatoes, sun-dried' family, so the identity matches. The problem is the packing descriptor. The USDA entry specifies 'packed in oil, drained', which is a packing-medium variant. Plain sun-dried tomatoes are most commonly sold dry (leathery, dehydrated), and the recipe does not ask for oil-packed. Under guideline F, a different packing medium is not substitutable, and under D, adding a modification to a plain ingredient is not the default. Even after draining, oil-packed tomatoes are softer and more pliable and carry residual oil and flavour, so the texture and taste differ and a diner could notice when the dish is prepared with them. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) are therefore not both met.

The ingredient is a 245g dinner roll, a small soft yeast-leavened bread roll typically made with enriched white flour, sugar, fat, and eggs or milk, with a soft crumb and thin crust. The USDA match is whole wheat bagel: a dense, chewy, boiled-then-baked ring made from whole wheat flour with a dark, glossy, firm crust and a tight crumb. Condition 1: a dinner roll could be replaced by a bagel in terms of handling, but the bagel is a different product (ring shape, boiled and baked, different dough) and would not be prepared the same way; it also would not serve the same role in the dish without changing its preparation (e.g., slicing, toasting behavior, baking). Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference in texture (chewy and dense versus soft and light), appearance (ring shape, dark crust versus golden soft roll), and flavour (whole wheat versus refined white enriched dough). Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw pork sausage meat, with the casings removed as a prep step. The USDA entry is 'Pork sausage, link/patty, unprepared', which is the same raw pork sausage product. Removing casings is handling the recipe does itself, which guideline C says does not change the match. Condition 1: the raw sausage can be used in place of the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since the casing is removed either way. Condition 2: the diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the sausage is the same product and the casing is not eaten or served. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is frozen brown rice that has been thawed, so it is already cooked rice that was frozen. The USDA entry 'Rice, brown, cooked, as ingredient' is cooked brown rice prepared for use in recipes. Condition 1: the thawed rice can be used in place of cooked brown rice without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is added ready to use rather than cooked from raw. Condition 2: the thawed rice should not look, taste or feel different from cooked brown rice in the dish, because rice is normally cooked and mixed into dishes and freezing does not show once it is cooked and thawed. Under guideline E, a frozen item that is normally cooked or mixed matches the plain cooked entry. The 'as ingredient' descriptor is USDA's standard wording for cooked rice used in recipes and does not indicate a flavour or modification. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain green tea, which is the standard caffeinated leaf tea. The USDA entry is 'Tea, hot, leaf, green, decaffeinated', so it differs in two ways. First, decaffeination is a modification of the plain product (guideline D: plain to modified version = no). Caffeine removal uses processing that can change flavour, and a diner could notice the difference. Second, the USDA entry describes a prepared hot beverage, while the ingredient is dry tea leaf, which is a different state (guideline F). Condition 1 fails because the match would change the preparation, and condition 2 fails because the flavour may differ. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is soy flour, a finely ground product made from defatted or full-fat soybeans and used as a dry flour in baking and cooking. The USDA match is soy sauce, a liquid fermented condiment made from soybeans, wheat, salt and water. These are not the same food: soy sauce is a liquid seasoning, not a flour. Condition 1 fails because soy sauce cannot replace flour without changing the preparation: it would add liquid, salt and fermented flavour, and the dough or batter would not form the same way. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would clearly taste the salty, savoury soy flavour and notice a difference in texture and appearance. Guideline F also applies: the raw/processed source relationship (soybean vs. processed condiment) and different product states are not substitutable. The quantity is irrelevant.

The ingredient is plain muenster cheese, the standard full-fat version. The USDA match is 'Cheese, Muenster, reduced fat', which is a modified version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a reduced/low-fat entry is not substitutable. Condition 2 also fails: reduced-fat muenster has less fat, so it melts differently, is firmer and drier, and a diner could notice the difference in texture and flavour. Quantity is ignored under guideline A.

The ingredient is raw goose egg, a whole egg from a different bird species. The USDA match is 'Egg foo yung, NFS', which is a prepared dish (a Chinese-style omelette containing eggs plus vegetables, meat or seafood, typically fried and served with gravy). It is not an egg product; it is a composite cooked dish. Condition 1 fails: using egg foo yung in place of a raw egg would change the preparation entirely, since the dish is already cooked and combined with other components. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, appearance and flavour between a whole egg and a fried omelette-style dish with additional ingredients. Guideline B does not apply because this is not a regional name for the same food, and guideline F rejects a composite product standing in for a single ingredient. The goose-versus-chicken egg difference is also not addressed by this match.

Malanga is a regional name for corms of the Xanthosoma genus, the same genus as yautía and tannier (tannia). The USDA entry 'Yautia (tannier), raw' describes the same raw root under other names, so it is the same food under another name (guideline B). The ingredient is fresh and raw, which matches the raw USDA entry, and the weight is ignored (guideline A). Cooking method, flavour, texture and appearance would not change, and a diner would not notice a difference between these closely related Xanthosoma roots. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned mackerel with no packing medium, cut or variety specified, so it is the generic canned product. The USDA entry 'Fish, mackerel, canned' is the same food under the same generic name and state (canned), so no change to the food itself is needed. The weight (120g) is decoration per guideline A. Condition 1: the canned mackerel can be used directly in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are already cooked and canned. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same canned fish type. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a sweetened prune puree, a smooth, blended product. The USDA entry is stewed dried plums (prunes) with added sugar, which is the whole or pieces-of-fruit form, not a puree. Condition 1: the sweetening matches, since the ingredient asks for the sweetened version, so the sugar is not the problem. However, using stewed prunes in place of a puree would change preparation: the fruit would need blending or pureeing first, and the USDA entry describes the fruit in its stewed state rather than a processed puree. Condition 2: in most dishes a diner would notice the difference. A puree gives a smooth, uniform texture and a different appearance from soft whole or chunked prunes, and that texture difference would show in the finished dish. Because the match is a different physical form (whole stewed fruit vs. blended puree), it fails both conditions.

The ingredient is uncooked (dry) rice vermicelli, a dried noodle product that must be boiled or soaked before use. The USDA match, 'Rice, cooked, NFS', is cooked rice grains, not noodles. Using it would change the preparation: the dry noodles would need cooking, while cooked rice is already prepared. Texture and appearance also differ. Cooked rice is a different state and product form (grains versus thin noodle strands), and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails because the dish's preparation would change, and condition 2 fails because taste, texture and appearance would differ. Guideline F rejects raw versus cooked states.

The ingredient is a pork rib roast, a roast cut from the rib section of the loin, usually cooked whole and roasted. The USDA entry is country-style ribs, which are cut from the blade end of the loin (near the shoulder), sold as thick bone-in or boneless strips, and typically braised or grilled. These are different cuts of pork. Under guideline F, a different cut of meat is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because the match would change the preparation from a whole roast to strips suited to braising or grilling. Condition 2 also fails because the shape, bone structure, and eating experience would differ. The quantity (290g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is fresh apricots, pitted. The USDA entry is Apricot, with skin, raw. The food is the same: fresh apricots in the raw state. Pitting is knife or handling work, which the guidelines say does not change the match (C). Apricots are normally eaten and cooked with their skin on, so 'with skin' is the default version of the plain ingredient (D). The quantity is ignored (A). Neither cooking method nor appearance, flavour or texture would change, so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a lemon-lime electrolyte drink, a flavoured product with a specific flavour profile. The USDA match is a branded sports drink (Powerade) with no lemon-lime flavour specified, and Powerade has its own sweetener, electrolyte and flavouring formulation. Substituting it would change the dish's flavour: the lemon-lime character and the taste of the formulation would differ, and a diner would likely notice. The category is close but not the same product, so guideline G (branded entry of the same plain product type) does not apply. Condition 1 is met in the sense that a liquid could be swapped without changing preparation, but condition 2 fails because taste would differ, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dry yeast, the 15g is only a quantity and is ignored, and 'proofed' describes handling done during the recipe (dissolving and activating in warm liquid), which does not change the match. The USDA entry 'Yeast' names only the food with no state, so per guideline E it is the generic food and matches dry, fresh, or plain yeast. Condition 1: the yeast can be used in place of the ingredient, and the same proofing step applies. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same leavening agent. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain 'chicken nuggets', which is a precooked, commonly frozen retail product. The USDA entry is the same food: chicken nuggets, precooked, frozen. The weight (150g) is ignored per guideline A. 'White meat' is the standard default for nuggets and the ingredient does not specify otherwise, so it is not a modified version. 'Not reheated' describes the product as bought, which is how a shopper would normally buy nuggets, so it does not change the match (guideline E). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the dish would reheat or cook the nuggets in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, because it is the same product type with the same taste, texture and appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh mustard greens, chopped, which is the raw vegetable as bought. Knife work does not change the food (guideline C). The USDA entry is 'Mustard greens, fresh, cooked, no added fat', which is the cooked form. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Using the cooked entry would change the dish: the greens would arrive already wilted and softened, so the cooking method and texture would differ, and a diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is canned peas and carrots, drained. The USDA entry is peas and carrots, canned, cooked, with no added fat. Both describe the same food in the same state: a canned, cooked mix of peas and carrots. The 250g is quantity and is ignored. Draining is handling that does not change the match. 'No added fat' is the standard plain canned product a shopper would normally buy, not a modified version. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Gram flour is the same food as chickpea flour, also called besan. Guideline B treats regional and culinary names for the same food as a match. The quantity (175g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: chickpea flour can replace gram flour without changing the preparation method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the two names refer to the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is caraway seed, the whole dried seed of Carum carvi, used as a spice. The USDA match is 'Spices, caraway seed', which is the same food under the standard name, so the identity matches. The quantity (6g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: caraway seed can be used directly in place of itself with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same whole spice. The entry does not name a ground, toasted, or otherwise modified state, so it is not a state mismatch under guideline F. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is shelled pinyon nuts, which are pine nuts from the pinyon pine. The USDA match is salted pistachio nuts, a different tree nut. Under guideline B these are not the same food under another name, so the match fails on identity. Condition 2 also fails: pinyon nuts have a soft, buttery, resinous flavour and a pale ivory colour, while salted pistachios are green, salty and distinctly flavoured. A diner would notice the difference. The quantity prefix is ignored, per guideline A. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is soy milk, a liquid plant-based milk, chilled. The USDA match is SILK Plain soy yogurt, a cultured, thick, tangy product. These are different foods, not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails: soy yogurt cannot replace liquid soy milk without changing how the dish is prepared, since its thickness and cultured nature would alter mixing, pouring and cooking behaviour. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the tangy flavour and thick, spoonable texture. The quantity and chilled state are irrelevant. Because both conditions are not met, the match is not substitutable.

Knockwurst is a finely ground, smoked, emulsified German sausage, usually pork and beef, in a casing that gives a distinct snap. Beef bologna is a different sausage: a cooked, emulsified cold cut, typically beef only, with a softer texture, no casing snap, and a different spice profile. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 is arguably met, since both are cooked sausages that could be heated or eaten in similar ways. Condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice the difference in texture (the casing snap is absent), flavour (smoke and seasoning differ), and possibly appearance. Under the strict criteria, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'Italian flatbread', a generic name. The USDA entry is 'Focaccia, Italian flatbread, plain', which names the same product both as focaccia and by the same descriptor. Under the guidelines, a regional or culinary name for the same food counts as the same food (B), and a plain ingredient matched to the standard default version is acceptable (D). The weight (55g) is ignored (A). 'Plain' matches the unflavoured default rather than a modified version. Condition 1: focaccia can be used in place of Italian flatbread without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: since the USDA entry names the same product, a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is ground veal, a minced meat product. The USDA match is 'Veal, chop', a whole-muscle cut (a loin or rib chop). Ground veal cannot be substituted with a chop without changing preparation: a chop is cooked whole or sliced, while ground veal is crumbled or shaped. Texture also differs, since a chop is a solid piece of meat and ground veal is loose and minced. A diner would notice the difference in appearance and mouthfeel. Guideline F rejects a different cut of meat, and this is a different form of meat altogether. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well.

The ingredient is lamb's kidneys, raw (no preparation or cooking stated beyond the 300g weight, which is ignored). The USDA entry is 'Lamb, variety meats and by-products, kidneys, raw', which is the same food under a standard USDA category name. Both are raw lamb kidneys, so the match is literally the same food. Substituting it would not change the cooking method, flavour, texture, or appearance, and a diner would not be able to tell the difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is unsalted sunflower seed butter, a plain product with no added flavour or modification. The USDA entry is 'Seeds, sunflower seed butter, without salt', which is the same food described in the same terms: sunflower seed butter with no added salt. Under guideline B it is literally the same food, and 'without salt' matches 'unsalted'. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation, since both are used as a spread or ingredient in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the product is the same and the salt content is identical. The 6g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

Almond paste is ground almonds mixed with a large amount of sugar (roughly equal parts or more sugar by weight), giving a dense, firm, sweet product used in baking and confectionery. Creamy almond butter is simply ground almonds, usually unsweetened and often roasted, with a soft spreadable texture. Condition 1 fails: almond paste cannot be swapped into recipes that call for it without changing the preparation, because almond butter lacks the sugar and firmness that make the paste structural in fillings and batters. Condition 2 fails: the sweetness, flavour and texture differ enough that a diner would notice. Guideline F also rejects a different product that looks close, and this is a different product with a different sugar and texture profile, so it is not an acceptable match.

The ingredient is a soft taco flour tortilla (wrap), and the USDA entry is a Mission Flour Tortilla in the soft taco size. The quantity (300g) is ignored per guideline A. The product type is the same: a wheat flour tortilla of soft taco size. Guideline G allows a branded entry of the same plain product type. The USDA descriptor '8 inch' only describes the standard size such tortillas are sold in, not a modification. Because it is the same product, the dish would be prepared the same way and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

'Vegetable spaghetti' is the common name for spaghetti squash, the same food as the USDA entry 'Squash, winter, spaghetti, raw' (guideline B: same food under another name). The 375g is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). The USDA entry is the plain raw form, and spiralizing or cutting the squash is handling that does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the squash can be used in place of the ingredient and cooked the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since it is the same vegetable with the same taste, texture and appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain orange juice, sold store-bought. The USDA entry 'Orange juice, 100%, NFS' is the generic 100% orange juice, with no added sweeteners, flavours, or modifications. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient directly, since the dish's preparation does not change when juice is swapped for juice. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the match is the same food, and 'NFS' only means the processing method is unspecified. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to the standard default version is substitutable. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cooked wholegrain rice. Wholegrain rice is rice with only the husk removed, so the bran and germ remain, which is the same food as brown rice under another name (guideline B). The USDA entry is brown rice, cooked, with no added fat. Both are in the cooked state, so no cooking method changes (condition 1). Plain cooked brown rice without added fat matches the default version of the food (guideline D). The quantity is ignored (guideline A). Taste, texture and appearance should be the same to a diner, since it is the same grain prepared the same way (condition 2). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'sweet Italian dressing', a standard full-calorie Italian-style dressing with added sugar, which gives it a noticeably sweeter flavour. The USDA entry is 'Salad dressing, italian dressing, reduced calorie'. Under guideline D, a plain or specified product matched to a reduced/low version is a modification, so this is not the same product. Reduced-calorie dressing contains less oil and often uses fillers or sweeteners, which changes mouthfeel, viscosity and flavour balance, so a diner would likely notice the difference. The entry also does not specify the sweet variant. Condition 1 might be met since it could be poured or tossed in the same way, but condition 2 fails because taste and texture would differ. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is salted fish, a preserved product that is salt-cured and usually dried or brined, and it would be used as a cured fish in the dish. The USDA match 'Fish, stick' is a breaded, pre-cooked or frozen processed product made from minced fish. The two differ in preservation method, state (cured versus breaded and cooked), flavour (intensely salty and cured versus mild and breaded), and texture and appearance (dense, flaky cured fish versus a breaded coating over a formed block). Using fish sticks would change how the dish is prepared, for example by requiring removal of the breading and altering soaking or desalting steps, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well.

The ingredient is chestnut flour, a finely ground, dried form of chestnuts. The USDA match is 'Chestnuts', which is the whole raw nut. Condition 1: Using whole raw chestnuts in place of flour would change the preparation. The nuts would need to be shelled, peeled, dried and milled, and they cannot be measured and stirred into batters as a flour. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference. Flour gives a fine, uniform, powdery texture and a different baked crumb, while whole chestnuts give chunks and a moist, starchy bite. Guideline F lists 'the raw plant/source vs the processed ingredient' as not substitutable, and this is that case. Guideline A (ignoring the 50g quantity) does not change this, and no naming equivalence applies. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is chokecherries prepared with sugar, so it is sweetened fruit. The USDA entry is raw, pitted chokecherries with no added sugar. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to an unsweetened or modified version is not acceptable, and the ingredient itself asks for the sugared version. Condition 1 is not met because the match omits an ingredient the dish calls for. Condition 2 is also not met because a diner would taste the difference between sweetened and unsweetened chokecherries. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is soy protein isolate (about 90% protein, with fat, carbohydrate and fibre largely removed). The USDA entry is soy protein concentrate produced by alcohol extraction (about 65-70% protein, with more residual carbohydrate, fibre and flavour compounds). These are different products, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 can fail because the two products have different protein content and functional properties, so a cook would not use them interchangeably without changing the recipe's hydration, binding or protein level. Condition 2 can fail because concentrate typically has a stronger beany, earthy flavour and a different texture and colour than isolate, which a diner could notice. Guideline F treats different processing states of the same ingredient as non-substitutable. Neither condition is clearly met.

The ingredient is plain fresh lemongrass (150g; the quantity is ignored). The USDA entry is 'SMART SOUP, Vietnamese Carrot Lemongrass', a branded prepared soup product containing carrot, lemongrass and other components. Condition 1 fails: a soup product is not a substitute for a raw herb/stalk; it cannot be added to a dish in place of fresh lemongrass without changing preparation, since it brings a whole liquid soup base with carrots and other ingredients. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the soup's carrot and broth flavour and notice a different dish. Per guideline F, a single ingredient versus a product containing it, and a processed product versus the raw source, are not substitutable. The entry is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply.

The ingredient is fresh oyster mushrooms, a specific variety with a distinct flavour, texture and appearance. The USDA entry is 'Mushrooms, NS as to form, cooked', a generic mushroom that is cooked and not identified as oyster. Condition 1 fails: the entry is a cooked product, while the recipe calls for a raw ingredient that the cook would prepare, so the cooking method and the stage of preparation would change. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice a difference, since the generic cooked mushroom differs from oyster mushrooms in flavour, texture and appearance. Guideline F excludes both a different variety with a different taste and a different state (raw vs cooked). The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh Granny Smith apple, diced. The USDA entry is Apples, granny smith, with skin, raw. Condition 1: Granny Smith is the same variety named in both, and 'raw' means uncooked; dicing is knife work the recipe performs and does not change the match (guideline C). 'With skin' is the normal way apples are sold and eaten, so it is the default version, not a modification (guideline D). The dish can therefore use this entry in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel, or see a difference between diced raw Granny Smith with skin and diced raw Granny Smith the ingredient describes, since the variety and state are identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is French bread that has been toasted, at 60g (the weight is ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry is 'Bread, French or Vienna, toasted', which is the same food under a standard name (B) and carries the same processing state. Guideline F rejects plain-versus-toasted mismatches, but here both sides are toasted, so that concern does not apply. Toasted bread is used as-is in the dish, so the preparation is unchanged, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is toasted fennel seeds (4g, quantity ignored). The USDA match is 'Spices, fennel seed', which is the raw/untoasted whole spice. Guideline F explicitly states that plain vs toasted is a different state and is not substitutable. Toasting changes the aroma and flavour of fennel seed (it becomes more nutty and intense), and a diner would likely notice the difference. Condition 1 is also not met, since using untoasted seeds would require a toasting step to be skipped and would change how the dish is prepared. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is smoked turkey, a processed, smoke-flavoured turkey product. The USDA match 'Turkey, NFS' is a generic, unspecified turkey entry with no state given, which would normally denote plain turkey meat of unspecified preparation. Under guideline F, a plain versus smoked/processed state is a difference in state, and smoking changes flavour, colour and texture noticeably. Guideline E does not apply because this is not a freezing issue. The generic entry does not name the smoked product, so a diner would likely notice the absence of smoky flavour. Condition 1 (same preparation) may be met in a loose sense, but condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste) fails because smoke flavour is absent.

The ingredient is amaranth flour, a raw, ground, dry product used in baking or thickening. The USDA match is amaranth grain that has been cooked, so it is a whole grain in a cooked, moist, porridge-like state. Condition 1 fails: it cannot replace the flour without changing preparation, since flour is measured and mixed into batters or doughs while cooked grain is a separately prepared whole food. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice whole cooked grains versus a fine flour in texture and appearance. Under the raw-versus-cooked and processed-versus-source rules, this is not a match.

The ingredient is dried goji berries, a specific dried fruit that is chewy, concentrated in flavour and sold dry. The USDA match is 'Berries, frozen', a generic frozen berry product. Condition 1 fails: frozen berries would need to be thawed or cooked, which changes preparation, and they cannot be used as a dry, shelf-stable ingredient in the same way. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (soft, juicy frozen fruit versus chewy dried berries), flavour (fresh-tart rather than concentrated and dried), and appearance. Guideline F also rules out a different state (dried versus frozen) and a different food, since goji is a distinct species and not the generic berry blend in the USDA entry. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is brie cheese, and the USDA entry 'Cheese, brie' is the same food. The quantity (275g) is ignored. 'Softened' describes handling (bringing the cheese to room temperature), which does not change the match, as with the other handling descriptors in the guidelines. Condition 1: brie can be used directly in place of softened brie without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cheese. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain pumpkin seeds explicitly specified as unsalted. The USDA match is pumpkin seeds that are salted. Condition 1: the seeds could physically be swapped in without changing preparation, since no cooking method changes. Condition 2: salted seeds taste noticeably saltier than unsalted ones, and a diner would likely notice the difference in flavour. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version (here, added sodium) is not substitutable, and the salt difference is a flavour change, which is explicitly disqualifying. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is unpopped popcorn kernels, which are raw, dried corn kernels that must be heated to pop. The USDA entry is 'Popcorn, ready-to-eat, plain', which is already popped and ready to eat. Condition 1 fails: the kernels cannot be used in place of popped popcorn without changing the preparation, since they would need to be popped first, which is a different cooking method. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste and see a clear difference between hard, unpopped kernels and light, expanded popped corn. This is a different state (raw vs. cooked/processed), which guideline F rules out. The quantity (300g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is melba toast with added salt, so it is a salted version of the plain product. The USDA entry is melba toast explicitly 'without salt.' Under guideline D, a plain product matched to a modified version (here, unsalted versus salted, a sodium-related modification) is not a match. The quantity (10g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 might be met since the item could be swapped in the same preparation, but condition 2 fails: a diner would taste the absence of salt, which is a noticeable difference in flavour. Since both conditions must hold, the match is not substitutable.

Malt syrup is made from malted barley and has a distinct malty, slightly toasted flavour and a darker colour. Corn syrup is made from corn starch and is a neutral, plain sweetener. They are different foods, not the same product under another name (guideline B does not apply). Substituting corn syrup would change the flavour and appearance of the dish, and a diner would likely notice the missing malt character. Condition 2 is not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain macaroni, cooked and drained. The USDA entry is 'Macaroni, vegetable, enriched, cooked', which is a variant made with added vegetable (typically spinach or tomato) that gives it a green or orange colour and a slightly different flavour. Condition 2 fails because a diner would see the colour difference in the dish and could taste the vegetable flavour. Condition 1 is not the main issue: cooking method is the same, but the product differs in appearance and flavour. The quantity and 'cooked and drained' handling do not change the match. Under guideline D and F, a plain ingredient matched to a flavoured or modified version is not substitutable. The default plain entry for cooked macaroni would be the correct match, not the vegetable variant.

The ingredient is smoked turkey breast, which is white meat from the breast. The USDA entry is smoked turkey drumstick, cooked, with skin and bone removed, which is dark meat from the leg. Guideline F says a different cut of meat is not substitutable, and this is a different cut from a different part of the bird. Condition 1 is not met: the drumstick is not a drop-in replacement for breast in the same preparation. Condition 2 is also not met: a diner would notice the difference in taste and texture, since dark meat is moister and richer than white breast meat, and the skin adds a visible and textural difference. Smoking is shared, but that does not offset the cut and skin differences. The quantity (145g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is pork hock, the lower leg or shank section of the pig, which is mostly skin, connective tissue, collagen and bone with relatively little lean meat. The USDA match is pork belly with skin, raw, a fatty cut from the side of the pig. These are different cuts with different fat, collagen and lean-meat content. Substituting belly for hock would change the texture (hock becomes gelatinous and fall-apart after long braising, while belly stays layered and rendered), the flavour profile and the appearance of the finished dish. Under guideline F, a different cut of meat is not substitutable, so condition 1 (no change to preparation or dish) and condition 2 (diner would notice a different texture and taste) both fail.

The ingredient is fresh asparagus spears, which are raw and uncooked. The USDA match is 'Asparagus, fresh, cooked, no added fat'. Condition 1: the match is the same food, but it is cooked, while the recipe uses it as a raw ingredient. Substituting it would change how the dish is prepared, because the cooking step would already be done and the recipe's own cooking would have to be altered or skipped. Guideline F explicitly lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Condition 2: cooking changes asparagus texture (softer, less crisp), colour (duller green), and flavour (milder, sweeter, less grassy), so a diner would likely notice the difference. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 likely fails too. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is cervelat, a cured, smoked, emulsified pork (and/or beef) sausage sold canned. The USDA match is raw beef chuck for stew, separable lean and fat. Condition 1: Cervelat is a processed, cured, smoked sausage that is ready to eat from the can; raw beef chuck is an uncooked whole-muscle cut. Substituting it would require entirely different preparation (cooking the raw meat, forming or seasoning it, omitting the cured/smoked character), so the preparation would change. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (cured, smoky, seasoned sausage flavour versus plain beef), texture (smooth emulsified sausage versus fibrous muscle meat), and appearance. The match is a different product and a different state (raw whole cut versus processed sausage), so it fails both conditions. Guideline F (different state, single ingredient vs processed product) applies.

Ingredient is 25g corn oil, a plain cooking oil. USDA match is 'Corn oil', which is the same food under the same name with no modifier, state, or blend. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Corn oil used in place of corn oil does not change preparation, and a diner would not perceive any difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh, peeled taro root, a raw starchy vegetable that is normally boiled, steamed, or baked. The USDA match is 'Snacks, taro chips', a fried or dehydrated snack product. Condition 1 fails: using taro chips would change the preparation, since the root must be cooked and cannot be substituted with a pre-fried, crisp snack. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (crisp and brittle versus soft and starchy), flavour (seasoned and fried versus plain), and appearance. Under guideline F, a raw source is not equivalent to its processed product. The quantity is ignored, per guideline A. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is canned figs, drained. The USDA match is raw fresh figs. Canned figs are heat-processed and packed in syrup, so they are softer, sweeter, and have a different texture and flavour from raw figs. Guideline F says raw vs cooked/processed is not substitutable, and the packing medium also changes the product. Guideline D's allowance for canned fruit in syrup covers how the product is normally sold, but it does not make canned figs the same as raw figs. Condition 1 may hold, since raw figs could be used in place of canned, but condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice the softer texture and different sweetness and appearance. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is shredded wheat cereal, the plain whole-wheat biscuit product sold under that name. The USDA entry 'Cereal, shredded wheat, plain' names the same product with no added flavour, sweetener, or modification. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to its standard default version is substitutable. Condition 1: the match is the same food, so it can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared (the leading 100g quantity is ignored per guideline A). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is shrimp cakes, which are patties made mainly from shrimp (often with binders, seasoning, and sometimes fish paste), typically cooked by frying or steaming. The USDA match is imitation crab meat, which is surimi, a processed fish paste usually made from pollock or similar white fish, flavoured to resemble crab and sold as flaked or stick-shaped pieces. These are different foods, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: imitation crab is not a cake-forming shrimp product and would change how the dish is prepared, since it cannot be shaped and cooked like shrimp cakes. Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste the difference between shrimp and surimi, and the texture (springy, fibrous surimi versus minced shrimp) and appearance would differ. Guideline F also applies: a different protein source is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh tamarind, the fruit of the tamarind tree. The USDA entry 'Tamarinds, raw' is the same food in its uncooked state. 'Fresh' corresponds to 'raw', and the leading '185g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the tamarind can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same fruit in the same form. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw Cornish hen liver. A Cornish hen is a small young chicken, so its liver is the same organ and food as chicken liver. The USDA entry 'Chicken, liver, all classes, raw' covers liver from all chicken classes, including young birds. Guideline B treats regional or culinary names of the same food as matches. Condition 1: chicken liver can replace Cornish hen liver without any change to the preparation, since both are raw and handled the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the organ is the same and the only difference is the size of the bird it came from. Both conditions hold.

Edamame is the young green soybean, so 'Soybeans, green, raw' is the same food under a different name (guideline B). The ingredient is listed as fresh, uncooked edamame, which matches the USDA 'raw' state. Shelling is handling that does not change the match (guideline C). The weight '30g' is ignored (guideline A). Since the food is the same and no cooking or processing difference is specified, the match is substitutable under both conditions. Diners would not perceive a difference from the ingredient itself, as the same green soybean is used.

Ingredient: plain croutons, crushed (150g). The leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Croutons, plain' is the same food under the same name, with no added flavour or modification. Crushing is knife/handling work that does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the croutons could be used in place of the ingredient, and the preparation (crushing, then using as a crumb or coating) stays the same. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the product is the same plain crouton. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is brown basmati rice, a specific long-grain variety with a distinct aroma and texture. The USDA entry is generic brown rice, cooked, with no added fat. Two differences make it non-substitutable. First, the variety differs: basmati has a different flavour and aroma from generic brown rice, which guideline F treats as a sibling variety with a different taste. Second, the state may differ: the ingredient gives no cooking state, and a 185g amount of rice in a recipe is most likely dry, uncooked weight, while the USDA entry is cooked. Raw and cooked are different states under guideline F, and cooking method and final weight would change. Because the variety differs and the state is at least uncertain, the match fails condition 2 (a diner could notice the difference in aroma and texture) and may fail condition 1.

1. Identity: 'Protein powder' is a generic high-protein powder sold for mixing into drinks, shakes, or batters. The USDA entry 'Nutritional powder mix, high protein, NFS' is a generic high-protein powder mix with the same primary function and no specific flavour, base, or added component named. 2. Preparation: Both are dry powders that are typically stirred into liquid or blended into other ingredients, so the cooking method would not change. 3. Sensory: Neither entry specifies a flavour, and the USDA entry's 'NFS' (not further specified) indicates a generic category, so no distinct taste, texture, or appearance is implied. Some brands differ in sweetness or flavouring, which is a real risk, but the generic match does not state a modified or flavoured version. Both conditions are plausibly met under the generic match.

Condition 1 (same preparation): The ingredient is plain shredded coconut, and the USDA entry is desiccated coconut, which is a close form of the same food. Changing the form alone would not alter cooking method. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference): The USDA entry is explicitly sweetened. The ingredient does not ask for a sweetened version, so this is a plain-to-modified mismatch under guideline D (sweetened versions of plain ingredients are not substitutable). A diner would taste the added sugar in the dish, changing its flavour. Because the sweetened descriptor changes taste, condition 2 fails, and the match is not substitutable.

The recipe calls for smoked braunschweiger, and the USDA entry is 'Braunschweiger (a liver sausage), pork' with no smoked descriptor, so it is the plain default. Guideline F lists plain vs smoked as a different state that is not substitutable. Condition 2 also fails: smoke flavour is a clear taste difference a diner would notice. The quantity (400g) is ignored. The base food, pork braunschweiger, is the same, but the smoked version the recipe requires is not what the entry describes.

The ingredient is fresh monkfish fillet, cut into chunks. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Fish, monkfish, raw' is the same food (monkfish) in its raw, uncooked state. Cutting into chunks is knife work that does not change the match (guideline C). Monkfish fillet is the standard edible flesh of the monkfish, so the USDA entry covers the same product. Condition 1: the raw monkfish could replace the fillet in the dish with the same preparation (cut into chunks, then cooked). Condition 2: a diner would not perceive a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same fish in the same raw state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is oat flour (ground oats, a cereal flour with oat flavour, protein and texture). The USDA match is arrowroot flour, which is a starch extracted from arrowroot tubers. These are different foods from different plant sources, not the same food under another name. Per guideline F, a different flour is not substitutable (e.g., bread flour vs cake flour). Arrowroot is nearly flavourless and behaves as a thickener with different gelling and binding properties, and it lacks oat's protein and wholegrain character, so baked goods or porridge would change in taste, texture and appearance. A diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would change (different hydration and binding behaviour), and condition 2 fails because taste and texture would visibly differ. The 70g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is boiled Chinese okra with no salt. 'Chinese okra' is a regional name for the sponge/dishcloth gourd (Luffa aegyptiaca, also called towelgourd), so the USDA entry names the same food under a different name (guideline B). The USDA entry is 'cooked, boiled, drained, without salt', which matches 'boiled' with 'no salt' and carries no added flavour or modification (guideline D). The 7g weight is ignored (guideline A). Preparation is the same, boiling, so the dish is not altered, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is flaxseed oil (20g, quantity ignored). The USDA match is 'Flaxseed oil', which is literally the same food with an identical name, so it is the same food rather than a sibling product or modified version. Condition 1: flaxseed oil can be used in place of itself with no change in preparation method. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same oil. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is brandy butter, a sweet British condiment made from butter, sugar and brandy, normally served cold as a spread or sauce. The USDA match is Brandy Alexander, a cocktail made from brandy, crème de cacao and cream. Condition 1 fails: a cocktail cannot replace a butter-based spread in a recipe without changing how the dish is prepared. It is a liquid with a different composition, not a fat-and-sugar spread. Condition 2 also fails: the flavour profile is different (chocolate-cream cocktail versus butter-sugar-brandy), and the texture and appearance would differ, so a diner would notice. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A. The match is not the same food under another name (guideline B) and is not a plain or standard version of it (guideline D).

The ingredient is guar gum, a seed gum used as a thickener and added as a cold-water slurry. The USDA entry 'Gums, seed gums (includes locust bean, guar)' explicitly names guar gum as one of its included items, so it is the same food under the USDA's grouped name (guideline B), not a different processed source. Condition 1: the entry can replace guar gum in the same slurry preparation with no change in cooking method. Condition 2: as a generic seed-gum entry that names guar, it describes the same thickener, so a diner would not notice a difference in texture or appearance. The main caveat is that locust bean gum, also in the group, has somewhat different hydration and viscosity, but the entry is the guar-inclusive category, so it is treated as a match.

Farina is a milled wheat product, coarsely ground from wheat endosperm, and is normally sold as a dry hot cereal. The USDA entry is a branded dry hot wheat cereal explicitly named 'Farina', so it is the same plain product type under a brand name (guideline G). It is dry, matching the 'dry farina' ingredient, and the 30g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: it can replace the farina without changing preparation, since both are cooked from dry in liquid or used dry in the same way. Condition 2: the taste, texture and appearance of the cooked result should be indistinguishable. Any difference in enrichment or brand formulation would be too minor for a diner to notice. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is garlic powder, a dried, ground spice made from garlic bulbs. The USDA match is Onions, white, raw, a fresh vegetable from a different Allium species with a distinct flavour profile. Condition 1: garlic powder is a dry seasoning used by sprinkling or mixing into dishes; raw white onion is a fresh, moist vegetable that would need chopping and would add water, bulk and a different texture, so it cannot replace the powder without changing preparation. Condition 2: diners would readily notice the difference, since garlic powder gives a concentrated garlic flavour while raw onion tastes sharp and sweet, and the texture and appearance would also differ. Guideline F rejects a different state (ground/dried vs raw) and a different food. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is a plain 'spinach dip', which the guidelines treat as the standard default version. The USDA match is 'Spinach dip, light', a reduced-fat modified version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a 'light' (reduced-fat) entry is a modification, not the same food. Light dips typically differ in fat content, which affects mouthfeel and flavour, so a diner could notice. The 'light' descriptor is not a normal default for spinach dip as sold under the plain name, so it does not qualify under the exception in D. Condition 2 therefore fails, and the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is pickle and pimiento loaf, a sliced luncheon meat. The USDA entry is the same named product, pickle and pimiento loaf, in its pork version. Slicing is preparation the recipe does itself and does not change the match (guideline C). The ingredient does not specify a meat, so the standard default version, the pork entry, is the plain-name match (guideline D). Using it in place of the ingredient would not change how the dish is prepared, and the product's taste, texture, and appearance are the same as the standard product a shopper would buy under this name. No modification, cut, or state change applies.

The ingredient is barley bread that is untoasted. The USDA entry is the same bread but toasted. Guideline F lists 'plain vs toasted' as a different state that is not substitutable. Toasting changes texture (crisper, drier crumb), colour (browned), and flavour (Maillard and caramelised notes), so a diner would notice. Toasting is also a cooking method that the recipe does not apply. Condition 1 fails because using toasted bread would change how the dish is prepared, and condition 2 fails because taste, texture and appearance would differ. The quantity and the shared food identity do not override this.

The ingredient is generic jam, which is normally a fruit preserve sweetened with sugar. The USDA entry is 'Jam or jelly, fruit juice sweetened', a modified version sweetened with fruit juice concentrate instead of sugar. Guideline D treats sweetened/unsweetened and similar modifications as non-matching when the plain ingredient is matched to a modified entry. Guideline F says a different sweetener is not substitutable. Condition 1 is arguably met, since jam can be used in the same way. Condition 2 fails: fruit-juice-sweetened spreads taste less sweet and have a different flavour profile, and a diner could notice the difference. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain pastry flour with no stated bleaching or enrichment. The USDA entry 'Flour, pastry' is the same product type, and 'unenriched, unbleached' describes one common way pastry flour is sold (unbleached pastry flour is a standard retail product). Guideline D treats such a descriptor as a normal sale form rather than a modification, so it is not a modified version of the ingredient. Both substitution conditions hold: it can be used in the same way without changing preparation, and the diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The only possible difference is a slight whiteness or tenderness contrast between bleached and unbleached versions, which is not meaningful enough to count as a noticeable change. Flour type (pastry, not bread or cake) matches, so this is not a case of a different flour under guideline F.

The ingredient is pak choi, which is the same vegetable as the USDA entry 'Cabbage, chinese (pak-choi)', so the food identity matches (guideline B). The USDA entry is American shad cooked by dry heat (baking, broiling or similar), a different preparation with no packing medium. Using it would change the preparation, since the ingredient is already cooked in the can and the match is cooked again by dry heat. A diner would likely notice the difference in moisture, softness and flavour, because canned shad is soft and moist while dry-heat cooked shad is firmer and drier. Guideline F rejects a different state or packing medium, and the canned-versus-dry-heat-cooked difference falls under that. The species is the same, but the state is not, so the two conditions are not both met.

The ingredient is feijoa, and the USDA entry is 'Feijoa, raw', which is the same fruit with no added state, cooking, or modification. The leading '250g' is only a quantity and is ignored per guideline A. Feijoa is normally sold and used fresh, so the raw entry matches the default form. Substituting it changes neither the preparation nor the taste, texture, or appearance of the dish. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is an unsweetened, fortified soy beverage, which is essentially soymilk with added calcium and vitamins. The USDA entry 'Soymilk (All flavors), enhanced' is the same product type: 'enhanced' is USDA's term for fortified, which the ingredient explicitly requests, so this is the matching fortified version rather than a modified one. 'All flavors' covers the unflavoured, unsweetened plain soymilk, so it does not introduce a sweetened or flavoured variant. The 75g quantity is ignored. Condition 1: soymilk can replace a fortified unsweetened soy beverage without changing preparation, since both are liquids used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the entry covers the plain unsweetened form and the fortification is the same. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a turkey drumstick that was frozen and then thawed. The USDA entry is the same cut (turkey drumstick) in raw form. Under guideline E, frozen meat that is normally cooked matches the raw entry when freezing doesn't show, and a thawed drumstick is handled like a fresh one. The 'meat only' descriptor names the same cut without skin, and the recipe does not specify skin, so it does not change the food being used. Cooking method, flavour, texture and appearance would not change in a way a diner would notice. The 300g weight is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned Atlantic mackerel (Scomber scombrus). The USDA entry is jack mackerel (Trachurus species), canned, drained solids. These are different fish species, not regional or trade names for the same food, so guideline B does not apply. Jack mackerel is a sibling species with a different, typically stronger and more pronounced flavour, a firmer and often drier texture, and a darker flesh colour than Atlantic mackerel. Guideline F rules out a sibling variety with a different taste. Draining the solids is standard handling and does not matter. Condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice the difference in taste and appearance. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a pumpkin flax granola, a ready-to-eat granola containing pumpkin and flax. The USDA entry is Nature's Path Organic FLAX PLUS Pumpkin Granola, a branded ready-to-eat cereal with the same two named components (pumpkin and flax) and the same product type (granola). Per guideline G, a branded entry of the same product type matches, and the flavour descriptor is part of what the recipe asks for, not an added modification. The 'Organic' and brand wording are standard descriptors of this product, not a change in the food. Condition 1: granola can be used directly in place of this granola without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since the same product type with the same components is being used. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked Colby Jack cheese. The USDA entry is plain Cheese, Colby Jack. Colby Jack is the same base cheese, so the product type matches. However, guideline F states that plain versus smoked is a different state and not substitutable. Smoking adds a distinct smoky flavour and often a darker surface, so a diner would notice the difference in taste and appearance. Condition 2 fails. Condition 1 is also doubtful, since the dish is served with the cheese and substituting plain cheese would change its flavour profile. Quantity (300g) is ignored per guideline A. Result: not substitutable.

The ingredient is guar gum, a thickening and stabilizing hydrocolloid derived from guar beans, used as a powder in cooking and baking. The USDA match is 'Chewing gum, sugarless', a confectionery product made from a gum base (synthetic or natural polymers), sweeteners or sugar alcohols, and flavourings. Condition 1 fails: chewing gum cannot be used in place of guar gum as a thickener or stabilizer; it would not hydrate or thicken the dish, and it is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice a difference in texture, sweetness, flavour, and appearance. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw apricots that have been peeled. The USDA entry is raw apricots with skin, which is the same food in its default state. Guideline C lists 'peeled' as knife work or handling that does not change the match, so the 'with skin' descriptor does not make it a different food. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the recipe itself does the peeling. Condition 2: once peeled, the fruit's taste and texture are the same, and the 'with skin' label describes the raw fruit before handling. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is chicken fat, and the USDA entry 'Fat, chicken' names the same food, so it is the same product under a standard name (guideline B). Quantity is ignored (A). Chicken fat is normally used as a rendered cooking fat, and the USDA entry is the generic chicken fat, which is the default version (D). Using it in place of chicken fat does not change the cooking method, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. It is not a different oil or fat type (F), since it is chicken fat itself. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried seedless golden raisins; the USDA entry is 'Raisins, golden, seedless', which is the same food under the same name. The leading weight (90g) is decoration and is ignored per guideline A. Golden raisins are the standard dried form of the grape sold as raisins, so the dried state matches the default product and no modification is implied. Condition 1: the raisins could be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried watermelon seeds, which are the seeds of a melon and are typically eaten roasted or salted in some cuisines. The USDA entry is sunflower seed kernels, dried, a different plant and a different food. Guideline B does not apply because these are not the same food under another name. Guideline F rejects matches between different source foods, and the two seeds differ in size, shape, flavour, and appearance, so a diner would notice the substitution. Condition 1 may hold in a loose sense, since both are dried seeds that can be used as snacks or garnish, but condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable. The 50g quantity is ignored per Guideline A.

The ingredient is a mixed dish of rice and beans, served leftover. The USDA entry 'Beans and white rice' names the same dish with the same two components, so it is the same food under a standard descriptor (guideline C). The leftover state is handling, not a change in cooking method. The ingredient does not specify brown rice or a particular bean, and white rice is the default for rice and beans, so no unstated modification is implied. The weight is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same dish with the same components. Both conditions are met.

Ingredient: kokum syrup, a syrup made from kokum fruit (Garcinia indica), which has a distinctive sour, tart, fruity flavour used in Indian cooking (e.g., sol kadhi, drinks). USDA match: Simple syrup, which is just dissolved sugar and water with no fruit flavour or acidity. Condition 1: Simple syrup could physically stand in for a liquid sweetener, so preparation method could be roughly unchanged. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference: kokum's sour, tart, fruity, slightly floral character is absent from simple syrup, and the colour (kokum syrup is typically deep pink/red) would also differ. Simple syrup is not the same food under another name; it is a different, unflavoured product. Per guideline F and B, this is not a same-food match, and the flavour change is clear. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a generic powdered sugar substitute, with no specific sweetener named. The USDA entry, 'Sugar substitute, powder, NFS', is the generic powdered form of the same product category, so it is the same food under a general name (guideline B). Preparation is unchanged, since a powdered sugar substitute is measured and used the same way as the entry describes (condition 1). Taste, texture, and appearance should match at the level the ingredient specifies, because neither side names a particular sweetener, so a diner would not reasonably notice a difference (condition 2). The 400g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a poppy seed dressing, a prepared condiment made from oil, vinegar or citrus, sugar or mayonnaise base, and poppy seeds. The USDA match is 'Spices, poppy seed', which is the dry seed alone. Condition 1: using bare poppy seeds in place of the dressing would change the preparation, because the dressing supplies liquid, emulsion, sweetness and acidity that the dish's method depends on. Condition 2: a diner would taste and feel the difference. The seeds lack the sweet-tart flavour and creamy or oily texture, and the appearance would change because the seeds would not coat the dish. Guideline F rules out a single ingredient standing in for a product that contains it, and a raw/dry spice versus a prepared product. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is turkey sausage, a processed meat product made from ground turkey with seasonings and typically casings. The USDA match is 'Oil, olive, salad or cooking', which is a plant-based fat. These are fundamentally different foods: a meat product versus an oil. Condition 1 fails because using olive oil in place of turkey sausage would change the dish entirely, removing the protein component and altering how it is prepared (sausage is cooked as a meat, olive oil is a cooking medium). Condition 2 also fails because a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. The quantity (85g) is irrelevant per the guidelines. This is not the same food under another name, nor a cut or preparation variant of it.

The ingredient is raw lamb tongue, a single cut of meat. The USDA entry is a prepared dish, 'Tongue pot roast, Puerto Rican style', which is cooked, seasoned and typically served in a sauce. It is not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails: using it in place of raw lamb tongue would mean the dish is no longer prepared by the original method, because the match is already a finished cooked preparation. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in flavour, texture and appearance, and the USDA entry does not identify lamb tongue at all (it is a generic tongue dish with Puerto Rican seasoning). The quantity is ignored, as the guidelines require. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is fresh fish roe, which is raw and would be cooked as part of the recipe. The USDA match is specifically 'cooked, dry heat', so it is already heat-treated. Condition 1 fails: using pre-cooked roe would change how the dish is prepared, since the cook would be applying heat to an already-cooked product or skipping a step the recipe expects. Condition 2 also fails: cooked roe has a firmer, set texture and a different appearance from raw fresh roe, which a diner could notice. Guideline F states that raw vs cooked is a different state and not substitutable. The 200g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is butterhead lettuce, torn, at 45g. The quantity is decoration per guideline A. Boston lettuce is the common American name for a butterhead-type lettuce, so it is the same type of food under a regional/trade name (guideline B). Tearing is handling and does not change the USDA match (guideline C). The USDA entry is raw, and the ingredient is presumably raw in a salad or garnish. Condition 1 is met: it can be torn and used in place of butterhead without changing preparation. Condition 2 is met: butterhead and Boston share the same soft, tender leaf texture, mild flavour and appearance, so a diner would not notice a difference. Although Boston is a named variety, it is the butterhead type itself, not a sibling variety with a different taste (unlike the F examples).

The ingredient is prepared horseradish, the standard condiment sold as a jarred or bottled product with vinegar and other typical ingredients. The USDA entry 'Horseradish, prepared' is the same food under the same name. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. The weight '250g' is decoration and is ignored. Both conditions are met.
