Frozen collards cooked from frozen would generally be acceptable under the frozen/cooked guidance, since freezing is not visible in cooked greens. The decisive difference is the added oil. The ingredient explicitly specifies cooking without fat, and the match has oil added during cooking. That changes the cooking method (no fat versus fat-cooked) and adds a richer, oily flavour and mouthfeel that a diner would likely notice. Under guideline D, a plain item mapped to a modified version (here, with added fat) is not a match. Condition 1 fails because the preparation changes, and condition 2 fails because the oil alters taste and texture. The quantity prefix is irrelevant.

The ingredient is cardoon (Cynara cardunculus), a distinct thistle-family vegetable that is related to the globe artichoke but is a different species. Cardoon is usually eaten as its leaf-stalks, which are fibrous and ribbed, while the USDA entry describes the globe artichoke flower bud. The two are not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), so the question is whether a diner would notice. They differ in taste (cardoon is more bitter, with an artichoke-like flavour but not the same), texture (stringy stalks versus tender bracts and heart), and appearance (stalks versus a bud). Substituting would change the dish's flavour, texture and appearance, and cooking preparation would differ too (cardoon stalks are typically peeled of fibres and blanched; artichokes are trimmed and the choke removed). Condition 1 and condition 2 both fail.

Masoor dal is the Indian name for split, dehulled red lentils, sold dried. USDA 'Lentils, pink or red, raw' is the same food under a regional name, and 'raw' here means the dried legume as bought (guideline C). Using it in place of masoor dal requires no change in cooking method, and the cooked dish would show no difference in taste, texture, or appearance because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is somen noodles, a thin Japanese wheat noodle normally bought dried. The USDA entry 'Noodles, japanese, somen, dry' is the same food under a more specific name, with the same product state (dry, uncooked). The 70g quantity is ignored per the guidelines. Condition 1: the noodles can be swapped in directly and cooked the same way, boiled until tender, with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product type. Both conditions are met.

Pak choi is a regional name for bok choy (Brassica rapa, Chinese white cabbage). The USDA entry 'Cabbage, bok choy, raw' is the same vegetable, uncooked, with no added state or modification. The quantity (225g) is ignored. Using this entry would not change preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is English muffins, split. The USDA entry 'Muffin, English' is the same food with no added modifier or preparation state. Splitting is handling (guideline C) and does not change the match. The weight is decoration (guideline A). Using the USDA entry in place of the ingredient would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, so both conditions hold.

The ingredient is dried fig (quantity 335g is ignored). The USDA match is 'Fig, dried', which is the same food with the same state: dried figs as bought. Condition 1: it can be used in place of dried figs without any change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is literally the same product. Per the guidelines, same food under the same name is substitutable.

The ingredient is smoked whitefish, a smoked fish product (a fish, plain or smoked, with a distinct flesh texture, flavour and appearance). The USDA match is Bean chips, a snack made from bean flour or whole beans, fried or baked into a crisp. These are not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails: bean chips cannot be used in place of smoked fish without changing the dish's preparation, since fish must be flaked, cured or cooked as fish and the chips are a dry, crunchy snack. Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (smoky fish vs. bean/salty snack), texture (flaky, moist fish vs. crisp chip) and appearance. Guideline F also excludes a different state and a different product category. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is duck liver, trimmed. The USDA match is chicken liver. The weight prefix is ignored per guideline A. Duck liver is not the same food as chicken liver, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 could be argued, since both are raw offal that can be cooked in similar ways. Condition 2 fails, though. Duck liver is noticeably richer, denser and more intense in flavour, and it has a firmer, creamier texture and a different colour and size. A diner would likely notice the difference, and guideline F rejects different-species substitutes that differ in taste. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain 'wheat crackers', which means the standard default wheat cracker. The USDA entry is 'Crackers, wheat, reduced fat', a modified version. The ingredient does not ask for reduced fat, and reduced-fat is not how wheat crackers are normally sold, so guideline D treats this as a plain-to-modified substitution. Condition 1 is about preparation: the cracker could be swapped in without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 is about the diner: reduced-fat crackers differ in taste, texture (less rich, often drier or crisper), and mouthfeel from standard crackers, and a diner could notice. Because the modified fat content changes the product, the match fails the sensory condition. The quantity (390g) is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is salami, cut into cubes, which is a plain cured meat. The USDA entry is a prepared sandwich: salami served on white bread. That is a different food with bread, and possibly condiments and other components. Condition 1 fails because a cook could not use a sandwich in place of cubed salami without changing the dish's preparation, since the bread would have to be removed and the salami separated out. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would notice the bread and other sandwich components. The quantity and knife work are ignored per the guidelines, but they do not change the fact that the match is a composite product, not the same food.

The ingredient is salted butter, a standard stick or block butter. The USDA entry is 'Butter, whipped, with salt', which is the same butter with air incorporated. Condition 1: whipped butter is less dense, so by weight it contains more air and less fat per gram. It can't be swapped gram-for-gram into a recipe that depends on solid butter, such as creaming for baking, laminating, or sautéing, without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: the diner would likely notice a difference in texture and mouthfeel, and possibly in how the dish spreads, sets, or browns. The entry is a different processed state of the same food, similar to the 'different state' cases in guideline F, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw okra pods, sliced (quantity and knife work are ignored per guidelines). The USDA match 'Fried okra' is okra that has been fried in oil, so it is a cooked and fat-modified product. Condition 1 fails: substituting fried okra for raw okra would change the cooking method, since the recipe calls for raw okra pods that would be cooked by the dish's own process, not pre-fried. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (crisp, breaded/oily coating versus tender-firm vegetable) and flavour (fried fat and coating versus fresh okra). Fried okra is a different state (cooked, fried) from raw, which guideline F explicitly marks as not substitutable.

The ingredient is reduced-fat canned refrigerated dough rounds, which are unbaked dough that the recipe presumably bakes. The USDA entry is 'Biscuits, plain or buttermilk, refrigerated dough, lower fat, baked', which is the finished, cooked product. Guideline C says unbaked ready-made products match their USDA product, but this USDA entry is specifically the baked form, so it is a different state. Guideline F says raw vs cooked is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using already-baked biscuits in place of raw dough would change the cooking method, since the dough would not be baked in the dish. Condition 2 also fails: the diner would notice differences in texture, rise, and appearance between raw-baked-in-dish dough and pre-baked biscuits. The brand and lower-fat descriptor match the ingredient, but the baked state is the decisive difference.

The ingredient is ground cloves, a whole-to-ground spice state that is already ground. The USDA match 'Spices, cloves, ground' is literally the same food: ground cloves. The leading '15g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: ground cloves can be used in place of ground cloves without any change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same spice in the same ground form. Both conditions are met.

Step 1: The ingredient is 'cream cheese spread', a softened cream cheese product. The USDA entry 'Cheese spread, cream cheese' names the same product type, so it is the same food under a near-identical name (guideline B). The 110g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Step 2: 'Softened' is handling that does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the spread can replace the ingredient in the same preparation without changing the method, since both are soft, spreadable cream cheese used at the same stage. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the USDA entry describes the same cream cheese spread product. Both conditions are met.

1) Same food? The ingredient is double-acting baking powder. The USDA entry is 'Leavening agents, baking powder, double-acting', so it names the same product type. The added 'straight phosphate' specifies the acid salt formulation (phosphate-based rather than sodium aluminum sulfate-based), not a flavoured or modified version. 2) Could it replace the ingredient without changing preparation? Yes. Both are double-acting leaveners used in the same way, at the same measure, in the same mixing and baking steps. 3) Would a diner notice? Not in a normal baked product. Both release gas in two stages, so rise and crumb are comparable, and any slight difference in acid-salt chemistry would not be perceptible in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Kishimen are flat, wide Japanese wheat noodles made from refined wheat flour, typically pale and smooth-textured. The USDA entry 'Noodles, whole grain, cooked' describes noodles made from whole-grain flour, which are darker, have a nuttier, more bran-like flavour, and a different, often firmer or chewier texture. The entry is not the same food under another name. Condition 1 is arguably met, since a cooked noodle could be swapped in without changing the cooking method. Condition 2 fails because a diner would likely notice the darker colour, the grainier flavour, and the different texture. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is a soft sandwich loaf, which in ordinary usage is a commercially sold soft white sandwich bread. The USDA entry 'Bread, white, commercially prepared' is the standard default version of that product, so it is the same food under a generic name (guideline B) and a plain ingredient matched to its default version (guideline D). The weight (300g) is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the bread can replace the loaf without changing preparation, whether it is used for crumbs, toasting, or layering. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since commercial soft sandwich loaves are typically white enriched bread. The match is not a modified or specialty version. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is plain pineapple juice (quantity ignored). The USDA match 'Pineapple juice, 100%' is the same food: unsweetened, 100% juice with no added flavour or modification, which is how pineapple juice is normally bought. Condition 1: it can directly replace the juice without changing preparation, since it is a liquid used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product type. Neither condition fails, so it is substitutable.

The ingredient is almond yogurt, a dairy-alternative yogurt made from almond milk with cultures and typically thickened and tangy. The USDA match is almond oil, a pressed fat from almonds with no fermentation, no tang, and a liquid oily texture. Condition 1: almond oil cannot be used in place of yogurt without changing preparation; it is not a fermented, spoonable product and would not behave as a yogurt in a recipe. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste (tangy dairy-like flavour versus neutral nutty oil), texture (creamy, thick versus oily) and appearance. The match is a different food product from a different category, not a regional name or a same-food variant. Neither condition is met, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is almond flour, and the USDA entry 'Flour, almond' names the same product with the words reordered. Almond flour is the standard default product, and the entry carries no modifier such as defatted, toasted, or flavoured. Substituting it would not change the preparation method, flavour, texture, or appearance of the dish, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met. The 10g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is a Valencia orange, which is a named orange variety. The USDA entry 'Oranges, raw, California, valencias' is the same variety, raw and uncooked, so the food itself matches. The region (California) is a sourcing detail, not a difference in the fruit. The 150g weight is ignored per guideline A. Guideline F's variety rule applies only to sibling varieties with different taste (e.g. navel vs blood orange), which does not apply here. Because the cultivar is identical, the dish would be prepared the same way and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Yuca is the Spanish/Latin American name for cassava (manioc). Yuca flour is cassava flour, so 'Flour, cassava' is the same food under another name (guideline B). It is a plain flour of the same source, so it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The quantity (175g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw dark-meat chicken, with no specific cut named, and the quantity is irrelevant. The USDA entry is raw, meat-only chicken from broilers or fryers, dark meat, thigh. Both are raw, uncooked poultry, so the cooking method is unchanged. Dark meat is a category that in practice is mostly thigh and drumstick, and thigh is its most typical cut, so the match is the same food under a more specific name rather than a different cut. Guideline F rejects different cuts such as pork belly versus pork loin, but here the ingredient does not specify a different cut. Diners would not reliably notice a thigh-based dark meat versus a thigh entry in the dish. The entry is meat only, and the ingredient does not mention skin, so there is no added difference. Both conditions are met, though the match is slightly less exact than a named cut would be.

The ingredient is boiled chayote that has been drained. The USDA entry is chayote fruit, cooked by boiling and drained, without salt. Both describe the same food in the same state (cooked and drained). The leading '4g' is quantity and is ignored. 'Drained' is handling that does not change the match. 'Without salt' is the default for a plain boiled vegetable, since no salt is named in the ingredient. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel, or see a difference.

The ingredient is dried salted jellyfish. The USDA entry 'Jellyfish, dried, salted' names the same product with the same state (dried) and treatment (salted). The leading '200g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the match is the same food, so it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since it would be soaked and desalted the same way. Condition 2: because it is the same product, a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is frozen, cooked chicken patties. The USDA entry 'Chicken patty, frozen, cooked' is the same product with the same state (frozen and cooked). Under guideline E, a frozen product matches the frozen USDA entry of the same product. Condition 1: the patties can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to cooking method, since both are already cooked and frozen. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product type in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 45g Alfredo sauce; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA match is literally 'Alfredo sauce', the same food under the same name, so it is the same product and the default version. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is a ready-made sauce used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, because it is the same named product with the same components. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is chorizo, sliced. The USDA entry is simply 'Chorizo', the generic food with no state or modification named. Slicing is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). The entry names the same product with no added flavour, cut, or preparation difference, so it is the standard default version (guideline D). Sliced chorizo would be used in the same way, with the same flavour, texture, and appearance as the USDA chorizo, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw chicken with the skin left on. The USDA entry is raw broiler or fryer chicken meat and skin, which is the same food in the same state. The recipe does not specify a cut, so the generic whole-bird-style entry is the standard default. Using it would not change the preparation, since skin-on raw chicken is cooked the same way either way. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. The quantity prefix is ignored under guideline A. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is plain cooked ham, minced. The USDA entry is Oscar Mayer ham, chopped, with natural juice. Both are the same food: ham that is already cooked, with knife work (mincing or chopping) that does not change the match. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. 'With natural juice' describes the ham's own juices in a packed chopped ham, not an added solution, flavouring, or reduced-sodium modification, so it is the standard way this product is sold. Substituting it would not change how the dish is prepared. A diner would see finely chopped ham in either case, with no meaningful difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain gouda cheese, and the USDA entry 'Cheese, Gouda or Edam' names gouda directly as the same product. Gouda and Edam are similar Dutch cheeses, and the entry is the standard default version rather than a modified, flavoured, or reduced-fat product. Condition 1: gouda can be used in place of this entry without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is cut, grated, or melted the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the match is the same cheese type. The 100g quantity is ignored per the guidelines. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Splenda sweetener packets, a branded tabletop sucralose sweetener. The USDA entry is 'Sweeteners, tabletop, sucralose, SPLENDA packets', which describes the same product in the same form. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. The leading '5g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is the same sweetener in the same packet format. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

Refried beans are mashed, cooked pinto (or similar) beans fried in fat into a paste. The USDA entry 'Fried green beans' refers to whole green bean pods (a vegetable, typically battered or breaded and fried). These are different foods: a legume paste versus a green vegetable. Condition 1 fails because using fried green beans would change the dish's preparation and form: you cannot mash and fry them into a refried bean texture. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would clearly notice a different flavour, texture, colour, and appearance. Not substitutable.

1) Identity: the ingredient is veal top round, the same cut named in the USDA entry 'Veal, leg (top round)'. The quantity (300g) is ignored. 2) State: 'fresh' corresponds to 'raw', which is uncooked, so the cooking method is unchanged. 3) Descriptor: 'separable lean and fat' is the standard way this cut is recorded and sold, with the fat left in as it comes. It is not a modification like a reduced-fat or lean-only version, so it reads as the default form of the cut (guideline D). 4) Substitution: the match is the same cut in the same raw state, so it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. A diner would not taste or see a difference beyond normal variation in trimming. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is rye flour, and the USDA entry 'Flour, rye' is the same food under a generic name. Rye flour is a plain, unmodified flour, and the entry names no processing state, blend, or modification. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the flour can replace rye flour directly in the recipe without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is an arepa, a Venezuelan/Colombian cornmeal flatbread. The USDA entry is 'Restaurant, Latino, arepa (unleavened cornmeal bread)', which names the same dish. Guideline B says the same food under the same name matches. The 50g weight is decoration (guideline A). The entry describes a cooked, ready-to-eat arepa, which is how the ingredient is normally bought and used, so the preparation method does not change. A diner would not taste or see a difference, so both conditions hold.

The ingredient is turkey ham, a processed deli-style turkey meat product. The USDA match is a turkey and ham sandwich on wheat bread, which is a composite food containing bread, condiments and possibly other components in addition to the meat. Under guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend or product containing it is not substitutable. Using the sandwich in place of turkey ham would change the dish: the bread and any spreads would be added, altering texture, appearance and flavour, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would change (bread and sandwich components would be introduced). Condition 2 also fails because a diner would notice bread and sandwich elements. The match does not meet either condition.

The ingredient is farmer's cheese, a fresh, unripened, crumbly cheese used as a standalone ingredient. The USDA match is a whole Papa John's thin-crust cheese pizza, a prepared dish with crust, sauce, and baked cheese. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: the pizza cannot replace crumbled farmer's cheese without changing the dish's preparation, since it adds a crust, sauce, and baking. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance. Both conditions must hold, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is roasted turkey breast, the plain default product. The USDA entry is light meat turkey, roasted, with skin eaten. Turkey breast is light meat, so the cut matches. The difference is the skin. The entry describes the product with skin included, while a plain 'roasted turkey breast' is normally served skinless, as in standard deli or carved breast. Including the skin changes the appearance (a browned, fattier outer layer) and the texture and fat content of each bite. A diner would likely notice the skin, and the dish's look and mouthfeel would change. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version is not substitutable. The skin-on entry fails condition 2, and it is not clearly the same default product, so it fails condition 1 as well.

The ingredient is fresh pomegranate seeds (arils), a fruit with a tart-sweet juicy flavour and crisp, juicy texture, red and glistening in appearance. The USDA match is 'Wheat, soft white', a cereal grain (typically dry, starchy, mild, and used as flour or whole grain). Condition 1: Wheat is not a substitute for pomegranate arils in any dish preparation; it would change the cooking method and structure entirely (grain requires milling/cooking, whereas arils are eaten raw as a garnish or mix-in). Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (sweet-tart fruit vs. bland grain), texture (juicy burst vs. starchy grain), and appearance (bright red arils vs. pale grain). Neither condition is met, and this is a different food rather than the same food under another name.

The ingredient is deglet noor dates, and the USDA entry is literally 'Dates, deglet noor', the same variety under the same name. The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the dates can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since the entry is the same food in the same state. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the identical variety. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is boneless, skinless chicken breast, raw by default since no cooking state is given. The USDA entry is broiler or fryer chicken, light meat (the breast), meat only (no skin or bone), raw. The light-meat designation is the breast cut, and 'meat only' corresponds to boneless and skinless. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same raw cut. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. The 225g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is seedless green grapes that have been roasted. The USDA entry is 'Grapes, green, seedless, raw', which is the same fruit but uncooked. Roasting is a cooking method that changes the grapes: it softens them, concentrates the sugars and produces a different flavour, and the skins wrinkle and collapse. Guideline F explicitly says 'plain vs toasted/smoked/roasted' and 'raw vs cooked' are not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because the dish would be prepared differently, since roasting is not done to the raw match. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would notice the softer texture, the wrinkled appearance and the altered flavour. The grape variety matches, but the processing state does not.

The ingredient is bay scallop meat, a specific small species (Argopecten irradians). The USDA entry is 'Mollusks, scallop, mixed species, raw', a blended category that covers several species, including large sea scallops. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F treats a sibling variety with a different taste or texture as not substitutable. Bay and sea scallops differ noticeably in size, sweetness and tenderness, and a mixed-species entry may be dominated by larger scallops. Condition 1 (same preparation) could plausibly hold, but condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture or appearance) is not reliably met. The leading '250g' is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is head cheese, a jellied cold cut made from pork head meat and set in its own gelatin. The USDA entry is 'Head cheese', which names the same product with the same name and no modifying descriptor. Guideline A says the leading weight is ignored, so 250g does not matter. Condition 1: it can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation, since it is already a ready-to-serve cold product. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'Ethiopian bread crumbs', a dried or toasted crumb product made from Ethiopian bread (typically injera or dabo-style breads, often teff-based and fermented). The USDA entry 'Bread, white, commercially prepared' is a generic wheat-flour sandwich loaf. Condition 1: swapping it in changes the preparation. Crumbs made from a fermented teff flatbread differ from crumbs made from a soft white loaf, so the dish would not be prepared the same way. Crumbs also need to be dried or toasted, while the USDA entry is a fresh loaf. Condition 2: the tang and earthy flavour of teff/fermented Ethiopian bread would not be matched by white bread, and the crumb texture and colour would differ. A diner would likely notice. The quantity (200g) is ignored. Neither condition holds, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a plain sliced chicken frankfurter used as a garnish. The USDA entry is 'Frankfurters or hot dogs and sauerkraut', a combined dish that includes sauerkraut as a component. Condition 1 fails: using it would add a sauerkraut component the recipe does not call for, so the preparation changes. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the sliver of sauerkraut in appearance, texture and flavour. The USDA entry is also a blend, not a single product (guideline F). The generic frankfurter entry is not specified as chicken, so the meat type may differ too. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh meat-filled tortellini: egg pasta enclosing a meat filling, sold raw and cooked in the dish. The USDA entry is plain enriched pasta, cooked, without filling. Condition 1 fails because the match is a different product: it lacks the meat filling, so the dish's preparation and components would change. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in taste and texture, since the filled pockets of meat and seasoning are absent. Guideline F rules out a plain product standing in for a composite one. Quantity is ignored. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is chia seeds (plain, presumably raw/dry as bought). The USDA match is 'Chia seeds', which is the same food under the same name. Quantity (25g) is ignored per guideline A. No cooking method change is implied, and the seeds are the same product with no added flavour, modification, or processing difference. A diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain margarine. The USDA match is 'Margarine-like spread, BENECOL Light Spread', a branded light, reduced-fat spread with added plant stanol esters. Condition 1: it is a different product with a lower fat content and higher water content than standard margarine. Its melting, browning and cooking behaviour would differ, so it could change how the dish is prepared (for example in creaming, frying or baking). Condition 2: a light spread with added stanol esters and less fat would likely change texture, mouthfeel and sometimes flavour, and a diner could notice. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient mapped to a 'light' or reduced-fat version as a modification, not a match. Guideline F also rejects a different fat. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is plain pork sausage, which the recipe treats as a raw meat product that will be cooked within the dish. The USDA entry is a different state and a modified product: it is already cooked (pan-fried), so it would change the preparation, since the recipe would need to cook raw sausage and the cooked version would be added at a different stage or would overcook. It is also reduced fat, which is a modification of the plain product (guideline D), so the flavour, juiciness and texture would differ. Guideline F rejects raw versus cooked states, and guideline D rejects a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced-fat version. Both conditions fail: the cooking method would change, and a diner could notice the difference in taste and texture. The quantity is irrelevant.

The ingredient is beef kidney, trimmed. The USDA entry is lamb kidney, raw. Trimming is knife work and does not change the match, and the 235g quantity is ignored. The question is whether lamb kidney is the same food as beef kidney. It is not. They are different animal species with different sizes, flavour profiles (lamb kidney is smaller and has a distinctly different, often more pronounced or gamey taste compared with the stronger, more mineral flavour of beef kidney), and different textures and appearance when cooked. Condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice a difference in taste and appearance. Condition 1 is also doubtful, since recipe timing and cooking may differ with the smaller lamb kidneys. Under the guidelines, a different-species variety with a different taste is not a substitutable match.

The ingredient is 'side pork, uncured', which is fresh, unsalted pork belly. The 'uncured' label rules out the salt-cured side pork sold as bacon. The USDA entry 'Pork, fresh, belly, raw' is the same raw, uncured cut under a different name, so it is the same food (guideline B). The leading '300g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A). The match is raw, which is the state the ingredient is in, and no cooking method is implied. Using pork belly therefore would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a fresh artichoke, trimmed. The USDA entry 'Artichokes, (globe or french), raw' is the same food: globe/French artichoke is the standard artichoke sold in shops. 'Trimmed' describes knife work (removing outer leaves and stem), which per guideline C does not change the match. The '150g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Freshness matches 'raw', and no cooking method, flavour, texture, or appearance differs from what a diner would expect. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a pickled egg, sliced: a hard-boiled egg preserved in a vinegar brine. The USDA match is raw, fresh whole egg. Condition 1 fails: a raw egg cannot be used in place of a pickled egg without changing the dish's preparation, since pickled eggs are already cooked and ready to eat, while raw egg must be cooked or used as is. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the sharp, vinegary flavour, the firm cooked white and yolk, and the characteristic pickled colour, none of which a raw egg has. This is a raw/cooked and processed-versus-plain difference (guideline F), so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a turkey frankfurter, a poultry sausage. The USDA match is a pork frankfurter, a different animal species. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Condition 1: the preparation could be similar, since both are cooked the same way, so the cooking method is not the main issue. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference. Turkey and pork frankfurters differ in flavour (pork is richer and fattier, turkey is leaner and milder), in texture, and often in colour and seasoning. Guideline F treats even different cuts of the same meat as non-substitutable, so a different species is a clearer case. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain coconut water. The USDA entry is 'Coconut water, unsweetened', the same product with one descriptor. Coconut water is naturally unsweetened and is normally sold that way, so the descriptor describes the standard product rather than a modified version (guideline D). Using it in place of the ingredient requires no change to preparation, since it is a liquid added in the same way. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the default product is unsweetened. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is toasted egg bread, and the USDA entry is 'Bread, egg, toasted'. Both name the same food, egg bread, in the same toasted state, so the match is literal. The 405g quantity is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is already toasted. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product in the same state. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is smoked lamb rib. The USDA entry is lamb rib, separable lean and fat, trimmed, choice, cooked, roasted, with no smoking. Guideline F says plain vs smoked is a different state, not a match. Condition 1: the match is roasted, so the dish would be prepared differently, since the smoking step would be lost. Condition 2: smoke flavour is a clear taste difference, and a diner would notice the missing smokiness. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable. The 150g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

Step 1: The ingredient is 'sea bass', a culinary name that usually refers to a saltwater species such as European sea bass (branzino) or Chilean sea bass (Patagonian toothfish). The USDA entry is 'Fish, bass, striped, raw', which is a different species, the striped bass (Morone saxatilis), a North American fish. Step 2: Guideline B requires the same food under another name, and these are different species rather than regional names for one fish, so the same-food exception does not apply. Step 3: Guideline F treats sibling varieties with different taste or texture as non-substitutable. Striped bass and sea bass differ in flesh texture, fat content and flavour, and Chilean sea bass in particular is much richer. Condition 2 is therefore not reliably met, since a diner could notice the difference. Step 4: Condition 1 holds in that the fish could be cooked the same way, but condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is roasted turkey drumstick meat with the skin removed before serving. The USDA entry is roasted turkey drumstick where the skin is not eaten, so the diner eats only the meat, the same as the ingredient. Condition 1: the match is the same food, roasted, in the same cut, and the skin removal is handling the recipe does itself (guideline C), so the dish is prepared the same way. Condition 2: the eaten portion is the same roasted meat, so taste, texture and appearance are unchanged. Nothing is reduced, modified, or swapped for a different cut or state. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is powdered milk, a dehydrated, unsweetened dairy product that is reconstituted or used dry. The USDA match is canned sweetened condensed milk, a thick, liquid product with added sugar. Condition 1 fails: powdered milk cannot replace condensed milk without changing the preparation, since it would need reconstitution and the sugar would have to be added separately. Condition 2 also fails: the sweetened condensed milk would make the dish sweeter and change its texture and consistency, which a diner would notice. Under the guidelines, sweetened is a modification of plain milk, and dry versus liquid/condensed is a different state. The entry is not the same food under another name.

The ingredient is extra-lean ground pork, a raw, minced pork product. The USDA entry is raw ground pork at 96% lean / 4% fat, which is the standard lean grade that sells as extra-lean. Both are the same cut and form (ground pork), in the same raw state. Condition 1: the match could replace the ingredient in the same recipe with the same preparation, since no cooking method, handling, or additional steps change. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the fat content is the same as what a shopper would buy as extra-lean. Under guideline D, the ingredient asks for the lean version and the matching lean entry counts. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is simple syrup, a home-made or commercial solution of sugar dissolved in water. The USDA entry is 'Simple syrup', which names the same product. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation, since both are used as liquid sweeteners. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food under the same name. The 150g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is tinned crabmeat, and the USDA match is 'Crab, canned', which is the same food under a different name. The weight prefix (300g) is decoration and does not affect the match. Using canned crab in place of tinned crabmeat requires no change to the cooking method, since the product is already cooked and is used as bought. Taste, texture and appearance should match, because a diner would not be able to tell tinned crabmeat from canned crab. Neither the packing medium nor the processing is described as differing from the standard tinned product. Both conditions are met.

Step 1: The ingredient is sheanut oil (the same oil from shea nuts), in its refined form. The USDA entry 'Oil, sheanut' is the same food and names no processing state, so under guideline E it is the generic food and matches a plain or refined version. Step 2: Cooking method is unchanged, since it is an oil used the same way. Refining mainly reduces the characteristic nutty aroma and colour of unrefined shea oil, so there could be some difference in flavour or smell. However, refined sheanut oil is the standard version sold for cooking and cosmetic use, and in most dishes its contribution is neutral and would not be noticed. The entry is the same oil type without a modifier like 'reduced' or 'flavoured', so guideline D's modified-version rule does not apply. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cooked eggplant with no added fat. The USDA entry is the same food, but prepared with added fat. Condition 1: using the fat-added entry would change how the dish is prepared, since the eggplant would arrive already cooked in fat, and the recipe specifically excludes added fat. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference. Fat-cooked eggplant is richer, glossier and softer, and it tastes of the added oil, so flavour, texture and appearance all change. Under guideline D, the ingredient asks for the plain version and the match is the modified version. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is sweetened condensed milk: thick, roughly 40% sugar, and typically used in recipes such as fudge, custards, or desserts where its sweetness and viscosity matter. The USDA match, evaporated milk whole, is unsweetened, thin, and has no added sugar. Condition 1 fails because replacing condensed milk with evaporated milk would require adding sugar and changing the preparation to get comparable thickness. Condition 2 fails because a diner would taste the lack of sweetness and notice the difference in texture. Guideline D treats sweetened versus unsweetened as a modification, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is uncooked millet seed, 85g (quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry 'Millet, raw' is the same food in its uncooked state, and millet is a grain typically sold as the dry seed, so 'raw' here means uncooked dry grain as bought. Condition 1: the raw millet can replace uncooked millet seed in any recipe with no change to preparation, since both are simply cooked later in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the food is the same raw grain. Both conditions are met, so it is substitutable.

The ingredient is raw ground elk (no cooking state is stated, so it is the plain raw product). The USDA match is 'Game meat, elk, ground, cooked, pan-broiled', which is a cooked product. Guideline F says a raw vs cooked difference is a different state and is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using a pre-cooked, pan-broiled product in place of raw meat changes how the dish is prepared, since the meat would not be cooked as part of the recipe. Condition 2 also fails: the diner would notice differences in texture, colour and flavour between raw-cooked-in-dish meat and pre-pan-broiled meat. The quantity (30g) is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is plain extra firm tofu, drained and pressed. Draining and pressing are handling steps that do not change the match (guideline C). The USDA entry is the same product, extra firm tofu. The only difference is the coagulant used in production: nigari (magnesium chloride) rather than the calcium sulfate common in many US tofus. Nigari is a standard, traditional coagulant, not a modification such as reduced sodium, flavouring, or a fat change, so guideline D's 'modified version' rule does not apply. Condition 1: extra firm tofu can be pressed, cubed, fried, or simmered in the same way, so the preparation is unchanged. Condition 2: both are extra firm and hold their shape similarly. Nigari tofu can taste slightly sweeter and smoother, but this is a subtle difference that would not usually be noticed in a finished dish. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 150g of whole wheat flour, a raw dry ingredient used to make roti dough, which is rolled and cooked at home. The USDA match is a commercially prepared, frozen, already-cooked flatbread. Condition 1 fails: the frozen bread cannot replace flour, because the dough would not be mixed, rolled, or cooked, so the preparation method changes entirely. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference between a freshly made roti and a commercial frozen product. Per guideline F, a raw flour versus a processed product made from it is not a match, and the quantity and the 'for rolling roti' phrasing do not change that.

The ingredient is dried kelp strips, a dehydrated product. The USDA match is 'Seaweed, kelp, raw', which is fresh, high-moisture seaweed. The guidelines treat raw versus dried as a different state (F: 'a different state: raw vs cooked, fresh vs dried herb'). Condition 1 fails: dried kelp is normally rehydrated or soaked before use, and 50g of dried kelp corresponds to a much larger weight of raw kelp, so the preparation and quantities would change. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (chewy and rehydrated versus fresh and crisp-tender) and appearance (dried, curled strips versus fresh green fronds). The quantity is ignored per guideline A and the match is judged on state alone. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is sliced beets labeled 'no salt added', a specification most commonly met by canned beets. The USDA entry 'Beets, canned, no salt added, solids and liquids' names the same food with the same no-salt-added modification, so the ingredient's own requested version matches (guideline D). Quantity is ignored (A). Canned beets are cooked, which could in principle conflict with a raw-beet reading (F), but the no-salt-added wording points to the canned or prepared product. The 'solids and liquids' qualifier means the packing liquid is included, which could matter if only the solids are used, but the sliced beets are the same food in the standard form. Both conditions are judged to hold, with some uncertainty.

The ingredient is radish relish, a condiment made from finely chopped radishes (often with vinegar, salt, sugar and other seasonings). The USDA match is horseradish sauce, a condiment made from grated horseradish root mixed with vinegar, sugar and salt, typically with a strong pungent heat. These are different foods: the base vegetable differs (radish vs horseradish root, though both are in the Brassicaceae family), and the flavour profile differs substantially (horseradish sauce is sharp and pungent; radish relish is milder, sweet-tangy, with a crisp chopped-vegetable texture). A diner would notice the difference in taste and texture, and the appearance also differs (creamy or pale sauce vs chunky relish). Radish relish is not the same food under another name, and the match is not a plain-to-standard equivalent. Condition 1 might loosely hold as a condiment swap, but condition 2 clearly fails. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dry soba noodles, which are uncooked and must be boiled as part of the recipe. The USDA match is 'Noodles, japanese, soba, cooked', which is already cooked. Using it would skip the cooking step, changing how the dish is prepared. The cooked noodles would also be softer and heavier by weight, since dry noodles absorb water, so the quantity and texture would differ. Guideline F says a different state (raw vs cooked) is not substitutable, and this pattern is a clear state mismatch. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 also fails because the cooked noodles would have a different texture and weight.

Cayenne peppers are a hot chili pepper cultivar. The USDA entry "Peppers, hot, cooked" is a generic hot-pepper category with no specific variety named, so it covers cayenne as a member rather than naming a different sibling variety. Guideline E treats a generic USDA entry as matching the specific food. Condition 1: cooked hot peppers can replace cooked cayenne without changing the preparation, since both are cooked the same way. Condition 2: the heat level and flavour of cayenne sit within the range of hot peppers, so a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is French dressing, and the USDA entry is 'French or Catalina dressing'. The USDA entry names French dressing directly, so it is the same product under the same name, which the guidelines treat as a match (B and D). Catalina dressing is a close, closely related sweet-tangy dressing that the entry explicitly groups with French. Condition 1: the dressing can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is a drop-in pourable dressing. Condition 2: the USDA entry is the generic product, so a diner would not reasonably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance compared with the standard French dressing they expected. The leading '30g' is quantity and is ignored (A). Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is fresh ground pork, which is raw meat that the recipe will cook. The USDA entry is 'Pork, fresh, ground, cooked', which describes meat that has already been cooked. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Using pre-cooked pork would change how the dish is prepared, since the meat would not be cooked during the recipe, and it would alter the texture and appearance (for example, browning, moisture, and firmness). A diner could notice the difference. Guideline C's handling of 'ground at home' applies to knife work and grinding, not to cooking state. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 likely fails too.

The ingredient is raw chicken necks. The USDA entry is raw broiler or fryer neck with meat and skin, which is the same cut from the same bird. Chicken necks are normally sold with skin attached, so the 'meat and skin' descriptor matches how a shopper would buy them. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match is raw, the same cut, and would be prepared the same way, so no change in cooking method. Condition 2: the diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same raw cut with its normal skin. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a fresh strip steak, which is the New York strip cut from the short loin. The USDA entry 'Beef, short loin (NY strip steak), raw' names the same cut under a trade name (guideline B), and 'raw' matches 'fresh' for uncooked meat (guideline C). The 400g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is the same cut and both are cooked the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cut of beef. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chocolate milk, a liquid beverage sold as a drink. The USDA entry is a frozen milk dessert, which is a different product with a different form (frozen, solid or semi-solid, not a liquid). Condition 1 fails: it cannot replace chocolate milk in a recipe without changing how the dish is prepared, since a frozen dessert would need thawing or melting and would not behave as a liquid. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (icy or creamy frozen versus liquid) and temperature. The entry is also milk-fat free, which is a modified version (guideline D) rather than the standard default of chocolate milk. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain rye bread cubes, a single food that the recipe will then season and cook in the stuffing. The USDA entry 'Bread stuffing' is a prepared dish, typically a mix of bread with seasonings, fat, and often onion and celery, and may be cooked or dry-mix. Condition 1 fails: using it in place of plain rye bread cubes would change the preparation, because the seasoning and fat would already be incorporated and the recipe's own seasoning step would be altered. Condition 2 also fails: the diner would taste added herbs and seasonings and see a different product. Per guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend or product containing it is not substitutable. The 100g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is dried rosemary sprigs, a dried herb with a distinctive pine-like, resinous flavour. The USDA match is Spearmint, dried, which is a different herb (Mentha spicata) with a sweet, minty flavour. They are not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 (same preparation): the dish could technically be prepared the same way with dried spearmint, so the method is not obviously altered. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste): spearmint would clearly change the flavour profile of the dish from savoury resinous rosemary to cooling mint, and a diner would notice. Guideline F explicitly says a different state or a sibling/different herb with a different taste is not substitutable. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is ranch dressing, a condiment used as a dressing or dip. The USDA entry is a complete composite menu item: a salad with crispy chicken, bacon, and other components. It is a product containing ranch dressing among many other ingredients, not the dressing itself. Guideline F says a single ingredient is not substitutable for a blend or product containing it. Using this salad in place of ranch dressing would change the dish entirely. The diner would get salad, chicken, and bacon instead of a dressing, so the dish's preparation and appearance would differ. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is sliced bamboo shoots and the USDA entry is Bamboo shoots, raw, which is the same food. Guideline A says the 100g quantity is irrelevant. Guideline C says knife work such as slicing does not change the match, so 'sliced' is handled by the recipe and the entry still applies. The ingredient does not specify a cooked or canned state, so the raw entry is the default version (guideline D). Condition 1: the raw shoots can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the recipe's own handling supplies the slicing. Condition 2: a diner would see the same food in the same form, with no difference in taste, texture or appearance attributable to the match. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh (raw) bamboo shoot, which is uncooked and typically needs preparation such as boiling before eating. The USDA entry is 'Bamboo shoots, cooked', which is a different state. Guideline F explicitly says raw vs cooked is not substitutable, because the dish would need a different preparation (the raw shoot would have to be cooked first, which changes the cooking method). Cooked bamboo shoot also differs in texture and possibly flavour and colour from a fresh raw shoot. Condition 1 fails because the match cannot be used in place of the fresh shoot without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 is also doubtful, since texture and taste differ between raw and cooked shoot. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Because condition 1 fails, the match is not substitutable.

Condition 1 (substitution without changing preparation): The ingredient is generic chocolate yogurt, and the USDA entry is chocolate yogurt. Both are eaten or mixed directly, so preparation is unchanged. The leading '150g' is quantity and is ignored. Under guideline D, flavoured yogurts are normally sold low fat, so the 'nonfat' descriptor reflects how chocolate yogurt is normally bought and is not a modification. The vitamin D fortification is a nutritional addition that does not change how the dish is made. Condition 1 is met. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference to a diner): Nonfat versus regular-fat chocolate yogurt differs somewhat in mouthfeel, but the guideline treats the normal low-fat version of flavoured yogurt as the standard default, and vitamin D fortification has no effect on taste, texture or appearance. A diner would not reasonably notice a difference from a typical chocolate yogurt. Condition 2 is met. Both conditions hold, consistent with the strawberry yogurt -> Yogurt, strawberry, low fat = yes pattern.

The ingredient is ground bay leaf, a powdered spice. The USDA entry 'Spices, bay leaf' is the whole dried leaf. Guideline F explicitly lists 'whole vs ground spice' as not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: whole leaves are typically added and removed from the dish, while ground bay is stirred in, so the preparation changes. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would see and taste the difference, since ground bay gives a gritty, more intense distribution of flavour and appearance, whereas whole leaves look like leaves. Quantity is ignored, per guideline A.

The ingredient is green leaf lettuce, and the USDA entry 'Lettuce, leaf, green, raw' is the same food: green leaf lettuce in its raw, uncooked state. The leading '35g' is only a quantity and is ignored. No cooking method is involved, so the preparation is unchanged. Green leaf lettuce is the standard variety of green leaf lettuce, and the USDA entry describes exactly that, with no added flavour, modification, or processing. A diner would see the same leaves with the same taste, texture and appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is '400g whole duck', meaning a whole bird (carcass with skin, meat, bones, and organs as sold). The USDA match is 'Duck, domesticated, liver, raw', which is only the liver organ of the duck. Condition 1 fails: using only the liver would not replace a whole duck in the dish; the preparation (roasting a whole bird versus cooking an organ) would change completely. Condition 2 fails: a diner would clearly notice a liver instead of a whole duck in taste, texture, and appearance. The quantity is ignored per guideline A, and the match is a different part of the animal, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply, since a liver is not the whole bird). Therefore it is not substitutable.

Condition 1: The ingredient is basil pesto, and the USDA entry is pesto with basil, ready-to-serve. Both are the same product type and both are used the same way, as a sauce or condiment, so the dish's preparation would not change. Condition 2: The entry is a plain basil pesto, not a flavoured or modified variant, so it does not add or remove a component. Homemade and commercial pesto differ in freshness and balance, but guideline G treats a branded entry of the same plain product type as a match, and the difference is one of brand and recipe rather than a different food. The 6g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are reasonably met.

The ingredient is canned condensed consomme, a clarified beef-based soup. The USDA entry is 'Soup, beef broth bouillon and consomme, canned, condensed', which names consomme explicitly, in the same canned condensed form. Under guideline B, the same food under the same name counts as a match. Condition 1: the condensed beef consomme can be used directly in place of the ingredient, with no change to cooking method, since both are canned condensed beef soups used the same way. Condition 2: the entry covers the standard default product (no modification, flavouring, or reduced-sodium descriptor), so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. The entry also includes beef broth bouillon, which is a closely related product, but it names consomme directly, so the match holds. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is vanilla Greek yogurt, with the leading '5g' ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry, Yogurt, Greek, vanilla, lowfat, names the same product type with the same flavour. Under guideline D, flavoured yogurts are typically sold low fat, so the 'lowfat' descriptor reflects how this product is normally sold and is not a modification. Condition 1: the yogurt can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same uncooked dairy product. Condition 2: the ingredient does not specify a fat level, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance between the standard vanilla Greek yogurt and this entry. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is soybean oil, a plain refined cooking oil. The USDA entry 'Oil, soybean lecithin' names a different product: soybean oil combined with or containing lecithin, an emulsifier. That makes it a modified or blended product rather than the same plain oil. Condition 1 fails because lecithin-containing oil behaves differently in cooking: it can foam, emulsify, and change how the oil disperses and browns. Condition 2 also fails because lecithin can alter flavour, mouthfeel and appearance. Guideline F rejects blends and specialty products versus the single home ingredient, and the same logic applies here. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain 'buckwheat flour', the default ground form of buckwheat. The USDA entry 'Buckwheat flour, whole-groat' names the same food. Whole-groat buckwheat flour is the standard form most often sold under the plain name, so it fits the plain-to-default rule (guideline D) and does not count as a different flour the way bread flour differs from cake flour (F). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient directly, since the cooking method is unchanged. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in a typical buckwheat flour product. The entry is the standard form, not a modified or blended one. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a combined item: pecans and dried cranberries together. The USDA match, 'Nuts, pecans, halves, raw', covers only the pecans. Condition 1 fails because using only pecans would omit the dried cranberries, so the dish would not be prepared the same way. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would notice the missing dried fruit's sweetness, chewy texture and red colour. The leading '50g' is ignored per guideline A. Guideline F's rule against a single ingredient standing in for a blend or mixture applies here, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a fresh navel orange, raw. The USDA entry is 'Oranges, raw, navels', which is the same food: a raw navel orange. The quantity (50g) is ignored per guideline A. The parenthetical about the Food Distribution Program is an administrative note and does not change the food. Condition 1: the orange can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same variety in the same raw state. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is drained clementine segments. Clementines are a mandarin-type citrus sold under a trade name, so the USDA entry 'Tangerines (mandarin oranges)' names the same food family and is a recognised match under the same-food-under-another-name rule. 'Drained' matches the USDA entry directly, and the knife work of segmenting does not change the match. Canned fruit is normally packed in juice or syrup, and the juice-pack entry is the normal default for that product, so the packing medium is not an unusual modification. Canned mandarin segments are the standard stand-in for clementine segments in recipes, and once canned and drained they look and taste essentially the same in a finished dish, so the cooking method, texture and appearance are unchanged and a diner would not notice a difference.

The ingredient is plain instant oats, dry. The USDA match is 'Cereals, oats, instant, fortified, with cinnamon and spice, dry', which is instant oats with added cinnamon and spice and fortification. Condition 1: the match could physically replace the oats in terms of preparation (dry oats, same cooking method), so the handling would be the same. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference, since cinnamon and spice flavour is added and the product's taste and appearance (speckled with spice) differ from plain instant oats. Guideline F and D treat a flavoured modification of a plain ingredient as not substitutable, and the flavour change is clearly noticeable. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is cashew butter, unsalted, a nut butter made from cashews. The USDA match is peanut butter, which is made from peanuts, a legume, with a different flavour profile (peanut is distinctly sweet-nutty versus the milder, buttery, slightly sweet cashew). These are different foods, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Guideline F states that a different source/product is not substitutable, and the flavour difference is noticeable to a diner in the finished dish. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the taste difference. Condition 1 is also questionable, since texture and oil content differ somewhat, though the preparation method would be similar. Because condition 2 fails, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is pike fillets that have already been baked. The USDA entry is 'Fish, pike, northern, cooked, dry heat'. Pike is the same food, and 'northern' is the species most commonly sold as pike, so this is the same food under a more specific name (guideline B). 'Dry heat' covers baking, roasting and broiling, so it matches the baked preparation. The cooking state also matches: the ingredient is already baked, so the USDA cooked entry describes it without changing how the dish is prepared (condition 1). A diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, since the USDA entry describes the same cooked fish (condition 2). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is top sirloin steak, a specific beef cut, sold raw. The USDA entry is 'Beef, top sirloin steak, raw', which is the same cut in the same raw state. The quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation, since it is the same raw cut and any cooking method applies identically. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is literally the same cut. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is raw Granny Smith apple, sliced. Sliced is knife work and does not change the match. The USDA entry 'Apple, baked' is a cooked product, and guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state. Condition 1 fails: baked apple cannot replace raw sliced apple without changing preparation, since the recipe would need cooking or would no longer be raw. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the softer texture, the lost tartness and crispness, and the caramelised, cooked flavour. Granny Smith is a tart variety, and the USDA entry does not specify variety, but the state difference alone is enough to reject the match.

The ingredient is a plain 'veal shank', which is normally sold bone-in with its surrounding fat and connective tissue. The USDA entry is 'separable lean only', which excludes the separable fat and, in practice, the bone and collagen-rich sinew that define a shank. Trimming done at home would be handling, but the USDA entry itself describes a different product from the default shank. Condition 2 also fails: a braised or stewed shank loses its gelatinous texture, marrow and bone-in appearance when only lean meat is used, and a diner would notice. Since the match is a modified cut rather than the standard default, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is canola oil, and the USDA entry 'Oil, canola' is the same food under its standard database name. Per guideline B, this is a literal match. The quantity (25g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: canola oil can replace canola oil with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same oil. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus (Opuntia), and the USDA entry 'Nopales, raw' is the same food under the same name. The quantity (200g) is irrelevant. The entry is raw, which is the plain uncooked form a cook would buy, and any trimming or dicing done in the recipe does not change the match. Substituting it would not change the cooking method, flavour, texture, or appearance, and a diner would not notice a difference.

The ingredient is canned garbanzo beans (chickpeas), drained. Under guideline B, garbanzo beans are the same food as chickpeas, but the USDA entry 'Pork and beans' is not chickpeas. It is a prepared product of navy beans (typically small white beans) baked or simmered in tomato sauce with pork, often with sugar and seasoning. Condition 1 fails: using it would change the dish's flavour profile, since it brings sweet tomato sauce and pork flavour that drained plain chickpeas lack, and it would change how the dish is prepared because the sauce would be included. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the sauce, colour, and taste differences, and the bean species differs (navy vs chickpea), so the texture and appearance would differ. Under guideline F, a different product with added ingredients is not a substitute. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is powdered sugar (confectioners' sugar), which is granulated sugar milled to a fine powder, usually with about 3% cornstarch added to prevent caking. The USDA entry is granulated sugar, which has coarse crystals. Condition 1 fails: powdered sugar is used for icing, frosting, dusting and some doughs, and granulated sugar cannot replace it there without changing how the dish is prepared. It would also not dissolve or incorporate the same way in those recipes. Condition 2 fails: the crystal size changes texture (grittiness in frostings and whipped creams), appearance (no matte white dusting), and the cornstarch in powdered sugar changes flavour and mouthfeel. Guideline F rules out a different form of sugar, and this is not the same food under another name, so it is not a match.

The ingredient is Marion blackberries, a specific cultivated blackberry variety (a marionberry, bred from Chehalem and Olallie parents) grown commercially in Oregon. The USDA entry is wild blackberries, raw, from Alaska Native food data. Condition 1 is about preparation: both are raw berries used the same way, so preparation could be unchanged. Condition 2 is about the diner's experience: wild and cultivated blackberries differ in size, seed content, sweetness and acidity, and marionberries have a distinctive tart, complex flavour. This is a different variety or source rather than the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and guideline F treats a sibling variety with a different taste as not substitutable. A diner could notice the difference, so condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is a raw beef chuck blade roast. The USDA entry is the same cut, Beef chuck blade roast, raw. The extra descriptors (separable lean and fat, trimmed to 1/8" fat, choice grade) describe the standard retail form of this roast, which is how a shopper would normally buy it. The ingredient does not ask for a leaner trim, a different grade, or any modification, so the standard default version applies (guideline D). The quantity (185g) is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the same cut can replace the ingredient without changing the cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same cut at the usual trim. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried rosemary, and the USDA entry is 'Spices, rosemary, dried', which is the same product under a standard name. The 15g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both are dried, so there is no fresh-versus-dried or whole-versus-ground mismatch under guideline F. Using the USDA entry would not change the cooking method, flavour, texture, or appearance, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is key lime, a distinct citrus variety (Citrus aurantiifolia) that is smaller, more acidic, and more aromatic than the common Persian/Tahiti lime. The USDA entry 'Limes, raw' is the generic lime. Key lime is not simply another regional name for the same fruit, so guideline B does not apply. It is closer to a sibling variety with a different taste (guideline F, like navel vs blood orange). Condition 1 (same preparation) is plausibly met, since the fruit is used the same way. Condition 2 fails: key lime's distinctive tartness and floral aroma would be noticeable in a dish such as key lime pie or a key lime-flavoured preparation. The weight (110g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain croaker, a fish sold fresh or frozen, with no cooking state or modification stated. The USDA entry 'Fish, croaker' names the same food with no state descriptor, so under guideline E it is the generic food and matches fresh or plain versions. Condition 1: the fish can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same species group and the recipe handling (cutting, cooking) applies identically. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same fish. The quantity (235g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 150g duck liver, a plain raw ingredient; the quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Duck, domesticated, liver, raw' is the same food (domesticated duck liver, uncooked) with no modification, cut, or processing mismatch. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with the same preparation, since raw duck liver is the default form in which it is bought and handled. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is literally the same food in the same raw state. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is strawberry Greek yogurt, and the USDA entry is Yogurt, Greek, strawberry, DANNON OIKOS, which is the same product type under a brand name. Guideline G says a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. Guideline D says flavoured yogurts are typically low fat and that a strawberry yogurt is not a modified version, so the descriptor does not make it differ from what a shopper would normally buy. Condition 1: the yogurt can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the quantity is ignored (Guideline A) and no cooking method changes. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same flavoured Greek yogurt. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a combined item: clams plus diced potato. The USDA entry 'Clams, raw' covers only the clams. Condition 1 fails because using clams alone would change the dish's composition, since the potato would be missing. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the absence of the diced potato in taste, texture and appearance. Guideline F also applies: a single ingredient does not substitute for a blend or combination that contains it. The quantity and the knife work (diced) do not change this.

The ingredient is fresh green chili pepper, which is raw and uncooked. The USDA entry is canned hot green chili peppers, with seeds excluded and only the solids kept, so it is a processed, preserved product. Guideline F lists a different state (raw vs cooked/processed) as not substitutable. Canning also softens the texture, and the packing brine or acidity changes the flavour, so a diner would notice the difference. The 5g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would change from using fresh pepper to using a drained canned product. Condition 2 fails because taste and texture would visibly differ. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is ground cayenne pepper, a dried, ground spice made from the chili pepper Capsicum annuum, used for heat and flavour. The USDA match is hot pepper sauce, a liquid condiment typically made from fermented or vinegar-based chili peppers, with vinegar, salt and often other ingredients. Condition 1 fails: hot pepper sauce cannot be used in place of ground cayenne without changing how the dish is prepared. It adds liquid, acidity, salt and moisture, which alters the cooking method and the dry-spice structure of the recipe. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in flavour (vinegar tang, salt, fermented notes), texture (wetness) and appearance (colour and speckling of ground spice versus a liquid sauce). Per guideline F, a whole/ground spice is not the same as a processed product, and the raw/dry state differs. The quantity is ignored. Not the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is diced chicken ham, a processed chicken product. The USDA entry 'Ham, minced' refers to ham, which is normally pork-based. Diced versus minced is only knife work and does not change the match. The meat source is the key difference: chicken ham and pork ham are different foods with different flavour, texture and colour. A diner would likely notice the difference in taste and appearance, so the match fails condition 2. Under the guidelines, a different meat source is treated as a different food, not a trade name for the same product.

The ingredient is plain 'soy flour' and the USDA entry is 'Flour, soy, defatted', which is the standard soy flour sold to home cooks. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matches the standard default version, and defatted soy flour is that default. The 45g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Soy flour is used as is, with no change to cooking method. Taste, texture and appearance should not differ noticeably from the default product a shopper would buy as soy flour.
