The main risk is that a full-fat soy flour was intended, which would be a different product (guideline F), but the ingredient does not specify it, so the default applies.

1) The ingredient is 50g of summer berry oatmeal, a dry, flavoured oatmeal product; the 50g quantity is ignored per guideline A. 2) The USDA entry is a dry cereal, QUAKER oatmeal REAL MEDLEYS summer berry, which is the same product type (dry summer berry oatmeal) under a brand name. Guideline G normally rejects branded entries with added flavour, but here the flavour is what the ingredient itself asks for, so guideline D applies and the matching flavoured entry counts. 3) Preparation is unchanged: both are dry oatmeal cooked the same way. 4) Taste, texture and appearance should match, since both are summer berry flavoured oatmeal, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 15g of toasted squash seeds, used as a casserole topping. The USDA match is 'Squash, summer, casserole with tomato and cheese', which is a prepared dish containing summer squash cooked with tomato and cheese, not squash seeds. Condition 1 fails: the match is a whole cooked vegetable dish, not a seed garnish, so it cannot be used in place of toasted seeds without changing preparation (the seeds would be toasted separately and sprinkled on top, while the match is a cooked casserole component). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture (crunchy toasted seeds versus soft cooked squash with tomato and cheese), and appearance. The match is the flesh of the vegetable in a prepared dish, not the seeds, and the toasted state is not represented. Per guideline F (raw/processed source versus processed ingredient, and different states), this is not substitutable. The quantity is ignored per guideline A.

Pinyon kernels are the edible seeds of pinyon pines (Pinus edulis and related species), which are a type of pine nut. Under guideline B, regional or alternate names for the same food count as a match, so 'Pine nuts' is the same food under another name. The 100g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Both are raw nut kernels used the same way in cooking, with no change to preparation. Any flavour or size variation between pinyon and other pine nut species is a sibling-variety difference that a diner would not reliably notice in a typical dish, and the USDA entry is the generic pine nut, which covers pinyon. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned sprouted mung beans, drained. The USDA entry is 'Beans, mung, mature seeds, sprouted, canned, drained solids', which names the same food in the same state (canned, sprouted, drained). The weight prefix is decoration and is ignored. Condition 1: the entry can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation, since draining is the same handling the recipe would do. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same canned, drained product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned fava beans, drained. The USDA entry is 'Broadbeans (fava beans), mature seeds, canned'. Fava beans and broad beans are the same food under different names (guideline B). Both are canned, so the processing state matches. 'Drained' is handling the recipe does itself and does not change the match (guideline C). The 150g weight is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the canned beans can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same canned bean.

The ingredient is plain cheddar cheese, quantity irrelevant (guideline A). The USDA entry is 'Cheese, cheddar', with the parenthetical note 'Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program', which is an administrative descriptor about the program scope, not a modification of the product (guideline D/C). It is the same food as the plain default cheddar, so no change to preparation is needed and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is ground turkey patties, cooked, specified as 'lean'. The USDA match is ground turkey at 85% lean / 15% fat, broiled. Quantity is ignored. Cooking state is acceptable: the ingredient says only 'cooked', and broiled is a cooked state, so the cooking-method condition is not the problem. The problem is the fat content. Under USDA definitions, 'lean' means under 10% fat, while 85% lean contains 15% fat. The ingredient explicitly asks for a lean product, and the match is a regular-fat product. Guideline D treats a modified version of a plain ingredient as a non-match, and guideline F treats differing product characteristics as non-substitutable. Higher fat content changes juiciness, mouthfeel and flavour of cooked patties, and a diner could plausibly notice the richer, moister, greasier result. Condition 2 is therefore not met.

The ingredient is goose fat. The USDA entry 'Fat, goose' names the same food, rendered goose fat, so this is the same product under a plain name (guideline B). The '50g' quantity and the '(optional)' note do not affect the match (guideline A). Nothing in the entry indicates a modified, flavoured, or processed version, and no state or preparation differs from the plain ingredient. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing the cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same fat.

The ingredient is honey mustard used as a dip, and the USDA entry is 'Honey mustard dip', which names the same product. The '100g' quantity is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, because it is the same dipping sauce served the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food under a near-identical name (guidelines B and D). Neither the match nor the ingredient is described as modified, flavoured differently, or in a different state. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is unsweetened almond milk, and the USDA match is 'Almond milk, unsweetened', which is the same product under the same descriptor. The leading weight '375g' is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: the diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same unsweetened almond milk. Guideline D treats the modifier 'unsweetened' as matching when the ingredient itself asks for that version. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a salted sunflower seed spread, which is the same food as sunflower seed butter with added salt, just under a different name. The quantity (3g) is decoration and is ignored. The USDA entry's note about the Food Distribution Program describes the entry's origin, not a change to the food. Condition 1: the spread can replace the USDA food with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since both are salted sunflower seed butter. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 315g of lime wedges, served as an accompaniment (fresh lime fruit, used raw as a garnish). The USDA match is 'Frozen novelties, ice type, lime', which is a frozen confection (like a sorbet-style popsicle or ice pop) flavoured with lime. Condition 1: Lime wedges cannot be substituted with a frozen lime ice pop without changing how the dish is prepared; a frozen novelty is not a fruit garnish that can be cut and served alongside a dish. Serving it would also change the preparation entirely, since it is a sweetened, frozen dessert product rather than a raw fruit. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference: the frozen, sweetened, dense, icy texture and appearance differ from fresh citrus wedges, and the flavour is sweetened and processed rather than the tart fresh juice and peel of lime. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply, since the match is a processed frozen dessert, not the raw fruit). Both conditions fail.

1. Ignoring the 585g weight, the ingredient is raw bone-in chicken thighs. The USDA entry is raw chicken thigh from broilers or fryers, the same cut and species. 2. Bone-in is the form in which thighs are normally sold, and the USDA thigh entry reflects that whole bone-in cut, so the cut matches rather than being a different one. 3. Bone-in thighs are normally sold skin-on, so 'meat and skin' is the standard default version, not a modified one. Cooking method, appearance and texture would be unchanged. 4. 'Raw' matches the uncooked ingredient. Any handling such as trimming does not alter the match. 5. Both conditions hold: the match could replace the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference.

The ingredient is 'ground pork, sweet Italian style', which is pork seasoned as Italian sausage meat, typically with fennel, garlic, salt and other spices. The USDA match 'Pork, ground, raw' is plain unseasoned ground pork. Condition 1: the match could physically replace the meat and the cooking method would be unchanged. Condition 2: the seasoning changes the flavour noticeably (fennel and sweet spice notes are obvious to a diner), so a diner would notice a difference. Per guideline F, a single ingredient versus a seasoned product containing it is not substitutable, and the leading weight is ignored. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried tofu (dehydrated bean curd, pressed). The USDA match is fresh extra firm tofu prepared with nigari, which retains its water content. Guideline F lists 'a different state (fresh vs dried)' as not substitutable. Pressing fresh extra firm tofu removes some water but does not produce the dense, chewy texture of dried tofu, so the cooking behaviour and texture would differ. A diner would likely notice the firmer, chewier, more concentrated texture of dried tofu versus fresh extra firm tofu. The match fails both conditions.

Condition 1 (same preparation): the ingredient is plain grated parmesan, and the USDA entry is also dry grated parmesan, so the form and cooking use are the same. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference): the USDA entry is specifically reduced-fat. Guideline D treats reduced-fat as a modification of a plain ingredient, not the standard default version. Reduced-fat parmesan has a lower fat content, which changes its flavour, melt and mouthfeel, so a diner could notice the difference. Condition 2 is not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain water crackers, a flour-and-water cracker with a neutral, mild flavour and a pale, uniform appearance. The USDA match is 'Crackers, cheese', a different product with added cheese, which changes the flavour, and typically the colour and texture. Condition 1 (same use in the dish without changing preparation) could be met, since both are crackers, but condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the cheese flavour and the different appearance. Per guideline F, a flavoured variant is a different product, not the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is beef frankfurters that have been heated. The USDA entry, 'Frankfurter, beef, heated', is the same food with the same state (cooked/heated) and the same component (beef). Per guideline B, the same food under another name counts. The quantity (300g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the frankfurter could replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are already heated and need no further cooking change. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the USDA entry describes the same heated beef frankfurter. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain sliced deli roast beef, with no request for a low-sodium version. The USDA entry is beef luncheon meat, which matches the product type, but it is specifically the reduced-sodium modified version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced-sodium entry is not substitutable. Condition 1 is arguably met because the preparation would not change, but condition 2 fails: reduced sodium changes the flavour, and a diner could notice the lower salt content compared with ordinary deli roast beef. The weight (300g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is provolone cheese, a plain cheese named by type with no stated modification. The USDA entry 'Cheese, provolone' is the same food under the identical name, so it is the standard default version (guideline D). The leading weight of 150g is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Provolone is normally sold as a semi-hard cheese, and the USDA entry describes that same product, so the cheese can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation (condition 1). A diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance because it is the same product (condition 2). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh pork breakfast sausage, crumbled. The USDA entry is the generic 'Pork sausage', which carries no state descriptor (no cooked, smoked, dried or flavoured qualifier), so it falls under the plain-name default rule (D) and matches the fresh, uncooked product as commonly sold. Breakfast sausage is the standard form of fresh pork sausage in the US market, so the generic entry represents the same food under its general name. Crumbling is knife or handling work and does not change the match (C). Condition 1: the generic sausage can be crumbled and cooked in the same way, so the preparation does not change. Condition 2: the diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since the seasoning profile of breakfast sausage is the default for fresh pork sausage. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw Pacific cod. The USDA entry is 'Fish, cod, Pacific, raw (may have been previously frozen)', which is the same species in the same raw state. The parenthetical note about previous freezing reflects normal frozen-then-thawed fish sold as fresh, which guideline E treats as matching the raw entry since freezing does not visibly change the fish when it is cooked. The leading weight of 195g is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the fish could be used in place of the ingredient with the same preparation, since it is the same raw food and the cooking method is unchanged. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, as it is the same species in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain tortilla chips, the standard default product. The USDA entry is 'Tortilla chips, reduced fat, flavored', which is a modified version on two counts: it is reduced fat and it is flavored. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced-fat or flavoured version is not a match. Condition 1 can be met, since the chips could physically be swapped in. Condition 2 fails: flavouring changes taste, and reduced fat changes texture and mouthfeel, so a diner could notice the difference. The flavouring is not a normal descriptor of how plain tortilla chips are sold, so the modification does not fall under the exception for normally-sold products.

The ingredient is trout roe, the unfertilized eggs of the trout, which are sold and eaten as small, firm, translucent pearls. The USDA match, 'Fish, trout, NFS', is the flesh of the whole fish with no state specified. Roe is a different food from fish meat, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: roe is used whole as a garnish or topping, while fish flesh would need to be cooked, flaked, or filleted, which changes how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in texture (burst pearls versus flaky or firm flesh) and appearance (glossy orange eggs versus opaque meat). Guideline F's point about a raw source versus a processed ingredient applies by analogy: the roe and the flesh are different parts of the animal. The quantity of 400g is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain American cheese, the standard default product. The USDA match is 'Cheese, American, reduced sodium', a modified version with lower sodium content. Guideline D says a plain ingredient matched to a reduced-sodium version is not substitutable. Reduced-sodium cheese also tastes different, since salt contributes to flavour, so a diner could notice the difference. Condition 1 (same preparation) is arguably met, but condition 2 (no noticeable taste difference) is not reliably met, so the match fails. The 50g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain yogurt, the default unmodified product. The USDA match is 'Yogurt, plain, nonfat', which is a fat-modified version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced or fat-free version is not a match. Condition 1: nonfat yogurt behaves differently in cooking. It separates or thins more under heat and gives a different mouthfeel in sauces and baking, so the preparation can change. Condition 2: nonfat yogurt is noticeably thinner and less creamy, with a sharper tang than whole-milk plain yogurt, so a diner could detect the difference in taste and texture. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

Ingredient: 97% lean ground beef, 150g (quantity ignored per guideline A). USDA match: Beef, ground, 97% lean meat / 3% fat, raw. This is the same product under its standard descriptor: the lean percentage is identical and the entry is raw, which is the uncooked state a home cook would start from (guideline C). Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation; it is browned, simmered or formed the same way, and the ground form matches. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the fat content and grind are the same. No cut, fat type, or processing difference exists between the two. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is teff flour, a fine flour milled from teff grain, with a distinctive mild, slightly nutty, molasses-like flavour and a particular texture. The USDA match is vital wheat gluten, which is a concentrated wheat protein powder (about 75-80% protein) made by washing wheat flour to remove starch. It is a different food from teff flour: it comes from a different grain, is a processed protein isolate rather than a whole-grain flour, and has no comparable flavour. Condition 1 fails: it would change the dish, since gluten provides elasticity and structure but no bulk starch or teff flavour, so baked goods, porridge or injera-type preparations would behave differently and the batter or dough handling would change. Condition 2 fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture (chewy, elastic rather than the tender, earthy crumb of teff) and appearance. Per guideline F, a different flour is not substitutable. The quantity is ignored. Not substitutable.

Textured soy protein (TVP/TSP) is an extruded, dehydrated, chewy, granular product made from defatted soy flour or concentrate. Soy protein isolate is a fine, powdery, highly refined protein ingredient. They are different processed forms, not the same food under another name. Substituting isolate would change the preparation: TSP is typically rehydrated and simmered, whereas isolate is usually whisked or blended into liquids, so it could not be used in place without altering the method. It would also change the texture and appearance of the dish, since TSP gives a chunky, meaty bite that isolate cannot reproduce, and a diner would notice a difference. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is raw clams (the 'optional' note and the 530g quantity are decoration and ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry 'Clams, raw' is the same food, uncooked, with no added modification, so it is the standard default version (guidelines B, C, D). Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are raw clams. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same raw food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fennel bulb, a plain vegetable. The USDA entry 'Fennel, bulb, raw' is the same food in the same state: the raw bulb. The quantity (10g) is decoration and is ignored. No cooking method is implied, and the bulb can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Taste, texture, and appearance are identical, since the diner would be eating the same raw fennel bulb. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cooked hyacinth beans with no added salt. The USDA entry is hyacinth beans, mature seeds, cooked, boiled, without salt. It is the same food in the same state (cooked), and 'without salt' matches 'unsalted'. The quantity prefix '4g' is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are already cooked and unsalted. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the product is the same boiled, unsalted hyacinth bean.

The ingredient is roasted pinon nuts, unsalted, at 150g. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Pinon Nuts, roasted (Navajo)', which is the same food: pinon nuts, roasted. The '(Navajo)' qualifier is a regional/cultural naming descriptor for the same nut, not a different variety with a different taste (guideline B). The entry names no added salt, so it matches the plain, unsalted default (guideline D). Condition 1: the nuts can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are already roasted and used as-is. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same roasted pinon nut with no added flavour or salt. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned skipjack tuna, drained. Canned tuna is precooked (retorted or steamed during canning), so it is a cooked, flaked, processed product. The USDA match is 'Fish, tuna, fresh, skipjack, raw', which is uncooked whole fish. Guideline F says raw vs cooked is a different state and not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using raw tuna would change the preparation, since it would need cooking or would be eaten raw, and it would not be the flaked, ready-to-use product the recipe assumes. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, appearance (pale flaked canned tuna vs raw red-pink flesh) and flavour (canned tuna's characteristic taste). The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is sweetbreads, the thymus or pancreas glands of calves or lambs. The USDA entry is 'Sweetbreads', which is literally the same food under the same name. It carries no cooking state, cut, or modifier (no 'cooked', 'fried', or 'flavoured'), so it is the generic food. The quantity prefix '30g' is decoration and is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same food and needs the same treatment such as soaking, blanching, and sautéing. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the identical product.

The ingredient is drumstick pods that have been boiled and salted. The USDA entry is drumstick pods, cooked, boiled, drained, with salt. Both describe the same food in the same state: boiled and salted. The word 'drained' is handling that does not change the product, and 'with salt' corresponds to 'salted'. The weight prefix is ignored per guideline A. Cooking method is unchanged, and a diner would not taste or see a difference, so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a reduced-sodium fish broth, which is a modified version of plain fish broth. The USDA entry 'Fish broth' names no sodium state, so it is the standard default version with regular sodium. Guideline D says a plain entry does not match a modified ingredient when the ingredient itself asks for the modified version. Condition 1 is arguably met because the broth could be used in the same preparation. Condition 2 fails: regular broth has noticeably more salt, so a diner could taste the difference. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried pears, and the USDA entry is 'Pear, dried', which is the same food in the same state. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the dried pear could replace the ingredient in the recipe without any change to preparation, since no cooking method or handling is altered. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same dried pear product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'brandy' and the USDA match is 'Brandy', which is the same food under the same name. Per guideline A, the 260g quantity is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since no cooking method or handling differs. Condition 2: the match is the same product, so a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is roasted peanuts. The USDA match is almonds, dry roasted, without salt added. Condition 1: Peanuts and almonds are different nut species, and the ingredient is a peanut, not an almond. Guideline B does not apply because peanut and almond are not regional or culinary names for the same food. Guideline F rules out substituting a different food that is merely similar. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference in taste (peanut vs almond flavour) and texture. The roasting state matches, but the food itself does not. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw round steak, cut into strips. Cutting into strips is handling and does not change the match, so the cut itself is not the issue. The USDA entry, however, is specifically cooked and braised, which is a different state from raw (guideline F: raw vs cooked is not substitutable). Using pre-braised meat in place of raw steak would change the cooking method, since the recipe would need to cook the steak, and the diner would notice differences in texture, moisture, and appearance. The entry also specifies bottom round, separable lean and fat, trimmed to 0" fat, which is a cut-and-state detail beyond the plain 'round steak'. Condition 1 fails because the preparation changes, and condition 2 fails because taste, texture, and appearance would differ.

The ingredient is fresh pork hock, an uncured raw cut of pork. The USDA match is 'Pork, pickled pork hocks', which is a cured product (pickled/brined, typically with salt and curing agents). Under guideline F, a different state (raw vs cured/processed) is not the same food, and the pickling changes flavour (salty, tangy, cured) and texture and appearance (pink or grey cured colour). Guideline D also treats added solutions/additives as a modification. Cooking would also differ: pickled hocks are usually cooked to be tender and are already salted, so substituting them would alter the dish's seasoning and flavour, and a diner would notice the cured taste. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable taste difference) are both not met.

The ingredient is beef and pork mortadella, a cured emulsified sausage. The USDA entry 'Mortadella, beef, pork' names the same product with the same components (beef and pork). Under guideline B and D, this is the same food under a near-identical name and the standard version. Quantity (110g) is ignored per guideline A. Cooking method is unaffected, since mortadella is normally served sliced or cubed without further preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance between the two.

The ingredient 'chicken fillet' most commonly means boneless chicken breast (white meat), and the 300g quantity is decoration per guideline A. The USDA match is dark meat thigh, meat only, raw, which is a different cut. Guideline F says a different cut of meat is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: substituting thigh for breast changes the cut and the cooking behaviour (thigh is fattier and needs longer cooking to stay tender). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the darker colour, richer flavour, and different texture of thigh meat. Since both conditions are not met, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is cantaloupe fruit pieces canned in syrup, so it is a solid fruit preserved in a sweet liquid. The USDA match, cantaloupe nectar, is a pureed or juiced beverage product. Condition 1 fails: a cook could not swap nectar for canned cantaloupe pieces without changing the dish's preparation, since the fruit would be liquid rather than chunks. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance, because the fruit would no longer be solid pieces. Guideline F rules out a processed or different-state product that is not the same food in the same form, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient 'Greenland turbot' is a trade name for Greenland halibut (Reinhardtius hippoglossoides), the same species as the USDA entry 'Fish, halibut, Greenland, raw'. Under guideline B, a regional or trade name for the same food counts as a match. The '200g' quantity is ignored (A). 'Fillet' is a cut/handling form of the raw fish and does not change the match (C). Both entries are raw, so cooking method is unchanged, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance because it is the same fish. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a raw whole turkey. The USDA entry is 'Turkey, whole, skin (light and dark), raw', which is the same food in its uncooked state. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matches its standard default version. A whole turkey is normally sold with skin on, and it includes both light and dark meat, so the 'skin (light and dark)' descriptor just describes how a whole bird is normally sold. Under condition 1, it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Under condition 2, a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The 180g weight is ignored per guideline A. The match is the same food, so it is substitutable.

The ingredient is watercress, a leafy green (Nasturtium officinale) eaten raw or lightly cooked, with a peppery, bitter taste and crisp leaves. The USDA match is golden seedless raisins, which are dried grapes: sweet, chewy, and dark-golden in appearance. They are not the same food under another name (condition B does not apply), and they are not a cut, variety, or preparation of watercress. Condition 1 fails because raisins cannot take watercress's place without changing how the dish is prepared (the leaves would be replaced by a dried, sweet fruit). Condition 2 fails because a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (sweet vs peppery), texture (chewy vs crisp) and appearance (dried fruit vs green leaves). Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain haddock, with the 100g quantity disregarded per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Fish, haddock, NFS' (not further specified) is the same food with no added processing, preparation, or state descriptor, so it is the generic default for haddock (guidelines B and D). Its NFS wording means it covers haddock regardless of form, so it does not change the cooking method. Haddock as bought is the same fish, so the dish would be prepared the same way and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Chinese chives (Allium tuberosum, also called garlic chives), a member of the onion/allium family with flat leaves and a garlic-onion flavour. The USDA match is Cabbage, Chinese (Brassica rapa, bok choy or napa-type cabbage), cooked. These are different plants from different families with different flavour, texture and appearance. Chinese cabbage is not a regional or trade name for Chinese chives, so guideline B does not apply. Substituting cooked cabbage would change the taste (mild and sweet versus garlicky), the texture, and the appearance, and a diner would notice. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh milkfish, deboned, weighing 225g. The weight is decorative and ignored. The USDA entry 'Fish, milkfish, raw' is the same species in the same uncooked state. Deboning is knife work that does not change the match. The fish is fresh, so the raw entry matches. Using the USDA entry would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient 'anhydrous butter oil' is a plain, standard product: butterfat with the water and milk solids removed. The USDA entry 'Butter oil, anhydrous' names the same food under the same name, so it is the same product, not a sibling or modified version. Quantity (25g) is ignored per the guidelines. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is used the same way (melted or added as a fat). Condition 2: the diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is literally the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 96% lean ground pork, given with no cooking state, so it is raw meat that the recipe will cook. The USDA match is 'Pork, ground, 96% lean / 4% fat, cooked, pan-broiled.' Same cut and lean percentage, but the match is cooked and pan-broiled. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Using pre-cooked, pan-broiled pork would change the cooking method, since the recipe would otherwise cook the raw meat, and it would change texture and appearance (browning and a firmer, drier texture). A diner could notice the difference. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would change. Condition 2 is also likely to fail because the cooked meat looks and tastes different from raw meat that is cooked within the dish. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient 'cowpeas' refers to the bean/seed of the cowpea plant, usually bought dried or as fresh shelled peas. The USDA entry 'Cowpeas, leafy tips, raw' is the leaves and shoot tips of the same plant, a leafy green vegetable. This is a different plant part, not the same food under another name, so it fails condition 1 (it would change the dish) and condition 2 (a diner would taste and see leafy greens instead of beans). The weight of 50g is ignored per the guidelines. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is whole flaxseeds, which are intact, hard, oval seeds. The USDA match is ground flaxseed, a processed form with a powdery, meal-like texture. Condition 1: ground flax can be used in some recipes, but it changes preparation. Whole seeds are often added unground or toasted, while ground flax is typically mixed in as a meal, and the recipe's handling and method would change. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in appearance and texture, since whole seeds are visible and crunchy while ground flax is fine and uniform. Guideline F treats whole versus ground forms as a different state that is not substitutable, and the same logic applies here. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is generic fruit preserves, which shoppers normally buy sweetened with sugar. The USDA entry specifically describes jams and preserves sweetened with fruit juice. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a sweetened-with-a-different-agent version is a modification, so it is not the standard default. Condition 2 also fails: juice-sweetened preserves are typically less sweet and can differ in flavour and set, so a diner could notice the difference. Quantity is ignored, and the USDA entry is not the same product under another name. Neither condition is clearly met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is canned mackerel, drained. Canned fish is already cooked during processing and packed in oil or water, with a flaked, soft texture and a distinct flavour. The USDA match is 'Fish, mackerel, Atlantic, raw', which is uncooked whole or fillet fish. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Using raw mackerel would change the preparation: it would need cooking, and it would not be flaked or ready to eat as canned fish is. A diner would also notice differences in texture, appearance and taste. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 likely fails too.

The ingredient is pickled pork kidney, a cured and preserved product. The USDA entry 'Kidney' is a generic, unprocessed organ meat with no pickling or species specified. Condition 1 fails: using raw kidney would require skipping or redoing the pickling step, which changes how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in flavour (sharp, acidic, brined taste versus mild, metallic raw or cooked kidney), texture (firmer, cured), and appearance (pickled versus plain). Guideline F rules out a different state (pickled/processed versus raw), and guideline D treats a modified form as not matching the plain entry. The ingredient is not the same food under another name, so the match is not acceptable.

The ingredient is taro chips, a snack food made from sliced, fried taro. The USDA entry is 'Taro chips', which names the same product with the same components. The quantity prefix (165g) is decoration and is ignored. Under guideline B, the match is literally the same food, and the default version of a plain product matches under guideline D. Using the USDA entry would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is crispy battered poultry skin, meaning skin from a bird that has been coated in batter and fried. The USDA entry is chicken (broilers or fryers) skin only, cooked, fried, with batter. Condition 1: the entry is cooked, fried and battered, which matches the prepared state of the ingredient. It is also skin only, so no meat is added. Poultry skin with no species named defaults to chicken, the standard poultry, so the species is the same food under a general name (guideline B). Using it in place of the ingredient would not change the preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference between chicken skin fried in batter and battered poultry skin, since the food is the same and both are crisp, battered and fried. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'mandarin orange', a general name for the Citrus reticulata group. A clementine is a seedless hybrid within that group, and in many markets (especially the UK) clementines are sold and labelled as mandarins. Under guideline B, this is close to the same food under a common name, not a different food. The weight '200g' is decoration (guideline A). The match is raw fresh fruit, so no cooking method changes. Appearance, texture and flavour are close enough that a diner would not reliably notice a difference. Clementines are sweeter and usually seedless, but this is a within-group variation, not a different food like navel versus blood orange. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a combination of two different foods: lotus seeds and goji berries. The USDA match, 'Seeds, lotus seeds, raw', covers only the lotus seeds. Goji berries are not represented at all, so the match would omit half the ingredient. Condition 1 fails because using only lotus seeds would change the dish's composition and preparation. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would notice the missing goji berries in taste, texture (dried, chewy, sweet berries), and appearance (their red colour). The quantity and the raw/dried state of the lotus seeds do not change this conclusion.

The ingredient is plain smooth peanut butter. The USDA entry, 'Peanut butter, smooth style, with salt', is the same food in its standard form. Salted smooth peanut butter is the default product a shopper buys under that name, so the 'with salt' descriptor is not a modification (guideline D). The parenthetical about the Food Distribution Program is an administrative note and does not change the product. The quantity (5g) is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation, since both are spreads or mix-ins used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because salted smooth peanut butter is what is normally served. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chunky peanut butter that is explicitly unsalted. The USDA entry is chunk-style peanut butter with salt. Both are the same base food, so the question is whether the added salt changes the dish. Guideline D treats a reduced or low-sodium version as a modification, and the reverse applies here: the ingredient asks for unsalted, and the match contains added salt. Salt is readily detectable in peanut butter, so a diner could taste the difference. Condition 1 may hold, since the peanut butter could be swapped in without changing preparation. Condition 2 fails because the taste would change. The 5g quantity is ignored per guideline A. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is lamb sweetbreads (thymus gland). The USDA match is lamb kidney, raw, from New Zealand. Sweetbreads are the thymus gland (or sometimes pancreas), not kidney; these are different organs with different textures, flavours, and appearance. Kidney has a strong, distinctly mineral/urinary flavour and a dense, fibrous texture with a central medulla, whereas sweetbreads are prized for a delicate, creamy, mild taste and tender texture. Cooking methods also differ: sweetbreads are typically blanched, then pan-fried or braised, while kidney is usually sautéed briefly or stewed to avoid toughness and ammonia notes. Per guideline F, a different cut or organ is not substitutable, and the diner would clearly notice the difference in taste and texture. Guideline B (same food under another name) does not apply because kidney and thymus are not the same food. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is cashew nut oil, a pressed oil extracted from cashew nuts. The USDA match is 'Cashews, unroasted', which is the raw whole nut itself. Condition 1: cashew nut oil cannot be used in place of raw cashews without changing how the dish is prepared; raw nuts are solid and must be chopped, ground, or soaked, whereas oil is a liquid fat used for frying, dressing, or finishing. The substitution would alter the cooking method and the dish's structure. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in texture, appearance, and flavour, since oil lacks the solid, crunchy nut structure and carries no nut particles. Per guideline F, the raw source is not substitutable for the processed ingredient (e.g., gelatin powder vs pork skin; a different fat vs another). Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is salted egg yolk, a cured product. Its defining features are added salt, a firmer and drier texture from curing, and a distinctive savoury flavour. The USDA match is 'Egg, yolk, raw, fresh', an uncured, unsalted raw yolk. Using it would change flavour (no salt or cured taste) and texture (soft and liquid rather than firm and sandy), and a diner would notice. Under guideline F, a processed ingredient is not interchangeable with its raw source, and under guideline D, a modified version differs from the plain entry. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste or texture) both fail.

The ingredient is uncooked (raw) spelt grain, which must be cooked or baked as part of the recipe. The USDA match is 'Spelt, cooked', which is already cooked. Guideline F states that raw versus cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Using cooked spelt would change how the dish is prepared, since the grain would not be cooked in the recipe, and the texture and appearance would differ from raw grain going through the cooking process. The quantity (400g) is irrelevant under guideline A. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is a mix of safflower seeds and pumpkin seeds. The USDA match is only pumpkin seeds, unsalted. Condition 1: substituting only pumpkin seeds changes the composition of the dish, since safflower seeds are absent, so the mix is not reproduced. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice a difference in appearance and flavour, because safflower seeds are visibly different (smaller, whiter/greyish, different taste) and the mix would no longer be a blend. Guideline F rejects a single ingredient versus a blend containing it. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

"Rooster sauce" is the common name for Huy Fong Sriracha, the chile-garlic sauce sold with a rooster label. The USDA entry "Sauce, hot chile, sriracha" describes that same product. Under guideline B, a regional or trade name for the same food counts as a match. Quantity is ignored under guideline A. Both conditions hold: the sauce can be used without changing preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference, since it is the same product.

The ingredient is peach-flavoured Greek yogurt, with no fat level specified. The USDA entry is Greek yogurt, nonfat, peach, from Chobani, so the food type and flavour both match. Guideline D says flavoured yogurts are typically low fat, so the nonfat descriptor describes how this product is normally sold and is not a modification. Guideline G allows a branded entry of the same product type, and the Chobani peach flavour matches the peach in the ingredient. The 250g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same peach Greek yogurt. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain beef bologna, the standard default product. The USDA match is 'Beef, bologna, reduced sodium', which is a modified version: its sodium content is deliberately lowered. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced-sodium version as not a match, because the ingredient does not ask for that version. Condition 1 (preparation) is met, since bologna is used as-is in the same way. Condition 2 is not met: reduced sodium lowers the salt level, which changes taste and can be noticed by a diner. The quantity (405g) is ignored per guideline A. The two foods are not literally the same product, so guideline B does not apply.

The ingredient is a blend of two foods: cottage cheese and sour cream, blended together. The USDA match is only 'Cheese, cottage, dry curd', a single ingredient with no cream. Under guideline F, a single ingredient does not substitute for a blend or product containing it. Condition 1 fails: the recipe calls for the cottage cheese and sour cream to be blended, and dry curd cottage cheese alone cannot reproduce the blended mixture without adding the sour cream. Condition 2 also fails: dry curd is crumbly, dry and low in fat, whereas the blend is smooth, creamy and rich. A diner would notice the difference in texture, mouthfeel and richness. Because both conditions are not met, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is simmered corn and butter beans. Butter beans are the same food as lima beans, a regional name under guideline B. The USDA entry is succotash made from corn and lima beans, so it names the same dish with the same two components (guideline D). Simmering and boiling are both moist-heat cooking in water, so the preparation method does not change. The entry is cooked and drained, which matches a ready-to-serve simmered side. 'Without salt' is the plain default, since the ingredient does not mention salt. The quantity is ignored (guideline A). Taste, texture and appearance should be essentially the same, so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Monterey Jack cheese, a plain cheese with no stated modification or state. The USDA entry 'Cheese, monterey' is the same cheese under its alternate name (Monterey Jack is also sold as 'monterey'), so it falls under guideline B. The leading weight '335g' is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). No cooking method, flavour, texture, or appearance differs between the two, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain sliced bacon, the standard default product. The USDA entry is 'Bacon, pre-sliced, reduced/low sodium, unprepared'. Pre-sliced and unprepared are compatible with sliced bacon in the recipe, so the food itself is the same product. The 'reduced/low sodium' descriptor is a modification, not how bacon is normally sold by default. Guideline D says a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced/low sodium version is not a match, and the ingredient does not ask for that version. Condition 1 (same preparation) is arguably met, but condition 2 fails: reduced-sodium bacon is noticeably less salty and has a different flavour profile, so a diner could notice the difference. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is peanut milk, a liquid plant-based milk made by blending peanuts with water. The USDA match is peanut oil, a pure extracted fat. These are different products, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Condition 1 fails: swapping peanut oil for peanut milk would change the liquid content, the fat-to-water ratio, and how the dish is prepared, since milk is typically whisked, poured, or heated while oil is measured as a fat. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the difference, since peanut oil lacks the milk's creaminess, body, and dairy-like mouthfeel. Guideline F rejects a different fat or oil in place of the original, and a processed product versus its source. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is low-fat milk, a dairy liquid. The USDA match is chia seeds, a dry seed from the Salvia hispanica plant. Condition 1 fails: chia seeds cannot replace milk in a recipe without changing how the dish is prepared, since milk is a liquid and chia seeds are dry seeds that would need hydrating and would change the cooking method. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. The match is not the same food under another name, and it is not a modified version of milk. Quantity is irrelevant. Therefore it is not substitutable.

Condition 1: The ingredient is a chicken leg with the skin removed. The USDA entry is 'Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh', which is the same cut, since a chicken leg is the drumstick and thigh together. 'Skin not eaten' corresponds to the skinless state the ingredient specifies. 'NS as to cooking method' is a generic descriptor, and the ingredient names no cooking method, so it does not conflict. The match could replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: The food is the same cut and state, so a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned lotus seeds, which are pre-cooked and packed in water or syrup, so they are soft and ready to eat. The USDA match is 'Seeds, lotus seeds, raw', which is uncooked, hard, dried seed. Condition 1 fails: using raw seeds would require soaking and cooking to soften them, which changes the preparation method. Condition 2 also fails: the dish would show a clear difference in texture and taste, since raw seeds are hard and starchy while canned seeds are tender. Guideline F rejects raw versus processed or cooked states, and a different packing medium, so this is not a valid match.

The ingredient is canned sardines packed in tomato sauce. The USDA entry is Atlantic sardine canned in oil, drained solids with bone. It is the same fish, so the food identity matches. However, the packing medium differs: tomato sauce versus oil. Guideline F says a different packing medium is not substitutable. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the difference, since tomato sauce adds acidity, sweetness and savoury flavour that oil packing does not, and the sauce would be missing from the dish. The drained-solids basis does not remove the sauce difference, because the sauce flavours the fish itself. Condition 1 is therefore not met either, since using oil-packed sardines would change the flavour of the dish. Both conditions cannot be satisfied, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a sweet miso glaze, which is miso blended with sweetening and flavouring components such as sugar, mirin or sake, and is used as a sweet, sticky coating. The USDA entry 'Miso sauce' is a general miso-based sauce without the sweetened glaze character. Condition 1 is not clearly met: a glaze is applied and caramelises differently from a generic miso sauce, so the preparation may change. Condition 2 is not met: a diner would taste the difference in sweetness and flavour. Under guideline D and F, a sweetened or flavoured version is not the same as the plain product, so this is not a substitutable match.

The ingredient is grilled shrimp (190g; weight ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry is 'Shrimp, grilled', which is the same food in the same prepared state: grilled shrimp. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since the shrimp is already grilled and no further cooking method is implied. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same grilled shrimp product. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is dried catfish, flaked (a fish product, dried and flaked). The USDA match is Bulgur, dry, which is a cereal grain product made from cracked wheat. These are entirely different foods: different food group (fish vs cereal grain), different protein and fat content, different flavour, and different texture and appearance. Bulgur would not be used in place of dried catfish without changing the dish's preparation, flavour, and appearance, and a diner would immediately notice the difference. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails. Quantity is ignored per the guidelines, and the match is not a regional name or same-food variant.

The ingredient 'pitanga' is the Brazilian name for the Surinam cherry (Eugenia uniflora). The USDA entry 'Pitanga, (surinam-cherry), raw' is the same fruit under its common English name, so this is the same food under another name (Guideline B). The '300g' quantity is decoration and is ignored (Guideline A). 'Raw' means uncooked, which matches fresh pitanga used as a fruit (Guideline C). No modification, processing, or state change is implied. Condition 1: the fruit could be used in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the identical fruit. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is hemp seeds (hulled hemp hearts, a nut-like seed with a nutty flavour, soft texture, and green-brown speckled appearance). The USDA match is enriched long-grain white rice, raw. These are different foods: hemp seeds are an oilseed, while rice is a cereal grain. Rice is starchy, has a neutral flavour, and is typically cooked before eating, whereas hemp seeds are eaten raw or sprinkled onto dishes for crunch and nutty taste. Using rice in place of hemp seeds would change the flavour, texture, and appearance of the dish, and a diner would notice the difference. Guideline F also rules out a raw plant source being matched to a different processed or different-category ingredient. Condition 1 fails (the preparation would change, since hemp seeds are not used the way rice is), and condition 2 fails (taste, texture, and appearance differ). The match is not substitutable.

Queso blanco is a fresh, moist, mild white Latin American cheese. Queso seco is a dry, aged, hard, salty grating cheese. The USDA entry is the dry, aged form, not the fresh, moist one the ingredient describes. Guideline F treats a different state (fresh vs dried) as non-substitutable. Although both are white Latin American cheeses, the dry, salty, hard texture of queso seco differs from the softer, milder queso blanco, so a diner would likely notice the difference in taste and texture, and the dish's preparation could also change. Condition 1 and condition 2 are not both met.

The ingredient is sapodilla, a fruit, with the weight (175g) being decorative and ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Sapodilla, raw' is the same food in its plain, uncooked, default form. It is therefore the same food under the same name (guideline B), and 'raw' simply means uncooked, which matches a plain ingredient (guideline C). Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since no cooking or processing is implied. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same fruit in its standard form. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is '50g soy nuts' and the USDA match is 'Soy nuts'. The leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry uses the same plain name as the ingredient, so it is the same food with no added modifier, flavour or state descriptor (guideline B and D). Using it in place of the ingredient would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is unflavored gelatin powder, a dry, plain, unsweetened gelatin. The USDA entry 'Gelatins, dry powder, unsweetened' is the same product in dry powder form. The 'unsweetened' descriptor does not make it differ from what a shopper normally buys under the name 'unflavored gelatin powder', since that product is sold unsweetened by default (guideline D). The quantity (5g) is ignored (guideline A). Used in place of the ingredient, it requires no change to preparation: it is dry powder, blooms and dissolves the same way. A diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, because unflavored gelatin is flavourless and unsweetened. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'horseradish and sour cream', a blend of two components (effectively horseradish cream). The USDA match 'Horseradish' covers only the horseradish root or condiment alone, with no sour cream. Under guideline F, a single ingredient does not substitute for a blend or product containing it. Replacing the horseradish-and-sour-cream mixture with plain horseradish would change the flavour (milder, no dairy richness), the texture (no creamy base), and the appearance (no creamy sauce), and a diner would notice the difference. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 and condition 2 both fail.

The ingredient is toasted raisin multigrain bread, which is multigrain bread containing raisins, served toasted. The USDA entry 'Bread, multigrain, with raisins, toasted' names the same product with the same components (multigrain, raisins) and the same state (toasted). Condition 1: it can be used directly in place of the ingredient, and the preparation is unchanged because the bread is already toasted. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same food in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is rosehips, and the USDA entry is 'Rose Hips, wild', which is the same food. The parenthetical '(Northern Plains Indians)' is a source or cultural label, not a processing state, preparation, or modification such as sweetened, dried, or flavoured. The entry names no state (no raw, cooked, dried or frozen), so under guideline E it is the generic food and matches the plain ingredient. Condition 1: rosehips can be used in place of the ingredient without changing the preparation, since the recipe handling is unaffected. Condition 2: the diner would taste and see the same rosehips, so no difference would be noticed. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a pasilla chile, a dried chilaca pepper with a dark, mildly hot, raisin-like flavour. The USDA entry is fresh, raw serrano, a different pepper variety with a green, bright, much hotter profile. Condition 1 fails: swapping them changes the dish's preparation, since the pasilla is normally used dried, rehydrated, toasted, or ground into sauces, while serrano is used fresh. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the much higher heat, the brighter flavour, and the different colour and texture. This is a sibling variety with a different taste and a different state (dried vs fresh), so it is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). The quantity is irrelevant.

The ingredient is heavy whipping cream, which is the standard US retail product sold as heavy cream. The USDA entry 'Cream, heavy' names the same product under its generic name (guideline B). The quantity (300g) is ignored (guideline A). 'Cold' is a handling descriptor and does not change the match (guideline C). Heavy whipping cream is the plain default version, not a modified one (guideline D). Using the USDA heavy cream entry would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not taste or see a difference, so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh cayenne chili pepper, thinly sliced, a raw fresh vegetable used as a whole-pod vegetable. The USDA entry 'Spices, pepper, red or cayenne' is the dried, ground spice. Guideline F says a different state (fresh vs dried, whole vs ground spice) is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: slicing fresh peppers cannot be replaced by a dry powder without changing the preparation, since the ground spice cannot be sliced and would be added as powder. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (crisp, sliced pieces vs fine powder dispersed through the dish), appearance, and the fresh, grassy heat profile versus the dried, ground flavour. The entry is not a same-food name variant (guideline B does not apply), and the 5g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is quail breast meat, ground. Grinding at home does not change the match (guideline C). The USDA entry is 'Quail, meat and skin, raw', which includes skin. Breast meat is a specific cut, and the USDA entry is a whole-bird mix of meat and skin. Guideline F treats a different cut as not substitutable. Including skin also raises the fat content and changes the flavour, texture and appearance of the ground product. A diner would likely notice the richer, fattier taste and texture. Condition 1 (same preparation) can be met, but condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture or appearance) is not. The match is therefore not substitutable.

1. Quantity (10g) is ignored per guideline A. 2. The ingredient is low-salt sliced roast beef, a sliced deli meat. The USDA entry is prepackaged or deli beef luncheon meat, which is the category sliced deli roast beef is sold under. 3. The ingredient asks for the reduced-sodium version, and the USDA entry is 'reduced sodium', so the modified-version rule in D gives a match. 4. Condition 1: the sliced product can be used in the same way with no change to preparation. 5. Condition 2: a diner would not reasonably notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance between sliced reduced-sodium deli beef and the USDA reduced-sodium deli beef luncheon meat entry. The main residual uncertainty is whether a generic luncheon-meat entry might include formed or restructured beef that differs from whole-muscle roast, but the entry names the same deli product category, so I treat it as a match.

The ingredient is plain raw chicken gizzards; 'sliced' is knife work and does not change the match. The USDA entry is 'Stewed gizzards, Puerto Rican style', a cooked dish that has been stewed and seasoned. Condition 1 fails: using it in place of raw gizzards would change the cooking method, since the gizzards are already cooked and would not be prepared as the recipe intends. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the added Puerto Rican seasonings and see a stewed, cooked product rather than raw sliced gizzards. Raw versus cooked and plain versus seasoned are both state differences that rule out a match under guideline F.

The ingredient is jarred pepper sauce, a processed condiment: a liquid or paste made from peppers with vinegar, salt and other additives, cooked and preserved in a jar. The USDA match is 'Peppers, hot, raw', which is the fresh, uncooked whole pepper. Guideline F rules out a raw plant source standing in for a processed ingredient. Condition 1 fails: a fresh pepper cannot be swapped in for a sauce without changing the preparation, since the vinegar, salt and liquid form are lost. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (solid chunks versus smooth sauce), appearance, and flavour (no vinegar or preservative tang). Because neither condition holds, the match is not substitutable.

Step 1: Identify the ingredient. In UK usage, 'pilchards, tinned' refers to canned Sardinops or Sardina pilchardus, which is the same fish that is sold as 'sardines' in most other markets. Guideline B treats regional and trade names for the same food as matches, so pilchards are sardines. Step 2: Check the USDA entry. 'Fish, sardines, canned' is the generic canned sardine entry. It names no packing medium, no added sauce, and no modification, so it matches the plain tinned product. Step 3: Condition 1 (preparation). Canned fish is eaten straight from the tin, so it can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Step 4: Condition 2 (sensory). Tinned pilchards and canned sardines are the same species and product type, so a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. A tomato-sauce or oil packing difference would be a sensory change, but the USDA entry is generic and does not specify a medium, so it is not treated as a modification here. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw Fuji apple. The USDA entry is 'Apples, raw, fuji, with skin', which is the same food, raw, with the same variety. The quantity (30g) is ignored per guideline A. Eating apples with the skin on is the standard default, so 'with skin' does not change the match (guideline D). The parenthetical about the Food Distribution Program is a trade-program note that does not alter the food. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same variety in the same raw state. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is fresh prune plums, pitted, which is a raw fruit. The USDA match is dried plums (prunes), uncooked, which is a dehydrated, processed form. Guideline F says a different state (fresh vs dried) is not substitutable, so the match fails on that basis. Condition 1: swapping dried prunes for fresh plums changes the preparation. Fresh plums must be cut, cooked or baked and release juice, while dried prunes are dense, chewy, and often need rehydrating or cook down differently. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in texture (soft and juicy versus chewy and wrinkled), appearance (skin, colour, shape), and flavour (fresh tartness versus concentrated sweetness). Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is canned anchovies packed in oil, drained. The USDA entry is European anchovy canned in oil, drained solids, which is the same food in the same packing medium and the same drained state. Per guideline A, the 30g quantity is ignored. Per guideline B, anchovy is the same food under a regional or trade name. Per guideline F, the packing medium (oil) matches, so there is no packing mismatch. Condition 1: the anchovies could replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the product is the same canned anchovy in oil, drained. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a generic frosted mini corn cereal. The USDA entry is Malt-O-Meal Frosted Mini Spooners, a branded frosted mini corn cereal. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type counts as a match. The 'frosted' and 'mini' descriptors match the ingredient, and the entry adds no extra flavour or modification such as reduced sugar. Condition 1: it is eaten dry or with milk, so it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: it is the same product category, so a diner would not reasonably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions hold. The quantity (100g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is smoked tabasco peppers, a specific variety that has been smoked, typically dried. The USDA entry is generic 'Peppers, hot, cooked', which is a cooked fresh hot pepper with no smoking. Guideline F lists 'plain vs smoked' and 'raw vs cooked' as different states that are not substitutable. Condition 2 also fails: smoke flavour is strongly noticeable in taste and aroma, and the smoked peppers' colour and texture differ from cooked fresh peppers. Using the USDA match would change the dish's flavour, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is salted roasted cashews, a tree nut. The USDA match is roasted salted peanuts, which are a legume. These are different foods, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Guideline F also rules out substitutes that differ in source. Cashews and peanuts differ noticeably in flavour (cashews are sweeter and buttery, peanuts are more earthy), and in texture and shape, so a diner would likely notice the swap. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plantain slices sauteed in butter. The USDA entry is plantain cooked with butter or margarine, so it names the same food prepared the same way. Sliced is only knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). The entry explicitly covers butter, so the cooking method (sauteeing in fat) is unchanged. Condition 1 is met: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. For condition 2, the plantain, the fat type and the cooked state are the same, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is strawberry yogurt powder, a dried dairy product (yogurt solids) flavoured with strawberry. The USDA match is a strawberry beverage powder, dry mix, which is a sugar-based drink mix (like a Kool-Aid-style product) with little or no dairy. Condition 1: it is not the same food under another name, and it would change the dish's composition and preparation, since a drink mix lacks the protein, fat, and tang of yogurt and would be dissolved or mixed differently. Condition 2: a diner would taste the difference. A sweet, artificially flavoured drink powder would lack the tangy, creamy dairy flavour and milk-solid texture of yogurt powder. Neither condition is met, so this is not substitutable.

Chayote (Sechium edule) is a distinct vegetable from zucchini (Cucurbita pepo summer squash). It is not the same food under a regional or trade name, so guideline B does not apply. Chayote is firmer and starchier, with a different flavour and a different texture after cooking. Cubed chayote would hold its shape and crunch differently from cubed zucchini, which softens and releases more water. A diner would likely notice the difference in texture and taste, so condition 2 fails. Cubing does not change the match, but the underlying food is different, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is light cream, a liquid dairy cream of roughly 18-30% milkfat that is unsweetened and unflavoured. The USDA match is 'Light ice cream, vanilla', a frozen, aerated, sweetened, vanilla-flavoured dessert. Condition 1 fails: ice cream cannot be used in place of liquid cream without changing how the dish is prepared. It would not whip, pour, or emulsify the same way, and it would melt or chill the dish. Condition 2 also fails: the vanilla flavour, sweetness, and frozen, airy texture would be noticed. Guideline F rules out a different product form, and guideline D treats flavoured or sweetened versions of a plain ingredient as modified. This is not the same food under another name, so the match is rejected.

The ingredient is beef sirloin tip, a specific cut (the knuckle/tip portion of the sirloin, usually from the top sirloin or round area). The USDA entry is bottom sirloin tri-tip roast, which is a different anatomical cut from a different primal area. Guideline F states that a different cut of meat is not substitutable, and a diner or cook would notice differences in texture, grain, and cooking behaviour. The frozen-then-thawed state is not a problem under guideline E, since frozen meat matches fresh meat. The USDA entry is also specified as trimmed to 0" fat and as a roast, which adds further mismatch, but the cut difference alone is sufficient. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) are not reliably met.

The ingredient is bran flakes, a ready-to-eat cereal made mainly from wheat bran and wheat flour, usually with sugar, malt and salt. The USDA entry, Cereal, wheat flakes, is a different product: flaked whole wheat, typically unsweetened and unmalted. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Bran flakes are typically sweeter, crisper and more bran-forward, and they carry a malt or sugar flavour. In a dish, especially one eaten as cereal, mixed into bakes, or used as a crunchy coating, a diner would likely notice the difference in flavour, texture and appearance. The quantity (250g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fine semolina flour, and the USDA match is semolina in the coarse and semi-coarse grind. Both are durum wheat semolina, so the base food is the same. However, the grind differs. Fine semolina has a smooth, powdery texture, while coarse semolina is gritty and granular. Substituting coarse semolina would change how the dish is prepared (for example, it absorbs liquid differently and may need more hydration or time) and would change its texture and appearance (grittier crumb, bite, or surface). A diner would likely notice the difference in a dish such as a semolina cake, pudding, or dough. Condition 1 (no change in preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance) are not both met.

The ingredient is sweetened acerola juice, which is acerola juice with added sugar. The USDA entry, 'Acerola juice, raw', is the plain unsweetened juice. Guideline D says a plain ingredient matched to a modified version is not a match, and 'sweetened' is a listed modification. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the juice could be swapped in mechanically. Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste the difference in sweetness, and the flavour is changed. Because the sweetening is the defining feature of the ingredient, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is red grapes packed in heavy syrup. The USDA entry is canned Thompson Seedless grapes in heavy syrup pack, solids and liquids. The packing medium matches, since both are heavy syrup, so that part is fine. The variety does not. Thompson Seedless is a specific cultivar, typically green/white, while the ingredient specifies red grapes. Guideline F treats a sibling variety with a different taste as not substitutable, and the colour difference is visible, so a diner would notice a change in appearance. Both conditions are therefore not met. The 19g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is whole pitted green olives, a single raw-type fruit product. The USDA match 'Olive tapenade' is a prepared spread or paste that blends olives with capers, anchovies, olive oil and seasonings. Under guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend containing it is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because tapenade cannot replace whole olives without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is a paste rather than a solid fruit to slice or add whole. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the smooth, spreadable texture and the added capers, anchovy and oil flavours instead of plain olives. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is abalone, a marine mollusk (sea snail) with firm, chewy texture and a distinct briny, sea-flavoured taste. The USDA match is almond paste, a sweet, dense paste made from ground almonds and sugar. These are entirely different foods: almond paste is a nut-and-sugar confection, not a seafood. Condition 1 fails because almond paste cannot stand in for abalone in a dish without changing its preparation (abalone is typically sliced and quickly cooked or braised, while almond paste is a sweet baking ingredient). Condition 2 fails because a diner would immediately notice sweet almond flavour and a paste texture instead of seafood. The weight is irrelevant under the guidelines. Not the same food under another name, so not substitutable.

The ingredient is turkey liver, frozen and then thawed. The USDA entry 'Turkey, all classes, liver, raw' is the same food (turkey liver) in its uncooked state. Under guideline E, frozen meat that is thawed matches the fresh/raw entry when freezing does not visibly change the food and it is normally cooked. Turkey liver is normally cooked, so thawing leaves no visible difference. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are raw turkey liver to be cooked by the recipe. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance once cooked. The 'all classes' label only indicates the bird class, not a different product. Both conditions are met.

Chèvre is the French term for goat's milk cheese, and the usual form sold under that name is a soft, fresh goat cheese. The USDA entry 'Cheese, goat, soft type' names the same food under a generic English name, so it counts as the same food under another name (guideline B). The quantity '200g' is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: a soft goat cheese can replace chèvre in a recipe without changing the preparation method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same kind of cheese. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is sliced almonds. The USDA match is plain unsalted almonds, which is the same food. Slicing is knife work, and guideline C says sliced does not change the match. Unsalted matches the plain default, since the ingredient names no salt or flavour. Neither condition is broken: the cooking method is unchanged, and taste and texture come from the same nut. The only visible difference is the cut shape, which guideline C treats as handling, not a change of food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked chinook salmon, and the USDA entry is 'Fish, salmon, chinook, smoked', which names the same fish in the same processed state. The 180g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Guideline F rejects plain-versus-smoked mismatches, but this is not one: the recipe asks for smoked salmon and the USDA entry is smoked. Guideline D says that when the ingredient itself calls for a processed version, the matching entry is a yes.
