Condition 1: pecans can be used in place of pecans with no change to preparation; the quantity (35g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since this is the same food under its plain name, and 'NFS' (not further specified) simply means the generic form that matches fresh, raw, or prepared pecans. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is american cheese, a processed cheese product (typically pasteurized process cheese food with emulsifiers, salt, and milk solids, sold as slices or loaf). The USDA match is soy chips, a snack made from soybeans, usually fried or baked and crunchy. Condition 1 fails: soy chips cannot replace american cheese in a recipe such as a melt, sauce, or sandwich without changing how the dish is prepared, since they do not melt or emulsify. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (salty, savoury dairy versus crisp soy snack), texture (smooth and melting versus crunchy), and appearance. Different food entirely, so it is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Not substitutable.

The ingredient is a Venezuelan-style arepa made from cornmeal (masarepa), a savory, grilled or baked corn cake. The USDA entry, Arepa Dominicana, is a different regional dish. Dominican arepas are typically sweeter, often made with sugar, butter, and other added ingredients, and are prepared and eaten differently. Condition 1 fails because substituting it would change the recipe's preparation and flavour profile. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in taste and texture. The 100g quantity is ignored. This is not the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

Step 1: The ingredient is fresh wax pepper, a specific pepper variety (a yellow, thin-walled, mildly tangy chili pepper, often sold pickled or fresh). Quantity is ignored. Step 2: The USDA entry 'Peppers, raw, NFS' is a not-further-specified catch-all. It does not name wax peppers, and it could represent sweet green bell peppers, hot chilies, or other varieties. Guideline B (same food under another name) does not apply, because the entry is not literally wax pepper. Guideline F treats a sibling variety with a different taste as not substitutable. Condition 1: the preparation could be the same (raw, chopped), so this is met in principle. Condition 2: a diner could notice a difference in heat, flavour and colour (for example, a green bell pepper in place of a yellow wax pepper), and the entry does not guarantee a match. Condition 2 is not reliably met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain rice bran, the outer layer milled from rice. The USDA entry 'Rice bran, crude' is the same food: the raw, unprocessed bran as it comes off the milling step. 'Crude' describes the unrefined default form rather than a modified version such as stabilized, defatted, or flavoured. Condition 1: it can be used in place of rice bran without changing preparation, since it is the same material used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met. The 200g quantity is ignored per the guidelines.

The ingredient is fresh shelled peanuts, weight 145g (quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry 'Peanuts, raw' is the same food in its uncooked state. Shelled peanuts are simply the nut without its shell; the USDA raw entry describes the nut itself, and shelling is handling that does not change the match (guideline C). Fresh peanuts are the raw nut, so there is no cooking-method, flavour, texture or appearance difference. A diner would not be able to tell the difference. Condition 1 (same use without changing preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) are both met.

The ingredient is beef tenderloin, and the USDA entry 'Beef, steak, tenderloin' describes the same cut of beef. The quantity prefix is ignored (guideline A). The USDA name carries no cooking state, so it is the generic food and matches the plain raw ingredient (guideline E). Condition 1: the same cut can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cut, not a different cut (guideline F does not apply). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is turkey tail, and the USDA entry is 'Turkey, tail', which is the same food under the same name. Per guideline B, literal matches count. The leading '300g' is decoration and is ignored (A). The USDA entry has no cooking state or modification that would differ from the plain ingredient, so the match is the standard default version (D). Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same cut. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is ground sage, a dried spice in ground form. The USDA entry 'Spices, sage, ground' is the same food in the same state (ground dried sage). Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Ground versus whole/fresh is the only state distinction that matters here, and both sides are ground. No cooking method change is needed, and a diner would not taste a difference between the two. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 200g of toasted oatmeal bread. The USDA entry is 'Bread, oatmeal, toasted', which names the same food (oatmeal bread) in the same state (toasted). The leading weight is ignored per guideline A. Guideline F rejects plain-versus-toasted mismatches, but here both sides are toasted, so that rule does not apply. Condition 1: the match is already toasted, so it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference between the two, since both are toasted oatmeal bread. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is farmer cheese, a dry, crumbly, pressed fresh curd cheese with a firm, drier texture and a mild tangy flavour. The USDA match is Cheese, Ricotta, a soft, moist, grainy whey-based cheese. Farmer cheese is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1: farmer cheese is typically drained, pressed or crumbled into doughs and fillings such as pierogi, blintzes and cheesecake, and ricotta's higher moisture would change how the mixture binds and is handled. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the softer, wetter, sweeter-tasting ricotta in place of the firmer, drier farmer cheese, so the taste and texture would differ. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is rutabagas, the same vegetable as the USDA entry 'Rutabagas, raw'. Guideline B confirms the same food under the same name counts. The quantity (170g) is ignored per guideline A. No cooking method is implied by the ingredient, and the entry is raw, which matches the plain uncooked ingredient (guideline C). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the identical food in its default form. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried sweet cherries. The USDA entry is dried tart cherries that are sweetened. Two differences matter. First, tart and sweet cherries are different varieties with different flavour profiles, and guideline F says a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable. Second, the entry is sweetened, and guideline D treats a sweetened version of a plain product as a modification that is not a match. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would likely notice the tart, more acidic flavour and the sugar coating compared with sweet dried cherries. The ingredient's 130g quantity is ignored, as guideline A requires. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is raw turkey tail, a specific cut of whole turkey that is cooked as a piece (roasted, braised, or similar) and keeps its bone, skin and fat structure. The USDA match is cooked ground turkey, a different cut and a processed form. Using it would change the cooking method, since it is already cooked and minced rather than raw and whole-cut. It would also change texture and appearance, because ground meat has no tail cut structure. Guideline F rejects raw vs cooked and different cuts of meat, so the two conditions are not met.

The ingredient is cashew butter, a smooth paste made by grinding cashews. The USDA match is 'Cashews, honey roasted', which is whole or pieces of cashew nuts coated in honey and roasted. Condition 1 fails: cashew butter cannot replace whole honey-roasted cashews without changing the preparation, because the nuts would need grinding and the paste form would not be reproduced. Condition 2 fails: honey roasting adds sweetness and a sugary coating, so a diner would notice the flavour difference, and the texture changes from a smooth paste to firm, crunchy pieces. Under guideline F, a flavoured or roasted state differs from the plain product, and a whole nut differs from a processed nut butter. The ingredient is not the same food as the match, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried pink beans, a dried legume sold as bought. The USDA entry is pinto beans, mature seeds, sprouted, raw. Pink beans are a different bean variety from pinto, a sibling with a somewhat different flavour and appearance, which Guideline F says is not substitutable. The USDA entry is also sprouted, a different state from dried beans. Sprouted beans are germinated, cook faster, and have a different texture and taste from dry mature seeds. Either difference would change the dish, and a diner could notice. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain buttermilk. The USDA entry 'Milk, buttermilk, fluid, cultured, lowfat' is the same food. Per guideline D, buttermilk is typically sold as low fat, so the 'lowfat' descriptor reflects how the product is normally sold and is not a modification. Condition 1: it can replace buttermilk in any recipe with no change in preparation. Condition 2: the diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since this is the standard cultured fluid buttermilk. Both conditions are met.

Sazon is a dry spice blend (typically coriander, cumin, oregano, garlic, annatto, and salt) used in small amounts to season a dish. The USDA entry is a packet mix for yellow rice with seasoning, unprepared. It is a different product: it contains rice and is meant to be cooked in water or stock into a rice dish. Condition 1 fails because using it in place of sazon would change the preparation. The dish would need rice, liquid, and a different cooking method, and it would no longer be a seasoned dish with the same components. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would notice the added rice, the altered texture, and the yellow colour and flavour profile of a rice dish. The quantity is ignored, per the guidelines. The entry is a product that includes the seasoning as a component rather than the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient 'cape gooseberry' is Physalis peruviana, also sold as poha or golden berry. The USDA entry 'Groundcherries, (cape-gooseberries or poha), raw' explicitly names cape gooseberries as one of its items, so it is literally the same food under a trade/regional name (guideline B). The quantity '250g' is decoration (guideline A). The USDA entry is raw, which matches a plain fresh ingredient, and any handling such as halving or husking does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: it is the same fruit, so taste, texture and appearance are the same and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient 'side meat' is a regional culinary name. In Southern US cooking it commonly refers to salt-cured pork belly or fatback, which is what 'salt pork' is. Under guideline B, regional names for the same food count as the same food. The USDA entry 'Pork, cured, salt pork, raw' describes that same salt-cured pork fat, in the same raw state, and the 6g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Used in place of side meat, it would be prepared the same way (rendered or simmered for seasoning) and would give similar flavour, texture and appearance. Some uncertainty remains because 'side meat' can also mean smoked or streaky bacon-style cuts, but the salt pork match is the most consistent reading.

The ingredient is 'jujube tea', a processed product (a tea or infusion made from jujube, typically dried and steeped or a prepared drink). The match is 'Jujube, raw', which is fresh whole fruit. Condition 1 fails: fresh fruit cannot replace a tea without changing how the dish is prepared, since the tea would need to be brewed or infused and the fruit used whole or chopped. Condition 2 also fails: the diner would taste and see a different product, with a different flavour concentration, texture and appearance. Under guideline F, the raw source is not the same as the processed ingredient. The quantity (170g) is ignored, per guideline A. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is soy yogurt, a thick, cultured, tangy product. The USDA match is unsweetened soy milk, a thin, unfermented liquid. Quantity is ignored, and this is not the same food under another name. Soy milk is not a plain default version of soy yogurt, so guideline D does not apply. Condition 1 fails: soy milk cannot replace yogurt without changing how the dish is prepared, since yogurt contributes body, tang and thickness that a thin liquid does not. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in taste (no fermented tang), texture (thin versus thick and creamy) and appearance. Both conditions must hold, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is explicitly reduced-fat limburger cheese. The USDA entry 'Cheese, limburger' is the standard, full-fat product. Quantity (185g) is ignored. Condition 1: the reduced-fat cheese could be used in the same way, since it is still sliced or melted like limburger, so preparation would not change. Condition 2: reduced-fat cheese has lower fat, which changes texture (firmer, less creamy, less melt) and can slightly change flavour and mouthfeel. A diner could plausibly notice the difference. Guideline D treats reduced-fat as a modification, and a modified ingredient is not matched by the plain entry. Since the entry does not match the stated fat level, condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is plain 'canned hominy' with no colour specified. The USDA entry is 'Hominy, canned, yellow', a specific colour variety of corn hominy. Condition 1 (preparation) is likely met, since canned hominy is used the same way regardless of colour. Condition 2 is not clearly met. Yellow hominy looks visibly different from white hominy, and it has a slightly different, sweeter corn flavour, so a diner in a dish such as pozole could notice the difference. The ingredient does not ask for yellow, so the yellow entry is a specific sibling variety rather than the unmarked default. Under the guidelines, a sibling variety with a different appearance or taste is not substitutable.

The ingredient is pickled turnips, and the USDA entry is 'Turnip, pickled', which names the same food in the same processed state. The leading '400g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Pickling is the defining state of both, so the entry is not a raw, cooked, or different-product match. Nothing in the USDA name adds a flavour, colouring, or modification such as reduced sodium or added sweetener. Under guideline B, the same food under the same name is substitutable. Condition 1 holds because the entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, and condition 2 holds because a diner would not perceive a difference in taste, texture, or appearance for the same pickled turnip.

The ingredient is tapioca pearls, dried tapioca starch formed into small pellets that must be cooked (boiled and hydrated) before use, typically in bubble tea or desserts. The USDA entry is 'Babyfood, banana no tapioca, strained', a commercial infant food made from banana, with tapioca mentioned only as a minor ingredient, and it is already a cooked, puréed, strained product. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a plain form of tapioca. Condition 1 fails: it cannot be used in place of tapioca pearls without changing preparation, since the pearls require boiling to gelatinize and the baby food is a ready-to-eat purée. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in texture (chewy translucent pearls versus smooth purée) and appearance and flavour (banana versus neutral starch). Not substitutable.

The ingredient is pearl onions, which are small whole onions of the Allium genus (a variety/size of onion, typically sold raw or used whole in cooking). The USDA match, 'Onion dip, regular', is a creamy, dairy-based dip product, not an onion. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a cut, state, or processed form of onions. Using onion dip in place of pearl onions would change the dish's ingredients, flavour, texture and appearance, and a diner would immediately notice a dip rather than onions. Condition 1 fails (it would change how the dish is prepared, since whole onions cannot be swapped for a dip) and condition 2 fails (taste, texture and appearance all differ). Quantity is ignored per the guidelines.

The ingredient is 'queso seco', a dry, crumbly white Mexican cheese. The USDA entry 'Cheese, dry white, queso seco' names the same product under the same name. The '200g' quantity is ignored, and 'grated' is knife or handling work that does not change the match. Substituting the USDA entry requires no change to preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same cheese. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked kielbasa, sliced. The USDA entry is kielbasa, fully cooked, grilled. Both are the same base product, so the food identity is close. However, the match differs in processing state. The ingredient is smoked, and the entry is grilled. Guideline F says plain vs smoked/roasted is a different state and not substitutable. Grilling is a surface cooking method that leaves grill marks and a char flavour, and it does not reproduce smoke flavour. Condition 1 fails: the dish's preparation would change, since the smoked sausage would be replaced with a grilled one. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would likely notice the difference in smoky flavour and surface appearance. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

1. The ingredient 'guac' is a common abbreviation of guacamole, so it is the same food under a shortened name (guideline B). The 50g weight is ignored (guideline A).
2. 'Guacamole, NFS' is the generic USDA entry for guacamole with no modifying state or added components. It matches the default version of the food.
3. Condition 1: Guacamole can replace guac in a recipe without changing preparation, since both are used as a ready-to-serve or mixed dip/topping.
4. Condition 2: A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the food is the same.
5. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is garlic powder (or garlic paste), a plain seasoning in dried or paste form. The USDA entry, 'Garlic sauce', is a prepared condiment, typically an emulsified or oil-based sauce containing garlic together with other ingredients such as oil, egg, or acid. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a modified version of garlic powder. Condition 1 fails: using a prepared sauce in place of garlic powder or paste would change the moisture, fat content, and texture of the dish, and would add ingredients that alter its flavour profile. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would likely notice the added fat, creaminess, or sauce flavour, and the dish's appearance could change. Guideline F applies, since a single ingredient is not substitutable with a blended product that contains it.

The ingredient is sorghum flour, a whole-grain flour made from sorghum seeds with its own flavour, colour and gluten-free baking behaviour. The USDA match is chickpea flour (besan), which is made from ground dried chickpeas (legume, not a cereal grain). These are different foods, not regional names for the same product. Condition 1: substituting besan for sorghum flour changes the dish's preparation characteristics, since besan has a distinct absorbency, binding behaviour and protein/starch profile, so baked goods and batters would behave differently. Condition 2: besan imparts a noticeable beany, nutty flavour and a yellow tint and denser crumb that a diner would likely detect. Under guideline F, a different flour is not substitutable. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is chopped cashews. The USDA entry 'Nuts, cashew nuts, raw' is the same food (raw cashew nuts). Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Chopping is knife work that does not change the match per guideline C. Condition 1: raw cashews can be used in place of chopped cashews without changing preparation, since the recipe's chopping is done by the cook. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste or texture, because the match is the same nut in its raw form, and the only difference is the cut. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked link sausage, and the USDA entry is 'Sausage, smoked link sausage, pork and beef'. Both name the same product type: a smoked link sausage. The ingredient does not specify a meat blend, so it is the generic default. The USDA entry adds only the standard meat composition for this product. Condition 1: the sausage can be used in place of the ingredient without changing the preparation, since it is the same smoked link product and handling is the same. Condition 2: a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance between a generic smoked link sausage and a pork-and-beef smoked link sausage, because both are smoked, cured, link-form sausages. No cooking-method change, flavour change, or visible difference is implied. Both conditions are met.

Skirt steak is the inside skirt cut from the beef plate, so the USDA entry names the same cut ('plate steak, boneless, inside skirt'). Guideline C says trimming does not change the match, and 'trimmed to 0" fat' only describes how the meat is prepared for sale. Condition 1: the match is raw beef of the same cut, so it can be cooked in place of the ingredient with the same method. Guideline E says frozen meat matches the fresh/raw entry when freezing does not show, and thawed skirt steak looks and cooks the same as fresh. Condition 2: a diner would not taste or see a difference in the same cut of raw beef. The 'separable lean and fat' label is a USDA data category and does not describe a different product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is ground acorns, meaning the nut has been milled into meal or flour. The USDA entry is 'Nuts, acorns, dried', which describes whole dried acorn kernels. Guideline A says to ignore the 10g quantity. Guideline B does not apply, since this is the same food and not a different name. The key question is whether grinding is handling the recipe does itself. The guidelines list chopping, mincing and grinding at home only for meat or fish as handling. Grinding nuts is a change of physical state, similar to whole vs ground spice (guideline F). Using whole dried acorns would require the cook to grind them, which changes the preparation. Even if they were ground, the result would differ in texture and appearance from whole kernels. Condition 1 is therefore not met, and condition 2 is doubtful because a diner could notice whole nut pieces versus fine meal. Not substitutable.

The ingredient 'brat' is a clipped form of 'bratwurst', so the USDA entry 'Bratwurst' names the same food. The 75g weight is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the sausage can be used in place of the ingredient without changing the preparation, since it is the same product handled the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same sausage under its full name. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is a sliced raisin loaf, which is ordinary raisin bread, untoasted by default. The USDA entry is the same food (wheat bread with raisins), so the base product matches. However, the USDA entry specifies 'toasted'. Guideline F says plain versus toasted is a different state, not a substitute. Toasting changes colour, crispness, texture and aroma, and a diner would notice a toasted slice where they expected soft bread. The ingredient does not ask for toasting, and the quantity and knife work (sliced) do not change the match. Because the toasted state changes the dish's texture, appearance and flavour, the match fails condition 2 and the cooking/preparation check.

The ingredient is cornmeal, a dried and ground product made from dried maize kernels. The USDA match is 'Corn, sweet, yellow, raw', which is fresh sweet corn on the cob or kernels. Condition 1: replacing cornmeal with fresh raw sweet corn would change the preparation. Cornmeal is a dry, milled powder used in batters, breads or porridge, while raw corn kernels are whole, moist, and need cutting or cooking. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in texture (grainy powder versus whole kernels) and appearance, and the flavour and moisture would also differ. Guideline F says the raw plant or source is not substitutable for the processed ingredient (e.g. cornstarch vs corn). The same logic applies here, so the match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is dried cherries, which are dehydrated, chewy, concentrated and sweet. The USDA match is frozen cherries, which are fresh fruit that has been frozen and is juicy and tart-sweet with a soft texture. Condition 1: dried cherries are added as a chewy, concentrated mix-in, while frozen cherries release liquid and soften during baking or cooking, so the preparation would change. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in texture (chewy versus juicy and soft) and in appearance (dark, shrivelled pieces versus plump fruit). Guideline F treats a different state (dried versus fresh or frozen) as not substitutable, and guideline E does not apply because freezing does not explain the dried-to-fresh change. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is cocoa butter, melted. The USDA entry 'Oil, cocoa butter' is the same food: cocoa butter is the fat itself, and melting it only changes its physical state, which is routine handling. Guideline B treats the same food under another name as a match, and guideline F's warnings about different fats do not apply because this is the same fat, not a substitute. Used in place of the melted ingredient, the match would not change preparation, flavour, texture or appearance, and the 19g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fish sauce, a fermented anchovy condiment. The USDA entry 'Sauce, fish, ready-to-serve' names the same product under a different label; it is the standard, unmodified fish sauce, with no added flavour, reduced-sodium version, or other modification. The '25g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: fish sauce can be swapped in directly as a liquid seasoning without changing the cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

Ingredient is 75g banana, peeled and sliced. USDA match is Banana, raw. Condition B: this is literally the same food (banana). Guideline C: peeling and slicing are knife work/handling the recipe does itself and do not change the match. Guideline A: the 75g quantity is ignored. Condition 1: raw banana can be used in place of peeled, sliced banana without altering preparation, since the recipe's own handling produces the sliced form. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the raw entry is the plain fruit that is then peeled and sliced. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried papaya, and the USDA entry is 'Papaya, dried', which is the same food in the same state. The quantity (135g) is ignored per the guidelines. Using this entry does not change the preparation, since both are dried papaya used the same way. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain shredded wheat cereal. The USDA entry is Quaker Shredded Wheat, a ready-to-eat cereal of the same plain product type under a brand name. Guideline G treats a branded entry of the same plain product type as a match. Condition 1: the cereal can be used in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation, since neither needs cooking and both are used as bought. Quantity (50g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2: the entry is not flavoured or modified (it is not sweetened, reduced-fat or otherwise altered), so it is the standard default version. Any difference between brands is a minor brand-level variation that the guidelines accept. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is leeks, specifically the bulb and lower leaves, weighing 75g; the leading quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Leeks, (bulb and lower leaf-portion), raw', which describes the same vegetable cut as the ingredient, with the same components (bulb and lower leaves). Per guideline C, 'raw' means uncooked, and any trimming or chopping done by the recipe does not change the match. Per guideline B, the inner or specified part of the same vegetable sold as the same thing counts as a match. Condition 1: the leeks could be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since the food is identical and raw. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same raw leek portion. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'powdered soy protein'. The leading weight (150g) is ignored per guideline A. Soy protein isolate is a powdered form of soy protein, and the ingredient does not specify concentrate or texturized protein, so the isolate powder is the standard default version of 'powdered soy protein' (guidelines B and D). Condition 1: the isolate is a dry powder, so it can be measured and mixed in the same way without changing the preparation. Condition 2: a powdered isolate is the usual product a shopper buys under this name, so a diner would not expect a different taste, texture, or appearance. The one residual risk is a concentrate-based powder with a slightly different flavour, but the ingredient does not specify that, so it is not grounds for rejection.

The ingredient is lamb neck, a specific cut of raw lamb meat, typically cooked by braising or slow-cooking on the bone. The USDA match is 'Lamb or mutton loaf', which is a processed, ground/formed meatloaf-style product containing lamb or mutton mixed with other ingredients and typically cooked as a loaf. Condition 1 fails: it cannot replace lamb neck without changing preparation, since lamb neck is a whole-muscle cut that is braised or stewed, while a loaf is a formed mixture baked in a pan. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would readily notice a loaf-style mixed product versus tender pieces of neck meat with bone and connective tissue in texture, appearance, and flavour. This is a different product form, not the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw lamb sirloin (cubed), a meat cut. The USDA match is cooked white rice with no added fat, a grain and an entirely different food category. Condition 1 fails: substituting cooked rice for lamb would completely change the dish's protein component, cooking method (lamb would be seared or braised, rice is boiled or steamed), and preparation. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice rice instead of lamb in taste, texture, and appearance. Cubing is knife work and does not change the match, but that does not rescue a different food altogether. Guideline F (different foods/states, raw vs cooked) and the general rule that a different food is not substitutable apply.

The ingredient is maitake mushrooms (Grifola frondosa), used as an optional garnish, quantity ignored. The USDA entry 'Mushrooms, maitake, raw' is literally the same food in its uncooked state. Condition 1: the match is the same raw ingredient, so it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation; the garnish use does not require any cooking change beyond what the recipe already does. Condition 2: a diner would see and taste the same maitake mushroom, with no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is raw quail egg white, an uncooked, liquid component used as-is in a recipe. The USDA entry, 'Egg white sandwich', is a prepared, cooked food product that includes bread (or a muffin) and typically other components, so it is a composite dish rather than an egg white. Condition 1 fails: using a cooked sandwich in place of raw egg whites would change how the dish is prepared, since the bread and cooking would have to be added or the egg would already be cooked. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, appearance and taste between raw egg white and a cooked sandwich. The entry is also not the same food under another name, and quail egg white is not interchangeable with chicken egg white sandwich. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is a raw lamb rack, a specific bone-in cut normally roasted or grilled without sauce. The USDA entry 'Lamb or mutton with gravy' is a cooked, prepared product that is served in gravy and comes from mixed lamb or mutton cuts. Condition 1 fails: using it would change the preparation, since the dish would need to be cooked from a raw product and could not be served as a plain roasted rack. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the gravy, the texture of the braised or stewed meat, and the altered appearance. Rule F rejects a different cut and a different state (raw vs cooked, plain vs sauced). The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is ripe guava (Psidium guajava, the common tropical guava). The USDA entry, 'Guavas, strawberry, raw', is a different species (Psidium cattleianum, strawberry guava). It is not the same food under another name. Strawberry guava is smaller, has a purplish-red skin, and tastes distinctly different, with a tangy, strawberry-like flavour, compared with the musky, sweet-tart flavour of common guava. Its flesh and seed appearance also differ. Under guideline F, a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable. Slicing does not change the match, and the quantity is ignored. Because a diner would likely notice the flavour and appearance difference, condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is fresh raspberries, weight irrelevant (guideline A). The USDA entry 'Raspberries, raw' is the same fruit in its uncooked, fresh state, which is exactly what 'fresh raspberries' denotes (guideline C: raw means uncooked, and fresh is the normal state). No cooking method change is implied, and the fruit's taste, texture and appearance are the same as the fresh fruit. A diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is lowfat half and half, and the USDA entry is 'Cream, half and half, lowfat', which names the same product. Guideline D says that when the ingredient itself asks for a low-fat version, the matching low-fat entry counts as a match. The leading '300g' is only a quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: lowfat half and half can be used in place of itself without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is amaranth seeds, which are the same food as amaranth grain. The USDA entry 'Amaranth grain, uncooked' is the raw, uncooked form, matching the plain ingredient as bought. Under guideline B, a regional or trade name for the same food counts as a match. Condition 1: the grain can replace the seeds with no change to preparation, since both are cooked or used the same way from the raw state. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. The weight of 150g is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried egg yolk, and the USDA entry 'Egg, yolk, dried' is the same food under the same state. Quantity (485g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same dried product used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would detect no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the food is identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'tequila, sweetened', meaning tequila with added sugar (a sweetened, flavoured spirit preparation). The USDA match 'Tequila Sunrise' is a cocktail made from tequila, orange juice, grenadine and often other mixers, so it contains multiple components beyond the tequila and has a different flavour, colour and appearance. Condition 1 fails: it is a mixed beverage, not a substitute that can be used in the same way without changing preparation. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice orange juice, grenadine colouring and fruitiness versus sweetened tequila. Per guideline F (a single ingredient vs a product containing it) and the rule against flavoured or modified versions, this is not substitutable.

The ingredient is pinto beans, with the leading 100g treated as decoration per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Pinto beans, NFS' (not further specified) names the same food with no added state, modification, or blend. Pinto beans are normally bought dry, and the generic entry covers the dried legume as bought, so no cooking-method change is implied. Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: the diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same bean. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is plain woven wheat crackers, the standard default product. The USDA match is specifically the reduced-sodium version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a modified entry (reduced sodium is explicitly listed) is not substitutable. The product is the same type and would be prepared the same way, so condition 1 is roughly met. Condition 2 fails because reduced-sodium crackers are noticeably less salty, so a diner could taste the difference. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is cockles, a bivalve mollusk (a shellfish eaten raw or cooked as a whole animal, with a distinct chewy texture and briny flavour). The USDA match is a condensed canned soup, New England clam chowder: a liquid, cream-based, thickened, seasoned soup containing chopped clam pieces, potato, onion, and dairy. Condition 1 fails: it cannot replace cockles without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is a prepared, concentrated soup base rather than a shellfish that can be cooked or served as-is. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance, because the cream-soup flavour and the potato/onion/liquid matrix are entirely different from whole cockle meat. Guideline F also applies: a processed product containing other ingredients is not the same as the plain food. Neither condition is met, so this is not substitutable.

The ingredient is low sodium tomato and vegetable juice, and the USDA entry is Tomato and vegetable juice, low sodium. These are the same product under the same name, with the same modification (low sodium), so guideline D's rule that a matching modified entry counts as a match applies. The 250g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the juice can be used directly wherever the ingredient is called for, with no change to cooking method. Condition 2: the juice is the same product, so a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is solid vegetable shortening, a plain home baking/cooking fat (typically a solid, hydrogenated or interesterified vegetable fat used for baking). The USDA entry is 'Shortening, industrial, soy (partially hydrogenated), pourable liquid fry shortening', which is an industrial/food-service specialty fat sold as a pourable liquid for deep frying. Under guideline F, industrial/food-service specialty fats are not substitutable for the home ingredient. Condition 1 fails: using a pourable liquid frying oil in place of a solid shortening changes the physical form and how the fat is incorporated (e.g., creaming or cutting into dough), so the preparation would change. Condition 2 also fails: the solid versus liquid state and the soy-based partially hydrogenated composition would alter texture (flakiness, structure, mouthfeel) and could be noticed by a diner. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain lime, and the USDA entry 'Lime, raw' is the same fruit in its uncooked form. The leading '150g' is only a quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: a raw lime can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since no cooking method is implied and any cutting or juicing is handling done by the recipe (guideline C). Condition 2: a diner would taste and see the same fruit, because the entry is the standard default version of lime (guideline D). Both conditions hold.

Maracuyá is the Spanish name for passion fruit, so the food itself is the same genus and type as the USDA entry 'Passion-fruit, (granadilla), purple, raw'. However, the USDA entry specifies the purple variety, while maracuyá in much of Latin America is commonly the yellow passion fruit (maracuyá amarilla). Condition 1 is met, since the fruit could be used in the same preparation as raw passion fruit. Condition 2 is not reliably met: purple and yellow passion fruit differ noticeably in acidity, sweetness and aroma, so a diner could taste the difference. Guideline F treats a sibling variety with a different taste as not substitutable, and the purple entry is a variety match only for some uses of the name. Because the variety is specified and the flavour would likely differ, the match fails.

Rice bran is the outer layer of the rice grain, removed during milling, used as a fibrous, nutty ingredient in cooking and baking. Rice paper is a thin, dried sheet made from rice flour or starch and water, used as a wrapper for fresh or fried rolls. These are different foods from different parts of the rice processing chain, not regional or trade names for the same product. Condition 1 fails: rice paper cannot replace rice bran without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is a sheet rather than a loose powder or granule and would not add bran's fibre and texture. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, appearance and flavour. The quantity (340g) is ignored per the guidelines.

The ingredient is 'toasted brazil nuts', while the USDA match is plain 'Brazil nuts' (the default raw entry). The quantity (120g) is irrelevant. Brazil nuts are the same food, so the food identity matches. However, guideline F explicitly lists plain vs toasted as a different state that is not substitutable. Toasting changes flavour (roasted, nutty, deeper taste), colour, and crunch. A diner would likely notice the difference, and the dish's preparation would be altered because the nuts would not be toasted. Condition 1 (no change to preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance) both fail.

The ingredient is veal shank, cubed. The USDA match is veal sirloin, separable lean only, raw. Guideline A means the 200g quantity is ignored. Veal shank and veal sirloin are different cuts from different parts of the animal. Shank is a muscle-heavy, collagen-rich cut that is typically braised to become tender and gelatinous, while sirloin is a leaner, more tender cut that cooks very differently. Guideline F explicitly states that a different cut of meat is not substitutable. Substituting sirloin would change the cooking method (braising vs. quick cooking) and the resulting texture and mouthfeel, and a diner would likely notice. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 also fails because the texture would differ. The cubing is handling and does not alter the cut.

The ingredient is uncooked long-grain white rice, rinsed. The USDA entry is raw, regular, enriched long-grain white rice, which is the same food in its standard default form. Rinsing is kitchen handling and does not change the match (guideline C). The weight is decoration (guideline A). Enrichment is the standard form of white rice sold in the US, so it is the default version (guideline D), not a modification. Cooking method is unchanged, since the rice is still raw and the cook would treat it the same way. A diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Montmorency cherries, which are the dominant variety of sour (tart) red cherry (Prunus cerasus). The USDA entry 'Cherries, sour, red, raw' describes that same fruit category in its raw, fresh state. 'Pitted' is knife or handling work and does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are raw fresh cherries used in the same way, and pitting is already handled. Condition 2: Montmorency is a sour red cherry, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance compared with the generic sour red cherry entry. Both conditions are met, and this is a regional or variety name for the same food (guideline B).

Bacon fat is rendered bacon drippings, which is what the USDA entry 'Animal fat, bacon grease' describes. Under guideline B these are the same food under different names. Condition 1: it can replace bacon fat in any recipe without changing the cooking method, since both are rendered pork fat used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because they are the same product. The quantity (500g) is ignored per guideline A. This is a household product, not an industrial or food-service fat, so guideline F does not apply. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is yellow mustard, the standard prepared condiment sold under that name. The USDA entry 'Mustard, prepared, yellow' is the same product under the same name. The quantity (100g) is decoration and is ignored. Substituting it changes no preparation method, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain 'popcorn' with no preparation, flavour, or state specified (the 75g is quantity, which is ignored). 'Popcorn, NFS' is the generic USDA entry for popcorn with no added flavour, modification, or unusual state. Per guideline E, a USDA entry that names only the food with no state matches the plain food. It is the same food under its standard name, so it can be used without changing preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance relative to the plain ingredient. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a dry, chicken-flavored rice and pasta mix, which is the product sold as Rice-A-Roni chicken flavor. The USDA entry is that same branded product in its unprepared (dry, uncooked) form. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. Under guideline C, an unprepared ready-made product matches its USDA product. The quantity (100g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the dry mix can be used directly in place of the ingredient, and the dish is prepared the same way (cooked with water or stock as the recipe directs). Condition 2: a diner would taste the same chicken-flavored rice and pasta, with no difference in flavour, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Concord grapes. Concord is a slip-skin American-type grape (Vitis labrusca), the variety the USDA 'American type (slip skin)' category is named for. The USDA entry is therefore the same food under a more general name, not a sibling variety. Quantity (165g) is ignored. The entry is raw, matching a raw fruit used as bought. Both conditions hold: the grapes can be used without changing preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the entry covers the same grape type.

The ingredient is chutney, a condiment. The USDA match is 'Chutney', which is literally the same food under the same name, so it is not a different food or a modified version. The quantity (30g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: chutney can be used in place of chutney without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is canned cannellini beans, which are fully cooked and packed in liquid, then drained. The USDA match is 'Beans, cannellini, dry', which is the uncooked dried legume. Condition 1 fails: dried beans would need soaking and long cooking, so the preparation method would change. The dish would also need extra cooking time and liquid, and the drained canned beans could not be replaced by dry ones without altering the recipe. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, since dry beans cooked from scratch are firmer, less uniform, and have a different skin and interior than canned beans. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state, and the same food in a different state does not qualify. The ingredient is the same bean, but its state differs, so it is not substitutable.

Granada is the Spanish word for pomegranate, so this is the same food under a regional or culinary name (guideline B). The quantity (110g) is ignored (guideline A). The USDA entry 'Pomegranates, raw' is the fresh fruit as bought, and the recipe does not change it (guideline C). Condition 1 holds: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 holds: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same fruit.

The ingredient is monk fruit (luo han guo), a small melon-like fruit sold fresh, dried, or as a concentrated sweetener extract. The USDA match, Fruit nectar, NFS, is a sweetened, diluted fruit beverage made from purees or juices. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Substituting it would change the dish's preparation: a liquid nectar cannot replace a solid fruit or a dry sweetener by weight. A diner would also taste a different, sweeter and juice-like flavour, and the texture and appearance would differ. Neither condition is met, and the quantity is ignored per guideline A.

Oat flour is commonly sold as ground whole oats, so 'Flour, oat, whole grain' is the same food under a more formal name. The quantity (35g) is ignored. Oat flour is normally sold as a whole-grain product, so the 'whole grain' descriptor just reflects how it is normally bought and does not count as a modification. Condition 1: it can replace oat flour without changing the preparation, since it is used the same way in baking or cooking. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same ground oat product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is explicitly cooked mulberries, while the USDA match is raw mulberries. Guideline F states that raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Cooking changes texture (softening, breaking down), appearance (colour deepening, skins splitting, a jammy look) and flavour (sweeter, less tart, cooked notes). Using raw fruit would therefore bypass the cooking step the recipe calls for, so condition 1 fails. A diner would also likely notice the difference in texture and appearance, so condition 2 fails. The food is the same species, so guideline B does not rescue it, because the difference is in preparation state, not name. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is a plain raw New Zealand lamb breast, which is normally sold with its fat. The USDA entry is 'separable lean only', meaning the separable fat has been removed. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version (here, trimmed of fat) is not a match. Condition 1 fails: lamb breast is typically braised or roasted to render its fat, so the lean-only cut would change how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in juiciness, texture and appearance, since the lean-only meat has far less fat and would cook drier and leaner. The entry is the same species and origin, but it is not the same cut as bought under the plain name.

The ingredient is plain shortening, a single fat. The USDA entry is Agutuk, a prepared traditional food made of fish whipped with shortening (Alaskan ice cream). It is a composite product, not the fat itself. Guideline F says a single ingredient versus a blend or product containing it is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using Agutuk in place of shortening would bring fish and whipped dish components into the recipe, changing preparation. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste fish and notice a different texture and appearance. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is 150g pig heart, i.e. raw pork heart; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Pork, fresh, variety meats and by-products, heart, raw', which is the same food (pig heart, raw, fresh) with USDA's standard naming. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is the same raw organ meat and any trimming or cubing is handler work that does not change the match. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a plain 'orange' with the weight as decoration, so the quantity is ignored. 'Orange, raw' is the standard default entry for a fresh orange, with no cooking, modification, or added flavour. Condition 1: an orange can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since it is the same fruit in its raw state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried apricots, chopped, which is the dried fruit as bought. The USDA match is 'Apricots, dried, sulfured, stewed, without added sugar'. Sulfured is the normal way dried apricots are sold, so that descriptor is acceptable under guideline D. 'Stewed' is different: the fruit has been cooked in water and is soft and plumped. Guideline F says raw/dry versus cooked is a different state and not substitutable. Using stewed apricots would change how the dish is prepared (the fruit would need no rehydration or cooking, and it cannot be chopped and used dry in the same way). It would also change texture and appearance: the pieces would be soft, moist and mushy rather than firm and chewy, so a diner would notice. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well.

The ingredient is sea cucumber, cleaned, which is an echinoderm (a marine invertebrate), not a fish. The USDA match is 'Fish, sea bass, mixed species, raw', which is a finned fish of the Serranidae/Moronidae families. These are different foods, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: sea bass cannot replace sea cucumber without changing the preparation, since sea cucumber is typically braised, stewed or rehydrated and has a gelatinous, firm, cartilage-like texture, whereas sea bass is a flaky fillet that would be cooked differently. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would readily notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is frozen basil pesto cubes, a frozen product that is thawed before use. The USDA match is ready-to-serve, shelf-stable pesto, a different product form. Condition 1: Guideline E lets a frozen product match its fresh or plain counterpart when freezing does not show and the food is normally cooked or mixed. Pesto cubes are often stirred into dishes, so swapping in a jarred pesto would not change the preparation method, which is a point in favour. Condition 2: Shelf-stable pesto is processed differently from frozen pesto, typically with more preservatives and different acidity, colour and texture. The shelf-stable product is usually darker and oilier, and it lacks the fresh-tasting character that frozen basil pesto keeps. A diner could plausibly notice the change in flavour and appearance. There is no frozen pesto entry in the USDA match, so the frozen-to-frozen rule in Guideline E cannot be applied. Because the flavour and appearance differences are likely to be noticeable, condition 2 is not met. The 2g quantity is ignored per Guideline A.

The ingredient is pecans, ground. The USDA match is 'Pecans, unroasted', which is raw pecans. Per guideline C, grinding is knife or handling work done at home and does not change the match. Guideline B says the same food counts, and this is the same nut in its uncooked state. Condition 1: raw pecans can replace ground pecans, since the grinding is done by the cook and the dish preparation is unchanged. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since the pecans are the same raw nut and the ground form is produced in the kitchen. The pattern matches guideline E for frozen nuts, where the same raw food matches without a visible difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh tofu, a plain, unfried soybean curd used as a base for cooking. The USDA match is 'Soybean curd, breaded, fried', which is a different product. Condition 1 fails: it is already breaded and deep-fried, so it cannot replace raw tofu without changing how the dish is prepared (the cook would have to skip frying, seasoning, or coating steps that the recipe expects to do itself). Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (crisp, oily breaded exterior versus soft, plain curd), appearance (golden coating), and flavour (fried batter). Fresh tofu is not the same food as breaded fried tofu, so this is not a naming variant under guideline B. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is raw kohlrabi, diced, intended for soup. The USDA match is 'Soup, vegetable with beef broth, canned, condensed', which is a processed, canned, condensed soup product containing beef broth, multiple vegetables, and likely other components. It is not the raw kohlrabi vegetable, nor is it a cut or inner part of kohlrabi. Condition 1 fails: substituting a canned condensed soup for a diced fresh vegetable would change the preparation (the soup would be a ready-made product rather than a vegetable added to soup-making). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in taste (beef broth flavour, no kohlrabi), texture (soft, diced vegetables vs. crisp kohlrabi pieces), and appearance. Guideline F applies: a single ingredient versus a blend or product containing it, and a processed product versus the raw source, are not substitutable. Quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is fish broth, a liquid stock made by simmering fish, bones and aromatics. The USDA match, 'Fish, NFS', is a generic entry for fish flesh, which is a solid food. Using it in place of broth would change the dish's preparation, since it would have to be cooked in or with liquid rather than used as a liquid. It would also change the flavour, texture and appearance, and a diner would notice the difference. This is a different food from a different state, not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well.

The ingredient is 'salsa', a prepared condiment made from tomatoes, onions, peppers, and seasonings, typically served cold or used as a topping or dip. The USDA match is 'Egg, whole, raw, fresh', which is a completely different food (an animal product, not a tomato-based sauce). Condition 1 fails: an egg cannot be used in place of salsa without changing the dish's preparation, since it has no acidity, chunky vegetable texture, or seasoning profile and would not serve the same role. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance. The quantity (20g) is ignored per the guidelines. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply.

The ingredient is frozen edamame, thawed. The USDA entry 'Edamame, frozen, unprepared' is the same food in the same frozen state, which is the match described in guideline E for a frozen product that is thawed. Quantity (30g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the frozen entry can replace the thawed ingredient without changing preparation, since the thawing is handled in the recipe and 'unprepared' describes the product as bought. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the product is the same edamame and freezing does not show once it is cooked or mixed. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain 'passion fruit' with no variety specified. The USDA entry 'Passion-fruit, (granadilla), purple, raw' is the purple passion fruit (Passiflora edulis), which is the standard passion fruit sold in most markets. 'Granadilla' is a regional/trade name for the same fruit, so under guideline B this is the same food under another name. The entry is raw, which matches a fresh fruit used as-is. The weight prefix '100g' is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since it is the default passion fruit. The only concern would be the yellow variety (a sibling with a different taste under guideline F), but the ingredient does not specify yellow, so the default purple match stands.

The ingredient is '210g ham and cheese spread' (quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry is 'Ham and cheese spread', which names the same product with the same components (ham and cheese). Under guideline B and D, a plain ingredient matching the standard default version of the same named product is a match. Condition 1: the spread could be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is a ready-to-use spread and no cooking method is involved. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product under the same name with the same components. Both conditions are met.

Ash gourd is the same food as wax gourd, also called Chinese preserving melon (Benincasa hispida), so this is a regional or culinary name for the same vegetable (guideline B). The USDA entry is 'cooked, boiled, drained, without salt', which matches the ingredient's 'boiled and drained' preparation. Boiling without added salt is the default way this vegetable is prepared, so no added salt difference applies (guideline D). The leading '1g' is decoration and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient with no change to the cooking method, since the dish is already boiled and drained. Condition 2: it is the same plant in the same prepared state, so a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance.

The ingredient is dried red dates, which are dried Chinese jujubes, the same fruit sold under a culinary/trade name (guideline B). The USDA entry 'Jujube, Chinese, fresh, dried' describes the dried Chinese jujube itself, so the food and its state match. Using it would not change how the dish is prepared, since it is the same dried fruit with the same taste, texture and appearance, so a diner would notice no difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is gluten-free pasta, and the USDA entry is 'Pasta, gluten free', which names the same product type with no cooking state or modifier attached. Under the guidelines, a USDA entry that names only the food with no state matches the generic food, so it covers the plain product as bought. Condition 1: the match is the same product, so it can replace the ingredient in the same preparation (boiling, sauce, etc.) without changing the method. Condition 2: because the match is the same kind of gluten-free pasta, a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions hold, and the 100g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is a frozen graham cracker pie crust, thawed. The USDA entry is a graham cracker cookie-type pie crust in ready-made form. Both are the same product type: a ready-made graham cracker crust with the same components. Guideline E says a thawed frozen product matches the frozen or generic USDA entry of the same product, and the USDA entry names no conflicting state. Condition 1: the crust can replace the ingredient directly, with no change to preparation (both are pressed into a pan and filled or baked the same way). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since both are graham cracker crusts of the same kind. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is 75g sweetened nectarine slices. The weight is ignored. The base food is nectarine, so the fruit itself matches 'Nectarines, raw'. However, 'sweetened' is a modification: the plain fruit has been given added sugar. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a modified version is not a match, and sweetened is listed explicitly as a modifier. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the added sweetness, which is a difference in flavour from the raw, unsweetened fruit. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the fruit could be cut and used in the same way, but the flavour change means the dish would be different. Because condition 2 fails, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is jack mackerel, a fish (oily saltwater fish of the Carangidae family, typically sold raw or as fillets). The USDA match is Cheese, Colby Jack, a dairy product made from cow's milk. These are entirely different foods: one is a raw animal-protein fish, the other a processed cheese. Condition 1 fails: a cheese cannot replace a fish without changing how the dish is prepared (fish would be cooked, grilled, or seared, whereas cheese would be melted, grated, or sliced, and the cooking method and dish structure would change). Condition 2 fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance. The quantity (410g) is irrelevant per guideline A, and there is no same-food naming equivalence per guideline B.

The ingredient is a mixture of two different fruits, sapodilla and mango, diced. The USDA entry 'Mangos, raw' covers only mango. Sapodilla is a distinct fruit, not a regional name for mango, so guideline B does not apply. Sapodilla has a different flavour (sweet, malty, often described as brown sugar or pear-like), a grainy, soft texture, and a brown flesh that differs in appearance from mango. Replacing it with mango alone would change the flavour, texture and appearance of the dish, and a diner would likely notice. This matches guideline F's rule that a single ingredient is not substitutable for a blend or combination containing it. Condition 1 (same preparation) can be met, but condition 2 (no noticeable difference) fails. Quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is baked acorn squash explicitly labelled unsalted. The USDA entry is baked acorn squash with salt added. Condition 1: the salted version would change the seasoning step, since the cook would be adding salt the recipe does not call for. Condition 2: a diner would likely taste the added salt, so the flavour differs. Guideline D treats a plain ingredient mapped to a sodium-modified version as not a match, and the ingredient's stated 'unsalted' requirement makes the salted entry the wrong version. Quantity is irrelevant. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is ground mustard seed. The USDA match is 'Spices, mustard seed, ground', which is the same food (ground mustard seed) under the same name. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: it can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since the product is the same ground spice. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Alaskan king crab with no stated preparation, so the plain, uncooked form is the default. The USDA entry 'Crustaceans, crab, alaska king, raw' is the same food under the same name, with the raw state matching the plain ingredient. Condition 1: the crab can be used in place of the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since any knife work or handling in the recipe does not alter the match. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance because it is the same species in the same uncooked state. The weight is ignored per the guidelines. Both conditions are met.

Condition 2: a diner would taste and see the same vegetable, since it is literally the same food with no processing or variety difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is flank steak, a specific beef cut. The USDA entry 'Beef, steak, flank' names the same cut with no modifying state such as cooked, smoked, or processed. The 560g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Under guideline E, an entry that names only the food with no state is the generic food, so it matches the plain cut. The match is the same food under the same name, so it could replace the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is plain cream cheese, softened, which by default means regular full-fat cream cheese. The USDA match is 'Cream cheese, fat free', a modified reduced-fat version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a fat-free or reduced-fat version is not a match. Condition 1 is about preparation: softening is handling that does not change the match, so the preparation itself would work. Condition 2 fails, though. Fat-free cream cheese has noticeably different taste (less richness), texture (firmer, sometimes rubbery or gummy, and it can behave differently when whipped or blended), and can appear different when spread or baked. A diner would likely notice the difference. Because condition 2 is not met, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is ground veal (raw, uncooked, ground). The USDA entry is 'Veal, ground, raw', which is the same food with the same state (raw, ground). Quantity (565g) is ignored per guideline A. Guideline E and C indicate that grinding meat is a handling step and does not change the match. Same cut/product, same state, no added modifications, so the dish preparation would be unchanged and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is cooked whole-wheat pasta. The USDA entry is 'Pasta, whole-wheat, cooked', which is the same food in the same state (cooked, whole-wheat). The parenthetical 'Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program' is a standard descriptor that USDA adds to many entries and does not change the product. The leading '160g' is quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are already cooked pasta. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same cooked whole-wheat pasta. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Bosc pears, sliced. The USDA entry is Pears, raw, bartlett. Both are raw fresh pears, so the knife work (sliced) does not change the match. However, Bosc and Bartlett are sibling varieties with different taste and texture. Bosc is firmer, denser and less juicy, with a spiced, more caramel-like flavour, while Bartlett is softer, juicier and sweeter. Guideline F says a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable. Because the two would differ in texture and flavour, a diner could notice the difference. Condition 2 therefore fails.

The ingredient is liverwurst, a cooked, spreadable pork liver sausage. The USDA entry 'Liverwurst spread' names the same food; 'spread' describes how liverwurst is commonly sold rather than a modified version, so it is the standard default product (guidelines B and D). Cubing is knife work the recipe performs and does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1 is met because the product can be cubed in the same way. Condition 2 is met because it is the same product, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste or flavour. Appearance and texture should be essentially the same for the same liverwurst product. No modification, blend, or different cut applies.

The ingredient is bottom round steak, which is the same cut that the USDA entry names (beef, round, outside round, bottom round, steak). The grade (choice) is the standard retail default, and 'raw' means uncooked, which matches. The USDA entry specifies 'separable lean and fat, trimmed to 0" fat'. Fat trimming is handling that a cook does, and guideline C treats 'trimmed' as not changing the match. Trimming a steak to lean-only changes its visible fat cap but not the cut, its cooking method, or the flavour a diner would notice in a normal preparation. Condition 1 is met because the steak could be cooked the same way. Condition 2 is met because the dish would look and taste essentially the same. The quantity is ignored.

'Navet' is the French name for turnip, so this is the same vegetable under a regional/culinary name (guideline B). The USDA entry 'Turnips, raw' is the uncooked, plain vegetable. The quantity prefix '250g' is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: turnips can replace navet with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is passion fruit pulp, which is the fruit's seeded, fibrous flesh used as a garnish. The USDA match is passion fruit juice, 100%, which is strained liquid with the pulp and seeds removed. Condition 1: the juice cannot replace the pulp as a garnish without changing how the dish is prepared. Pulp is spooned or scattered over the dish, while juice would be poured or drizzled, so the preparation changes. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Pulp contributes visible seeds, a thicker, grainy texture and a more intense appearance, while juice is smooth and translucent and lacks the seeds and visual garnish effect. Juice and pulp are different processed states of the fruit, so this is not a same-food naming match. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is raw leg of lamb, and the USDA entry is raw leg of lamb (whole leg, shank and sirloin included, trimmed to 1/4" fat, choice grade). It is the same food, and the same cut. The quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A. The trim specification and grade are the standard way a raw leg of lamb is sold, so under guideline D this is the default version of the plain ingredient, not a modified one. Condition 1: the lamb can be used in place of the leg of lamb with no change to the cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same raw cut with standard trimming. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chopped prunes, which are dried plums. The USDA entry 'Plums, dried (prunes), uncooked' names the same food under its common name, so it is the literal same product (guideline B). 'Chopped' is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). 'Uncooked' matches the raw dried product as bought. The weight is decoration (guideline A). Using the USDA entry would not change the preparation, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance.

The ingredient is canned blue crab, drained, about 145g. The USDA entry is Crustaceans, crab, blue, canned, which is the same food: blue crab packed in can. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Draining is handling that does not change the match (C). Canned crab is the standard default form of the product, so no modification applies (D). The USDA entry is the canned product itself, so it is the same state as the ingredient and no cooking method, flavour, texture or appearance differs. A diner would not notice any difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is haddock that has been steamed and then flaked. The USDA entry is haddock, steamed, which is the same food in the same cooked state. The leading '200g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Flaking is knife or hand handling, which does not change the match (guideline C). Using the USDA entry would not change how the dish is prepared, because the fish is already steamed and only needs flaking. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same steamed haddock. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried tilapia, a preserved, dehydrated fish product that is used as bought. The USDA entry is tilapia cooked with dry heat, a cooked fresh-fish product. Guideline F rules out a different state (raw/dried vs cooked), and the match would change both texture and appearance: dried tilapia is hard, dense and shelf-stable, while dry-heat cooked tilapia is moist, flaky and soft. The entry does not name a dried product, and the diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails because the ingredient is not used in the cooked form, and condition 2 fails because the eating texture and appearance would differ. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain salted butter (5g, quantity ignored). The USDA match is 'Lemon-butter sauce', a prepared sauce containing butter combined with lemon juice and other components. Condition 1: Substituting a lemon-butter sauce for salted butter would change the preparation, since it is a different product with added liquid and acidity, not a fat that can be used the same way. Condition 2: A diner would notice the lemon flavour and the different taste and texture. This is a blend containing butter rather than the same food under another name, and a flavoured modification of butter is not the standard default version. Under guideline F (a single ingredient vs a blend or product containing it) and guideline D (flavoured version is not a match), it fails both conditions.

The ingredient is canned plums, drained, which is simply canned plums with the liquid removed as a handling step. The USDA entry 'Plum, canned' names the same food in the same canned state, with no added flavour, modification, or unusual packing medium. Canned fruit is normally sold in syrup or juice, so the generic entry matches a shopper's default. Draining is handling, not a state change, so it does not alter the match. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is deli honey chicken, sliced: a sliced, honey-glazed chicken product sold at the deli counter.
