The USDA entry is Oscar Mayer Chicken Breast (honey glazed), a branded honey-glazed chicken breast product. The honey glaze, which defines the ingredient, is present in the match. Sliced is knife work or handling and does not change the match (guideline C). The branded entry is the same plain product type, with no added flavour beyond the honey glaze that defines the ingredient (guideline G). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is used as sliced deli meat in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because both are sliced honey-glazed chicken breast. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is triticale flour, a flour milled from a wheat-rye hybrid. The USDA match is whole-grain soft wheat flour, which is a different flour. Under guideline F, a different flour is not substitutable even when it looks close. Triticale has a different gluten structure, so doughs and batters behave differently. It also has a different flavour, a darker and more earthy colour, and a different crumb, so a diner would likely notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) both fail. The 400g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is fresh pork jowl. The USDA entry is 'Pork, fresh, variety meats and by-products, jowl, raw', which is the same cut, fresh and uncooked. The 'variety meats and by-products' label is just USDA's category wording for the jowl. The '100g' quantity is ignored. Condition 1: the jowl can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same raw cut. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is salted butter, a dairy fat made from churned cream. The USDA match is stick margarine, a vegetable-oil-based spread. They are different fats, which guideline F rules out as substitutable. Condition 1 can be met on paper, since both are solid fats used similarly in cooking. Condition 2 fails: butter's milk-derived flavour, its salt content (salted butter), and its browning behaviour differ from margarine's, so a diner would likely notice the difference in taste and possibly texture. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is clarified butterfat: milk solids and water removed, with no browning. The USDA entry is ghee, which is clarified butter cooked longer so the milk solids brown, giving a distinctive nutty, caramelised flavour and a slightly different aroma and colour. Guideline B (same food under another name) does not apply, because ghee is a distinct product from plain clarified butterfat, not a regional name for it. Guideline F treats a different fat, or a different state such as plain versus toasted, as not substitutable. Condition 1 (same preparation) could be met, since both are used as a cooking fat. Condition 2 is not met: a diner could notice the nutty, browned flavour of ghee in a dish that calls for clean clarified butterfat.

The ingredient is high fructose corn syrup, and the USDA entry 'Syrups, corn, high-fructose' is the same product under its full USDA name, so this is a same-food match (guideline B). The 20g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same syrup used in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a pupusa filled with both beans and cheese (quesillo or cheese is a defining component). The USDA entry, 'Pupusa, with beans', names only the bean filling. The dish is the same type of food, but the USDA entry omits the cheese, which is a component the ingredient explicitly specifies. Condition 1: the preparation would be the same, but the product is not the same composition. Condition 2: a diner would notice the absence of melted cheese in taste, texture (the stretchy, melted quality), and appearance. The USDA entry is a different filling combination, not the same food under another name, so it fails both conditions.

The ingredient is generic whole-grain snack crackers. The USDA entry is a wheat snack cracker (Wheat Thins), a whole-grain wheat cracker sold as a standard snack, so it is the same product type. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type counts as a match. Whole grain is the ingredient's own requirement, and Wheat Thins are made from whole grain wheat, so this is not a modified version. Wheat crackers are a common whole-grain snack, so the swap doesn't change how the dish is prepared (crushed, layered, or served as a snack, with no cooking-method change). Taste, texture and appearance are close enough that a diner would not reliably notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Atlantic pollock fillets, weight 100g (quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry is 'Fish, pollock, Atlantic, raw', which is the same species (Atlantic pollock) in the same raw, uncooked state. Fillets are a cut/form of the same fish, and cutting or portioning does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the raw Atlantic pollock could replace the fillets without changing preparation, since the same cooking methods apply. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same species and form. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cocoa butter, the pure fat extracted from cocoa beans. The USDA match is 'Hot chocolate / cocoa, dry mix, made with water', which is a prepared beverage made from cocoa powder, sugar, milk solids or nonfat dry milk, and other additives, reconstituted with water. This is not the same food: it is a sugary, flavoured, processed product, not a fat. Condition 1 fails: using a hot cocoa drink mix in place of cocoa butter would change the composition, moisture content, and preparation of the dish (it cannot be melted in as a fat for structure or mouthfeel, and it would add water, sugar, and milk solids). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste chocolate-sweetened drink flavour and notice a difference in texture and appearance. Quantity is ignored per the guidelines. Under guideline F, a different fat or a blend/product containing an ingredient is not a substitute, so the match is rejected.

The ingredient is sun-dried tomato, and the USDA entry 'Tomatoes, sun-dried' is the same food under its standard name. The quantity prefix is ignored. The recipe does not specify oil-packed, so the plain dried product is the default version (guideline D). The match is not a modified product, a different state (it is already dried, as the ingredient is), or a different cut. Condition 1 holds: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 holds: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. The only caveat is that if the ingredient were oil-packed, the packing medium would differ, but the ingredient does not state that.

The ingredient is peanut sauce, a prepared condiment typically made from peanut butter blended with oil, soy sauce, sugar, spices, coconut milk or other seasonings, and often served as a dipping or cooking sauce. The USDA match is 'Flour, chestnut', a dry, starchy powder milled from chestnuts. Condition 1: Chestnut flour cannot stand in for a liquid, emulsified, savoury-sweet sauce without changing how the dish is prepared; it would not coat, emulsify, or be cooked in the same way, and would require adding liquid and flavourings. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (sweet, nutty, savoury peanut flavour versus mild, slightly sweet chestnut flour), texture (smooth sauce versus dry powder or paste), and appearance. Both conditions fail, and this is a different food entirely, not a naming variant of the same product (guideline F: different state and a different food source).

The ingredient is pumpkin pie spice blend, a mixture of spices typically including cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, and cloves (sometimes allspice or cardamom in some blends). The USDA match is 'Spices, cardamom', which is a single spice (cardamom) rather than a blend. Per guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend containing it is not substitutable. Cardamom has a distinct citrusy, floral flavour that is not the dominant or characteristic profile of pumpkin pie spice, so the dish's flavour would change and a diner would notice. Condition 1 (substitution without changing preparation) could superficially hold, but condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste) fails. The quantity (10g) is irrelevant per guideline A.

The ingredient is amaranth flour, a finely milled, processed form of the grain. The USDA match is amaranth grain, uncooked, which is the whole raw seed. Guideline F says the raw source and the processed ingredient are not substitutable (cornstarch vs corn, for example). The exception for home grinding applies only to meat and fish, not grain. Condition 1 fails: whole grain cannot replace flour without changing how the dish is prepared, since it would need milling and would not blend or bind like flour. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the whole, unmilled seeds in texture and appearance. Because the match fails both conditions, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a mixture of two different foods, blue crab and shrimp, steamed. The USDA match covers only blue crab, cooked by moist heat. Condition 1 fails: the match is a single ingredient, while the recipe calls for a blend of crab and shrimp, so it cannot replace the ingredient as stated. This is the single-ingredient-vs-blend case in guideline F. Shrimp is a different food, so the match changes the dish's composition. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the absence of shrimp and the difference in flavour and texture. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain muesli, a generic unsweetened mix of oats, grains, nuts and dried fruit. The USDA entry is ALPEN, a branded ready-to-eat muesli-style cereal that is normally sweetened (sugar and/or honey, and typically a sweeter flavour profile). Under the guidelines, a branded entry of the same plain product type can match (G), but a branded entry with added sweetening or flavour does not (D, G). The word 'plain' signals the unsweetened default, so the sweetened Alpen product is a modified version. Condition 1: substituting it changes the sugar content and sweetness, so the preparation (for example, baking, soaking or toasting as a plain muesli would be used) would produce a different result. Condition 2: a diner would likely taste extra sweetness and notice a different flavour and texture from the ready-to-eat clusters or flakes. Neither condition is clearly met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a boneless rib roast, trimmed, with no stated grade or fat level. The USDA entry is a raw boneless rib eye roast trimmed to 1/8 inch fat, choice grade. A boneless rib roast is the rib eye roast, so this is the same cut under a different name (Guideline B). The ingredient is raw, which matches the USDA 'raw' state. 'Trimmed' is handling that does not change the match (Guideline C). 'Lip-on' and 'separable lean and fat' describe how the nutrient analysis was made rather than a different product, and the 1/8-inch trim is a standard trimmed state. The grade is unspecified, so the default choice grade is acceptable. The quantity is ignored (Guideline A). Condition 1: the meat can replace the ingredient with the same preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance.

The ingredient is plain 'corn flour', a finely ground corn product. The USDA entry 'Corn flour, yellow, degermed, unenriched' is the same product type, and degermed yellow corn flour is the standard default version sold as corn flour. The recipe does not specify a colour, so yellow is an acceptable default. It is not a cornstarch or masa product, and it is not a modified or blended version. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the same preparation, since corn flour is used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance beyond the normal variation between corn flours. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 185g quail, i.e. quail meat (the bird as a food, presumably raw or cooked meat). The USDA match is 'Quail egg, canned', which is a different food entirely: an egg product, not the bird's meat. Per guideline B, this is not the same food under another name; quail egg and quail meat are distinct foods. Per guideline F, a different food category (egg vs meat, and a canned processed product) changes the taste, texture and appearance of the dish, and a diner would clearly notice eating eggs rather than quail meat. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference) both fail. The weight is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is pigeon peas, a legume (Cajanus cajan). The USDA match, 'Pea salad', is a prepared dish of mixed components, not the legume itself. Condition 1 fails: using a pea salad in place of pigeon peas would change how the dish is prepared, since the peas would have to be cooked or otherwise incorporated, and the salad's other ingredients and dressing would be added. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance, since the salad is dressed and mixed while pigeon peas are a plain legume. Guideline B does not apply because 'pea salad' is not a regional name for pigeon peas. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh tripe, cut into strips. The USDA entry is raw beef tripe, the standard commercial form of tripe. Tripe is normally sold as beef stomach, so the two name the same food. Cutting into strips is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). The entry is raw, which matches fresh tripe as bought. Cooking would proceed the same way, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The leading weight of 200g is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked turkey Italian sausage. The USDA entry, 'Sausage, Italian, turkey, smoked', describes the same product: an Italian-style sausage made from turkey and smoked. The quantity prefix (260g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the sausage can be used directly in place of the ingredient with the same preparation, since the form and cooking method are the same. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the product is the same food with the same smoked state. The smoked descriptor matches the ingredient rather than changing it. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chicken liver, and the USDA entry 'Liver, chicken' is the same food under a reversed name order. The entry names no cooking state, so it is the generic food and matches fresh chicken liver. The quantity is ignored. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the recipe's handling applies equally to chicken liver. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried salted cod, a fish (Atlantic cod, Gadus morhua, cured by salting and drying). The USDA match is jellyfish, dried, salted, which is a different animal entirely, a cnidarian and not a fish. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Substituting jellyfish would change the taste, texture (cod flakes, jellyfish is crunchy and gelatinous), and appearance of the dish, and a diner would notice. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

Ingredient is Canadian bacon, cooked (100g; quantity ignored per guideline A). USDA match is 'Canadian bacon, cooked', which is literally the same food with the same state (cooked) and same name. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient with no change to preparation, since both are already cooked and need only the same handling. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked beef neck, a raw-or-cured beef cut that is smoked. The USDA entry is chicken broiler/fryer neck meat, cooked by frying. Three differences apply. First, the species differs: beef versus chicken. Guideline F treats a different cut of meat as not substitutable, and a different animal is a stronger difference than that. Second, the preparation differs: smoked versus fried. Guideline F says a different state (plain versus smoked or cooked) is not substitutable. Third, the flavour, texture and appearance would clearly differ: smoked beef has a smoky, cured profile and dense texture, while fried chicken neck has a crisp exterior and poultry flavour. Neither condition is met. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is plain yam, and the USDA entry is 'Yam, raw', which is the same food under the same name. The leading '500g' is quantity decoration and is ignored (guideline A). The entry is raw, which is the default state for a plain yam used as an ingredient, so it is the standard default version (guideline D). Condition 1: a raw yam can replace the ingredient without changing the preparation, since any cutting or cooking the recipe does applies equally to both. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is eye of round, a lean cut of beef from the round primal. The USDA entry is cooked, roasted chicken breast meat from broilers or fryers. These are different animal species, so this is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Eye of round is a beef cut that is typically cooked whole or sliced for roasting and carving. Substituting chicken breast would change the meat, flavour, and texture, and a diner would notice the difference. Also, the USDA entry is already cooked, while the ingredient is presumably raw. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails.

Ingredient is adobo sauce, a canned/jarred Mexican sauce made from chipotle or other dried chilies (often ancho/guajillo) blended with vinegar, tomato, garlic, and spices, typically with a smoky, tangy, and moist texture. USDA match is 'Spices, pepper, red or cayenne', which is a dry ground spice with no vinegar, tomato, or liquid component. Condition 1 fails: it cannot replace a wet sauce without changing preparation (no liquid, paste, or marinade base). Condition 2 fails: the flavour (smoky, tangy, saucy) and texture/appearance would be noticeably different. It is not the same food under another name, and the match is a single ingredient (dry spice) versus a blended product, which guideline F explicitly rules out. Quantity is ignored.

The ingredient is smoked Polish kielbasa, the traditional sausage, which is normally made from pork (often with some beef). The USDA entry is specifically a turkey-and-beef kielbasa. The name matches, but the USDA entry specifies a different protein base. Turkey and beef have different fat content, flavour, and texture from pork, and the sausage's characteristic taste and mouthfeel would change. The recipe's preparation would be the same, but a diner would likely notice eating turkey-beef sausage instead of traditional pork-based kielbasa. Under the guidelines, a different meat composition is a different product (cf. guideline F on cuts and blends), and the change would be noticeable in taste and texture. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is mandarin orange, a citrus fruit (Citrus reticulata, a mandarin/tangerine type). The USDA match is 'Oil, olive, salad or cooking', which is an edible fat extracted from olives. These are entirely different foods: one is a fresh fruit, the other is a vegetable oil. Under guideline B, this is not the same food under another name, since mandarin oranges are not olive oil and no regional or culinary alias applies. Condition 1 fails: substituting olive oil for mandarin orange would change how the dish is prepared (no segments, juice, or zest; a fat added instead of fruit). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. The quantity (10g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh sardines (raw, uncooked fish). The USDA match is 'Fish, sardines, canned', a processed product packed in oil or brine. Condition 1: substituting canned sardines for fresh would change the preparation. Fresh sardines are typically grilled, baked, or pan-fried, whereas canned sardines are already cooked and ready to eat, so the cooking method would be altered or skipped entirely. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Canned sardines have a softer, flakier texture, a distinctly stronger and oilier flavour from the packing medium and processing, and a different appearance. Guideline F explicitly lists 'raw vs cooked' and 'a different state' as not substitutable, and this is not the same food under another name, so the match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is thin-sliced deli turkey breast, a sliced, ready-to-eat deli product. The USDA entry, 'Turkey, prepackaged or deli, luncheon meat', is the standard USDA category for sliced deli turkey. Condition 1: the sliced product can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since both are eaten cold or used as-is in sandwiches, wraps or salads. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because both are the same kind of thin-sliced, cured or processed deli turkey. The quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A. The entry is a generic deli-turkey category rather than a specific breast-cut label, but it names the same product type, so it counts as a match under guideline B. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is unsalted dry roasted macadamia nuts. The USDA match is dry roasted macadamia nuts with salt added. Both are the same food and both are dry roasted, so the cooking state and nut type match. The difference is salt. The ingredient asks for unsalted, and the match adds salt. A diner would taste the added salt, so the flavour differs. Under guideline D, a salted version does not substitute for a plain or unsalted one, the same logic that makes reduced-sodium and standard versions non-equivalent. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the nuts could be swapped without changing preparation. Condition 2 fails because the taste difference is noticeable. Not substitutable.

Walnut kernels are the shelled edible part of the walnut, and English walnut (Juglans regia) is the standard walnut sold in shops. The USDA entry "Nuts, walnuts, english" is the same food under a formal name, so condition 1 holds: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 also holds: a diner would not taste or see a difference, since the match is the same nut. The weight prefix "40g" is ignored per guideline A. The entry carries no modification such as roasting, salting or flavouring, so there is no state difference to reject it on. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh, raw pike fillet, skinless. The USDA entry is pike (northern) cooked by dry heat. The food is the same species, so condition 1 is not the issue. The difference is the state: raw versus cooked. Guideline F explicitly lists raw vs cooked as not substitutable. Using a pre-cooked fish would change how the dish is prepared, since the cook would no longer be cooking raw fish through, and the diner would notice a different texture, appearance, and flavour. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is textured vegetable protein (TVP), a dried, rehydrated soy-based meat substitute that is a processed soy product with a spongy, granular texture and a bland flavour. The USDA match is 'Pork and vegetables, Hawaiian style', a prepared dish containing actual pork meat, vegetables, and presumably sauce and seasonings. Condition 1 fails: the match is a cooked, multi-component prepared dish rather than a dry protein ingredient, so using it in place of TVP would change the preparation (it cannot be rehydrated or used as a dry protein base; it would instead be a full cooked meal). Condition 2 fails: a diner would readily notice meat chunks, sweet-savoury sauce and vegetables versus a soy-based textured protein. This is not the same food under another name and is not a plain or standard version of TVP. Under rule F, a single ingredient versus a product containing other components is not substitutable.

The ingredient is squab (young pigeon), and the USDA entry explicitly says it includes squab, so the food identity matches. The problem is the state. The recipe ingredient is plain squab, which a shopper buys raw and then cooks as part of the recipe. The USDA entry is 'cooked'. Guideline F says raw vs cooked is a different state and not substitutable. Using pre-cooked meat would change how the dish is prepared, since the cooking step would be skipped or altered, and a diner could notice differences in texture, moisture and appearance. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 is also doubtful for the same reason. Therefore the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 25g golden raisins (dried grapes, a fruit ingredient used in baking or as a mix-in). The USDA match is 'Bagel, with raisins', a finished baked product. Condition 1: a bagel cannot replace raisins in a recipe. Using a bagel would change how the dish is prepared, since it is a whole baked bread product rather than a dried fruit that can be measured, chopped or folded in. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance, since a bagel contains bread dough, crust and chewy crumb rather than the small, chewy, sweet dried grapes. The match is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and it is a different food product (a composite baked good, not raisins). Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a mixture of corn and butter beans. In the US, butter beans are large lima beans, a regional name for the same legume, so the components match the USDA entry. The USDA entry 'Succotash, (corn and limas), raw' is the same combination of corn and lima beans in the uncooked state, which matches the ingredient as bought. The recipe does not indicate cooking, so the raw state is consistent. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since the beans are the same legume under another name and the corn is the same. Guideline B (regional names) and guideline C (same dish with the same components counts as a match) both apply. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pancake syrup, a standard sweetened table syrup, usually corn-syrup or sugar based and often maple-flavoured. The USDA match is 'Syrups, sugar free', a modified product that uses sugar substitutes instead of sugar. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a sweetened-versus-unsweetened or otherwise modified version is not a match. Condition 1 can be met, since it could be poured or used in the same way. Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste the difference, because sugar-free syrup has a different sweetness profile, often an aftertaste, and different viscosity and mouthfeel from sugar-based pancake syrup. Both conditions must hold, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'french dressing', a generic creamy/tangy sweet-tomato-style vinaigrette-type dressing (typically made with vegetable oil, vinegar, sugar, tomato paste or ketchup, paprika, and spices). The USDA match is 'Salad dressing, french, cottonseed, oil, home recipe'. It is the same food (French dressing) but specifies cottonseed oil as the oil base. Per guideline F, a different oil is not substitutable, since cottonseed oil can alter flavour and mouthfeel compared with the default vegetable oil typically used in French dressing. Condition 2 is therefore questionable: a diner might notice a difference in taste or mouthfeel from a specific oil. The weight is irrelevant (guideline A). The product is the same dish type, but the explicit oil specification is a modification in the same sense as the oil rule, so the match is not substitutable.

Nashi pear is the same fruit as the Asian pear (Pyrus pyrifolia), so this is a regional/trade name for the same food (Guideline B). The USDA entry 'Pears, asian, raw' is the uncooked, default form. The 30g weight is decoration and is ignored (Guideline A). Condition 1: the Asian pear can replace the nashi pear without changing preparation, since both are eaten raw or handled the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, because they are the same variety group with the same crisp, juicy texture and flavour. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'salt and sesame seeds (to taste)', a seasoning combination of salt plus sesame seeds. The USDA match is 'Salt, table', which covers only the salt component. Condition 1: substituting table salt alone would omit the sesame seeds, so the dish's preparation (sprinkling or coating with sesame seeds) would change. Condition 2: a diner would notice the absence of sesame seeds in taste, texture and appearance. The quantity prefix is ignored per guideline A. Because the match covers only one of the two named components and not the blend, it fails both conditions.

The ingredient is a vanilla-flavoured soy protein powder. The USDA entry, 'Beverages, Protein powder soy based', is the generic unflavoured soy protein powder. Condition 1 is about substitution: the powder could be used in the same way, with the same mixing and preparation, so the method is not the problem. Condition 2 fails. The vanilla flavour is the defining characteristic of the ingredient, and a diner would taste the difference from an unflavoured powder. Guideline D says a plain product matched to a flavoured or modified version is not substitutable, and the same logic applies in reverse here, since the USDA entry lacks the specified flavour. The quantity (5g) is ignored as instructed.

The ingredient is active dry yeast, a dehydrated granular product that is usually rehydrated in warm liquid before use. The USDA match is compressed (fresh) baker's yeast, a moist cake with a different water content and a different handling method. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Using it in place of active dry yeast changes the preparation: it must be crumbled or dissolved, and the quantity is not one-to-one, since fresh yeast is used at roughly twice the weight. That fails condition 1. Because the product's state and handling differ, the dough's rise and crumb can also differ, so a diner could plausibly notice the difference, which fails condition 2.

The ingredient is a fresh mustard pickle, a relish of pickled vegetables in a mustard-based, sweetened or spiced sauce. The USDA entry is sour cucumber pickles, which are brine- or vinegar-pickled whole or sliced cucumbers with dill or garlic flavouring. Condition 1: substituting sour pickles would change the dish's preparation. The mustard component and the chopped relish-style texture would be missing, so the dish would need reformulating. Condition 2: a diner would taste a clear difference. Mustard pickle has a yellow, mustard-sauce flavour and a sweet-sour profile, while sour cucumber pickles taste of dill and vinegar, and the appearance also differs. This is a different food, not a different name for the same food, so guideline B does not apply. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is grapefruit (peeled), a fresh citrus fruit with a distinct sour-bitter flavour and juicy texture. The USDA match is almond flour, a dry, finely ground nut product with no juice, acidity, or fruit character. Condition 1: almond flour cannot be used in place of grapefruit without changing preparation. Grapefruit would be eaten, segmented, juiced, or cooked as fruit, while almond flour is a powdered ingredient used in baking; it is not the same food under another name and is not a processing variant of grapefruit. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (sweet-nutty versus tart-bitter citrus), texture (dry powder versus juicy segments), and appearance. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable. The quantity (10g) is ignored per the guidelines.

1. The ingredient is cooked flounder, flaked. The USDA entry is flatfish (flounder and sole species), cooked, so it is the same food (flounder) in the same state (cooked). 2. The ingredient does not specify a cooking method, so the USDA's 'dry heat' descriptor is the standard cooked default rather than a modification that changes the food. 3. 'Flaked' is knife or handling work and does not change the match (guideline C). 4. Condition 1: the cooked dry-heat flounder can replace the flaked cooked flounder without changing how the dish is prepared. 5. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same species, cooked and flaked. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw button mushrooms (the standard fresh, uncooked mushroom, with quantity ignored). The USDA match 'Fried mushrooms' is a cooked product prepared by frying, typically in oil or fat, which changes the cooking state and adds fat and flavour. Condition 1 fails: using fried mushrooms in place of raw button mushrooms would alter the cooking method, since the recipe would call for raw mushrooms that are then cooked by the recipe, and the fried product has already been cooked. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the added oil, browned appearance, altered texture and seasoning differences compared with plain mushrooms. Per guideline F, raw versus cooked is a different state and is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fish cakes, a formed and usually fried or steamed product made mainly from minced or pureed fish, often with starch or flour binders and seasonings. The USDA match is rice cake, which is a rice-based product (puffed rice cake or Korean-style rice cake). These are not the same food under different names. Substituting rice cake would change the main ingredient, which alters taste, texture and appearance: a fish cake has a fish flavour and a dense, springy or patty-like texture, while a rice cake is starchy and bland or chewy. A diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails because the preparation and composition would change, and condition 2 fails because taste and texture would differ. The quantity is ignored.

The ingredient is nonfat chocolate milk, and the USDA entry is Chocolate milk, fat free (skim), which is the same food. The ingredient itself specifies nonfat, so the fat-free entry matches the requested version rather than being an unwanted modification (guideline D). The quantity (95g) is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the milk can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is a liquid used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

Tartar sauce is a mayonnaise-based condiment with chopped pickles or relish and capers, giving it a creamy, tangy, herbal flavour and a pale, opaque, speckled appearance. USDA 'Seafood sauce' is a different product, typically a cocktail-style sauce built on ketchup or chili with horseradish, and it has a red-orange colour and a different flavour profile. Condition 1 fails: it is a different sauce, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the change in flavour (sweet-tomato-horseradish versus creamy-pickle) and in appearance (red versus pale). Guideline F's principle that a different product with a different flavour is not substitutable applies here.

The ingredient is low-fat soy flour, and the USDA entry is 'Soy flour, low-fat', which is the same product under nearly identical naming. The ingredient itself asks for the low-fat version, so the matching low-fat entry is correct (guideline D). The quantity (250g) is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the flour can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: the same product gives the same taste, texture and appearance, so a diner would notice no difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain teriyaki sauce, and the USDA entry is 'Sauce, teriyaki, ready-to-serve', which is the same product under a standard descriptor. The leading 75g is quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: teriyaki sauce can be used directly in place of the ready-to-serve teriyaki sauce, with no change in cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since both are the same ready-made teriyaki sauce. Both conditions are met.

The quantity (2g) is ignored per guideline A. The ingredient is plain hubbard squash, which is a raw vegetable used as an ingredient in a recipe. The USDA match is 'Squash, winter, hubbard, baked, with salt', which is a cooked product with added salt. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. The match also adds salt, which is a modification from the plain ingredient (guideline D). Substituting baked, salted squash would change how the dish is prepared, since the squash would not be raw and would arrive already seasoned, and a diner could notice the difference in texture and flavour. Condition 1 fails, and so does condition 2.

The ingredient is hoisin sauce, a thick, sweet-savory Chinese condiment made from fermented soybeans, sugar, garlic, vinegar and spices, used here as a glaze. The USDA match is 'Chicken with mole sauce', which is a prepared dish of chicken in a Mexican chili-and-chocolate sauce. Condition 1: Hoisin is a standalone sauce used for glazing; substituting a dish that already contains chicken and a mole sauce would change the preparation (you would be glazing with a pre-cooked chicken dish rather than a sauce) and the component being applied. Condition 2: A diner would clearly notice the difference: mole is chili-, cocoa/chocolate- and spice-based with a dark, earthy profile, while hoisin is sweet, soy-fermented and garlicky with a glossy, sticky glaze. The flavour, texture and appearance all differ, and the match is a different food rather than the same food under another name. Both conditions fail, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is raw casaba melon (Cucumis melo, inodorus group), cubed. Cubing is knife work and does not change the match, so the question is whether 'Winter melon, cooked' is the same food. It is not. Winter melon (Benincasa hispida) is a different species, usually sold as a gourd-like vegetable, and this entry is cooked. Condition 1 fails: using cooked winter melon in place of raw casaba changes the preparation, since the dish would need cooked rather than fresh fruit. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (soft and cooked versus crisp and juicy), flavour (mild and watery versus sweet and musky), and appearance. Guideline F also rules out a raw-versus-cooked state difference and a different variety. The match is not substitutable.

Bacalao is the Spanish/Portuguese name for salt cod, meaning Atlantic cod that has been dried and salted. The USDA entry 'Fish, cod, Atlantic, dried and salted' describes the same product under a standard name, so it is the same food rather than a different cut or processed derivative. Condition 1: it can be used in place of bacalao without changing preparation, since the same soaking and desalting steps apply to both. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is honey mustard, a condiment made from mustard seed or prepared mustard blended with honey, giving a sweet-tangy yellow sauce. The USDA match is 'Honey butter', a spread made from butter blended with honey. These are different foods: honey mustard's defining component is mustard (pungent, sharp, vinegar-based flavor), while honey butter has a dairy fat base with no mustard. Condition 1: substituting honey butter for honey mustard would change the dish's flavour profile and would alter the sauce or glaze's base (dairy fat versus vinegar/mustard emulsion), so the preparation outcome changes. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the absence of the sharp mustard tang and the creamy, buttery mouthfeel versus a tangy, pourable condiment. Neither condition is met, and the entries are not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). The entry is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 300g ground elk, which is raw ground elk meat. The USDA entry is 'Elk, free range, ground, raw (Shoshone Bannock)', which is also raw ground elk. The leading weight is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the same raw ground meat can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to cooking method. Condition 2: 'free range' describes how the animal was raised and the parenthetical names a producer. Neither changes the taste, texture, or appearance of the ground meat in a way a diner would notice, and it is not a different cut, a blend, or a processed or cooked state. Per guideline G, a branded or sourced entry of the same plain product counts. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked herring. The USDA entry is Atlantic herring, kippered. Kippering is a traditional curing method (split, salted, then smoked), so kippered herring is a smoked herring. It is the same fish and the same smoked product under a more specific culinary name, which guideline B treats as a match. Its state (smoked, ready to eat) matches the ingredient, so it does not fall under the 'plain vs smoked' exclusion in F. Substituting it would not change how the dish is prepared. A diner would not reasonably notice a difference, since kippered herring is one of the common forms of smoked herring. The entry is substitutable.

The ingredient is medjool date paste, a smooth, pureed product. The USDA entry is whole medjool dates, the fruit as sold. Condition 1: using whole dates in place of paste would change preparation, because the dates would need to be pitted and blended or mashed before they could do what the paste does. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice. Paste gives a smooth, uniform texture and appearance, while whole dates are chunky, fibrous and visibly pieces of fruit. Guideline F treats a processed form differing in state from the whole source as not substitutable. The fruit is the same, but the product and its state differ, so the match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is bacon grease, the rendered fat left after cooking bacon. The USDA entry is cooked bacon meat, reduced sodium, which is the solid meat product, not the fat. Under guideline F, a single fat is not the same as the source meat or processed product. The entry is also a modified version (reduced sodium) with no basis in the ingredient, which guideline D treats as a mismatch. Using cooked bacon meat in place of 100g of bacon grease would change the ddish's fat content, texture, and flavour: the diner would get solid pieces where the recipe calls for liquid fat, and the grease would not coat or cook the food the same way. Conditions 1 and 2 both fail.

Pig's ears are the ears of a pig, which is exactly what 'Pork, ears' describes. It is the same food under a different name, so guideline B applies. The quantity (400g) is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry names only the food with no processing or cooking state, so it is the generic food and matches the plain ingredient (guideline E). Condition 1: the match can replace pig's ears without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference, since it is the same cut of the same animal part. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is crisp rice cereal, a ready-to-eat puffed rice product (the Rice Krispies type). The USDA entry is 'Cereals ready-to-eat, RALSTON CRISP RICE', a branded crisp rice cereal of the same product type. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is used as sold, with no cooking method change. Condition 2: it is the same kind of puffed rice cereal, so taste, texture and appearance should be essentially indistinguishable to a diner. The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is bottled Russian dressing, and the USDA entry is simply 'Russian dressing', which is the same product under the same name. The leading '250g' is only a quantity and is ignored. 'Bottled' describes how the product is normally sold, not a modification. Condition 1: the match can directly replace the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same dressing. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried turnip flakes, a dehydrated product. The USDA match is 'Turnip, raw', which is fresh, uncooked turnip. Guideline F explicitly lists a different state (fresh vs dried, raw vs processed) as not substitutable. Dried flakes have lost most of their water, so the same weight carries far more concentrated material, and they must be rehydrated or cooked before use. Using fresh raw turnip would change how the dish is prepared (it would need chopping, cooking or soaking, and different liquid and timing) and would change its texture and bulk. The 305g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 fails because the preparation changes, and condition 2 likely fails because the texture and appearance would differ. Not substitutable.

Hard bean curd is a common name for firm tofu, so 'Tofu, hard' is the same food under a culinary name (guideline B). The USDA descriptor 'prepared with nigari' names the coagulant used to make hard tofu, which is the normal way this product is made and sold, not a modified version (guideline D). The quantity is irrelevant (guideline A). Hard tofu prepared with nigari has the same firm texture, pale appearance and mild taste a diner would expect from hard bean curd, and it can be used in the same preparation without changing the cooking method. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain skim milk, a liquid dairy product. The USDA match is Cheese, ricotta, part skim milk, which is a solid-to-semi-solid cheese made from whey and milk. Condition 1 fails: substituting ricotta for skim milk changes the preparation. Liquid milk cannot be used as ricotta, and ricotta cannot be poured or measured as a liquid in the same way, so the cooking method would change. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in taste, texture (creamy and grainy versus thin and liquid), and appearance. This is a different food, not a name variant of the same food, and no guideline makes cheese equivalent to milk.

The ingredient is fresh lemongrass. The USDA entry 'Lemon grass (citronella), raw' is the same plant under a common alternate name (citronella is the widely used synonym for lemongrass). Its state is raw, which matches fresh. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is used the same way (bruised, sliced, or minced). Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chow mein noodles used as an optional garnish, which in most recipes means the crispy fried noodles sold in cans or bags. The USDA entry 'Noodles, chow mein' names the same product under the same name, so it is the same food rather than a different one (guideline B). Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is a ready-to-use garnish that is added without cooking. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same kind of product. The quantity (30g) and the 'optional' label do not affect the match (guideline A). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh ricotta cheese (the weight is irrelevant). The USDA entry 'Cheese, Ricotta' is the same food under its standard name, with no stated modification such as reduced fat, low sodium, or added flavour. Ricotta is a fresh cheese, and the USDA entry does not specify a dried or processed state, so it matches the plain fresh product. Substituting it would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 125g of strip steak, cut into strips, which is raw, uncooked beef steak. The cut-into-strips handling does not change the food. The USDA match is 'Beef, cured, breakfast strips, cooked', a cured, cooked, bacon-style product. Condition 1 fails: it cannot replace raw steak strips without changing the cooking method, since steak strips would be cooked in a different way and the dish would not be prepared the same. Condition 2 also fails: the diner would taste the curing, smoky salty flavour, and would see a different texture and appearance. It is a different food (a cured product, not a steak cut), so the same-food exception does not apply.

The ingredient is banana powder. The USDA entry is 'Bananas, dehydrated, or banana powder', which names banana powder explicitly as the same product. Condition 1: the entry is the same food in the same form, so it can replace the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. The quantity (500g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions hold.

1. Identity: The ingredient is sirloin steak, beef. The USDA entry is 'Beef, steak, sirloin', which is the same cut. The leading '100g' is quantity and is ignored (guideline A).
2. Modifiers: The ingredient names no fat trim, cooking state, or processing. 'NS as to fat eaten' is a generic fat-content descriptor, the default for sirloin steak, so it is not a modified version (guideline D).
3. Cooking state: 'As eaten' entries describe meat as it is consumed, which is the typical nutritional representation for steak used in a recipe. The ingredient is a plain steak that the recipe cooks, so the entry represents the same food the diner eats.
4. Conditions: The same cut of beef can be used without changing preparation. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the food is the same sirloin steak.
5. Both conditions are met.

1) The ingredient is a specific cut, roasted duck breast (skinless). The USDA entry is 'Duck, domesticated, meat only, cooked, roasted', which covers meat from the whole bird, including dark leg and thigh meat, not breast alone. 2) Guideline F says a different cut of meat is not substitutable. Duck breast is mostly light meat with a firmer, leaner texture and a milder flavour, while whole-bird meat includes darker, richer, more fibrous leg meat. A diner could notice the difference in texture, flavour and appearance (colour). 3) Both are cooked and roasted and both are skinless, so the preparation state matches, but the cut does not. The condition on taste, texture and appearance fails.

The ingredient is dried adzuki beans that have been soaked, so they are uncooked dried legumes as bought. The USDA entry is cooked, boiled beans with added salt. Guideline F rejects a difference in state (raw vs cooked), and guideline C says the dried-legume match is the 'mature seeds, raw' entry, not a cooked one. Using pre-cooked, salted beans would change the cooking method: the recipe calls for soaked dried beans that still need to be cooked, while the match is already cooked. It would also add salt flavour and a softer, cooked texture that a diner could notice. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 likely fails too, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is crisphead lettuce, which is the same food as iceberg lettuce. The USDA entry 'Lettuce, iceberg (includes crisphead types), raw' explicitly names crisphead types as included. The weight prefix is irrelevant. Both are raw, so the preparation is unchanged. Iceberg lettuce is the standard crisphead variety, so a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Natto is fermented whole soybeans with a sticky texture, strong aroma, and distinctive umami flavour. Bean sprouts, raw are germinated mung bean sprouts: crisp, watery, and mild. They are a different food, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails because bean sprouts cannot replace natto without changing the dish's preparation (natto is eaten as is or stirred with condiments, and sprouts would need different handling). Condition 2 fails because a diner would clearly notice the difference in texture (sticky vs crisp), flavour (fermented vs mild), and appearance. Quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is cod, a white-fleshed whitefish with a mild, flaky texture. The USDA match is Pacific and jack mackerel, raw, a fatty, oily, dark-fleshed fish with a strong flavour. It is a different species and a different fish family, not a regional or trade name for cod, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: cod and mackerel call for different cooking methods and seasonings, and substituting one for the other would change how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would readily notice the stronger, oilier taste, darker flesh and different texture. The weight (225g) is ignored per guideline A. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is chicken feet, optional, 200g; the quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA match is 'Chicken feet', which names the same food with no added state, preparation or modification. Chicken feet are a raw/generic poultry part and the entry names only the food, so it matches the plain default version (guidelines B and D). Condition 1: the match can be used in the same dish without changing preparation, since the ingredient is simply chicken feet. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is wild hog, which is the same animal as wild boar. The USDA entry 'Game meat, boar, wild, raw' is the raw wild boar meat, so it is the same food under a regional name (guideline B). The weight '170g' is ignored (guideline A). The ingredient gives no cut, and the entry is generic wild boar meat, which can stand in for wild hog without changing the cooking method. The entry is raw, which matches fresh raw wild hog. Condition 1 is met: it can be used in place of the ingredient without changing the preparation. Condition 2 is met: a diner would not notice a difference, since it is the same meat. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is plain trout fillets, which are raw fish in the standard sense. The USDA match is trout that has been baked or broiled and coated, meaning it is cooked and has a breaded or battered coating. Condition 1 fails: using a pre-cooked, coated product changes the cooking method, since the fillets would not be prepared in the dish as raw fish. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the coating, the cooked texture, and the altered appearance and flavour. The match is a different state (cooked and coated versus raw), which guideline F treats as not substitutable. Guideline A says the 100g quantity is irrelevant.

The ingredient is oyster mushrooms, weight 75g (quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry 'Mushrooms, oyster, raw' is literally the same food, raw and uncooked, with no added components or processing. Condition 1: the raw oyster mushroom can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since the recipe handling (slicing, sautéing, etc.) does not change the match. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same species in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is rice wine (Chinese huangjiu/Shaoxing-style or Japanese mirin/sake-type cooking wine), an alcoholic fermented beverage used as a cooking liquid that adds acidity, aroma and savoury depth. The USDA match is 'Rice milk', a non-alcoholic dairy-alternative beverage made from rice, with a sweet, mild, milky flavour. Condition 1: rice milk could be poured into a dish in place of rice wine, but it does not behave the same way in cooking. It lacks alcohol and acidity, so marinades, deglazing and braising would be prepared differently and the liquid would not reduce or tenderise the same way; with rice milk, a dairy-like liquid, it could curdle in acidic or high-heat applications. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference, since the dish would taste creamy and sweet rather than wine-savoury and aromatic, and the appearance and texture could change. This is a different food product, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is dried peach halves, which is the same food as dried peaches. Halving is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). USDA's 'Peaches, dehydrated (low-moisture), sulfured, uncooked' is the dried peach product as normally sold; sulfuring is the standard treatment for dried peaches, so it is not a modification (guideline D). The dish would not be prepared differently, and a diner would not taste or see a difference between dried peach halves and this entry. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked herring fillets, used as a garnish. The USDA match is Atlantic herring, pickled. Condition 1: Pickled herring is cured in a vinegar brine, not smoked, so swapping it in would change the preparation and the processing state. Guideline F treats smoked versus plain or processed states as different foods. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference. Pickled herring is sharp and acidic, with a softer, moister texture and a different appearance, while smoked fillets have a smoky flavour and a firmer, flaky texture. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

Tallow is rendered beef or mutton fat, while lard is rendered pork fat. Under guideline F, a different fat is not substitutable. Swapping them changes flavour, since beef tallow has a distinct beefy taste and pork lard a different one. It also changes texture and performance in cooking, such as crispness, mouthfeel and how the fat sets when chilled. The weight is decoration under guideline A and does not affect the answer. Condition 2 fails because a diner could notice the difference in flavour and texture.

The ingredient is a plain processed cheddar cheese, which is the standard default product. The USDA entry is the same product type (pasteurized process cheddar or American), but it is specified as low sodium. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced/low sodium version is a modification, not a match. The ingredient does not ask for low sodium, so the modified entry does not qualify. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the cheese could be swapped in the same preparation. Condition 2 fails: sodium reduction changes saltiness and flavour, and a diner would likely notice a blander, less salty cheese. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain ground pork (quantity ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry 'Pork, ground' is the same food under the same name, with no cooking state, seasoning, or modification indicated. Ground pork is commonly sold raw, and the USDA entry with no state descriptor is the generic food. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is lean ground beef (cattle). The USDA match is ground bison, which is a different animal species, not the same food under another name. Guideline B covers regional or trade names for the same food, and that does not apply here. Bison has a distinctly different flavour (often described as sweeter and more gamey), a different fat profile and a slightly different texture. A diner would likely notice the difference, and the dish's flavour would change. Guideline F rejects different cuts of meat and different products that look close, and a different species is a stronger case of the same principle. The 'raw' and 'ground' descriptors match the ingredient's state, but they do not resolve the species difference. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is pickled flounder fillets, a fish preserved by curing in vinegar or brine, usually with added spices, salt, and sugar. The USDA entry 'Fish, flounder, NFS' is the generic, unprocessed fish with no pickling. Condition 1: substituting plain flounder would change the preparation, since the pickling step (curing and marinating) is absent. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Pickled fish has a firmer, cured texture, a sharp acidic and seasoned flavour, and a different appearance from plain fish. Guideline F says a raw or plain item is not substitutable for a processed one, and a modified preparation changes flavour and texture. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is cracked wheat, a raw grain product (crushed wheat kernels) used in cooking, such as in pilafs, salads, or porridge. The USDA entry 'Bread, cracked-wheat' is a baked bread product. It is not the same food under another name, and it is not the raw grain. Substituting bread would change how the dish is prepared (the grain must be cooked or soaked, while bread is already baked) and would change its texture, appearance, and flavour. A diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails as well. Per the guidelines, a processed or different-state product is not a match for the raw source.

The ingredient is chicken rib, with no preparation or state specified, so it defaults to raw chicken ribs. The USDA entry 'Chicken, neck or ribs' explicitly names ribs as one of its included cuts, so it is the same food under the same name (guideline B). The weight is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are raw chicken pieces for the same cooking methods. Condition 2: the entry covers ribs directly, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The entry also includes neck, which is a different cut, but that does not make the ribs themselves a different food. The match is acceptable.

The ingredient is cooked mung beans, and the USDA entry is 'Mung beans, cooked'. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A. The food is literally the same (mung beans), and the state matches (cooked, not raw or dried). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since no cooking step or handling differs. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the food and its cooked state are identical. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried goji berries, and the USDA entry is 'Goji berries, dried', which is the same food in the same state. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same dried product used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the product is identical. The quantity (300g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sweetened flaked coconut, which is dried coconut meat with added sugar. The USDA entry is dried coconut meat that is sweetened, in a shredded/desiccated cut. Both are the same food: sweetened, dried coconut meat. The difference is cut size and form, which guideline B and C treat as the same food in a different cut, since knife work or cut form does not change the match. Flaked and shredded/desiccated sweetened coconut are routinely interchanged in baking and as toppings without changing the preparation. The fine desiccated texture may be slightly different from larger flakes, but it is the same product type and the same sweetened dried state, so the match is acceptable under the guidelines. Condition 1 is met because it can replace the ingredient without changing method. Condition 2 is met because the taste and general texture of sweetened dried coconut are the same, and the cut difference is minor enough that a diner would not reasonably identify a different food.

1) The ingredient is yellow fine corn flour, which is the same product as USDA's 'Flour, corn, yellow, fine meal'. The 375g quantity is ignored per guideline A. 2) Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient in any recipe with no change in preparation, since both are finely ground yellow corn. 3) Condition 2: 'enriched' means B vitamins and iron were added. This does not change taste, texture, colour or appearance, so a diner would not notice. 4) Enrichment is a nutrient addition rather than a flavour, texture or processing change, and enriched corn flour is a standard retail form. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is honey mustard dressing, a plain product type, and the USDA entry is 'Salad dressing, honey mustard, regular', which is the same food under a standard name. The quantity prefix (250g) is decoration and is ignored. 'Regular' is the default version rather than a reduced-fat, light, or flavoured modification, so guideline D does not reject it. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation, since it is used as a dressing or condiment in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product type. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is turkey bologna, a processed, emulsified, cured luncheon meat, frozen and then thawed. The USDA match 'Turkey, canned' is canned turkey meat, a different product. Using it would change the texture from a sliceable, smooth, seasoned bologna to canned turkey's firmer, shredded or chunky meat, and would change the flavour, since bologna carries curing salts, spices and smoke notes. The two are not the same food under another name, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 1 (same preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture or appearance) both fail. The frozen/thawed status does not change this, because the match is a different product rather than the same food in another state.

The ingredient is extra firm tofu: a pressed, water-packed curd that holds its shape when cubed and can be pan-fried, baked or stir-fried. The USDA entry is silken tofu, extra firm. Silken tofu is made by a different process, is smooth and custard-like, and is much more delicate even in its firm version. Condition 1: cubed silken tofu would not hold its shape or take the same cooking methods (pan-frying, baking, stir-frying) without falling apart, so the preparation would change. Condition 2: a diner would notice the much softer, smoother, more custardy texture and the different appearance. It is the same soy food family but not the same product, and the guideline F-style differences in processing and texture rule it out. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is octopus, chopped (a seafood/mollusk). The USDA match is 'Oil, olive, salad or cooking', which is a plant-derived fat. Condition 1: octopus cannot be replaced by olive oil without changing the dish's preparation; it is a different food entirely, not the same food under another name, and the chopping is handling that does not change the identity. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance between octopus and olive oil. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain 'liqueur' with no flavour or type specified, and the USDA entry 'Liqueur' is the generic food with no added modifier. Under guideline B, the same food under the same name matches. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to the standard default version is substitutable. Guideline A means the 200g quantity is ignored. Condition 1 holds: the liqueur can be added in place of the USDA liqueur without changing the preparation method. Condition 2 is met on the information given, since the recipe does not name a specific liqueur, so no specific flavour difference can be identified. The annotator should note that a diner could notice a different liqueur type (e.g., coffee vs orange) if the actual product differs, but the ingredient as written is generic, so the match is acceptable.

The ingredient is fried chicken drumstick meat, which has been pulled (shredded by hand). The USDA entry is cooked, fried chicken leg meat from broilers or fryers, meat only, so the food is the same: fried chicken drumstick meat. Pulling is handling that the recipe itself does, and guideline C says such handling does not change the match. The ingredient does not mention skin, so the 'meat only' descriptor is consistent with it. Condition 1: the entry can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since the fried state is identical and the pulling is done by the cook. Condition 2: a diner would not taste or see a difference, because the meat is the same fried drumstick meat, shredded either way. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked mackerel, a fish that has been smoked, which gives it a distinct smoky flavour, a firmer and drier texture, and a characteristic golden-brown appearance. The USDA match is 'Fish, mackerel, salted', which is mackerel preserved by salting, typically with a firm, salty, cured texture and no smoke flavour. Guideline F lists 'plain vs toasted/smoked/roasted' as a different state that is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because salted mackerel would change how the dish is prepared: it usually needs soaking or desalting and would not be used as a direct swap for flaked smoked fish. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would taste the lack of smoke and the salty, cured flavour, and would notice a different texture and appearance. The quantity (400g) is irrelevant.

The ingredient is self-rising flour, a standard product made from soft white wheat flour with leavening (baking powder) and salt added. The USDA entry 'Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, self-rising, enriched' names the same product with the same components, and the 'enriched' descriptor is how this flour is normally sold. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the same recipe without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is wild duck, a 400g quantity (ignored per guideline A), with skin explicitly optional. The USDA entry is wild duck meat and skin, raw, which is the same food, the same species and the same raw state, so guideline B applies. Skin is a component the ingredient permits, so a recipe using skin-on duck still matches what the ingredient specifies. Condition 1 holds: the entry can replace the ingredient without changing the cooking method, since the recipe already allows skin. Condition 2 holds: the diner eats wild duck either way, and the skin is an intended option rather than a different food. The only difference is whether skin is present, which the ingredient itself leaves open. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sliced turkey breast, prepackaged (deli-style sliced turkey breast, 130g; weight is ignored). The USDA entry is 'Turkey breast, sliced, prepackaged', which names the same food, the same cut (turkey breast), the same form (sliced), and the same packaging (prepackaged). Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is the same product in the same form. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same sliced turkey breast product. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is pork ear, a specific cut of pork offcut that is typically sold raw and is used in dishes where its gelatinous, cartilaginous texture is central. The USDA match is 'Pulled pork in barbecue sauce', a cooked, shredded pork shoulder product already combined with sweet tomato-based barbecue sauce. Condition 1 fails: pork ear cannot be substituted without changing preparation, since the recipe would need to handle a raw cut with a distinct texture, whereas the match is a fully cooked, sauced product. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would readily notice the difference in texture (crisp or gelatinous cartilage versus shredded soft meat), appearance (skin and cartilage structure versus shredded strands) and flavour (smoky sweet sauce versus plain pork). Guideline F also applies, since this is a different cut and a different state (raw versus cooked, plain versus sauced). The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is carambola (star fruit), a fresh tropical fruit with a crisp texture, sweet-tart flavour and distinctive star-shaped cross-section. The USDA match is Ostrich, tenderloin, raw, which is a red meat cut from an bird. This is not the same food under another name, and it is not a cut or variant of the same food. Condition 1 fails: an ostrich tenderloin cannot be used in place of star fruit without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is meat requiring cooking rather than a fruit eaten fresh or used in fruit preparations. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'condensed milk' with the quantity (200g) ignored per guideline A. Under the plain name, a shopper buys sweetened condensed milk, the standard default product, so the 'sweetened' descriptor reflects how the product is normally sold rather than a modification (guideline D). The USDA entry 'Milk, condensed, sweetened' is therefore the same food under its standard name. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

Soybean curd is the same food as tofu, a regional or culinary name for it. The USDA entry is named identically, with no added state, flavour, or modification such as reduced fat, sweetening, or a different coagulant described. Under guideline B, the same food under another name is substitutable. The quantity (100g) is decoration and is ignored under guideline A. Using the same food in the same preparation would not alter the cooking method, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is refried pinto beans. The USDA entry is refried red beans (canned), which in this context means a different bean variety, typically red kidney-type beans, not pinto. Pinto and red beans are sibling varieties with different flavour, texture and colour (refried pinto is a pale brownish-pink, while refried red beans are darker red). Guideline F rejects sibling varieties with a different taste, so the first condition (no change in dish) may be met in terms of preparation, but the second fails: a diner would likely notice the difference in flavour and appearance. The 85g quantity is ignored. Not the same food under another name, so not substitutable.

The ingredient is a mixture of two different foods, mullet and shrimp, both cooked. The USDA match covers only one of them, striped mullet cooked with dry heat, and contains no shrimp. Under guideline F, a single ingredient does not substitute for a blend or product containing it. Shrimp is also a different food from fish, with a different texture and flavour, so a diner would notice the difference. The quantity (265g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 fails because the dish's composition would change, and condition 2 fails because a diner would notice missing shrimp.

The ingredient is fresh (raw) swordfish, which the cook will prepare in the recipe. The USDA entry is swordfish that is already cooked by dry heat. Under guideline F, raw vs cooked is a different state, so the match fails. Substituting pre-cooked fish would change the cooking method (the dish would need no cooking or a different one), and a diner would notice differences in texture, moisture, and appearance. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 also fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is bread and butter pickles, a sweet-sour cucumber pickle preserved in a vinegar, sugar and spice brine, typically with sliced cucumbers and onions. The USDA entry is pickle and pimiento loaf, pork, a processed luncheon meat loaf made from pork and ground pork with chopped pickles and pimientos. Condition 1 fails: the match is a processed meat product, not a pickle, so it cannot be substituted for pickles without changing the dish's composition and preparation. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the presence of meat, a different texture, and a different flavour profile. The entry only shares the word 'pickle' and is not the same food under another name, so neither condition is met.

The ingredient is store-bought marinara, a ready-made tomato-based pasta sauce. The USDA entry 'Sauce, pasta, spaghetti/marinara, ready-to-serve' names the same product type, sold ready to use. Condition 1: it can replace the marinara directly, since it is a ready-to-serve jar or can of the same sauce, so no cooking method changes. The quantity (20g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2: the USDA entry describes the standard commercial marinara, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. The 'ready-to-serve' descriptor matches how marinara is normally bought, so it is not a modification (guideline D). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain smoked turkey. The USDA entry is smoked turkey breast with added lemon pepper flavour and a 97% fat-free modification. Guideline D treats flavoured and fat-reduced versions of a plain ingredient as modifications, so they do not match the standard default. The lemon pepper seasoning would change the flavour, and the fat-free leaner composition would change texture and mouthfeel compared with standard smoked turkey. A diner would likely notice the lemon pepper taste. The quantity (5g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is cornbread crumbs, which are baked cornbread that has been dried or toasted and broken into crumbs.
