The USDA entry is a dry mix: an unbaked powder of cornmeal, flour, leavening, sugar and similar, meant to be reconstituted and baked. Condition 1 fails: substituting the dry mix would change preparation. It is uncooked and would need to be baked or otherwise cooked, unlike the ready-to-use crumbs, so the cooking method changes. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice a difference in texture and taste, since raw or unbaked mix would be gritty, floury and dense rather than crisp or toasted. Under guideline F, a different state (unbaked mix vs baked, dried product) is not a match, so the answer is no.

The ingredient is 'pita chips' and the USDA entry is 'Pita chips'. They name the same product. The leading '200g' is only a quantity and is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the USDA pita chips can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since no cooking method is implied. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met, so the match is substitutable.

The ingredient is plain fruit yogurt. The USDA entry is 'Yogurt, fruit, low fat', which is the same product type. Under guideline D, fruit yogurts are normally sold as low fat, so the 'low fat' descriptor reflects how the product is typically bought rather than a modification. The '11g protein/8 oz' suffix is a product-label descriptor of the same yogurt type, not a change in composition that would be noticed. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient in the same preparation, since yogurt is used as-is and the handling does not change. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same fruit yogurt sold under the standard low-fat profile. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient 'pasta rings with spinach filling' describes spinach-filled tortellini, which are ring-shaped stuffed pasta. The USDA entry 'Tortellini, spinach-filled, no sauce' names the same product with the same components (pasta shell plus spinach filling), so it is the same food under a different name (guideline B). The 'no sauce' descriptor matches a plain ingredient with no sauce mentioned, so it is not a modification (guideline D). Condition 1: the entry can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same stuffed pasta. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain cream cheese (320g, quantity ignored). The USDA match is 'Puffs, fried, crab meat and cream cheese filled', which is a fried snack food containing crab meat and cream cheese as a filling, not cream cheese itself. Condition 1: cream cheese cannot be substituted for this product without changing preparation; the entry is a fried, pre-made appetizer that contains other components, and using it in place of plain cream cheese would require the dish to be a different fried item rather than a cream cheese ingredient. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice a difference in taste, texture and appearance, since the fried crispy shell and crab meat flavour are absent in plain cream cheese. Per guideline F, a single ingredient versus a product containing it is not substitutable. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is plain puffed rice cereal used as a topping. The USDA entry is QUAKER Puffed Rice, a branded plain puffed rice ready-to-eat cereal. Under guideline G, a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. Condition 1: it can be used as the topping without changing preparation, since both are dry, ready-to-eat puffed rice. Condition 2: it has no added flavour or modification, so taste, texture and appearance match the generic product. The 160g weight is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain bread crumbs, a dry, crisp, usually unsweetened product used for coating, binding, or topping. The USDA entry is coffee cake, crumb or quick-bread type, a sweet, moist, baked cake with added sugar, fat, and often spices or fruit. Condition 1 fails: coffee cake cannot be used in place of bread crumbs without changing preparation, since it would need to be crumbled or dried, and it would not coat or bind the way crumbs do. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the sweetness, moist cake texture, and altered appearance. The quantity is ignored under guideline A. This is a different food, not a regional name or a standard variant of the same product (guideline B), so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is ground chicken, a minced meat typically made from chicken breast and/or thigh. The USDA entry is 'Chicken, stewing, meat only, raw', which describes meat from mature stewing hens. Condition 1: Ground chicken is a ground product, while stewing chicken is a whole-cut meat from older birds. Using it in place of ground chicken would require mincing it, and the result would not be a ground-meat equivalent, so the preparation would change. Guideline F rejects a different cut or type of meat, and guideline C's 'ground at home' allowance only applies when the USDA entry is the same food. Condition 2: Stewing hen meat is tougher, darker and more strongly flavoured than typical ground chicken. A diner would likely notice the difference in taste and texture in a patty, meatball or sauce. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is raw pork spleen. The USDA entry is 'Pork, fresh, variety meats and by-products, spleen, raw', which is the same food with the same state (raw, fresh) and the same cut (spleen). The '250g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the spleen could replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same raw food and the USDA descriptors only describe its category. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same organ meat in the same raw state. Both conditions are met, so it is substitutable.

1. Ignoring the 10g quantity, the ingredient is salted, toasted sesame seeds. The USDA entry is toasted sesame seed kernels with salt added, so salt and toasting both match. 2. The USDA entry adds 'decorticated', meaning hulled. The ingredient does not specify hulled or unhulled seeds, so the plain default is not clearly hulled. Per guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified or processed version is not substitutable. 3. Hulled (decorticated) kernels are visibly paler and ivory, while unhulled toasted seeds are darker tan or brown. Texture and flavour also differ slightly, so a diner could notice the difference in appearance. 4. Because the ingredient does not call for decortication and the match changes appearance, the two conditions are not clearly met.

The ingredient is amaranth seed, and the USDA entry is amaranth grain, uncooked. Amaranth seed is the grain as bought, so this is the same food under a different name (guideline B). The USDA entry is raw/uncooked, which matches a recipe ingredient that is used uncooked or cooked by the recipe itself (guideline C). Condition 1: the grain can replace the seed without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same raw grain. Both conditions are met.

1. Identity: The ingredient is explicitly cuttlefish (Japanese cuttlefish, 'ika'). The USDA entry is cuttlefish, mixed species, raw. Japanese cuttlefish is a cuttlefish species, so this is the same food under a regional name (Guideline B). The 'mixed species' wording covers the species sold as cuttlefish, and 'raw' matches an uncooked ingredient. 2. Quantity (40g) is ignored (Guideline A). 3. Preparation: the match is raw, so the dish's cooking method is unchanged, and any knife work or sashimi-style slicing is handled by the recipe (Guideline C). 4. Taste, texture and appearance: cuttlefish species are closely related and similar in flavour and texture, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is purslane that has been boiled and drained with no salt added. The USDA entry is purslane, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt. Condition 1: the USDA entry describes the same food in the same prepared state (boiled and drained, unsalted), so it could replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. The weight (15g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 2: a diner would taste, feel and see the same boiled, drained, unsalted purslane, since 'no salt added' matches 'without salt'. No modification, flavour change or different food is involved. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain Monterey Jack cheese, whose standard default version is full-fat. The USDA match is 'Cheese, monterey, low fat', a modified version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced-fat version is not a match. Low-fat Monterey Jack has less fat, so it melts differently, is drier and firmer, and has a different mouthfeel and flavour. A diner would likely notice the difference in a dish using 485g of cheese. The quantity is ignored, as guideline A requires. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is crumbled soybean curd, which is tofu: a plant-based soy product. The USDA entry is 'Cheese, cottage, dry curd', a dairy product made from milk curds. These are different foods, not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Substituting dry curd cottage cheese would change the flavour from soy to dairy, and a diner would notice a tangy, milky taste and a different mouthfeel. Condition 2 fails even though the crumbled appearance is somewhat similar, and the swap would also alter the dish's taste profile, so condition 1 is not cleanly met either. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is dry beef bouillon powder, which is added directly to a dish and dissolved during cooking. The USDA entry describes a beef broth or bouillon powder that has already been prepared with water, so it is a reconstituted liquid. That is a different state from the dry powder. Condition 1 fails: substituting a prepared liquid for 10g of dry powder changes how the dish is prepared, because the cook would need to account for added water, and 10g of the prepared product carries far less seasoning and solids than 10g of powder. Condition 2 also fails: the added water and much lower concentration of seasoning would change the dish's flavour and possibly its moisture content. The quantity is ignored per guideline A, and the shared product name does not outweigh the difference in state, per guidelines C and F.

The ingredient is canned chicken liver pate. The USDA entry is 'Pate, chicken liver, canned', which is the same food under the same name, with the same product form (canned). Quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A. Canned pate is shelf-stable and served as is, so there is no cooking-method change; it could be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Taste, texture, and appearance are the same because the entry describes the same product. No modification, flavour, cut, or state difference applies. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh goji berries (Lycium barbarum), a specific fruit. The USDA entry 'Berries, frozen' is a generic category, typically mixed frozen berries such as strawberries, blueberries or raspberries. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Condition 1: goji berries are normally eaten fresh or dried, not cooked or baked, so substituting frozen berries would change the dish's preparation and flavour profile. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Goji berries are small, red, and chewy with a distinctive mild, earthy-sweet taste, while frozen mixed berries thaw to soft, juicy fruit of different colour, texture and flavour. Guideline E allows frozen-for-fresh only where the freezing does not show and the food is normally cooked or mixed, which is not the case here. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is colby cheese that was frozen and then thawed. The USDA entry 'Cheese, colby' is the same food in its default form. Guideline E says frozen cheese for cooking matches the standard entry because freezing does not visibly change it in a cooked dish. The quantity (500g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the cheese can be used in place of the thawed colby without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the cheese is the same type and freezing is not visible in the finished dish. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is jarred sofrito, a ready-made version of the same seasoning base (peppers, onions, garlic, herbs, oil). The USDA entry, 'Sauce, sofrito, prepared from recipe', is the generic sofrito entry with the same components. Under guideline C, USDA's standard descriptor does not make it a different food. Under guideline D, jarred sofrito is its normal retail form, so the plain-named default matches. Condition 1: it can be added in the same way, with no change to cooking method. Condition 2: sofrito is a cooked-in flavour base, so a diner would not reasonably notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance from a comparable sofrito. Quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is skinless duck breast, a specific cut. The USDA entry 'Duck, domesticated, meat only, raw' is a generic mix of all duck meat, not breast specifically. 'Meat only' does match the skinless part, so the skin condition is satisfied. However, guideline F states that a different cut of meat is not substitutable. Breast and leg meat differ in texture, fibre, colour and fat distribution, and a breast is typically seared or roasted to medium-rare while leg meat is usually cooked long and slow. Using the mixed-cut entry would therefore change how the dish is prepared (cooking method and doneness) and could change texture and appearance. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 is doubtful for the same reasons. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a turkey frankfurter, which is a turkey hot dog under another name. The USDA entry 'Hot dog, turkey' describes the same product, so this is the same food under a culinary/regional name (guideline B). Condition 1: a turkey hot dog can replace a turkey frankfurter without changing how the dish is prepared, since both are cooked and used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same kind of sausage. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain Greek yogurt, the standard unflavoured product. The USDA entry is 'Yogurt, Greek, low fat milk, flavors other than fruit', which differs in two ways. First, it is flavoured ('flavors other than fruit'), and guideline D treats a plain ingredient replaced by a flavoured version as a modification. Second, it is low fat, while plain Greek yogurt is sold as whole or nonfat, so low fat is a modified fat level. Condition 1 is not clearly met, since the flavouring would change the flavour of the dish, and condition 2 fails because a diner could taste the added flavouring and the different fat content. The product is not the default plain version, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried oregano, a dried herb sold as a whole/ground spice product. The USDA match is a ready-to-serve spaghetti/marinara sauce, which is a tomato-based pasta sauce containing many components (tomatoes, water, sugar, salt, onion, garlic, possibly other herbs and oils). Condition 1: substituting this for dried oregano would fundamentally change the dish; a sauce adds volume, liquid, tomato base, sugar and salt, and cannot serve as a seasoning in place of a dried herb. The preparation would be altered. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance, since the dish would gain a tomato sauce flavour and consistency rather than the herbal note of oregano. Guideline F explicitly rejects dried herbs replaced by other products, and blends or products containing the item rather than a single ingredient. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is plain whey protein powder, a single ingredient. The USDA entry is 'Nutritional powder mix (Isopure)', a branded nutritional product that is a blend and typically contains flavouring, sweeteners and other additives beyond whey protein. Guideline F rejects a single ingredient matched to a blend or product containing it. Guideline G rejects a branded entry with an added flavour or modification. The quantity is ignored, per guideline A. Condition 1 may be met, since the powder could be measured and mixed in the same way. Condition 2 fails: the flavour, sweetness and possibly texture of the blend would differ from plain whey powder, and a diner could notice. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried tarragon, a distinct herb with a pronounced anise-like flavour. The USDA match is dried chervil, a different herb with a milder, parsley-like, subtly anise taste. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Condition 1: chervil could be swapped in mechanically, since both are dried herbs added in the same way, so the preparation would not change. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the flavour difference, because tarragon's characteristic anise note is much stronger than chervil's. Guideline F treats sibling varieties with different taste as not substitutable. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is smoked sturgeon, a specific species (Acipenseridae), skinned. The USDA entry is whitefish, mixed species, smoked, which is a different fish family (Coregonus, such as lake whitefish and cisco) and a mixed-species blend rather than a single species. Guideline F rejects substitution across different species with different taste and texture, and rejects a single ingredient replaced by a blend. Smoked sturgeon has a firm, meaty, rich texture and a distinct flavour that a diner would likely notice compared with mild, flaky smoked whitefish. Smoking and skinning do not bridge this gap, so the match fails both conditions: the dish's flavour and texture would change, and the diner would notice a different fish.

Chapati and roti are the same flatbread under two names, so the USDA entry is the same food (guideline B). The ingredient is plain and the USDA entry is the plain, default version, with no modifier such as sweetened, low-fat or flavoured (guideline D). The weight '65g' is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: a commercially prepared plain roti can replace a homemade chapati in the same dish without changing how it is prepared, since it is served as-is or warmed. Condition 2: the main differences are that commercial versions may be softer, more uniform, and packaged, with possible minor additives. These are small and are the normal variation between homemade and shop-bought versions of the same flatbread, not a different food, so a diner would not reasonably notice a different dish. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is spaghetti sauce with meat, a ready-made tomato-based sauce containing ground meat. The USDA entry is 'Spaghetti sauce with meat', which names the same product with the same components. Quantity (15g) is ignored per guideline A. The match is the same food under the same name, with no cooking method change, no flavour, texture or appearance difference implied, and no modified version (not reduced-fat, low-sodium, or flavoured). Condition 1 is met because it can directly replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2 is met because a diner would not notice a difference, as it is the same product type. Per guideline D and B, this is a plain ingredient mapped to its standard default version.

1. Identity: The ingredient is dungeness crab and the USDA entry is Crustaceans, crab, dungeness, raw. This is the same food, so guideline B applies. 2. State: The ingredient does not specify cooked or raw, so it is a plain ingredient, and guideline D treats the standard default version as the match. The 'raw' descriptor is the plain default, not a modification. 3. Quantity: The 255g weight is ignored per guideline A. 4. Condition 1: The match could replace the ingredient without changing the preparation, since the recipe's own handling determines cooking. 5. Condition 2: Given the unspecified state, a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance attributable to the entry. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is green tea ice cream, a frozen dessert made with cream, milk, sugar, and matcha/green tea flavouring. The USDA match is iced green tea, brewed, unsweetened, a non-dairy, unsweetened beverage. Condition 1: it cannot replace ice cream in preparation; the ingredient is a frozen dairy dessert, while the match is a liquid beverage with no fat, no frozen state, and no creamy structure, so the preparation would change. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in texture (liquid versus creamy frozen), appearance, and sweetness (unsweetened versus sweetened ice cream). Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried cranberries, pureed, which is a dried fruit reduced to a paste. The USDA match is Cranberry sauce, a cooked, wet product made from fresh or frozen berries with water and added sugar. Under condition 1, using the sauce would change the preparation: the dried fruit's concentrated, low-moisture paste would be replaced by a cooked, liquid-based sauce, so the recipe's moisture balance and method would shift. Under condition 2, a diner would likely notice the difference in texture (smooth dried-fruit paste versus jellied or whole-berry sauce), in appearance, and in flavour (dried cranberries are concentrated and often sweetened differently from cooked sauce). The guidelines treat dried versus cooked or processed states as different (guideline F, 'a different state'), and the pureeing does not bridge that gap. Quantity is ignored. Because the dried and cooked states differ and the diner would likely notice, the match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is canned bockwurst, a ready-to-eat, heat-processed sausage. The USDA entry is 'Bockwurst, pork, veal, raw', an uncooked product. Under guideline F, raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: the raw sausage would need cooking before it could replace the canned product, which changes how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 also fails: a raw bockwurst differs in texture, colour and flavour from a cooked, canned one, and a diner would notice. The 150g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is cooked broccoli and cauliflower, and the USDA entry is the same food in the same state: broccoli and cauliflower, cooked. The ingredient names no added fat or seasoning, so the default plain version, 'no added fat', is the standard match (guideline D). The 280g weight is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are already cooked and need no further cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same vegetable mix prepared the same way. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh loganberries used as an optional garnish, which is normally served raw and whole. The USDA match is 'Loganberries, frozen', a different state. Guideline E says frozen matches fresh only when the food is normally cooked or mixed and freezing does not show. A garnish is served uncooked, and thawed frozen loganberries are softer, more watery, and may bleed juice, so the appearance and texture would visibly differ. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would change from serving fresh berries to serving thawed ones. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would notice the softer texture and altered appearance. The quantity (100g) and the 'optional' label do not affect this. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is store-bought almond paste. The USDA entry 'Nuts, almond paste' names the same product under the same name. Guideline B and D treat a plain ingredient matched to its standard default product as the same food. The quantity (200g) is decoration per guideline A. Condition 1: the paste can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is goose liver pate, a specific product made from goose liver with a rich, mild, buttery flavour. The USDA entry is generic 'Pate, liver, not specified, canned', which covers pate made from an unspecified animal liver, most often pork or chicken, and does not name goose. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 is arguably met in that both are spreads served cold from a tin, but the canned generic pate would be a different product. Condition 2 fails: the source animal, and therefore the flavour, colour and mouthfeel, would differ in a way a diner could notice. Guideline F rejects a different source with a different taste profile. The quantity (55g) is irrelevant under guideline A. Conclusion: not substitutable.

The ingredient is chicken salami, a cured, fermented, smoked processed meat product made from chicken. The USDA match is Alcoholic beverage, creme de menthe, 72 proof, a sweet mint-flavoured liqueur. Condition 1: Using creme de menthe in place of chicken salami would completely change how the dish is prepared; salami is sliced or cubed and cooked or served as a cured meat, whereas creme de menthe is a liquid spirit that cannot be used as a meat substitute in the same role. Condition 2: A diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (sweet mint liqueur vs savoury cured meat), texture (liquid vs firm sliced meat), and appearance. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable. No guideline about same-food naming applies, since the two items are entirely different foods.

Step 1: Identity. Filberts are hazelnuts under another name (guideline B), so the food is the same. Step 2: Preparation. The ingredient is 'toasted' and the USDA entry is 'dry roasted', which describes the same process (dry heat roasting without oil). Toasted and dry roasted are the same state, so this is not the plain-vs-roasted mismatch described in guideline F. Step 3: Salt. 'Unsalted' corresponds to 'without salt added', so there is no sodium modification. Step 4: Condition 1 holds, since the match can be used directly without changing preparation. Condition 2 holds, since a diner would not taste or see a difference between toasted filberts and dry-roasted hazelnuts without salt. Quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is turkey kielbasa, a smoked, seasoned sausage made from turkey meat. The USDA match, 'Turkey sandwich on wheat', is a composed sandwich consisting of sliced turkey meat, bread, and typically condiments and vegetables. These are not the same food. Condition 1 fails: the sausage cannot be used in place of a sandwich without changing how the dish is prepared, since it would need to be cooked as a link (grilled, simmered, or browned) rather than served as a bread-based sandwich, and the bread and assembly would be added. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would readily notice the difference in texture, appearance (a link versus a bread-enclosed sandwich), and flavour (smoked, seasoned sausage versus deli turkey on bread). The match is not a regional or trade name for the same product, and it is not a different cut of the same meat; it is a prepared composite dish. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 'frozen buttermilk biscuits' with no stated baked state. Frozen biscuits sold to home cooks are most commonly unbaked dough that is baked before serving. The USDA entry is 'Biscuits, plain or buttermilk, frozen, baked', which is a fully cooked product. Condition 1: swapping a frozen raw-dough biscuit for a pre-baked one changes the preparation, since the dough would no longer be baked in the recipe. Guideline F treats raw versus cooked as a different state, not a substitute. Condition 2: the texture, rise, and browning of a baked biscuit differ from those of a biscuit baked from frozen dough, so a diner could notice. The match is also not clearly the same product, because the ingredient does not specify a baked product. Both conditions are not reliably met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain lima beans, drained. The USDA entry is a mixed product, 'Lima beans and corn, cooked, no added fat', so it contains corn as well as lima beans. Under guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend containing it is not substitutable. The corn kernels would also be visible and change the dish's appearance and taste, so both conditions fail. The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is 500g of alfalfa sprouts that are rinsed and drained. The USDA entry is 'Alfalfa sprouts, raw', which is the same food in its uncooked state. Per guideline A the quantity is ignored, and per guideline C rinsing and draining are handling steps that do not change the match. Condition 1: the sprouts could be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since the recipe already treats them as raw and rinsed. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same raw sprout.

The ingredient is 300g lactose-free milk, a liquid dairy milk with lactose removed. The USDA match is Glutino Gluten Free Wafers, Milk Chocolate, a branded chocolate-covered wafer biscuit. Condition 1: milk cannot be substituted by a wafer cookie. Milk is a liquid used for liquid volume, emulsification, and moisture; a solid chocolate wafer would require entirely different preparation (it would not dissolve or blend in the same way, and would change the batter or sauce structure). Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (chocolate, sweetness, wafer crunch) and texture and appearance. The match is a different food product with added flavour and components, not the same food under another name, and not a modified version of plain milk. Therefore neither condition is met.

The ingredient is plain 'fenugreek' with no stated form (whole, ground, or leaves), and the quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Spices, fenugreek seed' is the same spice under its default name, so the plain-ingredient default rule (D) applies. Guideline F rejects whole vs ground spice only when the ingredient specifies a state, which it does not here. Any grinding needed for a recipe is home handling (guideline C), so the preparation is unchanged. Condition 1 is met. Condition 2 is met, since the diner would taste the same fenugreek flavour. The only real ambiguity is that 'fenugreek' could mean the leaves (methi), but the seed is the standard spice default, so I treat this as a match.

The ingredient is plain soft margarine. The USDA match is 'Margarine-like, vegetable oil spread, stick or tub, sweetened.' Quantity is ignored per guideline A. The match is not the same plain product: it is a vegetable oil spread (a margarine-like product, typically lower in fat than margarine) and it is explicitly sweetened. Guideline D lists 'sweetened' as a modification, so a plain ingredient mapped to a sweetened version is not a match. Condition 1 is therefore questionable: the sweetened spread is not a drop-in replacement for plain margarine in this recipe. Condition 2 also fails, because added sweetness and the different fat composition could change flavour, texture and browning in a way a diner might notice. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain sliced deli turkey, the standard default product. The USDA entry is 'Turkey, prepackaged or deli, luncheon meat, reduced sodium', a modified version. Guideline D says a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced-sodium version is not a match, because the ingredient does not ask for reduced sodium. Condition 1 is arguably met, since the slices could be swapped in without changing preparation. Condition 2 fails: reduced-sodium turkey has a noticeably different, blander salt profile, and a diner could plausibly notice the difference in flavour. The quantity (150g) is ignored per guideline A.

Palmito is the Spanish/Portuguese name for hearts of palm, so the USDA entry 'Hearts of palm, canned' is the same food under another name (guideline B). The weight '50g' is decoration (guideline A). 'Drained' is handling that does not change the match (guideline C), and canned hearts of palm is the normal way this product is sold, so the canned descriptor does not count as a modification (guideline D). The dish would be prepared the same way, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'winged beans', which in ordinary cooking usually means the whole green pods, eaten fresh or stir-fried. The USDA entry is specifically the immature seeds (the beans inside the pods), raw. Guideline B allows an inner part of the same vegetable when it is sold as the same thing, as with celery hearts, but immature seeds are not usually sold under the name 'winged beans'. Condition 1: using seeds in place of pods would change preparation, since pods must be trimmed and sliced or shelled differently and the seeds are a separate component. Condition 2: a diner would notice pods versus loose seeds in taste, texture and appearance. Both conditions are not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 200g turkey egg; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Egg, turkey, whole, fresh, raw', which names the same food: turkey eggs, whole, fresh, uncooked. Under guideline B, this is literally the same food, not a sibling variety or a different product. Condition 1: the raw whole turkey egg can be used exactly where the ingredient is used, with no change to preparation. Condition 2: because it is the same food, a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is beef tongue, and the USDA entry is 'Beef, variety meats and by-products, tongue, raw', which is the same food named in USDA's standard category wording. The quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A. The 'raw' descriptor means uncooked, which matches a recipe ingredient that has not been cooked. Nothing in the recipe handling changes the match, and no modified, flavoured, or different cut is involved. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance because it is the same food in the same state, so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh (uncooked) turkey breast, which will be cooked as part of the recipe. The USDA match is turkey breast meat only, cooked and roasted. Guideline F explicitly says raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Using pre-roasted meat would change the cooking method, since the dish would no longer cook the turkey from raw, and it would change the texture and appearance of the meat as cooked in the dish. A diner could notice the difference. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 is also doubtful. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is 'French crescent roll', a term usually used for the refrigerated, shortening-based crescent-style dough sold in the US, which is typically unbaked and softer and sweeter than a croissant. The USDA entry 'Croissant' is a finished, baked, laminated butter pastry. Condition 1: a baked croissant cannot replace raw or refrigerated crescent dough without changing how the dish is prepared (it would not be shaped, proofed, or baked as the recipe expects). Condition 2: even if the ingredient were a baked crescent roll, its softer crumb, lower butter content and sweeter flavour differ from a croissant's flaky, laminated texture, and a diner could notice. Because the two conditions are not met, the match is not substitutable. The weight '155g' is ignored as instructed.

The ingredient is plain feta cheese, with the quantity (40g) ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Cheese, feta' is the same food under the same name, so it is the standard default version (guideline D). Using it in place of the ingredient requires no change in preparation, since feta is a plain cheese used as bought. A diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the match is the same product. Both conditions are met.

Minced chicken and ground chicken are the same food under different regional names. The '250g' quantity is decoration and is ignored. 'Raw' in the USDA entry means uncooked, and the recipe's mincing or grinding does not change the match. Substituting raw ground chicken would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Step 1: The ingredient is pink sugar substitute packets, which are the saccharin-based tabletop sweetener (Sweet'N Low). The USDA entry is tabletop saccharin (sodium saccharin), the same product type. Per guideline B, this is the same food under another name. The quantity (6g) is ignored per guideline A. Step 2: Condition 1 is met because the entry is used the same way, as a tabletop sweetener added to food or drink, with no change to preparation. Step 3: Condition 2 is met because the sweetening agent is the same saccharin, so taste, texture and appearance should be indistinguishable to a diner. Pink packets may contain small amounts of dextrose or other carriers, but these are bulking agents at trace levels and do not change the sweetness profile in a way a diner would notice. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is eggnog, a sweetened, spiced dairy beverage made from milk or cream, eggs, sugar, and typically nutmeg and sometimes alcohol. The USDA match is heavy whipping cream, fluid: unsweetened, unspiced, without egg, and with a high fat content (about 36%). Condition 1: Using heavy cream in place of eggnog would change the dish. Eggnog contributes egg richness, sweetness, and spice flavour, and it is a liquid that is typically served as a drink or used in custards and batters where the eggs contribute structure. Heavy cream lacks these components, so the preparation would change (for example, custard setting or sweetening would not occur as intended). Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference in taste because eggnog's characteristic flavour (sweet, nutmeg-spiced, egg-custard notes) is absent from plain cream. Texture and appearance would also differ, since eggnog is a thinner, pale yellow, custard-like liquid. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is edam, a semi-hard cheese (a pressed, cooked-curd cheese that is typically aged and eaten or melted). The USDA match is a chocolate milk drink, which is a sweetened, flavoured beverage made from milk plus cocoa and sugar. Condition 1: edam cannot be substituted for a chocolate milk drink without changing preparation. A liquid sweetened drink cannot be grated, sliced, melted or otherwise handled like a solid cheese, so the cooking method and dish structure would change. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference. The chocolate milk drink would add sweetness, cocoa flavour and a liquid texture, and the cheese's savoury, nutty, salty profile and solid texture would be absent. Guideline F also rules out a different state and product type, and guideline D rules out a flavoured/modified version of a plain dairy base. Both conditions fail, so this is not substitutable.

The ingredient is butter oil, essentially anhydrous milkfat (ghee-like), which is almost pure butterfat with virtually no water or milk solids. The USDA match, 'Butter, light', is a reduced-fat butter with roughly half its weight as water and added ingredients. Condition 1: substituting it would change preparation. Butter oil is used for high-heat cooking and frying because it has no water to spatter or burn, and it can't be used in the same way as a water-containing spread. Light butter would foam, spatter and scorch differently, so the method changes. Condition 2: the diner would notice a difference in texture, mouthfeel, browning and flavour, since the lower fat content and added water change how the dish cooks and tastes. Under guideline D, a reduced-fat version is a modified product, not the plain one, and under guideline F a different fat is not substitutable. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is queso fresco, a fresh Mexican cheese, crumbled. The USDA entry 'Cheese, fresh, queso fresco' names the same food. Crumbling is knife or hand handling and does not change the match (guideline C). The quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the cheese can be used as-is in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same product. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same cheese in the same crumbled form. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is ground allspice that has been toasted. The USDA match is plain ground allspice, with no indication of toasting. Condition 1 is about whether the match can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared. Toasting is a separate preparation step, so using untoasted ground allspice skips it and changes the preparation. Condition 2 is about taste. Toasting allspice changes its flavour, making it more aromatic and nutty and less sharp, so a diner would likely notice the difference. Guideline F explicitly lists 'plain vs toasted' as not substitutable. The quantity (2g) and the 'for serving' note do not change this. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient 'agave spirit' is a broad category covering tequila, mezcal, and other agave-distilled spirits, not one specific product. The USDA entry 'Tequila' is only one member of that category, so it is not literally the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). Agave spirits differ in flavour: mezcal is typically smoky and tequila is not, and tequila ages vary in colour and oak character. Using tequila where the recipe calls for an unspecified agave spirit could therefore change the taste of the dish, and a diner could notice if the original spirit was mezcal or another agave spirit. Condition 2 is not reliably met, so the match is not substitutable.

Ingredient: 235g enoki mushroom (quantity ignored per guideline A). USDA match: 'Mushroom, enoki' is the same food under the same name, with no cooking state, preparation, or modification indicated. Enoki is commonly sold fresh, so the USDA entry matches the plain ingredient (guideline D/B). Condition 1: enoki can be used in place of enoki with no change in preparation, since it is the identical product. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the food is literally the same. Both conditions are met.

1. The ingredient is frozen amaranth leaves, thawed. The USDA match is Amaranth leaves, raw, which is the same food in fresh form. Guideline B treats this as the same food, so the question is whether the frozen-and-thawed state changes it. 2. Guideline E says a frozen item matches the fresh/raw entry when the food is normally cooked or mixed and freezing does not show. Amaranth leaves are normally cooked like spinach or chard, not eaten raw in most dishes. 3. Condition 1: the thawed leaves can be used in place of raw leaves without changing the preparation, since both would be cooked or mixed into the dish the same way. 4. Condition 2: freezing leaves that are cooked in the dish does not visibly change their taste, texture, or appearance in the finished dish. Any softening from freezing is minor and would not be noticed by a diner. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a cooked mixture of beans and white rice, with the quantity ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry names the same dish with the same two components, beans and white rice. Under guideline C, a USDA entry that names the same dish with the same components is a match. Neither entry specifies a bean variety, and the USDA entry carries no raw or dry state, so it is consistent with a cooked dish. Condition 1: the match could replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same combination of cooked beans and white rice. Both conditions are met.

Genoa salami is a specific style of Italian dry-cured pork salami. The USDA entry 'Salami, Italian, pork' is the general category that includes Genoa-style salami rather than a different sibling variety such as Milano or Hungarian. Condition 1: both are cured, sliced, ready-to-eat meat products, so the dish is prepared the same way. Condition 2: the difference between Genoa and a generic Italian pork salami is modest, mainly in seasoning intensity, and a diner would not reliably notice a change in taste, texture, or appearance in a typical dish. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'hot sauce', a generic term for a chili-pepper condiment. The USDA entry 'Hot pepper sauce' names the same product under a different name. Under guideline B, a regional or culinary name for the same food counts as a match. The quantity (10g) and the word 'optional' are irrelevant under guideline A. Condition 1: the sauce is used as a condiment or seasoning and can be swapped in without changing preparation. Condition 2: since both are the same generic pepper-based condiment, a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance attributable to the naming. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is anise seeds, crushed. The USDA entry, 'Spices, anise seed', names the same food with no processing state, so it is the generic whole seed. Condition 1: crushing is a handling step the cook performs (comparable to chopping or crushing in the recipe itself), so the same seed can be used and the cook would crush it, leaving the preparation unchanged. Condition 2: the food is still anise seed, not ground anise or an extract, so the diner would not notice a difference in flavour, texture or appearance beyond the crushing the recipe calls for. The 'whole vs ground' rule does not apply because crushing is not grinding to a powder. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a fresh plum, a Prunus fruit (stone fruit, typically sweet and juicy). The USDA entry is Java-plum (jambolan), Syzygium cumini, a different genus and family from plum. It is a distinct fruit with a markedly different flavour (astringent, sour, tannic) and appearance (small, oblong, dark purple). It is not a regional or trade name for plum, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in taste and texture. Quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 is also doubtful, since the dish would be prepared differently with a different fruit. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh Jerusalem artichokes (the tuber, a plant commonly called sunchoke). The USDA entry 'Jerusalem-artichokes, raw' is the same food in its raw, uncooked state, and 'fresh' describes the raw state the recipe calls for. The quantity (45g) is ignored per guideline A. No cooking method, flavour, texture or appearance differs between the two, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a generic 'chicken seasoning blend', a commercial or home seasoning mix whose exact composition varies but commonly includes salt, garlic, onion, paprika and other flavourings. The USDA entry 'Spices, poultry seasoning' is a traditional herb blend, typically sage, thyme, marjoram, rosemary and black pepper, with no salt or other flavour components. It is not literally the same product under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 is likely met, since it could be sprinkled in the same way with no change in preparation. Condition 2 is not met: the flavour profile differs, and a diner would likely notice the difference in taste, particularly the missing salt and garlic or onion notes that chicken seasonings usually carry. Because the composition differs, this is a blend-versus-different-blend mismatch rather than an equivalent product.

The ingredient is dry corn gluten-free pasta. The USDA entry, 'Pasta, gluten-free, corn, dry', describes the same product: dried corn-based gluten-free pasta sold as bought. The leading '100g' is quantity and is ignored. Using the USDA product in place of the ingredient requires no change to cooking method, since both are dry pasta boiled in water. Taste, texture and appearance are the same, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is edam cheese powder, a dried, powdered form of edam. The USDA entry 'Cheese, Gouda or Edam' is the solid natural cheese. Both are the same cheese type, so the food identity overlaps, but the state differs: a powder is a dried, ground product, while the USDA entry is a solid block. Guideline F treats a different state as non-substitutable. Using solid edam in place of the powder would change how the dish is prepared, since the powder blends or dissolves into a dish and cannot be grated or sliced in the same way. It would also change the texture and appearance of the finished dish, and a diner could notice the difference. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 likely fails too.

The ingredient is 400g pork tenderloin, boneless; the quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Pork, loin, tenderloin, boneless, raw' is the same cut: pork tenderloin is the boneless tenderloin from the loin, and the entry is raw, which matches a fresh raw tenderloin. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient with no change in preparation, since the same cut is simply cooked as usual. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cut in the same raw state. Both conditions are met, so it is substitutable.

The ingredient is pickled herring, a fish (Clupea species) preserved in brine or vinegar, typically served as a fillet. The USDA match is Okra, pickled, a vegetable (Abelmoschus esculentus) preserved in brine or vinegar. These are entirely different foods: one is an animal protein, the other a plant pod. Substituting okra for herring would change the dish's flavour, texture (flaky fish versus crisp, slippery pod), and appearance (fish fillet versus cut okra pods), and a diner would immediately notice they were eating something different. The shared feature of pickling is a preservation method, not identity of food. Condition 1 and condition 2 both fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is an almond croissant, a pastry filled with almond cream (frangipane) and usually topped with sliced almonds. The USDA match is a chocolate croissant, which is filled with chocolate. Condition 1 is about whether it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation; the pastry format is similar, so that part is plausibly met. Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste chocolate instead of almond and would see the absence of the almond topping and the different filling. The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Different flavour with the same base product is not a same-food-under-another-name case (guideline B), and the filling difference is a flavour change (guideline F-style reasoning on distinct products). Therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is palm oil, melted. The USDA entry 'Oil, palm' is the same product, palm oil, with no state or modifier attached. Melting is handling the recipe does itself and does not change the food, so it does not alter the match (guideline C). Condition 1: palm oil can be used in place of melted palm oil without changing the preparation, since the recipe melts it anyway, and the USDA entry is the oil in its plain form. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference, because it is the same oil. It is not a different oil, blend or processed fat (guideline F does not apply), and the 65g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is egg roll wrappers, the thin dough sheets used to wrap a filling. The USDA entry 'Egg roll, meatless' is a finished, filled egg roll product, not the wrapper dough. Using it would change the dish: the filling and cooked product would be added as a whole item rather than wrapping a filling, so the preparation method and the final dish would differ. A diner would also notice a different food (a pre-filled, pre-cooked roll with a vegetable filling versus a wrapper sheet). Condition 1 fails because the preparation changes, and condition 2 fails because the diner would taste a different product. Not the same food under another name, and not a wrapper product.

The ingredient is a cooked mixture of pinto beans and brown rice, and the leading 100g is decoration (guideline A). The USDA entry names the same dish with the same two components. It has no state descriptor, so it is the generic food and matches the cooked version (guideline E). Pinto beans and brown rice cooked together is the standard way this dish is prepared and served, so using this entry would not change the cooking method. A diner would not taste, feel, or see a difference between the two. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is tomato puree explicitly labelled 'uncooked'. The USDA match is 'Tomatoes, cooked, as ingredient', so the state differs: uncooked versus cooked. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a non-substitutable state difference. Condition 1 fails because using cooked tomatoes changes the preparation the recipe calls for, since the puree would not be cooked in the dish. Condition 2 also fails because cooked tomato has a different flavour (sweeter, less bright and fresh) and a different texture and colour from uncooked puree, which a diner could notice. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is turkey bacon, cooked, used as an optional garnish; the leading weight is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry is 'Turkey bacon, cooked', which names the same food in the same state (cooked). Condition 1: the match could replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are already cooked and serve as a garnish. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product in the same cooked state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is watermelon pepitas, meaning the hulled kernels of watermelon seeds. The USDA entry 'Seeds, watermelon seed kernels, dried' is the same food under a descriptive name: watermelon seed kernels. Guideline B covers same food under another name. The 'dried' descriptor reflects how the kernels are normally stored and sold, not a modification such as roasting, salting or flavouring. The ingredient line gives no roasted, toasted or salted state, so the plain default applies (guideline D). Condition 1: the kernels can replace the pepitas with no change to preparation, since no cooking method is implied. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the food is the same kernel. Both conditions are met.

Confectioners' sugar is the same product as powdered sugar, and the USDA entry 'Sugar, white, confectioner's, powdered' names it directly under a trade name. Guideline B says the same food under another name counts as a match. Using it in place of confectioners' sugar does not change how the dish is prepared, since it dissolves, dusts, or mixes the same way. The taste, texture and appearance are the same, so a diner would not notice a difference. The leading '250g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is braised veal shank, a cooked, braised cut of veal. The USDA entry is Veal, shank (fore and hind), cooked, braised, which is the same cut in the same prepared state. Condition 1: the match is already braised, so it can replace the ingredient in the same dish without changing the preparation method. Condition 2: a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference between braised veal shank and this entry. The 'separable lean and fat' wording is USDA's standard way of describing the cut and does not indicate a different food. The recipe does not specify bone-in or trimmed, so the default cut is assumed. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chuck roll, a cut of beef (the shoulder roast). The USDA match 'Roll, garlic' is a bread roll flavoured with garlic, a baked bakery product. It is not the same food under another name and it is not a beef cut. Substituting it would change the food category entirely, from raw meat that is cooked as a roast or braise to a baked bread product, so the cooking method, flavour, texture and appearance would all change. Condition 1 fails, and a diner would immediately notice they were eating bread rather than beef, so condition 2 fails too.

The ingredient is 35g bread flour, a plain wheat flour made from hard wheat with high protein content, used for bread and yeasted doughs. The USDA match is a gluten-free bread product made with tapioca starch and brown rice flour. This is a finished baked bread, not a flour, and it is not the same food under another name. It is a different product type (bread rather than flour) with different components (no wheat, tapioca starch and brown rice flour instead of wheat flour). Substituting it would change how the dish is prepared, since it cannot be used as a flour ingredient in a dough, and a diner would notice differences in taste, texture and appearance. Under guideline F, a different flour is not substitutable, and this is a far more distant mismatch. Condition 1 fails and condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is yautia, a root vegetable also known as tannier (malanga/cocoyam, Xanthosoma sagittifolium). The USDA entry 'Yautia (tannier), raw' explicitly names the same food under its alternate name, so it is the same food under another name (guideline B). The quantity (75g) is irrelevant (guideline A). Neither the ingredient nor the match specifies a cooking state beyond raw, and the match is the plain uncooked root, which is the default form of the ingredient (guidelines C and D). Condition 1: it can be used directly in place of the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference, since it is the same vegetable. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cantaloupe, a muskmelon with orange flesh and a distinct musky aroma and sweetness. The USDA match is honeydew, a different melon variety with pale green flesh and a milder, different flavour. This is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply). It is a sibling variety with a different taste (guideline F). Condition 1 might be met, since both are diced raw melon, but condition 2 fails: a diner would see green rather than orange flesh and would taste a noticeably different melon.

Borlotti beans are the same bean as cranberry (Roman) beans, so the food identity matches under guideline B. The USDA entry is 'mature seeds, cooked, boiled, with salt', which describes the same legume in a cooked, salted state. Canned beans are normally sold cooked and salted, so this matches what a shopper would buy under the plain name. 'Drained' is handling that does not change the match (guideline C). The quantity is ignored (guideline A). The bean is cooked in both cases and the salt is the usual canned-bean seasoning, so the dish would not change in preparation, taste, texture or appearance.

The ingredient is a turkey frankfurter, a standard processed sausage. The USDA entry 'Frankfurter, turkey' names the same product with the same component (turkey), just in a different word order. Under guideline B, this is the same food under another name. Quantity is ignored (A). Frankfurters are normally sold ready-to-eat and are prepared by heating, so the match does not change the preparation method. Taste, texture and appearance should be the same for the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain adzuki beans, the dried legume as bought. The USDA match is Yokan, a processed Japanese confection made from adzuki beans and sugar, which is a sweetened, gelled bean paste product. Using it in place of beans would change the dish's preparation: the beans would not cook, soak, or simmer as the recipe expects, and the added sugar and gel structure would change flavour and texture. Anyone eating the dish would notice the difference. Under guideline F, a single ingredient versus a processed product containing sugar and other ingredients is not a match. The condition for being substitutable fails on both counts.

Farmer cheese is a dry, firm, crumbly pressed fresh cheese, usually sold as a block or log and often sliced or crumbled. Cottage cheese, the USDA entry here, is a moist, loose curd product that is usually sold with cream or whey. Condition 1: in many recipes (fillings, spreads, pierogi, blintzes), cottage cheese could be substituted, but it would often need draining, pressing, or a texture change to behave like farmer cheese. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference in texture, since farmer cheese is denser and more crumbly, while cottage cheese has visible moist curds and a looser, creamier mouthfeel. The entry is a different product rather than the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Because the texture and appearance would differ, condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is a formed, processed chicken patty that is barbecue-flavoured. The USDA entry is rotisserie broiler chicken with skin, a whole-bird or piece product cooked by rotisserie. Condition 1 fails: using rotisserie chicken would change the preparation, since a patty is formed and typically pan-fried or baked, not rotisserie-cooked. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (intact muscle versus a formed, uniform patty) and appearance (skin, bone-in pieces, roasted surface versus a shaped patty). The USDA entry is not the same food under another name, and the structure and cooking method both differ, so it is not a match.

The ingredient is colby cheese (a semi-soft American cheese, mild and mellow, closely related to cheddar but with a higher moisture content and a softer, more open texture). The USDA entry 'Cheese, colby' is the same named cheese type with no modifiers such as reduced fat, sodium, or flavoured additions. Guideline A says the leading weight of 240g is decoration and is ignored. Guideline B and D: a plain ingredient mapped to the standard default version of the same food matches. Condition 1: the colby cheese can be used in place of the colby cheese in the recipe without changing preparation, since it is the same product. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance because it is the same cheese. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is shelled, flaked crab meat, the edible meat picked from the shell. The USDA entry 'Crab, soft shell' is a whole molted crab eaten shell and all. It is a different product, not another name for the same food. Condition 1 fails: the recipe would need to be reworked, since soft shell crabs are not flaked and have no shell to remove. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance, because the dish would contain whole or pieced soft shell crab rather than flaked meat. Guideline F (different state or form of the same source) supports rejection.

The ingredient is bottled lemon juice, a plain bottled product. The USDA entry 'Lemon juice, 100%, canned or bottled' is the same food: 100% lemon juice in bottled form, which is the standard default version a shopper would buy under this name. The quantity (685g) is decoration and is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient in any recipe without changing preparation, since no cooking or handling differs. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product type and no added flavour or modification is present. Both conditions are met.

Luo han guo is the Chinese name for monk fruit, so 'luo han guo sweetener' is a monk fruit sweetener under another name (guideline B). The USDA entry 'Sugar substitute, monk fruit, powder' is the same product type in powdered form. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient directly with no change to preparation, since both are used as powdered sugar substitutes and the 1g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Condition 2: the entry is the plain monk fruit sweetener, not a flavoured or modified version, so a diner would not normally detect a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is caraway rye bread, a light rye loaf flavoured with caraway seeds. The USDA entry covers marble rye and pumpernickel. Condition 1 is arguably met, since both are sliced breads that could be served in the same way. Condition 2 fails. Marble rye is swirled light and dark dough, often with cocoa, so it has a visibly marbled appearance that caraway rye does not. Pumpernickel is a dark, dense, molasses-sweetened rye with a markedly different taste and texture from a light caraway rye. A diner would notice the difference in colour, flavour and crumb. The entry also describes two different breads rather than the same product, so it is not the same food under another name.

The ingredient is roquefort cheese, and the USDA entry 'Cheese, roquefort' is the same food under the same name. The leading '35g' is quantity and is ignored. 'Crumbled' is knife or hand handling that does not change the match (guideline C). The USDA entry names no modification, preparation, or added flavour, so it is the standard default product (guideline D). Using it in place of the ingredient would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same cheese in the same form.

Black currants (Ribes nigrum) and red/white currants (Ribes rubrum/sativum) are different species with clearly different flavour. Black currants are more intense, musky and tart, while red and white currants are milder and more acidic. Their colour also differs: dark purple-black versus red or pale. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. It is a sibling variety with a different taste, which guideline F lists as not substitutable. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in flavour and appearance. The quantity (80g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is dried rockfish, a preserved product that has been dried (and usually salted) before sale. The USDA entry is rockfish, Pacific, mixed species, raw, which is fresh, uncooked fish. Guideline F says a different state, such as raw versus dried, is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because rehydrating or using fresh fish would change the preparation: dried fish needs soaking or long cooking and is used differently from fresh fillets. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the difference in texture, chewiness, and flavour between dried and fresh fish. The species match is not enough to override the change in state.

The ingredient is dried rosemary (a dried herb, the leaves of Rosmarinus officinalis). The USDA match is 'Spices, oregano, dried', a different herb with a distinctly different flavour profile (oregano is earthy and pungent with marjoram-like notes, while rosemary is piney, resinous and camphorous). Condition 1: oregano could be added in the same quantity at the same stage, so the preparation method would not change in a mechanical sense. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in flavour, since rosemary and oregano are not interchangeable in taste and are used to give distinct characters to dishes. Guideline F treats different herbs/sibling varieties with different tastes as not substitutable, and guideline B does not apply because these are not the same food under another name. Therefore condition 2 fails and the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a canola oil spread that is unsalted. The USDA entry is a margarine-like vegetable oil spread at 60% fat, with salt. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 (use without changing preparation) is arguably met, since a spread can be swapped in for a spread. Condition 2 fails. The ingredient specifies unsalted, and the match specifies salted. Under guideline D, a salted version of a plain or unsalted product is a modified version, and salt is a perceptible taste difference that a diner would notice, especially in a spread eaten on its own or in a recipe where salt level matters. The match also names generic 'vegetable oil' rather than canola, which under guideline F is a different oil. Because the salt difference alone changes taste, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain pecan halves that have been toasted. The USDA entry is pecans that have been honey roasted, meaning they are coated or cooked with honey, so they are sweetened and flavoured. Guideline F lists plain versus toasted or roasted as a different state, and guideline D treats an added flavour as a modification. Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste the honey sweetness and see the glossy, sugary coating, which differs from plain toasted pecans. Condition 1 also fails, because a recipe calling for toasted pecans would change in flavour and sweetness if honey-roasted nuts were substituted. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is dairy-free coconut yogurt, which is a yogurt made from coconut milk. The USDA entry 'Yogurt, coconut milk' describes the same product type under a more formal name, so it is the same food (guideline B). Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient in any recipe. It is used the same way, with no change to cooking method or preparation. Condition 2: the USDA entry is the generic coconut milk yogurt, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance compared with the ingredient as named. Brand-level variation exists, but the generic entry describes the same product category. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is brioche buns, an enriched bread made with butter, eggs, and sugar, with a rich flavour, tender crumb, and golden, glossy crust. The USDA match is plain commercially prepared white bread, which is lean, with a firmer crumb and a neutral flavour. Condition 1: brioche buns are not the same food as white bread under another name, and they are typically served as buns rather than sliced loaf bread, so swapping them would change the dish's preparation and presentation. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the richer, more buttery, softer texture and the difference in flavour and appearance. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is ground cardamom, a distinct spice with a citrusy, floral, eucalyptus-like aroma and flavour. The USDA match is allspice, ground, which is a different spice (from Pimenta dioica, tasting of clove, cinnamon and nutmeg). Condition 1: allspice could physically replace cardamom in a dish, so the preparation method would not change, but this is a sibling spice rather than the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference in flavour, since cardamom's aromatic profile is not reproduced by allspice. Guideline F explicitly rejects different-food substitutions that change flavour, and the weight (15g) is irrelevant. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is homemade chicken stock, and the USDA entry is 'Soup, stock, chicken, home-prepared', which is the same food under the same preparation method. The quantity (300g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the stock can be used in place of the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is a liquid used the same way in cooking. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same homemade chicken stock. Both conditions are met.

Condition 1: The ingredient is a sugar-free chocolate syrup, and the USDA entry is HERSHEY'S Sugar Free chocolate-flavored syrup. Guideline D says that when the ingredient asks for a modified version (here, sugar-free), the matching modified entry counts. Guideline G says a branded entry of the same plain product type counts. The quantity (200g) is ignored per guideline A. Using the syrup in place of the ingredient requires no change in preparation, so condition 1 is met. Condition 2: Both are chocolate syrups sweetened without sugar, so the flavour, texture and appearance should be the same in the finished dish. Nothing in the USDA entry adds a flavour or modification beyond what the ingredient requests, so a diner would not notice a difference. Condition 2 is met.

The ingredient is jarred burdock root that has been drained, so it is a processed, packed product, typically pre-cooked or pickled/brined and softened. The USDA match is 'Burdock root, raw', which is fresh, uncooked root. Condition 1: using raw burdock would change the preparation, since the jarred product is already cooked or pickled and tender, while raw root must be peeled, cut and cooked before it can be eaten, so the method changes. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Raw burdock is fibrous, crisp, and earthy-bitter, while jarred burdock is softer and carries packing-liquid flavour, so taste and texture differ. Guideline F excludes raw versus processed or cooked states and different packing media. The 'drained' descriptor reinforces that the ingredient is a packed, processed product rather than the raw root. Neither condition is met.

1. Identity: the ingredient is edamame (immature soybeans), and the USDA entry is Edamame, cooked. It is the same food, so this is not a different-food case.
2. Raw vs cooked: the ingredient does not specify raw, and edamame is normally sold frozen and pre-cooked (blanched) and eaten cooked. Rule E treats plain foods as matching their standard, normally-cooked form when handling does not show. The cooked entry therefore represents the default way edamame is bought and served.
3. Condition 1 (preparation): using cooked edamame in place of the ingredient does not change how the dish is prepared, since the usual handling is to cook or thaw and then add it.
4. Condition 2 (diner perception): a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance when the edamame is the normal cooked product.
5. Caveat: if the recipe explicitly calls for raw edamame, the cooked entry would not match, but the ingredient string gives no such indication.

The ingredient is plain summer sausage, ground for serving. The USDA entry is summer sausage in stick form with cheddar cheese added. Condition 1: the dish could be prepared with the cheddar stick in place of plain summer sausage, but the cheese is an added component, so the preparation would differ: it would need different handling and would no longer be plain sausage. Condition 2: a diner would notice the cheddar, which changes flavour and visible appearance (cheese pieces or marbling). Per guideline F, a product containing an added ingredient is not a match for the plain version. The pork-and-beef base and the 'summer' name match, but the cheddar modification and stick form make it a different product. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is beef consomme in its undiluted (concentrated) form, as sold in condensed cans. The USDA entry is beef consomme prepared with an equal volume of water, meaning it is already diluted to a ready-to-eat strength. This is the same food, but in a different state of concentration. Condition 1 fails: substituting the diluted product for the undiluted one changes the preparation, because the cook would need to adjust the amount, add less water, or reduce the liquid to reach the same concentration. The guidelines say to ignore the weight, so the 5g figure does not help. Condition 2 also fails: the diluted product would give a weaker beef flavour and a thinner body than the concentrated product, which a diner could notice. Since the two conditions are not both met, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is coconut sugar, made from the sap of the coconut palm, and the match is USDA 'Sugar, brown', which is cane sugar with added molasses. Guideline F says a different sugar is not substitutable. Coconut sugar has a distinct caramel/butterscotch-like flavour, a different colour and granule texture, and different moisture and sweetness behaviour. Condition 1 can be argued, since it can be used in the same cooking method. Condition 2 fails because a diner would likely notice the flavour difference. Coconut sugar is not the same food as brown sugar under another name, so guideline B does not apply. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is Pacific cod that was frozen and then thawed. The USDA entry is raw Pacific cod, with a note that it may have been previously frozen. Condition 1: the same food, uncooked, can be used in place of the thawed fish without changing the preparation, and the thawing is handling that does not alter the match (guideline E). Condition 2: thawed cod that is normally cooked is not distinguishable from fresh raw cod in taste, texture, or appearance, and the USDA wording explicitly covers previously frozen fish. Both conditions hold. The 200g quantity is ignored (guideline A).

Ingredient: boneless striploin, uncooked. This is a beef cut known as New York strip (striploin is the same cut as the short loin strip steak). USDA entry: 'Beef, short loin (NY strip steak), raw' - the same cut, explicitly named as NY strip steak, and raw matches uncooked. Quantity (135g) is ignored. Boneless is a handling/trim descriptor that does not change the cut; the USDA entry is for the steak itself. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the striploin without changing preparation (same cut, same cooking method). Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance since it is the same cut of beef. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is liquid cottonseed oil, a common refined edible oil used for cooking and frying. The USDA entry is 'Oil, industrial, cottonseed, fully hydrogenated', which is an industrial, food-service specialty fat that has been fully hydrogenated. Full hydrogenation converts the oil into a solid or semi-solid fat at room temperature, so it is not liquid and cannot be used in place of liquid oil without changing how the dish is prepared (it would need melting, and would behave differently in frying or mixing). It also differs in texture and mouthfeel, and in flavour and appearance in the finished dish. Guideline F explicitly excludes industrial/food-service specialty fats and different states of the same source (hydrogenated vs liquid). Condition 1 fails, and a diner would likely notice the texture difference, so condition 2 also fails.

The ingredient is frozen great northern beans, thawed. The guidelines say a thawed frozen product should match the frozen USDA entry of the same product, and the closest frozen entry would be the correct target.
