Condition 2 also fails: a diner would readily notice the difference in texture (creamy sauce vs. crumbled meat), appearance, and flavour (milk-based gravy vs. seasoned chicken meat). It is not the same food under another name, and it is not a plain-to-standard version of the same product.

The ingredient is plantain leaves, used as an edible or aromatic wrapper (similar to banana leaves). The USDA match is 'Plantains, green, raw', which is the fruit of the plantain plant, not its leaves. This is a different food, not a regional or trade name for the same item, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: the fruit cannot wrap the dish, so the preparation would change. Condition 2 also fails: the leaf's aroma, colour, and the leaf-wrapped appearance would be absent, and a diner would notice a different food. The quantity and 'optional' qualifier are irrelevant under guideline A.

1) The ingredient is cooked ground pork with no stated fat content or cooking method. The USDA entry is also cooked ground pork, so the raw/cooked state matches. 2) The USDA entry adds two specifics the ingredient does not state: an 84% lean / 16% fat ratio and pan-broiling. Pan-broiling renders and drains fat, which typically leaves meat drier and firmer and can change appearance. 3) Because the USDA entry is a particular pan-broiled, 84/16 product rather than the plain default, a diner could plausibly notice a difference in texture, juiciness and fat content, and the cooking-method descriptor is not neutral. 4) The match therefore does not clearly satisfy the condition that the diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Judged as not substitutable, with the caveat that this is a borderline call.

The ingredient is canned pink beans, a legume (pinto-type bean) sold drained. The USDA match is canned pink salmon, drained solids, which is a fish. These are different foods: a legume versus an animal protein. The shared word 'pink' is only a colour descriptor and does not make them the same food. Guideline B (same food under another name) does not apply, and guideline F (a different food is not substitutable) rules out the match. Using salmon for beans would change the flavour, texture and appearance of the dish, and a diner would immediately notice. Substitutable is false.

The ingredient 'Mexican flatbread, thin' is a tortilla, the standard Mexican flatbread. The '50g' weight is decoration and is ignored. 'Thin' describes the normal form of a tortilla rather than a modified product. The USDA entry 'Tortilla, NFS' is the generic, unspecified tortilla, so it names the same food without adding a modification or a different state. Condition 1: a tortilla can be used in place of a thin Mexican flatbread without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since the generic entry covers the same product type. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is '150g beet greans, chopped', which is almost certainly beet greens (a typo). Beet greens are the leafy tops of the beetroot plant. The USDA match, 'Green peas, raw', is the immature seed of a pea pod, a legume. These are different foods, not trade or regional names for the same thing (guideline B). The 'chopped' descriptor is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C), and the weight is ignored (guideline A). Substituting peas for beet greens would change flavour (sweet, starchy peas versus earthy, slightly bitter greens), texture (tender pea seeds versus leafy tissue), and appearance (round green peas versus dark leafy pieces). A diner would notice the difference, so condition 2 fails. Condition 1 also fails because peas are not a leafy green that can be used as a direct replacement without changing the dish. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is canned pimentos, drained, and the USDA entry is 'Pimento, canned', which is the same food in the same canned form. The '400g' weight is decoration and is ignored. 'Drained' describes handling the recipe does itself, not a change in state, so it does not alter the match. Condition 1: the canned pimento can be used directly in place of the drained canned pimento without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'all-fruit preserves', meaning a preserve sweetened with fruit juice or concentrate instead of added sugar. The USDA entry 'Jams, preserves, marmalades, sweetened with fruit juice' describes that same product type. Under guideline D, when the ingredient itself asks for the modified version (here, the fruit-juice-sweetened form), the matching modified entry counts as a match. Condition 1: the preserve is spread or cooked into the dish in the same way, so the preparation does not change. Condition 2: the sweetener is fruit juice in both, so taste, texture and appearance should be essentially the same and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh jujubes, halved. The USDA entry, 'Jujube, Chinese, fresh, dried', is a dried fruit product. Halving is knife work and does not change the match, but the state is the problem. Guideline F lists 'a different state' (fresh vs dried) as not substitutable. Condition 1 fails in part: a cook would not prepare dried jujubes the same way as fresh ones, since dried fruit is typically rehydrated or used differently. Condition 2 also fails: dried jujubes are wrinkled, chewy, and more concentrated in sweetness, so a diner would notice the difference in texture and taste. The entry's label is contradictory ('fresh' and 'dried'), but the descriptor that matters is 'dried', and the entry does not clearly describe the fresh fruit. Neither condition holds, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient 'soybeans' is a plain, unspecified form, and the leading '20g' is ignored per guideline A. Under guideline C, 'mature seeds, raw' for beans denotes the dried legume as bought, which is the standard form in which soybeans are purchased for cooking. It is the same food with no added processing, flavouring or modification. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the dried beans are used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same bean. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Gruyere cheese that was frozen and then thawed. The USDA entry 'Cheese, gruyere' is the plain, generic food with no state or modification descriptor. Guideline E says frozen cheese intended for cooking matches the standard entry because freezing does not show once the cheese is melted or mixed. Condition 1: the cheese can replace the thawed Gruyere without changing the preparation method. Condition 2: once thawed and used in a cooked dish, a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance from the same cheese. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient 'tomato concentrate' is the same food as tomato paste, a concentrated tomato product commonly called tomato concentrate or tomato purée in some regions (guideline B). The USDA entry 'Tomato, paste, canned' is the standard plain version. The 'without salt added' descriptor does not make it a modified version here, since the recipe ingredient names no sodium modification and unsalted tomato paste is a normal default purchase. The 8g quantity is ignored (guideline A). Using it in place of tomato concentrate would not change preparation, flavour, texture, or appearance, so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 30g chutney, and the USDA match is simply 'Chutney'. The quantity is decoration and is ignored. The USDA entry names the same food with no modifying state, so it is the generic default version of the ingredient (guideline B and D). Condition 1: the chutney could be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is a ready-to-serve condiment with no cooking step involved. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product type. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain cooked pumpkin, and the qualifier "unsalted" specifies that no salt is added. The USDA entry is the same food (pumpkin, cooked, boiled, drained), so the food identity matches. However, the USDA entry is explicitly "with salt," which is a salted modification of the plain product. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a modified version (such as one with added salt or solution) is not substitutable. Using salted pumpkin in place of unsalted would change the flavour, since a diner would taste the salt, and the seasoning of the dish would differ. Condition 2 therefore fails, and the match is rejected.

Condition 1: The ingredient is fresh grouper fillet, which is raw fish. The USDA entry is raw grouper of mixed species. Both are uncooked, and a fillet is the standard way grouper is sold, so the same cooking method applies. The weight (250g) is ignored per the guidelines. Condition 2: Grouper species differ slightly in flavour and texture, but the mixed-species entry is the generic grouper product, and a fillet of unspecified grouper is what it represents. Raw grouper prepared the same way would not show a noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance to a diner. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a good-quality peach. The USDA match is raw nectarines. Nectarines are botanically a smooth-skinned variety of peach, but they are sold and eaten as a distinct fruit. They differ from peaches in skin (smooth and no fuzz), often in flavour (a sharper, more tart profile), and sometimes in flesh texture. Guideline B covers names for the same food, not sibling varieties. Guideline F explicitly says sibling varieties with a different taste are not substitutable. Condition 2 fails because a diner could notice the missing fuzz and the flavour difference. Condition 1 is also doubtful, since a peach-based dish would be prepared with a different fruit profile. The quantity (280g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is thinly sliced turkey breast, and the USDA entry is sliced turkey breast sold prepackaged. Both are the same food in the same form, so this is not a different cut or a different state. Slicing is handling the recipe does itself, and 'sliced' in the USDA name describes the same product. 'Prepackaged' describes how sliced turkey breast is normally sold, not a modification such as added solution or a flavoured variety. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same sliced turkey breast. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is explicitly fat-free cream cheese, softened. The USDA entry 'Cheese, cream, fat free' is the same product with the same descriptor. The ingredient itself asks for the fat-free version, so the matching modified entry counts under guideline D. 'Softened' is handling (room temperature) and does not change the match under guideline D's handling rules. Cooking method, taste, texture and appearance would be the same, so both conditions hold.

Strong white flour is the British/Irish name for bread flour, a high-protein white wheat flour. The USDA entry 'Wheat flour, white, bread, enriched' is the same product under a standard name, so it counts as the same food under another name (guideline B). Guideline F rules out bread flour vs cake flour, but that does not apply here because the ingredient is bread flour. 'Enriched' is the standard default for US-sold white bread flour, so it is not a modification (guideline D). The quantity in cups is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing the method, since the flour is used the same way. Condition 2: the protein content and gluten behaviour match, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance.

The ingredient 'peer' is a typo for 'pear', so it is the same fruit as the USDA entry 'Pear, raw'. The leading '220g' is quantity and is ignored. 'Ripe' describes the normal state a pear is bought and eaten in, so a raw pear matches a ripe pear without changing preparation. Condition 1: a raw pear can replace a ripe pear with no change to how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since this is the same food in its default raw state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh cape gooseberries (Physalis peruviana), a small golden-orange fruit in a papery husk with a tropical, tart-sweet flavour. The USDA entry is 'Gooseberries, canned, light syrup pack', which describes the Ribes genus (European/North American gooseberries), a different species from the cape gooseberry. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Even setting species aside, the match is canned rather than fresh, and it is packed in light syrup, which is a different packing medium (guideline F). Condition 1 fails: the dish would need its preparation changed (draining syrup, adjusting sugar, using a different fruit). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in flavour (syrup sweetness, Ribes taste), texture (soft canned fruit), and appearance (green or red Ribes versus golden Physalis). Not substitutable.

The ingredient is salt-packed capers (pickled flower buds of the caper bush, Capparis spinosa), rinsed. The USDA match is dill or kosher dill pickles, which are cucumbers. These are different foods, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: capers are used whole as a briny, sharp garnish or sauce component, and cucumber pickles would be cut, sliced or chopped, which changes preparation. Condition 2 fails: capers have a distinct floral, pungent, mustard-like flavour and a small round bud texture, while dill pickles taste strongly of dill and vinegar, have a crisp watery texture, and look different. A diner would notice the difference. The quantity (3g) is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient 'chile negro' is a dried Mexican chile. In common usage, especially in the US, 'chile negro' is a regional name for the dried chilaca pepper, which is the same food sold as pasilla. The USDA entry 'Peppers, pasilla, dried' is therefore the same food under another name (guideline B), and it is in the same dried state as the ingredient (guideline C). The quantity '2' is decoration (guideline A). Using it would not change the preparation (toasting, soaking and blending work the same), and a diner would not notice a difference in flavour, texture or appearance. One caveat: 'chile negro' can occasionally refer to other varieties such as chilhuacle negro, but the standard reading of the name matches pasilla. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is apple juice concentrate, which is a concentrated product that is normally diluted or used as a flavour base. The USDA entry is ready-to-drink apple juice, reconstituted from concentrate, with added vitamin C and shelf-stable processing. Under guideline D, 'with added vitamin C' is an added-additive modification, so it is not the plain default product. Condition 1: using 250g of reconstituted juice in place of 250g of concentrate would supply far less apple solids, sugar and flavour, and the recipe's dilution, reduction or sweetness balance would change, so the preparation would not be the same. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice a weaker, less concentrated apple flavour and different sweetness. Because the concentrate and the ready-to-drink juice are different products and the match carries an added vitamin C modification, the match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is plain ravioli with no sauce. The USDA entry is 'Ravioli, NS as to filling, no sauce', which is the same food with the same state (no sauce) and an unspecified filling. The recipe does not name a filling, so the generic 'not specified as to filling' entry is the standard default version. Cooking method is unchanged, and a diner would not notice a difference, since the recipe itself does not fix a filling. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is glutinous rice flour, a raw, milled dry ingredient used as a component in a recipe. The USDA match is 'Cake made with glutinous rice', a finished, prepared baked or steamed dessert. Condition 1 fails: the cake cannot replace the flour without changing how the dish is prepared, since it would have to be used as a finished product rather than mixed, hydrated, and cooked. Condition 2 also fails: the match is a different food, not the same food under another name, and a diner would notice the difference in texture, structure, and flavour. The match is a processed dish rather than the flour itself, so it is not the same food under another name.

The ingredient is beef oxtails. The USDA entry 'Beef, oxtails' names the same cut with no cooking state, preparation, or added components, so it is the generic food and matches fresh or plain versions (guideline E). The 200g weight is decoration (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same cut and needs no different cooking method. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is mole sauce specifically requested as reduced sodium. The USDA match 'Mole sauce' is the plain, standard-sodium entry, so it is the same food but not the modified version the recipe asks for. Under guideline D, a plain entry is not a valid substitute for a reduced-sodium ingredient, because reduced sodium changes the taste (less salt) and the recipe calls for that specific version. Condition 2 also fails: a diner could notice the difference in saltiness. The ingredient is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 500 g of baked barbecue wings, which is a cooked chicken wing dish with BBQ sauce. The USDA entry is chicken wings with barbecue flavour and glaze, heated in a conventional oven, which is the same dish with the same components. The weight is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the match is already cooked and only needs heating, which is the same cooking method as baking the wings, so the preparation does not change. Guideline E treats a frozen product that is thawed and cooked as matching when freezing does not show in the finished dish. Here the frozen state is how pre-cooked BBQ wings are normally sold, and the descriptor 'glazed' matches the sauced wings the ingredient describes. Condition 2: the flavour (barbecue) and appearance (sauced, oven-heated wings) match. Any remaining difference in texture between home-baked and commercially reheated wings is minor and would not reasonably be noticed by a diner in this dish. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is oyster mushroom, a specific variety with a distinct flavour and texture, presented as a raw, as-bought food. The USDA match is 'Mushrooms, NS as to form, cooked': a generic mushroom type of unspecified form that has been cooked. Guideline B does not apply because this is not the same food under another name; oyster mushrooms are a distinct variety from the unspecified generic mushroom. Guideline F treats raw versus cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails because using pre-cooked mushrooms changes the preparation: the dish would need the cooking step removed or altered. Condition 2 fails because a diner would likely notice the difference in flavour, texture and appearance between oyster mushrooms and cooked generic mushrooms. Both conditions are not met.

Condition 1: The ingredient is a single ingredient, tapioca flour, toasted. The USDA entry is a finished product, gluten-free rolls, made from a blend of brown rice flour, tapioca starch and potato starch. Per guideline F, a single ingredient does not match a blend or product that contains it, and a different flour or starch is not interchangeable. Substituting bread rolls for flour would change how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: Even ignoring the change in preparation, tapioca flour toasted would give a distinct toasted, nutty flavour and a different texture. A diner would notice a baked roll in place of the flour. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is cottonseed oil (plain, refined cooking oil; the quantity 80g is ignored). The USDA match is 'Cottonseed oil', which is the same food with the same name and no modification, state, or blend. Condition 1: cottonseed oil can be used in place of cottonseed oil without any change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would detect no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the identical product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is crumbled chicken sausage, a meat product made from ground chicken with seasonings, typically cooked as crumbles in a skillet. The USDA match is 'Sausage gravy', which is a sausage-based cream gravy (pork sausage pieces in a white roux/milk sauce), a wet, saucy preparation. Condition 1 fails: substituting a gravy for crumbled sausage would change the preparation, since you cannot crumble and brown a gravy the way you would sausage meat; it is a sauce, not a meat ingredient. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would readily notice a creamy gravy instead of dry, browned chicken sausage crumbles, and the flavour, texture and appearance differ substantially. Not the same food under another name, and it is a different product type (a sauce containing sausage vs. the sausage itself, plus a different meat source). Therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain applesauce, a puréed apple product. The USDA entry 'Cookie, applesauce' is a baked cookie made with applesauce as an ingredient, which is a different food product, not the same food under another name. Using it in place of applesauce would change the dish: it adds flour, sugar, fat and baked structure, and the diner would notice a different taste, texture and appearance. Condition 1 fails because the match is a finished baked good rather than the plain ingredient. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would notice the difference. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is reduced sodium ketchup, and the USDA match is 'Ketchup, reduced sodium', which is the same product under the same name. Guideline D says that when the ingredient itself asks for the modified version, the matching modified entry is a yes. The 90g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the ketchup can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same condiment with the same sodium level.

The ingredient is chicken bratwurst, a whole cased sausage that is sliced and typically cooked, so it keeps a firm, sliceable texture and a casing. The USDA match, chicken spread, is a spreadable, emulsified or paste-like product, not a sausage. Substituting it would change the texture from firm pieces to a soft paste, and the appearance and cooking method would also change. A diner would notice the difference. Slicing is handling and does not change the match, but the product itself is different. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails too.

The ingredient is '145g ground pork' with no stated cooking state, so it is treated as raw ground pork, the default form. The USDA match is 'Pork, ground, 96% lean / 4% fat, cooked, crumbles', which is cooked and crumbled. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using pre-cooked crumbles in place of raw ground pork would change how the dish is prepared, since the meat would not brown or cook through in the same way and would need different timing or handling. Condition 2 also fails: the texture, moisture and appearance of cooked crumbles differ from raw ground pork, and a diner could notice the difference. The 96% lean specification is a further difference from a default ground pork entry. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is reduced-fat canned dough rounds that are fried. The USDA entry is refrigerated biscuit dough, lower fat, baked. The product type and reduced-fat descriptor align, so the food identity is close. However, condition 1 fails: the ingredient is fried, while the USDA entry is baked. Frying versus baking is a change of cooking method, and the dish's preparation would therefore differ. Condition 2 also fails in practice: fried dough absorbs oil and develops a crisp, blistered, golden surface and a richer flavour that baked biscuit dough does not have, so a diner would likely notice the difference. Because the cooking method and resulting texture and flavour change, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is sunflower oil (high oleic), a liquid cooking fat. The match is a snack food: sunflower seed kernels that have been oil roasted, without salt. These are different foods. The match is a solid seed product, not an oil, so it cannot be used in place of the oil without changing how the dish is prepared. Substituting roasted seed kernels for oil would also change texture, appearance, and flavour, since the diner would notice solid roasted seeds rather than a liquid fat. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 fails too. The quantity prefix is ignored per the guidelines. Under guideline F, a different oil or fat is not substitutable, and a processed seed product is not the same as the oil it could yield.

The ingredient is ready-to-eat popcorn. The USDA entry 'Popcorn, ready-to-eat, NFS' names the same food under a generic descriptor (NFS, not specified as flavoured, sweetened or otherwise modified). Condition 1: the match can be used directly in place of the ingredient, since no cooking or preparation step changes. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same ready-to-eat popcorn product. The 30g quantity is ignored per the guidelines. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 100g overripe bananas, chopped. The weight is decoration (guideline A). The USDA entry 'Bananas, overripe, raw' is the same food at the same ripeness stage, so the ripeness rule in F (ripe vs overripe) does not apply. 'Raw' means uncooked, which matches a plain fresh ingredient. Chopping is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is used raw and chopped the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same overripe banana. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is brie, a specific soft-ripened cow's milk cheese with a white rind, creamy interior and mild, buttery flavour. The USDA match, 'Cheese ball', is a mixed spread product, typically cream cheese blended with other cheeses, seasonings, and often rolled in nuts or herbs. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: using a cheese ball would change the preparation, since it is a shaped, seasoned spread rather than a wedge that is baked or served as a whole piece. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste added seasonings and notice a different texture and appearance. The quantity (500g) is ignored per guideline A. Guideline F's principle applies: a processed or blended product is not substitutable for the plain ingredient.

The ingredient is fontina cheese, a single cheese, used melted. The USDA match is 'Cheese fondue', a prepared dish made from cheese blended with wine, starch and often kirsch or other seasonings. Under guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend or product containing it is not substitutable. Using fondue would change the flavour (wine and kirsch notes, Swiss-style character rather than fontina's), and the texture would differ because of added starch and the fondue's preparation. A diner could notice the difference. Condition 1 is also doubtful, since the dish would be built around a ready-made fondue rather than melted fontina. Condition 2 fails on taste and texture, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain pork tenderloin, the standard raw cut. The USDA entry is a branded, pre-treated product: HORMEL ALWAYS TENDER is a pork tenderloin injected with a solution, and this variant is peppercorn-flavoured. Under guideline G, a branded entry with an added flavour or modification does not match. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a flavoured or additive-treated version is not substitutable. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste peppercorn and notice the altered texture from the added solution. The entry is not a substitute for plain pork tenderloin.

Ingredient is green split peas, which are dried green peas split for cooking; the 25g quantity is ignored. USDA entry 'Peas, green, split, mature seeds, raw' is the dried split legume as bought (guideline C: 'mature seeds, raw' for peas is the dried legume as bought). It is literally the same food under the same name. Using it changes no preparation step, and the diner would see and taste the same split green peas. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh pomegranate seeds (arils), a fruit with juicy, tart-sweet arils. The USDA match is 'Wheat, soft white', a cereal grain (typically dry kernels, or flour-related). These are entirely different foods: a fruit versus a grain. Substituting wheat kernels for pomegranate arils would change the dish's flavour (tart, sweet, juicy versus starchy, bland), texture (crisp, juicy pop versus hard, dry kernel), and appearance (red jewel-like seeds versus pale tan grains). Condition 1 fails because the preparation would also have to change, and condition 2 fails because a diner would clearly notice. The quantity (25g) is irrelevant per the guidelines.

The ingredient is crab meat, the edible flesh of crab. The USDA entry 'Crab' names only the food with no preparation state, so under guideline E it is the generic food and matches fresh, thawed, or plain versions. Crab meat is the crab's edible flesh, so it is the same food under the generic name, not a different cut or product (guideline B). The recipe's handling (picking, flaking, or folding the meat) does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the generic crab entry can replace crab meat without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the food is the same crab flesh. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain cottage cheese, served as an accompaniment (for serving). The USDA entry 'Cheese, cottage, NFS' is the generic cottage cheese entry, which matches the plain, standard product (guideline D: cottage cheese -> Cheese, cottage, creamed, is a yes). The quantity (125g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the cheese could be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is simply served as is. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food under a generic name; the NFS (not further specified) label covers the standard fat-level variants that are sold under the plain name. No modification, flavouring, or state change is implied. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked sausage with no meat specified, so the default version applies. The USDA entry is 'Sausage, smoked link sausage, pork', which names the same product type: a smoked link sausage. The smoking is already part of the ingredient's description, so it is not a state mismatch (guideline F does not apply because both are smoked). Pork is the standard default for smoked sausage, and the ingredient does not call for another meat, so no cut or species change is implied. The sausage would be prepared the same way (sliced, browned or simmered) and would look and taste the same to a diner. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh lychee (135g, quantity ignored). The USDA entry is simply 'Lychee', which is the generic food with no processing state, preparation, or modification stated. Per guideline E, a USDA entry naming only the food matches fresh, thawed, or plain versions. Lychee is the same fruit under the same name, so the same plant source and form are involved. Condition 1: it can be used in place of fresh lychee without changing preparation (peeling, pitting, and serving are identical). Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the generic entry describes the same fruit as normally bought. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is high fructose corn syrup. The USDA entry 'Syrups, corn, high-fructose' is the same food under another name, so it is the same product rather than a modified version, a different sweetener, or a processed derivative of corn. Guideline B covers same-food name variants, and the 20g quantity is decoration per guideline A. Condition 1: HFCS can be used in place of itself with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a 50/50-style mix of two different berries, loganberries and raspberries, both frozen. The USDA match covers only loganberries, frozen. Condition 1: using loganberries alone would drop half of the specified fruit, so the recipe's fruit composition changes, even though the preparation method (frozen berries for cooking) would be the same. Condition 2: loganberries and raspberries differ in flavour (loganberries are tarter and more wine-like), colour and seed character, so a diner would likely notice the change. Guideline F rejects a single ingredient standing in for a blend containing it. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is ground pork that has been cooked, with no fat ratio or cooking method specified. The USDA entry is ground pork, cooked, at 84% lean / 16% fat, prepared by pan-broiling. Condition 1: the ingredient is cooked ground pork, so the entry is the same food in the same state (cooked). The unspecified ingredient is not altered by the entry's 16% fat level, which sits within the normal range for ground pork, and the entry does not change how the dish is prepared, since the recipe calls for cooked meat either way. Condition 2: a diner would not reliably notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance between cooked ground pork at this fat level and cooked ground pork prepared by another method. Per guideline D, a plain ingredient matches the standard default version. The weight (110g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is camembert cheese, a soft-ripened cheese typically sold as a whole round or wedge. The USDA entry 'Cheese, camembert' is the same food under the same name, so it is the standard default version of the product. The quantity (35g) is ignored per guideline A. Camembert is normally used as-is (served, baked, or melted), and the USDA entry describes the same product with no modification, processing, or added flavour. Swapping in the USDA entry would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is thousand island dressing, reduced fat. The USDA entry is 'Salad dressing, thousand island dressing, reduced fat', which names the same product with the same modifier (reduced fat). The leading weight of 75g is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the dressing can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: it is the same food under the same name, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met, and the match follows the rule that a matching modified entry is substitutable when the ingredient itself asks for that version.

The ingredient is fresh fiddleheads, the young coiled fronds of ostrich fern (Matteuccia struthiopteris), a common vegetable. The USDA match is 'Tree fern', a different plant from a different genus (Cyathea or similar), with its own taste and texture. This is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. The match is also cooked, while the ingredient is fresh/raw, and guideline F treats raw vs cooked as a different state. The tree fern would taste and look different from fiddleheads, so a diner would notice. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is a dry sauce mix, a powdered product that must be combined with liquid (and often butter or milk) before it becomes a sauce. The USDA entry 'Hollandaise sauce' is a finished, prepared emulsion of egg yolk, butter and lemon juice. Condition 1 fails: the dry mix would need to be reconstituted and cooked, so using the finished sauce would change how the dish is prepared. Guideline F also applies: a dry, unprepared product is a different state from the prepared sauce, and a powdered mix with its own thickeners and seasonings is not the same product as a traditional hollandaise. Condition 2 also fails, since the flavour, texture and composition of a mix-based sauce would not match a classic hollandaise. Both conditions are not met.

Bacalau is the Portuguese/Galician name for salt cod, which is Atlantic cod that has been dried and salted. The USDA entry 'Fish, cod, Atlantic, dried and salted' describes that same product. Under guideline B, a regional or culinary name for the same food counts as a match. The recipe would not need a different cooking method, since bacalau is normally soaked to rehydrate before cooking, and the USDA entry is the same dried-salted product. Quantity (400g) is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met: the dish's preparation is unchanged, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance.

The ingredient is sorghum syrup, made by boiling down juice from sorghum cane, a different grass from sugar cane. The USDA match is Syrup, Cane, made from sugar cane juice. These are different foods, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Sorghum syrup has a distinct earthy, grassy, slightly tangy flavour and a different sugar profile, while cane syrup is a milder, sweeter, more molasses-like product. Guideline F rules out a different sugar or syrup, so condition 2 fails: a diner would likely notice the flavour difference. Condition 1 is also doubtful, since the two syrups are used the same way but do not taste the same. Quantity is ignored. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is freeze-dried chives, a dehydrated herb. The USDA match is 'Chives, raw', which is fresh, uncooked chives. Guideline F states that a different state, including fresh versus dried herb, is not substitutable. Freeze-dried chives are a dried product that must be rehydrated or added directly, and they differ in texture (crisp and brittle rather than soft and moist) and in appearance (dull, flattened pieces rather than bright green stems). Condition 1 fails because using fresh chives in place of freeze-dried changes preparation, since fresh chives are typically added raw or chopped and freeze-dried ones may be added dry or rehydrated. Condition 2 also fails because a diner could notice the difference in texture and appearance. The 35g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Because the states differ, the match is not substitutable.

1. The ingredient is 100g graham cereal, a ready-to-eat cereal made from graham flour. The leading weight is decoration and is ignored (guideline A).
2. The USDA entry is Quaker Mother's Graham Bumpers, a branded ready-to-eat graham cereal. Guideline G says a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. The product is not flavoured or modified beyond what a shopper would normally buy under the plain name.
3. Condition 1: Graham cereal is used as a ready-to-eat ingredient, typically crushed, mixed or sprinkled. Bumpers are the same kind of product and can be used in the same way without changing preparation.
4. Condition 2: Bumpers are a graham cereal, so a diner would not expect a different food. Any small variation in sweetness or crumb size between brands is within the normal range of the same product type.
5. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 30g puffed corn, a processed cereal product made by heating and puffing corn kernels into a light, crisp, airy form. The USDA match, 'Corn grain, yellow', is raw, uncooked dried kernel corn. Condition 1 fails: puffed corn cannot replace raw kernels without changing preparation, since the puffing step is already done and raw kernels are hard and dense. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture and appearance, as puffed corn is light and crunchy while raw corn is hard and dense. This is the raw source versus a processed ingredient pattern (guideline F), so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is light cream, a dairy cream of roughly 18-30% fat that is liquid at room temperature and used unsweetened in cooking. The USDA entry is light vanilla ice cream, a frozen, sweetened, flavoured, aerated product. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Condition 1 fails: substituting frozen ice cream would change how the dish is prepared, since it cannot be poured, whisked, simmered or folded in the same way and would melt or freeze the preparation. Condition 2 also fails: the diner would taste added sugar and vanilla flavour and notice a frozen or creamy-solid texture instead of a liquid cream. Guideline F applies because this is a different product type with different composition and state. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is goose liver pâté, a processed product made from cooked, puréed liver blended with fat, seasonings and often other ingredients. The USDA match is 'Goose, liver, raw', which is uncooked whole liver. Condition 1 fails: pâté cannot be used in place of raw liver without changing preparation, since raw liver would need cooking and blending into a spread. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture, flavour and appearance, because raw liver is firm and unseasoned while pâté is smooth, spreadable and seasoned. Guideline F rules out raw versus processed or cooked states and a single ingredient versus a product containing it. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dry, ground espresso coffee, an uncooked, unbrewed solid. The USDA entry is a brewed beverage, restaurant-prepared espresso, which is a liquid already extracted with water. Condition 1 fails: substituting a brewed liquid for dry grounds changes the preparation. If used in a recipe, the brewed espresso adds water, changes the moisture and volume, and cannot be measured or incorporated as dry grounds would be. Condition 2 also fails: the dish would differ in taste intensity, texture, and appearance, for example in a rub, a dry mix, or a grind. This is a different state (dry ground vs brewed beverage), which guideline F rules out. It is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply.

The ingredient is soy nut butter, a spread made from ground roasted soy nuts. The USDA match is a baked cookie made with butter or sugar and fruit and/or nuts. These are different foods, not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails: a cookie cannot replace a spread as a 1 tbsp ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is a solid baked product rather than a paste. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste sugar, flour, butter and baked texture, and would notice a different food. The quantity is irrelevant under guideline A.

The ingredient is toasted pumpernickel bread, and the USDA entry is 'Bread, pumpernickel, toasted', which is the same food in the same state. Guideline F says plain vs toasted is not substitutable, but that applies when one side is plain and the other toasted. Here both are toasted, so the states match. The 80g weight is ignored per guideline A. Cooking method is unchanged because the bread is already toasted, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is salted duck egg, a cured egg with a strongly salty, savoury flavour, a firmer and oilier yolk, and a distinct appearance. The USDA entry 'Duck egg, cooked' is a plain cooked duck egg with no curing or added salt. Condition 1 fails: it would change the flavour and preparation the recipe relies on, and a salted egg cannot simply be replaced by an unsalted one in a dish that calls for it. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the missing salinity and different yolk texture. Per guideline D, adding salt is a modification from the plain item, so this is not the default version. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is yardlong beans, the long, fresh green pod vegetable (Vigna unguiculata subsp. sesquipedalis). The USDA entry 'Yardlong bean, raw' names the same food, and the weight prefix is irrelevant. Both are fresh, uncooked pods, so the cooking method is unchanged, and a diner would see and taste the same vegetable. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chicken bouillon cubes, a dry, concentrated, solid seasoning product that the cook dissolves in water. The USDA entry describes the finished soup, 'chicken broth or bouillon, dry, prepared with water', which is the liquid broth already made from dry bouillon. Condition 1 fails: using the prepared soup would skip the dissolving step, and the cook would have to work out how much liquid to add. The 15g of cubes is also a dry concentrate, so a prepared broth would bring a different water and salt balance. Condition 2 fails as well: the dish's salt and flavour intensity would shift, and the state difference between a dry cube and a prepared liquid is a different state under guideline F. The entry is not the same food under another name, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is a powdered sugar substitute, which is a generic product type. The USDA entry 'Sugar substitute, powder, NFS' is the same generic category: a powdered sugar substitute with the specific product not further specified. Under guideline B, this is the same food under a near-identical name, and under guideline D, a plain ingredient matches the standard default version. The quantity (2 cups) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the powder form can replace the ingredient in the same way, with no change to cooking method, since both are measured as a powder and used the same way. Condition 2: the entry is unspecified, as is the ingredient, so the match does not introduce a modification such as a flavour or added component. Sweetness and bulk can vary between brands, but the ingredient does not specify one, so this variation is not a mismatch with the ingredient as written. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cooked spelt, and the USDA entry is Spelt, cooked. They are the same food in the same state, and the quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the cooked grain can replace the ingredient directly without any change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same cooked grain. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is tiger shrimp (a species of shrimp), peeled. The USDA entry 'Shrimp, NFS' is the generic, not-further-specified shrimp entry. Per guideline E, a USDA entry that names only the food with no state or variety is the generic food and matches the ingredient. Peeling is knife or handling work and does not change the match (guideline C). Tiger shrimp is still shrimp, so this is the same food under a more general name (guideline B), not a sibling variety. The ingredient does not specify cooked or frozen, so no state mismatch is indicated. Condition 1: the shrimp can be prepared the same way. Condition 2: the generic entry does not assert a different species, so no difference in appearance or texture is implied by the match. Both conditions are met, though species-level flavour differences are a minor caveat.

The ingredient is a powdered tomato sauce product, a dry, concentrated, dehydrated form. The USDA match, 'Tomato sauce, for use with vegetables', is a ready-to-use liquid sauce, a different state and product form. Guideline F rules out a different state (dry vs wet, processed vs ready-to-use). Condition 1 fails: substituting 150g of liquid sauce for 150g of powder would add a large amount of moisture and change how the dish is prepared, since the recipe's liquid balance, mixing and cooking would all change. Condition 2 also fails: the dish's texture, consistency and concentration of tomato flavour would differ, and a diner could notice. The weight and quantity are ignored per guideline A. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain 'cottage cheese', which the guidelines map to the default entry 'Cheese, cottage, creamed'. The USDA match is 'Cheese, cottage, low fat', a reduced-fat version. Guideline D says a plain ingredient mapped to a low-fat or reduced-fat version is a modification and is not substitutable. The low-fat descriptor is not one that cottage cheese is normally sold with under its plain name, since the default is creamed. Using low-fat cheese would change the fat content, and so the mouthfeel and richness, of the dish, which a diner could notice. Condition 2 therefore fails. Condition 1 is not the deciding factor: the cheese could physically replace the ingredient without changing preparation, but the taste and texture difference means the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is beef sirloin tip, which is the knuckle/sirloin tip cut from the round-adjacent top sirloin area. The USDA entry is bottom sirloin tri-tip roast, a different primal sub-cut from the bottom sirloin with a different muscle structure, grain, and fat distribution. Guideline F states that a different cut of meat is not substitutable, and the cut here is not the same food under another name. The freezing and thawing (guideline E) and the trimming descriptor are not the deciding issue, because the cut itself differs. A diner could notice a difference in texture and tenderness, and the cooking method could also be affected. Condition 1 and condition 2 are therefore not both met.

The ingredient is butternut squash (plain, presumably raw, uncooked, weight-decorated as 75g; the quantity is ignored per guideline A). The USDA entry 'Squash, winter, butternut, raw' is literally the same food, a raw butternut squash. Nothing in the recipe description indicates cooking or processing that would be altered by the match, and the raw state matches the plain ingredient. Condition 1: it could replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since any handling such as peeling, cubing or roasting applies equally to either. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture or appearance because it is the same vegetable in the same raw state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is star fruit, which is the common name for carambola. USDA lists 'Carambola, (starfruit), raw', which is the same fruit under its regional/trade name (guideline B). The quantity (50g) is ignored (guideline A). The entry is raw, matching a plain fresh star fruit with no cooking implied (guideline C). Condition 1: the match can be used in place of the ingredient with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain cooked ham, the standard default version. The USDA match is 'Pork, cured, ham, low sodium, lean and fat, cooked', which is a modified version: it is specifically low sodium. Guideline D says a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced/low sodium version is not a match, because the ingredient does not ask for that version. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would likely notice the reduced saltiness compared with standard cooked ham, so the taste differs. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is regular ketchup, a plain condiment whose standard default version contains the usual sodium level. The USDA match is 'Ketchup, reduced sodium', which is a modified version with lower sodium content. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a reduced/low sodium modified version is not the same product, and the modification is not a normal way the plain product is sold. Condition 1: the ketchup could physically be swapped in without changing preparation, so the cooking method is unaffected. Condition 2: sodium reduction noticeably changes taste; a diner tasting the ketchup would likely perceive the flatter, less salty flavour, so a difference in taste would be noticed. Because the second condition fails, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is cream of wheat, a farina-type hot cereal made from wheat middlings. The USDA entry is literally 'Cream of wheat, NFS', the same named product with no stated preparation state (no 'cooked', 'dry', or 'prepared' qualifier). Under guideline E, an entry that names only the food is the generic food and matches the plain product. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with the same preparation, since it is the same cereal to be cooked as usual. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh raw taro root, peeled, which is a starchy root vegetable to be cooked. The USDA match is 'Snacks, taro chips', a processed, typically fried and seasoned snack. Condition 1 fails: it cannot replace raw taro root in a recipe without changing the preparation, since taro chips are already cooked, dried or fried, and would not be boiled, roasted or otherwise prepared as the root would be. Condition 2 also fails: the chips differ greatly in texture (crisp and brittle versus firm and starchy), flavour (salted or seasoned versus neutral) and appearance, and a diner would notice. Per guideline F, the raw source versus the processed product is not a match, and the quantity is irrelevant.

The ingredient 'poori' is the Indian deep-fried puffed wheat flatbread, also spelled 'puri'. The USDA entry 'Bread, puri' names the same food under its alternate spelling, which falls under guideline B (same food under another name). The weight '30g' is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the ingredient is the ready-made bread itself, so the USDA entry can replace it with no change to how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: it is the same product, so a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is purple corn meal, a misspelled but recognizable name for ground whole-grain purple corn. The USDA entry, 'Corn flour, whole-grain, blue (harina de maiz morado)', explicitly identifies itself as purple corn flour, the Spanish name for the same ground whole-grain purple corn. 'Meal' and 'flour' are regional and trade naming variants for ground corn here, so under guideline B this is the same food under another name. Both are whole-grain, so there is no added modification, and neither the cooking method nor the purple colour and corn flavour should change. A slight difference in grind fineness is possible, but it is a naming and grind variant of the same product, not a different food, so the match holds.

The ingredient is plain "tapioca" with the leading weight ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry "Tapioca, pearl, dry" is the standard default form of tapioca as sold, uncooked and dry, so it matches under guideline D. Using it would not change the preparation method, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance once the dish is cooked as the recipe directs. Tapioca starch or flour would be a different product, but the plain name maps to the pearl entry by default. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh marjoram leaves, used as a fresh herb. The USDA match is 'Spices, marjoram, dried', which is a dried herb. Guideline F explicitly lists fresh vs dried herb as a state difference that makes items non-substitutable. Substituting dried for fresh would change the flavour (dried herbs are more concentrated and lose some aromatic volatiles) and appearance (leaves are crushed or whole dried flakes rather than fresh green leaves). Condition 1 fails in that the preparation would change (quantity and timing of addition differ for dried herbs), and condition 2 fails because a diner could notice the taste and appearance difference. Therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is a vegetarian canned luncheon meat, a processed meat analogue, typically made from soy protein, wheat gluten, or mycoprotein, and designed to be meat-free. The USDA entry is pork with ham, canned (Spam). These are different foods: one is a plant-based product and the other is a pork product. Guideline F rules out substituting a processed product for a different base ingredient. Condition 2 also fails: the dish's intended vegetarian character changes, and a diner would notice pork instead of a plant-based product in taste, texture, and appearance. Spam's fat content, salty flavour, and firm pink-tinged texture differ from typical vegetarian luncheon meat. The optional label does not change the substitution analysis. Condition 1 is arguably met only in a superficial sense (both are minced canned luncheon-style meat), but condition 2 fails, and the swap would also change the dish's dietary identity.

The ingredient is mortadella, a specific Italian cured emulsified pork sausage (finely textured, with visible fat cubes, typically sliced thin for charcuterie). The USDA entry is 'Bologna sandwich on wheat', which is a prepared sandwich consisting of bread plus bologna, not a meat product by itself. Condition 1 fails: the match is a complete assembled dish including bread, so it cannot be used in place of sliced mortadella without changing the preparation (the diner would receive bread, condiments and a sandwich form rather than plain sliced meat). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would clearly notice the difference in appearance and texture between sliced cured meat and a sandwich on wheat bread. Bologna is at best a related American cousin of mortadella, not the same food, and the entry is a composite dish rather than the ingredient. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is sweet potato leaves, a fresh vegetable normally sold and used raw or cooked as a leafy green. The USDA entry 'Sweet potato leaves, raw' is the same food in the same uncooked state. The quantity (300g) is ignored. Condition 1: the leaves can be used in place of the ingredient without changing the preparation, since the USDA entry describes the same food as bought. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same plant part in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is beef heart, cubed and cooked. The USDA match is beef heart from New Zealand, but it is listed as raw. The food itself is the same, and cubing is knife work that does not change the match. The cooked/raw difference is a different state, though, and guideline F explicitly says raw vs cooked is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: using raw heart would require the cook to apply the heat that the recipe's cooked ingredient has already had, so the preparation changes. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice raw versus cooked meat in texture, colour and taste. The 'optional' label and the 100g quantity do not affect the decision.

The ingredient is 'spinach and artichoke dip' (the leading 70g is ignored). The USDA entry is 'Spinach and artichoke dip', which names the same dish with the same components. Condition 1: it could replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are a ready-to-serve dip used as-is. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same food under the same name. Guideline B and the rule that same-named dishes with the same components match both apply. No modification, state, or cut difference is present. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pork chop, a cut of pork meat. The USDA match is olive oil (Oil, olive, salad or cooking), a plant-derived fat. They are not the same food under another name. Substituting oil for pork would change the dish fundamentally: it is a different food category (animal meat vs. vegetable fat), the protein would be absent, and a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance. Guideline F also rules out substitutions of a different kind of ingredient. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is raw lamb tongue, a plain meat cut to be cooked by the recipe. The USDA entry is a finished, seasoned dish ('Tongue pot roast, Puerto Rican style'), so it is already cooked and flavoured with seasonings and sauce. Using it in place of raw lamb tongue would change the preparation: the recipe's own cooking and seasoning would be skipped or duplicated. Diners would also notice the difference in flavour, texture and appearance. The USDA entry is a prepared dish rather than the same plain food under another name, and tongue pot roast is typically beef tongue, so the species may also differ. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 is likely to fail as well.

The ingredient is Canadian bacon, a cured and smoked pork loin (back bacon) product, typically sold pre-cooked as round medallions with a lean, firm, ham-like texture and a mild pork flavour. The USDA match is Turkey bacon, cooked, which is a different meat (turkey rather than pork), usually made from turkey thigh or processed turkey meat formed into strips with a different fat profile, flavour and texture. Under guideline F, a different cut or type of meat is not substitutable. Condition 1: turkey bacon could be heated in a similar way, but it is a different product from the ingredient and would change the dish's flavour base. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in taste (turkey versus smoked pork), texture (strips versus firm round slices, different fat and moisture), and appearance. Both conditions fail, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is colby cheese powder, a dehydrated, processed form of colby cheese, usually sold as a dry seasoning or mix component. The USDA match, 'Cheese, colby', is the natural block or sliced cheese. Condition 1 fails: the powder cannot replace the block cheese without changing preparation. It would be added dry or dissolved into a sauce, not grated, melted, or cubed. Condition 2 also fails: the powder has a different texture, a more concentrated and dusty flavour, and a different appearance (a powdery coating rather than cheese pieces). Guideline F treats a different state (dried or processed vs. natural) as not substitutable, so the match is rejected.

Ingredient: pecan halves, the default plain form of pecans; quantity (20g) is ignored. USDA entry: Nuts, pecans, halves, raw. This is the same food in the same plain state. 'Halves' matches the ingredient directly, and 'raw' means uncooked, which is the default for pecan halves used in a recipe unless the recipe calls for toasting, which is not stated. Using the USDA halves entry would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

Condition 1: The ingredient is a canned, ready-to-drink meal replacement shake. The USDA entry is a ready-to-drink nutritional drink or shake. Both are the same product type and can be used without changing preparation, since neither requires cooking or mixing. Condition 2: Ensure Plus is a branded product in this category, and under guideline G a branded entry of the same plain product type matches. Meal replacement shakes do differ in flavour, sweetness and calorie content between brands and varieties, so a diner might notice a difference in a specific case. However, the ingredient does not name a brand, flavour or formulation, so the generic category match is the relevant comparison. Both conditions are met on that basis.

The ingredient is smoked pork fillet, a smoked (processed) pork cut. The USDA match is 'Pork, tenderloin', which is the raw/fresh unsmoked pork tenderloin. Pork fillet is in fact the same cut as tenderloin, so the cut matches. However, guideline F states that plain versus smoked is a different state, and the smoked preparation changes flavour, colour, and texture, which a diner would notice. The match is therefore the unsmoked version of the food, not the smoked product. Condition 1 might be met if the dish were cooked from raw, but the recipe calls for smoked meat, so the substitution would change the dish's flavour and appearance. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the absence of smoke flavour and the different appearance.

The ingredient is 1 cup of ripe bananas, chopped. Chopping is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C), so the question is whether 'overripe' matches 'ripe'. Guideline F explicitly lists a different ripeness (ripe vs overripe) as not substitutable, because overripe bananas are noticeably sweeter, softer, and more intensely flavoured, and their texture and appearance (darker skin and flesh) differ. Condition 1 (same preparation) is arguably met, but condition 2 fails: a diner could notice the difference in flavour and texture. The match is therefore not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh ground pork, which is raw meat that the recipe will cook. The USDA entry is 'Pork, fresh, ground, cooked', which is already cooked. Guideline F states that raw vs cooked is a different state and is not substitutable. Using pre-cooked pork would change the cooking method, since the meat would not need or receive the same cooking, and would change texture and appearance (for example, it would not brown or firm up the same way). Condition 1 therefore fails. Condition 2 also fails, because a diner could notice differences in texture and appearance. The match is the same food only in its cooked state, not the raw state the ingredient calls for.

The ingredient is plain ketchup described only as 'good-quality', which does not request a reduced-sodium product. The USDA entry is 'Ketchup, reduced sodium', a modified version of the standard product. Guideline D says a plain ingredient matched to a reduced/low-sodium version is not a match. Reduced sodium also changes taste: the product is less salty, and a diner could notice this. Condition 2 therefore fails. Quantity is ignored per guideline A, and 'good-quality' does not imply the modified variant.

The ingredient is plain brussels sprouts with the quantity given as a decorative leading weight, which is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Brussels sprouts, raw' is literally the same food in its uncooked, default form. No cooking method is implied by the ingredient, so the match does not alter preparation. Taste, texture and appearance are identical between the raw USDA entry and the plain ingredient. Both conditions are met.

Apple butter is a cooked, concentrated, sweetened and typically spiced apple purée reduced to a thick, smooth spread. 'Apple, baked' is whole or sliced apple flesh cooked in its own form, with a chunky texture and milder, less concentrated flavour. Condition 1 fails: apple butter is a spread or ingredient that would be measured and mixed in, while baked apple is a solid fruit preparation that would have to be mashed and seasoned to approximate it, which changes preparation. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (smooth, dense paste vs. soft pieces) and in flavour (concentrated sweetness and spice vs. plain baked apple). Apple butter is a processed product, not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is bottled, unsweetened black tea, which is the same product as USDA's 'Tea, iced, bottled, black, unsweetened'. The 'iced' descriptor just describes how bottled black tea is normally served and sold, so it does not change the product. Bottled and unsweetened both match the ingredient. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same liquid used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not taste or see a difference, because it is the same bottled unsweetened black tea. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is full-fat soy flour, which retains the oil from the soybean (typically around 20% fat) and is used in baking and cooking for its richness, moisture, and flavour. The USDA match, Soy flour, defatted, has had most of the fat removed, which is a different processed product with a different fat content. Under guideline F, a different fat or processed state is not substitutable. Removing fat changes the flavour (less richness, more bean-forward or drier taste), the texture (drier, different crumb and moisture retention, different browning and absorption), and the appearance (lighter colour in some uses). A diner would plausibly notice the difference in a 400g quantity used as a major component. Guideline A says to ignore quantity, so the large amount does not change the analysis. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would be altered by different liquid absorption and fat needs, and condition 2 fails because taste and texture would differ noticeably.

The ingredient is beef neck bones, and the USDA entry is 'Beef, neck bones', which is the same food under the same name. The entry gives no cooking state, so it is the generic raw cut, matching the plain ingredient as bought. The quantity (1 lb) is ignored per guideline A. Swapping one for the other would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is spaghetti squash that has been cooked (375g cooked vegetable spaghetti). The USDA entry is the same food, but raw. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that makes items non-substitutable. Cooking changes texture (raw squash is firm and crunchy, while cooked squash separates into soft strands) and flavour, and a diner would notice the difference. Cooking is not knife work or handling of the kind listed in guideline C, so the raw entry does not match the cooked ingredient. Condition 1 fails because the dish cannot be prepared with raw squash in place of cooked without changing the method. Condition 2 fails because the texture and taste differ.

The ingredient is dried salted cod (bacalao), a salt-cured and air-dried product that must be soaked and desalted before use. The USDA entry is fresh Atlantic cod that has been cooked by dry heat. The two differ in state (cured and dried versus fresh and cooked), so the cooking method would change: the dish would need soaking and desalting rather than cooking from cooked fish. Flavour would differ because of the salt curing and drying, and texture would differ because dried salt cod is dense and firm while dry-heat cooked cod is flaky and moist. A diner would notice the difference. Although both come from cod, guideline F treats a different processed state as not substitutable, so the match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is fresh papaya. The USDA match is dried papaya. Dried papaya is a processed, dehydrated product with a much higher sugar concentration, chewy leathery texture, and concentrated flavour, and it is a different state from fresh fruit. Per guideline F, raw/fresh versus processed/dried is a different state and not substitutable. Using dried papaya in place of fresh would change the texture, flavour and appearance of the dish, and a diner would notice. The weight (135g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would change, and condition 2 fails because taste and texture would differ.

The ingredient is black olives that have been sliced. Sliced is knife work the recipe performs, so per guideline C it does not change the match. The USDA entry 'Olives, black' names the same food with no state or modification, so it is the generic food. Condition 1: the olives can be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, since slicing is done by the cook. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance between the USDA olive and the sliced black olive. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain yogurt, a fresh, unsweetened, cultured dairy product. The USDA match is frozen yogurt, a separate product that is typically sweetened, flavoured, and churned or frozen. Condition 1: it cannot be used in place of plain yogurt without changing preparation. Frozen yogurt would need to be thawed or it would stay solid, and it would not behave like plain yogurt in marinades, sauces, or baking. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Frozen yogurt is sweeter, has a cold, icy or creamy-frozen texture, and differs in taste and appearance from plain yogurt. Guideline D's allowance for normally low-fat flavoured yogurts does not apply, because frozen yogurt is a different product state (frozen dessert) rather than a flavoured version of plain yogurt. Both conditions fail.

1. Identity: the ingredient is guacamole with tomatoes, and the USDA entry is 'Guacamole with tomatoes'. These are the same dish with the same components, so the match is on identity (guideline D/B).
2. Frozen/thawed: guideline E says a USDA entry that names only the food, with no state (fresh, frozen, or cooked), is the generic food and matches fresh, thawed or plain versions. The USDA entry has no state descriptor, so the thawed product matches it.
3. Preparation: the ingredient is used as guacamole, the same way the USDA food is used. Thawing does not change how the dish is prepared, so condition 1 holds.
4. Sensory check: thawed guacamole can be slightly softer or darker than fresh, but the guidelines treat the generic entry as covering thawed versions. Condition 2 is judged against the generic food, so no meaningful difference is assumed here.
5. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient 'burger rolls' is the same food as a hamburger bun under another name (guideline B). The USDA entry 'Roll, white, hamburger bun' is the default plain version, with no modifying descriptor such as sweetened, toasted, or flavoured (guideline D). The leading quantity and the word 'large' are decoration and do not change the match (guideline A). Condition 1: a hamburger bun can replace a burger roll without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since they are the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cooked pumpkin with salt added. The USDA entry is pumpkin, cooked, boiled, drained, with salt, so it is the same food in the same state (cooked) with the same added seasoning (salt). Guideline A says to ignore the leading 1g. The 'boiled, drained' wording describes the standard way cooked pumpkin is prepared and does not change the product. Condition 1: the ingredient is already cooked and salted, so the match could replace it without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would not taste or see a difference, since the salt level and cooked texture are the same. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is a combination of two foods: paneer cubes and chopped spinach. The USDA entry 'Cheese, paneer' is the same food as the paneer component (condition B and D are met for that part). However, it contains no spinach, so using it in place of the ingredient would drop one of the two components. That changes the dish's preparation and appearance: the green chopped spinach would be missing, and a diner would notice the difference in appearance, flavour and texture. Condition 1 (no change to how the dish is prepared) and condition 2 (diner would not notice a difference) both fail. The quantity (30g) is ignored per guideline A. Not substitutable.

Choucroute is the French name for sauerkraut, so this is the same food under a regional or culinary name (guideline B). The USDA entry 'Sauerkraut' is the standard default version of the product, with no modification or added flavour (guideline D). Quantity is ignored (guideline A). Sauerkraut can be used in place of choucroute without changing the preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is eggnog, and the USDA entry is 'Eggnog', which is the same food under the same name. The leading '30g' is quantity and is ignored. 'Chilled' describes how the product is stored and served, so it does not change the match (guideline C). Eggnog is normally sold chilled, so the standard default version matches (guideline D). Using the USDA eggnog in place of chilled eggnog would not change how the dish is prepared, and a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is cooked spiny lobster meat. The USDA entry is spiny lobster (mixed species), cooked by moist heat, which describes the same food in the same state (cooked meat). The weight is decoration and is ignored. The 'moist heat' descriptor only states how the lobster was cooked, which is the normal way cooked lobster is prepared and sold, so it is the standard default version rather than a modified one. Substituting it would not change how the dish is prepared, since the meat is already cooked. A diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same species in the same cooked state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is fresh beech mushrooms (shimeji), a distinct mushroom species with small clustered stems, small caps, and a nutty, slightly sweet flavour with a firm, crisp-tender texture. The USDA match is shiitake mushrooms, raw, a different species with larger caps, a meatier and more smoky or earthy flavour, and a chewier texture. Condition 1: the two are not the same food under another name, and substituting shiitake changes the appearance of the dish (cluster form and cap size) and how it cooks, since shiitake caps and stems are handled differently and typically need longer cooking. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the different flavour, texture and look. Under guideline F, a different variety with a different taste is not substitutable. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is smoked haddock. The USDA entry, 'Fish, haddock, NFS', is plain haddock with no smoking specified. Under guideline F, a plain ingredient versus a smoked version is a different state. Smoking adds a strong flavour and changes the texture and appearance, and a diner would notice the difference. The match therefore fails condition 2 (taste, texture and appearance would differ), and it also fails condition 1 because smoking is a processing step the plain fish does not undergo. Quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is ketchup, with a typo ('ketcup'), used as an optional dip. The leading '250g' quantity is decoration and is ignored. The USDA entry 'Ketchup' is the same plain product under the standard name, with no modifier such as low-sodium, reduced-sugar, or flavoured. Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient for dipping without changing preparation.
