Product identity: 'quinoa pasta' is a quinoa-based pasta, and the USDA entry is a branded (Ancient Harvest) gluten-free corn and quinoa pasta. That is the same product type, so the identity check passes under guidelines B and G. State: the ingredient is listed as plain 'quinoa pasta' with no preparation stated, so the default is dry, uncooked pasta as bought. The USDA entry is 'cooked'. Guideline F treats raw versus cooked as a different state, not a match. Preparation: using cooked pasta in place of dry pasta changes how the dish is prepared, because the pasta would not be boiled in the recipe, which fails condition 1. Taste and texture: cooked pasta in the dish would be noticeably different from dry pasta that is cooked within it, which affects condition 2 as well. The 35g weight is ignored per guideline A. Because the state differs, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is sliced pepperoni, a cured sausage. The USDA entry is 'Pepperoni, beef and pork, sliced', which is the same product with the standard beef and pork composition and the same sliced form. Knife work (sliced) does not change the match (guideline C). The default pepperoni is a beef and pork product, so this is the plain standard version rather than a modified one (guideline D). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is used the same way in the dish. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same sliced pepperoni. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 'baloney, sliced'. 'Baloney' is a common regional spelling and name for bologna, the same cured sausage product. Under guideline B, regional and trade names for the same food count as the same food. The weight (150g) is ignored per guideline A, and 'sliced' is knife work that does not change the match (guideline C). Condition 1: the bologna can be used in place of baloney with no change to how the dish is prepared. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is mustard oil, a pressed oil extracted from mustard seeds and used as a cooking fat or flavouring. The USDA entry, Mustard greens, fresh, cooked, fat added, is a cooked leafy vegetable with fat added. These are different foods, not the same food under another name, so condition B does not apply. Using cooked greens in place of an oil would change the dish's composition: the diner would get solid vegetable matter instead of a liquid fat with mustard's pungent flavour. Condition 1 fails because the preparation would change, and condition 2 fails because taste, texture and appearance would all differ. Guideline F also rules out a source plant versus its processed ingredient.

The ingredient is crushed pineapple, a fruit product with visible fruit pieces and pulp that stays in the dish. The USDA entry is 100% pineapple juice, a liquid with the pulp removed. Condition 1 fails: juice cannot replace crushed fruit without changing how the dish is prepared, since it adds liquid volume and drops the solid fruit that would normally be stirred or folded in. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the missing fruit pieces and the different texture and appearance. This is the raw/processed and form difference the guidelines treat as non-substitutable. The 100g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is pickled egg, sliced: a hard-boiled egg preserved in a vinegar brine, typically with added salt, spices and sometimes beet or other colouring. The USDA match is raw whole egg. Condition 1 fails: a raw egg cannot stand in for a pickled egg without changing the preparation, since the pickling step is the defining process and a raw egg would need cooking and brining. Condition 2 fails: the raw egg is uncooked, has a liquid yolk and white rather than a firm set texture, and lacks the sour, salty, spiced flavour and the characteristic pickled appearance. A diner would clearly notice. Raw vs processed/pickled is a different state, so it is not a same-food match under the annotation guidelines.

The ingredient is kiwi fruit, and the USDA match is 'Kiwi fruit, raw', which is literally the same food. The leading '300g' quantity is ignored per guideline A. The plain ingredient maps to the standard default raw version (guideline D), and 'raw' simply means uncooked, which is the state in which kiwi fruit is normally eaten or used (guideline C). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same fruit in the same state. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is veal shank, a specific cut from the leg that is tough, rich in connective tissue, and normally braised or stewed until tender. The USDA match is veal sirloin, separable lean only, raw, a different cut from a different section of the animal. Guideline F explicitly lists a different cut of meat as not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: sirloin is leaner and more tender, so it would not be prepared the same way as shank (the long, slow cooking needed to break down shank's collagen would leave sirloin dry and tough). Condition 2 also fails: the texture, mouthfeel, and body of the sauce would differ, and a diner would likely notice. The cubing is handling and does not change the match, and the 200g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain cheese-filled tortellini (the standard default product, with no sauce implied by 'plain'). The USDA entry 'Tortellini, cheese-filled, no sauce' is the same food with the same components (cheese-filled pasta, unsauced). Guideline D treats a plain ingredient matched to its standard default version as a match, and 'no sauce' simply describes the plain state rather than a flavoured or modified version. Quantity (210g) is ignored per guideline A. The product can be used in the same preparation without changing cooking method, flavour, texture, or appearance, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is pumpkin pie spice blend, a mixture of ground spices typically including cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, and cloves (sometimes allspice or cardamom in smaller amounts). The USDA match is 'Spices, cardamom', which is a single spice (cardamom) with a distinct, strong floral-citrusy flavour. Condition 1: Cardamom could be used in place of the blend mechanically, since both are ground spices added in the same way, so the preparation method is unchanged. Condition 2: A diner would notice the difference. Pumpkin pie spice's characteristic warm cinnamon-nutmeg-clove profile would be replaced by cardamom alone, clearly altering the flavour. Per guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend containing it is not substitutable. The quantity (10g) is ignored. Therefore the match fails both the flavour condition and the blend-versus-single-ingredient rule.

The ingredient is dried figs, a whole dried fruit. The USDA match is 'Cookie, fig bar', a baked sandwich-style cookie with a fig paste filling inside a dough. Condition 1 fails: dried figs cannot replace a fig bar without changing preparation, since the dish would need a baked, processed product instead of whole fruit. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (soft, chewy whole fruit vs. a crisp or soft baked cookie), appearance, and flavour (added sugar, flour, fat, and spices). This is not the same food under another name, and it is a processed product rather than the raw or dried source (guideline F). Not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain catfish fillets (raw, uncooked, default version). The USDA match is 'CRACKER BARREL, farm raised catfish platter', a branded restaurant-style prepared platter. Condition 1: a platter is a ready-made dish (typically breaded and fried, served with sides in a restaurant product), so using it in place of raw catfish fillets would change the preparation method, since the fillet would need to be cooked from raw rather than used as a finished, coated product. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance, because breading, seasoning and frying are added and the item is not the same food as plain catfish fillet. The match is a prepared product with added components, not the same plain food under another name, so it does not satisfy either condition.

The ingredient is pickled turkey sausage, so the meat is turkey. The USDA entry 'Pickled sausage' does not name a meat, and USDA's generic pickled sausage is typically pork-based. Turkey and pork are different meats with different flavour, fat content and texture. A diner would likely notice the difference, and the entry does not name the same product. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is braunschweiger, a German smoked liver sausage. The USDA entry is the same product: Braunschweiger (liver sausage), pork. The word 'smoked' in the ingredient describes how braunschweiger is normally made and sold, so it is not a modification that the USDA entry lacks (guideline D). The weight '400g' is ignored (guideline A). Using the USDA entry in place of the ingredient would not change preparation, and a diner would not taste, feel or see a difference because it is the same food.

The ingredient is cooked peppers and onions, and the USDA entry is peppers and onions, cooked, with no added fat. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. The food is the same (peppers and onions) in the same state (cooked), so the components match (guideline B and C). The ingredient does not specify any added fat, so the plain default is cooked without added fat. Guideline C treats a standard descriptor on the same dish as still a match, as with 'cooked, fat added' for buttered peas and carrots. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since the recipe already calls for cooked peppers and onions. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the ingredient itself names no fat or flavour that the USDA entry lacks.

The ingredient is smoked milkfish, which is milkfish that has been smoke-processed. The USDA match is 'Fish, milkfish, raw', which is unsmoked, uncooked fish. Smoking changes the flavour (smoky, more savoury), the texture (firmer, drier flesh), and the appearance (colour and surface). A diner would notice the difference in taste and texture. Guideline F explicitly lists 'plain vs toasted/smoked/roasted' as a different state that is not substitutable. The weight '200g' is ignored per guideline A. Because the match changes the flavour and texture and would not be undetectable to the diner, condition 2 fails, and condition 1 also fails because the recipe would need smoking to be prepared as intended.

The ingredient is barley flour (ground barley grain, a whole-grain-type flour). The USDA entry is 'Barley flour or meal', which is the same food under the same name. Quantity (285g) is ignored per guideline A. The product is the plain flour as normally sold, with no modification, flavour, or cooking state difference. Using it in place of barley flour would not change preparation, taste, texture, or appearance, so both conditions are met.

The ingredient is toasted wheat bread, and the USDA entry is 'Bread, wheat, toasted', which is the same food in the same state. The 30g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the toasted wheat bread can be used directly in place of the USDA toasted wheat bread without changing preparation, since both are already toasted. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the food is the same product in the same toasted state. The plain-vs-toasted rule in F applies only when one side is toasted and the other is not, which is not the case here. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a fresh artichoke, which in culinary use means the globe artichoke (Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus), the flower bud of a thistle. The USDA entry is Jerusalem artichoke (sunchoke), a tuber from a sunflower species (Helianthus tuberosus). These are different plants, not regional or trade names for the same food. Condition 1 fails: a Jerusalem artichoke has a different preparation profile (peeled tuber rather than trimmed bud, different cooking times and methods). Condition 2 fails: a diner would taste a starchy, sweet, nutty tuber in place of a tender, vegetal bud, and the texture and appearance would differ. The quantity is irrelevant. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is cashew butter. The word 'ground' describes how the nuts were processed into a paste, which is what cashew butter already is, so it is the same food under a descriptive name (guideline B). The USDA entry 'Cashew butter' is the plain, standard product with no added flavour, sweetener, or modification (guideline D). Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since no cooking method or handling differs. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is nonfat peach Greek yogurt. The USDA entry is Yogurt, Greek, nonfat, peach, CHOBANI, which describes the same product: nonfat Greek yogurt with peach flavour, from a brand. Quantity (75g) is ignored per guideline A. Guideline G says a branded entry of the same product type matches, and the entry adds no modification beyond what the ingredient asks for (nonfat and peach are both stated in the ingredient). Condition 1: the yogurt can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: the flavour, fat level and texture are the same, so a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is sweetened rice milk. The USDA match is unsweetened rice milk. Guideline D states that sweetened/unsweetened is a modification, so a plain ingredient mapped to a modified version is not acceptable, and the same applies when the ingredient itself asks for the sweetened version and the match is unsweetened. Condition 1: swapping sweetened for unsweetened rice milk would not change the cooking method in the abstract, but the sugar content is a different product. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the absence of sweetness in a drink or in a dish where the sweetened milk contributes flavour, so the taste differs. Both conditions are not clearly met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh loquats, sliced. The USDA match is Apple, baked, which is a cooked apple product. Condition 1: loquats are a different fruit from apples and would not be substituted for apples without changing the preparation. Apple, baked implies the fruit has been cooked and is typically softened and sweetened or spiced, whereas fresh loquats are raw and eaten uncooked or used raw in the dish, so the cooking state differs and the preparation would change. Condition 2: loquats have a distinct sweet-tart, apricot-like flavour with a juicy texture and a different appearance (small, orange, with large seeds), while baked apple is soft, cooked, and apple-flavoured. A diner would readily notice the difference. The match is a different food (not a regional name for the same food) and differs in state (raw vs baked), so it does not qualify under the guidelines.

The ingredient is ramen noodles: wheat-flour noodles, typically sold fresh or dried, made from wheat flour, water, salt and kansui (alkaline agent), giving them a yellow colour, chewy springy texture and distinct flavour. The USDA match is 'Rice noodles, dry', which is made from rice flour and is a different food: different base grain, different texture (more brittle and less elastic), different colour (white versus yellow), and different taste. Condition 1 fails because rice noodles require a different preparation (soaking or brief boiling rather than the boiling time and handling ramen needs, and they do not carry the kansui-alkaline character), so the cooking method would change. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would notice the difference in texture, flavour and appearance. This is not the same food under another name, and it is not a plain/default version of the same product, so guideline B does not apply. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is 200 g of extra-lean ground turkey. The weight is decoration (guideline A). In US retail, 'extra-lean' ground turkey is conventionally the 93% lean / 7% fat product, so the USDA entry 'Turkey, ground, 93% lean, 7% fat, raw' is the same food under a common descriptor (guideline B). The entry is raw, which matches the uncooked ingredient, and the recipe's handling does not change the match (guideline C). Ground meat is normally cooked or mixed, so the match holds (guideline E). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same cut and form of ground turkey. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the fat content is the same as what a shopper would buy as extra-lean. Both conditions are met.

Chicken flats and drumettes are the two segments of a chicken wing, the flat (middle section) and the drumette (upper section). The USDA entry is for broiler or fryer wing, meat and skin, raw, which is the same food as a whole wing. Guideline B treats a cut or part of the same food as a match. Guideline C says that raw handling such as separating the wing into segments does not change the match. Flats and drumettes are normally sold skin-on, which matches the USDA entry's inclusion of skin. Using the wing entry would not change the cooking method, since wing segments are cooked the same way. The diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because the pieces are the same chicken wing parts. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is turkey breast, which is the light meat of the turkey. The USDA entry 'Turkey, light meat, skin not eaten' describes the same cut: the breast, with the skin excluded. Skin not eaten is the standard default way to eat it, not a modification, and the entry names no cooking state, so it is the generic food. Condition 1: the match could replace turkey breast in the same preparation without changing the method. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same meat. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain kefir, the standard unflavoured fermented milk. The USDA entry is a lowfat kefir with added strawberry flavour. Condition 1: swapping in strawberry kefir would not change the preparation method, but it fails condition 2. Guideline D says a plain ingredient matched to a flavoured or modified version is not substitutable. The guideline's exception for flavoured yogurt applies because flavoured yogurt is what shoppers normally buy under the yogurt name. Plain kefir is normally sold unflavoured, so strawberry kefir differs from what a shopper would expect. A diner would taste strawberry, and the lowfat descriptor also departs from the default. Both conditions are not met.

The ingredient is a yellow apple with skin on, with no specific variety named. Golden Delicious is a yellow-skinned apple and is the standard example of that category, so it fits the ingredient's description. The USDA entry specifies 'with skin', which matches 'skin on'. Both are raw, so no cooking change applies. The ingredient's stated 40g is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1 is met because the match can replace the apple without changing preparation. Condition 2 is met because a diner would not reliably distinguish a Golden Delicious from another yellow apple, since the recipe does not specify a variety and the guideline on sibling varieties applies to named varieties with different taste, such as Fuji vs Granny Smith.

The ingredient is 'egg substitute', a manufactured product, typically liquid egg whites with added gums, colouring, stabilisers and flavourings, and usually without yolk. The USDA match is 'Egg, whole, raw, fresh', which is the plain whole egg. Condition 1: an egg substitute is a different product from a whole egg, so using whole egg changes the ingredient, though it could often be used in the same cooking method. Condition 2: a diner could notice differences. Whole egg has yolk fat, richer flavour, and a yellow colour that egg-white-based substitutes lack or only partly match, and texture can differ in scrambled, custard or binding uses. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient is not interchangeable with a modified or additive-containing version, and under guideline F, a processed product is not the same as its raw source. The weight prefix is ignored. Both conditions are not met, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried oregano (a dried herb). The USDA match is 'Spices, oregano, dried', which is the same food: dried oregano leaves. Guideline F explicitly lists fresh vs dried herb as a state difference, but here both sides are dried, so that distinction does not apply. The quantity (5g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: dried oregano can directly replace dried oregano with no change in preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice any difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same spice. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain fresh mangosteen. The USDA entry is canned mangosteen in syrup. Condition 1: canned fruit cannot replace fresh fruit without changing preparation. Fresh mangosteen is eaten or used raw, while the canned version is already cooked or processed and sealed in syrup, so the dish's preparation changes. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference. Canned fruit in syrup is sweeter, softer, and has a different texture and flavour from fresh mangosteen. Guideline D says canned fruit is normally in syrup, but that does not make it the plain fresh fruit. Guideline F rejects a different state (fresh vs processed) and a different packing medium (syrup pack). Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is a dry pico de gallo seasoning blend. Pico de gallo seasoning is a blend of spices and herbs (typically including chili pepper, onion, garlic, cumin, salt, and sometimes cilantro/lime notes), not a single ingredient. The USDA match 'Spices, pepper, red or cayenne' is a single spice (ground cayenne/red pepper) with no other components. Per guideline F, a single ingredient versus a blend containing it is not substitutable. Condition 1 fails: swapping in cayenne alone changes the flavour profile of the seasoning, since the blend's cumin, garlic, onion and other components would be missing. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would taste the difference, as the dish would lose the characteristic pico de gallo seasoning flavour and be overly hot and one-dimensional. Quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is custard apple (Annona squamosa, also called sugar apple), a tropical fruit in the genus Annona. The USDA match is Apples, dried, sulfured, which is Malus domestica, a different fruit. This is not a regional or trade name for the same food, so guideline B does not apply. Custard apple has a creamy, sweet, custard-like flesh with a distinct aroma, while dried sulfured apple is firm, chewy, tart-sweet, and has the sulfur-treated appearance of dried apple. A diner would notice the difference in taste, texture, and appearance. Quantity and knife work (sliced) are ignored per guidelines A and C. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is sunflower oil, and the USDA entry is 'Sunflower oil', which is the same food. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. 'Mixed' describes handling (it is mixed into the recipe), which does not change the match per guideline C. Condition 1: the oil can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same oil. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a porterhouse steak, a specific beef cut from the short loin. The USDA entry is the same cut, described as raw porterhouse steak with separable lean and fat trimmed to 1/8" fat. Condition 1: the steak can replace the ingredient without changing preparation. Cooking method stays the same (grilling, pan-searing or broiling), and the 1/8" trim is the standard retail trim, so the steak is prepared as usual. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same cut with normal fat trimming. The grade descriptor 'choice' is a standard grade for this cut and does not change the match, and the weight is ignored per guideline A. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is Italian salami, a cured sausage. The USDA entry is 'Salami, Italian, pork', which names the same product. Italian salami is conventionally made from pork, so the USDA entry is the standard default version and not a modified, different-cut, or processed variant. The '300g' quantity and '(optional garnish)' note are decoration and do not affect the match. Condition 1: the salami can be used as a garnish in place of the USDA item with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same food. Both conditions are met.

The recipe specifies unsalted butter, and the USDA match is salted butter. Salted butter contains added salt, so it differs from the ingredient in flavour. Condition 1 (no change in preparation) is arguably met, since butter is used as a garnish either way. Condition 2 fails: as a garnish, the butter is eaten largely unmixed, so a diner would likely taste the added salt. Salted vs unsalted is a sodium modification of the plain product, which the guidelines treat as a flavour change, so the match is not substitutable.

Condition 1: The ingredient is oatmeal bread that has been toasted, and the USDA entry is 'Bread, oatmeal, toasted', which names the same product in the same state. The ingredient already calls for toasted bread, so the match requires no change to cooking method or handling. 'Good-quality' describes a grade of the same product, not a modification such as a flavour or reduced-fat version. Condition 2: Toasted oatmeal bread in the USDA entry is the same food, so a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is 1 lb of raw ground pork, with no specified lean ratio or cooked state. The USDA match is 'Pork, ground, 84% lean / 16% fat, cooked, crumbles', so it is a cooked product. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Using pre-cooked crumbles would change the cooking method, since raw pork must be cooked in the dish, and the texture, appearance and moisture would differ from raw ground pork. The match fails condition 1 because it cannot be used without changing how the dish is prepared, and it fails condition 2 because a diner could notice the difference in texture and appearance. The lean percentage is not the deciding issue; the cooked state is.

The ingredient is a whole chicken, which is a raw, uncooked bird that the recipe will prepare itself. The USDA match is 'Chicken, broiler, rotisserie, BBQ, skin', which is a cooked product that has already been roasted on a rotisserie and seasoned with barbecue flavouring, with skin included. Condition 1 fails: using a pre-cooked, BBQ-flavoured bird would change the cooking method, since the recipe would need raw chicken to be cooked and the match is already cooked. Condition 2 also fails: the diner would taste barbecue seasoning and rotisserie browning, and the appearance and texture would differ from a plain raw-cooked whole chicken. Per guideline F, raw vs cooked and plain vs flavoured are not substitutable, and the weight is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is green leaf lettuce, wilted (the word 'wilded' is read as 'wilted'). The USDA entry is 'Lettuce, wilted, with bacon dressing', a prepared dish. Condition 1: the match adds a bacon dressing, which is a component the recipe does not call for. Using it would change the dish's preparation, since the lettuce would arrive already dressed. Condition 2: a diner would taste bacon fat, smoke and sweet-sour dressing, which the plain green leaf lettuce does not have. The match is not the same food under another name (guideline B), and it adds a flavour (guideline F/G-style modification). Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is leftover cooked fajita meat, and the USDA entry 'Fajita, beef or pork' is the same dish: cooked fajita meat seasoned in the standard fajita style. The ingredient does not name the protein, so the USDA entry's beef-or-pork scope fits it; the amount (100g) is ignored per guideline A. Leftover fajita meat is already cooked, which matches the cooked USDA product, and reheating does not change the match. The USDA name matches the ingredient's dish and components, so under guideline C it is a match. Condition 1 holds because it can be used directly without changing preparation. Condition 2 holds because a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same fajita-style meat. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is raw Pacific cod, a plain fish with no stated cooking or coating. The USDA entry is 'Fish, cod, baked or broiled, coated', which is a cooked, breaded or coated product. Guideline F rules out a raw-versus-cooked state difference, and the coating adds a visible and tasted difference. Using the cooked, coated entry would change how the dish is prepared (the fish would arrive already cooked and breaded) and a diner would notice the coating and altered texture. Condition 1 fails, and condition 2 also fails. The cod species matches, but the product state does not.

The ingredient is plain 'woven wheat crackers', which a shopper would normally buy as the standard product. The USDA entry is 'Crackers, woven wheat, reduced fat', a modified version with a reduced fat content. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a reduced/low modified version is not a match, and reduced fat is not how woven wheat crackers are normally sold. The cooking method would not change, but the fat content differs from the standard product, so a diner could notice a difference in taste and texture. Condition 2 is not met.

The ingredient is fresh turkey sausage, a raw or fresh poultry sausage that must be cooked before eating. The USDA match, 'Pickled sausage', is a different product: it is preserved in brine or vinegar, typically a ready-to-eat processed meat, and its flavour is sour and tangy. Condition 1 fails because it would change how the dish is prepared, since fresh sausage is cooked and pickled sausage is not. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would taste the sour, pickled flavour and notice a different meat and texture. Ignoring the quantity and the minor spelling 'turky' does not change this. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain tartar sauce, and the USDA match is 'Tartar sauce', which is the same food under the same name with no added modifier or different state. Quantity (30g) is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: tartar sauce can directly replace tartar sauce without any change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is smoked turkey meat, and the USDA entry is smoked turkey (light or dark meat, skin not eaten), so the food itself matches. The entry does not specify a cut, and the 150g quantity is ignored per guideline A. The skin descriptor is handling, not a modification. Both are smoked, so the flavour issue does not arise. However, the ingredient is smoked meat, so the match is not in question. The remaining question is whether the entry's cut mix (light or dark) and its smoked state fit the ingredient. Smoked turkey meat is a smoked product, so the entry's smoked state matches. Light or dark mix is a generic turkey meat blend, which is the standard default for unspecified turkey meat. Both conditions are met: the same smoked turkey could be used without changing preparation, and a diner would not taste a difference.

The ingredient is white bean sauce, a fermented soybean condiment that is lighter in colour and milder, and is often made with a different flavour profile. The USDA match is black bean sauce, a fermented black soybean product that is darker, saltier, and more pungent. These are sibling products with different flavour and appearance, not the same food under another name. Guideline F applies: a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable. Using black bean sauce would change the dish's flavour and colour, and a diner would notice the difference. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient 'paw-paw' is a recognized alternate spelling and regional name for the pawpaw (Asimina triloba), the same fruit as the USDA entry 'Pawpaw, peeled, seeded, raw'. Under guideline B, this is the same food under another name. The weight '220g' is decoration (guideline A). 'Peeled, seeded' describes handling the recipe itself and does not change the match (guideline C), and 'raw' means uncooked, which fits a fresh fruit used as an ingredient. The default version of the plain fruit is the entry matched, with no modification, flavouring or sweetening (guideline D). Neither a change in cooking method nor a difference in taste, texture or appearance is implied. One caveat: in Australian and some other usage, 'paw paw' refers to papaya, which would be a different food. The ingredient string as written most directly names the pawpaw, so the match is accepted, though the regional ambiguity is noted.

The ingredient is dried cod, ground to a powder at home. Per guideline C, grinding is handling the recipe does itself and does not change the match. The USDA entry is the same food, Atlantic cod. The added descriptor 'dried and salted' is the normal form in which dried cod is sold, since shoppers typically buy dried cod as salt cod (bacalao), so under guideline D it is the standard default version rather than a modification. Condition 1 is met: the same dried cod can be used without changing the preparation. Condition 2 is plausibly met: a diner would not notice a difference from the standard product. The main uncertainty is that 'dried cod' is not explicitly salted, and stockfish is unsalted, which would make the salt level differ. Applying the default-version rule, the match is accepted.

The ingredient is cold-pressed flax oil. The USDA entry, 'Oil, flaxseed, cold pressed', is the same product under a standard name. The quantity (100g) is ignored. Condition 1: the oil can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since it is used as a liquid fat and the cooking method stays the same. Condition 2: the oil is identical, so a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dry milk powder, a shelf-stable dehydrated product. The USDA entry is 'Milk, dry, reconstituted, nonfat', which is milk with water added back, so it is a liquid-state product. Using it in place of 100g of powder would change the dish's preparation: the liquid and water content would be different, so the recipe's hydration and method would need to change. It also carries the 'nonfat' modifier, which the plain ingredient does not specify. Condition 1 (no change to preparation) is not met. Because the state differs (dry powder vs reconstituted liquid), a diner or the dish's texture and structure could also change, so condition 2 is doubtful. The match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain 'turkey ham', an unspecified deli-style turkey ham. The USDA entry is the same food type (turkey ham, sliced, prepackaged or deli), so the product identity and the cut/form match. The concern is the descriptor 'extra lean'. Guideline D treats reduced-fat or lean-modified versions of a plain ingredient as a modification, not the default. Extra lean turkey ham is a specifically marketed lower-fat variant, which can be drier and firmer than standard turkey ham, so a diner could plausibly notice a texture difference. The 'normally sold this way' exception does not clearly apply, because a shopper buying plain turkey ham would not necessarily get the extra lean version. Preparation would not change, but the descriptor alters the product relative to the plain name, so the match fails the taste/texture condition.

The ingredient is frozen potato wedges, and the USDA entry is the same food in the same state: 'Potato wedges, frozen'. Per guideline E, a frozen product matches the frozen USDA entry of the same product. The parenthetical about the USDA Food Distribution Program is a standard descriptor and does not change the food. The 215g quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the frozen wedges can be used in place of the ingredient with the same preparation, such as baking or frying from frozen. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same frozen potato product.

The ingredient is powdered creamer, a non-dairy cream substitute sold in powder form for coffee and similar uses. The USDA entry 'Cream substitute, powdered, light' names the same product type under the standard USDA designation. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient directly, since both are added as powders to beverages or batters with no change to preparation. Condition 2: the 'light' descriptor reflects how powdered creamers are normally sold, not a modification of the plain product, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is green olive tapenade, pitted. The USDA entry is 'Olive tapenade', which is the generic product with no colour or olive-type specified. Tapenade is classically made from black olives, and green and black olive tapenades differ noticeably in colour (pale olive-green versus dark purple-black) and in flavour (green olives are firmer, tangier and more bitter). Guideline E lets a stateless generic entry match fresh or plain versions of the same food, but here the ingredient names a specific sub-variety that the entry does not confirm, and the variety changes taste and appearance. Condition 1 is met, since the tapenade would be used the same way. Condition 2 is not reliably met, because a diner could notice the difference in colour and flavour, as with a sibling variety under guideline F. The pitting is handling and does not affect the match.

Filberts are the same nut as hazelnuts; 'filberts' is a regional/trade name for hazelnuts, so the USDA entry 'Nuts, hazelnuts or filberts, raw' names the identical food. The quantity (75g) is decoration and is ignored. The ingredient is plain and unspecified, so the standard raw default matches. Condition 1: the nuts can be used in place of filberts without changing preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is literally the same food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a light creamy Italian dressing. The USDA entry, Creamy Italian dressing, light, describes the same product with the same descriptor (light) and only differs in word order. Condition 1: it can directly replace the ingredient in the same way, with no change to preparation, since both are used as a ready-made dressing. Condition 2: the same product type and fat level means no difference in taste, texture, or appearance is expected. The quantity prefix (50g) is ignored per guideline A. Because the ingredient itself asks for the light version, the matching light entry qualifies per guideline D. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is bacon grease, melted. The USDA entry 'Animal fat, bacon grease' is the same food under its standard name. Melting is preparation handling, which the guidelines say does not change the match. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing the preparation, since the grease is simply used in its liquid state. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same rendered bacon fat. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is wild plums, a plain fresh fruit with no preparation or processing stated. The USDA entry 'Plums, wild (Northern Plains Indians)' is the same food, a wild plum, identified by a regional/cultural name. Under guideline B, same food under another name counts as a match. The entry names no processed state such as dried, canned, or cooked, so it corresponds to the fresh fruit. Condition 1: it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since both are used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not detect a difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same fruit. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a plain, uncooked 'pork shank', which is a raw meat cut. The USDA entry is 'Pork, fresh, leg (ham), shank half, separable lean only, cooked, roasted'. It is the same cut, but it is cooked and roasted, and it is lean only. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state, not substitutable. Substituting cooked, roasted meat for raw meat would change how the dish is prepared, since the meat would need no cooking and would not brown or render in the same way. A diner would also notice differences in texture, appearance and flavour. Condition 1 fails, so the match is not substitutable. The quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is 75g unsalted almonds; the quantity is ignored per guideline A. The USDA entry 'Almonds, unsalted' is the same food with the same descriptor (unsalted), so it is the same product under the same name. Condition 1: it can be used directly in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, since the entry is the same unsalted almond. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is fresh chile negro, a fresh chile that is the fresh form of the pasilla/chilaca pepper. The USDA match is 'Peppers, pasilla, dried', which is the dried form. Guideline B could treat these as the same food under different names, but the states differ. Guideline F explicitly says fresh and dried items are not substitutable (fresh vs dried herb is given as an example, and the same logic applies to produce). Condition 1 fails: a dried pepper must be rehydrated, toasted, or soaked before use, and cannot be used as-is where a fresh chile is called for. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in texture (leathery and wrinkled versus fleshy), appearance, and flavour concentration. Because the match changes both preparation and sensory qualities, it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is fresh, uncooked pompano fillet. The USDA entry is 'Fish, pompano, fried', which is a cooked, breaded-and-fried product. Substituting it would change the cooking method: the recipe would need raw fish, but the match is already fried, so the dish could not be prepared the same way. Diners would also notice the difference in texture (crisp, oil-absorbed coating versus tender raw-to-cooked flesh) and appearance (golden fried exterior). Guideline F treats raw versus cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. The match fails condition 1 and condition 2.

The ingredient is pearl barley, which is pearled (polished) barley sold dry and uncooked. The USDA entry 'Barley, pearled, raw' describes the same food: pearled barley in its uncooked state. The leading '370g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: pearled barley can be used directly in place of the ingredient with the same preparation, such as simmering in liquid, with no change to the cooking method. Condition 2: the cooked grain would show no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is green seedless grapes, which are European grapes (Vitis vinifera) sold as a table grape. The USDA entry is muscadine grapes, a different species (Vitis rotundifolia) native to the southeastern United States. It is not the same food under another name. Muscadines have a thick skin, a tough pulp, a different and musky flavour, and usually contain large seeds, whereas green seedless grapes have a thin skin, sweet flesh, and no seeds. Condition 1 is not met: the match would change the dish's flavour, texture and appearance. Condition 2 is not met: a diner would notice the difference in taste, texture and seeds. Muscadine is a sibling variety with a different taste (guideline F), so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is liver from a Cornish hen, which is a young chicken, typically a Cornish cross bird. The USDA entry 'Chicken, liver, all classes, raw' covers liver from chickens of all classes, including young birds such as broilers and fryers, and Cornish hens fall within that. The entry is raw, matching the fresh ingredient, and the 100g weight is decoration. Condition 1: the liver can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since the handling and cooking are the same. Condition 2: liver from a young chicken differs little in taste, texture, or appearance from chicken liver of the 'all classes' mix, and a diner would not notice a difference. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is butternut squash that has been baked. The USDA entry is the same food, winter squash (butternut), prepared by the same method (baked). The quantity '5g' and the word '(divided)' are decoration and are ignored under guideline A. The 'without salt' descriptor is the default for plain baked squash, since the ingredient names no seasoning or salt, so it is not a modification (guideline D). Cooking method matches, so the dish would not be prepared differently. Taste, texture and appearance would also be the same, because the USDA entry describes the same baked butternut squash. Both conditions are met.

Condition 1: The ingredient is hi-oleic sunflower oil, a sunflower oil bred for high oleic acid (typically over 80%). The USDA entry is sunflower oil with less than 60% linoleic acid, which is the standard linoleic-type sunflower oil. Both are liquid vegetable oils and could be used in the same cooking method, but guideline F treats a different oil as not substitutable even when the oils look close. The fatty acid profile differs, which changes oxidative stability and smoke point, so frying or high-heat behaviour may change. Condition 1 is therefore not clearly met. Condition 2: The two oils are similar in colour, taste and texture, and a diner might not notice a difference in a finished dish. However, the oils are different products, and the oil-type rule in guideline F is explicit. Because condition 1 is not met under the guidelines, the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is queso anejo, an aged Mexican cheese. The USDA entry 'Cheese, mexican, queso anejo' names the same cheese, so it is the same food under the same name (guideline B). The quantity (75g) is ignored (guideline A). Condition 1: the match is the same product as bought, so it can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, such as crumbling or grating. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture, or appearance, because it is the same cheese. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a combined entry: 15g of semolina plus salt to taste. The USDA match, 'Semolina, unenriched', covers only the semolina. The semolina part is the same food, and the weight is ignored per guideline A. However, the ingredient also calls for salt, which the match does not represent. Using unsalted semolina in place of semolina-and-salt would change the flavour of the dish, and a diner would likely notice the lack of seasoning. Condition 2 therefore fails, because the match does not reproduce the full ingredient's taste.

The ingredient is a blend: peanut and raisin trail mix. It contains peanuts and raisins, and usually other components and seasoning. The USDA match is a single ingredient, roasted unsalted peanuts. Guideline F says a single ingredient versus a blend containing it is not substitutable. Using only peanuts would drop the raisins, which a diner would taste and see. The match also differs in salt content from typical trail mix. Condition 1 fails because the dish would not be prepared the same way without the raisins. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the missing raisins and different flavour and texture.

The ingredient is cocoa butter, the pressed fat from cocoa beans. The USDA entry 'Oil, cocoa butter' is the same food under its standard database name, so the identity matches (guideline B). 'Melted' describes handling before use, like chopped or softened, and does not change the food (guideline C). Condition 1: cocoa butter can be used directly in place of the melted version, since the recipe would melt it anyway, so the preparation does not change. Condition 2: the fat is the same product, so a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is smoked beef neck bones. The USDA entry is plain beef neck bones, with no smoking indicated. Guideline F states that plain vs smoked is a different state and not substitutable. Smoking changes flavour and appearance, and a diner would notice the smoky taste. The quantity is irrelevant, and the cut (neck bones) matches, but the smoked processing does not. Condition 2 fails, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is chicken bratwurst, a sliced sausage link that is cooked as a whole sausage and keeps a firm, casing-bound texture. The USDA match, chicken spread, is a soft, spreadable paste with a different composition and texture. Substituting it would change the cooking method, since a spread cannot be sliced and browned like a sausage. It would also change the texture and appearance, and a diner would notice they were eating a paste rather than sausage. The two products are not the same food under different names, so condition 1 fails, and condition 2 also fails.

The ingredient is beef liver, sliced. The USDA entry is raw beef liver from the variety meats and by-products category, so it is the same food. Slicing is knife work and does not change the match (guideline C). The '(optional)' note and the 345g weight are decoration and do not affect the match (guideline A). Condition 1: the raw liver can replace the sliced liver without changing preparation, since the cook slices it the same way. Condition 2: a diner would see and taste the same beef liver. Both conditions hold.

The ingredient is salted macadamia nuts, with no mention of roasting. The USDA entry is dry roasted with salt added. Guideline F treats a plain versus roasted state as a different state, not a substitute. Adding roasting changes the flavour, aroma, and colour, and a diner could notice that difference. The salt matches, and the nut is the same, but the ingredient does not specify roasting, so the roasted entry is a modified version. Condition 2 is not met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is powdered light creamer. The USDA entry, 'Cream substitute, powdered, light', is the same product type under USDA's standard name: a powdered creamer in the light (reduced-fat) variety. Guideline B treats same food under another name as a match, and guideline D says that when the ingredient itself asks for a modified version (here, light), the matching modified entry counts. Condition 1: it can be used directly in place of powdered light creamer, since both are dry powders added in the same way, so preparation does not change. Condition 2: the same powdered light creamer product would be used, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance. Both conditions are met. The 60g quantity is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is beef shank, a leg cut that is usually bone-in and rich in connective tissue. The USDA entry is beef chuck for stew, a shoulder cut with different fat and connective-tissue distribution. Guideline F says a different cut of meat is not substitutable (beef brisket vs beef chuck is the given example). Condition 1 is not met: the match is a different cut, so the dish's preparation would not be unchanged in the way the recipe intends. Condition 2 is also not met: shank typically breaks down into a more gelatinous, distinctly textured result when braised, so a diner could notice a difference in texture. Quantity and the 'cut in pieces' handling do not change the match. Because the cuts differ, the match fails.

The ingredient, lactase-treated milk, is milk with the lactose broken down by the lactase enzyme, which is the same product sold as lactose-free milk. The USDA entry 'Milk, lactose free, whole' is therefore the same food under another name, and because the ingredient itself specifies the lactose-reduced version, the matching modified entry counts (guideline D). Condition 1: it can be used in place of the ingredient with no change to preparation, since it is whole milk handled the same way. Condition 2: the enzyme-treated milk is the same product, so the diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance beyond what the ingredient itself already implies. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is orange roughy fillets as bought, which are raw and uncooked. The USDA match is 'Fish, roughy, orange, cooked, dry heat', so it is a cooked product. Guideline F lists raw vs cooked as a different state that is not substitutable. Using the cooked entry would also change the dish's preparation, since the fish would need cooking before it could be used as raw fillets, and a diner could notice the difference in texture and appearance. The species matches, but the state does not, so condition 1 fails. Condition 2 would also likely fail, because cooked fish looks and feels different from raw fish. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is beef sirloin tip, a specific cut from the round/knuckle area. The USDA entry is bottom sirloin tri-tip roast, a different primal cut with a different muscle structure, shape, and typical texture. Guideline F states that a different cut of meat is not substitutable (e.g., pork belly vs pork loin; beef brisket vs beef chuck). The entry also specifies 'separable lean and fat, trimmed to 0" fat, choice' while the ingredient only says 'good-quality' with no fat trimming specified, adding further mismatch. Freezing and thawing are not the issue, since frozen meat matches fresh under guideline E. The quantity is ignored under guideline A. Because the cut differs, the cooking method and eating experience could change, so the two conditions are not both met.

The ingredient is plain fried tofu cubes, a single food that is fried. The USDA entry is a mixed dish: tofu combined with vegetables (excluding carrots, broccoli and dark-green leafy vegetables, and potatoes) and a soy-based sauce. Condition 1 fails: using this entry would add vegetables and sauce, changing the dish's composition and flavour. Also, the entry does not indicate fried tofu, so the cooking state differs. Condition 2 fails: a diner would notice the added vegetables, sauce and different appearance. The entry is not the same food under another name, so guideline B does not apply. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is white corn meal, a standard ground dried corn product. The USDA match is whole-grain blue corn flour (harina de maiz morado). Condition 1: the match is a different product. It is a flour rather than a meal, it is whole-grain (bran and germ retained) where cornmeal is typically degermed or simply ground, and it is made from blue corn rather than white. Substituting it would change the dish's texture and the grind, and it would not be prepared the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice. The blue colour would visibly alter the appearance of cornbread, tortillas, or batter, and the whole-grain flour has a more pronounced, earthier, nuttier flavour and a coarser, heavier texture. Guideline F also rules out a different variety with a different taste and appearance. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried chives that have been toasted. The USDA match is fresh chives, raw. Condition 1 fails: the recipe calls for a dried, toasted product, and fresh raw chives cannot replace it without changing the preparation (the toasting step would be lost, and dehydrated chives are rehydrated or crumbled differently from fresh stems). Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice the difference in flavour (toasted, concentrated, dried onion notes versus fresh, grassy, green chives), texture (brittle and crisp versus soft and moist) and appearance (dark, dry flakes versus bright green stems). Guideline F explicitly rejects fresh versus dried herb and plain versus toasted, and the quantity (500g) is ignored as instructed. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is plain Swiss cheese, which shoppers normally buy as the standard full-fat version. The USDA entry is 'Cheese, Swiss, nonfat or fat free', a modified reduced-fat version. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient matched to a fat-free/reduced-fat version is not a match. Condition 1: the swap would not change the preparation method, since both are cheese that can be melted or sliced. Condition 2: a diner would likely notice the difference. Fat-free Swiss is firmer, rubbery, and melts poorly compared with full-fat Swiss, and its flavour is noticeably milder. The weight (55g) is ignored as instructed. Because the taste and texture difference is noticeable, condition 2 fails.

The ingredient is plain 'kelp' with no preparation or state stated, so the default version applies. The USDA entry 'Seaweed, kelp, raw' is the same food in its uncooked form, so it is the same food under the standard name. The 60g weight is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the raw kelp can replace the ingredient without changing how the dish is prepared, since no cooking method is implied. Condition 2: with no state specified, a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance from the default form. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain sunflower oil. The USDA entry 'Oil, sunflower, linoleic (less than 60%)' is sunflower oil, the standard default grocery version, which is typically sold as linoleic or mid-oleic sunflower oil. The '(less than 60%)' descriptor describes the fatty acid profile of the normal product rather than a modification such as a flavouring or additive. Condition 1: it can replace the oil in any recipe without changing the cooking method. Condition 2: the taste, texture and appearance of the dish would not noticeably change. It is not a different oil like canola, and the quantity is ignored. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is dried marjoram leaves, and the USDA entry is 'Spices, marjoram, dried'. Both describe the same food in the same state: dried marjoram. The 12g weight is decoration (guideline A). Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is used the same way. Condition 2: a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture or appearance, because it is the same dried herb. The fresh-versus-dried rule (F) does not apply because both are dried. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is plain cream cheese, softened. Softening is handling that does not change the product (guideline C), and the quantity is irrelevant (guideline A). The USDA entry 'Cream cheese, regular, plain' is the standard default version of the same product (guideline D). It could be used in place of the ingredient without changing preparation, and a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is chipotle ketchup, a ketchup flavoured with chipotle chilli (smoky, spicy). The USDA match is plain 'Ketchup, restaurant', which is a standard tomato ketchup with no chipotle or other added flavouring. Condition 1: swapping plain ketchup for chipotle ketchup would not change the cooking method, but the ingredient is specifically a flavoured version, so the match is a plain ingredient standing in for a modified/flavoured one. Condition 2: a diner would taste the absence of smoky chipotle heat, so the flavour differs noticeably. Guideline D says a flavoured version is a modification, and guideline F says flavour changes are not substitutable. The match fails on flavour, so it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is frozen guacamole, thawed. The USDA entry is 'Guacamole with tomatoes', a fresh, unfrozen product. Condition 1 (same preparation): guacamole is normally served fresh, not cooked or mixed after freezing, so thawing is not hidden the way it is for frozen peas or berries used in baking. Condition 2 (no noticeable difference): thawed guacamole typically shows visible browning, a watery or grainy texture, and a changed mouthfeel compared with fresh guacamole, and a diner would likely notice. The USDA entry also adds tomatoes, which is an added ingredient relative to the plain product, so the flavour and appearance may differ from the ingredient as specified. Both conditions are not reliably met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain raisin bread. The USDA entry is raisin bread that has been toasted. Under guideline F, 'plain vs toasted' is a different state, not a substitute. Toasting changes colour, crispness, and flavour, and a diner would likely notice the difference in texture and appearance. Condition 2 therefore fails. Condition 1 also fails because toasting is a cooking step that alters the bread's preparation. The quantity prefix is ignored per guideline A.

Step 1: The ingredient is avocado, and the USDA entry is Hass avocado, which is the same food. 'Peeled' describes handling that the recipe itself performs, and 'mashed' is likewise knife or hand work done in the kitchen, so neither changes the match under guideline C. Step 2: Condition 1 holds because raw peeled Hass avocado can be mashed in place of mashed avocado without changing how the dish is prepared. Condition 2 holds because mashing the peeled raw fruit produces the same taste, texture and colour a diner would expect. The quantity prefix is ignored per guideline A.

The ingredient is plain cranberry juice, which is normally 100% cranberry juice, tart and unsweetened. The USDA entry, Cranberry juice cocktail, is a sweetened product, diluted to roughly a quarter juice with added sugar. Under guideline D, a plain ingredient mapped to a sweetened version is a modification and does not match. Condition 2 also fails: the sweetness and milder cranberry flavour would be noticeable in the finished dish. Condition 1 might be met in terms of preparation, but the taste difference means the match fails.

The ingredient is rendered bacon fat (a pure animal fat, solidified) weighing 290g. The USDA match is 'Bacon bits', which is a processed, cooked meat product (usually textured/cured pork pieces, often with added seasonings, preservatives and flavourings), not a fat. Condition 1: Bacon bits cannot replace rendered fat in a recipe, since it provides no fat phase for frying, greasing, roasting or shortening, so the cooking method would change. Condition 2: a diner would clearly notice the difference in texture (solid fat versus crisp meat pieces) and appearance and flavour profile. Per guideline F, a different fat or a processed product differing in state is not substitutable, and the bacon bits are a processed product rather than the same food. Both conditions fail.

Condition 1: The ingredient is starfruit that is grilled, so the recipe requires a heat-cooking step. The USDA match is 'Carambola, (starfruit), raw', which is the uncooked fruit. Using raw starfruit would skip the grilling, so the preparation changes. Guideline F treats raw vs cooked as a different state, and the knife-work exception in C does not cover applying heat. Condition 1 fails. Condition 2: Grilling softens the flesh, caramelises the sugars, and leaves char marks, so a diner would notice differences in flavour, texture and appearance. Condition 2 also fails. The food is the same species (guideline B), but the cooked state makes the match unacceptable.

The ingredient is fish broth, a liquid stock made by simmering fish bones, trimmings and aromatics. The USDA entry 'Fish, NFS' is generic fish flesh, a solid food, not a stock or broth. This is the raw source versus a processed ingredient, which guideline F rules out. Using fish flesh in place of broth would change the dish's liquid base, flavour, and texture, and a diner would notice. Condition 1 (no change in preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste or texture) both fail. Guideline A says quantity is irrelevant, so the 200g does not affect the result.

The ingredient is fresh horseradish (a pungent root, Armoracia rusticana), grated. The USDA match is Pumpkin, raw, which is a different plant entirely (a squash-family fruit with mild, sweet, vegetal flavour and a soft, dense flesh). Condition 1 fails: pumpkin cannot stand in for horseradish in the same preparation, since grating horseradish yields a sharp, volatile, pungent condiment-style ingredient and pumpkin would not provide that heat or pungency. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would immediately notice the absence of horseradish's sharp bite and the difference in colour and texture of the grated product. Guideline B does not apply because this is not the same food under another name, and no processing or cut description makes pumpkin equivalent to horseradish.

The ingredient is canned crab, i.e. crab meat (a plain seafood ingredient, packed in water or brine). The USDA match 'Crab salad' is a prepared dish made with crab meat plus mayonnaise-type dressing and typically other ingredients such as celery, onion, seasonings. Condition 1: Crab salad cannot be used in place of canned crab without changing the preparation, because the dish is already dressed and mixed; a recipe calling for crab meat would be altered by adding dressing and extra components. Condition 2: a diner would notice the difference in taste, texture and appearance, since mayonnaise-based dressing and added vegetables change flavour and texture compared with plain crab meat. Crab salad is a different product (a composed/modified version), not the same food under another name. Therefore it is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried rosemary, a dried herb. The USDA match is 'Spices, rosemary, dried', which is the same food (dried rosemary leaves) under the standard USDA name. Quantity (15g) is ignored. Guideline F explicitly says fresh vs dried herb is a different state, but here both sides are dried, so that distinction does not apply. The entry is not a blend, not a modified version, and not a different variety. Condition 1: dried rosemary can replace dried rosemary without any change to preparation. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, since it is the same product. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is a combined item, navy beans plus diced ham. The USDA entry covers only navy beans (cooked, boiled, without salt) and has no ham. Under the guidelines, a single ingredient does not substitute for a blend or combination that contains it (F). The leading '5g' is ignored (A). Condition 1 fails because the ham is an element of the dish's preparation that the match cannot supply, so the dish would have to be prepared differently. Condition 2 fails because a diner would notice the missing ham in taste, texture and appearance. The ingredient also does not specify cooked beans, so the match would be an assumption. Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is cooked artichoke hearts, meaning the inner, edible part of the globe artichoke after cooking. The USDA entry is globe or French artichokes, cooked by boiling, drained, with salt. Under guideline B, the inner part or a cut of the same vegetable sold as the same thing counts as the same food. The entry is cooked, which matches the ingredient. The 'with salt' and 'drained' descriptors describe a standard boiled preparation, and the ingredient names no modified version, so guideline D treats it as the default. The quantity is ignored per guideline A. Condition 1: the entry can replace cooked hearts without changing the preparation, since it is the same cooked vegetable. Condition 2: the taste and texture of boiled globe artichoke are those of cooked artichoke hearts, so a diner would not notice a difference beyond the trivial presence of salt, which is a standard seasoning for this food. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is lotus root that has been boiled and salted. The USDA entry is lotus root, cooked, boiled, drained, with salt. It is the same food in the same state: both are cooked by boiling and both are salted. The quantity prefix is irrelevant. Cooking method, flavour, texture and appearance all match, so a diner would not notice a difference. Condition 1 and condition 2 both hold.

The ingredient is a chocolate hazelnut spread, and the USDA entry is literally 'Chocolate hazelnut spread', the same food under the same name. The leading '45g' is only a quantity and is ignored. Condition 1: the spread can be used directly in place of the ingredient, since it is a spread, so the preparation does not change. Condition 2: the USDA entry describes the same product type, so a diner would not notice a difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient '100g turkey roll' most plausibly refers to a processed deli turkey roll, a sliced or formed meat product. The USDA match 'Egg roll, with chicken or turkey' is a prepared dish: a wrapper of dough filled with shredded meat and vegetables, typically fried or baked. Condition 1 fails because the match cannot be used in place of turkey roll without changing how the dish is prepared. It is not a meat ingredient that could be cooked or sliced the same way. Condition 2 also fails because a diner would immediately notice a difference in texture, appearance and taste between sliced turkey meat and an egg roll. It is not the same food under another name (guideline B does not apply), and it is a different product type with added components (guideline F). Neither condition is met.

The ingredient is ghee, which is clarified butter: the water and milk solids are removed, leaving almost pure milkfat. The USDA match is butter without salt, which contains roughly 15-18% water and milk solids. Condition 1 fails because ghee has a higher smoke point and does not splatter or brown the way butter does, so using butter changes how the dish is cooked. Condition 2 also fails because ghee has a richer, nuttier flavour and a different mouthfeel, and butter's milk solids change the appearance when melted or heated. Guideline F says a different fat is not substitutable, and ghee and butter are different fats. The quantity (10g) is ignored.

The ingredient is toasted multigrain bread, and the USDA entry is 'Bread, multigrain, toasted', which is the same food in the same state. Condition 1: the USDA item is already toasted, so it can replace the ingredient without any change to how the dish is prepared, and the quantity is irrelevant. Condition 2: a diner would taste and see the same toasted multigrain bread, so there is no noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is rendered goose fat, a pure fat used as a cooking medium. The USDA entry is cooked, roasted goose meat and skin, a whole tissue containing lean meat, skin and fat. These are different foods: a single fat versus a composite meat product. Using the roasted meat and skin in place of rendered fat would change how the dish is prepared, since it cannot be melted, poured or used to fry or roast in the same way. It would also change flavour, texture and appearance, and a diner would notice solid pieces of meat rather than fat. Per guideline F, the processed ingredient is not the same as the raw or cooked source. The match fails both conditions.

The ingredient is chickpea flour (besan), a finely ground, raw, dry product made from dried chickpeas. The USDA entry 'Chickpeas, from dried, no added fat' describes whole chickpeas that have been cooked from dried, so it is a cooked, intact legume. Guideline F rejects a raw or source food standing in for a processed ingredient, and a cooked food standing in for a raw one. Using whole cooked chickpeas in place of flour would change the dish's preparation: the flour would need to be ground and cooked into a batter, dough or paste, and it cannot simply be swapped in. A diner would also notice the difference in texture and appearance, since a gram-flour dish (such as pakoras, socca or batter) would not look or feel the same with whole chickpeas. Both conditions fail.

The ingredient is plain boiled lotus root with no salt specified. The USDA entry is the same food (lotus root, cooked, boiled, drained), so the base food matches. The difference is the 'with salt' descriptor, which means the boiled root was salted. Under the guidelines, a plain ingredient mapped to a modified or seasoned version is not a match, and added salt is a flavour change. A diner could plausibly taste the added salt, so condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste) is not met. The quantity of 1 tbsp is ignored per guideline A. Result: not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried pear ("dryed" is a spelling error), a plain dried fruit used as-is. The USDA entry is Pears, dried, sulfured, uncooked, which is the same food in the dried, uncooked state. The only extra descriptor is 'sulfured.' Guideline D says dried fruits such as apricots, apple and peaches are typically sold sulfured, so this descriptor reflects how the product is normally sold rather than a modification. Condition 1: it can replace dried pear with no change in preparation, since neither needs cooking. Condition 2: sulfuring is a common, mild treatment that a diner would not reliably notice in taste, texture or appearance compared with the standard dried pear a shopper buys. Both conditions hold.

Puffed wheat is a ready-to-eat puffed whole-grain cereal: wheat kernels pressurised and expanded, so it is light, crisp and airy. Cream of wheat is a granular farina-type product made from ground wheat middlings, which is cooked into a smooth porridge. They are different processed products, not the same food under another name. Condition 1 fails: puffed wheat is used as a crisp, dry ingredient (e.g. in bars, brittles, or as a crunchy topping), and cream of wheat would change the preparation because it needs cooking with liquid and would not stay crisp. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would notice a dense, soft, grainy texture instead of a light, crunchy one. Neither condition holds, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is plain cranberries, with the weight (30g) being irrelevant. The USDA match is 'Cranberries, raw', which is the same food in its uncooked state. Condition 1: the match can replace the ingredient without changing preparation, since it is the same raw fruit used in the same way. Condition 2: a diner would notice no difference in taste, texture or appearance, because the fruit is the same. Nothing in the recipe context indicates a sweetened, dried or cooked version was intended, and the ingredient does not specify any modification. Both conditions are met.

The ingredient is American cheese (misspelled 'amercan'), a processed cheese product made from cheddar and other cheeses with emulsifiers, milk solids and salt, sold in slices or blocks. The USDA match is 'Soy chips', a crispy snack food made from soy flour or soybeans, typically fried or baked and seasoned. Condition 1: soy chips are not a cheese and cannot be used in place of American cheese in a dish without changing how it is prepared; cheese melts, slices or is shredded, whereas soy chips are a crunchy snack that does not melt. Condition 2: a diner would immediately notice the difference in taste (no dairy, salty snack flavour rather than cheese), texture (crisp and brittle rather than soft, creamy, meltable) and appearance. Neither condition is met, so the match is not substitutable.

The ingredient is dried papaya, a dehydrated product with chewy texture, concentrated sweetness, and a darker appearance. The USDA match is 'Papayas, raw', which is fresh, uncooked fruit with soft, juicy flesh and a much milder flavour. Guideline F rejects a difference in state (raw vs dried), so the match is not interchangeable. Using fresh papaya would change the dish's texture and flavour, and a diner would notice the difference. Weight is ignored per guideline A, and the name 'papaya' alone does not make the two the same food, since the dried form is a processed product. Condition 1 (no change in preparation) and condition 2 (no noticeable difference in taste, texture, or appearance) are both unmet.

The ingredient is soy nut butter, a spread made from roasted or raw soy nuts (soybeans), with a distinct legume-based flavour and a thick, paste-like texture. The USDA match, 'Cookie, butter or sugar, with fruit and/or nuts', is a baked cookie product containing fruit and/or nuts. It is not a nut butter, not a soy product, and not a spread. Condition 1 fails: substituting a baked cookie for a soy nut butter would change the preparation, since the ingredient is a spreadable paste used as is, and the cookie is a solid baked good with flour, sugar and fat. Condition 2 also fails: a diner would readily notice the difference in taste (sweet baked cookie versus savoury-toasted soy flavour), texture (crumbly, baked versus smooth paste), and appearance. The match is not the same food under another name, and it is not a modified version of the plain ingredient; it is an entirely different product category. Not substitutable.

The ingredient is a plain tri-tip roast, and the USDA entry is the same cut (beef bottom sirloin, tri-tip roast), raw. Guideline F says a different cut is not substitutable, but this is the same cut under its standard name. The entry's descriptors are 'separable lean and fat', 'trimmed to 0" fat' and 'all grades'. Guideline C lists 'trimmed' among handling descriptors that do not change the match, and the recipe does not specify a fat level, so the plain ingredient maps to the standard raw version. Condition 1: the meat can replace the tri-tip with the same cooking method, since raw beef tri-tip is cooked the same way. Condition 2: the main visible difference would be the fat cap, which is a handling/trimming variation rather than a different food. Taste, texture and appearance of the same cut would not be noticeably different to a diner. Both conditions are met.

Condition 1 (preparation): The ingredient is mango nectar, and the USDA entry is also mango nectar, so the product type and preparation method match. The quantity prefix is ignored. Condition 2 (taste, texture, appearance): The ingredient specifies the Ataulfo variety, a sweeter, creamier, lower-fibre mango with a distinct flavour. The USDA entry is generic and does not name a variety, so it may be made from different mangoes such as Tommy Atkins, with different sweetness, acidity and colour. Guideline F states that a sibling variety with a different taste is not substitutable.
